Bernoulli’s inequality supplies one at once: (1 + h)^n \ge 1 + nh > nh. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want --------------------------------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 0 < \abs{r} < 1 \abs{r}^n below every \varepsilon > 0 for large n h \coloneqq  rac{1}{\abs{r}} - 1 > 0, so \abs{r}^n =  rac{1}{(1 + h)^n} enough: (1 + h)^n bounded below by Cn @fd2:thm-bernoulli: (1 + h)^n \ge 1 + nh > nh \abs{r}^n <  rac{1}{nh}: the bounding step of the method with C =  rac{1}{h}; the gap is closed ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The proof follows these rows from top to bottom. It then finishes with the choice of the threshold and the forward proof, using the bound 1/(nh). (a) Let r 
e 0. Then 0 < \abs{r} < 1, since the absolute value of a non-zero number is positive. Reciprocals reverse the order of positive numbers, so 1/\abs{r} > 1/1 = 1, that is, h > 0. By the choice of h, 1 + h = 1/\abs{r}, so \abs{r} = 1/(1 + h) and \abs{r}^n = 1/(1 + h)^n. Since h \ge -1, Bernoulli’s inequality (@fd2:thm-bernoulli) gives (1 + h)^n \ge 1 + nh > nh . For n \ge 1, nh > 0 as a product of positive numbers. So 0 < nh < (1 + h)^n, and taking reciprocals reverses the inequality: \abs{r}^n = 1/(1 + h)^n < 1/(nh). (b) If r = 0, then r^n = r^{n-1} \cdot 0 = 0 for every n \ge 1, so \abs{r^n - 0} = 0 < \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0 and every n \ge 1. So N \coloneqq 1 works for every \varepsilon > 0. Let r 
e 0 and \varepsilon > 0, and let h be as in (a). Then h\varepsilon > 0. Since 
R is Archimedean, @fd3:prp-archimedean-reciprocal gives N \in 
Z_{>0} with 1/n < h\varepsilon for every n \ge N. This N depends on \varepsilon and on r, through h. Let n \ge N. Then n \ge 1, and \abs{r^n} = \abs{r}^n by induction on n, since \abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}. By (a), \abs{r^n - 0} = \abs{r}^n <  rac{1}{nh} <  rac{h\varepsilon}{h} = \varepsilon . This proves r^n 	o 0. @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a) (\abs{r} > 0 for r 
e 0), (b) (\abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}); @fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (b) (reciprocals reverse <). @fd2:prp-power-laws ((1/x)^n = 1/x^n); @fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b) (x^n = x^{n-1} x); @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (products of positives). Part (a) is the useful half. It gives an explicit bound, valid for every n \ge 1, from which a threshold can be read off for any tolerance. From @prp-power-null (a), find an N with (0.9)^n < 0.01 for every n \ge N. Here r = 0.9 =  rac{9}{10}, so h =  rac{10}{9} - 1 =  rac{1}{9} and (0.9)^n < \dfrac{1}{n/9} = \dfrac{9}{n} for n \ge 1. Now  rac{9}{n} \le  rac{1}{100} exactly when n \ge 900. So N = 900 works: for n \ge 900, (0.9)^n < 9/n \le 0.01. The bound is wasteful, since already (0.9)^{44} < 0.01. That costs nothing: the definition asks for some threshold, not the least. The same steps handle a power in a denominator under a numerator that is a power of n: write the base as 1 + h, keep one term of the expansion, and invert. [Method: bound a power from below] How it goes. To make a quotient small when its denominator contains r^n with r > 1: 1. Write r = 1 + h with h > 0. 2. Keep one term of the expansion: (1 + h)^n \ge nh by Bernoulli’s inequality, or (1 + h)^n \ge  inom{n}{k} h^k by @cor-binomial-real (b). Take k one more than the power of n on top. 3. Bound  inom{n}{k} below by c\,n^k for n \ge n_0. 4. Invert, and finish with the method of @fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition. When to use it. Quotients n^p / r^n. Powers \abs{r}^n with \abs{r} < 1, through 1/\abs{r} = 1 + h. The n-th roots of Section 1.5. Common mistakes. One mistake is to choose k too small: then the bound does not tend to 0. Another is to use the binomial bound with h < 0. In @exm-binomial-bound the base was 2, and k = 2 gave n/2^n \le 2/(n - 1) for n \ge 2. The same steps work for every base r > 1. The numerator is n, to the first power, so k = 2. [Powers Beat n] Let r > 1 and h \coloneqq r - 1. Then \dfrac{n}{r^n} \le \dfrac{4}{nh^2} for every integer n \ge 2, and \dfrac{n}{r^n} 	o 0. Follow @exm-method-power-lower-bound step by step. Write r = 1 + h. Keep the term k = 2, which is of order n^2. Bound n(n - 1) below by  rac12 n^2. Invert, multiply by n, and finish the limit with C = 4/h^2. Let n \ge 2. Since r > 1, h > 0. By @cor-binomial-real (b) with x = h and k = 2 \le n, and since  inom{n}{2} \cdot 2 = n(n - 1), r^n = (1 + h)^n \ge  inom{n}{2} h^2 =  rac{n(n - 1)}{2} h^2 . Since n \ge 2,  rac{n}{2} \ge 1, so n - 1 \ge  rac{n}{2} \ge 0. Multiplying the inequalities 0 \le  rac{n}{2} \le n - 1 and 0 \le n \le n, between non-negative numbers, gives n(n - 1) \ge  rac{n^2}{2}. Hence r^n \ge  rac{n^2 h^2}{4} > 0. Inverting, which reverses the inequality, and multiplying by n > 0,  rac{n}{r^n} \le n \cdot  rac{4}{n^2 h^2} =  rac{4}{nh^2} . For the limit, n/r^n > 0, so the distance to 0 is n/r^n \le C/n for n \ge 2, with C \coloneqq 4/h^2. Let \varepsilon > 0, choose an integer N' > C/\varepsilon, and let N \coloneqq \max\{2, N'\}. It depends on \varepsilon and r. For n \ge N, \abs{n/r^n - 0} \le C/n \le C/N < \varepsilon. So n/r^n 	o 0. @prp-binomial-factorial (c) ( inom{n}{2} \cdot 2 = n(n - 1)); @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (c) (larger denominator, smaller quotient), (d) (multiplying inequalities). With k = 1, that is, Bernoulli’s inequality, the same steps give only n/r^n < n/(nh) = 1/h. That bound does not tend to 0. The choice of k is the whole difference. A comparison with a power can also run the other way: a sequence that is hard to handle directly is bounded by a geometric one, and @prp-power-null finishes. [Factorials beat powers of two] Show that \dfrac{1}{n!} \le \dfrac{1}{2^{n-1}} < \dfrac{2}{n} for every integer n \ge 1, and hence that \dfrac{1}{n!} 	o 0. The first inequality. We show n! \ge 2^{n-1} for n \ge 1, by induction on n. For n = 1: 1! = 1 = 2^0. Suppose n! \ge 2^{n-1}. Also n + 1 \ge 2, and both inequalities are between non-negative numbers, so we may multiply them: (n + 1)! = n! \, (n + 1) \ge 2^{n-1} \cdot 2 = 2^n . Here 2^{n-1} > 0, as a power of a positive number, and n! \ge 2^{n-1} > 0. So inverting reverses the inequality, and 1/n! \le 1/2^{n-1}. The second inequality. By @prp-power-null (a) with r =  rac12, h = 2 - 1 = 1, we have ( rac12)^n <  rac1n for n \ge 1. Since 1/2^{n-1} = ( rac12)^{n-1} = 2 \cdot ( rac12)^n,  rac{1}{2^{n-1}} = 2 \Bigl(  rac12 \Bigr)^n <  rac{2}{n} . The limit. So 0 < 1/n! < 2/n for n \ge 1: a bound C/n with C = 2. Given \varepsilon > 0, take an integer N > 2/\varepsilon. It depends on \varepsilon only. Then N \ge 1, and for n \ge N, \abs{1/n! - 0} < 2/n \le 2/N < \varepsilon. Hence 1/n! 	o 0. @fd2:def-sum-product ((n + 1)! = n! \, (n + 1)); @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d) (multiplying inequalities), (c) (larger denominator, smaller quotient); @fd2:prp-power-laws (1/2^{n-1} = 2 ( rac12)^n), (e) (2^{n-1} > 0).  rac{1}{n^2} \le \varepsilon is not  rac{1}{n^2} < \varepsilon. The definition of a limit asks for the strict inequality. A threshold chosen to make the bound at most \varepsilon can miss it. For \varepsilon = 1, the choice N \coloneqq 1/\varepsilon = 1 gives, at n = N = 1, the distance  rac{1}{1^2} = 1, which is not < 1. Ask for N > C/\varepsilon, strictly. Change one hypothesis of @cor-binomial-real (b): keep k = 2 and allow h < 0. At h = -1, n = 2 the claim would read (1 - 1)^2 \ge  inom{2}{2}(-1)^2, that is, 0 \ge 1, which is false. What breaks is the step that keeps one term of a sum. That step needs every term non-negative, and with h < 0 the terms  inom{n}{j} h^j alternate in sign. Bernoulli’s inequality survives for -1 \le h < 0, because its proof is an induction, not a dropped sum. So for 0 < \abs{r} < 1 the method first passes to 1/\abs{r} = 1 + h with h > 0, as the proof of @prp-power-null did. It never expands (1 + (r - 1))^n directly. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the negation of “a_n 	o 0” with all its quantifiers. 2. In @exm-first-estimate, on what does N depend? Could it depend on n? 3. Name the method used: \dfrac{n}{n^3 + 7} \le \dfrac{1}{n^2} for n \ge 1. 4. True or false: if \abs{a_n} \le \dfrac{5}{n} for every n \ge 10, then a_n 	o 0. (a) \exists \varepsilon > 0 \ \  orall N \in 
N \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \  igl( n \ge N \wedge \abs{a_n} \ge \varepsilon  igr), as in the negation after @fd3:def-sequence-limit-ordered-field with a = 0. (b) On \varepsilon only. It cannot depend on n: N is chosen before n is named, and the claim is about every n \ge N. (c) Bounding the distance by shrinking the denominator, the bounding step of @fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition. Here we keep the dominant term n^3 and drop the positive 7, as in @exm-method-dominant-term. So n^3 + 7 \ge n^3 > 0 and n/(n^3 + 7) \le n/n^3 = 1/n^2. (d) True. Given \varepsilon > 0, take an integer N' > 5/\varepsilon and N \coloneqq \max\{10, N'\}. For n \ge N, \abs{a_n - 0} \le 5/n \le 5/N < \varepsilon. B. Practice [B1: Say which method, then complete it] Show that a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{n + 5}{2^n} 	o 0. Start: write 2 = 1 + 1. By @cor-binomial-real (b) with k = 2, 2^n \ge \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2} \ge \dfrac{n^2}{4} for n \ge 2. Say which method this is, then complete it. The method: bound the power from below, as in @exm-method-power-lower-bound. The numerator is handled by keeping its dominant term, as in @exm-method-dominant-term. Let n \ge 5. Then n + 5 \le 2n. By the start, 2^n \ge n^2/4 > 0, so 1/2^n \le 4/n^2. Multiplying, 0 < a_n \le 2n \cdot  rac{4}{n^2} =  rac{8}{n} . Let \varepsilon > 0, take an integer N' > 8/\varepsilon and N \coloneqq \max\{5, N'\}. For n \ge N, \abs{a_n - 0} \le 8/n \le 8/N < \varepsilon. Hence a_n 	o 0. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (c) (larger denominator, smaller quotient), (d) (multiplying inequalities). [B2: Put the proof in order] The claim is a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{2n + 1}{n + 1} 	o 2. Put the lines below in an order that proves it, and say which line does not belong. 1. Let \varepsilon > 0. 2. For n \ge N, \abs{a_n - 2} = \dfrac{1}{n + 1} < \dfrac{1}{n} \le \dfrac{1}{N} < \varepsilon. 3. Choose N \in 
N with N > 1/\varepsilon and N \ge 1. 4. Choose N \coloneqq n + 1. 5. Hence a_n 	o 2. 6. \abs{a_n - 2} = \Bigl\lvert \dfrac{2n + 1 - 2n - 2}{n + 1} \Bigrvert = \dfrac{1}{n + 1} for every n \in 
N. An admissible order is (i), (iii), (vi), (ii), (v). Line (vi) uses nothing chosen, so it may also come first: (vi), (i), (iii), (ii), (v). Line (ii) must come after (iii), since it uses N. It must also come after (vi), since it uses the formula for the distance. In (ii), 1/n \le 1/N holds because a larger denominator gives a smaller quotient, and 1/N < \varepsilon follows from N > 1/\varepsilon. The line that does not belong is (iv): it makes N depend on n, but N must be fixed before n is named, and n ranges over all numbers \ge N. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (c) (larger denominator, smaller quotient); @fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (b) (reciprocals reverse <). [B3: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one. In parts (a), (b), (c) and (e), a_n denotes the n-th term of the sequence in question. 1. \dfrac{n^2 + 1}{n^3} 	o 0. 2. \dfrac{n}{n + 1} 	o 0. 3. \dfrac{(-1)^n}{n} 	o 0. 4. For every \varepsilon > 0, every integer n \ge 1/\varepsilon has \dfrac{1}{n^2} < \varepsilon. 5. \dfrac{2^n}{n!} 	o 0. (a) True. For n \ge 1, n^2 + 1 \le 2n^2, so 0 < a_n \le 2n^2/n^3 = 2/n. Given \varepsilon > 0, take an integer N > 2/\varepsilon. Then N \ge 1, and for n \ge N, \abs{a_n} \le 2/n \le 2/N < \varepsilon. (b) False. For n \ge 1, 2n \ge n + 1, so  rac{n}{n + 1} \ge  rac12. Take \varepsilon \coloneqq  rac12. For every N \in 
N, the index n \coloneqq \max\{N, 1\} \ge N has \abs{a_n - 0} \ge  rac12 = \varepsilon. This is the negation of A1 (a). (c) True. \abs{a_n - 0} = \abs{(-1)^n}/n = 1/n, since \abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y} and \abs{(-1)^n} = 1. Given \varepsilon, an integer N > 1/\varepsilon works, as in (a). (d) False. Take \varepsilon = 1 and n = 1 \ge 1/\varepsilon. Then 1/n^2 = 1, which is not < 1. The non-strict 1/n^2 \le \varepsilon does not give the strict 1/n^2 < \varepsilon. (e) True. For n \ge 3, n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \prod_{k=3}^{n} k. Also 2^n/n! = \prod_{k=1}^{n} (2/k), by induction on n from 2^{n+1}/(n+1)! = (2^n/n!) \cdot (2/(n+1)). So  rac{2^n}{n!} =  rac{2}{1} \cdot  rac{2}{2} \cdot \prod_{k=3}^{n}  rac{2}{k} \le 2 \cdot 1 \cdot  rac{2}{n} =  rac{4}{n} . Every factor  rac{2}{k} with 3 \le k < n lies in (0, 1], so their product lies in (0, 1]. The last factor, k = n, is kept. Given \varepsilon > 0, take an integer N' > 4/\varepsilon and N \coloneqq \max\{3, N'\}. For n \ge N, \abs{a_n} \le 4/n \le 4/N < \varepsilon. @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) (\abs{xy} = \abs{x} \abs{y}); @fd3:exm-first-sequences-ordered-field (d) (\abs{(-1)^n} = 1); @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d) (multiplying inequalities); @fd2:def-sum-product (the recursion of products and factorials, for 2^n/n! = \prod_{k=1}^n (2/k) and the splitting of n!). C. Going deeper [C1: Chapter check: a rational limit] Prove from the definition that a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{3n^2 - n}{n^2 + 4} 	o 3. Let \varepsilon > 0. The goal is an N with \abs{a_n - 3} < \varepsilon for every n \ge N. The distance. For every n, a_n - 3 =  rac{3n^2 - n - 3(n^2 + 4)}{n^2 + 4} =  rac{-(n + 12)}{n^2 + 4} , so \abs{a_n - 3} = \dfrac{n + 12}{n^2 + 4}. The bound. Let n \ge 1. Then n + 12 \le n + 12n = 13n, and n^2 + 4 \ge n^2 > 0, so 1/(n^2 + 4) \le 1/n^2. Multiplying, \abs{a_n - 3} \le 13n/n^2 = 13/n. The threshold. Choose an integer N > 13/\varepsilon. Then N \ge 1, and N depends on \varepsilon only. For n \ge N, n \ge 1, so \abs{a_n - 3} \le  rac{13}{n} \le  rac{13}{N} < \varepsilon , where the middle step holds because n \ge N and the last because N > 13/\varepsilon. Hence a_n 	o 3. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: fixes \varepsilon > 0 arbitrary and states the goal. - 3: computes \abs{a_n - 3} exactly. - 3: bounds it by C/n (or C/(n + 1)) on a stated range n \ge n_0, with each inequality justified. - 2: chooses N before n, depending only on \varepsilon, and ends the chain with a strict < \varepsilon. Slips that lose the step. Letting N depend on n. Bounding in the wrong direction, that is, shrinking a numerator or enlarging a denominator. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (c) (larger denominator, smaller quotient), (d) (multiplying inequalities). [C2: Squares over powers] Let r > 1 and h \coloneqq r - 1. Show that \dfrac{n^2}{r^n} 	o 0. Start: by @cor-binomial-real (b) with k = 3, r^n \ge \dfrac{n(n - 1)(n - 2)}{6} h^3 for n \ge 3. Say which method this is, then complete it. [Hint 1] Bound n - 1 and n - 2 below by multiples of n, for n \ge 4. [Hint 2] For n \ge 4, n - 2 \ge  rac{n}{2}, since this rearranges to  rac{n}{2} \ge 2. Find a similar bound for n - 1, then multiply. The method: bound the power from below, as in @exm-method-power-lower-bound. The start wrote r = 1 + h and kept one term, with k = 3, one more than the power of n on top. What remains is to bound n(n - 1)(n - 2) below and finish the limit. The lower bound. Let n \ge 4. Then n - 1 \ge  rac{3n}{4}, since this rearranges to  rac{n}{4} \ge 1. Also n - 2 \ge  rac{n}{2}, since this rearranges to  rac{n}{2} \ge 2. Both sides of both inequalities are non-negative. So we may multiply them, with 0 \le n \le n as the third factor, and get n(n - 1)(n - 2) \ge n \cdot  rac{3n}{4} \cdot  rac{n}{2} =  rac{3n^3}{8}. Hence r^n \ge  rac{3n^3}{8 \cdot 6} h^3 =  rac{n^3 h^3}{16} > 0 \qquad (n \ge 4) . The limit. Inverting, which reverses the inequality, and multiplying by n^2 > 0, we get \dfrac{n^2}{r^n} \le \dfrac{16}{nh^3} for n \ge 4. Let \varepsilon > 0, take an integer N' > \dfrac{16}{h^3 \varepsilon} and N \coloneqq \max\{4, N'\}. It depends on \varepsilon and r. For n \ge N, \Bigl\lvert  rac{n^2}{r^n} - 0 \Bigrvert \le  rac{16}{nh^3} \le  rac{16}{Nh^3} < \varepsilon . Hence n^2/r^n 	o 0. What a complete answer needs. (6 points) - 1: names the method (bounding a power from below). - 2: linear lower bounds for n - 1 and n - 2 on a stated, justified range n \ge n_0. - 1: their product, with non-negativity checked, and the inversion, with positivity stated. - 2: the choice of N, and the strict chain ending in < \varepsilon. Slips that lose the step. Using n - 1 \ge  rac{3n}{4} or n - 2 \ge  rac{n}{2} without the range n \ge 4. Multiplying inequalities without checking that the factors are non-negative. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d) (multiplying inequalities, twice), (c) (larger denominator, smaller quotient).

title: 1.5 Roots and Rational Powers
content:
Roots and Rational Powers Number Systems, Chapter 6 found \sqrt a as the supremum of the numbers whose square stays below a (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). The same construction gives every n-th root, and the factorization of t^n - s^n from Section 1.1 makes it work for every exponent. Roots then give powers with rational exponents, a^{m/n}, once we check that the value does not depend on how the fraction  rac{m}{n} is written. These are the “real powers” of the chapter title as far as this chapter goes: rational exponents of positive reals. Chapter 8 extends them to every real exponent. The section ends with two estimates that make the limits \sqrt[n]{a} 	o 1 and \sqrt[n]{n} 	o 1 routine. n-th roots For n = 2, Number Systems, Chapter 6 built the square root as the supremum of a set (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). An exercise there did the same for cube roots (@fd3:exr-measuring-by-rationals-b2). For a general exponent the construction is the same. Only the estimate for (s + h)^n needs a new tool, and @lem-difference-of-powers supplies it. Here n \cdot 1_{
R} is written n. Powers in 
R are those of @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring with R = 
R. They follow the same recursion as @fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (b). For example, 2 is the cube root of 8: it is non-negative, and 2^3 = 8. No other non-negative number has cube 8. The lemma says the same for every a \ge 0 and every exponent n \ge 1. [Real n-th Roots] Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1. 1. If s, t \in 
R and 0 \le s < t, then s^n < t^n. 2. For every a \in 
R with a \ge 0 there is exactly one b \in 
R with b \ge 0 and b^n = a. We write \sqrt[n]{a} \coloneqq b. For n = 2 it is the square root \sqrt a of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. Part (a) is the factorization t^n - s^n = (t - s)(t^{n-1} + t^{n-2}s + \dots + s^{n-1}): both factors are positive. For (b), let s be the supremum of the set S of non-negative y with y^n \le a, and rule out s^n < a and s^n > a. If s^n < a, we want h > 0 with (s + h)^n \le a. Working backwards: for 0 < h \le 1, the same factorization writes (s + h)^n - s^n as h times a sum of n terms, each at most (s + 1)^{n-1}. So (s + h)^n - s^n \le h \cdot n(s + 1)^{n-1}, and it is enough that this be at most half the room a - s^n. That gives h \coloneqq \min\{1, (a - s^n)/(2n(s + 1)^{n-1})\}. If s^n > a, we want h > 0 with (s - h)^n \ge a still, which makes s - h a smaller upper bound. Now s^n - (s - h)^n \le h \cdot n s^{n-1}, and it is enough that this equal the excess s^n - a. That gives h \coloneqq (s^n - a)/(n s^{n-1}). Before reading on: where is completeness used, and why must h \le 1 in the first case? Three facts are used throughout. All three rest on @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), or equality. 1. A power of a non-negative real number is non-negative, and a power of a positive one is positive. This is induction on the exponent. 2. If 0 \le y \le 1, then y^k \le y for every k \ge 1. If y \ge 1, then y^k \ge y. Both are induction, with y^{k+1} = y^k y. 3. If 0 \le x \le x' and 0 \le y \le y', then xy \le x'y \le x'y'. Each step multiplies by a non-negative number. (a) By @lem-difference-of-powers in the commutative ring 
R, t^n - s^n = (t - s) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} t^k s^{n-1-k} . Every term of the sum is \ge 0, and the term with k = n - 1 is t^{n-1} > 0, since t > s \ge 0. So the sum is \ge t^{n-1} > 0. Also t - s > 0. Hence t^n - s^n > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). (b) Uniqueness. If b, c \ge 0 and b 
e c, say b < c, then b^n < c^n by (a); so at most one non-negative b has b^n = a. Existence. If a = 0, then b \coloneqq 0 works, since 0^n = 0^{n-1} \cdot 0 = 0. Let a > 0, and let S \coloneqq \{ y \in 
R : y \ge 0 	ext{ and } y^n \le a \} . Put m \coloneqq \min\{1, a\} > 0. Since 0 < m \le 1, m^n \le m \le a, so m \in S. Put M \coloneqq \max\{1, a\}. If y > M, then y > 1, so y^n \ge y > M \ge a and y 
otin S; hence M is an upper bound of S. Since 
R is a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), S has a supremum; let s \coloneqq \sup S. Then s \ge m > 0. Case s^n < a. Let h \coloneqq \min\Bigl\{ 1,  rac{a - s^n}{2n(s + 1)^{n-1}} \Bigr\} . It depends only on a, n and s, and h > 0, since a - s^n > 0 and 2n(s + 1)^{n-1} > 0. By @lem-difference-of-powers, (s + h)^n - s^n = h \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (s + h)^k s^{n-1-k} . Since 0 \le s < s + h \le s + 1, each term satisfies (s + h)^k s^{n-1-k} \le (s + 1)^k (s + 1)^{n-1-k} = (s + 1)^{n-1}. This uses (a) or equality, the third fact, and the rule for adding exponents. A sum of n terms, each at most (s + 1)^{n-1}, is at most n (s + 1)^{n-1}. Hence (s + h)^n \le s^n + h \cdot n(s + 1)^{n-1} \le s^n +  rac{a - s^n}{2} < a . So s + h \in S, and s + h > s, against s being an upper bound of S. Case s^n > a. Let h \coloneqq  rac{s^n - a}{n s^{n-1}} , which depends only on a, n and s, and is positive. Since a > 0, we have s^n - a < s^n \le n s^n, so h < s^n/(n s^{n-1}) = s/n \le s; thus 0 < s - h < s. By @lem-difference-of-powers and the same bound, with 0 < s - h < s, each of the n terms of \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} s^k (s - h)^{n-1-k} is at most s^{n-1}, so s^n - (s - h)^n \le h \cdot n s^{n-1} = s^n - a , that is, (s - h)^n \ge a. Now let y \in S. If y > s - h, then (a) gives y^n > (s - h)^n \ge a, against y \in S. So y \le s - h, and s - h is an upper bound of S smaller than s, against s being the least upper bound. Both cases are impossible, so s^n = a by trichotomy, and b \coloneqq s \ge 0 works. For n = 2, the number \sqrt[2]{a} is non-negative and squares to a, so it is \sqrt a, by the uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. @fd3:def-complete-ordered-field (bounded sets have suprema); @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a) (adding exponents); @prp-sum-order (b), (c) (one term of a sum of non-negative terms; termwise bound). The two values of h were found by working backwards from what we wanted. Each depends on a, n and s only. Completeness was used once, to produce s. For a > 0 the root is positive, since 0^n = 0 
e a. For instance \sqrt[3]{8} = 2 and \sqrt[4]{4} = \sqrt 2, since 2^3 = 8 and (\sqrt 2)^4 =  igl((\sqrt 2)^2 igr)^2 = 4, and both are non-negative. In this chapter the symbol \sqrt[n]{a} is used only for non-negative real a. Chapter 8 adds odd roots of negative reals, and Chapter 3 shows why it could not mean “the” n-th root of a complex number. The last example already used the working principle of this section. To identify a root, we do not compute it: we take a candidate, check that it is non-negative, and check that its n-th power is a. Uniqueness in part (b) does the rest. Each equation between roots follows this way from a rule for powers. [Rules for n-th Roots] Let n, m \ge 1 be integers and a, b \in 
R with a, b \ge 0. 1. \sqrt[n]{ab} = \sqrt[n]{a} \, \sqrt[n]{b}. 2. \sqrt[n]{a^m} =  igl( \sqrt[n]{a}  igr)^m. 3. \sqrt[m]{\sqrt[n]{a}} = \sqrt[mn]{a}. 4. If a < b, then \sqrt[n]{a} < \sqrt[n]{b}. Each of (a)–(c) says that some non-negative number is a certain root. So we raise the right side to the relevant power, compute with the laws of powers, and let the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b) identify it. Number Systems identified inverses the same way (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules): name the defining property, check it, use uniqueness. Part (d) is the converse of part (a) of @lem-reals-nth-root, proved by contradiction. Write x \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{a} and y \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{b}, so x, y \ge 0, x^n = a and y^n = b. Powers and products of non-negative reals are non-negative (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), by induction for powers). (a) The number xy is \ge 0, and (xy)^n = x^n y^n = ab by @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (c). By the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b), xy = \sqrt[n]{ab}. (b) The number x^m is \ge 0, and by @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (b), used twice with mn = nm, (x^m)^n = x^{mn} = (x^n)^m = a^m . By uniqueness, x^m = \sqrt[n]{a^m}. (c) Let z \coloneqq \sqrt[m]{x}, so z \ge 0 and z^m = x. By @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (b), z^{mn} = (z^m)^n = x^n = a. By uniqueness with the exponent mn \ge 1, z = \sqrt[mn]{a}. (d) Let a < b, and suppose y \le x. If y = x, then b = y^n = x^n = a. If y < x, then b = y^n < x^n = a by @lem-reals-nth-root (a), since 0 \le y. Both contradict a < b. So x < y. Part (d) and @lem-reals-nth-root (a) together say that for non-negative reals, a < b holds if and only if \sqrt[n]{a} < \sqrt[n]{b}: taking an n-th root and raising to the n-th power both preserve strict order. That two-way comparison is how roots are compared without computing them, as in @exm-rational-power-computations below. Simplify \sqrt[3]{\sqrt{64}} in two ways. By @lem-root-rules (c) with m = 3, n = 2, it is \sqrt[6]{64} = 2, since 2 \ge 0 and 2^6 = 64. Directly, \sqrt{64} = 8 (as 8 \ge 0 and 8^2 = 64), and \sqrt[3]{8} = 2. Integer powers A rational exponent  rac{m}{n} may have a negative numerator, so before we can define a^{m/n} we need a^m for negative integers m. There is only one sensible choice. If the law a^{m+k} = a^m a^k is to survive, then a^{-k} a^k = a^0 = 1, so a^{-k} has to be the inverse of a^k. For instance, 2^{-3} must be the inverse of 2^3 = 8, which is  rac18 =  igl( rac12 igr)^3. The definition makes this so, and it works in every field. Chapter 3 meets it again in 
C, in an exercise. Integer Powers Let F be a field, a \in F with a 
e 0, and n \in 
N. Put a^{-n} \coloneqq  igl( a^{-1}  igr)^n , where the right side is the power of @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring. Only n = 0 could clash with the earlier meaning: -0 = 0, and both readings give 1, since a^0 = 1 = (a^{-1})^0. For n \ge 2 the symbol a^{-n} is new. At n = 1 it already meant the inverse, and the definition agrees with it: (a^{-1})^1 = a^{-1}. The base must be non-zero, since 0 has no inverse. For instance, in 
R, 2^{-3} =  igl( rac12 igr)^3 =  rac18. [Laws of Integer Powers] Let F be a field, let a, b \in F with a 
e 0 and b 
e 0, and let m, n \in 
Z. 1. a^{m+n} = a^m a^n. 2. (a^m)^n = a^{mn}. 3. (ab)^n = a^n b^n. 4. a^n 
e 0 and a^{-n} = (a^n)^{-1}. 5. If F is an ordered field and a > 0, then a^n > 0. 6. If F is an ordered field, a > 1 and m < n, then a^m < a^n. Each law is known for exponents in 
N (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring). A negative exponent is a natural one applied to a^{-1}, and (a^{-1})^k = (a^k)^{-1} lets us move the inverse wherever it is needed. So each law splits into sign cases, and each case reduces to 
N. The other cases reduce to natural exponents in the same way. One case shows the pattern: (a) with m \ge 0 > n. Write n = -k with k \ge 1. We use (d) for natural exponents, (a^{-1})^k = (a^k)^{-1}, proved first among the sign cases below. If m \ge k, then a^m = a^{m-k} a^k, so a^m a^{-k} = a^{m-k} \, a^k (a^k)^{-1} = a^{m-k} = a^{m+n} . If m < k, then a^{-k} = (a^{-1})^{m} (a^{-1})^{k-m} and a^m (a^{-1})^m = (a a^{-1})^m = 1, so a^m a^{-k} = (a a^{-1})^m \, (a^{-1})^{k-m} = (a^{-1})^{k-m} = a^{-(k-m)} = a^{m+n} . Both computations use only the laws for natural exponents, parts (a) and (c) of @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring, together with that identity and 1^m = 1. Throughout, exponents written j, k, \ell are in 
N, and laws “for 
N” are @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring. Note 1^k = 1 for every k (induction: 1^{k+1} = 1^k \cdot 1). (d) Natural exponents. For k \in 
N, a^k 
e 0 by part (d) for 
N, and a^k (a^{-1})^k = (a a^{-1})^k = 1^k = 1 by part (c) for 
N. By @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a), a^{-k} = (a^{-1})^k = (a^k)^{-1}, and it is non-zero, since its product with a^k is 1 
e 0. Negative exponents. For n = -k with k \ge 1, a^n = (a^k)^{-1} 
e 0, and (a^n)^{-1} = ((a^k)^{-1})^{-1} = a^k = a^{-n} by @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a). So (d) holds for every n \in 
Z. In particular, for every n \in 
Z, a^{-n} =  igl( a^{-1}  igr)^{n} , 	ag{$\ast$} by the definition for n \ge 0, and for n = -k < 0 because both sides equal a^k: the right side is ((a^{-1})^{-1})^k = a^k. (e) Both m, n \ge 0: part (a) for 
N. Both negative: let m = -j and n = -k. By the definition and part (a) for 
N applied to a^{-1}, a^{m+n} = (a^{-1})^{j+k} = (a^{-1})^j (a^{-1})^k = a^m a^n . Mixed signs. The case m \ge 0 > n is the computation above. The case m < 0 \le n is the same with m and n exchanged, since F is commutative. (f) n = k \ge 0. If m \ge 0, this is part (b) for 
N. If m = -j < 0, then (a^m)^k = ((a^{-1})^j)^k = (a^{-1})^{jk} = a^{-jk} = a^{mk}, by part (b) for 
N applied to a^{-1}. n = -k < 0. Since a^m 
e 0 by (d), the definition and (d) give (a^m)^{-k} = ((a^m)^{-1})^k = (a^{-m})^k, and the case just proved, with exponents -m \in 
Z and k \ge 0, gives (a^{-m})^k = a^{-mk} = a^{mn}. (g) n = k \ge 0: part (c) for 
N. n = -k < 0: ab 
e 0 and (ab)^{-1} = a^{-1} b^{-1} (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)), so (ab)^{-k} = (a^{-1} b^{-1})^k = (a^{-1})^k (b^{-1})^k = a^{-k} b^{-k} . (h) For k \in 
N, a^k > 0 by induction: a^0 = 1 > 0, and if a^k > 0, then a^{k+1} = a^k a > 0 \cdot a = 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c). (This is the proof of @fd2:prp-power-laws (e), which works in any ordered field.) For n = -k < 0, a^{-1} > 0 by @fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (a), so a^n = (a^{-1})^k > 0 by the case just proved. (i) First, a^\ell > 1 for every \ell \ge 1, by induction: a^1 = a > 1, and if a^\ell > 1, then a^{\ell+1} = a^\ell a > 1 \cdot a = a > 1, by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) with the positive factor a. Now let m < n, and put \ell \coloneqq n - m \ge 1. By (a), a^n = a^m a^\ell, and a^m > 0 by (e). Multiplying a^\ell > 1 by a^m > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives a^n > a^m. Compute 2^{-3} \cdot 4^{2} and  igl( rac23 igr)^{-2} in 
R. 2^{-3} =  igl( rac12 igr)^3 =  rac18 and 4^2 = 16, so the product is  rac{16}{8} = 2. (Alternatively, 4^2 = (2^2)^2 = 2^4 and 2^{-3} 2^4 = 2^1 by @prp-integer-power-laws (b), (a).) And  igl( rac23 igr)^{-2} =  igl( rac32 igr)^2 =  rac94, since the inverse of  rac23 is  rac32. Rational powers Which number should 8^{2/3} be? Reading the exponent as “square of the cube root” gives (\sqrt[3]{8})^2 = 2^2 = 4. But  rac23 =  rac46, and reading  rac46 the same way gives (\sqrt[6]{8})^4. That is 4 again, as it must be if the notation is to mean anything: its sixth power is 8^4 = 4096 = 4^6. A definition that picks one way of writing the exponent is a definition by representatives, and it is only a definition if every representative gives the same value. A rational power is a power of a root, and it does not matter which fraction names the exponent. Rational Powers Let a \in 
R with a > 0, and let r \in 
Q. Write r =  rac{m}{n} with m \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, and put a^r \coloneqq  igl( \sqrt[n]{a}  igr)^m . In words: take the n-th root of the base, which is positive since a > 0, and raise it to the integer power m of @def-integer-power. The base is strictly positive, so that negative m is allowed. Negative bases cannot be admitted at all; an example after the next proposition shows why. The definition chose one fraction for r, and every rational number has infinitely many. So there is something to check before a^r means anything. [Rational Powers Are Well Defined] Let a \in 
R with a > 0. If m, p \in 
Z and n, q \in 
Z_{>0} satisfy  rac{m}{n} =  rac{p}{q}, then  igl( \sqrt[n]{a}  igr)^m =  igl( \sqrt[q]{a}  igr)^p . For r = m \in 
Z, the number a^r is the integer power a^m of @def-integer-power, and for r =  rac1n it is \sqrt[n]{a}. Try it first (ten minutes): show (\sqrt[2]{a})^1 = (\sqrt[4]{a})^2, then say what the general proof must compare. The attempt runs into the fact that we cannot compute either root, so we cannot compare them directly. In the trial case, squaring the right side gives ((\sqrt[4]{a})^2)^2 = a, so it is the non-negative number with square a: uniqueness of square roots identifies it. In general, raise both candidates to the power nq, which clears both roots: the left side becomes a^{mq} and the right side a^{pn}, and mq = pn is what  rac{m}{n} =  rac{p}{q} means. Two positive numbers with the same nq-th power are equal by @lem-reals-nth-root (b). This is the method of @fd2:exm-method-well-definedness: two representatives, their relation unwound, equal outputs. Let u \coloneqq (\sqrt[n]{a})^m and v \coloneqq (\sqrt[q]{a})^p. The roots are positive since a > 0, so u, v > 0 by @prp-integer-power-laws (e). By @prp-integer-power-laws (b), used twice with m \cdot nq = n \cdot mq, u^{nq} =  igl( \sqrt[n]{a}  igr)^{mnq} = \Bigl(  igl( \sqrt[n]{a}  igr)^{n} \Bigr)^{mq} = a^{mq} , and in the same way v^{nq} =  igl( (\sqrt[q]{a})^{q}  igr)^{pn} = a^{pn}. Multiplying  rac{m}{n} =  rac{p}{q} by nq gives mq = pn. Hence u^{nq} = v^{nq}, with nq \ge 1, and the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b) with exponent nq gives u = v. For r = m \in 
Z, use the representative  rac{m}{1}: \sqrt[1]{a} = a, since a \ge 0 and a^1 = a, so a^r = a^m. For r =  rac1n, use  rac{1}{n}: a^r = (\sqrt[n]{a})^1 = \sqrt[n]{a}. So a^r depends on r alone, and the two special cases say that the new notation extends the old: a^{3}, a^{-2} and a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a} all mean what they meant before. Negative bases do not have rational powers. The real number -2 has cube -8, so one might want (-8)^{1/3} = -2. But  rac13 =  rac26, and read through  rac26 the power would be the square of a sixth root of -8, and no real number has sixth power -8, since an even power is \ge 0. Reading  rac26 as “sixth root of the square” gives ((-8)^2)^{1/6} = 64^{1/6} = 2, positive. No value is independent of the representative, which is why @def-rational-power asks for a > 0. With well-definedness in hand, the laws come almost for free. For instance, 8^{1/3} \cdot 8^{1/3} = 2 \cdot 2 = 4, and 8^{2/3} = 4 as computed above: the first law below says this always works. Any two rational exponents can be written over one denominator. Then most laws become statements about integer powers of one root \sqrt[n]{a}. [Laws of Rational Powers] Let a, b \in 
R with a > 0 and b > 0, and let r, s \in 
Q. 1. a^{r+s} = a^r a^s. 2. (a^r)^s = a^{rs}. 3. (ab)^r = a^r b^r. 4. a^r > 0. 5. If a > 1 and r < s, then a^r < a^s. 6. If a < b and r > 0, then a^r < b^r. Write r =  rac{m}{n} and s =  rac{p}{n} over a common denominator n > 0; @prp-rational-power-well-defined allows any representative. Then a^r = c^m and a^s = c^p with c \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{a}, and (a), (d), (e) become laws of integer powers of c (@prp-integer-power-laws). Write r =  rac{m'}{n'} and s =  rac{p'}{q'} with n', q' > 0, and put n \coloneqq n'q' > 0, m \coloneqq m'q', p \coloneqq p'n'. Then r =  rac{m}{n} and s =  rac{p}{n}. Let c \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{a} > 0. By @prp-rational-power-well-defined, a^r = c^m and a^s = c^p. (a) Since r + s =  rac{m + p}{n}, @prp-rational-power-well-defined gives a^{r+s} = c^{m+p}. Adding integer exponents, c^{m+p} = c^m c^p = a^r a^s. (b) Let a > 1. Then c > 1: otherwise c \le 1, and either c = 1 and a = 1^n = 1, or 0 < c < 1 and a = c^n < 1^n = 1 by @lem-reals-nth-root (a); both contradict a > 1. From r < s, multiplying by n > 0, we get m < p. By @prp-integer-power-laws (f), a^r = c^m < c^p = a^s. @prp-integer-power-laws (a) (adding integer exponents). Keep r =  rac{m}{n}, c = \sqrt[n]{a} as above. (d) a^r = c^m > 0 by @prp-integer-power-laws (e), since c > 0. (e) Here it is convenient to write s =  rac{p}{q} with its own denominator q > 0. Let w \coloneqq a^r, which is positive by (d). Let u \coloneqq w^s = (a^r)^s and v \coloneqq a^{rs}, where rs =  rac{mp}{nq}. Both u and v are positive by (d). Every change of the form (x^i)^j = x^{ij} = (x^j)^i below is @prp-integer-power-laws (b). By the definition, w^n = (c^m)^n = (c^n)^m = a^m, and u^q = \Bigl(  igl( \sqrt[q]{w}  igr)^p \Bigr)^q = \Bigl(  igl( \sqrt[q]{w}  igr)^q \Bigr)^p = w^p . Hence u^{nq} = (u^q)^n = (w^p)^n = (w^n)^p = (a^m)^p = a^{mp} . Also v = (\sqrt[nq]{a})^{mp}, so v^{nq} =  igl( (\sqrt[nq]{a})^{nq}  igr)^{mp} = a^{mp}. So u^{nq} = v^{nq}, and the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b) with exponent nq gives u = v. This covers m \le 0 and p \le 0 as well, because only integer-power laws were used. (f) By @lem-root-rules (a), \sqrt[n]{ab} = \sqrt[n]{a} \, \sqrt[n]{b}, and both factors are positive. By @prp-integer-power-laws (c), (ab)^r =  igl( \sqrt[n]{a} \, \sqrt[n]{b}  igr)^m =  igl( \sqrt[n]{a}  igr)^m  igl( \sqrt[n]{b}  igr)^m = a^r b^r . (g) Let a < b and r > 0. Since r =  rac{m}{n} > 0 and n > 0, m \ge 1. Let d \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{b}. By @lem-root-rules (d), 0 < c < d. By @lem-reals-nth-root (a) with the exponent m \ge 1, a^r = c^m < d^m = b^r. Part (e) needs a > 1: for a = 1 every power is 1, and for 0 < a < 1 the order reverses, as Exercise C1 shows. Part (f) needs r > 0: for r = 0 both sides are 1. [Rational powers by hand] Compute 27^{2/3} \cdot 9^{-1/2} and  igl( rac{16}{81} igr)^{-3/4}. Which is larger, 2^{1/2} or 3^{1/3}? Since 3 \ge 0 and 3^3 = 27, \sqrt[3]{27} = 3, so 27^{2/3} = 3^2 = 9. Since \sqrt{9} = 3, 9^{-1/2} = 3^{-1} =  rac13. The product is 9 \cdot  rac13 = 3. Since  rac23 \ge 0 and  igl( rac23 igr)^4 =  rac{16}{81}, \sqrt[4]{16/81} =  rac23. So  igl( rac{16}{81} igr)^{-3/4} =  igl( rac23 igr)^{-3} =  igl( rac32 igr)^3 =  rac{27}{8}. For the comparison, raise both to the sixth power, which clears both roots: by @prp-rational-power-laws (b), (2^{1/2})^6 = 2^3 = 8 and (3^{1/3})^6 = 3^2 = 9. Both numbers are positive. If 2^{1/2} \ge 3^{1/3}, then 8 \ge 9 by @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (or equality), which is false. So 2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}. Means and estimates with roots Section 1.3 proved the inequality between the means in the form a_1 \cdots a_n \le A^n, without roots, because none were available. With n-th roots it takes its familiar shape. For the two numbers 2 and 8, the geometric mean is \sqrt{2 \cdot 8} = 4, and the arithmetic mean is  rac{2 + 8}{2} = 5. [Geometric Mean Below Arithmetic Mean] Let n \ge 1 be an integer and let a_1, \dots, a_n \in 
R with a_k \ge 0 for every k. Then \sqrt[n]{a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n} \le  rac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k , with equality if and only if a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_n. This is @thm-am-gm with an n-th root taken on both sides. The theorem bounds the product G^n, and the root turns that bound into one on G. Taking roots preserves order by @lem-root-rules (d). @exm-method-am-gm (bounding the product). Let A \coloneqq  rac1n \sum a_k \ge 0 and G \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{a_1 \cdots a_n} \ge 0. By @thm-am-gm (a), G^n = a_1 \cdots a_n \le A^n. If G > A, then G^n > A^n by @lem-reals-nth-root (a), since A \ge 0; so G \le A. If G = A, then a_1 \cdots a_n = A^n, and @thm-am-gm (b) gives a_1 = \dots = a_n. Conversely, if all a_k are equal, then a_1 \cdots a_n = A^n by @thm-am-gm (b), so G = \sqrt[n]{A^n} = A by uniqueness, as A \ge 0. The last results of this chapter turn roots into estimates. How close to 1 is \sqrt[n]{a} for large n? Write the root as 1 + x with x \ge 0. Then a = (1 + x)^n, and a power of 1 + x is exactly what @exm-method-power-lower-bound bounds from below by one term. A lower bound on (1 + x)^n is an upper bound on x. For instance, \sqrt[3]{8} = 2, and part (a) below gives the bound \sqrt[3]{8} \le 1 +  rac{8 - 1}{3} =  rac{10}{3}. [Two Root Estimates] 1. If a \in 
R, a \ge 1 and n \ge 1 is an integer, then 1 \le \sqrt[n]{a} \le 1 + \dfrac{a - 1}{n}. 2. If n \ge 2 is an integer, then 1 \le \sqrt[n]{n} \le 1 + \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{n - 1}}. The method of @exm-method-power-lower-bound, read for a root: write the root as 1 + x, keep one term of (1 + x)^n, solve for x. For (a), Bernoulli’s term nx suffices, because the left side a is fixed. For (b) the left side is n, which grows, so the linear term gives only x \le  rac{n-1}{n}; the quadratic term  inom{n}{2} x^2 is needed. In both parts let y be the number in question, y \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{a} or y \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{n}, and let x \coloneqq y - 1. Since \sqrt[n]{1} = 1 (as 1 \ge 0 and 1^n = 1), @lem-root-rules (d) gives y \ge 1 whenever the radicand is \ge 1, with equality if it is 1. So x \ge 0, which is the left inequality in both parts. (a) By @fd2:thm-bernoulli (with x \ge 0 \ge -1), a = (1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx. So nx \le a - 1, and dividing by n > 0, x \le  rac{a - 1}{n}. (b) Recall  inom{n}{2} =  rac{n(n-1)}{2}. By @cor-binomial-real (b) with k = 2 \le n, n = (1 + x)^n \ge  rac{n(n - 1)}{2} x^2 . Dividing by  rac{n(n-1)}{2} > 0 gives x^2 \le  rac{2}{n - 1}. Let w \coloneqq \sqrt{2/(n - 1)} \ge 0. If x > w, then x^2 > w^2 =  rac{2}{n-1} by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), since x, w \ge 0; so x \le w. @prp-binomial-factorial (c) (the value of  inom{n}{2}). Both bounds are explicit for every n, so a threshold for any tolerance can be read off. The limit statements follow at once by @fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition. [Roots tend to one] Show that \sqrt[n]{a} 	o 1 for every real a \ge 1, and that \sqrt[n]{n} 	o 1. First limit. By @prp-root-estimates (a), \abs{\sqrt[n]{a} - 1} = \sqrt[n]{a} - 1 \le  rac{a - 1}{n} for n \ge 1. If a = 1, the sequence is constant. If a > 1, let \varepsilon > 0, choose an integer N > (a - 1)/\varepsilon, so N \ge 1; it depends on a and \varepsilon only. For n \ge N, \abs{\sqrt[n]{a} - 1} \le  rac{a-1}{n} \le  rac{a-1}{N} < \varepsilon. Second limit. By @prp-root-estimates (b), \abs{\sqrt[n]{n} - 1} \le \sqrt{2/(n - 1)} for n \ge 2. Let \varepsilon > 0 and choose an integer N > 1 + 2/\varepsilon^2; then N \ge 2, and N depends on \varepsilon only. For n \ge N, n - 1 > 2/\varepsilon^2 > 0, so  rac{2}{n - 1} < \varepsilon^2 (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (b)). Square roots preserve strict order between non-negative numbers (@lem-root-rules (d) with n = 2). So \sqrt{2/(n-1)} < \sqrt{\varepsilon^2} = \varepsilon. Hence \abs{\sqrt[n]{n} - 1} < \varepsilon. Find an N with \sqrt[n]{5} < 1.01 for every n \ge N. By @prp-root-estimates (a) with a = 5, \sqrt[n]{5} \le 1 +  rac4n. And 1 +  rac4n < 1.01 exactly when  rac4n <  rac{1}{100}, that is, n > 400. So N = 401 works. (The bound is generous: already \sqrt[162]{5} < 1.01. The definition asks for some threshold, not the least.) [Looking ahead] Chapter 8 defines a^x for every real x through the exponential function and checks that it agrees with the a^r of this section; the analysis volumes construct the exponential itself. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Where does the proof of @lem-reals-nth-root use that 
R is complete? 2. Why is h \le 1 imposed in the case s^n < a of that proof? 3. Run the first steps of the existence proof for n = 3, a = 8: what are m, M and s? 4. Compute 8^{-2/3}. 5. True or false: (a^r)^s = a^{rs} for all real a > 0 and all r, s \in 
Q. (a) Once: to produce s \coloneqq \sup S, from a non-empty set bounded above. Nothing else in the proof needs it. (b) So that s + h \le s + 1. Then each of the n terms (s + h)^k s^{n-1-k} is at most (s + 1)^{n-1}, a bound that does not involve h, and h can be solved for. Without h \le 1 the terms would grow with h. (c) m = \min\{1, 8\} = 1, M = \max\{1, 8\} = 8, and s = \sup\{ y \ge 0 : y^3 \le 8 \} = 2: the proof shows s^3 = 8, and 2 is the non-negative number with cube 8. (d) \sqrt[3]{8} = 2, so 8^{-2/3} = 2^{-2} =  rac14. (e) True: @prp-rational-power-laws (b). B. Practice [B1: Simplify] Simplify, for real a, b > 0: 1. 32^{3/5}; 2.  igl( a^{1/2} b^{-1/3}  igr)^6; 3. \dfrac{4^{3/2}}{8^{2/3}}. (a) \sqrt[5]{32} = 2, since 2^5 = 32; so 32^{3/5} = 2^3 = 8. (b) By @prp-rational-power-laws (c) and (b), (a^{1/2} b^{-1/3})^6 = (a^{1/2})^6 (b^{-1/3})^6 = a^{3} b^{-2}. (c) 4^{3/2} = (\sqrt 4)^3 = 2^3 = 8 and 8^{2/3} = (\sqrt[3]{8})^2 = 2^2 = 4, so the quotient is  rac84 = 2. [B2: Compare without a calculator] Put 3^{1/3}, 2^{1/2} and 5^{1/5} in increasing order. Justify your answer. Raise all three to the power 30, a common multiple of 3, 2, 5. By the law (a^r)^s = a^{rs}, (3^{1/3})^{30} = 3^{10} = 59049 , \quad (2^{1/2})^{30} = 2^{15} = 32768 , \quad (5^{1/5})^{30} = 5^{6} = 15625 . All three numbers are positive, and for positive x, y, x^{30} < y^{30} forces x < y: otherwise y \le x and y^{30} \le x^{30} by @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (or equality). Hence 5^{1/5} < 2^{1/2} < 3^{1/3}. @prp-rational-power-laws (b) (powers of powers). [B3: An explicit N] Find an N such that \sqrt[n]{n} < 1.1 for every n \ge N. By @prp-root-estimates (b), \sqrt[n]{n} \le 1 + \sqrt{2/(n - 1)} for n \ge 2, so it suffices that \sqrt{2/(n - 1)} < 0.1. Both sides are non-negative. Squaring and taking square roots both preserve strict order between non-negative numbers. So this holds exactly when  rac{2}{n - 1} < 0.01, that is, when n - 1 > 200. So N = 202 works: for n \ge 202, \sqrt[n]{n} \le 1 + \sqrt{2/(n-1)} < 1.1. @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (squaring preserves order); @lem-root-rules (d) (square roots preserve order). C. Going deeper [C1: Chapter check: powers of a base below one] Let a \in 
R with 0 < a < 1, and let r, s \in 
Q. Prove: 1. if r < s, then a^r > a^s; 2. if r > 0, then a^r < 1. Put b \coloneqq  rac1a. Since 0 < a < 1, @fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (b) gives b >  rac11 = 1. For every t \in 
Q, 1^t = 1: with t =  rac{m}{n}, \sqrt[n]{1} = 1 by uniqueness (as 1 \ge 0 and 1^n = 1), and 1^m = 1 for every m \in 
Z by @prp-integer-power-laws (d). So, by @prp-rational-power-laws (c), a^t b^t = (ab)^t = 1^t = 1 , and a^t = (b^t)^{-1} for every t \in 
Q. (i) Let r < s. By @prp-rational-power-laws (e), applied to the base b > 1, b^r < b^s, and both are positive by part (d). Reciprocals reverse the order between positive numbers (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (b)), so a^r = (b^r)^{-1} > (b^s)^{-1} = a^s . (ii) Let r > 0. By (i) with the exponents 0 < r, a^r < a^0, and a^0 = 1, since by @prp-rational-power-well-defined a^0 is the integer power a^0 = 1. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: reduces to a base above one, b =  rac1a > 1, with the reason. - 3: the link to that base, a^t = (b^t)^{-1} from (c) of the laws and 1^t = 1. - 2: the law (e) applied to a base above one, not to a. - 2: the reversal of order under reciprocals, with positivity from (d). - 1: (ii) from (i), with a^0 = 1. Alternatively, over a common denominator r =  rac{m}{n}, s =  rac{p}{n}: - 3: c = \sqrt[n]{a} \in (0, 1) with the reason, and m < p. - 2: c^{p-m} < 1, with the reason (for instance (1/c)^{p-m} > 1). - 2: c^p = c^m c^{p-m} < c^m, using c^m > 0. - 2: the conclusion a^r = c^m > c^p = a^s. - 1: (ii) from (i), with a^0 = 1. Slips that lose the step: applying (e) to a base a < 1. [C2: The compound sequence is bounded] Show that  igl( 1 +  rac1n  igr)^n < 3 for every integer n \ge 1. [Hint 1] Expand by the binomial theorem and compare the term  inom{n}{k}  rac{1}{n^k} with  rac{1}{k!}. [Hint 2] By @prp-binomial-factorial (c),  inom{n}{k} \dfrac{1}{n^k} = \dfrac{1}{k!} \displaystyle\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}  rac{n - j}{n}. Let n \ge 1. By @thm-binomial-commutative-ring with x =  rac1n, y = 1, \Bigl( 1 +  rac1n \Bigr)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}  inom{n}{k}  rac{1}{n^k} . The term k = 0 is 1. Let 1 \le k \le n. By @prp-binomial-factorial (c),  inom{n}{k} k! = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} (n - j), and n^k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} n, so  inom{n}{k}  rac{1}{n^k} =  rac{1}{k!} \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}  rac{n - j}{n} . For 0 \le j \le k - 1 \le n - 1, the factor  rac{n - j}{n} lies in (0, 1]. So the product lies in (0, 1], by induction on the number of factors. Hence the term is at most  rac{1}{k!}, and  rac{1}{k!} \le  rac{1}{2^{k-1}} by @exm-geometric-comparison. Comparing termwise and summing the geometric series with ratio  rac12, \Bigl( 1 +  rac1n \Bigr)^n \le 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \Bigl(  rac12 \Bigr)^{k-1} = 1 + 2\Bigl( 1 -  rac{1}{2^n} \Bigr) = 3 -  rac{2}{2^n} < 3 , where the last step uses  rac{2}{2^n} > 0. Together with @exm-am-gm-compound, which showed that the sequence increases, this says the compound sequence is increasing and bounded above by 3. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d) (products of factors in (0, 1]); @prp-sum-order (a) (termwise comparison); @fd2:prp-geometric-sum (the geometric sum). What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 3: the binomial expansion, with each term written in the factorial form. - 3: the termwise bound  inom{n}{k} n^{-k} \le  rac{1}{k!}, with the factors  rac{n-j}{n} shown to lie in (0, 1], and  rac{1}{k!} bounded by a summable comparison sequence (for instance  rac{1}{2^{k-1}}), with reason. - 2: the comparison sum evaluated exactly (geometric or telescoping). - 2: the strict inequality < 3, with its reason. Slips that lose the step: bounding  inom{n}{k} n^{-k} by  rac{1}{k!} without the factor-by-factor reason, or summing the comparison series to infinity. R. Review [R1] Compute \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}  rac{1}{\sqrt{k} + \sqrt{k + 1}} for n \ge 1. The tool is telescoping (@exm-method-telescoping). Since k + 1 > 0, \sqrt{k+1} > 0, so \sqrt k + \sqrt{k+1} > 0. Since (\sqrt{k+1} - \sqrt k)(\sqrt{k+1} + \sqrt k) = (k + 1) - k = 1,  rac{1}{\sqrt k + \sqrt{k + 1}} = \sqrt{k + 1} - \sqrt k . With b_j \coloneqq \sqrt{j + 1} and j = k - 1, @thm-telescoping (a) gives \sum_{k=1}^{n}  igl( \sqrt{k + 1} - \sqrt k  igr) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (b_{j+1} - b_j) = b_n - b_0 = \sqrt{n + 1} - 1 . [R2] Compute \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n}  inom{n}{k} (-2)^k for n \in 
N. By the binomial theorem (@thm-binomial-commutative-ring) in 
R with x = -2 and y = 1, the sum is (-2 + 1)^n = (-1)^n. [R3] Prove that \dfrac{n + \sqrt n}{n^2 + 1} 	o 0. The first tool is keeping the dominant term (@exm-method-dominant-term). The second is proving a limit from the definition (@fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition). For n \ge 1, n \le n^2, so \sqrt n \le \sqrt{n^2} = n by @lem-root-rules (d) (or equality). Here \sqrt{n^2} = n by uniqueness, since n \ge 0. Hence the numerator is at most 2n. The denominator is at least n^2 > 0, so 0 <  rac{n + \sqrt n}{n^2 + 1} \le  rac{2n}{n^2} =  rac{2}{n} \qquad (n \ge 1) . Let \varepsilon > 0 and choose an integer N > 2/\varepsilon; then N \ge 1, and N depends on \varepsilon only. For n \ge N the distance to 0 is at most 2/n \le 2/N < \varepsilon. The look-alike tool, the quotient rule for limits, does not apply to the fraction as written: neither the numerator nor the denominator converges.

title: Chapter Review
content:
Chapter Review Summary Finite sums obey the rules of @lem-ring-finite-sums in every commutative ring, and a sum whose terms are differences telescopes (@thm-telescoping). The binomial theorem holds in every commutative ring with coefficients defined by Pascal’s rule (@thm-binomial-commutative-ring). In the real numbers it bounds a power from below by one or two of its terms (@cor-binomial-real). Bernoulli’s inequality becomes strict (@lem-bernoulli-strict) and extends to products, and the arithmetic mean bounds the geometric mean (@thm-am-gm). With these, geometric sequences, n/r^n and 1/n! tend to zero. Every non-negative real has a unique non-negative n-th root (@lem-reals-nth-root). The powers a^{m/n} of a positive real are well defined and obey the laws of powers (@prp-rational-power-laws). What is open: powers with irrational exponents, which Chapter 8 defines through the exponential function, and the limit of the compound-interest sequence, which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 4 identifies. Proof methods in this chapter - Telescoping (@exm-method-telescoping). When a sum has terms b_{k+1} - b_k, the middle cancels and only the ends survive. Introduced in Section 1.1, where it sums reciprocals and squares and proves the difference of powers. Its “verification form” checks a guessed closed form instead of finding it. - Bound a product by a power (@exm-method-am-gm). Replace the factors by their arithmetic mean, which is easy to compute, and let the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality turn the product into a power. Introduced in Section 1.3. - Keep the dominant term (@exm-method-dominant-term). In a quotient of sums, keep the term that grows fastest and absorb the others into it from some index on. The quotient is then bounded by a quotient of single powers. Introduced in Section 1.4. - Bound a power from below (@exm-method-power-lower-bound). Write a base above one as 1 + h and keep one term of the expansion, by Bernoulli or by the binomial theorem. This makes r^n at least a multiple of a power of n. Introduced in Section 1.4, with exercises B1 and C2. - Recalled from earlier volumes. Proving a limit from the definition (@fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition); induction on the last term (@fd2:exm-method-induction-step); well-definedness (@fd2:exm-method-well-definedness). Constructing a point as a supremum, from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 6 (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), is run again in Section 1.5. Terms - arithmetic mean, geometric mean: (a_1 + \dots + a_n)/n and \sqrt[n]{a_1 \cdots a_n}, compared in @thm-am-gm. - binomial coefficient: the natural number  inom{n}{k} given by Pascal’s rule, never by a quotient of factorials (@def-binomial-coefficients). - integer power: a^{-n} \coloneqq (a^{-1})^n for a 
e 0 in a field (@def-integer-power). - natural multiple: n \cdot a, the sum of n copies of a, with its laws (@lem-natural-multiples). - n-th root: the unique b \ge 0 with b^n = a, written \sqrt[n]{a} (@lem-reals-nth-root). - rational power: a^{m/n} \coloneqq (\sqrt[n]{a})^m for a > 0 (@def-rational-power). - telescoping sum: a sum of terms b_{k+1} - b_k, equal to the difference of its ends (@thm-telescoping). Results used from earlier volumes Nothing in the chapter is borrowed: everything is proved from the results below. No other chapter of this volume is used, since this chapter comes first. Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: - induction (@fd1:ax-induction); - strengthening a claim before inducting (@fd1:exm-strengthen-the-claim). Sets and Functions, Chapter 3: - the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion) and induction in practice (@fd2:thm-induction); - finite sums and products (@fd2:def-sum-product) and powers (@fd2:def-power); - the laws of powers (@fd2:prp-power-laws); - the sum of the first n numbers (@fd2:prp-sum-first-n) and the geometric sum (@fd2:prp-geometric-sum); - a finite list of reals has a largest term (@fd2:prp-finite-max); - Bernoulli’s inequality for real numbers (@fd2:thm-bernoulli), used in Sections 1.2–1.5. Sets and Functions, Chapter 5: - well-definedness, as a proof method (@fd2:exm-method-well-definedness). Number Systems: From 
N to 
R: - its 
N and the 
N of Sets and Functions are the same (@fd3:cor-omega-identification), from its Chapter 1; - commutative rings and fields (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) and the algebra of a ring (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra), from its Chapter 2; - the rules of an ordered ring, including the multiples of its Section 2.4 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules), and 
Z as an ordered ring (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring); - reciprocals reverse the order (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order), from its Chapter 3; - the rules of an ordered field (@fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves), the absolute value (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field) and fractions in a field (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules), from its Chapter 4; - the natural numbers inside an ordered field (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-naturals-in-ordered-field); - the Archimedean property (@fd3:prp-archimedean-reciprocal); - limits of sequences (@fd3:def-sequence-limit-ordered-field), the first limits (@fd3:exm-first-sequences-ordered-field), only the tail matters (@fd3:prp-tail-change-ordered-field), and how to prove a limit from the definition (@fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition); - the completeness of 
R (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:def-complete-ordered-field), from its Chapter 5; - a complete ordered field is Archimedean (@fd3:thm-cof-complete-archimedean), from its Chapter 6; - square roots in 
R (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots) and a point constructed as a supremum (@fd3:exr-measuring-by-rationals-b2), from its Chapter 6, which Section 1.5 runs for every exponent. Threads - From sums to Cauchy–Schwarz. The rules for finite sums of Section 1.1 are what Chapter 9 uses to prove the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Chapter 4 uses the same sums with terms in a field. - Binomial theorem and Fermat. The binomial coefficients are defined without division because Chapter 4 needs them in 
F_p, where p! is zero. There (x + y)^p = x^p + y^p. - Rational to real powers. Section 1.5 stops at rational exponents. Chapter 8 defines a^x for every real x from the exponential function. Analysis on the Real Line proves the facts about the exponential that Chapter 8 borrows.

title: Divisibility and Congruences
content:
Divisibility and Congruences Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2 built 
Z out of pairs of natural numbers and proved it an ordered ring, but it said nothing about which integers divide which. Sets and Functions, Section 3.2 did, for the school integers: it proved division with remainder, showed that every integer from 2 on has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of prime factorization aside as a fact it neither proved nor used. This chapter proves that arithmetic again for the constructed 
Z, and goes further, using the ordered-ring axioms and two properties of the order of 
Z: there is no integer strictly between 0 and 1 (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), and a non-empty set of integers with a lower bound has a least element (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element). Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5 drew division with remainder from the second property (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder), and this chapter starts there; the field 
Q enters for lowest terms and in a few examples and exercises. Then one move does most of the work. In a set of integers closed under sums and under multiplication by any integer, the least positive element divides every element, and dividing by it with remainder is how one sees this. Applied to the combinations ax + by, it makes the greatest common divisor a combination of a and b (Bézout’s theorem), and the Euclidean algorithm computes it. Multiplying that combination by a third integer gives Euclid’s lemma, that a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors, and with it the uniqueness of prime factorization and the lowest terms of a rational number. The second half returns to the clock of Sets and Functions, Section 5.2. There, and again for 
Z and 
Q in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3, each sum and product of classes was checked separately to be well defined. Section 2.3 makes the check once, for the quotient of any commutative ring by an ideal, and 
Z/n
Z becomes a commutative ring with n elements on which, for n \ge 2, no order fits. In it the classes that can be divided by are exactly the classes of the integers coprime to n. So 
Z/p
Z is a field with p elements for every prime p, and two congruences with coprime moduli have exactly one class of solutions modulo the product of the moduli, the Chinese remainder theorem. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 builds 
R in the same shape, as classes of rational Cauchy sequences whose difference is null (the null sequences play the part of the ideal), though it checks its operations directly; Chapter 7 of this volume runs division with remainder, gcd and unique factorization again for polynomials over a field. Two integers, one theory. Sets and Functions, Chapters 1, 3 and 5 proved its facts about divisibility for the school integers, from school facts such as the closure of 
Z under +, - and \cdot (@fd2:prp-integers-closed). This chapter keeps their definitions of divisibility, prime and congruence (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime, @fd2:def-congruence), read word for word on the ring of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2, and proves the results again; no proof in it cites a result of Sets and Functions about integers. Each such result has a twin here: transitivity of divisibility (@fd2:prp-divides-transitive) and even or odd (@fd2:thm-even-or-odd), from its Chapter 1, are @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b) and @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a); the others are named in the section that proves them: division with remainder (@fd2:thm-division-algorithm) and the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N (@fd2:prp-divides-partial-order) in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5; a prime factor of every n \ge 2 (@fd2:thm-prime-factor) and lowest terms (@fd2:lem-lowest-terms) in Section 2.2; and the arithmetic of congruence classes (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic) in Section 2.3. Nothing earlier was circular: the earlier chapters used these facts about the school integers as stated facts, and this chapter proves them for the constructed ones. What you need. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 1–3, chiefly Sections 2.3–2.5, and Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–5, chiefly Sections 1.1, 3.2 and 5.2. From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3: the commutative ring 
Z and its algebra (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra), its order, the rules for inequalities and discreteness (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules, @fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring), the least element of a set of integers bounded below (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element), the copy of 
N inside 
Z (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers), the lemma that a rule on classes is a function when equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs (@fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes), the two-element field that cannot be ordered (@fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), and the field 
Q with 
Z inside it and its order (@fd3:def-rational-operations, @fd3:thm-rationals-field, @fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals, @fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field); and from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5, division with remainder, the rules for divisibility and parity (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd). From its Chapter 1, the citing rule of its Section 1.4 (@fd3:cor-omega-identification), by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, @fd3:thm-omega-recursion) apply to 
N; and powers and parity on 
N (@fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity), used in review exercise R2. From Sets and Functions, Section 1.1, the definitions of divisibility and prime (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime); from its Section 3.3, finite products (@fd2:def-sum-product), used in Section 2.2 as a pattern for products of lists; from its Section 5.2, equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition) and congruence (@fd2:def-congruence); from its Section 5.3, suprema and the divisibility order (@fd2:def-order-supremum, @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm), in a remark of Section 2.1 and in Section 2.2’s B2. From Sets and Functions, Chapters 1 and 2: products, equality of functions, bijections and their composites (@fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-bijective, @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective); and from its Section 4.1, finite sets and equinumerous sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-equinumerous-properties), to count 
Z/n
Z, with more on finite sets (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy, @fd2:exr-finite-sets-c2) in Section 2.4’s B3 and C2. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 8, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for Section 2.2’s B1 and C2 and Section 2.4’s C2. A few results are compared with and not used: the twins listed above; Euclid’s argument in Logic and Proof, Section 8.1’s C1 (@fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1) in Section 2.2’s C3; a rule on classes that is not a function (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map) in Section 2.3’s C1; lowest terms in Sets and Functions, Section 3.2’s C2 (@fd2:exr-induction-in-practice-c2) in Section 2.2; and, in the review exercises, the countable product of Sets and Functions, Section 4.2 (@fd2:exr-countable-sets-b2, @fd2:thm-product-countable) in R2, the two proofs that \sqrt 2 is not rational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two) in R3. From Chapter 1 of this volume, review exercise R1 uses the laws of powers in a commutative ring (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring) and the difference of powers (@lem-difference-of-powers). Time. About 20 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm. The combinations a
Z + b
Z and the multiples n
Z, the greatest common divisor with \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0, Bézout’s theorem (the least positive combination is the gcd, and every combination is a multiple of it), coprime integers, and the Euclidean algorithm as a recursion that keeps the set of combinations fixed, with back-substitution for the coefficients. - Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Euclid’s lemma from the Bézout identity, a prime dividing a product of primes equal to one of them, coprime divisors, the least divisor above 1 as a prime, existence and uniqueness of non-decreasing prime factorizations by comparing the largest primes, a monoid in which factorization is not unique, and lowest terms in 
Q. - Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n. Ideals as the subsets that a quotient needs, the quotient ring R/I of a commutative ring by an ideal, the failure for 
Z \subseteq 
Q, the ideals of 
Z as the sets n
Z, and 
Z/n
Z as a commutative ring with n elements that no order fits when n \ge 2. - Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Units of a commutative ring, the units of 
Z/n
Z as the classes coprime to n with inverses from back-substitution, 
Z/n
Z a field exactly when n is prime, and the Chinese remainder theorem for two coprime moduli, with the failures when the moduli share a factor; the review exercises reach back to Chapter 1 of this volume, Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 1 and 3, Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, and Sets and Functions, Chapter 4. Named moves - Least positive element, then divide. Take the least positive element d of a set of integers closed under integer combinations; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than d, so it is 0. This proves Bézout’s theorem in Section 2.1 and the description of the ideals of 
Z in Section 2.3, and Section 2.2’s B2 and Section 2.3’s C2 use it for common multiples and for sets closed under subtraction. - Multiply the Bézout identity. From 1 = ax + by, multiply by c: c = acx + bcy, and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about common divisors into an equation, and it gives Euclid’s lemma in Section 2.2; in Section 2.4 the same identity, read modulo n, gives inverses, and read modulo m and modulo n at once, the Chinese remainder theorem. - Compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. An operation on classes a + I is well defined because a change of representative is an element of I, and multiplying it by the other argument keeps it in I. This is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2’s check one argument at a time, now made once for every commutative ring and every ideal.

title: 2.1 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content:
The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm Number Systems, Section 2.5 gave the constructed integers a relation a \mid b and a division with remainder (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder). This section asks what two integers have in common. Here is a concrete version. A machine accepts only coins worth 12 and 42 units, and gives change in the same coins. Which amounts can be paid exactly? Paying x coins of the first kind and y of the second, with negative numbers for coins received as change, pays 12x + 42y. So 42 - 3 \cdot 12 = 6 can be paid, and hence every multiple of 6; and since 6 divides both 12 and 42, nothing else can. Why 6, and why exactly the multiples of 6? The answer is a theorem about every pair of integers, and its proof is the main move of this chapter. Integer combinations The amounts 12x + 42y form a set that deserves a name. Integer Combinations Let a, b, n \in 
Z. The set of integer combinations of a and b is a
Z + b
Z \coloneqq \{ ax + by : x, y \in 
Z \} , and the set of multiples of n is n
Z \coloneqq \{ kn : k \in 
Z \}. So n
Z is the set of m \in 
Z with n \mid m (@fd2:def-divides), and a
Z + b
Z is written as one symbol: it is defined directly, not as a sum of two sets. Three closure properties hold for every a, b \in 
Z. For x, y, x', y', m \in 
Z, the ring laws of @fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) give  egin{aligned} (ax + by) + (ax' + by') &= a(x + x') + b(y + y'), \ -(ax + by) &= a(-x) + b(-y), \ m(ax + by) &= a(mx) + b(my), \end{aligned} so a
Z + b
Z is closed under +, under -, and under multiplication by any integer. It contains 0 = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 0, a = a \cdot 1 + b \cdot 0 and b = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1. Taking b = 0 gives n
Z + 0
Z = \{ nx + 0y \} = \{ xn : x \in 
Z \} = n
Z, by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6); so n
Z has the same three properties. Examples: - 12
Z + 42
Z contains 12, 42, 30 = 42 - 12 and 6 = 12 \cdot (-3) + 42 \cdot 1, so it contains every multiple of 6, by the third closure property. - 2
Z + 3
Z = 
Z: it contains 1 = 2 \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot 1, and with it m \cdot 1 = m for every m \in 
Z. - The degenerate case: 0
Z + 0
Z = \{0\} (the case n = 0 above, since 0
Z = \{ k \cdot 0 : k \in 
Z \} = \{0\} by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). It is the only case in which a
Z + b
Z has no positive element (if a 
e 0, one of a, -a is a positive element, by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h); likewise for b), and the theorem below must exclude it. Non-example by minimal change. Allow only paying, with no change given: \{ 12x + 42y : x, y \in 
N \}. It contains 12 and 42 and is closed under +, but not under -: it contains no negative integer, since x, y \ge 0 give 12x + 42y \ge 0. Nor does it contain 6: a non-zero element has x \ge 1 or y \ge 1, so it is at least 12. The coefficients must range over all of 
Z. The greatest common divisor An integer d is a common divisor of a and b if d \mid a and d \mid b. Every pair has the common divisor 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). For the coins, 6 is a common divisor of 12 and 42, and the question was why it is the one that matters. The greatest common divisor is the largest integer that divides both. [Greatest Common Divisor] Let a, b \in 
Z. If (a, b) 
e (0, 0), the greatest common divisor \gcd(a, b) is the greatest element, for \le, of the set of common divisors of a and b. We set \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0. In words: among all integers dividing both a and b, take the largest. The definition says “the greatest element”, so it owes us a proof that there is one. Well-definedness. Let (a, b) 
e (0, 0), and let D be the set of common divisors of a and b. It is non-empty, since 1 \in D. Say a 
e 0 (otherwise b 
e 0, and the same argument runs with b). By @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h), one of a, -a is positive; call it c. Every d \in D satisfies d \le c: if d > 0, then d \mid c by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d), and d \le c by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e); if d \le 0, then d \le 0 < c. So D is bounded above, and by @fd3:prp-integer-least-element it has a greatest element. Since 1 \in D, that element is at least 1. Hence \gcd(a, b) \ge 1 whenever (a, b) 
e (0, 0), and \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a), since the condition “d \mid a and d \mid b” is symmetric in a and b. Examples: - \gcd(4, 6) = 2. A positive common divisor d satisfies d \le 4, by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), and d \ge 1, so d \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} by discreteness (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), applied repeatedly. Now 4 
mid 6 and 3 
mid 4, because 6 = 1 \cdot 4 + 2 and 4 = 1 \cdot 3 + 1 have non-zero remainders (the divisibility test after @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder), while 2 divides both. So the greatest common divisor is 2. - \gcd(-5, 5) = 5: the common divisors of -5 and 5 are the divisors of 5 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), and the greatest is 5, by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). - \gcd(1, b) = 1 for every b \in 
Z: a common divisor d divides 1, so d = \pm 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), and the greater is 1. Why the convention for (0, 0). Every integer divides 0, so 0 and 0 have no greatest common divisor for \le, and some value has to be chosen. The value 0 is the one that keeps clauses (c) and (e) of the theorem below true for (0, 0), as the remark after it shows. It also matches @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm of Sets and Functions, Section 5.3, where 0 is the top of (
N, \mid), divisible by everything. Listing divisors one by one, as in the first example, is slow. The Euclidean algorithm below replaces the list by one division per step, and Bézout’s theorem is what makes it work. Bézout’s theorem Here is the answer to the coin question for every pair of integers: the payable amounts are exactly the multiples of the greatest common divisor, and the greatest common divisor is itself payable. Bézout’s Theorem Let a, b \in 
Z, not both 0, and let S \coloneqq (a
Z + b
Z) \cap 
Z_{>0}. 1. S has a least element d, and d = ax_0 + by_0 for some x_0, y_0 \in 
Z. 2. d \mid a and d \mid b. 3. Every common divisor of a and b divides d. 4. d = \gcd(a, b). In particular, \gcd(a, b) = ax + by for some x, y \in 
Z. 5. a
Z + b
Z = d
Z. Try it first (ten minutes): for a = 12 and b = 42, list the positive numbers 12x + 42y you can reach. Which is the least, and why should the least one divide 12? The obvious plan starts from the greatest common divisor and tries to write it as ax + by. It stalls: the definition of \gcd(a, b) says nothing about combinations, so there is nothing to build x and y from. The attempt on 12 and 42 suggests starting at the other end. The positive combinations 12, 42, 30, 18, 6, \dots have a least element, and it was found as a combination. Why should it divide 12? Divide 12 by it. The remainder is 12 minus a multiple of a combination, so it is again a combination, and it is smaller than the least positive one. So it cannot be positive: it is 0. Once the least positive combination d is known to divide a and b, the rest is bookkeeping: every common divisor divides the combination d, so none exceeds it. Before reading on: where is the minimality of d used, and where its positivity? (a) Suppose a 
e 0; if a = 0, then b 
e 0, and the argument is the same with b in place of a. Both a = a \cdot 1 + b \cdot 0 and -a = a \cdot (-1) + b \cdot 0 lie in a
Z + b
Z, and by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h) one of them is positive. So S 
e \emptyset. Every element of S is positive, so 0 is a lower bound, and by @fd3:prp-integer-least-element S has a least element d. Since d \in a
Z + b
Z, there are x_0, y_0 \in 
Z with d = ax_0 + by_0. (b) Since d \in 
Z_{>0}, @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a) gives q, r \in 
Z with a = qd + r and 0 \le r < d. Then r = a - qd = a - q(ax_0 + by_0) = a(1 - qx_0) + b(-qy_0) , so r \in a
Z + b
Z. If r > 0, then r \in S and r < d, contradicting the minimality of d. Hence r = 0, and a = qd, that is, d \mid a. Dividing b by d in the same way gives d \mid b. (c) Let c \mid a and c \mid b. By @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c), c \mid ax_0 + by_0 = d. (d) By (b), d is a common divisor of a and b. Let c be any common divisor. If c > 0, then c \mid d by (c), and c \le d by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), since d > 0. If c \le 0, then c \le 0 < d. So d is the greatest common divisor: d = \gcd(a, b) by @def-integer-gcd, and \gcd(a, b) = ax_0 + by_0. (e) (\supseteq) Let k \in 
Z. Then kd = k(ax_0 + by_0) = a(kx_0) + b(ky_0) \in a
Z + b
Z. (\subseteq) Let x, y \in 
Z. By (b), d \mid a and d \mid b, so d \mid ax + by by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c), that is, ax + by \in d
Z. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: the minimality of d is used once, in (b), to force the remainder r to be 0. The positivity of d is used twice: to divide by d at all (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder needs a positive divisor), and in (d), where c \le d for positive c comes from @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) and for the other c from 0 < d. (The step r \in S uses the positivity of r, not of d, which is why the case r = 0 is split off.) The proof of (b) is the move this chapter is built on, and we give it a name: least positive element, then divide. Take the least positive element d of a set closed under integer combinations; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than d, so it is 0. Section 2.2 uses the move again for common multiples, and Section 2.3 for sets closed under subtraction. For the coins, the theorem says: the payable amounts form 12
Z + 42
Z = d
Z, where d is the least positive payable amount, and d = \gcd(12, 42). The Try-it-first list finds d = 6 = 12 \cdot (-3) + 42 \cdot 1. Clause (c) says that \gcd(a, b) is greatest also for divisibility, not only for \le. For a, b \in 
N, not both 0, it is the infimum of \{a, b\} in (
N, \mid) (@fd2:def-order-supremum): it divides both, and every c \in 
N dividing both divides it. This is the mirror image of @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm, where the supremum is the least common multiple. For general a, b \in 
Z, let a' be the one of a, -a that lies in
