title: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:
Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic Section 2.1 gave every pair of integers, not both zero, a greatest common divisor, and wrote it as a combination ax + by (@thm-integers-bezout). This section spends that identity. Take 60. It splits as 2 \cdot 30, as 6 \cdot 10, as 4 \cdot 15, and every way of splitting it further, until no factor splits again, ends with the same primes 2, 2, 3, 5. Sets and Functions, Section 3.2 proved, for the school integers, that every integer at least 2 has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of the full splitting aside. Here we prove both, for the integers of Number Systems, Chapter 2. The key is a property of primes that the definition (“no positive divisors except 1 and itself”) does not obviously give: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. As in Number Systems, Section 2.5, numerals are the natural numbers of those names, and their sums and products may be computed in 
N (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers (a)). Euclid’s lemma The definition of a prime p speaks about the divisors of p. The property we want speaks about the numbers that p divides. Something has to connect the two, and the connection is the Bézout identity of Section 2.1. We first prove a version for any divisor that shares no factor with one of the two numbers multiplied. Euclid’s Lemma Let a, b, c \in 
Z. If a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1, then a \mid c. The hypothesis \gcd(a, b) = 1 is a statement about common divisors, which is hard to use directly. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination it is the same as an equation 1 = ax + by, and an equation can be multiplied. Multiplying it by c writes c as acx + bcy. The first term is a multiple of a on sight, and the second is one because bc is. Suppose a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination there are x, y \in 
Z with ax + by = 1. Since a \mid bc, there is k \in 
Z with bc = ka (@fd2:def-divides). Multiplying the identity by c, with (F7), (F9), (F5) and (F6), c = c(ax + by) = a(cx) + (bc)y = a(cx) + a(ky) = a(cx + ky) . Since cx + ky \in 
Z, this shows a \mid c. We call the method of this proof multiply the Bézout identity: from 1 = ax + by, multiply by c and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about divisors into an equation, which is where the work can be done. Each hypothesis has a job. Without \gcd(a, b) = 1 the conclusion fails: 4 \mid 2 \cdot 6 = 12, but 4 
mid 6, since 6 = 1 \cdot 4 + 2 leaves a non-zero remainder (uniqueness in @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a)); here \gcd(4, 2) = 2. The common factor 2 of 4 and 2 let 4 divide the product without dividing 6. Lists, products and prime factorizations To say that a factorization is unique, we must first say what a factorization is. The products 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 and 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 are equal and use the same primes, and we want to count them as one. We do so by writing the primes in order, smallest first. A factorization also has a length, and the length may be 0: the number 1 is the product of no primes at all. Products of lists are defined by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product. That definition was made for sequences of real numbers, and we use it as a pattern, as Number Systems, Section 1.4 allows for definitions read on a new number system, with the ordered field 
Q (@fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field) in place of

Hence a \mid acx + bcy (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)). So a \mid c. Line (i) comes first, and (ii) needs its hypothesis \gcd(a, b) = 1. Lines (iii), (iv) and (v) each need only (ii): (iii) multiplies its equation, and (iv) and (v) mention its x and y; (v) also uses the hypothesis a \mid bc of (i). None of these three uses another of them. Line (vi) needs both (iv) and (v), but not (iii), since acx + bcy is just an expression in a, b, c, x, y. Line (vii) rewrites (vi) through the equation of (iii), so it needs both and comes last. The admissible orders are therefore those that start (i), (ii), end with (vii), and place (vi) after (iv) and (v); there are eight. For example, (i), (ii), (iv), (v), (vi), (iii), (vii) is admissible: (iii) may come anywhere before (vii). The distractor (ii′) cites a “fact” that is not available as a step for arbitrary a. For a prime a it is @cor-prime-divides-product (b), which is proved from this lemma, so citing it here is circular. For a general integer a the line is the lemma itself in a weaker form, so citing it is circular again; only special cases are available (for a = \pm 1, a \mid b by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a), with (d) for -1), and the proof must work for every a. Either way the line uses what has not been established, which is (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The distractor (iii′) divides in 
Z, where there is no division: a may be 0 (\gcd(0, 1) = 1), and then the line divides by 0; for a 
e 0, 1/a is not an integer unless a = \pm 1. Divisibility is defined by multiplication (@fd2:def-divides), not by fractions. [B2: The least common multiple] Let a, b \in 
Z_{>0}, and let M \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z_{>0} : a \mid m 	ext{ and } b \mid m \}. Prove that M has a least element L, and that L \mid c for every c \in 
Z with a \mid c and b \mid c. The first part of a proof is given. ab > 0 by (O4), and a \mid ab, b \mid ab, so ab \in M; and 0 is a lower bound of M. By @fd3:prp-integer-least-element, M has a least element L. Let c \in 
Z with a \mid c and b \mid c. By @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a), c = qL + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < L. Since r = c + (-q)L, and a divides c and L, a \mid r (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)); likewise b \mid r. The last step is blank. Say which method this is, then complete it. The method is least positive element, then divide: the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than its least positive element, so it is not positive. Completion: if r > 0, then r \in 
Z_{>0} is a common multiple of a and b, so r \in M, and r < L, against the choice of L. Hence r = 0 (as r \ge 0), and c = qL, that is, L \mid c. The same argument proved @thm-integers-bezout (b), with the set of positive combinations in place of M. This is the twin of @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm, now on the constructed 
Z. [B3: Two factorizations and a gcd] Find the prime factorizations of 1001 and of 2^{10} - 1, proving that each entry is prime. Then show that \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 in two ways. First, use the factorizations to write 1001 = 11 \cdot 91 and 1023 = 11 \cdot 93: show \gcd(91, 93) = 1, and deduce \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 from a Bézout identity for 91 and 93 (@cor-coprime-iff-combination). Second, use the Euclidean algorithm. Hint: the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime shortens each primality check. Do not use the school rule “the gcd is the product of the shared primes”: this chapter does not prove it. Factorizations. 1001 = 7 \cdot 143 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13, and 2^{10} - 1 = 1024 - 1 = 1023 = 3 \cdot 341 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 31. So the prime factorizations are (7, 11, 13) and (3, 11, 31), both non-decreasing, once the entries are known to be prime. The primes 3 and 7 are covered by the small-primes remark above. For 11, 13 and 31 we use the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime: it suffices that no d \ge 2 with d \cdot d \le p divides p. - p = 11 and p = 13: d \in \{2, 3\}, since d \ge 4 gives d \cdot d \ge 16. The divisions 11 = 5 \cdot 2 + 1 = 3 \cdot 3 + 2 and 13 = 6 \cdot 2 + 1 = 4 \cdot 3 + 1 leave non-zero remainders. - p = 31: d \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}, since d \ge 6 gives d \cdot d \ge 36. The divisions 31 = 15 \cdot 2 + 1 = 10 \cdot 3 + 1 = 7 \cdot 4 + 3 = 6 \cdot 5 + 1 leave non-zero remainders. A non-zero remainder means d 
mid p, by the uniqueness in @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a). By @thm-fundamental-arithmetic these are the only prime factorizations. The gcd from the factorizations. We have 1001 = 11 \cdot 91 and 1023 = 11 \cdot 93. First, \gcd(91, 93) = 1: a common divisor of 91 and 93 divides 93 - 91 = 2, so a positive one is 1 or 2 (discreteness), and 2 
mid 91 = 45 \cdot 2 + 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination, 91x + 93y = 1 for some x, y \in 
Z; indeed 91 \cdot 46 - 93 \cdot 45 = 4186 - 4185 = 1. Multiplying by 11, 1001 \cdot 46 - 1023 \cdot 45 = 11 . So every common divisor of 1001 and 1023 divides 11, and a positive one is at most 11. Since 11 is itself a common divisor, \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11. The gcd by the algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers): 1023 = 1 \cdot 1001 + 22, 1001 = 45 \cdot 22 + 11, 22 = 2 \cdot 11 + 0. The last non-zero remainder is 11. @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c) (divides every combination); @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) (positive divisor is smaller); @def-integer-gcd. C. Going deeper [C1: Chapter check: unique factorization] Prove that two prime factorizations of the same positive integer are equal: the uniqueness half of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic. You may cite @thm-euclid-lemma-integers and @cor-prime-divides-product. The proof of uniqueness in @thm-fundamental-arithmetic is a complete answer. Its steps, in order: set up P(k) for non-decreasing lists of primes of length k and arbitrary length l, with equal products; base case k = 0, where a non-empty list of primes cannot have product 1; in the step, l \ge 1, then p_{k+1} = q_j \le q_l and q_l = p_i \le p_{k+1} by @cor-prime-divides-product (c) (proved from Euclid’s lemma by induction on the length of the product) and the order of the lists; so p_{k+1} = q_l; cancel this non-zero factor (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)); apply P(k) to the shortened lists. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: sets up an induction on the length of one list (or a least counterexample), with the statement quantified over all lengths of the other list, and proves the base case. - 3: shows that the largest (or any chosen) prime of one list divides the other product, and identifies it with an entry of the other list by Euclid’s lemma for products of several factors (cited as @cor-prime-divides-product (c), or proved by induction from Euclid’s lemma). - 2: uses the symmetric step and the non-decreasing order to get equality of the two chosen extreme entries (both largest, or both smallest). - 1: justifies the cancellation by the absence of zero divisors. - 2: applies the induction hypothesis (or minimality) to the shortened lists and concludes equality of length and entries. Slips that lose the step: using the uniqueness of the factorization of a smaller number without an induction or a least counterexample set up; applying Euclid’s lemma for two factors to a product of many with no induction. Canceling a prime without noting that it is non-zero costs 1 point and does not lose the step. A least-counterexample proof on n (the least positive integer with two different factorizations) maps to the same points: its set-up and the case n = 1 take the first 2, and “the cofactor m in n = m p_k has only one factorization” takes the last 2. A proof that compares the smallest entries p_1 = q_1 earns the same points, provided it proves (for example by induction on the length) that a product equals its first entry times the product of the re-indexed list (p_2, \dots, p_{k+1}), and states the re-indexing of the shortened lists (p_2, \dots, p_{k+1}) and (q_2, \dots, q_l) before applying the induction hypothesis; asserting that identity without proof costs the 1 cancellation point. [C2: Find the error] Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. Let m, n, c \in 
Z. If m \mid c, n \mid c and \gcd(m, n) = 1, then mn \mid c. Argument. (1) Write c = mk and c = nl with k, l \in 
Z. (2) Then c^2 = c \cdot c = (mk)(nl) = mn \cdot kl. (3) So mn \mid c^2. (4) Hence mn \mid c. Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, and give a counterexample to the step. The claim is true: it is @prp-coprime-divisors-product. The argument does not prove it. Lines (1)–(3) are correct. The failing line is (4). It rests on a general “fact”: x \mid c^2 implies x \mid c. That has not been proved, and it is false, so the line cites nothing: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A counterexample to the step: x = 4, c = 2, with 4 \mid 4 = c^2 and 4 
mid 2 (a positive divisor of 2 is at most 2, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). There is no counterexample to the conclusion, which is true. A sign that something is wrong: the argument never uses \gcd(m, n) = 1, and without that hypothesis the claim is false (4 \mid 12, 6 \mid 12, 24 
mid 12). The repair is the proof of @prp-coprime-divisors-product, which spends the coprimality in Euclid’s lemma. [C3: There is no last prime] Prove that no finite list contains every prime: for every list of primes (p_1, \dots, p_k), with k \in 
N, there is a prime that is not an entry of the list. [Hint 1] Consider N \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i + 1, and ask which primes can divide it. [Hint 2] First prove, by induction on k, that every entry of a list of primes divides its product, and that the product is at least 1. A lemma on products. For a list of primes (p_1, \dots, p_k), write P_j \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i for j \le k. We prove, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) on j, the statement “if j \le k, then P_j \ge 1 and p_i \mid P_j for every i \le j”. Base j = 0: P_0 = 1 (the recursion of @def-prime-factorization), and there are no entries to check. Step: let j + 1 \le k; then j \le k, so the statement holds for j, and P_{j+1} = P_j p_{j+1} by the recursion. Each p_i with i \le j divides P_j, which divides P_{j+1}, so p_i \mid P_{j+1} (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b)); and p_{j+1} \mid P_{j+1} by @fd2:def-divides. Since P_j \ge 1 > 0 and p_{j+1} \ge 2 > 0, P_{j+1} > 0 \cdot p_{j+1} = 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so P_{j+1} \ge 1 by discreteness (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)). The new prime. Let N \coloneqq P_k + 1. Then N \ge 2, so its least divisor q \ge 2 is prime (@lem-least-divisor-prime), and q \mid N. If q = p_i for some i, then q \mid P_k by the lemma, so q divides N - P_k = 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), and q = \pm 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), against q \ge 2. So q is a prime that is not an entry of the list. For the empty list, N = 2 and q = 2. For (2, 3, 5, 7), N = 211, which happens to be prime; for (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), N = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509 is not, and the new prime is 59. The proof promises a new prime factor of N, not that N itself is prime. This is the direct proof asked for in part (c) of @fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1, now on the constructed 
Z and including the empty list. Its two school facts are replaced by @lem-least-divisor-prime and @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c). What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: defines N as the product plus 1 and shows N \ge 2, with a reason that the product is positive. - 2: shows that each p_i divides the product, by an induction or a cited result. - 2: produces a prime factor q of N, citing @lem-least-divisor-prime or an equivalent. - 3: shows q is not any p_i, since it would divide 1. - 1: concludes with the quantifiers in order: for every list there is a prime outside it. Slips that lose the step: claiming that N is prime; assuming “the set of primes is finite” and taking its product without a list (no list, no product).

title: 2.3 Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n
content:
Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 turned the school integers into a clock, 
Z/n, and checked by hand that its sum and product are well defined (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic). Number Systems, Chapters 2 and 3 made the same kind of check twice more, for 
Z and for 
Q, each time through @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes and a computation special to the formula. This section makes the check once, for every commutative ring and every subset of the right kind, called an ideal. The integers modulo n, now a ring, are the first example. Number Systems, Chapter 5 builds 
R in the same shape, from classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals that differ by a null sequence, and checks its operations there directly; Chapter 7 runs division with remainder, gcd and unique factorization again for polynomials over a field. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), with a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). What a quotient needs Let I \subseteq R, and call a and b related when they differ by an element of I: a \sim_I b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a - b \in I . For R = 
Z and I the multiples of n, this is congruence modulo n. We want two things: \sim_I should be an equivalence relation, and the sum and product of classes should be computable on representatives. Each wish makes a demand on I. - Reflexivity, a - a \in I, needs 0 \in I. - Symmetry: b - a = -(a - b), so it needs I to be closed under negatives. - Transitivity: a - c = (a - b) + (b - c), so it needs I to be closed under sums. - The sum on classes. Changing a to a' changes a + b to a' + b, and the difference is a - a' again: no new demand. - The product on classes. Changing a to a' changes ab to a'b, and the difference is (a - a')b: an element of I multiplied by an arbitrary element of R. So I must swallow such products. The last demand contains the second: -x = (-1)x. Three clauses remain, and they get a name. An ideal is a set of allowed errors: it contains 0, it is closed under adding errors, and an error multiplied by anything is still an error. [Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring. A subset I \subseteq R is an ideal of R if 1. 0 \in I; 2. for all a, b \in I, a + b \in I; 3. for all a \in I and all r \in R, ra \in I. In words: (I1) and (I2) say that I contains 0 and is closed under addition; (I3), absorption, says that multiplying an element of I by any element of the ring, inside I or not, lands in I. The ring element r in (I3) ranges over all of R, and that is what separates (I3) from mere closure under multiplication, where r would have to lie in I. Two consequences are used constantly. First, an ideal is closed under negatives and differences: for a \in I, -a = (-1)a \in I by (I3), since (-1)a = -(1 \cdot a) = -a by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F7) with (F6); then a - b = a + (-b) \in I for a, b \in I, by (I2). Second, if 1 \in I, then I = R, since every r = r \cdot 1 \in I by (I3). Examples. - The degenerate cases: \{0\} and R itself are ideals of R. For \{0\}: 0 + 0 = 0 and r \cdot 0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). For R, every clause asks for an element of R. They are the two extremes: “no error allowed” and “everything allowed”. - For n \in 
Z, the multiples n
Z = \{ kn : k \in 
Z \} form an ideal of 
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations): 0 = 0 \cdot n; kn + ln = (k + l)n; r(kn) = (rk)n. In particular the even integers 2
Z form an ideal. - For a, b \in 
Z, the combinations a
Z + b
Z form an ideal of 
Z, by the closure properties in @def-integer-linear-combinations; @thm-integer-ideals-principal below records this. Non-examples by minimal change. 
N \subseteq 
Z satisfies (I1) and (I2), but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = -1: (-1) \cdot 1 = -1 
otin 
N, since -1 < 0 (1 > 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in 
Z by @fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring, then (a)) while 
N = \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). And 
Z \subseteq 
Q satisfies (I1), (I2) and is even closed under negatives and products, but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = 1/2: (1/2) \cdot 1 = 1/2 
otin 
Z. (If 1/2 = m \in 
Z, then 2m = 1, but 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd and so not of the form 2m, by @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a).) In both cases the ring element r comes from outside the subset, which is exactly what (I3) allows. Why these clauses. Each clause was forced by one of the five wishes above, and dropping one loses its wish: without (I1) or (I2), \sim_I is not reflexive or not transitive; without (I3), the product on classes can fail, as the warning after the next theorem shows for 
Z \subseteq 
Q. The quotient ring The payoff is a single theorem that builds a ring of classes from any ideal. We write [a], or [a]_I when the ideal must be named, for the class of a under \sim_I, and R/I for the quotient set R/{\sim_I} (@fd2:def-quotient-set). [Quotient Ring by an Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring and I an ideal of R. 1. Setting a \sim_I b \iff a - b \in I defines an equivalence relation \sim_I on R, and the class of a is [a] = a + I \coloneqq \{ a + x : x \in I \}. 2. The rules [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b], [a] \cdot [b] \coloneqq [ab] and -[a] \coloneqq [-a] are well defined on R/I \coloneqq R/{\sim_I}. 3. R/I, with these operations, is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The quotient map q \colon R 	o R/I, q(a) \coloneqq [a], satisfies q(a + b) = q(a) + q(b), q(ab) = q(a) q(b) and q(1) = [1]. 4. [a] = [0] if and only if a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] if and only if I = R. In words: (a) and (b) say that classes modulo an ideal can be added, multiplied and negated through any representatives; (c) says that the result obeys every ring law, and that passing to classes respects the operations; (d) says that the elements of I are exactly those that become 0, and that the quotient collapses to the zero ring exactly when I is everything. A change of representative is an element of I. The equivalence-relation clauses ask that such changes can be reversed and chained, which is closure under negatives and sums. The operations ask that a change in one argument produce a change in the output: for the sum the change is the same element of I, and for the product it is that element multiplied by the other argument, which (I3) keeps in I. The ring laws are then laws of R read on classes. Before reading on: where is “ra \in I for every r \in R” used, and why does closure under + not suffice for the product? (a) Let a, b, c \in R. (Eq1): a - a = 0 \in I, by (F4) and (I1). (Eq2): if a - b \in I, then b - a = -(a - b) \in I, since I is closed under negatives; here (a - b) + (b - a) = 0 by (F1)–(F4), so b - a = -(a - b) by the uniqueness of negatives (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). (Eq3): if a - b \in I and b - c \in I, then a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) \in I, by (F2)–(F4) and (I2). So \sim_I is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). For the class: if x \sim_I a, then x - a \in I and x = a + (x - a) \in a + I; conversely, for y \in I, (a + y) - a = y \in I, so a + y \sim_I a. Hence [a] = a + I. (b) We check the hypotheses of @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes (b), with X = R and the relation \sim_I, for the maps (a, b) \mapsto a + b and (a, b) \mapsto ab. Let a \sim_I a', so a - a' \in I, and let b \in R. Then  egin{aligned} (a + b) - (a' + b) &= a - a' \in I , \ ab - a'b &= (a - a')b = b(a - a') \in I , \end{aligned} by (F1)–(F4) in the first line, and by (F9), (F6) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) in the second, where the membership is (I3) with r = b: the ideal absorbs b. This is the first hypothesis. Since a + b = b + a and ab = ba ((F1), (F6)), the second hypothesis is the first with the two arguments exchanged. For the negative we check the hypothesis of @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes (a) for a \mapsto -a: (-a) - (-a') = -(a - a') \in I, by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a) and closure under negatives. Hence the three rules define functions. (c) Every element of R/I is a class [a] (@fd2:def-quotient-set). Each axiom of @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field other than (F8) is an equation, and by (b) both of its sides, read on classes, are the classes of the two sides of the same equation in R. For example, for (F9), [a] igl([b] + [c] igr) = [a][b + c] = [a(b + c)] = [ab + ac] = [ab] + [ac] = [a][b] + [a][c] , using (F9) in R in the middle; for (F3), [a] + [0] = [a + 0] = [a]; for (F4), [a] + (-[a]) = [a] + [-a] = [a + (-a)] = [0]; for (F7), [a][1] = [a \cdot 1] = [a]. The laws (F1), (F2), (F5) and (F6) go the same way. So R/I is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The equations for q are the definitions in (b) read from right to left, and q(1) = [1] by definition of q. (d) [a] = [0] holds if and only if a \sim_I 0 (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)), that is, a - 0 \in I; and a - 0 = a + 0 = a, since -0 = 0 (0 + 0 = 0 and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). So [a] = [0] \iff a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] \iff 1 \in I. If 1 \in I, then I = R, since r = r \cdot 1 \in I for every r \in R by (I3); and if I = R, then 1 \in I. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Absorption with an arbitrary r \in R, the full force of (I3), is used exactly once in the proof of (a) and (b): in the product, at ab - a'b = (a - a')b, where the change of representative a - a' \in I is multiplied by an arbitrary b \in R. Elsewhere (I3) enters only with r = -1, through closure under negatives (-x = (-1)x), and otherwise the proof uses (I1) and (I2). Closure under + does not suffice for the product because b need not lie in I: the product changes by a multiple of the error, not by a sum of errors. We call this move compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. It is the move of Number Systems, Chapter 2’s “one argument at a time”, now with the change of representative recorded as one element of I. Closure under + and - is not enough for the product. 
Z \subseteq 
Q contains 0 and is closed under sums and negatives, and these are all that the proof of (a) and of the sum and negative in (b) used. So “x - y \in 
Z” relates rationals by an equivalence relation, and [x] + [y] \coloneqq [x + y] is well defined on its classes. But [x][y] \coloneqq [xy] is not: [1/2] = [3/2], since 3/2 - 1/2 = 1 \in 
Z, while 	frac12 \cdot 	frac12 = 	frac14 , \qquad 	frac32 \cdot 	frac12 = 	frac34 , \qquad 	frac34 - 	frac14 = 	frac12 
otin 
Z . One class, two products in different classes. The missing clause is (I3): 
Z is not an ideal of 
Q. The ideals of the integers In 
Z every ideal is as simple as possible: the multiples of one number. The proof is the move that gave the gcd in Section 2.1. [Ideals of the Integers] 1. For all a, b \in 
Z, a
Z + b
Z is an ideal of 
Z. In particular n
Z is an ideal of 
Z for every n \in 
Z. 2. Every ideal I of 
Z equals n
Z for exactly one n \in 
N: n = 0 if I = \{0\}, and otherwise n is the least positive element of I. For (b), take the least positive element n of I. Its multiples lie in I by absorption. Conversely, divide any a \in I by n: the remainder a - qn lies in I and is smaller than n, so it is not positive, and it is 0. This is least positive element, then divide once more. (a) 0 = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 0 \in a
Z + b
Z (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), and @def-integer-linear-combinations shows that a
Z + b
Z is closed under sums and under multiplication by any integer. These are (I1)–(I3). Since n
Z = n
Z + 0
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations), n
Z is an ideal. (b) Existence. If I = \{0\}, then I = 0
Z, since k \cdot 0 = 0 for every k (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). Otherwise I has an element a 
e 0, and -a \in I as well; one of a, -a is positive (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h)). So I \cap 
Z_{>0} is non-empty, with lower bound 0, and has a least element n (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element). By (I3), kn \in I for every k \in 
Z, so n
Z \subseteq I. Conversely, let a \in I. By @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a), a = qn + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < n. Then r = a + (-q)n \in I, by (I3) and (I2). If r > 0, then r is a positive element of I smaller than n, against the choice of n. So r = 0, and a = qn \in n
Z. Hence I = n
Z. Uniqueness. Let n
Z = m
Z with n, m \in

title: 2.4 Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem

Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem Section 2.3 made 
Z/n
Z a commutative ring, and @exm-integers-mod-six put two of these rings side by side. In 
Z/5
Z every non-zero class has a partner whose product with it is [1], so we may divide by it. In 
Z/6
Z the class [2] has no such partner: the products [2][x] are only [0], [2], [4]. Which classes can be divided by, and for which moduli can all non-zero classes? This section answers both questions with the gcd of Section 2.1, and finds a field with p elements for every prime p. It then solves two congruences at once, the Chinese remainder theorem, by the move of Section 2.2, multiply the Bézout identity: write 1 as a combination and multiply. Throughout, n \in 
Z_{>0} and classes are taken in 
Z/n
Z unless another modulus is named. Two classes are equal exactly when their representatives are congruent: [u] = [v] \iff u - v \in n
Z \iff n \mid u - v . The first equivalence is @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) for the relation of @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (a); the second is the definition of n
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations) read with @fd2:def-divides. We call it the class test. Products of classes are computed on representatives, [u][v] = [uv] (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (b)). Units of a commutative ring In 
Z/6
Z the equation [2][x] = [1] has no solution, while [5][x] = [1] has the solution [x] = [5]. The elements that can be divided by are the ones that solve “u times something is 1”, and they deserve a name in every commutative ring at once. A unit is an element that has a multiplicative inverse in the ring itself. [Unit of a Commutative Ring] Let R be a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field). An element u \in R is a unit of R if there exists v \in R with uv = 1. The set of units of R is written R^{	imes}. For a unit u, the element v is unique; it is written u^{-1} and called the inverse of u. In words: u is a unit when the equation ux = 1 can be solved inside R. The definition asks for one solution; it does not ask u to be non-zero. Well-definedness of u^{-1}. Let uv = 1 and uv' = 1. Then, by (F7), (F5) and (F6), v = v \cdot 1 = v(uv') = (vu)v' = (uv)v' = 1 \cdot v' = v' . So the inverse is unique, and the notation u^{-1} names one element. Closure. The element 1 is a unit, since 1 \cdot 1 = 1. If u is a unit, so is u^{-1}, with (u^{-1})^{-1} = u, because u^{-1} u = u u^{-1} = 1 by (F6). If u and w are units, then (uw)(u^{-1} w^{-1}) = (u u^{-1})(w w^{-1}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 , reordering the four factors by (F5) and (F6); so uw is a unit and (uw)^{-1} = u^{-1} w^{-1}, by uniqueness. A unit is not a zero divisor. If u is a unit and ux = 0, then x = (u^{-1} u) x = u^{-1}(ux) = u^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 , by u^{-1} u = 1 (above) and 1 \cdot x = x \cdot 1 = x ((F6), (F7)) in the first equality, (F5) in the second, and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) in the third. So a unit times a non-zero element is never 0. Examples. - The integers. 
Z^{	imes} = \{ 1, -1 \}. Indeed 1 \cdot 1 = 1 and (-1)(-1) = 1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). Conversely, uv = 1 says u \mid 1, so u = 1 or u = -1 by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g). - The rationals. 
Q^{	imes} = 
Q \setminus \{0\}: every non-zero rational has an inverse by (F8) (@fd3:thm-rationals-field), and 0 is not a unit, since 0 \cdot v = 0 
e 1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). - The integers modulo six. By the multiplication table of @exm-integers-mod-six, the units of 
Z/6
Z are [1] and [5], and [5]^{-1} = [5]. - The zero ring \{0\} of Number Systems, Section 2.3, where 1 = 0. Here 0 \cdot 0 = 0 = 1, so 0 is a unit and R^{	imes} = R. This degenerate case is why “every non-zero element is a unit” is not by itself the definition of a field. A non-example by minimal change. Change 5 to 2 in the third example. The class [2] \in 
Z/6
Z is non-zero, like [5], but [2][3] = [6] = [0]: it is a zero divisor, so by the paragraph above it is not a unit. Concretely, the clause “there exists v with uv = 1” fails: the products [2][x] for x = 0, \dots, 5 are [0], [2], [4], [0], [2], [4], and [1] is not among them. Why this definition. With units, the field axiom (F8) reads: every non-zero element is a unit. So a field (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) is exactly a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 in which R^{	imes} = R \setminus \{0\}; when 1 
e 0, the element 0 is never a unit, since 0 \cdot v = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). The definition asks for an inverse in R, not in some bigger ring: 2 \in 
Z has the inverse 1/2 in 
Q, and it is still not a unit of 
Z. “Non-zero and not a zero divisor” does not make an element a unit. In 
Z there are no zero divisors at all (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), yet 2 is not a unit, since 2 
mid 1. The paragraph above proves only one direction: a unit is never a zero divisor. So “not a unit” must be checked against the definition, or, in 
Z/n
Z, by the next theorem. The units of a commutative ring are closed under products and inverses and contain 1: they form what Chapter 5 calls a group. Here we only need to find them in 
Z/n
Z. Which classes are units In 
Z/6
Z the units [1] and [5] are the classes of the integers coprime to 6, and the non-units [0], [2], [3], [4] share a factor with 6. The equation [a][x] = [1] says n \mid ax - 1, that is, ax + ny = 1 for some integer y: a Bézout identity. So the question is answered by Section 2.1. [Units Modulo n] Let n \in 
Z_{>0} and a \in 
Z. Then [a] is a unit of 
Z/n
Z if and only if \gcd(a, n) = 1. In that case, for any x, y \in 
Z with ax + ny = 1, [a]^{-1} = [x]. Both directions translate between one equation in 
Z/n
Z and one equation in 
Z. A solution of [a][x] = [1] is an integer combination ax + ny = 1, and @cor-coprime-iff-combination says that such a combination exists exactly when \gcd(a, n) = 1. The class test does the translation. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \gcd(a, n) = 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination there are x, y \in 
Z with ax + ny = 1. Let x, y be any such pair. Then ax - 1 = -ny = (-y)n, so n \mid ax - 1, and by the class test [ax] = [1]. Hence [a][x] = [ax] = [1], where the first equality is the definition of the product on classes (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (b)). So [a] is a unit, and [x] is its inverse, which is unique (@def-ring-unit); thus [a]^{-1} = [x] for every such pair. (\Rightarrow) Suppose [a] is a unit. Every element of 
Z/n
Z is the class of an integer (@fd2:def-quotient-set), so [a][x] = [1] for some x \in 
Z. Then [ax] = [1], so n \mid ax - 1 by the class test: ax - 1 = yn for some y \in 
Z. Hence ax + n(-y) = 1, and \gcd(a, n) = 1 by @cor-coprime-iff-combination. This proves the theorem. The theorem turns “is [a] invertible?” into a gcd, and the Euclidean algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers) computes the gcd. Back-substitution, as in @exm-euclidean-algorithm-run, then produces the x with ax + ny = 1, and with it the inverse. Whether \gcd(a, n) = 1 depends only on the class [a], since by the theorem it is equivalent to a statement about [a]; so any representative may be used. [Inverting a class modulo sixty] Decide whether [17] and [12] are units of

N 	imes 
N. The tool is unique factorization, @thm-fundamental-arithmetic. The powers are those of 
N = \omega (@fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity), carried into 
Z, which preserves products (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers); b^0 = 1 and b^{j+1} = b^j \cdot b. A factorization. For m, n \in 
N, let L_{m,n} be the list of length m + n whose first m entries are 2 and whose last n entries are 3. Its entries are prime, by the small-primes remark of Section 2.2, and it is non-decreasing, since 2 \le 3. Its product is 2^m 3^n. Indeed, with P_j the product of the first j entries, the recursion of @def-prime-factorization and induction on j \le m give P_j = 2^j (P_0 = 1 = 2^0; P_{j+1} = P_j \cdot 2 = 2^{j+1}), and then induction on i \le n gives P_{m+i} = 2^m 3^i. So L_{m,n} is a prime factorization of 2^m 3^n, which is positive, being a product of positive integers (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)). Uniqueness. If 2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'}, then L_{m,n} and L_{m',n'} are prime factorizations of the same positive integer, so they are equal (@thm-fundamental-arithmetic): m + n = m' + n', with equal entries. Suppose m < m'. Then the entry of index m' is 2 in L_{m',n'}, and in L_{m,n} it is 3, since m < m' \le m + n: a contradiction. Exchanging the two lists rules out m' < m. So m = m', and then n = n' by canceling m in m + n = m' + n'. This is line (vii) of @fd2:exr-countable-sets-b2, which was not available when that exercise was set; @fd2:thm-product-countable proves the same injectivity by parity instead. Q satisfies x^2 = p. This is the school argument of @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, now with every step citable. The case 2. Suppose x \in 
Q and x^2 = 2. By @prp-rationals-lowest-terms, x = a/b with a \in 
Z, b \in 
Z_{>0} and \gcd(a, b) = 1. By @fd3:def-rational-operations, x^2 = a^2/b^2, and 2 = 2/1, so a^2 = 2b^2 (@fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals (b)). Then a^2 is even, so a is even by @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (b): a = 2c with c \in 
Z. Then 4c^2 = 2b^2, and canceling the non-zero factor 2 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f), applied to 2(b^2 - 2c^2) = 0) gives b^2 = 2c^2. So b is even as well. Now 2 divides a and b, hence divides \gcd(a, b) = 1 (@thm-integers-bezout (c), (d)), so 2 \in \{1, -1\} (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)): a contradiction. A prime p. The same argument works with “p \mid” in place of “even”: from a^2 = p b^2, p \mid a \cdot a, so p \mid a by @cor-prime-divides-product (b); a = pc gives p^2 c^2 = p b^2, so b^2 = p c^2 (cancel p 
e 0), and p \mid b in the same way. Then p \mid \gcd(a, b) = 1, against p \ge 2. Comparison. The proof in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 3 (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two) needed neither parity nor gcd: it descended to a smaller denominator using order alone. The argument here is shorter, but it stands on lowest terms, and lowest terms stands on Bézout (@prp-rationals-lowest-terms uses @cor-coprime-iff-combination). [R4] Find all x \in 
Z with 6x \equiv 4 \pmod{10}. Answer: the class 4 + 5
Z. The tool is to divide the congruence by \gcd(6, 10) = 2, and then invert a unit (@thm-units-mod-n). Since 6x - 4 = 2(3x - 2) and 10 = 2 \cdot 5, 10 \mid 6x - 4 \iff 5 \mid 3x - 2 : if 2(3x - 2) = 10k = 2(5k), cancel 2 
e 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)); conversely, multiply 3x - 2 = 5k by 2. So the condition is [3][x] = [2] in 
Z/5
Z. There [3]^{-1} = [2], since 3 \cdot 2 = 6 = 5 + 1. Multiplying by [2], [x] = [2][2] = [4]; and conversely [3][4] = [12] = [2]. So the solutions are exactly the x \equiv 4 \pmod{5}. Check: 6 \cdot 4 - 4 = 20 and 6 \cdot 9 - 4 = 50 are multiples of 10. Why the look-alikes fail. “Multiply by [6]^{-1} in 
Z/10
Z” fails: \gcd(6, 10) = 2, so [6] is not a unit there (@thm-units-mod-n). Canceling the 2 from every term but keeping the modulus gives 3x \equiv 2 \pmod{10}, and that is wrong: it keeps 4 and loses 9 (6 \cdot 9 - 4 = 50, while 3 \cdot 9 - 2 = 25). The modulus must be divided too. The Chinese remainder theorem is not a look-alike that fails: splitting 10 = 2 \cdot 5, @thm-chinese-remainder-two (b) turns the condition [6]_{10}[x]_{10} = [4]_{10} into [0]_2 [x]_2 = [0]_2, which always holds, and [x]_5 = [4]_5, since [6]_5 = [1]_5; so it is a second route to the same answer. Note also that the answer is a class modulo 5, not modulo 10: it is the two classes [4]_{10} and [9]_{10}.

title: Complex Numbers
content:
Complex Numbers No real number squares to -1: in an ordered field a non-zero square is positive (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), so x^2 + 1 = 0 has no solution in 
R. The usual remedy, “invent a symbol i with i^2 = -1”, leaves open why such a symbol is safe when “a number z with 0 \cdot z = 1” is not. This chapter does not invent anything. It takes pairs of real numbers, objects the reader already trusts, adds them coordinate by coordinate, and multiplies them by the one formula that i^2 = -1 would force. Then it checks, law by law, that nothing breaks: the complex numbers 
C form a field in the sense of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2, and they contain 
R as the pairs (a, 0). Every later volume that computes with complex numbers, from inner products in linear algebra to roots of unity in algebra, starts from this field. Two habits of 
R do not survive the passage. No order on 
C is compatible with its arithmetic, and no choice of “the” square root of each complex number keeps the rule \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{xy}. One new habit takes the place of order: measure a complex number by its modulus, a non-negative real, and compute with \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u}, which is algebra. The first four sections need nothing but the real numbers, and they reach far: division, the triangle inequality, and square roots and the quadratic formula without a single angle. The picture of multiplication as a turn and a stretch does need angles, and angles need cosine and sine, which belong to analysis. The chapter borrows exactly five facts about them, says so in one place, and derives everything else from those five: the familiar special values, De Moivre’s formula, the n different n-th roots of every non-zero complex number, and the roots of unity. It ends with a look ahead at the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, which Chapter 7 proves without the borrowed facts. What you need. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R above all, and in it chiefly Chapters 2, 4 and 6. From its Chapter 5: the real numbers as a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:def-complete-ordered-field), the standing setting of the whole chapter. From its Chapter 6: square roots of non-negative reals, existing and unique (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), which define the modulus in Section 3.2 and build complex square roots in Section 3.4; the uniqueness of the complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness), which lets Section 3.5 carry the borrowed facts over to our 
R; the automorphism theorem (@fd3:thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity), used in the solution of review exercise R1 and compared there with the two such maps of 
C. From its Chapters 2 and 3: the axioms of a field and of an ordered field and their rules (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:def-ordered-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules), used on nearly every page; the finite ring that cannot be ordered (@fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), compared with in Section 3.4; and the gap at \sqrt 2 in 
Q (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two), which shows in Section 3.2 why the modulus needs completeness. From its Chapter 4: the rules for fractions in a field (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules), the absolute value of an ordered field (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), which the modulus extends and whose triangle inequality Section 3.3 reproves by a new route, and the natural numbers and powers in an ordered field (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field); a remark of Section 3.4 recalls its exercise on fields with a square root of -1 (@fd3:exr-rules-and-absolute-value-c1). From its Section 2.5: division with remainder, divisibility and parity in 
Z (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd), in Exercise B1 of Section 3.1 and in Sections 3.5 and 3.6. From its Chapter 1: the citing rule by which induction and recursion apply to 
N (@fd3:cor-omega-identification). From Sets and Functions: ordered pairs and Cartesian products, Chapter 1 (@fd2:def-ordered-pair, @fd2:def-cartesian-product); injective maps, Chapter 2 (@fd2:def-injective); divisibility, Section 1.1 (@fd2:def-divides); finite sums, Section 3.3 (@fd2:def-sum-product), in Section 3.3; finite sets, Section 4.1 (@fd2:def-finite), for counting n-th roots; and congruence modulo n and the classes 
Z/n, Section 5.2 (@fd2:def-congruence, @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic, @fd2:prp-integers-mod-n), in Exercise C2 of Section 3.4. From Logic and Proof: induction, Chapter 4 (@fd1:ax-induction); the contrapositive, Chapter 2 (@fd1:prp-contrapositive), in Exercise B3 of Section 3.1; and the catalogue of what a proof may not do, Chapter 8 (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), in the proof-ordering and find-the-error exercises of Sections 3.4 and 3.6. From Chapter 1 of this volume: the laws of powers and the difference of powers in a commutative ring, Section 1.1 (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring, @lem-difference-of-powers), which Section 3.1 recalls for 
C and Sections 3.2, 3.5 and 3.6 use; real n-th roots, Section 1.5 (@lem-reals-nth-root), in Section 3.6; and integer powers in a field, Section 1.5 (@def-integer-power), in Exercise C1 of Section 3.5. From Chapter 2 of this volume: the ring 
Z/n
Z, Section 2.3 (@def-integers-mod-n-ring, @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal, @thm-integers-mod-n-ring), in review exercise R2. Section 3.4 also proves the complex square roots that Logic and Proof, Section 7.1 took as a school fact. Nothing from linear algebra is used, and nothing from analysis before the box of borrowed facts in Section 3.5. Which real numbers. The chapter builds 
C on the real numbers of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5, whose elements are classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals (@fd3:def-reals-cauchy-classes). No proof looks inside a real number: every step uses only that 
R is a complete ordered field. By the uniqueness theorem of that volume’s Chapter 6 (@fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness), any complete ordered field would give the same 
C, up to the one isomorphism between the two fields. What this chapter borrows. Everything in Sections 3.1–3.4, and in Section 3.5 up to its box of borrowed facts, is proved from the real numbers. From that box on, five facts (T1)–(T5) about \cos, \sin and \pi are used without proof: the circle identity, the addition formulas, where the cosine equals 1, that every point of the unit circle is reached, and the sign of the sine on the first half turn. Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 7 defines the two functions and the number and proves the five facts. No other fact about cosine and sine is used, and the results that rest on the five say so in their dependency ledgers. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Complex Numbers as Pairs of Reals. 
C defined as 
R 	imes 
R with the product that i^2 = -1 would force; the real numbers inside 
C as the pairs (a, 0), which makes a + bi honest notation and i^2 = -1 a computation; a product with one sign changed, which has zero divisors; the laws of arithmetic, which make 
C a commutative ring with 1 
e 0; and powers and the factorization of z^n - w^n, recalled from Chapter 1, where they are proved for every commutative ring. - Conjugate, Modulus, and Division. The conjugate and the modulus, a non-negative real square root and the place where the completeness of 
R enters; the modulus as an extension of the absolute value of 
R; the rules for conjugate and modulus, with \abs{zw} = \abs{z}\abs{w} proved by squaring; the inverse \conj{z}/\abs{z}^2 of a non-zero z; the theorem that 
C is a field in which 
R is closed under the field operations; and division by the conjugate of the denominator. - The Triangle Inequality. Why the trapping proof for ordered fields cannot run in 
C; comparing squares of non-negative reals; real and imaginary parts at most the modulus; the triangle inequality, by expanding \abs{z + w}^2 and recognizing the cross term as a real part; and three variants: the reverse inequality, the inequality for n terms, and a lower bound for the modulus of a sum. - Square Roots, Quadratic Equations, and the Missing Order. An explicit formula for a square root of a complex number, built from two real square roots, and the count of exactly two square roots of every non-zero number; the quadratic formula with complex coefficients; the proof that no order makes 
C an ordered field; and why no choice of square roots keeps the product rule \sqrt{z}\sqrt{w} = \sqrt{zw}. - The Unit Circle and Polar Form. The unit circle 
T, closed under products and inverses, and every non-zero number as a length times a direction in exactly one way, all without angles; the five borrowed facts about cosine and sine; e^{i	heta} as an abbreviation for \cos	heta + i\sin	heta, multiplication as “multiply moduli, add angles”, and polar form, unique up to a multiple of 2\pi in the argument; De Moivre’s formula; and the values of cosine and sine at \pi/6, \pi/4, \pi/3, \pi/2 and \pi, derived from the five facts. - Higher Roots, Roots of Unity, and a Look Ahead. The unique non-negative n-th root of a non-negative real, recalled from Chapter 1; exactly n solutions of z^n = c for every non-zero c, listed by polar form; the roots of unity, the set \mu_n, and the sums of their powers; a look ahead at the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra; the conjugate of a solution of an equation with real coefficients as a second solution; and review exercises on the maps of 
C to itself that respect sums, products and 1 and send 
R into 
R, on 
Z/n
Z and \mu_n, on the triangle inequality of an ordered field, and on the equation \conj{z} = z^2. Named moves - Compare real and imaginary parts. One equation between complex numbers is two equations between real numbers: for real a, b, c, d, a + bi = c + di if and only if a = c and b = d. It is named in Section 3.1, where it proves the laws of arithmetic; Section 3.4 uses it to turn w^2 = z into two real equations, and Section 3.5 to turn e^{i	heta} = 1 into \cos	heta = 1 and \sin	heta = 0. The warning of Section 3.1 marks the hypothesis it needs: the four numbers must be real. Exercise C1 of Section 3.1 proves the same uniqueness of parts in any field that contains 
R and a square root of -1. - Square the modulus. The modulus is a square root, and square roots do not expand; its square \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u} is a product, and products do. So square, expand with conjugates, bound or compare the real numbers that appear, and take the non-negative square root back, which is legitimate because non-negative reals compare as their squares do. Section 3.2 uses it first, for \abs{zw} = \abs{z}\abs{w}; Section 3.3 names it and runs it in full for the triangle inequality. Exercise B2 of Section 3.3 leaves the last step to you, and Exercise C2 of Section 3.3 the last half. - Multiply moduli, add angles. In polar form a product is the product of the moduli and the sum of the arguments, so an equation z^n = c splits into a real equation r^n = ho for the length and an angle condition n	heta \in \alpha + 2\pi
Z. It is named in Section 3.5, after the multiplication theorem, and gives De Moivre’s formula there; Section 3.6 uses it to solve z^n = c and to count the solutions. The warning of Section 3.6 shows what goes wrong when the angle condition is read as an equation n	heta = \alpha: all roots but one are lost.

title: 3.1 The Complex Numbers as Pairs of Reals
content:
The Complex Numbers as Pairs of Reals The equation x^2 + 1 = 0 has no real solution. In an ordered field every square is non-negative (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) for a non-zero element, and 0^2 = 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so x^2 + 1 \ge 0 + 1 = 1 > 0 for every real x (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (e)). For most of school mathematics this gap is harmless. Later volumes cannot live with it: the linear-algebra volumes meet real matrices, such as a rotation of the plane, whose most useful data are not real numbers. This section builds the complex numbers, the number system that closes the gap, and proves that they obey the familiar laws of arithmetic. Standing setting. Throughout the chapter, 
R is the complete ordered field built in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). In particular 
R is a field in the sense of @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, and every rule that book proved for ordered fields holds in it. No proof below looks inside a real number. Letters a, b, c, d, e, f, x, y stand for real numbers, and z, w, u, v for complex numbers, unless we say otherwise. Building the new numbers The quick way to introduce complex numbers is to say “invent a symbol i with i^2 = -1 and compute as usual”. That raises a fair worry. How do we know that such a symbol does not lead to a contradiction, the way “invent a number z with 0 \cdot z = 1” does? The answer is to build the new numbers out of objects we already trust: pairs of real numbers. Here is the recurring expression that suggests the definition. If we pretend i^2 = -1 and expand, we get (a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bd\, i^2 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i . So a “number a + bi” is really the pair (a, b), and the product should be the pair (ac - bd, ad + bc). We take this formula as the definition, so nothing is pretended. A complex number is a pair of real numbers, multiplied as if i^2 = -1. [Complex Numbers] The set of complex numbers is 
C \coloneqq 
R^2 = 
R 	imes 
R = \{ (a, b) : a, b \in 
R \} , the Cartesian product of @fd2:def-cartesian-product, with addition and multiplication defined for all (a, b), (c, d) \in 
C by  egin{aligned} (a, b) + (c, d) &\coloneqq (a + c, \; b + d) , \ (a, b)(c, d) &\coloneqq (ac - bd, \; ad + bc) . \end{aligned} We write i \coloneqq (0, 1). For z = (a, b) \in 
C, the real part of z is \operatorname{Re} z \coloneqq a and the imaginary part of z is \operatorname{Im} z \coloneqq b. In words: addition is coordinate by coordinate, as for points of the plane. Multiplication is the formula found by expanding. Both right-hand sides are pairs of real numbers, computed with the operations of 
R, so both operations are functions 
C 	imes 
C 	o 
C. The point i is the point one unit up the vertical axis. The real part and the imaginary part of z are its two coordinates, and both are real numbers. There is nothing to check for well-definedness: a pair determines its coordinates, by the characteristic property of ordered pairs (@fd2:def-ordered-pair), (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . In the language of the definition: two complex numbers z and w are equal if and only if \operatorname{Re} z = \operatorname{Re} w and \operatorname{Im} z = \operatorname{Im} w. So one equation between complex numbers is two equations between real numbers. This is the first named move of the chapter, compare real and imaginary parts, and the proofs of @prp-reals-embed-complex and @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws below rest on it. The equation that motivated everything is now a computation: i \cdot i = (0, 1)(0, 1) = (0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1, \; 0 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0) = (-1, 0) . To read the right-hand side as “-1”, we have to see the real numbers inside 
C. The real numbers inside the complex numbers The real number a should be the point (a, 0) on the horizontal axis. Before we write a for (a, 0), we check that nothing is lost: different real numbers stay different, and adding or multiplying two real numbers gives the same answer in 
C as in 
R. The Real Numbers inside the Complex Numbers Let \iota \colon 
R 	o 
C be the map \iota(a) \coloneqq (a, 0). Then \iota is injective (@fd2:def-injective), and for all a, c \in 
R, \iota(a + c) = \iota(a) + \iota(c) , \qquad \iota(ac) = \iota(a)\, \iota(c) , \qquad \iota(1) = (1, 0) . Moreover (a, b) = \iota(a) + \iota(b)\, i for all a, b \in 
R, and i \cdot i = \iota(-1). Each claim is one application of the definitions: write both sides as pairs and compare coordinates. The facts about 
R needed are that 0 is neutral for addition (so subtracting 0 changes nothing), that 1 is neutral for multiplication, and that a product with 0 is 0, which kills the extra terms of the multiplication formula. Let a, c \in 
R. If \iota(a) = \iota(c), then (a, 0) = (c, 0), so a = c by @fd2:def-ordered-pair; hence \iota is injective. By @def-complex-numbers, \iota(a) + \iota(c) = (a + c, \; 0 + 0) = (a + c, \; 0) = \iota(a + c) , and, since a \cdot 0 = 0 \cdot c = 0 \cdot 0 = 0 in 
R (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), \iota(a)\, \iota(c) = (ac - 0 \cdot 0, \; a \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot c) = (ac, \; 0) = \iota(ac) . The equation \iota(1) = (1, 0) is the definition of \iota. Next, for a, b \in 
R, \iota(b)\, i = (b, 0)(0, 1) = (b \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1, \; b \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0) = (0, b) , so \iota(a) + \iota(b)\, i = (a, 0) + (0, b) = (a, b). Finally i \cdot i = (-1, 0) = \iota(-1) by the computation before the proposition. Identification. From now on we write a for \iota(a) and regard 
R as a subset of 
C. In particular 0 = (0, 0) and 1 = (1, 0). This is a convenient abuse of notation made honest by the injective embedding, exactly as Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.2 wrote n for the integer \iota(n): because \iota is injective, different real numbers stay different, and because it preserves + and \cdot, a sum or product of real numbers is the same whether computed in 
R or in 
C. With this convention the proposition reads (a, b) = a + bi \quad 	ext{for all } a, b \in 
R , \qquad i^2 = i \cdot i = -1 . So the notation a + bi is honest: it is a computation with the definitions, not a new symbol. Comparing real and imaginary parts now reads: for a, b, c, d \in 
R, a + bi = c + di \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . For z = a + bi with a, b \in 
R we have \operatorname{Re} z = a and \operatorname{Im} z = b. A real number a = a + 0i is a complex number whose imaginary part is 0, and 0 = 0 + 0i is the only complex number with both parts 0. The point i = 0 + 1i has real part 0 and imaginary part 1. The rule “a + bi = c + di gives a = c and b = d” needs a, b, c, d to be real. Without that it fails: 0 + 1 \cdot i = i + 0 \cdot i, yet 0 
e i. Before comparing parts, write each side as a + bi with a and b known to be real. [First Computations in 
C] Compute (2 + 3i)(1 - i), the products i \cdot i, (i \cdot i) \cdot i and  igl((i \cdot i) \cdot i igr) \cdot i, and the product (a + bi)(a - bi) for real a, b. Here 1 - i is 1 + (-1)i. By the multiplication rule with a = 2, b = 3, c = 1, d = -1, (2 + 3i)(1 - i) =  igl(2 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot (-1) igr) +  igl(2 \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot 1 igr) i = 5 + i . We already know i \cdot i = -1 = (-1, 0). Then (i \cdot i) \cdot i = (-1, 0)(0, 1) = (0 - 0, \; -1 + 0) = (0, -1) = -i , writing -i for 0 + (-1)i, and  igl((i \cdot i) \cdot i igr) \cdot i = (0, -1)(0, 1) =  igl(0 - (-1), \; 0 + 0 igr) = (1, 0) = 1 . Finally, with a - bi = a + (-b)i, (a + bi)(a - bi) =  igl(a^2 - b(-b) igr) +  igl(a(-b) + ba igr) i = a^2 + b^2 , where a^2 = aa and b^2 = bb are computed in 
R. This product is a real number, and it is non-negative, since a^2 \ge 0 and b^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) for a non-zero real, and 0^2 = 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so a^2 + b^2 \ge 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). We meet it again in Section 3.2, as the square of the length of a + bi. The last product is the first hint of how division will work: multiplying a + bi by a - bi lands in the real numbers, where division is familiar. Compute (1 + i)(1 + i). Is \operatorname{Im}(3 - 4i) equal to -4i? By the multiplication rule, (1 + i)(1 + i) = (1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 1) + (1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 1)i = 2i. No: 3 - 4i = 3 + (-4)i with 3, -4 \in 
R, so \operatorname{Im}(3 - 4i) = -4, a real number. The number -4i is not real, since its imaginary part is -4 
e 0. A non-example by minimal change. Change one sign in the multiplication rule: define (a, b) * (c, d) \coloneqq (ac + bd, \; ad + bc) , which is what expanding gives if we pretend j^2 = +1 instead. Addition is unchanged. This product is still commutative, by commutativity in 
R, and (1, 0) is still an identity element: (a, b) * (1, 0) = (a + 0, \; 0 + b) = (a, b). But (1, 1) * (1, -1) =  igl(1 - 1, \; -1 + 1 igr) = (0, 0) , so two non-zero elements multiply to zero. Division breaks down too: (1, 1) * (c, d) = (c + d, \; d + c) can never equal the identity element (1, 0), because that would need c + d = 1 and d + c = 0 at once. So the non-zero element (1, 1) has no inverse. The single sign in ac - bd is what makes division possible, as Section 3.2 will show. Exercise B3 finds every element that goes wrong in this way. Why this definition. We could have tried to postulate a number i with i^2 = -1, but a postulate is only as safe as the consistency of what it asserts. Pairs of reals are sets we already have, so 
C exists as soon as 
R does, and every law we want must now be proved. The multiplication formula is not a free choice either: Exercise C1 shows that in any field K containing 
R, whose sum and product agree with those of 
R on real numbers, and containing a square root j of -1, the product of a + bj and c + dj is forced to be (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)j. The minimal change above shows that a different formula really does give a different, and worse, system. The laws of arithmetic Before computing freely, we should confirm that rearranging, regrouping and expanding brackets are legal in 
C. The definition does not promise this; it has to be checked. [Arithmetic Laws in 
C] For all z, w, u \in 
C: 1. z + w = w + z and zw = wz; 2. (z + w) + u = z + (w + u) and (zw)u = z(wu); 3. z(w + u) = zw + zu; 4. z + 0 = z, z \cdot 1 = z, and z + (-z) = 0, where -(a + bi) \coloneqq (-a) + (-b)i for a, b \in 
R. Every law reduces to the corresponding law for real numbers once both sides are written as pairs and compared part by part. Addition is coordinate by coordinate, so its laws are immediate. For multiplication the only real work is associativity: expand both sides and see that they produce the same four terms in each coordinate. Let z = a + bi, w = c + di and u = e + fi with a, b, c, d, e, f \in 
R. In each part we compute both sides with @def-complex-numbers and compare real and imaginary parts, using the field laws of 
R (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) and the algebra of @fd3:prp-ring-algebra. Since addition acts coordinate by coordinate, the laws for addition in (a), (b) and (d) are the same laws in 
R, applied to each coordinate; for (d), z + 0 = (a + 0) + (b + 0)i = z and z + (-z) = (a + (-a)) + (b + (-b))i = 0. (a) By definition zw = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i and wz = (ca - db) + (cb + da)i. These are equal because real multiplication and addition are commutative. (b) Expanding with the definition twice gives  egin{aligned} (zw)u &=  igl((ac - bd)e - (ad + bc)f igr) \ &\qquad +  igl((ac - bd)f + (ad + bc)e igr)i \end{aligned} and  egin{aligned} z(wu) &=  igl(a(ce - df) - b(cf + de) igr) \ &\qquad +  igl(a(cf + de) + b(ce - df) igr)i . \end{aligned} Multiplying out with the distributive law of 
R, both real parts equal ace - adf - bcf - bde, and both imaginary parts equal acf + ade + bce - bdf. Hence (zw)u = z(wu). (c) We have w + u = (c + e) + (d + f)i, so  egin{aligned} z(w + u) &=  igl(a(c + e) - b(d + f) igr) +  igl(a(d + f) + b(c + e) igr)i \ &=  igl((ac - bd) + (ae - bf) igr) +  igl((ad + bc) + (af + be) igr)i , \end{aligned} which is zw + zu by the definitions of the product and the sum. (d) With 1 = 1 + 0i, we get z \cdot 1 = (a \cdot 1 - b \cdot 0) + (a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1)i = a + bi = z. The equations for addition were shown above. This proves the proposition. In the language of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.3, the proposition checks the axioms of a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field): (a) is (F1) and (F6), (b) is (F2) and (F5), (c) is (F9), and (d) is (F3), (F7) and (F4). Moreover 1 
e 0 in 
C, since (1, 0) 
e (0, 0) by @fd2:def-ordered-pair, as 1 
e 0 in 
R. So 
C, with the operations of @def-complex-numbers, is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0. Every result proved for commutative rings therefore holds in 
C without a new proof. From @fd3:prp-ring-algebra: 0, 1 and negatives are unique, -(-z) = z, z \cdot 0 = 0, (-z)w = -(zw), (-z)(-w) = zw, and (z + w)^2 = z^2 + 2zw + w^2, where z^2 \coloneqq zz. The remaining field axiom (F8), inverses of non-zero elements, is the subject of Section 3.2. From now on we compute in 
C exactly as in 
R: expand brackets, collect terms, and replace i^2 by -1. The proposition is what makes that habit legitimate. For instance, (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 - abi + abi - b^2 i^2 = a^2 + b^2 agrees with @exm-complex-arithmetic. Powers and a factorization Powers and finite sums in any commutative ring, and in particular in 
C, were set up in Chapter 1, Section 1.1. There z^n is defined by the recursion z^0 \coloneqq 1, z^{n+1} \coloneqq z^n z, the laws of powers are proved from the ring axioms alone (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a)–(c), and (d) for a field), and the difference of powers z^n - w^n = (z - w) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z^k w^{n-1-k} is proved (@lem-difference-of-powers). Nothing in those proofs used an order, so they apply to R = 
C unchanged, and we use them from here on. Section 3.6 uses the difference of powers again. For a real number a, the power a^n is the same whether computed in 
R or in 
C. Indeed \iota(a^0) = \iota(1) = 1, and if \iota(a^n) = \iota(a)^n, then \iota(a^{n+1}) = \iota(a^n a) = \iota(a^n)\,\iota(a) = \iota(a)^{n+1}, by @prp-reals-embed-complex; induction (@fd1:ax-induction) does the rest. So the identification of 
R with a subset of 
C is safe for powers too. In the notation of powers, @exm-complex-arithmetic computed i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i and i^4 = 1; by @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a), (b), every multiple of 4 gives i^{4q} = (i^4)^q = 1^q = 1, since 1^{q+1} = 1^q \cdot 1 and induction give 1^q = 1. Exercise B1 turns this into a rule for every power of i. Compute i^{10} and (1 + i)^4, citing the parts of @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring you use. By (a) and (b), i^{10} = i^{8} i^{2} = (i^4)^2 i^2 = 1^2 \cdot (-1) = -1. By (b), (1 + i)^4 =  igl((1 + i)^2 igr)^2 = (2i)^2, and by (c), (2i)^2 = 2^2 i^2 = 4 \cdot (-1) = -4, using (1 + i)^2 = 2i from the first Quick check. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Compute (2 - i)(3 + 4i), and the real and imaginary parts of i(1 + i). 2. True or false, with a reason: the equation (a, b) = a + bi, for a, b \in 
R, needs a proof. 3. Which laws in @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws need a genuine computation, and which follow coordinate by coordinate from the same laws in 
R? 4. True or false, with a reason: if z \in 
C and z^2 = 0, then z = 0. Prove it by comparing real and imaginary parts, without using that 
C is a field. (a) (2 - i)(3 + 4i) = 6 + 8i - 3i - 4i^2 = 6 + 4 + 5i = 10 + 5i. And i(1 + i) = i + i^2 = -1 + i, so \operatorname{Re} igl(i(1 + i) igr) = -1 and \operatorname{Im} igl(i(1 + i) igr) = 1. (b) True. The symbols a, b and i denote the pairs (a, 0), (b, 0), (0, 1), and a + bi is a sum and a product of pairs. That it equals (a, b) is a computation with @def-complex-numbers; it is part of @prp-reals-embed-complex. (c) The laws for addition, in (a), (b) and (d), hold coordinate by coordinate. Commutativity of multiplication, distributivity and z \cdot 1 = z are one-line computations. Associativity of multiplication is the one law that needs a genuine expansion: both sides have four terms in each part, and they agree only after multiplying out. (d) True. Let z = a + bi. Then z^2 = (a^2 - b^2) + 2abi, so z^2 = 0 gives a^2 - b^2 = 0 and 2ab = 0, by comparing parts. Since 2 
e 0 in 
R and 
R has no zero divisors (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)), a = 0 or b = 0. If a = 0, then -b^2 = 0, so b^2 = 0 and b = 0 by the same rule; if b = 0, then a^2 = 0 and a = 0. So z = 0. (Once Section 3.2 has shown that 
C is a field, this follows at once from @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d) in 
C.) B. Practice [B1: Powers of i] Let n \in 
N, and let r be the remainder of n on division by 4. Prove that i^n = i^r. Hence compute i^{2026}. By division with remainder (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, with n \in 
N \subseteq 
Z and divisor 4) there are integers q, r with n = 4q + r and 0 \le r < 4. Also q \ge 0: if q \le -1, then n \le -4 + r < 0, which is false. So q, r \in 
N. By @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a) and (b), and i^4 = 1 (@exm-complex-arithmetic), i^n = i^{4q} i^r = (i^4)^q i^r = 1^q i^r = i^r , where 1^q = 1 by induction on q (1^{q+1} = 1^q \cdot 1). So i^n is 1, i, -1, -i according as r = 0, 1, 2, 3. Hence, since 2026 = 4 \cdot 506 + 2, i^{2026} = i^2 = -1. [B2] 1. Use @lem-difference-of-powers to factor z^3 - 1 and z^4 - 1 in 
C, and check the second factorization at z = i. 2. Verify (1 + i)^4 = -4 using (1 + i)^2 = 2i and @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring. Hence show that, for every z \in 
C, z^4 + 4 =  igl(z - (1 + i) igr) igl(z^3 + (1 + i) z^2 + 2i z + (-2 + 2i) igr) . (a) With n = 3 and n = 4, z^3 - 1 = (z - 1)(1 + z + z^2) , \qquad z^4 - 1 = (z - 1)(1 + z + z^2 + z^3) . At z = i: the left side is i^4 - 1 = 0, and on the right 1 + i + i^2 + i^3 = 1 + i - 1 - i = 0, so both sides are 0. (b) By (b) of the proposition with m = n = 2, and then (c), (1 + i)^4 =  igl((1 + i)^2 igr)^2 = (2i)^2 = 2^2 i^2 = -4 . Let w \coloneqq 1 + i. Then w^2 = 2i and w^3 = w^2 w = 2i(1 + i) = -2 + 2i. By @lem-difference-of-powers with n = 4, whose sum is w^3 + z w^2 + z^2 w + z^3, z^4 - w^4 = (z - w) igl(z^3 + w z^2 + w^2 z + w^3 igr) . Since w^4 = -4, the left side is z^4 + 4, and substituting w, w^2, w^3 gives the displayed factorization. In particular 1 + i is a root of z^4 + 4. [B3: The zero divisors of the minimal change] Let * be the product (a, b) * (c, d) \coloneqq (ac + bd, \; ad + bc) on 
R^2 of the non-example in this section. Call a non-zero p \in 
R^2 a zero divisor if p * q = (0, 0) for some non-zero q \in 
R^2. Prove that a non-zero (a, b) is a zero divisor if and only if a^2 = b^2, that such an (a, b) has no inverse (no q gives (a, b) * q = (1, 0)), and that if a^2 
e b^2, then (a, b) * (ta, -tb) = (1, 0) for t \coloneqq (a^2 - b^2)^{-1}. First, for any real t, (a, b) * (ta, -tb) =  igl(t a^2 - t b^2, \; -tab + tab igr) =  igl(t(a^2 - b^2), \; 0 igr) . If a^2 
e b^2, then a^2 - b^2 
e 0 has an inverse in 
R, and t \coloneqq (a^2 - b^2)^{-1} gives (1, 0). (\Leftarrow) Let (a, b) 
e (0, 0) with a^2 = b^2. Then (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2 = 0, so b = a or b = -a (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d) in 
R). If b = a, then (a, a) * (1, -1) = (a - a, \; -a + a) = (0, 0); if b = -a, then (a, -a) * (1, 1) = (a - a, \; a - a) = (0, 0). In both cases the second factor is non-zero, so (a, b) is a zero divisor. Such an element also has no inverse: (a, a) * (c, d) =  igl(a(c + d), \; a(c + d) igr) has equal coordinates and (a, -a) * (c, d) =  igl(a(c - d), \; -a(c - d) igr) has opposite coordinates, while (1, 0) has neither, since 1 
e 0 and 1 
e -0 = 0. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive). Let a^2 
e b^2, and suppose (a, b) * (c, d) = (0, 0), that is, ac + bd = 0 and ad + bc = 0. Multiply the first equation by a and the second by b, and subtract: a^2 c + abd - abd - b^2 c = 0, that is, (a^2 - b^2) c = 0. Multiply the first by b and the second by a, and subtract: (b^2 - a^2) d = 0. Since a^2 - b^2 
e 0 and 
R has no zero divisors, c = 0 and d = 0. So the only q with (a, b) * q = (0, 0) is q = (0, 0), and (a, b) is not a zero divisor. No associativity of * was needed. For example, (1, 1) is a zero divisor, as in the text, and (2, 1) is not: (2, 1) * (2/3, -1/3) = (4/3 - 1/3, \; -2/3 + 2/3) = (1, 0). C. Going deeper [C1: There is only one way to adjoin a square root of minus one] Let K be a field (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) with 
R \subseteq K, such that the sum and the product of K, applied to two real numbers, are their sum and product in 
R. Let j \in K with j^2 = -1. 1. Show that 0, 1, negatives and inverses of non-zero real numbers are the same in K as in 
R. 2. Show that if a + bj = c + dj with a, b, c, d \in 
R, then a = c and b = d. 3. Let \varphi \colon 
C 	o K, \varphi(a + bi) \coloneqq a + bj for a, b \in 
R. Show that \varphi is injective, \varphi(1) = 1, and \varphi(z + w) = \varphi(z) + \varphi(w), \varphi(zw) = \varphi(z)\varphi(w) for all z, w \in 
C. [Hint 1] For (a), start from 0 + 0 = 0 and 1 \cdot 1 = 1 in 
R and cancel in K: add the negative of 0_{
R}; for 1, multiply by the inverse of 1_{
R}, which exists because 1_{
R} 
e 0_{
R} = 0_K. For -a and a^{-1}, use that each is the only element with its property (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a), @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). For (b), ask what happens if b 
e d. [Hint 2] For (b): suppose b 
e d. Then (d - b) j = a - c, and d - b is a non-zero real number. (a) In 
R, 0_{
R} + 0_{
R} = 0_{
R}; the same equation holds in K, since the sum of K on reals is that of 
R. Adding -0_{
R} (the negative in K) to both sides gives 0_{
R} = 0_K. Next, 1_{
R} \cdot 1_{
R} = 1_{
R} in K, and 1_{
R} 
e 0_{
R} = 0_K; multiplying by the inverse of 1_{
R} in K gives 1_{
R} = 1_K. For a \in 
R, the real negative -a satisfies a + (-a) = 0_{
R} = 0_K in K, so it is the negative of a in K, by uniqueness of negatives (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). Likewise, for real a 
e 0, the real inverse satisfies a a^{-1} = 1_{
R} = 1_K in K, so it is the inverse of a in K (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). So sums, products, differences and quotients of real numbers computed in K are real numbers. (b) Suppose a + bj = c + dj, and suppose, for contradiction, that b 
e d. Then (d - b) j = a - c, with d - b a non-zero real number, so j = (a - c)(d - b)^{-1}, which is real by (a). Then j^2 is the square of a real number, computed in 
R. Here j 
e 0, since 0^2 = 0 
e -1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so j^2 > 0 in 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). But j^2 = -1 < 0 in 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (a)), and 0 < j^2 < 0 contradicts (O1). Hence b = d, and then a = c by adding -bj to both sides. (c) The map is a function, since a + bi determines a and b (@prp-reals-embed-complex). It is injective by (b): a + bj = c + dj gives a = c and b = d, so a + bi = c + di. Also \varphi(1) = \varphi(1 + 0i) = 1 + 0j = 1. For z = a + bi and w = c + di, the field laws of K give \varphi(z) + \varphi(w) = (a + c) + (b + d)j = \varphi(z + w) , and, with j^2 = -1,  egin{aligned} \varphi(z)\varphi(w) &= ac + adj + bcj + bd j^2 \ &= (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)j = \varphi(zw) , \end{aligned} by @def-complex-numbers. This proves (c). So any field that contains 
R and a square root j of -1 contains an exact copy of 
C, namely \{ a + bj : a, b \in 
R \}, and its arithmetic is forced to be the arithmetic of @def-complex-numbers. Chapter 4 meets more fields of this shape, built from a smaller field and one new element, such as \{ a + bi : a, b \in 
Q \}. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) identifies 0 and 1 of 
R in K by cancellation, and negatives and inverses of reals by uniqueness. - 3: (b) shows that b 
e d would make j real, with the division justified by d - b 
e 0. - 2: (b) derives the contradiction from j^2 > 0 in 
R (with j 
e 0) and -1 < 0, naming the ordered-field rule. - Second route for (b): squaring (b - d)j = c - a with j^2 = -1, and noting by (a) that the result is an equation between real numbers, earns the 3 points; concluding from (c - a)^2 + (b - d)^2 = 0 that a = c and b = d, from squares \ge 0 in 
R, naming the ordered-field rule, earns the 2 points. - 1: (c) injectivity, from (b). - 2: (c) the sum and the product, expanding with j^2 = -1 and comparing with @def-complex-numbers. Fatal errors (0 for the step): treating j as i (the point is that K is any field); claiming j^2 \ge 0 in K (there is no order on K).

title: 3.2 Conjugate, Modulus, and Division
content:
Conjugate, Modulus, and Division Section 3.1 built 
C and showed that it is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 (@prp-complex-arithmetic-laws). One field axiom is still missing: (F8), which asks for an inverse of every non-zero element. To divide by 3 + 4i, we want a number to multiply by that lands in the real numbers, where division is familiar. The product (a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2 of @exm-complex-arithmetic shows which number does the job. This section gives its two ingredients names, the conjugate and the modulus, proves the rules they obey, and concludes that 
C is a field. Conjugate and modulus A complex number z = a + bi is a point (a, b) of the plane. Two pieces of plane geometry turn out to be algebra in disguise: the mirror image of z in the horizontal axis, and the distance of z from 0. The mirror image changes the sign of b. The distance, by Pythagoras, is the square root of a^2 + b^2, the very number that appeared in @exm-complex-arithmetic. Square roots of non-negative real numbers exist and are unique in every complete ordered field (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), so we may use them in 
R: for x \in 
R with x \ge 0, \sqrt{x} is the unique y \in 
R with y \ge 0 and y^2 = x. Conjugating reflects a point in the real axis; the modulus is its distance from the origin. Conjugate and Modulus Let z = a + bi \in 
C with a, b \in 
R. The complex conjugate of z is \conj{z} \coloneqq a - bi . The modulus (or absolute value) of z is the real number \abs{z} \coloneqq \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} , the non-negative square root of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots in 
R. In words: the conjugate keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part, \operatorname{Re} \conj{z} = \operatorname{Re} z and \operatorname{Im} \conj{z} = -\operatorname{Im} z. The modulus is a real number, never negative, and its square is a^2 + b^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z)^2. Well-definedness. Since z determines a and b (compare real and imaginary parts, Section 3.1), the right-hand sides depend only on z. The square root exists because its argument is non-negative: a^2 \ge 0 and b^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), with 0^2 = 0 when the number is 0), so a^2 + b^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)). And 
R is complete (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), which is the hypothesis of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. This is where the completeness of 
R enters the chapter. Over 
Q alone the definition would break down at once: \abs{1 + i} would have to be a rational number whose square is 2, and there is none (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two). Examples. A point with integer distance. For z = 3 + 4i: \conj{z} = 3 - 4i, and \abs{z} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5. The last step is the uniqueness clause of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots: 5 \ge 0 and 5^2 = 25, so 5 is the non-negative square root of 25. The unit i. \conj{i} = \conj{0 + 1i} = 0 - 1i = -i, and \abs{i} = \sqrt{0 + 1} = 1, since 1 \ge 0 and 1^2 = 1. The degenerate case z = 0. \conj{0} = 0 and \abs{0} = \sqrt{0} = 0. For z = -2i = 0 + (-2)i: \conj{z} = 0 - (-2)i = 2i and \abs{z} = \sqrt{0 + 4} = 2, since 2 \ge 0 and 2^2 = 4. For z = 1 - i: \conj{z} = 1 + i and \abs{z} = \sqrt{1 + 1} = \sqrt{2}. In neither case is \conj{z} = z: comparing imaginary parts, \conj{z} = z needs \operatorname{Im} z = -\operatorname{Im} z, that is \operatorname{Im} z = 0, and both numbers have non-zero imaginary part. Why this definition. The square root is what makes the modulus a length. Without it, the simpler quantity N(z) \coloneqq a^2 + b^2 would do some of the same jobs: it is z \conj{z}, and it vanishes only at 0. But on real numbers it is N(a) = a^2, not \abs{a}, so it does not extend the absolute value: N(2) = 4. And it is not a sensible distance: N(1 + 1) = 4, while N(1) + N(1) = 2, so the “side” from 0 to 2 would be longer than the two sides through 1. The modulus keeps the convenient algebra of N, since \abs{z}^2 = N(z), and adds the right size. Section 3.3 exploits exactly this square. The modulus squared is z \conj{z}, not z z.
