Rules for conjugate and modulus The following rules are used constantly, in this chapter and much later for complex inner products. They say that conjugation respects both operations, and that the modulus respects products. [Properties of Conjugation and Modulus] For all z, w \in 
C: 1. \conj{z + w} = \conj{z} + \conj{w} and \conj{\conj{z}} = z; 2. \conj{zw} = \conj{z} \, \conj{w}; 3. z \conj{z} = \abs{z}^2 and z + \conj{z} = 2 \operatorname{Re} z; 4. \abs{zw} = \abs{z} \, \abs{w} and \abs{\conj{z}} = \abs{z}; 5. \abs{z} = 0 if and only if z = 0. Parts (a)–(c) and (e) are direct computations with real and imaginary parts. For (d), expanding \abs{zw} directly is legitimate but messy, since a square root of a long sum appears. It is cleaner to square: by (c) a squared modulus is a product with a conjugate, and (b) lets the conjugate split across the product. Two non-negative real numbers with the same square are equal, and that brings us back from squares to moduli. Let z = a + bi and w = c + di with a, b, c, d \in

Also z + \conj{z} = (a + a) + (b - b)i = 2a = 2 \operatorname{Re} z. (d) By (c), then (b), then @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws to regroup and reorder the four factors, \abs{zw}^2 = (zw)\,\conj{zw} = z w \conj{z} \, \conj{w} = (z \conj{z})(w \conj{w}) = \abs{z}^2 \abs{w}^2 . In 
R, \abs{z}^2 \abs{w}^2 =  igl(\abs{z} \abs{w} igr)^2 (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (c)), and \abs{z} \abs{w} \ge 0: it is 0 if one factor is 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), and positive otherwise, since a product of two positive elements of an ordered field is positive ((O4) of @fd3:def-ordered-ring-and-field). So \abs{zw} and \abs{z}\abs{w} are both non-negative real numbers whose square is \abs{z}^2 \abs{w}^2. By the uniqueness clause of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots they are equal. Finally \abs{\conj{z}} = \sqrt{a^2 + (-b)^2} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = \abs{z}, since (-b)^2 = b^2 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). (e) If z = 0, then \abs{z} = \sqrt{0} = 0. Conversely, let \abs{z} = 0, so a^2 + b^2 = \abs{z}^2 = 0. If a 
e 0, then a^2 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)) and b^2 \ge 0, so a^2 + b^2 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), a contradiction; hence a = 0. Then b^2 = 0, and the same rule gives b = 0. So z = 0. This proves the theorem. The proof of (d) is our first use of a move that runs through the whole chapter: a statement about a modulus \abs{u} becomes a statement about \abs{u}^2 = u \conj{u}, which is algebra; we compute there, and come back by taking non-negative square roots. Section 3.3 names it, square the modulus, and uses it to prove the triangle inequality. Two remarks on what the theorem says. First, (a) and (b) say that conjugation respects sums and products, and it fixes 1. Not every reflection does: the reflection in the vertical axis, z \mapsto -\conj{z}, respects sums, but it sends 1 to -1, and 1 \cdot 1 = 1 to -1, while the product of the images is (-1)(-1) = 1. Second, (d) says that the size of a product is the product of the sizes. In the plane picture, multiplying by w stretches every length by \abs{w}; Section 3.5 completes this picture with angles. Q. By @prp-complex-inverse, z^{-1} =  rac{a}{a^2 + b^2} +  rac{-b}{a^2 + b^2}\, i , whose parts are quotients of rational numbers by a non-zero rational number, hence rational. So all five operations stay in 
Q(i). For example, (1 + 2i)^{-1} =  rac15 -  rac25 i \in 
Q(i). Chapter 4 calls a subset of a field a subfield when it contains 0 and 1 and has these closure properties. 
Q(i) contains 0 = 0 + 0i and 1 = 1 + 0i, and it is one of the examples there. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the copy of 
Q in 
R is closed under +, \cdot, negatives and inverses of non-zero elements, with a reason (@fd3:thm-rational-embedding (a), (c)). - 2: z + w, -z and \conj{z} have rational real and imaginary parts. - 2: zw = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i has rational parts. - 3: for z 
e 0, a^2 + b^2 is non-zero (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)) and rational, and the formula of @prp-complex-inverse then gives rational parts. - 1: the conclusion that all five operations stay in 
Q(i). Fatal errors (0 for the step): dividing by a^2 + b^2 without first using z 
e 0 to show it is non-zero; assuming without a reason that 
Q \subseteq 
R is closed under the operations.

title: 3.3 The Triangle Inequality
content:
The Triangle Inequality The modulus of Section 3.2 measures a complex number by a real one. Picture z = a + bi as the point (a, b) of the plane: by Pythagoras, \abs{z} = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} is its distance from the origin, and \abs{z - w} is the distance between the points z and w. In a triangle, one side is never longer than the other two together. This section proves the algebraic form of that fact, \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w}, from the definitions alone. The picture motivates it; no step of the proof uses it. Why the old proof does not transfer For an ordered field, Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 proved \abs{x + y} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y} by trapping (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)). Each of x and y lies between \pm its absolute value, -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x} (part (c) there); adding the two traps traps x + y between \pm(\abs{x} + \abs{y}), and part (d) reads that as the inequality. That route needs x \le \abs{x}: a comparison between x itself and a number. For a complex z, “z \le \abs{z}” compares a complex number with a real one, and 
C has been given no order in which to make the comparison. Section 3.4 shows that no order compatible with the arithmetic of 
C exists (@prp-complex-not-orderable). So the proof must compare real numbers only. Two kinds of real number are at hand. Moduli are real, and so are real parts. The device that connects them to the arithmetic of 
C is the identity \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u} of @thm-conjugate-properties (c). A modulus is a square root, and square roots do not add well; its square is a product, and products expand. So we will compare squares and then come back. Comparing squares. Coming back from squares to the numbers needs one rule about the real numbers. Let p, q \in 
R with p \ge 0 and q \ge 0. Then p \le q \iff p^2 \le q^2 , \qquad\qquad p = q \iff p^2 = q^2 , and likewise with < on both sides. The strict form is @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g). For the first equivalence: if p < q, then p^2 < q^2 by (g), and if p = q the squares agree. Conversely, if p^2 \le q^2 and yet q < p, then (g) gives q^2 < p^2, which contradicts p^2 \le q^2 by trichotomy (O1); so p \le q. The second equivalence follows from the first, applied in both directions, and trichotomy. In words: for non-negative reals, squaring neither creates nor destroys a comparison. Both hypotheses p \ge 0 and q \ge 0 matter: (-2)^2 > 1^2, and yet -2 < 1. The real part is at most the modulus The single estimate the proof needs is that a real part never exceeds the modulus. It comes with two companions, which say that the modulus and the “taxicab size” \abs{\operatorname{Re} u} + \abs{\operatorname{Im} u} are comparable. [Real and Imaginary Parts against the Modulus] For every u \in 
C, \abs{\operatorname{Re} u} \le \abs{u} , \qquad \abs{\operatorname{Im} u} \le \abs{u} , \qquad \abs{u} \le \abs{\operatorname{Re} u} + \abs{\operatorname{Im} u} . In particular \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u}. Here \abs{\operatorname{Re} u} is the absolute value of a real number. By @prp-modulus-of-real it is the same whether it is read as the absolute value of the ordered field 
R from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field) or as the modulus of a complex number that happens to be real, so the lemma has only one reading. Every quantity in the lemma is a non-negative real, so compare squares. The square of \abs{u} is x^2 + y^2, and the squares of \abs{x} and \abs{y} are x^2 and y^2, each at most the sum; the square of \abs{x} + \abs{y} is the sum plus the non-negative cross term 2\abs{x}\abs{y}. Write u = x + yi with x, y \in 
R. By @def-conjugate-modulus and the defining property of the square root (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), \abs{u} \ge 0 and \abs{u}^2 = x^2 + y^2. Since y^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) if y 
e 0; 0^2 = 0 otherwise), adding x^2 gives x^2 \le x^2 + y^2 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). Also \abs{x}^2 = x^2 and \abs{x} \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), (b)). Hence \abs{x}^2 \le \abs{u}^2, with both \abs{x} and \abs{u} non-negative, and comparing squares gives \abs{x} \le \abs{u}. The same argument with the roles of x and y exchanged gives \abs{y} \le \abs{u}. Then \operatorname{Re} u = x \le \abs{x} by @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c), so \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u}. For the last inequality, expand with @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d):  egin{aligned}  igl( \abs{x} + \abs{y}  igr)^2 &= \abs{x}^2 + 2 \abs{x} \abs{y} + \abs{y}^2 \ &= x^2 + y^2 + 2 \abs{x} \abs{y} \ge x^2 + y^2 = \abs{u}^2 , \end{aligned} where the inequality holds because \abs{x}\abs{y} \ge 0 as a product of non-negative reals, so 2 \abs{x}\abs{y} \ge 0, and @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) adds it. Both \abs{x} + \abs{y} and \abs{u} are non-negative, so comparing squares gives \abs{u} \le \abs{x} + \abs{y}. This proves the lemma. For u = 3 - 4i the three inequalities read 3 \le 5, 4 \le 5 and 5 \le 7. For u = 2 they read 2 \le 2, 0 \le 2 and 2 \le 2: a real u makes the first and third equalities. The inequality \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} is strict for u = -1, where it reads -1 \le 1; the absolute value inside the first inequality is what makes it sharp for real u of either sign. Find a non-zero u \in 
C with \operatorname{Re} u = 0. What do the three inequalities of @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus say for it? For example u = 2i, with \operatorname{Re} u = 0, \operatorname{Im} u = 2 and \abs{u} = \sqrt{0 + 4} = 2. The inequalities read 0 \le 2, 2 \le 2 and 2 \le 0 + 2. Any u = yi with y 
e 0 works the same way: \abs{u} = \abs{y}, so the second and third inequalities are equalities. The triangle inequality We can now state the theorem. Its proof is the first full run of the move this chapter is built around. [Triangle Inequality for Complex Numbers] For all z, w \in 
C, \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w} . Try it first (ten minutes): show \abs{z + w}^2 \le (\abs{z} + \abs{w})^2 by expanding both sides with \abs{u}^2 = u \conj{u}, and note which term you cannot yet bound. Expanding the left side with \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u} and conjugation of sums gives \abs{z}^2 + z\conj{w} + \conj{z}w + \abs{w}^2; the right side is \abs{z}^2 + 2\abs{z}\abs{w} + \abs{w}^2. Everything matches except the cross term z\conj{w} + \conj{z}w, and an attempt usually stops there: it looks like a complex number, and complex numbers cannot be compared with 2\abs{z}\abs{w}. The way out is to notice that \conj{z} w is the conjugate of z \conj{w}, so the cross term is u + \conj{u} = 2 \operatorname{Re} u with u = z\conj{w}: a real number after all. A real part is at most the modulus, and \abs{z\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\abs{w}. Squares compare, so the moduli do. Before reading on: where is \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} used, and why may we compare squares? Let z, w \in 
C. By @thm-conjugate-properties (c), then (a), then @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws (c) together with (a) and (b) (distributivity, commutativity, associativity),  egin{aligned} \abs{z + w}^2 &= (z + w)\,\conj{(z + w)} = (z + w)(\conj{z} + \conj{w}) \ &= z\conj{z} + z\conj{w} + \conj{z}w + w\conj{w} . \end{aligned} By @thm-conjugate-properties (b) and (a), \conj{z\conj{w}} = \conj{z}\,\conj{\conj{w}} = \conj{z} w. So with u \coloneqq z\conj{w}, the two middle terms are u + \conj{u} = 2 \operatorname{Re} u, by @thm-conjugate-properties (c). Using (c) once more for z\conj{z} and w\conj{w}, \abs{z + w}^2 = \abs{z}^2 + 2 \operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) + \abs{w}^2 . Every term here is real, and sums and products of real numbers are the same in 
C as in 
R (@prp-reals-embed-complex), so the inequalities below take place in the ordered field 
R. By @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus, \operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) \le \abs{z\conj{w}}, and by @thm-conjugate-properties (d), \abs{z\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\,\abs{\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\,\abs{w}. Adding this inequality to itself (2a = (1 + 1)a = a + a by distributivity) and then adding \abs{z}^2 + \abs{w}^2 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) twice), and expanding the square with @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d), \abs{z + w}^2 \le \abs{z}^2 + 2\abs{z}\abs{w} + \abs{w}^2 =  igl( \abs{z} + \abs{w}  igr)^2 . Both \abs{z + w} and \abs{z} + \abs{w} are non-negative real numbers, so comparing squares gives \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w}. This proves the triangle inequality. The proof answers its prompt in two lines. \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} is used once, to bound the cross term 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) by 2\abs{z\conj{w}}. Comparing squares is legitimate because the two quantities being compared, \abs{z + w} and \abs{z} + \abs{w}, are both non-negative; without that, a smaller square would say nothing about the numbers. This route has a name in this chapter: square the modulus. The modulus is a square root, and square roots are hard to handle; its square \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u} is a product, so square, expand with conjugates, bound or compare the real numbers you get, and take the non-negative square root back. Section 3.2 used the same move once already, for \abs{zw} = \abs{z}\abs{w} (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)). The linear algebra volumes take the same route, square, expand, bound the cross term, for the length of a vector in an inner product space. The square of the modulus is u\conj{u}, not u^2. Expanding \abs{z + w}^2 as (z + w)^2 = z^2 + 2zw + w^2 gives nonsense: for z = w = i, (z + w)^2 = (2i)^2 = -4, while \abs{z + w}^2 = \abs{2i}^2 = 4. The cross term of the correct expansion is z\conj{w} + \conj{z}w, and only that form is real. The inequality can be strict: for z = 1 and w = -1, the left side is \abs{0} = 0 and the right side is 2. For real z, w, every modulus in the statement is the absolute value of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 (@prp-modulus-of-real), and the theorem is @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), reached by a different route. Compute \abs{3 + 4i} + \abs{-3 + 4i} and \abs{(3 + 4i) + (-3 + 4i)}, and check them against the triangle inequality. \abs{3 + 4i} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5 and \abs{-3 + 4i} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5, so the right side is 10. The sum is 8i, and \abs{8i} = \sqrt{0 + 64} = 8. Indeed 8 \le 10. In the picture, the two points and 8i are three corners of a parallelogram with the origin as the fourth, and the diagonal 8 is shorter than the two sides 5 + 5. Three variants Three consequences are used often enough to be stated once: a lower bound for the modulus of a difference, the inequality for any finite number of terms, and a lower bound for the modulus of a sum. [Variants of the Triangle Inequality] Let z, w \in 
C. 1. (Reverse triangle inequality.)  igl| \abs{z} - \abs{w}  igr| \le \abs{z - w}. 2. For every n \in 
N with n \ge 1 and all z_1, \dots, z_n \in 
C, \displaystyle \Bigl| \sum_{k=1}^{n} z_k \Bigr| \le \sum_{k=1}^{n} \abs{z_k}. 3. \abs{z} - \abs{w} \le \abs{z + w}. In (a), the outer bars are the absolute value of the real number \abs{z} - \abs{w}. In words: (a) says that two points at distance \abs{z - w} from each other have distances from the origin that differ by at most that much; (b) says that a path of n steps is at least as long as the straight line from start to end; (c) says that adding w can lower the modulus by at most \abs{w}. For (a), split z as (z - w) + w and apply the theorem; that bounds \abs{z} - \abs{w} from above, and swapping z and w bounds it from below. For (b), add one term at a time. For (c), apply (a) to z and -w. (a) Since z = (z - w) + w, @thm-complex-triangle-inequality gives \abs{z} \le \abs{z - w} + \abs{w}, so \abs{z} - \abs{w} \le \abs{z - w}. Exchanging z and w gives \abs{w} - \abs{z} \le \abs{w - z}. Moreover w - z = (-1)(z - w), so by @thm-conjugate-properties (d), \abs{w - z} = \abs{-1}\,\abs{z - w} = \abs{z - w}, where \abs{-1} = 1 by @prp-modulus-of-real. Let t \coloneqq \abs{z} - \abs{w} \in 
R. We have shown t \le \abs{z - w} and -t \le \abs{z - w}, that is, -\abs{z - w} \le t \le \abs{z - w}: if -t < \abs{z - w}, then -\abs{z - w} < -(-t) = t by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a), and if -t = \abs{z - w}, then -\abs{z - w} = -(-t) = t. By @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), \abs{t} \le \abs{z - w}. (b) By induction on n \ge 1 (@fd1:ax-induction, through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b), applied to the statement for n = m + 1, m \in 
N), with the sums defined by appending the last term, as for real sums (@fd2:def-sum-product). For n = 1, both sides are \abs{z_1}. Suppose the inequality holds for n, and let z_1, \dots, z_{n+1} \in 
C. Then  egin{aligned} \Bigl| \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} z_k \Bigr| &= \Bigl| \sum_{k=1}^{n} z_k + z_{n+1} \Bigr| \le \Bigl| \sum_{k=1}^{n} z_k \Bigr| + \abs{z_{n+1}} \ &\le \sum_{k=1}^{n} \abs{z_k} + \abs{z_{n+1}} = \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} \abs{z_k} , \end{aligned} by @thm-complex-triangle-inequality, then the induction hypothesis with @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b). (c) Apply (a) to z and -w. Since z - (-w) = z + w (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)) and \abs{-w} = \abs{-1}\abs{w} = \abs{w} as in (a), it reads  igl| \abs{z} - \abs{w}  igr| \le \abs{z + w}. By @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c), \abs{z} - \abs{w} \le  igl| \abs{z} - \abs{w}  igr|. This proves the corollary. Part (b) with n = 2 is the theorem itself, so the corollary contains it. Chapter 7 uses (b) and (c) to show that a polynomial expression of degree at least 1 is large in modulus when \abs{z} is large, a step towards the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. Take z = 5 and w = 3i. Compute both sides of (a) and of (c). \abs{z} = 5 and \abs{w} = 3, so \abs{z} - \abs{w} = 2. For (a): \abs{z - w} = \abs{5 - 3i} = \sqrt{34}, and 2 \le \sqrt{34} because 2^2 = 4 \le 34 (comparing squares). For (c): \abs{z + w} = \abs{5 + 3i} = \sqrt{34} too, and again 2 \le \sqrt{34}. Both bounds are far from sharp here; (a) is an equality when w = 0, for instance. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-complex-triangle-inequality. 1. Where in the proof is \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} used, and for which u? 2. Why may the proof pass from \abs{z + w}^2 \le (\abs{z} + \abs{w})^2 back to \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w}? 3. Run the proof on z = 3 and w = 4i: compute the cross term 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}), then both sides of the squared inequality. 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 5. True or false: \abs{z + w} = \abs{z} + \abs{w} for all z, w \in 
C. Justify your answer. (a) Once, to bound the cross term: with u = z\conj{w}, 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) \le 2\abs{z\conj{w}}. (b) Both \abs{z + w} and \abs{z} + \abs{w} are non-negative reals, and for non-negative reals p \le q if and only if p^2 \le q^2 (comparing squares, from @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) and trichotomy). (c) \conj{w} = -4i, so z\conj{w} = 3 \cdot (-4i) = -12i, with real part 0: the cross term is 0. Then \abs{z + w}^2 = 9 + 0 + 16 = 25 and (\abs{z} + \abs{w})^2 = (3 + 4)^2 = 49, and 25 \le 49. So \abs{3 + 4i} = 5 \le 7. (d) Square both sides and expand with \abs{u}^2 = u\conj{u}: everything matches except the cross term, which is 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}). A real part is at most the modulus, and \abs{z\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\abs{w}, so the squares compare, and so do the non-negative moduli. (e) False. For z = 1 and w = -1, \abs{z + w} = 0, but \abs{z} + \abs{w} = 2. B. Practice [B1: The equality case] Let z, w \in 
C. Prove that \abs{z + w} = \abs{z} + \abs{w} if and only if z\conj{w} is a non-negative real number, that is, \operatorname{Im}(z\conj{w}) = 0 and \operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) \ge 0. Hint: trace the proof of the triangle inequality and ask where an inequality could be strict. Let u \coloneqq z\conj{w} = x + yi with x, y \in 
R. By the proof of @thm-complex-triangle-inequality,  egin{aligned} \abs{z + w}^2 &= \abs{z}^2 + 2x + \abs{w}^2 , \  igl( \abs{z} + \abs{w}  igr)^2 &= \abs{z}^2 + 2\abs{u} + \abs{w}^2 , \end{aligned} the second because \abs{z}\abs{w} = \abs{u} (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)). Both moduli are non-negative, so (comparing squares) \abs{z + w} = \abs{z} + \abs{w} holds if and only if the squares are equal, that is, if and only if 2x = 2\abs{u}, that is, x = \abs{u}. It remains to show that x = \abs{u} holds exactly when y = 0 and x \ge 0. If x = \abs{u}, then x \ge 0, and squaring gives x^2 = x^2 + y^2, so y^2 = 0 and y = 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e): a non-zero square is positive). Conversely, if y = 0 and x \ge 0, then \abs{u} = \sqrt{x^2} = x, since x \ge 0 and x^2 = x^2 (uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). Hence \abs{z + w} = \abs{z} + \abs{w} if and only if z\conj{w} is a non-negative real number. For instance z = 1 + i, w = 2 + 2i: z\conj{w} = (1 + i)(2 - 2i) = 4 \ge 0, and indeed \abs{3 + 3i} = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt 2 = \sqrt 2 + 2\sqrt 2 = \abs{1 + i} + \abs{2 + 2i}. In the picture: equality holds exactly when one of z, w is 0 or they point in the same direction from the origin. The linear algebra volumes prove the version for n terms. [B2: A distance that does not change] Let z \in 
C with \abs{z} = 1. Prove that \abs{z - w} = \abs{1 - \conj{z}w} for every w \in 
C. The first two steps are done:  egin{aligned} \abs{z - w}^2 &= \abs{z}^2 - z\conj{w} - \conj{z}w + \abs{w}^2 , \ \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}^2 &= 1 - z\conj{w} - \conj{z}w + \abs{z}^2\abs{w}^2 , \end{aligned} both by expanding u\conj{u} with @thm-conjugate-properties. Name the move, then complete it. The move is square the modulus: compare the squares, which are algebra, and take the non-negative square roots back. Substitute \abs{z}^2 = 1 into both lines. The first becomes 1 - z\conj{w} - \conj{z}w + \abs{w}^2, and so does the second, since \abs{z}^2\abs{w}^2 = \abs{w}^2. So \abs{z - w}^2 = \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}^2. Both \abs{z - w} and \abs{1 - \conj{z}w} are non-negative, and non-negative reals with equal squares are equal (comparing squares). Hence \abs{z - w} = \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}. (For the record, the given lines. Conjugation respects differences: \conj{-v} = \conj{(-1)v} = \conj{-1}\,\conj{v} = -\conj{v} by @thm-conjugate-properties (b), @prp-modulus-of-real and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c), so with (a), \conj{u - v} = \conj{u} - \conj{v}; and \conj{1} = 1 by @prp-modulus-of-real. Then (z - w)(\conj{z} - \conj{w}) = z\conj{z} - z\conj{w} - w\conj{z} + w\conj{w}, and \conj{1 - \conj{z}w} = 1 - z\conj{w}, so (1 - \conj{z}w)(1 - z\conj{w}) = 1 - z\conj{w} - \conj{z}w + (z\conj{z})(w\conj{w}).) [B3] Prove that \abs{z} \le \abs{\operatorname{Re} z} + \abs{\operatorname{Im} z} \le \sqrt 2 \, \abs{z} for every z \in 
C, and, for each of the two inequalities, find a non-zero z for which it is an equality. The first inequality is the last part of @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus. For the second, write z = x + yi. Both sides are non-negative (\sqrt 2 \ge 0 by @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), so it suffices to compare squares. The right side squared is (\sqrt 2)^2 \abs{z}^2 = 2(x^2 + y^2), and the left side squared is x^2 + 2\abs{x}\abs{y} + y^2, using \abs{x}^2 = x^2 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b)). Their difference is  egin{aligned} 2(x^2 + y^2) -  igl( x^2 + 2\abs{x}\abs{y} + y^2  igr) &= \abs{x}^2 - 2\abs{x}\abs{y} + \abs{y}^2 \ &=  igl( \abs{x} - \abs{y}  igr)^2 \ge 0 , \end{aligned} a square in the ordered field 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So (\abs{x} + \abs{y})^2 \le 2\abs{z}^2, and \abs{x} + \abs{y} \le \sqrt 2\,\abs{z}. Equality: z = 1 gives 1 = 1 + 0 in the first; z = 1 + i gives 1 + 1 = 2 = \sqrt 2 \cdot \sqrt 2 in the second. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the triangle inequality] State and prove the triangle inequality for complex numbers. Your proof must include a proof that \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} for every u \in 
C. Statement. For all z, w \in 
C, \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w}. The estimate. Let u = x + yi with x, y \in 
R. Then \abs{u}^2 = x^2 + y^2 \ge x^2 = \abs{x}^2, since y^2 \ge 0. Both \abs{x} and \abs{u} are non-negative, so \abs{x} \le \abs{u} by comparing squares (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) with trichotomy). Hence \operatorname{Re} u = x \le \abs{x} \le \abs{u} (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c)). The inequality. Let z, w \in 
C. By @thm-conjugate-properties (a)–(c),  egin{aligned} \abs{z + w}^2 &= (z + w)(\conj{z} + \conj{w}) = \abs{z}^2 +  igl( z\conj{w} + \conj{z\conj{w}}  igr) + \abs{w}^2 \ &= \abs{z}^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) + \abs{w}^2 . \end{aligned} By the estimate and @thm-conjugate-properties (d), 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) \le 2\abs{z\conj{w}} = 2\abs{z}\abs{w}. Hence \abs{z + w}^2 \le (\abs{z} + \abs{w})^2. Both \abs{z + w} and \abs{z} + \abs{w} are non-negative, so comparing squares gives \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w}. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: proves \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u}, with a reason for passing from squares to moduli. - 3: expands \abs{z + w}^2 with conjugates and identifies the cross term as 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}), a real number. - 2: bounds the cross term by 2\abs{z}\abs{w}, citing \abs{z\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\abs{w}. - 1: concludes \abs{z + w}^2 \le (\abs{z} + \abs{w})^2. - 2: takes square roots, justified by the non-negativity of both sides. A second route, with coordinates z = a + bi, w = c + di: expanding (a + c)^2 + (b + d)^2 and isolating the cross term 2(ac + bd) earns the 3 points of the second line; proving ac + bd \le \abs{z}\abs{w}, for instance from (ac + bd)^2 \le (a^2 + b^2)(c^2 + d^2), which follows from (ad - bc)^2 \ge 0, earns the 2 points of the third line if proved, not if quoted; the last two lines are marked as above. The 2 points for \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} are still owed on that route, since the problem asks for it. Fatal errors (0 for the step): writing z \le \abs{z} or any inequality between non-real complex numbers; dropping the conjugate, as in \abs{u}^2 = u^2. [C2: Inside the unit disc] Let z, w \in 
C with \abs{z} < 1 and \abs{w} < 1. Prove that \abs{z - w} < \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}. Here is the start of a proof: square both sides and expand. Name the move, then complete it. The move is square the modulus. Both sides are non-negative, so it is enough to show \abs{z - w}^2 < \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}^2 (comparing squares, strict form: @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). Expanding each as u\conj{u}, exactly as in @exr-triangle-inequality-b2,  egin{aligned} \abs{z - w}^2 &= \abs{z}^2 - z\conj{w} - \conj{z}w + \abs{w}^2 , \ \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}^2 &= 1 - z\conj{w} - \conj{z}w + \abs{z}^2\abs{w}^2 . \end{aligned} The non-real terms cancel in the difference:  egin{aligned} \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}^2 - \abs{z - w}^2 &= 1 - \abs{z}^2 - \abs{w}^2 + \abs{z}^2\abs{w}^2 \ &=  igl( 1 - \abs{z}^2  igr) igl( 1 - \abs{w}^2  igr) . \end{aligned} Since 0 \le \abs{z} < 1, comparing squares gives \abs{z}^2 < 1^2 = 1, so 1 - \abs{z}^2 > 0; likewise 1 - \abs{w}^2 > 0. A product of two positive reals is positive ((O4)). So the difference is positive, \abs{z - w}^2 < \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}^2, and \abs{z - w} < \abs{1 - \conj{z}w}. In particular 1 - \conj{z}w 
e 0. Since \abs{1 - \conj{z}w} = \abs{1 - z\conj{w}} (a modulus is unchanged by conjugation, @thm-conjugate-properties (d)), the inequality says that \abs{z - w}/\abs{1 - \conj{w}z} < 1 for all z, w in the open unit disc: the map z \mapsto (z - w)/(1 - \conj{w}z) sends the open unit disc into itself, a fact complex analysis builds on. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: reduces to the squared inequality, with the non-negativity of both sides as the reason. - 3: expands both squares with conjugates. - 3: factors the difference as (1 - \abs{z}^2)(1 - \abs{w}^2). - 2: shows both factors positive, from \abs{z}, \abs{w} < 1, and concludes strictly. Fatal errors (0 for the step): expanding \abs{z - w}^2 as (z - w)^2; comparing z\conj{w} with a real number.

title: 3.4 Square Roots, Quadratic Equations, and the Missing Order
content:
Square Roots, Quadratic Equations, and the Missing Order Logic and Proof, Section 7.1 needed, in one of its checks, the fact that every complex number has a complex square root, and took it there as a school fact about polar form. This section proves it, with no angles at all: a square root of a complex number is built from two square roots of non-negative reals, which Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 6 provides (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). The quadratic formula follows, for complex coefficients. Then we see what 
C has lost on the way from 
R: it has no order compatible with its arithmetic, and the rule \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{xy} has no complex version. Square roots from real square roots The question is: given z = a + bi, find w = x + yi with w^2 = z. Since w^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + 2xyi, comparing real and imaginary parts turns the question into two real equations, x^2 - y^2 = a , \qquad 2xy = b . The answer is an explicit formula in a, b and \abs{z}. [Square Roots of Complex Numbers] Let z = a + bi \in 
C with a, b \in 
R and z 
e 0, and let r \coloneqq \abs{z}. Put s \coloneqq 1 if b \ge 0 and s \coloneqq -1 if b < 0, and x \coloneqq \sqrt{ rac{r + a}{2}} , \qquad y \coloneqq s \sqrt{ rac{r - a}{2}} , \qquad w \coloneqq x + yi . Then: 1. w^2 = z; 2. for u \in 
C, u^2 = z if and only if u = w or u = -w; 3. w 
e -w. For z = 0: u^2 = 0 if and only if u = 0. In words: every non-zero complex number has exactly two square roots, w and -w, and the formula finds one of them; 0 has exactly one. Try it first (ten minutes): find w with w^2 = 3 + 4i by writing w = x + yi. What do you do with the two equations you get? For 3 + 4i the two equations are x^2 - y^2 = 3 and 2xy = 4. The natural attempt eliminates y = 2/x and arrives at x^4 - 3x^2 - 4 = 0, a quartic; it can be solved, but it hides what is going on, and in general it needs the quadratic formula before we have it. The missing piece is a third equation, and it comes from the modulus. If w^2 = z, then \abs{w}^2 = \abs{w^2} = \abs{z} by @thm-conjugate-properties (d), that is, x^2 + y^2 = r. Now the first equation and the third give x^2 and y^2 by adding and subtracting: x^2 = (r + a)/2, y^2 = (r - a)/2. That fixes x and y up to sign, and the second equation 2xy = b says which signs go together: xy has the sign of b. For 3 + 4i: r = 5, x^2 = 4, y^2 = 1, xy > 0, so w = \pm(2 + i). The proof runs this forward: define x and y by the formulas, check w^2 = z, and get “only \pm w” from the field axioms. Before reading on: why does the sign of b decide whether x and y have the same sign? The proof uses one small rule about real square roots: for p, q \in 
R with p, q \ge 0, \sqrt{p}\,\sqrt{q} = \sqrt{pq} . Both sides are non-negative (a product of non-negative reals is non-negative), and the square of the left side is (\sqrt p)^2 (\sqrt q)^2 = pq, by commutativity; so the left side is the non-negative number whose square is pq, which is the right side by the uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots. The rule is about non-negative reals only; the last part of this section shows that it has no complex version. The roots exist. By @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus, \abs{a} = \abs{\operatorname{Re} z} \le r, so -r \le a \le r (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). Hence r + a \ge 0 and r - a \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), (b)). Halving keeps this: for p \ge 0, either p > 0 and then p/2 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (b), with \varepsilon = p), or p = 0 and then p/2 = 0 \cdot (1/2) = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). So (r + a)/2 \ge 0 and (r - a)/2 \ge 0. So the two square roots in the definition of x and y exist (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). (a) Since s^2 = 1, x^2 - y^2 =  rac{r + a}{2} - s^2 \,  rac{r - a}{2} =  rac{r + a}{2} -  rac{r - a}{2} = a . For the imaginary part, the rule for real square roots gives  egin{aligned} 2xy &= 2s\sqrt{ rac{r + a}{2}}\sqrt{ rac{r - a}{2}} = 2s\sqrt{ rac{r^2 - a^2}{4}} \ &= s\sqrt{r^2 - a^2} = s\sqrt{b^2} = s\abs{b} = b . \end{aligned} Here the third equality is 2\sqrt{t/4} = \sqrt{4}\sqrt{t/4} = \sqrt{t}, by the same rule and \sqrt 4 = 2; the fourth uses r^2 = a^2 + b^2 (@def-conjugate-modulus); the fifth holds because \abs{b} \ge 0 and \abs{b}^2 = b^2 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), (b)), with uniqueness in @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots; and the last because s\abs{b} = b by the definitions of s and of \abs{b} (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field), in each of the two cases b \ge 0 and b < 0. Hence w^2 = (x^2 - y^2) + 2xyi = a + bi = z, by the multiplication rule of @def-complex-numbers. (b) Let u \in 
C. Since 
C is a commutative ring, (u - w)(u + w) = u^2 - w^2 (@prp-complex-arithmetic-laws, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). If u^2 = z, then u^2 - w^2 = z - z = 0 by (a), so (u - w)(u + w) = 0. Since 
C is a field (@thm-complex-numbers-field), it has no zero divisors (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)), so u - w = 0 or u + w = 0, that is, u = w or u = -w. Conversely w^2 = z by (a), and (-w)^2 = w^2 = z by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c). (c) First w 
e 0, since w^2 = z 
e 0 and 0^2 = 0. Suppose w = -w. Then 2w = w + w = 0. But 2 = 1 + 1 
e 0 in 
C: it is the real number 2, which is positive in 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)), and 
R \subseteq 
C by the injective embedding of @prp-reals-embed-complex. So 2w = 0 with 2 
e 0 and w 
e 0 contradicts the absence of zero divisors. Hence w 
e -w. Finally, for z = 0: 0^2 = 0, and if u^2 = u \cdot u = 0, then u = 0 by @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d). This proves the proposition. The answer to the prompt: x is non-negative by construction, and y is s times a non-negative number, so xy is s times a non-negative number, and 2xy must equal b. If b > 0, then x and y must both be non-zero with the same sign; if b < 0, opposite signs. When b = 0 the choice of s does not matter, because then one of x, y is 0. The proposition proves what Logic and Proof, Section 7.1 assumed, and it is stronger: it counts the roots. It uses only the field 
C, its modulus, and square roots of non-negative reals; no angle, cosine or sine appears. That matters later: Chapter 7 proves the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra using square roots in exactly this form. [Square Roots of 5 - 12i] Find all w \in 
C with w^2 = 5 - 12i. Write w = x + yi with x, y \in 
R. Comparing real and imaginary parts in (x^2 - y^2) + 2xyi = 5 - 12i gives x^2 - y^2 = 5 \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad xy = -6 . Taking moduli, by @thm-conjugate-properties (d), x^2 + y^2 = \abs{w}^2 = \abs{5 - 12i} = \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13. Adding and subtracting, x^2 = 9 and y^2 = 4, so x = \pm 3 and y = \pm 2. Since xy = -6 < 0, x and y have opposite signs. Hence w = 3 - 2i or w = -3 + 2i. Check: (3 - 2i)^2 = 9 - 12i + 4i^2 = 5 - 12i, and (-3 + 2i)^2 = (3 - 2i)^2. The formula of @prp-complex-square-roots gives the same root: a = 5, b = -12 < 0, so s = -1; r = 13, x = \sqrt{18/2} = 3 and y = -\sqrt{8/2} = -2. By part (b) there are no other roots. Find the square roots of -4 and of 2i. For -4: a = -4, b = 0, r = 4, so x = \sqrt{0} = 0 and y = \sqrt{8/2} = 2; the roots are \pm 2i, and indeed (2i)^2 = -4. For 2i: a = 0, b = 2, r = 2, so x = \sqrt{1} = 1 and y = 1; the roots are \pm(1 + i), and (1 + i)^2 = 1 + 2i - 1 = 2i. The quadratic formula With square roots in hand, a quadratic equation with complex coefficients is solved exactly as in school: complete the square. The only difference is that we never need to ask whether the discriminant is negative. [Quadratic Formula over the Complex Numbers] Let a, b, c \in 
C with a 
e 0, and let d \in 
C be a square root of b^2 - 4ac (one exists by @prp-complex-square-roots). Then for z \in 
C, az^2 + bz + c = 0 \iff z =  rac{-b + d}{2a} \ 	ext{ or } \ z =  rac{-b - d}{2a} . The two solutions coincide if and only if b^2 - 4ac = 0. Here a, b, c are complex numbers, in a departure from the chapter’s habit of reserving these letters for reals; the statement is the school formula, and keeps its letters. The choice of d does not matter: the other square root is -d (@prp-complex-square-roots (b)), which swaps the two solutions. Complete the square, as in school: after multiplying by 4a, the equation says that 2az + b is a square root of b^2 - 4ac. The square roots of b^2 - 4ac are exactly d and -d, and solving the two linear equations 2az + b = \pm d gives the formula. Multiply by 4a and complete the square. By the ring laws (@prp-complex-arithmetic-laws) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d), 4a(az^2 + bz + c) = 4a^2z^2 + 4abz + 4ac = (2az + b)^2 - (b^2 - 4ac) . Now 4a 
e 0, since 4 
e 0 in 
C (as for 2 in the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots (c)) and a 
e 0, and 
C has no zero divisors (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)). So az^2 + bz + c = 0 if and only if (2az + b)^2 = d^2, that is, (2az + b - d)(2az + b + d) = 0, as in the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots (b). By the absence of zero divisors again, this holds if and only if 2az + b = d or 2az + b = -d. Since 2a 
e 0, these say z = (-b + d)/(2a) or z = (-b - d)/(2a). The two solutions coincide if and only if d = -d, that is, 2d = 0, that is, d = 0 (as 2 
e 0). And d = 0 if and only if d^2 = 0 (no zero divisors), that is, b^2 - 4ac = 0. This proves the corollary. Example. Solve z^2 - (3 + i)z + (2 + 2i) = 0. Here a = 1, and the discriminant is (3 + i)^2 - 4(2 + 2i) = (8 + 6i) - (8 + 8i) = -2i . The formula of @prp-complex-square-roots, applied to -2i (real part 0, imaginary part -2 < 0, modulus 2), gives x = \sqrt{2/2} = 1 and y = -\sqrt{2/2} = -1, so d = 1 - i; indeed (1 - i)^2 = 1 - 2i - 1 = -2i. The solutions are z =  rac{(3 + i) + (1 - i)}{2} = 2 \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad z =  rac{(3 + i) - (1 - i)}{2} = 1 + i . Check: their sum is 3 + i and their product is 2 + 2i, the negative of the middle coefficient and the constant term, as they should be for (z - 2)(z - (1 + i)). No order on the complex numbers In 
R, and in every ordered field, a non-zero square is positive (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). In 
C, i is non-zero and its square is -1. If 
C carried an order of the kind 
R has, -1 would have to be positive, and so would 1. That is already the proof. [The Complex Numbers Cannot Be Ordered] There is no relation < on 
C with which (
C, +, \cdot, <) is an ordered field in the sense of @fd3:def-ordered-ring-and-field. Suppose < is a relation on 
C with which 
C is an ordered field. Since i = (0, 1) 
e (0, 0) = 0, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) gives i^2 > 0, that is, -1 > 0 (@prp-reals-embed-complex: i \cdot i = -1). Since 1 
e 0 in the field 
C, the same part (e) gives 1 > 0. Adding, by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), 0 = 1 + (-1) > 0 + 0 = 0. But 0 < 0 is impossible: (O1), with both elements equal to 0, says that exactly one of 0 < 0 and 0 = 0 holds, and 0 = 0 does. So no such relation exists. The proof never asks whether i > 0 or i < 0: part (e) covers both at once. It also never assumes that the hypothetical order agrees with the order of 
R on real numbers. It concludes 1 > 0 and -1 > 0 in whatever order is supposed, and that is the contradiction. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 showed, in an exercise (@fd3:exr-rules-and-absolute-value-c1), that a field containing a square root of -1 cannot be ordered, and named the complex numbers as such a field; the proposition proves that fact for 
C on its own. Compare @fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable, and the integers modulo 3 of Exercise C2 below: there the obstacle to an order is n \cdot 1 = 0 for some n \ge 1. That obstacle is absent here, since n \cdot 1 in 
C is \iota(n \cdot 1), the image of the real number n \cdot 1 > 0 of 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)), which is non-zero as \iota is injective. (The identity n \cdot 1 = \iota(n \cdot 1) is proved by @fd1:ax-induction on n, as for powers in Section 3.1: 0 \cdot 1 = 0 = \iota(0), and if n \cdot 1 = \iota(n \cdot 1), then (n + 1) \cdot 1 = \iota(n \cdot 1) + \iota(1) = \iota((n + 1) \cdot 1) by @prp-reals-embed-complex.) The obstacle in 
C is i^2 = -1 instead. An inequality z < w between complex numbers means nothing: by @prp-complex-not-orderable no order on 
C is compatible with its arithmetic. Apart from arguments that suppose an order on 
C in order to reach a contradiction (the proof above and Exercises B2 and C2), every inequality in this chapter compares real numbers in the order of 
R: moduli, real parts, imaginary parts, or quantities proved to be real, as 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) was in Section 3.3. Writing i > 0 leads, by the proof above, to 0 > 0; so does writing i < 0. Is the following a proof that 
C cannot be ordered? “Every real square is \ge 0, and i^2 = -1 < 0. So i is not a square of anything, a contradiction.” No. The argument proves nothing about orders on 
C. “-1 < 0” is a statement in 
R’s order, and a hypothetical order on 
C need not agree with it on the reals; the argument never even introduces the hypothetical order. And “i is not a square” is false: i = (\pm(1 + i)/\sqrt 2)^2 by @prp-complex-square-roots. The correct proof works inside the supposed order, where i^2 > 0 because i 
e 0. The square-root rule does not survive In 
R, \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y} = \sqrt{xy} for x, y \ge 0: that is the rule for real square roots used above. A non-zero complex number has two square roots and no preferred one, and no way of preferring one keeps the rule alive. No choice of “the” square root \sqrt{z} of each complex z can satisfy \sqrt{z}\sqrt{w} = \sqrt{zw} for all z, w \in 
C. Whatever is chosen for \sqrt{-1}, it is i or -i (@prp-complex-square-roots (b)), and in both cases \sqrt{-1} \cdot \sqrt{-1} = (\pm i)^2 = -1. But \sqrt{(-1)(-1)} = \sqrt{1}, and the rule itself forces \sqrt{1} = 1: since \sqrt{1} is a square root of 1, 1 = \sqrt{1} \cdot \sqrt{1} = \sqrt{1 \cdot 1} = \sqrt{1}. So the rule would give -1 = 1, which is false in 
C (the real parts -1 < 1 differ). So in this volume the symbol \sqrt{\phantom{x}} is applied only to non-negative reals; for any other z, say “a square root of z” and solve w^2 = z. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. True or false: if z, w \in 
C and z^2 = w^2, then z = w. Justify your answer, and state what is true. 2. Run the formula of @prp-complex-square-roots on z = -4: compute a, b, r, s, x, y and both square roots. 3. Where in the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots is r \ge \abs{a} used? 4. State the idea of the proof of @prp-complex-square-roots in two sentences. (a) False: z = 1, w = -1 have z^2 = w^2 = 1 and z 
e w. What is true: z^2 = w^2 implies z = w or z = -w, since (z - w)(z + w) = z^2 - w^2 = 0 and 
C has no zero divisors (this is the argument of @prp-complex-square-roots (b)). (b) a = -4, b = 0, r = \abs{-4} = 4, s = 1 (as b \ge 0), x = \sqrt{(4 - 4)/2} = 0, y = \sqrt{(4 + 4)/2} = 2. So w = 2i, and the square roots are \pm 2i. (c) To take the square roots at all: r \ge \abs{a} gives r + a \ge 0 and r - a \ge 0, so \sqrt{(r + a)/2} and \sqrt{(r - a)/2} exist. (d) Comparing parts gives x^2 - y^2 = a and 2xy = b; taking moduli gives a third equation x^2 + y^2 = r, and the first and third give x^2 and y^2 by adding and subtracting. The signs are then fixed by 2xy = b, and the absence of zero divisors shows that \pm w are the only roots. B. Practice [B1] 1. Find all w \in 
C with w^2 = -3 + 4i. 2. Hence solve z^2 + 2z + 4 - 4i = 0. (a) Write w = x + yi. Comparing parts, x^2 - y^2 = -3 and xy = 2. Taking moduli (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)), x^2 + y^2 = \abs{-3 + 4i} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5. Adding and subtracting, x^2 = 1 and y^2 = 4. Since xy = 2 > 0, x and y have the same sign, so w = 1 + 2i or w = -1 - 2i, and by @prp-complex-square-roots (b) there are no others. Check: (1 + 2i)^2 = 1 + 4i - 4 = -3 + 4i. (b) By @cor-complex-quadratic-formula with a = 1, b = 2, c = 4 - 4i: the discriminant is 4 - 4(4 - 4i) = -12 + 16i = 4(-3 + 4i), with square root d = 2(1 + 2i) = 2 + 4i by (a), since (2(1 + 2i))^2 = 4(1 + 2i)^2. So z =  rac{-2 + (2 + 4i)}{2} = 2i \qquad 	ext{or} \qquad z =  rac{-2 - (2 + 4i)}{2} = -2 - 2i . Equivalently, completing the square, z^2 + 2z + 4 - 4i = (z + 1)^2 - (-3 + 4i), so z + 1 = \pm(1 + 2i). Check: (2i)^2 + 2(2i) + 4 - 4i = -4 + 4i + 4 - 4i = 0. [B2: Put the proof in order] The nine lines below include the seven lines of a proof of @prp-complex-not-orderable, shuffled, and two lines that do not belong. Write the seven lines in an order that makes a proof, and say what is wrong with each of the other two. 1. i^2 = -1, so -1 > 0. 2. Since i 
e 0, we have i > 0. 3. Suppose < is a relation on 
C that makes 
C an ordered field. 4. 0 < 0 is impossible by (O1), so no such relation exists. 5. So i^2 > 0, because non-zero squares are positive in an ordered field. 6. 1 
e 0, so 1 = 1^2 > 0. 7. i^2 = -1 < 0, because -1 < 0 in 
R. 8. i 
e 0, since i = (0, 1) 
e (0, 0). 9. Adding, 0 = 1 + (-1) > 0 + 0 = 0. An admissible order is (iii), (viii), (v), (i), (vi), (ix), (iv). The constraints are what each line uses: (v), (vi), (i), (ix) and (iv) work in the supposed order, so they come after (iii); (v) also uses (viii); (i) uses (v); (ix) uses (i) and (vi); (iv) uses (ix). Line (viii) is a fact about 
C and uses no order, so it may stand anywhere before (v), even before (iii); line (vi) may stand anywhere after (iii) and before (ix). For instance (iii), (vi), (viii), (v), (i), (ix), (iv) and (viii), (iii), (v), (i), (vi), (ix), (iv) are also admissible. The admissible orders are exactly those that respect these constraints. Line (ii) drops a case: from i 
e 0, trichotomy (O1) gives i > 0 or i < 0, and the line keeps only the first. That is (N7) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, a missing case. Line (v) needs neither case, which is why the proof does not split. Line (vii) cites a reason that is not available: the supposed order on 
C is arbitrary, and nothing says that it agrees with the order of 
R on the real numbers. The proposition is about every relation on 
C, and (vii) quietly replaces “every” by “one that extends 
R’s order”. (The inequality -1 < 0 does hold in any ordered field, by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) applied to 1 > 0, so the line could be repaired by citing that; as written its reason is (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, a fact that is not available.) [B3] Let a, b, c \in 
R with a 
e 0 and b^2 - 4ac < 0. Prove that the equation az^2 + bz + c = 0 has exactly the two solutions z =  rac{-b + i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a} \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad z =  rac{-b - i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a} in 
C, and that they are conjugate to each other. Since 4ac - b^2 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a)), q \coloneqq \sqrt{4ac - b^2} exists, q > 0, and d \coloneqq iq satisfies d^2 = i^2 q^2 = -(4ac - b^2) = b^2 - 4ac. So @cor-complex-quadratic-formula with this d gives exactly the two solutions displayed, and they are distinct since b^2 - 4ac 
e 0. Since a, b, q are real and 2a 
e 0, the two solutions are - rac{b}{2a} +  rac{q}{2a}\, i \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad - rac{b}{2a} -  rac{q}{2a}\, i , with the same real part and opposite imaginary parts: each is the conjugate of the other (@def-conjugate-modulus). For instance z^2 - 2z + 5 = 0 has b^2 - 4ac = -16, q = 4, and the solutions 1 \pm 2i. C. Going deeper [C1: Find the error] Here is an argument. Claim. For z, w \in 
C, if z^2 = w^2, then z = w or z = -w. Proof. If w = 0, then z^2 = 0, so z = 0 = w, since 
C has no zero divisors. If w 
e 0, put u \coloneqq z/w, which exists because 
C is a field; then u^2 = z^2/w^2 = 1. Taking square roots, u = \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1. In particular, u = 1 or u = -1. Multiplying by w, z = w or z = -w. Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails and the reason, give a counterexample to that line, and repair the argument. The claim is true: it is the argument of @prp-complex-square-roots (b), and it also follows directly from (z - w)(z + w) = z^2 - w^2 = 0 and the absence of zero divisors in 
C. The argument does not prove it. The failing line is “u = \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1”. It uses the rule “u = \sqrt{u^2} whenever u^2 is a non-negative real”, which is neither proved nor true: it is a general “fact” of the kind (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue forbids. The symbol \sqrt{\phantom{x}} is defined only on non-negative reals, and u is a complex number; even for real u, \sqrt{u^2} = \abs{u}, not u. Counterexample to the step: u = -1 has u^2 = 1, but \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1 
e u. The next line, “u = 1 or u = -1”, is a valid weakening of u = 1 (a disjunction follows from either part), so it is not itself an error; it only papers over the loss of the root -1 one line earlier. The rest of the argument (the case w = 0, the division, and multiplying back by w) is correct. Repair: replace the two middle lines by “Then (u - 1)(u + 1) = u^2 - 1 = 0, and 
C has no zero divisors, so u = 1 or u = -1.” Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the claim is true, with a reason. - 3: names the line u = \sqrt{u^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1 as the failing one, and its illegal rule u = \sqrt{u^2}. - 2: a counterexample to that step (u = -1, or any u with u^2 = 1, u 
e 1). - 3: a correct repair, by factoring u^2 - 1 and using no zero divisors (or by @prp-complex-square-roots (b) applied to z = 1). Fatal errors (0 for the step): declaring the claim false; naming the “In particular” line instead of the \sqrt{\phantom{x}} line as the failing one, since it is a valid weakening. [C2: A second proof that there is no order] 1. Use @prp-complex-square-roots to give a second proof of @prp-complex-not-orderable in which the element i is never mentioned. 2. Say why the argument in (a) does not need the special element i. 3. Is the converse of the principle behind (a) true? That is: if a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 admits no order, must -1 be a square in it? Test the ring 
Z/3
Z. [Hint 1] In an ordered field, which elements can be squares? For (c), list the squares of the three classes. (a) Suppose < makes 
C an ordered field. Every square is then \ge 0: a non-zero square is positive by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), and 0^2 = 0. First, -1 
e 0, since otherwise 1 = -(-1) = -0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), against 1 
e 0 in the field 
C (@thm-complex-numbers-field). By @prp-complex-square-roots (a), applied to the non-zero number -1, some d \in 
C has d^2 = -1. So -1 = d^2 \ge 0, and as -1 
e 0, -1 > 0. By part (e) again, 1 > 0. Adding (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), 0 = 1 + (-1) > 0, which (O1) forbids. This is the argument of @fd3:exr-rules-and-absolute-value-c1, with the square root of -1 supplied by a formula. (b) The argument uses only that -1 is a square in 
C, and that is a property of the field, not of any named element. It does not matter that the formula of @prp-complex-square-roots, applied to -1, happens to produce i (a = -1, b = 0, r = 1: x = 0, y = 1). The same argument shows that no field in which -1 is a square can be ordered; in particular no field in which every element is a square. (c) No. The ring 
Z/3
Z has the class operations [a] + [b] = [a + b] and [a][b] = [ab], well defined by @fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic, and each law of a commutative ring holds because it holds for representatives in 
Z. Its three elements are [0], [1], [2], pairwise different (@fd2:prp-integers-mod-n), so [1] 
e [0]. No relation makes it an ordered commutative ring: in an ordered commutative ring with 1 
e 0, 1 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), so 1 + 1 + 1 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b)), while here [1] + [1] + [1] = [3] = [0]. with squares [0]^2 = [0], [1]^2 = [1], [2]^2 = [4] = [1]. So the squares are [0] and [1], while -[1] = [2]. Hence -1 is not a square in 
Z/3
Z, and yet the ring cannot be ordered: the obstacle there is 3 \cdot [1] = [0], not a square root of -1.

title: 3.5 The Unit Circle and Polar Form
content:
The Unit Circle and Polar Form Addition in 
C is addition of arrows in the plane: (a, b) + (c, d) = (a + c, b + d) puts the second arrow at the tip of the first. Multiplication has a picture too, and Section 3.2 already holds half of it: the modulus of a product is the product of the moduli (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)). The other half is about angles, and angles need the functions cosine and sine, which this volume does not construct. This section first proves everything about directions that needs no angle at all, then states exactly five facts about cosine and sine that it borrows, and from those five builds the polar form of a complex number and the rule “multiply the lengths, add the angles”. Length and direction Every non-zero complex number should be a length times a direction. The length is the modulus. The directions are the complex numbers of length 1, and they deserve a name. The unit circle is the set of complex numbers at distance 1 from 0. We write 
T \coloneqq \{ u \in 
C : \abs{u} = 1 \} for the unit circle. For u = x + yi with x, y \in 
R, the condition \abs{u} = 1 says \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = 1, that is, x^2 + y^2 = 1: both sides of the first equation are non-negative, so it holds exactly when the squares agree (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). So 
T is the circle of radius 1 about 0 in the plane. It contains 1, -1, i and -i, and also 	frac35 + 	frac45 i, since 	frac{9}{25} + 	frac{16}{25} = 1. It does not contain 1 + i, whose modulus is \sqrt 2 
e 1. The next proposition collects what the multiplication of 
C does on 
T. None of it uses an angle. [The Unit Circle] 1. 1 \in 
T. If u, v \in 
T, then uv \in 
T. If u \in 
T, then u 
e 0 and u^{-1} = \conj{u} \in 
T. 2. For every z \in 
C with z 
e 0 there is exactly one pair (r, u) with r \in 
R, r > 0, u \in 
T and z = ru, namely r = \abs{z} and u = z / \abs{z}. 3. For z \in 
C with z 
e 0: 1/z = \conj{z} if and only if \abs{z} = 1. Every part is a statement about moduli, so each follows from the rules of Section 3.2: moduli multiply, u\conj{u} = \abs{u}^2, and only 0 has modulus 0. For (b), divide z by its length; for the uniqueness, take moduli of z = ru. (a) By @prp-modulus-of-real, the modulus of the real number 1 is its absolute value, which is 1; so 1 \in 
T. If \abs{u} = \abs{v} = 1, then \abs{uv} = \abs{u}\abs{v} = 1 by @thm-conjugate-properties (d). Let u \in 
T. Then u 
e 0, since \abs{0} = 0 
e 1 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)). By @thm-conjugate-properties (c), u \conj{u} = \abs{u}^2 = 1, so \conj{u} satisfies the defining equation of u^{-1}. Since 
C is a field (@thm-complex-numbers-field), inverses are unique (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)), and u^{-1} = \conj{u}. Finally \abs{\conj{u}} = \abs{u} = 1 by @thm-conjugate-properties (d). (b) Existence. Let r \coloneqq \abs{z}. Then r \ge 0, and r 
e 0 because z 
e 0 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)); so r > 0, and its inverse r^{-1} is a positive real number (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (a)). By @thm-complex-numbers-field the inverse of r in 
C is this real number, so u \coloneqq z / \abs{z} = r^{-1} z is defined, and z = r u. By @thm-conjugate-properties (d) and @prp-modulus-of-real, \abs{u} = \abs{r^{-1}} \abs{z} = r^{-1} r = 1, where \abs{r^{-1}} = r^{-1} because the absolute value of a positive real number is the number itself (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field). So u \in 
T. Uniqueness. Let z = r u with r > 0 and u \in 
T. Taking moduli, \abs{z} = \abs{r} \abs{u} = r \cdot 1 = r, again by @thm-conjugate-properties (d) and @prp-modulus-of-real. Then u = r^{-1} z = z / \abs{z}. So the pair is the one named in the statement. (c) Since inverses are unique, 1/z = \conj{z} holds if and only if z \conj{z} = 1, that is, by @thm-conjugate-properties (c), if and only if \abs{z}^2 = 1 = 1^2. Both \abs{z} and 1 are non-negative, so by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) neither can be strictly smaller than the other, and \abs{z}^2 = 1 holds if and only if \abs{z} = 1. Part (b) is the picture we wanted: z = \abs{z} \cdot u, a length times a direction, and both factors are forced. Part (a) says that the directions are closed under multiplication and inversion and contain 1; Chapter 5 calls a set with these properties, under an associative product, a group, and 
T is one of its first examples. Part (c) is a practical test: on the unit circle, and only there, dividing by z is the same as conjugating. Write z = 3 + 4i as r u with r > 0 and u \in 
T. What is 1/u? By @prp-unit-circle (b), r = \abs{3 + 4i} = 5 and u = 	frac35 + 	frac45 i. By (a), 1/u = \conj{u} = 	frac35 - 	frac45 i. Check:  ig(	frac35 + 	frac45 i ig) ig(	frac35 - 	frac45 i ig) = 	frac{9}{25} + 	frac{16}{25} = 1. So far a direction is a point u of 
T, and multiplying two directions gives a third. What we cannot yet say is how much a direction turns the plane. For that we need to measure positions on the circle by a real number, an angle, so that multiplying directions adds angles. That is a job for cosine and sine. What this volume borrows about cosine and sine An angle should be a real number 	heta that walks around the circle: a point (\cos	heta, \sin	heta) on 
T, moving as 	heta moves, returning to its start after a full turn of length 2\pi. Defining such functions needs limits of functions, by power series or by integrals. This volume develops no limits of functions, so it does not define cosine and sine. Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 7 does: there \cos and \sin are defined by power series, \pi is defined as twice the least positive zero of \cos, and the facts below are proved. Its 
R is a complete ordered field, so by @fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness it is our 
R, up to the one order-preserving field isomorphism; the functions and the number carry over along it. We write 2\pi
Z \coloneqq \{ 2\pi k : k \in 
Z \}, the integer multiples of 2\pi in 
R. What This Volume Borrows about Cosine and Sine There are functions \cos, \sin \colon 
R 	o 
R and a real number \pi > 0 with the following properties. They are assumed here and proved in Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 7. 1. \cos^2	heta + \sin^2	heta = 1 for every 	heta \in 
R. 2. For all 	heta, \varphi \in 
R,  egin{aligned} \cos(	heta + \varphi) &= \cos	heta \cos\varphi - \sin	heta \sin\varphi , \ \sin(	heta + \varphi) &= \sin	heta \cos\varphi + \cos	heta \sin\varphi . \end{aligned} 3. For 	heta \in 
R: \cos	heta = 1 if and only if 	heta \in 2\pi
Z. 4. For every (x, y) \in 
R^2 with x^2 + y^2 = 1 there is 	heta \in 
R with \cos	heta = x and \sin	heta = y. 5. \sin	heta > 0 whenever 0 < 	heta < \pi. In words: (T1) puts the point (\cos	heta, \sin	heta) on the unit circle; (T2) is the pair of addition formulas; (T3) says that the cosine reaches 1 exactly at the multiples of a full turn; (T4) says that every point of the circle is reached; (T5) says that during the first half turn the point stays in the upper half plane. This box is where the chapter borrows. Like @fd1:ax-induction, which Logic and Proof assumed and Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 proved, it is a statement assumed in one volume and proved in another. Nothing in Sections 3.1–3.4, and nothing in this section above the box, uses it. From here on we use these five facts about \cos, \sin and \pi and no others: no value such as \cos(\pi/3) = 	frac12, no periodicity, no picture of a graph. Whatever else we need, we derive, and each proof that uses one of the facts names it by its number. Two consequences come at once. - \cos 0 = 1, by (T3), since 0 = 2\pi \cdot 0 \in 2\pi
Z. Then (T1) gives \sin^2 0 = 1 - 1 = 0, so \sin 0 = 0, because a non-zero real number has a positive square (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). - \cos(2\pi k) = 1 and \sin(2\pi k) = 0 for every k \in 
Z, by (T3) and then (T1) in the same way. The five facts are about \cos, \sin and \pi only. A school fact such as \sin(\pi/6) = 	frac12 is not among them, and a proof in this volume may not quote it: @exm-special-angles below derives the few values we use. Nor do the facts say that \cos and \sin are “periodic with period 2\pi” as functions; that is true, and derivable from (T2) and (T3), but no proof here needs it. Polar form With angles available, we can name the point of 
T at angle 	heta. e^{i	heta} is the point of the unit circle at angle 	heta. Polar Form For 	heta \in 
R we write e^{i	heta} \coloneqq \cos	heta + i \sin	heta . Let z \in 
C with z 
e 0. A polar form of z is an expression z = r e^{i	heta} with r \in 
R, r > 0, and 	heta \in 
R. Then 	heta is an argument of z. In words: the first line is an abbreviation, not an exponential. Until Chapter 8 this volume has no exponential function. Even there, e^{i	heta} stays an abbreviation, because Chapter 8’s \exp takes only real arguments. The only rule of exponents we will use for e^{i	heta} is the one proved below (@thm-polar-multiplication (a)). Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 7 shows that e^{i	heta} is indeed the value of the complex exponential function at i	heta; the notation anticipates that, and the linear algebra volumes write their roots of unity with it. The exponent may be written in any form equal to i	heta with 	heta real, and the symbol then means e^{i	heta}: for example e^{-i	heta} = e^{i(-	heta)}, e^{2\pi i} = e^{i \cdot 2\pi}, e^{in	heta} = e^{i(n	heta)} and e^{-2\pi i} = e^{i(-2\pi)}. This is unambiguous, because the real number 	heta is determined by i	heta (it is its imaginary part). The second part asks for a positive real r and allows any real 	heta. The point e^{i	heta} lies on 
T. Indeed \abs{e^{i	heta}} = \sqrt{\cos^2	heta + \sin^2	heta} = \sqrt 1 = 1, by @def-conjugate-modulus and (T1). So r e^{i	heta} is a length r times a direction, as in @prp-unit-circle (b), and that proposition gives r = \abs{z} for every polar form of z. Examples. - e^{i0} = \cos 0 + i \sin 0 = 1, by the consequences of the box. So 1 = 1 \cdot e^{i0} and 5 = 5 e^{i0} are polar forms. - e^{2\pi i} = \cos 2\pi + i \sin 2\pi = 1, by the second consequence with k = 1. So 1 = 1 \cdot e^{2\pi i} as well: 0 and 2\pi are both arguments of 1, and they differ, since \pi > 0. - The number 0 has no polar form, since \abs{r e^{i	heta}} = r > 0. A non-example by minimal change. Allow r < 0: then -1 = (-1) \cdot e^{i0} looks like a polar form of -1 with argument 0. The clause that fails is r > 0, and it matters: with negative r allowed, the length could no longer be read off as \abs{z}, and 1 = 1 \cdot e^{i0} and -1 = (-1) e^{i0} would share the argument 0. We will see in @exm-special-angles that -1 = 1 \cdot e^{i\pi} is a genuine polar form. The examples already show why the definition says an argument: 1 = e^{i0} = e^{2\pi i}. How much freedom there is, exactly, is part (b) of @prp-polar-form below. First, the reason for the notation: these numbers multiply the way exponentials do. [Multiplication in Polar Form] 1. e^{i	heta} e^{i\varphi} = e^{i(	heta + \varphi)} for all 	heta, \varphi \in 
R. 2. e^{i0} = 1, and (e^{i	heta})^{-1} = e^{-i	heta} = \conj{e^{i	heta}} for every 	heta \in 
R. 3. If r, s \in 
R with r, s > 0 and 	heta, \varphi \in 
R, then (r e^{i	heta})(s e^{i\varphi}) = rs \, e^{i(	heta + \varphi)}, and this is a polar form of the product. Multiply out (\cos	heta + i\sin	heta)(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi) with the rule of @def-complex-numbers: the real and imaginary parts that appear are exactly the right-hand sides of the addition formulas (T2). The rest is bookkeeping with inverses and moduli. (a) By the multiplication rule of @def-complex-numbers,  egin{aligned} e^{i	heta} e^{i\varphi} &= (\cos	heta\cos\varphi - \sin	heta\sin\varphi) + (\cos	heta\sin\varphi + \sin	heta\cos\varphi) i \ &= \cos(	heta + \varphi) + i \sin(	heta + \varphi) , \end{aligned} where the second equality is (T2), with the two products in the imaginary part reordered by commutativity in 
R. The right-hand side is e^{i(	heta + \varphi)}. (b) e^{i0} = 1 was shown in the first example above. By (a) with \varphi = -	heta, e^{i	heta} e^{-i	heta} = e^{i0} = 1, so e^{-i	heta} is the inverse of e^{i	heta}, by uniqueness of inverses in the field 
C (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (a)). Since e^{i	heta} \in 
T, its inverse is also its conjugate (@prp-unit-circle (a)). (c) By @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws (commutativity and associativity of \cdot), (r e^{i	heta})(s e^{i\varphi}) = (rs)(e^{i	heta} e^{i\varphi}), and (a) turns this into rs \, e^{i(	heta + \varphi)}. Here rs > 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c) (multiply 0 < r by s > 0), so this is a polar form. In words: to multiply two complex numbers, multiply their moduli and add their arguments. This is the chapter’s third named move, multiply moduli, add angles. Multiplying by a fixed w = s e^{i\varphi} therefore turns the plane about 0 by the angle \varphi and stretches it by the factor s. The picture shows z, w and zw for \abs{z} = 1.5, \abs{w} = 1.2, and arguments of 20^\circ and 50^\circ (a full turn being 360^\circ, that is, 2\pi). The arrow for zw has length 1.5 	imes 1.2 = 1.8 and makes the angle 20^\circ + 50^\circ = 70^\circ with the positive real axis: it is the arrow for z, turned by the argument of w and stretched by the modulus of w. The small arc marks the argument of z, the large arc the extra turn by the argument of w, and the dashed arc is part of the unit circle, where the numbers e^{i	heta} live. Now the freedom in the argument. Every non-zero number has a polar form, and its arguments are determined up to a whole number of full turns. [Existence and Uniqueness of Polar Form] 1. Every z \in 
C with z 
e 0 has a polar form, and every polar form z = r e^{i	heta} has r = \abs{z}. 2. For r, s \in 
R with r, s > 0 and 	heta, \varphi \in 
R, r e^{i	heta} = s e^{i\varphi} \iff r = s 	ext{ and } 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z . (a) By @prp-unit-circle (b), z = \abs{z} \cdot u with u = x + yi \in 
T, so x^2 + y^2 = 1. By (T4) there is 	heta \in 
R with \cos	heta = x and \sin	heta = y, that is, u = e^{i	heta}. Hence z = \abs{z} e^{i	heta}, with \abs{z} > 0. Conversely, if z = r e^{i	heta} is a polar form, then e^{i	heta} \in 
T, and the uniqueness in @prp-unit-circle (b) gives r = \abs{z}. (b) Suppose first that r e^{i	heta} = s e^{i\varphi}. The number r e^{i	heta} is non-zero: r 
e 0, e^{i	heta} \in 
T is non-zero (@prp-unit-circle (a)), and a product of non-zero elements of the field 
C is non-zero (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)). So both sides are polar forms of the same non-zero number, and r = s by (a). Multiplying by r^{-1} gives e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi}. In the other direction, if r = s, the two sides are equal exactly when e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi}. So it remains to show that e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} if and only if 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z. Multiplying by e^{-i\varphi}, and back by e^{i\varphi}, shows that e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} holds if and only if e^{i	heta} e^{-i\varphi} = e^{i\varphi} e^{-i\varphi}, that is, by @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and (b), if and only if e^{i(	heta - \varphi)} = 1. Comparing real and imaginary parts, this says \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1 and \sin(	heta - \varphi) = 0. The second condition follows from the first: by (T1), \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1 gives \sin^2(	heta - \varphi) = 0, hence \sin(	heta - \varphi) = 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} if and only if \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1, and by (T3) that holds if and only if 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z. Existence came from (T4), and uniqueness from (T3), with (T1) helping and (T2) entering through @thm-polar-multiplication. “Comparing arguments” therefore always means comparing them up to a multiple of 2\pi, and the next warning is the trap this sets. From e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} one may not conclude 	heta = \varphi: e^{i0} = e^{2\pi i} = 1, and 0 
e 2\pi. Only 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z follows (@prp-polar-form (b)). Forgetting this loses solutions as soon as an equation is solved for an angle; Section 3.6 meets an equation where it would lose all but one of them. Powers Repeating @thm-polar-multiplication gives powers. The powers z^n are those of the recursion z^0 = 1, z^{n+1} = z^n z of Chapter 1, Section 1.1. [De Moivre’s Formula] For every 	heta \in 
R and every n \in 
N,  igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^n = e^{in	heta} , \quad 	ext{that is,} \quad (\cos	heta + i\sin	heta)^n = \cos n	heta + i \sin n	heta . Consequently (r e^{i	heta})^n = r^n e^{in	heta} for every real r > 0, and this is a polar form. A power is a repeated product, and each new factor e^{i	heta} adds 	heta to the argument, by @thm-polar-multiplication (a). So induction on n, along the recursion z^{n+1} = z^n z. We use @fd1:ax-induction on n, read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b); here n	heta is the product in 
R of n \cdot 1_{
R} and 	heta (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a)). For n = 0, the left side is (e^{i	heta})^0 = 1 by the recursion, and the right side is e^{i0} = 1 by @thm-polar-multiplication (b). Suppose (e^{i	heta})^n = e^{in	heta} for some n \in 
N. Then  igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^{n+1} =  igl(e^{i	heta} igr)^n e^{i	heta} = e^{in	heta} e^{i	heta} = e^{i(n	heta + 	heta)} = e^{i(n+1)	heta} , by the recursion, the induction hypothesis, @thm-polar-multiplication (a), and (n + 1) \cdot 1_{
R} = n \cdot 1_{
R} + 1_{
R} (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field (a)) with distributivity in 
R. This proves the formula for every n \in 
N. For the consequence, @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (c) gives (r e^{i	heta})^n = r^n (e^{i	heta})^n = r^n e^{in	heta}. The power r^n is the same whether it is computed in 
R or in 
C, since the embedding of 
R in 
C preserves powers (Section 3.1), and r^n > 0 because a product of positive reals is positive (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c); induction on n, with r^0 = 1 > 0). For a negative exponent, z^{-n} is the integer power of @def-integer-power (
C is a field, by Section 3.2), and Exercise C1 below proves the matching formula; nothing in the text uses it. The five borrowed facts give no particular value of \cos or \sin except at multiples of 2\pi. Every other value this chapter uses is derived next, from (T1)–(T5) and the algebra of Sections 3.1–3.4. [Special Angles] Show, using only (T1)–(T5) and the results proved so far, that  egin{aligned} &e^{i\pi} = -1, \qquad e^{i\pi/2} = i, \qquad e^{i\pi/3} = 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i, \ &e^{i\pi/6} = 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} + 	frac12 i, \qquad e^{i\pi/4} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} + 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} i . \end{aligned} Each value is found the same way: a power of the unknown point is a point we already know, and (T5) chooses between the candidates. Since \pi > 0, each of \pi/2, \pi/3, \pi/4, \pi/6 lies strictly between 0 and \pi, so (T5) gives \operatorname{Im} e^{i	heta} = \sin	heta > 0 for each of them. (i) e^{i\pi} = -1. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi}. By @thm-de-moivre, u^2 = e^{2\pi i} = 1, so (u - 1)(u + 1) = u^2 - 1 = 0, and since 
C has no zero divisors (@thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d)), u = 1 or u = -1. Suppose u = 1. Then \cos\pi = 1, so \pi = 2\pi k for some k \in 
Z by (T3); dividing by \pi 
e 0 gives 1 = 2k in 
R, an equation between images of integers. The embedding of 
Z into 
R, through 
Q (@fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals) and \kappa (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), is injective and preserves + and \cdot, so 1 = 2k holds in 
Z. But 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, and an odd integer is not of the form 2k (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a)). So u 
e 1, and e^{i\pi} = -1. (ii) e^{i\pi/2} = i. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi/2}. By @thm-polar-multiplication (a), u^2 = e^{i\pi} = -1 = i^2, so (u - i)(u + i) = 0 and u = \pm i. Since \operatorname{Im} u > 0 and \operatorname{Im}(-i) = -1 < 0, u = i. (iii) e^{i\pi/3} = 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi/3}. By @thm-de-moivre, u^3 = e^{i\pi} = -1. Multiplying out shows (u + 1)(u^2 - u + 1) = u^3 + 1 = 0. Now u 
e -1, since \operatorname{Im} u > 0; so u^2 - u + 1 = 0. By @cor-complex-quadratic-formula with a = 1, b = -1, c = 1, and d \coloneqq \sqrt 3\, i, a square root of b^2 - 4ac = -3 (indeed (\sqrt 3\, i)^2 = 3 i^2 = -3), u =  rac{1 + \sqrt 3\, i}{2} \quad 	ext{or} \quad u =  rac{1 - \sqrt 3\, i}{2} . Since \operatorname{Im} u > 0, u = 	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i. (iv) e^{i\pi/6} = 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} + 	frac12 i. Since \pi/6 = \pi/2 + (-\pi/3), @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and (b) give e^{i\pi/6} = e^{i\pi/2} e^{-i\pi/3} = i \cdot \conj{e^{i\pi/3}} = i \Bigl(  rac12 -  rac{\sqrt 3}{2} i \Bigr) =  rac{\sqrt 3}{2} +  rac12 i , by (ii) and (iii). (v) e^{i\pi/4} = 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} + 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} i. Let u \coloneqq e^{i\pi/4}. By @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and (ii), u^2 = e^{i\pi/2} = i. The formula of @prp-complex-square-roots for z = i (so a = 0, b = 1, r = \abs{i} = 1) gives the square root w = \sqrt{1/2} + \sqrt{1/2}\, i, and \sqrt{1/2} = 1/\sqrt 2, since both are non-negative and square to 	frac12. By @prp-complex-square-roots (b), u = w or u = -w, and \operatorname{Im} u > 0 rules out -w. So u = w. Comparing real and imaginary parts turns these into values of \cos and \sin: --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 	heta 0 \pi/6 \pi/4 \pi/3 \pi/2 \pi ------------ ---------- ----------- ----------- ----------- ---------- ---------- \cos	heta 1 \sqrt 3/2 1/\sqrt 2 1/2 0 -1 \sin	heta 0 1/2 1/\sqrt 2 \sqrt 3/2 1 0 --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- These are the familiar values, now proved from the five facts. Two special cases of the rotation picture are worth isolating. Multiplying by i = e^{i\pi/2} turns the plane by a quarter turn, counterclockwise; two quarter turns make a half turn, and this is the picture behind i^2 = -1 = e^{i\pi}. And multiplying by e^{-i	heta} = \conj{e^{i	heta}} undoes the turn by 	heta (@thm-polar-multiplication (b)). Powers that are tedious to expand become one line in polar form. [A Power via Polar Form] Compute (\sqrt 3 + i)^6. We have \sqrt 3 + i = 2  igl( 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} + 	frac12 i  igr) = 2 e^{i\pi/6}, by @exm-special-angles (iv). By @thm-de-moivre and @exm-special-angles (i), (\sqrt 3 + i)^6 = 2^6 e^{i \cdot 6\pi/6} = 64 \, e^{i\pi} = -64 . By hand: (\sqrt 3 + i)^2 = 3 + 2\sqrt 3\, i - 1 = 2 + 2\sqrt 3\, i = 2(1 + \sqrt 3\, i), and (1 + \sqrt 3\, i)^3 = (1 + \sqrt 3\, i)(-2 + 2\sqrt 3\, i) = -2 - 6 = -8, so (\sqrt 3 + i)^6 =  igl(2(1 + \sqrt 3\, i) igr)^3 = 8 \cdot (-8) = -64 (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (b), (c)), the same answer. Use polar form to compute (1 + i)^8, and check the answer with (1 + i)^2 = 2i. By @exm-special-angles (v), 1 + i = \sqrt 2  igl( 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} + 	frac{1}{\sqrt 2} i  igr) = \sqrt 2 \, e^{i\pi/4}. By @thm-de-moivre, (1 + i)^8 = (\sqrt 2)^8 e^{i \cdot 8\pi/4} = 16 \, e^{2\pi i} = 16, since (\sqrt 2)^8 =  igl((\sqrt 2)^2 igr)^4 = 2^4 = 16 and e^{2\pi i} = 1. Check: (1 + i)^8 =  igl((1 + i)^2 igr)^4 = (2i)^4 = 16 i^4 = 16, by @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (b), (c). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Give a polar form of -2 and of 3i. 2. True or false: if e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi}, then 	heta = \varphi. Justify your answer. 3. In @prp-polar-form, which of the borrowed facts (T1)–(T5) gives the existence of a polar form, and which gives the uniqueness of the argument up to 2\pi
Z? 4. Which results of Sections 3.1–3.5 use none of the borrowed facts? Is @prp-unit-circle among them? (a) -2 = 2 e^{i\pi} and 3i = 3 e^{i\pi/2}, by @exm-special-angles (i) and (ii); the moduli 2 and 3 are positive, as a polar form requires. (Any \pi + 2\pi k, respectively \pi/2 + 2\pi k, with k \in 
Z, is also an argument, by @prp-polar-form (b).) (b) False. e^{i0} = 1 = e^{2\pi i}, but 0 
e 2\pi since \pi > 0. What is true is 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z (@prp-polar-form (b)). (c) Existence: (T4), which provides an angle for the point z/\abs{z} of 
T. Uniqueness: (T3), which turns \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1 into 	heta - \varphi \in 2\pi
Z; (T1) is used alongside it, to see that \sin(	heta - \varphi) = 0 follows from \cos(	heta - \varphi) = 1, and (T2) enters through @thm-polar-multiplication, which turns e^{i	heta} = e^{i\varphi} into e^{i(	heta - \varphi)} = 1. (d) Everything in Sections 3.1–3.4, and the part of this section before @ax-cosine-sine; after the box, only Exercise C2, which is set up to avoid them. In particular @prp-unit-circle uses none of them: its proof uses only the modulus rules of Section 3.2, the field properties of 
C, and order facts about 
R from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R. B. Practice [B1] Compute (1 - \sqrt 3\, i)^6. We have 1 - \sqrt 3\, i = 2  igl( 	frac12 - 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i  igr) = 2 \, \conj{e^{i\pi/3}} = 2 e^{-i\pi/3}, by @exm-special-angles (iii) and @thm-polar-multiplication (b). By @thm-de-moivre, (1 - \sqrt 3\, i)^6 = 2^6 e^{-6i\pi/3} = 64 \, e^{-2\pi i} = 64 , since -2\pi = 2\pi \cdot (-1) \in 2\pi
Z, so \cos(-2\pi) = 1 and \sin(-2\pi) = 0 by (T3) and (T1), and e^{-2\pi i} = 1. [B2: Symmetries of Cosine and Sine] Prove that for every 	heta \in 
R:  egin{aligned} &\cos(-	heta) = \cos	heta, \quad \sin(-	heta) = -\sin	heta, \quad \cos(	heta + \pi) = -\cos	heta, \ &\sin(	heta + \pi) = -\sin	heta, \quad \cos	heta = \sin(	heta + \pi/2) . \end{aligned} Hint: write each left side as a part of some e^{i\psi}, and compute that e^{i\psi} with @thm-polar-multiplication. By @thm-polar-multiplication (b), e^{-i	heta} = \conj{e^{i	heta}}, that is, \cos(-	heta) + i \sin(-	heta) = \cos	heta - i \sin	heta. Comparing real and imaginary parts gives \cos(-	heta) = \cos	heta and \sin(-	heta) = -\sin	heta. By @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and @exm-special-angles (i), e^{i(	heta + \pi)} = e^{i	heta} e^{i\pi} = -e^{i	heta}, that is, \cos(	heta + \pi) + i \sin(	heta + \pi) = -\cos	heta - i \sin	heta. Comparing parts gives the next two identities. By @thm-polar-multiplication (a) and @exm-special-angles (ii), e^{i(	heta + \pi/2)} = i e^{i	heta} = i\cos	heta - \sin	heta. Comparing imaginary parts gives \sin(	heta + \pi/2) = \cos	heta. (Comparing real parts gives, in addition, \cos(	heta + \pi/2) = -\sin	heta.) [B3] Let 	heta \in 
R. Show that \abs{e^{i	heta} - 1}^2 = 2 - 2\cos	heta. Hence show again that e^{i	heta} = 1 if and only if \cos	heta = 1. Let u \coloneqq e^{i	heta}, so u \conj{u} = \abs{u}^2 = 1. Squaring the modulus, by @thm-conjugate-properties (a)–(c), \abs{u - 1}^2 = (u - 1)\conj{(u - 1)} = (u - 1)(\conj{u} - 1) = u\conj{u} - (u + \conj{u}) + 1 = 2 - 2 \operatorname{Re} u , and \operatorname{Re} u = \cos	heta. Hence \abs{u - 1}^2 = 2 - 2\cos	heta. Now u = 1 if and only if \abs{u - 1} = 0 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)), if and only if \abs{u - 1}^2 = 0 (a real number is 0 exactly when its square is: 0^2 = 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), and a non-zero square is positive by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), if and only if 2 - 2\cos	heta = 0, that is, \cos	heta = 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Triple Angles and Negative Powers] 1. Prove that \cos 3	heta = 4\cos^3	heta - 3\cos	heta and \sin 3	heta = 3\sin	heta - 4\sin^3	heta for every 	heta \in 
R. 2. For z \in 
C with z 
e 0 and n \in 
N, let z^{-n} be the integer power of @def-integer-power, so that z^{-n} = (z^{-1})^n. Show that (e^{i	heta})^{-n} = e^{-in	heta} for every 	heta \in 
R and n \in 
N. (a) Write c \coloneqq \cos	heta and s \coloneqq \sin	heta. By @thm-de-moivre, \cos 3	heta + i \sin 3	heta = (c + is)^3. Now (c + is)^2 = (c^2 - s^2) + 2cs\, i, and  egin{aligned} (c + is)^3 &=  igl((c^2 - s^2) + 2cs\, i igr)(c + is) \ &= (c^3 - 3cs^2) + (3c^2 s - s^3) i . \end{aligned} Comparing real parts and using s^2 = 1 - c^2 (T1), \cos 3	heta = c^3 - 3c(1 - c^2) = 4c^3 - 3c. Comparing imaginary parts and using c^2 = 1 - s^2, \sin 3	heta = 3(1 - s^2)s - s^3 = 3s - 4s^3. (b) By @thm-polar-multiplication (b), (e^{i	heta})^{-1} = e^{-i	heta} = e^{i(-	heta)}. By @thm-de-moivre applied to -	heta, (e^{i	heta})^{-n} = (e^{i(-	heta)})^n = e^{in(-	heta)} = e^{-in	heta}. Nothing else in this chapter uses negative powers of complex numbers. [C2: Points on the Circle without Angles] For t \in 
R put u_t \coloneqq  rac{1 + it}{1 - it} . 1. Show that u_t is defined, that u_t \in 
T, and that u_t 
e -1. 2. Show that every u \in 
T with u
