e -1 equals u_t for exactly one t \in 
R, namely t = \operatorname{Im} u / (1 + \operatorname{Re} u). 3. Compute u_{1/2} in the form a + bi. Use none of the borrowed facts (T1)–(T5). [Hint 1] For (b), on the unit circle the conjugate is the inverse: \conj{u} = 1/u. [Hint 2] Clearing the denominator, u = u_t is equivalent to u - 1 = it(u + 1), and u + 1 
e 0, so t is determined; it remains to show that (u - 1)/ igl(i(u + 1) igr) is real. (a) The real part of 1 - it is 1, so 1 - it 
e 0 and the quotient is defined. The numbers 1 + it and 1 - it are conjugate, so they have the same modulus (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)), which is non-zero. From u_t (1 - it) = 1 + it and @thm-conjugate-properties (d), \abs{u_t} \abs{1 - it} = \abs{1 + it} = \abs{1 - it}, and canceling the non-zero real number \abs{1 - it} gives \abs{u_t} = 1. If u_t = -1, then 1 + it = -(1 - it) = -1 + it, so 1 = -1, which is false. So u_t 
e -1. (b) Let u \in 
T with u 
e -1, and let t \in 
R. Since 1 - it 
e 0, the equation u = u_t is equivalent to u(1 - it) = 1 + it, that is, to u - 1 = it(u + 1) . Since i(u + 1) 
e 0, this holds if and only if t = t_0, where t_0 \coloneqq (u - 1)/ igl(i(u + 1) igr) \in 
C. So at most one real t has u_t = u, and one does exactly when t_0 is real. Using u\conj{u} = 1, (u - 1)(\conj{u} + 1) = u\conj{u} + u - \conj{u} - 1 = u - \conj{u} = 2i \operatorname{Im} u , where u - \conj{u} = 2i \operatorname{Im} u by @def-conjugate-modulus (with u = a + bi, (a + bi) - (a - bi) = 2bi); and (u + 1)(\conj{u} + 1) = \abs{u + 1}^2 = 2 + 2\operatorname{Re} u, by @thm-conjugate-properties (a), (c). This is a positive real number, since u + 1 
e 0. Multiplying numerator and denominator of (u - 1)/(u + 1) by \conj{u} + 1 = \conj{u + 1} 
e 0, t_0 =  rac{1}{i} \cdot  rac{2i \operatorname{Im} u}{2 + 2\operatorname{Re} u} =  rac{\operatorname{Im} u}{1 + \operatorname{Re} u} , a real number. So exactly one t \in 
R has u_t = u, namely t_0. (c) Multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate 1 + 	frac12 i of the denominator, u_{1/2} =  rac{(1 + 	frac12 i)^2}{1 + 	frac14} =  rac{	frac34 + i}{	frac54} =  rac35 +  rac45 i . Check against (b): \operatorname{Im} u / (1 + \operatorname{Re} u) = 	frac45 / 	frac85 = 	frac12. So the map t \mapsto u_t is a bijection from 
R onto 
T \setminus \{-1\}, and it was found with no angle. For rational t, the point u_t has rational coordinates: the computation in (c) with t in place of 	frac12 gives u_t =  igl((1 - t^2) + 2t\, i igr)/(1 + t^2), and t = 1/2 gives the point (3/5, 4/5) behind the right triangle with sides 3, 4, 5. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: 1 - it 
e 0 with a reason, and \abs{u_t} = 1 from the equal moduli of conjugates. - 1: u_t 
e -1. - 2: u = u_t rewritten as a linear equation in t, with u + 1 
e 0 used to solve it uniquely. - 3: shows that the unique solution is real and equals \operatorname{Im} u / (1 + \operatorname{Re} u), with 1 + \operatorname{Re} u 
e 0 justified (for example by multiplying by \conj{u + 1} and using u\conj{u} = 1, with 2 + 2 \operatorname{Re} u > 0). - Second route (coordinates u = x + yi, x^2 + y^2 = 1): the two lines above (5 points) become 2 for splitting u - 1 = it(u + 1) into x - 1 = -ty and y = t(1 + x), showing x 
e -1 (otherwise u = -1) and so t = y/(1 + x) is forced; and 3 for checking that this t satisfies x - 1 = -ty, using x^2 + y^2 = 1. - 2: (c) computed and checked. Fatal errors (0 for the step): writing u = e^{i	heta} and using a half-angle formula (borrowed facts, and values not derived here); dividing by 1 + \operatorname{Re} u without showing it is non-zero.

title: 3.6 Higher Roots, Roots of Unity, and a Look Ahead
content:
Higher Roots, Roots of Unity, and a Look Ahead Section 3.4 solved z^2 = c with real square roots alone. Polar form turns the general equation z^n = c into a question about lengths and angles: by De Moivre’s formula (@thm-de-moivre), raising to the n-th power raises the modulus to the n-th power and multiplies the argument by n. The angle part is a linear equation for a real number, with the ambiguity 2\pi
Z of @prp-polar-form attached. The length part is the real equation r^n = ho with ho > 0, and Chapter 1 already showed that it has exactly one positive solution. This section recalls that, solves z^n = c, counts the solutions, studies the case c = 1, and ends with a look ahead at polynomial equations in general. Real n-th roots Chapter 1, Section 1.5, proved that every real number a \ge 0 has exactly one non-negative n-th root \sqrt[n]{a}, by the move construct a point as a supremum (@lem-reals-nth-root), and that 0 \le s < t gives s^n < t^n (@lem-reals-nth-root (a)). We use both here, with the difference of powers (@lem-difference-of-powers) behind them, for the roots of complex numbers below. Solving the equation z to the n equals c Now the main result. Every non-zero complex number has exactly n different n-th roots, and polar form lists them. [n-th Roots of a Complex Number] Let n \in 
N with n \ge 1, and let c \in 
C with c 
e 0. Let c = ho e^{i\alpha} be a polar form of c (@prp-polar-form), and for k \in 
Z put z_k \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{ho} \; e^{i(\alpha + 2\pi k)/n} . 1. For z \in 
C: z^n = c if and only if z = z_k for some k \in 
Z. 2. For k, l \in 
Z: z_k = z_l if and only if n \mid k - l (@fd2:def-divides). 3. The map \{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\} 	o \{ z \in 
C : z^n = c \}, k \mapsto z_k, is a bijection. So c has exactly n n-th roots (@fd2:def-finite). In particular every non-zero complex number has an n-th root, and every u \in 
T has one in 
T. Write the unknown in polar form, z = r e^{i	heta}. De Moivre turns z^n = c into r^n e^{in	heta} = ho e^{i\alpha}, and the uniqueness half of polar form splits that into a real equation for the length, r^n = ho, and an equation for the angle, n	heta \in \alpha + 2\pi
Z. The first has one solution, r = \sqrt[n]{ho}. The second has the solutions 	heta = (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n, one for each integer k. Different k can give the same point, and they do exactly when the angles differ by a whole number of turns, that is, when n \mid k - l. So the k that matter are the remainders 0, \dots, n - 1. Before reading on: where is the uniqueness half of the polar form used, and where the uniqueness of the real n-th root? Here ho = \abs{c} > 0 by @prp-polar-form (a), so \sqrt[n]{ho} \ge 0 exists by @lem-reals-nth-root (b), and \sqrt[n]{ho} > 0, since 0^n = 0 
e ho. (a) Let z \in 
C. If z = 0, then z^n = 0^{n-1} \cdot 0 = 0 
e c (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), and z is no z_k, since every z_k has modulus \sqrt[n]{ho} > 0. So let z 
e 0, and fix a polar form z = r e^{i	heta} (@prp-polar-form (a)). By @thm-de-moivre, z^n = r^n e^{in	heta}, a polar form with r^n > 0. By @prp-polar-form (b), z^n = c \iff r^n = ho \ 	ext{ and } \ n	heta - \alpha \in 2\pi
Z . Since r > 0, the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b) gives r^n = ho \iff r = \sqrt[n]{ho}. And n	heta - \alpha = 2\pi k holds for a given k \in 
Z exactly when 	heta = (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n. (\Rightarrow) If z^n = c, then r = \sqrt[n]{ho} and 	heta = (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n for some k \in 
Z, so z = z_k. (\Leftarrow) If z = z_k, use the polar form r \coloneqq \sqrt[n]{ho}, 	heta \coloneqq (\alpha + 2\pi k)/n of z in the equivalence above. Both conditions on the right hold, so z^n = c. (b) The numbers z_k and z_l are given in polar form with the same modulus. By @prp-polar-form (b), z_k = z_l if and only if  rac{\alpha + 2\pi k}{n} -  rac{\alpha + 2\pi l}{n} =  rac{2\pi (k - l)}{n} \in 2\pi
Z , that is, if and only if 2\pi(k - l)/n = 2\pi m for some m \in 
Z. Multiplying by n/(2\pi), and back, this says k - l = mn, an equation between integers. So z_k = z_l if and only if n \mid k - l. (c) By (a), each z_k is a solution, so the map is into the set of solutions. Injective: let 0 \le l < k \le n - 1. Then 0 < k - l < n. If z_k = z_l, then n \mid k - l by (b), and since n > 0 and k - l > 0, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) gives n \le k - l, a contradiction. So z_k 
e z_l. Surjective: let z^n = c. By (a), z = z_k for some k \in 
Z. Division with remainder (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a)) gives k = qn + j with q \in 
Z and 0 \le j \le n - 1. Then n \mid k - j, so z = z_k = z_j by (b). Hence the map is a bijection. Composing it with the bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{0, \dots, n - 1\}, j \mapsto j - 1, shows that the set of solutions has n elements (@fd2:def-finite). Finally, z_0 is an n-th root of c. If \abs{c} = 1, then ho = 1 and \sqrt[n]{1} = 1, since 1 \ge 0 and 1^n = 1; so every z_k has modulus 1 and lies in 
T. The answer to the prompt: the uniqueness half of the polar form, @prp-polar-form (b), turns the one complex equation z^n = c into the two real conditions, and is used again in (b) to decide when two of the z_k coincide. The uniqueness of the real root forces the modulus, r = \sqrt[n]{ho}. The ambiguity 2\pi
Z in the angle is what produces n roots instead of one. Dividing the angle equation by n too early loses roots. From z^3 = 1, z = e^{i	heta}, one might write e^{3i	heta} = e^{i0}, “so 3	heta = 0 and z = 1”. But e^{3i	heta} = e^{i0} only gives 3	heta \in 2\pi
Z (@prp-polar-form (b)), and the angles 2\pi/3 and 4\pi/3 give two more cube roots of 1. Only the remainders 0, \dots, n - 1 of k matter, but all of them do. Roots of unity The most important case is c = 1. Roots of Unity Let n \ge 1 be an integer. Find all z \in 
C with z^n = 1, and draw them for n = 6. Apply @thm-complex-nth-roots with c = 1 = 1 \cdot e^{i0} (@thm-polar-multiplication (b)): ho = 1, \alpha = 0, and \sqrt[n]{1} = 1. The solutions are z_k = e^{2\pi i k / n} , \qquad k \in 
Z . Put \omega \coloneqq e^{2\pi i/n}. By @thm-de-moivre, z_k = (e^{2\pi i/n})^k = \omega^k for k \in 
N. By @thm-complex-nth-roots (c), there are exactly n solutions, 1, \; \omega, \; \omega^2, \; \dots, \; \omega^{n-1} , the n-th roots of unity. They lie on

The squaring proof of (a) is the one that survives: in the complex triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality) the cross term 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) is bounded by a comparison between real numbers, \operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u} (@lem-real-part-at-most-modulus), which replaces xy \le \abs{xy} here. [R4] Find all z \in 
C with \conj{z} = z^2. The tool: take moduli first. If \conj{z} = z^2, then \abs{z} = \abs{\conj{z}} = \abs{z^2} = \abs{z}^2 (@thm-conjugate-properties (d)), so \abs{z} igl(\abs{z} - 1 igr) = 0 and \abs{z} = 0 or \abs{z} = 1. If \abs{z} = 0, then z = 0 (@thm-conjugate-properties (e)), and z = 0 is a solution. If \abs{z} = 1, multiply \conj{z} = z^2 by z: 1 = z\conj{z} = z^3 (@thm-conjugate-properties (c)). So z is a cube root of unity: z = 1 or z = -	frac12 \pm 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i (the Check above). Conversely, each cube root of unity \zeta lies in 
T (Exercise B3), so \conj{\zeta} = \zeta^{-1} (@prp-unit-circle (a)), and \zeta^{-1} = \zeta^2 because \zeta \cdot \zeta^2 = \zeta^3 = 1. So each is a solution. The solutions are 0, 1, -	frac12 + 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i and -	frac12 - 	frac{\sqrt 3}{2} i. Why the look-alike tools are worse. Comparing real and imaginary parts, with z = x + yi, gives x^2 - y^2 = x and 2xy = -y, which can be solved, but only with a case split by hand (y = 0 or x = -	frac12). “Divide \conj{z} = z^2 by z” silently loses the solution z = 0. Polar form works, but it is not needed: the moduli settle \abs{z}, and the cube roots of unity can be found without angles, as in the Check.

title: Fields
content:
Fields Linear algebra solves equations by adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing by numbers that are not zero, and by nothing else. A field is a number system in which exactly these moves work, under the usual rules. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R already defined fields and built two of them, 
Q and 
R. Chapter 2 built the integers modulo a prime p, and Chapter 3 added 
C. This chapter studies fields as a kind of object in their own right. It covers the rules every field obeys, the finite fields 
F_p and how to compute in them, fields inside fields, maps between fields that respect both operations, and one number, the characteristic, that says whether 1 + 1 + \dots + 1 can ever be 0. That number decides whether “2x = 0, so x = 0” is a valid step, and the linear-algebra volumes ask about it again and again. Two facts organize the chapter. A homomorphism of fields is forced to be injective, because a non-zero element has an inverse and its image must have one too. And every field contains exactly one smallest subfield, a copy of 
Q or of exactly one 
F_p, onto which there is exactly one homomorphism. The chapter ends with the identity (x + y)^p = x^p + y^p, which holds in every field of characteristic p and fails for other exponents and in rings of composite characteristic. Fermat’s little theorem then takes a few lines: on 
F_p the map x \mapsto x^p is a homomorphism of 
F_p to itself, and the only such map is the identity. One definition, two books. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2 defined “field” (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), and the linear-algebra volumes cite the definition as @def-field. Section 4.1 restates it under that name with the clauses (F1)–(F9) numbered as both books number them. A remark there proves that the two definitions describe the same objects; they differ only in where the condition 1 
e 0 is filed, inside (F7) here and as a clause of its own in Number Systems. Where Number Systems or Chapter 2 already proved a result, this chapter cites it. So @thm-field-basic-properties takes parts (a), (d) and (e) and the uniqueness of negatives from @fd3:prp-ring-algebra, takes the uniqueness of inverses, the absence of zero divisors and the inverse identities of part (g) from the paragraphs on units after @def-ring-unit in Section 2.4, and proves cancellation and the fraction rules itself; and the proof of @thm-zp-field-iff-prime is a citation of @thm-integers-mod-prime-field from Section 2.4. What you need. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3, and Chapter 2 of this volume, above all; Chapter 3 of this volume, for examples; Chapter 1 of this volume, for the binomial theorem in Section 4.6, the natural multiples of Section 4.5 and the power laws; and smaller pieces of Sets and Functions and Logic and Proof. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3: commutative rings and fields and their algebra (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra), on nearly every page; the integers as a commutative ring (@fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring), for the non-examples of Section 4.1; the copy of 
N in 
Z (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers), in Sections 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 and for integer multiples in Section 4.5; the integers as an ordered ring (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring), for negative multiples in Section 4.5; and the least element of a set of integers bounded below (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element), which makes the characteristic well defined in Section 4.5; the multiples n \cdot a of the “Multiples” paragraph of its Section 2.4, which Section 4.5 extends to negative n; ordered fields and their rules (@fd3:def-ordered-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules), and the order on 
Q from its positive elements (@fd3:prp-order-from-positives), in a quick check of Section 4.1; the field 
Q, built as classes of pairs (@fd3:def-rationals-as-classes, @fd3:def-rational-operations, @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes, @fd3:thm-rationals-field, @fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals), which Section 4.5 maps into every field of characteristic 0; the irrationality of \sqrt 2 (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two), used in Section 4.3; and the two-element ring that cannot be ordered (@fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), compared with in Section 4.2. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5, and from Chapter 2 of this volume: division with remainder, parity and the rules for divisibility (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers); the gcd, Bézout’s theorem, Euclid’s lemma and the test for primes (@def-integer-gcd, @thm-integers-bezout, @cor-coprime-iff-combination, @thm-euclid-lemma-integers, @cor-prime-divides-product, @lem-least-divisor-prime); quotient rings and the rings 
Z/n
Z, with the example 
Z/6
Z (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal, @def-integers-mod-n-ring, @thm-integers-mod-n-ring, @exm-integers-mod-six); and units, their inverses modulo n, and the field 
Z/p
Z (@def-ring-unit, @thm-units-mod-n, @thm-integers-mod-prime-field). Section 4.2 gives these fields the name 
F_p that Section 2.4 left to this chapter. Its move “least positive element, then divide” proves @prp-characteristic-divides. - From Chapter 1 of this volume: the rules for natural multiples (@lem-natural-multiples), which Section 4.5 extends to integer multiples; powers in a commutative ring and their laws (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring), used in Sections 4.4 and 4.6; and, for Section 4.6, finite sums in a commutative ring, the binomial coefficients with their absorption identity, and the binomial theorem (@lem-ring-finite-sums, @def-binomial-coefficients, @prp-binomial-absorption, @thm-binomial-commutative-ring). - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 4–6, for examples, comparisons and a few exercises only: 
R as a complete ordered field containing 
Q (@fd3:thm-reals-field, @fd3:thm-reals-ordered-field, @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:def-rational-embedding, @fd3:thm-rational-embedding), from its Chapter 5; square roots in 
R and the theorem that 
R has no automorphism but the identity (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots, @fd3:def-cof-order-preserving-map, @fd3:thm-cof-field-automorphism-identity, @fd3:prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals), from its Chapter 6; and the fraction rules and the embedding of 
Q into an ordered field (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules, @fd3:prp-naturals-in-ordered-field, @fd3:thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field), from its Chapter 4, which remarks in Sections 4.1 and 4.5 compare with. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1: the citing rule by which induction and recursion apply to 
N (@fd3:cor-omega-identification), in Sections 4.4–4.6. From Sets and Functions, Chapter 1: power sets and sets cut out by a property (@fd2:def-power-set, @fd2:def-set-builder), which make the set of subfields containing a given set a set, in Section 4.3. - From Chapter 3 of this volume, for examples and review exercises only: 
C as a field containing 
R (@def-complex-numbers, @prp-reals-embed-complex, @prp-complex-arithmetic-laws, @prp-complex-inverse, @thm-complex-numbers-field); conjugation and its rules (@def-conjugate-modulus, @thm-conjugate-properties), the first automorphism of Section 4.4; complex square roots (@prp-complex-square-roots), compared with in Section 4.1 and used in Exercise R1 of Section 4.6; and the method by which 
C cannot be ordered (@prp-complex-not-orderable), reused in Exercise R3 of Section 4.6. - From Sets and Functions: functions, composition, bijections, inverse functions and images, and intersections of families of sets (@fd2:def-bijective, @fd2:def-composition, @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective, @fd2:def-inverse-function, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @fd2:def-image, @fd2:def-family-union-intersection), from its Chapters 1 and 2; primes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-prime, @fd2:def-quotient-set), from its Chapters 1 and 5; finite and infinite sets and the pigeonhole principle (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:exm-hilbert-hotel, @fd2:thm-pigeonhole, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy), from its Chapter 4. - From Logic and Proof: induction (@fd1:ax-induction), from its Section 4.2, and, for the five find-the-error exercises and the proof-ordering exercise of Section 4.3, the catalogue of moves that are not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), from its Section 8.6. No proof of a result rests on 
R or 
C: they enter through examples, remarks and exercises. Nothing from linear algebra is used, and polynomials appear only as equations between elements, never as objects; Chapters 6 and 7 build them. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 40 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Field Axioms and the First Examples. What elimination needs, and the definition of a field with the clauses (F1)–(F9) and its agreement with the definition in Number Systems; the rules of every field, collected from the commutative-ring rules with the fraction rules added; the two square roots \pm y, with 
Z/8
Z as the ring where there are more; one linear equation and a system of two, solved in any field; 
Q, 
R and 
C as fields; and 
N, 
Z, the zero ring and 
Z/6
Z as non-examples, each with the clause that fails. - Finite Fields from Modular Arithmetic. The arithmetic of 
Z/n
Z recalled, with the tables of 
F_2; Bézout’s lemma in the form the linear-algebra volumes cite, and 
Z/n
Z as a field exactly for prime n; the fields 
F_p, with inverses found by trial and by the Euclidean algorithm and the elimination of Section 4.1 run over 
F_5; why a non-zero class modulo a composite cannot always be divided by, and why 
F_p has no order; and, as an exercise, a field with four elements that is not 
Z/4
Z. - Subfields. Subfields, with examples and one-clause non-examples; the subfield test, which shows that a subfield is a field with the zero and one of the big field and reduces the check to 1, differences and quotients; 
Q(\sqrt 2) \subseteq 
R and 
Q(i) \subseteq 
C as subfields, with 
Z[i] failing only at inverses; the warning that \{[0], [3]\} \subseteq 
Z/6
Z is a field with another one; and intersections of subfields, the smallest subfield containing a set, and the prime subfield, which for 
F_p is 
F_p itself. - Field Homomorphisms. Homomorphisms, isomorphisms and automorphisms, and why \varphi(1) = 1 is required; the theorem that a homomorphism keeps 0, negatives and inverses, is injective, and maps its domain onto a subfield isomorphic to it; conjugation of 
C and of 
Q(\sqrt 2) as automorphisms, and 
R with none but the identity; and the pairs 
C 	o 
R, 
F_2 	o 
Q and 
Q 	o 
F_p with no homomorphism at all. - Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield. Integer multiples n \cdot a in a commutative ring, negative n included, with the proof for negative n in a second-reading fold; the characteristic, the theorem that n \cdot 1 = 0 exactly when \operatorname{char} F divides n (so 2 is invertible exactly when \operatorname{char} F 
e 2), and the theorem that it is 0 or a prime; its invariance under subfields and homomorphisms, and the characteristics of the standard fields; the prime subfield as the image of the unique homomorphism from 
Q or 
F_p, so that a homomorphism has no choice on it and 
Q and 
F_p have no automorphism but the identity; and finite fields, which have prime characteristic. - The Binomial Theorem, the Frobenius Map, and Fermat’s Little Theorem. The binomial theorem recalled from Chapter 1 (finite sums, binomial coefficients by Pascal’s rule and the theorem itself, all in a commutative ring); the prime dividing the middle coefficients of row p; the Frobenius map x \mapsto x^p, a homomorphism in characteristic p and an automorphism of a finite field; Fermat’s little theorem, with powers and inverses computed in 
F_7, 
F_{31} and 
F_{101}; and review exercises on complex square roots (Chapter 3), square roots in 
Q(\sqrt 2), fields that cannot be ordered, and the homomorphisms 
Q(\sqrt 2) 	o 
R. Named moves - Test inside the big field. For a subset K of a field L, the identities (F1), (F2), (F5), (F6) and (F9) hold in K because they hold for all elements of L; only closure and the elements 0, 1, -a and a^{-1} need checking. It is named in the Idea of the subfield test (@prp-subfield-test) in Section 4.3. Through that test it shows that 
Q(\sqrt 2) and 
Q(i) are fields and that an intersection of subfields is a subfield in Section 4.3, and that the image of a homomorphism is a subfield in Section 4.4. The warning of Section 4.3 marks its limit: inside a ring that is not a field, a subset can be a field whose one is not that of the ring, as \{[0], [3]\} \subseteq 
Z/6
Z is. - Push the equation through \varphi. To find \varphi(x), apply \varphi to an equation that x satisfies, such as a + (-a) = 0, aa^{-1} = 1, i^2 = -1 or p \cdot 1 = 0, and solve the resulting equation in the target field, where it often has only one solution. It is named in Section 4.4, after the proof of @prp-field-homomorphism-properties, whose parts (a) and (b) run it in full. Exercise B1 of Section 4.4 leaves its last step to you, and Exercise B2 there its last half. When the pushed equation has no solution in the target, it proves that no homomorphism exists (@exm-field-homomorphism-obstructions). Section 4.5 uses it for the uniqueness half of @thm-prime-subfield, and Exercise R4 of Section 4.6 to find the homomorphisms 
Q(\sqrt 2) 	o 
R. - Count copies of 1. A question about integers acting on a field becomes a question about the elements n \cdot 1: by @lem-integer-multiples, n \cdot a = (n \cdot 1)a, and n \mapsto n \cdot 1 respects sums and products. Then the move of Chapter 2, “take the least positive element, then divide by it”, turns “n \cdot 1 = 0” into “\operatorname{char} F divides n” (@prp-characteristic-divides). Section 4.5 names only the second step; the name “count copies of 1” is given here. Since a homomorphism sends n \cdot 1 to n \cdot 1, it has no choice on the prime subfield (@cor-homomorphisms-fix-prime-subfield). In Section 4.6 the same counting kills the middle terms of (x + y)^p, and that rigidity turns the Frobenius map of 
F_p into Fermat’s little theorem.

title: 4.1 The Field Axioms and the First Examples
content:
The Field Axioms and the First Examples Number Systems: From 
N to 
R defined fields (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) and built 
Q and 
R. Chapter 2 built, for each prime p, the field 
Z/p
Z, and Chapter 3 added 
C. This chapter looks at fields as a kind of object in their own right. Its first section restates the definition under the name that the linear-algebra volumes use, collects the rules that hold in every field, solves one and two linear equations in any field, and sorts the standard examples from the standard non-examples, naming in each case the clause that fails. What solving equations needs Here is a small system of equations, solved the way it is solved at school:  egin{aligned} 2x + 3y &= 7, \ x - y &= 1. \end{aligned} Subtract twice the second equation from the first: 5y = 5. Divide by 5: y = 1. Then x = 1 + y = 2. Check: 2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 1 = 7 and 2 - 1 = 1. List the moves. Equations were combined by sums and differences, one equation was scaled by a number, and one was divided by a number that is not zero. Silently, terms were also reordered, regrouped, and brackets were multiplied out. Elimination, the method the linear-algebra volumes run on systems of any size, uses these moves and nothing else. Now stay inside 
Z. The equation 2x = 1 has integer coefficients and no integer solution: 2x is even and 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd, and no integer is both (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a)). The move “divide by 2” leads out of 
Z. So the dividing line between 
Z and 
Q is division, and division by every non-zero element is what the definition must ask for. A field is a number system where you can add, subtract, multiply, and divide by anything non-zero, with the usual rules. The definition The definition lists the rules once, as clauses that can be checked and cited. The numbering is the one Number Systems used for commutative rings, and the one the linear-algebra volumes cite. [Field] A field is a set F together with two functions, addition + \colon F 	imes F 	o F, (a, b) \mapsto a + b, and multiplication \cdot \colon F 	imes F 	o F, (a, b) \mapsto a \cdot b = ab, satisfying the following clauses. 1. a + b = b + a for all a, b \in F. 2. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) for all a, b, c \in F. 3. There is an element 0 \in F such that a + 0 = a for every a \in F. 4. For every a \in F there is an element -a \in F such that a + (-a) = 0. 5. (ab)c = a(bc) for all a, b, c \in F. 6. ab = ba for all a, b \in F. 7. There is an element 1 \in F with 1 
e 0 such that a \cdot 1 = a for every a \in F. 8. For every non-zero a \in F there is an element a^{-1} \in F such that a a^{-1} = 1. 9. a(b + c) = ab + ac for all a, b, c \in F. We write a - b \coloneqq a + (-b), and a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1} for b 
e 0. Read the clauses in three groups. - (F1)–(F4) speak only of addition. The order and the grouping of a sum do not matter, 0 changes nothing when added, and each element can be undone by its negative. Subtraction is built from these. - (F5)–(F8) repeat those four statements for multiplication, with one change: an inverse is demanded only of a non-zero element. So division is defined only by non-zero elements, and no clause ever calls for division by 0. Clause (F7) also demands that the two neutral elements differ. - (F9), the distributive law, is the single bridge between the two operations: it alone mentions both, and multiplying out brackets rests on it, with (F6) for a bracket on the left. Mind the order of the quantifiers in (F3): there is one element 0 that works for every a. The weaker reading, “each a has its own z with a + z = a”, would let z change with a, and it is not what (F3) says. In (F4) the order is the other way round, as it has to be: the negative -a depends on a. Both operations are functions into F: a sum or product of two elements of F is again in F. For a candidate field cut out of a larger number system, that closure is where checking starts. We say “F is a field” when the two operations are understood, and write (F, +, \cdot) when they must be named. [The same definition in Number Systems] @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field calls a set with two operations a commutative ring when (F1)–(F7) and (F9) hold, its (F7) asking only for an element 1 with a \cdot 1 = a; it calls a commutative ring a field when, in addition, 1 
e 0 and (F8) hold. Clause by clause, these are the conditions of @def-field: the nine clauses are worded alike, and the only difference is where the condition 1 
e 0 is filed, inside (F7) here and as a separate clause there. So F is a field in the sense of @def-field if and only if it is a field in the sense of @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field. Every result that Number Systems proves for fields, or for commutative rings, therefore applies to every field of this chapter, and conversely. The separate filing there has a purpose: it lets the one-element set \{0\} count as a commutative ring (the zero ring) while keeping it out of the fields. Is 
Q_{>0}, the set of positive rationals with the usual + and \cdot of 
Q, a field? No. Addition and multiplication do map 
Q_{>0} 	imes 
Q_{>0} into 
Q_{>0} (@fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field, with (P1) of @fd3:prp-order-from-positives). But (F3) fails. An element z \in 
Q_{>0} with 1 + z = 1 would satisfy z = 0 + z = ((-1) + 1) + z = (-1) + (1 + z) = (-1) + 1 = 0 in the field 
Q, by (F1), (F3), (F4) and (F2), and 0 
otin 
Q_{>0}. (Once (F3) fails, (F4) cannot even be stated.) Rules that hold in every field The definition’s notation takes something for granted. The symbols 0, -a and a^{-1} are written as names of single elements, while (F3), (F4), (F7) and (F8) assert only that suitable elements exist. Were there two different zeros in some field, the symbols 0, a - b and a / b would be ambiguous. The next theorem removes the worry and collects the rules of school algebra that every field obeys. Most of it was proved in Number Systems for every commutative ring; we collect it under one name, citing the proofs there, and add the rules for fractions as part (g). [Basic Properties of Fields] Let F be a field and let a, b, c, d \in F. 1. The element 0 in (F3) is unique, and the element 1 in (F7) is unique. 2. (Cancellation) If a + b = a + c, then b = c. If ab = ac and a 
e 0, then b = c. 3. The negative -a in (F4) is unique, and for a 
e 0 the inverse a^{-1} in (F8) is unique. 4. 0 \cdot a = 0. 5. (-1)a = -a. 6. If ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0. 7. If b 
e 0 and d 
e 0, then bd 
e 0, (bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}, (b^{-1})^{-1} = b, and  rac{a}{b} +  rac{c}{d} =  rac{ad + bc}{bd}, \qquad  rac{a}{b} \cdot  rac{c}{d} =  rac{ac}{bd}. Work backwards from each goal to the clause that could produce it; each part then takes a few lines. For uniqueness, take two candidates and prove them equal. No clause says anything about 0 \cdot a, so for (d) we manufacture a place where (F9) can act: 0 = 0 + 0, distribute, cancel. In (f) the hypothesis a 
e 0 has exactly one use, which is to unlock (F8). The fraction rules in (g) come from one move: an element is identified by showing that it satisfies the defining equation of the element we want, and uniqueness finishes. By the remark after @def-field, F is a commutative ring in the sense of @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, so @fd3:prp-ring-algebra applies to it. (a) This is @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a). (b) Suppose a + b = a + c. Put -a in front of each side and regroup with (F2): this gives ((-a) + a) + b = ((-a) + a) + c. By (F1) and (F4), (-a) + a = a + (-a) = 0, so 0 + b = 0 + c, and by (F1) and (F3) this says b = c. Now suppose ab = ac and a 
e 0. By (F8), a^{-1} exists. Using (F7), (F8), (F6) and (F5),  egin{aligned} b &= b \cdot 1 = b(a a^{-1}) = (ba) a^{-1} = (ab) a^{-1} \ &= (ac) a^{-1} = (ca) a^{-1} = c (a a^{-1}) = c \cdot 1 = c. \end{aligned} (c) The negative is unique by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a). For a 
e 0, clause (F8) says that a is a unit of F in the sense of @def-ring-unit, and the inverse of a unit is unique (the well-definedness paragraph after @def-ring-unit). (d) By @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), a \cdot 0 = 0, and 0 \cdot a = a \cdot 0 by (F6). (e) By @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) with a = 1, (-1)b = -(1 \cdot b) for every b \in F; and 1 \cdot b = b \cdot 1 = b by (F6) and (F7). Applied to b = a, this gives (-1)a = -a. (f) Suppose ab = 0. If a = 0 there is nothing to prove, so suppose a 
e 0. By (F8), a is a unit of F (@def-ring-unit), and a unit is not a zero divisor (the paragraph after @def-ring-unit): from ab = 0 it follows that b = 0. So a = 0 or b = 0. (g) Let b 
e 0 and d 
e 0. If bd = 0, then (f) would give b = 0 or d = 0; so bd 
e 0. By (F8), b and d are units of F. A product of units is a unit, with (bd)^{-1} = b^{-1} d^{-1}, and the inverse of a unit is a unit, with (b^{-1})^{-1} = b (the closure paragraph after @def-ring-unit). Here b^{-1} 
e 0, since 1 
e 0 by (F7) and so 0 is not a unit (the paragraph “Why this definition” after @def-ring-unit); thus (b^{-1})^{-1} is also the inverse that (F8) supplies, by (c). For the sum, multiply out with (F9) and reorder with (F5) and (F6):  egin{aligned} (a b^{-1} + c d^{-1})(bd) &= a (b^{-1} b) d + c (d^{-1} d) b \ &= ad + cb = ad + bc, \end{aligned} by (F8) and (F7) and then (F6). Multiplying both ends by (bd)^{-1}, and using (bd)(bd)^{-1} = 1 with (F5) and (F7) on the left, gives a b^{-1} + c d^{-1} = (ad + bc)(bd)^{-1}, which is the first displayed rule. For the product, (F5) and (F6) give (a b^{-1})(c d^{-1}) = (ac)(b^{-1} d^{-1}) = (ac)(bd)^{-1}, by the formula for (bd)^{-1} just proved. This proves the theorem. From now on we use 0 + a = a and 1 \cdot a = a silently; they follow from (F1), (F3), (F6) and (F7). The larger gain is that any school identity whose proof uses only (F1)–(F9) is true in every field: for instance (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, where a^2 \coloneqq aa and 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d)), and (-a)(-b) = ab (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). Part (f) is the rule we will lean on most: a product of non-zero elements is non-zero. Finite Fields from Modular Arithmetic Every field of Section 4.1 is infinite. Chapter 2 has already met finite ones: it proved that the integers modulo a prime p form a field (@thm-integers-mod-prime-field). This section restates that result in the language of @def-field, gives these fields a name of their own, 
F_p, and computes in them: inverses, linear equations, and the elimination method of Section 4.1, now run modulo 5. Finite fields are not a curiosity; coding theory and computer algebra do linear algebra over them every day. Arithmetic modulo n, recalled Fix an integer n \ge 1. The ring

This is the class test of Section 2.3 (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (a), read with @def-integers-mod-n-ring). Sums and products are computed on representatives. The first example collects what is known about this arithmetic, in the language of @def-field. [Arithmetic on

Subfields The fields met so far sit inside one another.

C, and each is a field with the sum and product of the next: 
Q inside

N to

R inside 
C through @prp-reals-embed-complex. Between 
Q and 
R lies the set 
Q(\sqrt 2) of numbers a + b\sqrt 2 with a, b rational. Sums and products of two such numbers are again of that form, but is 1/(1 + 2\sqrt 2)? This section gives a short test that settles such questions once, and it finds, inside every field, a smallest field. Throughout, a - b \coloneqq a + (-b) and a/b \coloneqq ab^{-1} for b 
e 0, as in @def-field, and the rules of @thm-field-basic-properties are used freely, each cited by its letter. Fields inside fields A subset K of a field L inherits two operations, but only in a weak sense: a + b and ab are defined for a, b \in K, as elements of L. For K to be a field with these operations, the sum and the product must land in K, and the elements that the axioms (F3), (F4), (F7) and (F8) ask for must be found in K. The natural guess is that nothing else needs checking. A subfield is a subset that a field’s own arithmetic never leaves. [Subfield] Let L be a field. A subfield of L is a subset K \subseteq L such that - 0 \in K and 1 \in K; - K is closed under sums and products: a + b \in K and ab \in K for all a, b \in K; - K is closed under negatives: -a \in K for every a \in K; - K is closed under inverses: a^{-1} \in K for every non-zero a \in K. Here 0, 1, +, \cdot, -a and a^{-1} are those of L. In words: the first clause asks for the two special elements of L; the second says that the operations of L do not leave K; the last two say that the negatives and inverses which L provides already lie in K. Examples. - L itself is a subfield of L. It is the largest one, and the degenerate case: every clause holds because K = L. - 
Q in 
R. Under the identification of a rational q with \kappa(q) \in 
R, the embedding \kappa sends 0, 1, sums, products, negatives and inverses of rationals to the same things in 
R (@fd3:thm-rational-embedding (a), (c)). So all four clauses hold, and 
Q is a subfield of 
R. - 
R in

By (a), K_S \coloneqq  igcap \sK_S is a subfield of L. Every K \in \sK_S contains S, so S \subseteq K_S. And if K is a subfield containing S, then K \in \sK_S, so K_S \subseteq K. [Hint 1] For b \in K, which maps K 	o K can you build from b and the two operations? [Hint 2] The maps x \mapsto x + b and x \mapsto bx go from K to K. Why are they injective, and what does finiteness then give? A finite set has no injection onto a proper part. Let f \colon K 	o K be injective. If f were not surjective, its image f(K) (@fd2:def-image) would be a proper subset of K, and f, with codomain f(K), would be a bijection K 	o f(K), against @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy. So every injective map K 	o K is surjective. Zero. Let t \colon K 	o K, t(x) \coloneqq x + 1, a map into K because K is closed under + and 1 \in K. It is injective: x + 1 = x' + 1 gives 1 + x = 1 + x' by (F1), so x = x' by additive cancellation in L (@thm-field-basic-properties (b)). So it is surjective, and some x \in K has x + 1 = 1 = 0 + 1, so 1 + x = 1 + 0 by (F1); canceling, x = 0. So 0 \in K. Negatives. Let b \in K. The map x \mapsto x + b is injective in the same way, hence surjective, and 0 \in K is a value: x + b = 0 for some x \in K. By the uniqueness of negatives in L, x = -b. Inverses. Let b \in K, b 
e 0. The map x \mapsto bx goes from K to K and is injective by multiplicative cancellation in L, which uses b 
e 0. So it is surjective, bx = 1 for some x \in K, and x = b^{-1} by the uniqueness of inverses in L. So K is a subfield. Note that K 
e \emptyset need not be assumed: 1 \in K. Finiteness is needed. 
N \subseteq 
Q contains 1 and is closed under + and \cdot, and -1 
otin 
N. The argument breaks at “injective, hence surjective”: x \mapsto x + 1 is injective on 
N, and 0 is not a value. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: a finiteness argument with its reason: an injective map from a finite set to itself is surjective (@fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy, or a count), or pigeonhole on a sequence in K (@fd2:thm-pigeonhole). - 2: 0 \in K, from a translation map and cancellation, or from a repetition m \cdot 1 = n \cdot 1 with m < n and cancellation in L, before 0 is used. - 2: negatives, from surjectivity of x \mapsto x + b and uniqueness of negatives in L, or from a repetition i \cdot b = j \cdot b with i < j, giving -b = (j - i - 1) \cdot b. - 2: inverses, with the cancellation by b justified by b 
e 0 (injectivity of x \mapsto bx, or b^i = b^j with i < j giving b^{j - i} = 1 and b^{-1} = b^{j - i - 1}). - 2: a witness that finiteness is needed (
N \subseteq 
Q, or 
Z \subseteq 
Q for inverses). Fatal errors (0 for the step): using 0 \in K or -b \in K to build the translation before proving it; “injective, hence surjective” (or pigeonhole) without finiteness. [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument. Is its conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails and why. “
Q(\sqrt 2) is closed under inverses. (1) Let a + b\sqrt 2 \in 
Q(\sqrt 2) be non-zero. (2) Then (a + b\sqrt 2)^{-1} =  rac{1}{a} +  rac{1}{b\sqrt 2} =  rac{1}{a} +  rac{1}{2b}\sqrt 2 . (3) Both coefficients are rational, so the inverse lies in 
Q(\sqrt 2).” The conclusion is true (@exm-q-sqrt2-field). The argument does not prove it. Line (2) fails. Its first equality uses the general “fact” 1/(x + y) = 1/x + 1/y, which is neither proved nor true; so the line cites nothing, entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. It also divides by a and by b, either of which may be 0 (for \sqrt 2 = 0 + 1\sqrt 2, a = 0). The second equality, 1/(b\sqrt 2) = (1/(2b))\sqrt 2, is correct for b 
e 0. Counterexample to the step. x = y = 1 in 
Q: 1/(1 + 1) = 1/2, while 1/1 + 1/1 = 2. In the case at hand, a = b = 1: the formula gives 1 + 	frac12\sqrt 2, and (1 + \sqrt 2)(1 + 	frac12\sqrt 2) = 2 + 	frac32\sqrt 2 
e 1; the true inverse is -1 + \sqrt 2. Repair. Multiply by the conjugate, as in @exm-q-sqrt2-field: (a + b\sqrt 2)^{-1} = (a - b\sqrt 2)/(a^2 - 2b^2).

title: 4.4 Field Homomorphisms
content:
Field Homomorphisms Section 4.3 looked at fields inside fields. This section looks at maps between fields. Two such maps have appeared already. Complex conjugation z \mapsto \conj{z} turns sums into sums and products into products (@thm-conjugate-properties (a), (b)), and so does a + b\sqrt 2 \mapsto a - b\sqrt 2 on 
Q(\sqrt 2) (@exm-cof-sqrt2-conjugation). A map that respects both operations carries every equation that holds in one field to an equation in the other. That single observation decides where such a map can send an element, shows that it never collapses two elements, and rules out most maps between most pairs of fields. Throughout, F and L are fields, and n \cdot a for n \in 
N is the multiple of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.4 (“Multiples”): 0 \cdot a \coloneqq 0, (n + 1) \cdot a \coloneqq n \cdot a + a. Powers in a field are the powers of Section 1.1, defined in every commutative ring by the same recursion with products: a^0 \coloneqq 1 and a^{n+1} \coloneqq a^n a for n \in 
N. The power laws a^{m+n} = a^m a^n, (a^m)^n = a^{mn} and (ab)^n = a^n b^n hold in every commutative ring (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring), so in every field. Maps that respect both operations A homomorphism is a map that respects addition, multiplication and the number one. [Field Homomorphism] Let F and L be fields. A homomorphism (of fields) \varphi \colon F 	o L is a function such that, for all a, b \in F, \varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b) , \qquad \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) , \qquad \varphi(1) = 1 . A bijective (@fd2:def-bijective) homomorphism is an isomorphism; F and L are isomorphic, written F \cong L, if there is an isomorphism F 	o L. An isomorphism F 	o F is an automorphism of F. In words: the first clause says that adding and then mapping gives the same as mapping and then adding; the second says the same for multiplying; the third pins down the image of 1, where 1 on the left is 1_F and on the right 1_L. An isomorphism is a homomorphism that is also a one-to-one correspondence of elements, so F and L are then “the same field with the elements renamed”. Examples. - The identity \id_F \colon F 	o F is an automorphism. - Conjugation z \mapsto \conj{z} on 
C is a homomorphism by @thm-conjugate-properties (a), (b), since \conj{1} = 1; @exm-complex-conjugation-automorphism below shows that it is an automorphism. - The conjugation of 
Q(\sqrt 2), \sigma(a + b\sqrt 2) \coloneqq a - b\sqrt 2, is an automorphism (@exm-cof-sqrt2-conjugation). Why the clause \varphi(1) = 1. The zero map a \mapsto 0 satisfies the first two clauses, since 0 = 0 + 0 and 0 = 0 \cdot 0, and it carries no information about F at all. The third clause excludes it, and the next proposition shows that the third clause is exactly what forces a homomorphism to remember every element. The order-preserving field maps of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 6.1 (@fd3:def-cof-order-preserving-map), are the homomorphisms between ordered fields that also preserve <. From here on, F \cong L means isomorphic as fields, in the sense above; the relation of that chapter, an isomorphism that also preserves the order, is said in words, “isomorphic as ordered fields”. The two differ: the conjugation \sigma of 
Q(\sqrt 2) is an automorphism of the field, and it is not order-preserving, since 0 < \sqrt 2 while \sigma(\sqrt 2) = -\sqrt 2 < 0 = \sigma(0). What a homomorphism must do To find where a homomorphism sends an element, we take an equation that the element satisfies and apply \varphi to both sides. The equation in L that comes out often has only one solution. [Properties of Field Homomorphisms] Let \varphi \colon F 	o L be a homomorphism of fields, and let a, b \in F. 1. \varphi(0) = 0, \varphi(-a) = -\varphi(a) and \varphi(a - b) = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b). 2. If a 
e 0, then \varphi(a) 
e 0 and \varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}. 3. \varphi is injective. 4. The image \varphi(F) is a subfield of L, and \varphi, with codomain \varphi(F), is an isomorphism F 	o \varphi(F). 5. If \psi \colon L 	o M is a homomorphism of fields, then \psi \circ \varphi \colon F 	o M is a homomorphism. If \varphi is an isomorphism, its inverse function \varphi^{-1} \colon L 	o F is an isomorphism. The identity \id_F is an automorphism. 6. \varphi(n \cdot a) = n \cdot \varphi(a) and \varphi(a^n) = \varphi(a)^n for every n \in 
N. For (a) and (b) the equations to push through \varphi are 0 + 0 = 0, a + (-a) = 0 and aa^{-1} = 1; in L the results are equations with a unique solution, by cancellation and the uniqueness of negatives and inverses. For (c): a homomorphism cannot send a non-zero element to 0, because a non-zero element has an inverse, and then \varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(1) = 1 
e 0. Injectivity is that fact applied to a - b. The rest is bookkeeping with (a)–(c), and induction for (f). Before reading on: in the proof of (c), where is \varphi(1) = 1 used, and which map satisfies the other two clauses of @def-field-homomorphism but is not injective? (a) Since 0 + 0 = 0 in F, \varphi(0) + \varphi(0) = \varphi(0 + 0) = \varphi(0) = \varphi(0) + 0 , and additive cancellation in L (@thm-field-basic-properties (b)) gives \varphi(0) = 0. Next, a + (-a) = 0 gives \varphi(a) + \varphi(-a) = \varphi(a + (-a)) = \varphi(0) = 0, so \varphi(-a) is a negative of \varphi(a), and \varphi(-a) = -\varphi(a) by the uniqueness of negatives (@thm-field-basic-properties (c)). Finally, \varphi(a - b) = \varphi(a + (-b)) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(-b) = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b). (b) Let a 
e 0. Since aa^{-1} = 1, \varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(aa^{-1}) = \varphi(1) = 1 . If \varphi(a) = 0, the left side would be 0 \cdot \varphi(a^{-1}) = 0 (@thm-field-basic-properties (d)), and the display would read 0 = 1, against (F7) in L. So \varphi(a) 
e 0, and the display says that \varphi(a^{-1}) is an inverse of \varphi(a); by the uniqueness of inverses (@thm-field-basic-properties (c)), \varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}. (c) Let \varphi(a) = \varphi(b). By (a), \varphi(a - b) = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b) = 0. By (b), read contrapositively, an element whose image is 0 is 0; so a - b = 0, and a = b (add b to both sides, with (F2), (F1), (F4) and (F3)). So \varphi is injective. (d) We use @prp-subfield-test (c) for \varphi(F) \subseteq L. First, 1 = \varphi(1) \in \varphi(F). Next, two elements of \varphi(F) are \varphi(a), \varphi(b) with a, b \in F (@fd2:def-image), and \varphi(a) - \varphi(b) = \varphi(a - b) \in \varphi(F) by (a). If moreover \varphi(b) 
e 0, then b 
e 0, since \varphi(0) = 0; so by (b), \varphi(a)\varphi(b)^{-1} = \varphi(a)\varphi(b^{-1}) = \varphi(ab^{-1}) \in \varphi(F). Hence \varphi(F) is a subfield of L, a field with the operations of L (@prp-subfield-test (a)). The map \varphi \colon F 	o \varphi(F) still satisfies the three clauses, since the operations of \varphi(F) are those of L and its one is 1_L; it is surjective by the definition of the image, and injective by (c). So it is an isomorphism. (e) For the composite, (\psi \circ \varphi)(a + b) = \psi(\varphi(a) + \varphi(b)) = \psi(\varphi(a)) + \psi(\varphi(b)), likewise for products, and \psi(\varphi(1)) = \psi(1) = 1 (@fd2:def-composition). Now let \varphi be an isomorphism, with inverse function \varphi^{-1} \colon L 	o F (@fd2:def-inverse-function, which exists by @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse). For x, y \in L, \varphi igl(\varphi^{-1}(x) + \varphi^{-1}(y) igr) = \varphi(\varphi^{-1}(x)) + \varphi(\varphi^{-1}(y)) = x + y = \varphi igl(\varphi^{-1}(x + y) igr) , so \varphi^{-1}(x) + \varphi^{-1}(y) = \varphi^{-1}(x + y), because \varphi is injective. The same computation with products gives \varphi^{-1}(x)\varphi^{-1}(y) = \varphi^{-1}(xy). And \varphi(1) = 1 gives \varphi^{-1}(1) = 1. The function \varphi^{-1} is bijective, with inverse \varphi (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse); so it is an isomorphism. The identity satisfies the three clauses trivially and is bijective. (f) By induction on n (@fd1:ax-induction, read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification). For n = 0: \varphi(0 \cdot a) = \varphi(0) = 0 = 0 \cdot \varphi(a) by (a), and \varphi(a^0) = \varphi(1) = 1 = \varphi(a)^0. If the two formulas hold for n, then  egin{aligned} \varphi((n + 1) \cdot a) &= \varphi(n \cdot a + a) = n \cdot \varphi(a) + \varphi(a) = (n + 1) \cdot \varphi(a) , \ \varphi(a^{n+1}) &= \varphi(a^n a) = \varphi(a)^n \varphi(a) = \varphi(a)^{n+1} . \end{aligned} This proves the proposition. The answer to the prompt. In (c), \varphi(1) = 1 enters through (b): the display \varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = 1 is what makes \varphi(a) = 0 impossible. The zero map F 	o L satisfies the two other clauses, sends every element to 0, and is not injective. A map that respected sums and products but sent 1 to 0 would be the zero map: \varphi(a) = \varphi(a \cdot 1) = \varphi(a)\varphi(1) = \varphi(a) \cdot 0 = 0, by (F7), the product clause, \varphi(1) = 0, and @thm-field-basic-properties (d) with (F6) in L. We call the move of this proof push the equation through \varphi: to learn \varphi(x), apply \varphi to an equation that x satisfies, and solve the resulting equation in L. By (c) and (d), a homomorphism F 	o L is the same thing as a copy of F inside L: F \cong \varphi(F), a subfield of L. By (e) and @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective (c), composing isomorphisms gives isomorphisms, so \cong is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on any set of fields. A bijection that respects addition alone is not an isomorphism. The map f \colon 
Q 	o 
Q, f(x) \coloneqq 2x, is bijective (its inverse is x \mapsto x/2) and satisfies f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b), by (F9). But f(1 \cdot 1) = 2, while f(1)f(1) = 4; and f(1) = 2 
e 1. All three clauses of @def-field-homomorphism must be checked. Is a \mapsto -a a homomorphism 
Q 	o 
Q? No. It sends 1 to -1, and -1 
e 1 in 
Q: if -1 = 1, then 1 + 1 = 1 + (-1) = 0, while 1 + 1 = 2 \cdot 1 > 0 in the ordered field 
Q (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), @fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field). (In 
F_2, where -1 = 1, the same map is the identity.) It also fails the product clause: 1 \cdot 1 = 1 is sent to -1, while the product of the images is (-1)(-1) = 1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). It does respect sums, by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F9): -(a + b) = (-1)(a + b) = -a + (-b). Examples, and pairs of fields with no map between them [Conjugation and Other Automorphisms] 1. Show that conjugation z \mapsto \conj{z} is an automorphism of 
C, that it is not the identity, and that \conj{z} = z if and only if z \in 
R. 2. Let K be a subfield of L. Show that the inclusion K 	o L, x \mapsto x, is a homomorphism, and that it is not surjective when K 
e L. 3. Recall why a + b\sqrt 2 \mapsto a - b\sqrt 2 is an automorphism of 
Q(\sqrt 2). 4. Which automorphisms does 
R have? (i) By @thm-conjugate-properties (a), (b), \conj{z + w} = \conj{z} + \conj{w} and \conj{zw} = \conj{z}\,\conj{w}; and \conj{1} = \conj{1 + 0i} = 1 - 0i = 1 (@def-conjugate-modulus). So conjugation is a homomorphism. By @thm-conjugate-properties (a), \conj{\conj{z}} = z, so conjugation is its own inverse, hence bijective (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse): an automorphism. It is not the identity: \conj{i} = -i, and -i 
e i, since i - (-i) = 2i = (0, 2) 
e (0, 0). For the fixed elements, let z = a + bi with a, b \in 
R. Then \conj{z} = a - bi (@def-conjugate-modulus), and comparing parts (@def-complex-numbers), \conj{z} = z if and only if -b = b, that is 2b = 0, that is b = 0 (as 2 = 2 \cdot 1 > 0 in the ordered field 
R, @fd3:thm-reals-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h), so 2 
e 0, and by @thm-field-basic-properties (f)). And b = 0 says z = a + 0i = a \in 
R (@prp-reals-embed-complex). This fact is not among the parts of @thm-conjugate-properties; the two lines above prove it. (ii) The operations of K are those of L, and 1_K = 1_L (@prp-subfield-test (a)). So x \mapsto x satisfies the three clauses. If K

(iii) This is @exm-cof-sqrt2-conjugation, recalled and not proved again: unique representation makes the formula a function, the product formula of @exm-q-sqrt2-field with -b, -d in place of b, d shows that products go to products, and the map is its own inverse. title: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content:
Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield Add 1 to itself in 
Q and the sums 1, 1 + 1, 1 + 1 + 1, \dots never return to 0. In 
F_2 two copies of 1 already give 0, and in 
F_p it takes p copies. This one number decides whether “2x = 0, so x = 0” is a valid step, and Section 4.4 showed that homomorphisms respect it: there is none from 
F_2 to 
Q (@exm-field-homomorphism-obstructions (ii)). This section names the number, the characteristic, proves that it is 0 or a prime, and uses it to find the smallest subfield of every field: a copy of 
Q or of exactly one 
F_p. Throughout, F and L are fields (@def-field), 0 and 1 are the zero and one of the field in play, and we write 1_F when two fields are in play at once. Integer multiples The question “can 1 + 1 + \dots + 1 be 0?” is about the elements n \cdot 1. For n \in 
N these are already defined in every commutative ring. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.4 (“Multiples”) defines, for a commutative ring R and a \in R, by recursion on 
N = \omega, 0 \cdot a \coloneqq 0 , \qquad (n + 1) \cdot a \coloneqq n \cdot a + a \quad (n \in 
N) . So 1 \cdot a = a, 2 \cdot a = a + a, and n \cdot a is the sum of n copies of a. We need negative multiples too, because the divisibility arguments below write n = qc + r with q possibly negative. Negative multiples. Every integer is m or -m for some m \in 
N (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers (c)). For n \in 
Z with n < 0 we have -n > 0, so -n \in 
N by @fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (b), and we define n \cdot a \coloneqq - igl( (-n) \cdot a  igr) . So (-3) \cdot a = -(a + a + a). Extending the convention of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.4 (there for natural numbers), a dot with an integer on its left always means this multiple, and the product of two ring elements is written by juxtaposition, ab. When R = 
Z the two readings agree: for n \in 
N this is the remark after the definition of multiples in that section, and for n < 0, n \cdot a = -((-n)a) = -(-(na)) = na by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) and (a). The lemma below collects the rules for multiples. Parts (a)–(c) are the three identities that the linear-algebra volumes cite; part (d) extends everything to integer multiples. Integer Multiples Let R be a commutative ring, a, b \in R, and m, k \in 
N. 1. (m \cdot 1) + (k \cdot 1) = (m + k) \cdot 1. 2. (m \cdot 1)(k \cdot 1) = (mk) \cdot 1. 3. (m \cdot 1)\, a = m \cdot a. 4. The identities (a)–(c) hold for all m, k \in 
Z, and so do  egin{aligned} (m + k) \cdot a &= m \cdot a + k \cdot a , & (-m) \cdot a &= -(m \cdot a) , \ m \cdot (a + b) &= m \cdot a + m \cdot b , & (m \cdot a)\, b &= m \cdot (ab) , \ (mk) \cdot a &= m \cdot (k \cdot a) . & & \end{aligned} In words: integer multiples obey the rules one expects of “m copies of a”, with signs behaving as in 
Z. Since every field is a commutative ring (the remark after @def-field), the lemma holds in every field. For natural numbers everything is one induction each, on the recursion that defines m \cdot a: four rules for natural multiples (a sum law, a distributive law, a product law and a composition law, proved in Chapter 1 as @lem-natural-multiples) and then (a)–(c) as special cases with a = 1. Negative multiples are reduced to natural ones by writing an integer as a difference m_1 - m_2 of natural numbers; that bookkeeping is (d), and its proof is in the fold below. For natural numbers the four rules are @lem-natural-multiples (a)–(d), proved in Chapter 1: (a) is the sum law, (b) the distributive law, (c) the product law and (d) the composition law, and below we call them rules (i)–(iv), in that order: (m + k) \cdot a = m \cdot a + k \cdot a, m \cdot (a + b) = m \cdot a + m \cdot b, (m \cdot a) b = m \cdot (ab) and (mk) \cdot a = m \cdot (k \cdot a). Now (a) of the present lemma is rule (i) with a = 1. For (c), (m \cdot 1) a = m \cdot a is @lem-natural-multiples (e). For (b), (m \cdot 1)(k \cdot 1) = m \cdot (1 (k \cdot 1)) = m \cdot (k \cdot 1) = (mk) \cdot 1 by rule (iii), (F6) with (F7), and rule (iv). Part (d) is proved in the fold below. This proves the lemma. Every integer is a difference m_1 - m_2 of natural numbers, and a negative multiple is the negative of a natural one. So each identity of (d) splits into identities for natural multiples, which are rules (i)–(iv), combined with the ring rules for negatives. Only the composition law needs the four sign cases separately, and a table keeps them apart. Step 1: (-m) \cdot a = -(m \cdot a) for every m \in 
Z. If m > 0, then -m < 0 and the definition gives (-m) \cdot a = -((-(-m)) \cdot a) = -(m \cdot a). If m = 0, both sides are 0, since -0 = 0 (0 + 0 = 0 and uniqueness of negatives, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). If m < 0, the definition gives m \cdot a = -((-m) \cdot a), so -(m \cdot a) = (-m) \cdot a because -(-x) = x (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). Step 2: (m - k) \cdot a = m \cdot a - k \cdot a for m, k \in 
N. If m \ge k, then m - k \in 
N and (m - k) + k = m, so m \cdot a = (m - k) \cdot a + k \cdot a by rule (i) of the proof above; adding -(k \cdot a) to both sides gives the claim. If m < k, then by Step 1 and the first case (m - k) \cdot a = - igl( (k - m) \cdot a  igr) = - igl( k \cdot a - m \cdot a  igr) = m \cdot a - k \cdot a , the last step because (k \cdot a - m \cdot a) + (m \cdot a - k \cdot a) = 0 by (F1)–(F4), and negatives are unique. Step 3: the sum, distributive and product rules. By @fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers (c), every integer is a difference m_1 - m_2 of natural numbers (m = m - 0, -m = 0 - m). Let x = m_1 - m_2 and y = k_1 - k_2 with m_1, m_2, k_1, k_2 \in 
N. Then x + y = (m_1 + k_1) - (m_2 + k_2), and by Step 2 and rule (i),  egin{aligned} (x + y) \cdot a &= (m_1 \cdot a + k_1 \cdot a) - (m_2 \cdot a + k_2 \cdot a) \ &= (m_1 \cdot a - m_2 \cdot a) + (k_1 \cdot a - k_2 \cdot a) = x \cdot a + y \cdot a , \end{aligned} using -(u + v) = (-u) + (-v) (both are negatives of u + v) and (F1), (F2). In the same way, Step 2 with rules (ii) and (iii) gives x \cdot (a + b) = x \cdot a + x \cdot b and (x \cdot a) b = (m_1 \cdot a) b - (m_2 \cdot a) b = x \cdot (ab), the middle step by (F9) and (-u) b = -(ub) (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). From the distributive rule, x \cdot c + x \cdot (-c) = x \cdot 0, and x \cdot 0 = (x \cdot 1) 0 = 0 by the product rule just proved (with a = 1, b = 0) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b); so x \cdot (-c) = -(x \cdot c). Step 4: (xy) \cdot a = x \cdot (y \cdot a). Write x = \pm m' and y = \pm k' with m', k' \in 
N. In 
Z, (-m')k' = m'(-k') = -(m'k') and (-m')(-k') = m'k' (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). Each row of the table reduces both sides to rule (iv), using Step 1 and the last line of Step 3. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- x, y (xy) \cdot a x \cdot (y \cdot a) ----------------------- ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------------- m', k' (m'k') \cdot a m' \cdot (k' \cdot a) -m', k' -((m'k') \cdot a) -(m' \cdot (k' \cdot a)) m', -k' -((m'k') \cdot a) m' \cdot (-(k' \cdot a)) = -(m' \cdot (k' \cdot a)) -m', -k' (m'k') \cdot a -(m' \cdot (-(k' \cdot a))) = m' \cdot (k' \cdot a) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Step 5: (a)–(c) for integers. (a) is the sum rule with a = 1. (c): (x \cdot 1) a = x \cdot (1 a) = x \cdot a. (b): (x \cdot 1)(y \cdot 1) = x \cdot (1 (y \cdot 1)) = x \cdot (y \cdot 1) = (xy) \cdot 1, by the product rule and Step 4. This proves (d). Two readings of the lemma are used constantly. First, by (a) and (b) with (d), the map 
Z 	o R, n \mapsto n \cdot 1, turns sums of integers into sums in R and products into products, and sends 1 to 1 \cdot 1 = 1. Second, by (c) with (d), every multiple n \cdot a is a product in R, namely (n \cdot 1) a: to know how multiples behave, it is enough to know the elements n \cdot 1. In 
Z/n
Z these elements are the classes themselves: k \cdot [1] = [k] for k \in 
N (@thm-integers-mod-n-ring (d)), and for k < 0, k \cdot [1] = -((-k) \cdot [1]) = -[-k] = [k], since -[u] = [-u] in a quotient ring (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (b)). In 
Z/5
Z, compute (-3) \cdot [2] in two ways: by the definition of a negative multiple, and by (c) of @lem-integer-multiples, extended to integers by (d). By the definition, (-3) \cdot [2] = -(3 \cdot [2]) = -([2] + [2] + [2]) = -[6] = [-6] = [4], since -6 - 4 = -10 is divisible by 5. By (c) and (d), (-3) \cdot [2] = ((-3) \cdot [1])[2] = [-3][2] = [-6] = [4], using k \cdot [1] = [k] for k = -3. The characteristic The elements 1, 2 \cdot 1, 3 \cdot 1, \dots of a field either never reach 0, or reach it for some positive n. In the second case the first time they reach it is the number that matters. The characteristic counts how many copies of 1 add up to 0, and is 0 if no number of copies does. [Characteristic] Let F be a field. If there exists a positive integer n with n \cdot 1 = 0, the characteristic of F, written \operatorname{char} F, is the least such n. If there is none, \operatorname{char} F \coloneqq 0. In words: test n = 1, 2, 3, \dots in turn; \operatorname{char} F is the first n with n \cdot 1 = 0, and 0 if the test never stops. The same words define the characteristic of a commutative ring. Well-definedness. If the set S \coloneqq \{ n \in 
Z_{>0} : n \cdot 1 = 0 \} is non-empty, it is a non-empty set of integers bounded below by 1, so it has a least element by @fd3:prp-integer-least-element. So “the least such n” names exactly one integer. First examples. - 
F_2: 1 \cdot 1 = 1 
e 0 and 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = 0 by the table of @exm-finite-fields, so \operatorname{char} 
F_2 = 2. - 
F_3: 1 \cdot 1 = 1, 2 \cdot 1 = 2, 3 \cdot 1 = 3 = 0, and 1, 2 
e 0 in 
F_3, so \operatorname{char} 
F_3 = 3. - 
Q: n \cdot 1 = n 
e 0 for every n \ge 1, so \operatorname{char} 
Q = 0. The reason is the order of 
Q; the example at the end of the next subsection gives it. - The ring 
Z/6
Z, which is not a field: k \cdot [1] = [k] 
e [0] for k = 1, \dots, 5 and 6 \cdot [1] = [0], so it has characteristic 6. The degenerate case. In the zero ring \{0\} of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.3, 1 = 0, so 1 \cdot 1 = 1 = 0 and the characteristic is 1. It is the only ring of characteristic 1: characteristic 1 means 1 = 1 \cdot 1 = 0, and then every a = a \cdot 1 = a \cdot 0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). It is not a field. For fields, the clause 1 
e 0 of (F7) rules out characteristic 1, and that is the first step of the theorem below on which characteristics occur. Why 0 and not “infinity”. The convention \operatorname{char} F = 0 makes the next proposition read the same in every case: n \cdot 1 = 0 exactly when \operatorname{char} F divides n. For \operatorname{char} F = 0 this says n \cdot 1 = 0 only for n = 0, because 0 \mid n only for n = 0 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). The proposition is the form in which the characteristic is used. Its proof is the move of Chapter 2: take the least positive element, then divide by it. [The Characteristic Divides Every Vanishing Multiple] Let F be a field, c \coloneqq \operatorname{char} F, and n \in 
Z. 1. n \cdot 1 = 0 if and only if c \mid n. 2. n \cdot 1 is invertible in F if and only if c 
mid n. In particular 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1 is invertible in F if and only if \operatorname{char} F 
e 2. For c > 0, divide n by c with remainder, n = qc + r. The multiple c \cdot 1 is 0, so the rules of @lem-integer-multiples kill the part qc and leave n \cdot 1 = r \cdot 1. The remainder is smaller than c, and c was the least positive integer with a vanishing multiple, so r \cdot 1 = 0 forces r = 0. For c = 0 there is nothing to divide: no positive multiple vanishes, and negatives follow by a sign. (a) Case c = 0. We show n \cdot 1 = 0 iff n = 0, which is the claim since 0 \mid n iff n = 0 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). If n = 0, n \cdot 1 = 0. If n > 0, then n \cdot 1 
e 0 by @def-characteristic, since c = 0 means no positive multiple vanishes. If n < 0, then n \cdot 1 = -((-n) \cdot 1) with (-n) \cdot 1 
e 0; and -x = 0 would give x = -(-x) = -0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), so n \cdot 1 
e 0. Case c > 0. (\Leftarrow) If c \mid n, say n = qc with q \in 
Z, then by @lem-integer-multiples (b), which holds for integers by part (d), n \cdot 1 = (qc) \cdot 1 = (q \cdot 1)(c \cdot 1) = (q \cdot 1) \, 0 = 0 , the last step by @thm-field-basic-properties (d) and (F6). (\Rightarrow) Suppose n \cdot 1 = 0. By @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder there are q, r \in 
Z with n = qc + r and 0 \le r < c. By the sum rule of @lem-integer-multiples (d) and the computation just made, 0 = n \cdot 1 = (qc) \cdot 1 + r \cdot 1 = 0 + r \cdot 1 = r \cdot 1 , using (F1) and (F3) at the end. If r > 0, then r is a positive integer with r \cdot 1 = 0 and r < c, against the minimality of c in @def-characteristic. So r = 0, and n = qc, that is, c \mid n. (b) In a field an element is invertible if and only if it is non-zero: a non-zero element has an inverse by (F8), and 0 has none, since 0 \cdot y = 0 
e 1 (@thm-field-basic-properties (d), and 1 
e 0 by (F7)). So (b) is (a) negated. For n = 2: 2 \cdot 1 = (0 \cdot 1 + 1) + 1 = 1 + 1. The positive divisors of 2 are 1 and 2 (2 is prime), and 0 
mid 2; and c 
e 1, since 1 \cdot 1 = 1 
e 0. So c \mid 2 iff c = 2, and 1 + 1 is invertible iff c 
e 2. This proves the proposition. This is the form the linear-algebra volumes use, in sentences such as “\operatorname{char} F 
e 2, so 2 is invertible” and “m \cdot 1 is invertible when \operatorname{char} F 
mid m”. It also says that the integers n with n \cdot 1 = 0 are exactly the multiples of one integer, c, with nothing else vanishing by accident. In characteristic 2, 1 + 1 = 0, so -1 = 1 and x = -x for every x. The familiar step “x = -x, so 2x = 0, so x = 0” divides by 2 = 1 + 1, which is 0 there. In 
F_2, the element 1 satisfies 1 = -1 and 1 
e 0. This is why many later results, for instance about symmetric and alternating bilinear forms in the linear-algebra volumes, assume \operatorname{char} F 
e 2: by @prp-characteristic-divides (b), that is exactly the hypothesis that makes the step valid. [Completing the square in 
F_3] Solve x^2 + x + 1 = 0 in 
F_3 by completing the square. Since \operatorname{char} 
F_3 = 3 
e 2 (the first examples above), 2 = 1 + 1 is invertible by @prp-characteristic-divides (b); indeed 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 1, so 2^{-1} = 2. Also 4 = 1 
e 0, so x^2 + x + 1 = 0 holds if and only if 4(x^2 + x + 1) = 0 (one direction by @thm-field-basic-properties (d) and (F6), the other by (f)). By @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d), with the multiples regrouped by @lem-integer-multiples (b), (F5) and (F6), (2x + 1)^2 = 4x^2 + 4x + 1, so 4(x^2 + x + 1) = (2x + 1)^2 + 3 = (2x + 1)^2 , as 3 = 0 in 
F_3. So the equation says (2x + 1)^2 = 0, that is, 2x + 1 = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f), and x = 2^{-1}(-1) = 2 \cdot 2 = 1 by @prp-field-linear-equation (a), using -1 = 2. Testing all three elements agrees: x = 0, 1, 2 give 1, 3 = 0 and 7 = 1. In 
F_2 the method stops at the first step: there 2 = 0 and 4 = 0, so multiplying by 4 cannot be undone and 2 has no inverse. The characteristics found so far are 0, 2 and 3, and the ring 
Z/6
Z has characteristic 6. A field cannot. [The Characteristic Is Zero or a Prime] Let F be a field. Then \operatorname{char} F is 0 or a prime. This is the argument that showed 
Z/n
Z is not a field for composite n (@thm-zp-field-iff-prime), run inside F. If c = rs with smaller factors, then (r \cdot 1)(s \cdot 1) = c \cdot 1 = 0. A field has no zero divisors, so one of the two factors is already 0, at a multiple smaller than c. Let c \coloneqq \operatorname{char} F and suppose c > 0. Since 1 \cdot 1 = 1 
e 0 by (F7), c 
e 1, so c \ge 2. Suppose c is not prime. By @fd2:def-prime it has a positive divisor r 
otin \{1, c\}; write c = rs with s \in 
Z. Then s > 0, as r, c > 0, and s \mid c; r \le c and s \le c by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e); and s 
e 1, s 
e c, since s = 1 would give r = c and s = c would give r = 1 (cancel c 
e 0 in 
Z). So 1 < r < c and 1 < s < c. By @lem-integer-multiples (b), (r \cdot 1)(s \cdot 1) = (rs) \cdot 1 = c \cdot 1 = 0 , so r \cdot 1 = 0 or s \cdot 1 = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f). Either way a positive integer smaller than c has a vanishing multiple, against the minimality of c. Hence c is prime. This proves the theorem. So the possible characteristics of fields are 0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, \dots, and the example at the end of the next subsection shows that each of them occurs. The hypothesis “field” is used twice, at 1 
e 0 and at “no zero divisors”, and the ring 
Z/6
Z shows the second cannot be dropped: there [2][3] = [0]. The characteristic under subfields and homomorphisms The characteristic is computed from 0, 1 and + alone. A subfield has the same three, and a homomorphism carries them over, so both must preserve it. [Subfields and Homomorphisms Preserve the Characteristic] 1. If K is a subfield of L, then \operatorname{char} K = \operatorname{char} L. 2. If \varphi \colon F 	o L is a homomorphism, then \operatorname{char} F = \operatorname{char} L. 3. There is no homomorphism between two fields of different characteristic. (a) By @prp-subfield-test (a), K has the zero 0_L, the one 1_L, and the restricted addition of L. Hence n \cdot 1_K = n \cdot 1_L for every n \in
