Z, as Section 5.1 announced. C. Going deeper [C1: Dropping “disjoint”] @prp-disjoint-cycles-commute assumes that the supports are disjoint. 1. Find two transpositions that share exactly one point and do not commute. 2. Find two cycles in S_3 with the same support that do commute. 3. In the proof of @prp-disjoint-cycles-commute, which step fails for the pair of (a)? (a) (1\ 2) and (2\ 3) share only the point 2. By the table of Exercise B1, (1\ 2)(2\ 3) = (1\ 2\ 3) and (2\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 3\ 2), which differ (at 1: 2 versus 3). (b) (1\ 2\ 3) and (1\ 3\ 2) both have support \{1, 2, 3\}. They are inverse to each other (the inverse formula after @def-cycle), so both products are \id: (1\ 2\ 3)(1\ 3\ 2) = \id = (1\ 3\ 2)(1\ 2\ 3). More generally every permutation commutes with its inverse and with its own powers (@prp-group-power-laws (a)). So disjointness is sufficient for commuting, not necessary. (c) Case 1 at the point i = 1 \in \supp (1\ 2): the proof needs \sigma(i) = 2 
otin \supp 	au, so that 	au fixes it. Here 	au = (2\ 3) moves 2, so (	au\sigma)(1) = 	au(2) = 3, while (\sigma	au)(1) = \sigma(1) = 2. [C2: Powers of disjoint cycles] 1. Let \sigma = (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k) \in S_n be a k-cycle and m \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that \sigma^m = \id if and only if k \mid m. 2. Let \sigma be a k-cycle and 	au an l-cycle in S_n, disjoint. Prove that, for every m \in 
Z_{>0}, (\sigma	au)^m = \id if and only if k \mid m and l \mid m. 3. Deduce that the least m \ge 1 with (\sigma	au)^m = \id is the least positive common multiple of k and l. 4. Find the least m \ge 1 with  igl((1\ 2)(3\ 4\ 5) igr)^m = \id in S_5. [Hint 1] For (b): a power of 	au fixes every point that 	au fixes. [Hint 2] Converse of (b): evaluate \sigma^m	au^m = \id at a point of \supp \sigma. (a) Read the indices of the entries modulo k: for j \in 
Z let i_j \coloneqq i_t, where t \in \{1, \dots, k\} and j \equiv t \pmod{k}. Write j - 1 = kq + s with 0 \le s < k (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a)) and take t \coloneqq s + 1; t is unique because s is. Then \sigma(i_j) = i_{j+1} for every j, which is @def-cycle. By induction on m \in 
N (@fd1:ax-induction), \sigma^m(i_j) = i_{j+m} for every j: for m = 0 both sides are i_j, and \sigma^{m+1}(i_j) = \sigma(\sigma^m(i_j)) = \sigma(i_{j+m}) = i_{j+m+1}, using \sigma^{m+1} = \sigma\sigma^m (@prp-group-power-laws (a)). Every point off the cycle is fixed by \sigma, hence by \sigma^m. So \sigma^m = \id if and only if i_{j+m} = i_j for every j. Since the entries i_1, \dots, i_k are distinct, i_{j+m} = i_j holds exactly when j + m \equiv j \pmod{k}, that is, when k \mid m. (b) The supports are disjoint, so \sigma	au = 	au\sigma (@prp-disjoint-cycles-commute), and (\sigma	au)^m = \sigma^m	au^m by @prp-group-power-laws (d). If k \mid m and l \mid m, then \sigma^m = 	au^m = \id by (a), so (\sigma	au)^m = \id. Conversely, suppose \sigma^m	au^m = \id. Let x \in \supp \sigma. Then x 
otin \supp 	au, so 	au(x) = x, and by induction on m (@fd1:ax-induction) 	au^m(x) = x (Hint 1). Hence \sigma^m(x) = \sigma^m(	au^m(x)) = x. Also \sigma^m fixes every x 
otin \supp \sigma, since \sigma does. So \sigma^m = \id, and then 	au^m = \sigma^m	au^m = \id. By (a), k \mid m and l \mid m. (c) By (b), the m \ge 1 with (\sigma	au)^m = \id are exactly the positive common multiples of k and l. This set contains kl, and so it has a least element (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element), the least positive common multiple of k and l. By @exr-subgroups-c3, the common multiples of k and l are exactly the multiples of that number. (d) (1\ 2) and (3\ 4\ 5) are disjoint, of lengths 2 and 3. The positive common multiples of 2 and 3 start 6, 12, \dots (a common multiple of 2 is even, and 3 
mid 2, 4), so the least m is 6. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (a) the formula \sigma^m(i_j) = i_{j+m} with indices modulo k, proved by induction, and the points off the cycle fixed. - 1: (a) from distinctness of the entries to k \mid m, in both directions. - 2: (b) commuting from disjointness, cited, and (\sigma	au)^m = \sigma^m	au^m with the reason. - 3: (b) the converse: from \sigma^m	au^m = \id, uses disjointness of the supports to get \sigma^m = \id and 	au^m = \id. - 1: (c) and (d), the least element named. Second route: \sigma^m = 	au^{-m}, with \supp \sigma^m \subseteq \supp \sigma and \supp 	au^{-m} \subseteq \supp 	au, and these are disjoint, so both are \id; this earns the same 3 points if both inclusions are justified. Fatal errors (0 for the step): (\sigma	au)^m = \sigma^m	au^m without using that the cycles commute; “\sigma^m	au^m = \id so \sigma^m = 	au^{-m}, hence both are \id” with no use of disjointness.

title: 5.5 Transpositions Generate the Symmetric Group
content:
Transpositions Generate the Symmetric Group Section 5.4 wrote permutations in cycle notation and showed that every permutation breaks into disjoint cycles (@thm-disjoint-cycle-decomposition). One small computation there, (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3) in @exm-cycle-notation, says more than it seems to: a 3-cycle is two swaps. This section shows that every permutation of \{1, \dots, n\}, for n \ge 2, is a product of swaps of two points. The determinant of linear algebra is built on exactly this fact, and so is the sign of a permutation, which later volumes define. Throughout, n \in 
N, products of permutations are read right to left (@def-symmetric-group: \sigma	au = \sigma \circ 	au applies 	au first), and a product 	au_1 	au_2 \cdots 	au_r is the product of a list in the group S_n (@def-group-list-product), so brackets may be dropped (@prp-group-list-product-laws (b)). Cycles as products of transpositions Recall from @def-cycle that a transposition is a 2-cycle (a\ b), with a 
e b: it swaps a and b and fixes every other point. Two facts about it are used constantly below. - (a\ b) = (b\ a), since both swap a and b and fix the rest (@fd2:prp-function-equality). - A transposition is its own inverse: (a\ b)(a\ b) = \id. Indeed a \mapsto b \mapsto a, b \mapsto a \mapsto b, and every other point is fixed twice. Equivalently, the inverse of (a\ b) is (b\ a) = (a\ b) (@def-cycle). The computation (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3) has a pattern: both transpositions contain the first entry 1 of the cycle, and the one applied first is (1\ 2), which sends 1 to the next entry. Longer cycles follow the same pattern. [A Cycle Is a Product of Transpositions] Let k \ge 2, and let i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k \in \{1, \dots, n\} be distinct. Then (i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_k) = (i_1\ i_k)(i_1\ i_{k-1}) \cdots (i_1\ i_2) , a product of k - 1 transpositions. Read right to left, the factors are (i_1\ i_2), then (i_1\ i_3), and so on up to (i_1\ i_k). For k = 4: (1\ 2\ 3\ 4) = (1\ 4)(1\ 3)(1\ 2). Follow 2: the first factor (1\ 2) sends it to 1, the second sends 1 to 3, and the third fixes 3; so 2 \mapsto 3, as the cycle requires. Induct on the length. To pass from (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k) to (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k\ i_{k+1}), the only change is that i_k must now go to i_{k+1} instead of back to i_1, and i_{k+1} must go to i_1. One more swap of i_1 and i_{k+1}, applied after the shorter cycle, makes exactly this change. We prove, by @fd2:thm-induction with base 2 (read on \omega by @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)), the statement P(k): “for every list (i_1, \dots, i_k) of distinct points of \{1, \dots, n\}, the displayed equation holds”. Formal Polynomials At school a polynomial is “an expression in x”, and x is a number not yet chosen. Over the field 
F_2 of Chapter 4 this picture breaks at once: x^2 + x takes the value 0 at both elements, so as a function it is the zero function, yet we want it to have degree 2. This chapter therefore decides that a polynomial is its list of coefficients, a sequence with only finitely many non-zero entries, and that x is the name of a position, never a number. From that one decision it builds the polynomial ring R[x] over any commutative ring R of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2, and proves its laws with one device, check on monomials, extend by additivity, so that no double sum is ever reordered. It then attaches the degree and the leading coefficient, recovers “plugging in” as a ring homomorphism, and defines the derivative by its coefficients, with no limit in sight. Which school rules survive depends on R, and the chapter keeps count. Over 
Z/6
Z the degree of a product can drop, because [2][3] = [0]. Over 
Z/4
Z the polynomial 1 + [2]x is its own inverse. Over every finite ring with 1 
e 0 some non-zero polynomial vanishes at every element, so a polynomial is not its function. Over 
F_p the derivative of x^p is 0. Each result says what it needs from R: nothing at all, no zero divisors, a unit leading coefficient, finiteness with 1 
e 0, or, for the derivative, the characteristic of a field. The chapter ends where Chapter 7 begins, with R = F a field and division with remainder still to come. One construction, many rings. The linear-algebra companion defines polynomials over a field F, and its later chapters cite this chapter’s results with F a field. Every such statement is the case R = F of the statement proved here for a commutative ring, since a field is a commutative ring. Where a result really needs more than a commutative ring, the hypothesis is named at the point of use: no zero divisors (@thm-degree-of-product (b), @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors, @prp-polynomial-units), a unit leading coefficient (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), R finite with 1

Degree with \deg 0 = -\infty, the leading coefficient and monic polynomials; the degree of a sum; the degree of a product, whose top coefficient is \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q) in every commutative ring, so that degrees add exactly when that product is non-zero, as over a ring with no zero divisors or for a unit leading coefficient; integral domains, with R[x] an integral domain exactly when R is; the units of R[x] over an integral domain, and the non-constant unit 1 + [2]x over

The value p(c), roots, and evaluation respecting sums and products; ring homomorphisms and two impostors; the substitution principle, that one ring homomorphism R[x] 	o S extends a given \varphi \colon R 	o S and sends x to a given s, and only one; changing coefficients along \varphi, with reduction modulo n and the exact condition for the degree to drop, and the composition p \circ q; and the ring R^R of functions, with polynomial composition matching composition of functions and, over every finite ring with 1 
e 0, a non-zero polynomial whose function is 0. - The Formal Derivative. The derivative defined by (f')_k = (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1}, the role of the element n \cdot 1, and examples in five rings; the sum, product and power rules in every commutative ring, the product rule by checking on monomials; over a field, f' = 0 exactly for the constants in characteristic 0 and exactly for the polynomials in x^p in characteristic p; and review exercises that return to groups (Chapter 5), complex conjugation (Chapter 3) and countability (Sets and Functions, Chapter 4). Named moves - Compare coefficients. Two polynomials are equal if and only if their coefficients agree in every position, so an identity in R[x] is proved by computing the k-th coefficient of both sides for an arbitrary k. It is the “reduce to the level below” of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.3, now with sequences. Named in Section 6.1, it proves the additive laws and both distributive laws of R[x] in Section 6.2 and the linearity of the derivative in Section 6.5. - Check on monomials, extend by additivity. Two maps of up to three polynomial arguments that are additive in each argument, and agree when every argument is a monomial, agree everywhere (@lem-check-on-monomials). It proves commutativity and associativity of the product in Section 6.2, evaluation and substitution respecting products in Section 6.4, and the product rule in Section 6.5. Exercise B2 of Section 6.2 leaves its last step to you, and Exercise C2 of Section 6.4 its second half. - Look at the top coefficient. The coefficient of x^{\deg p + \deg q} in pq is \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q), and nothing sits above it; every question about the degree of a product becomes the question whether that one element of R is 0. It proves the degree formula in Section 6.3 and, through it, the absence of zero divisors and the units of R[x]; in Section 6.4 it shows that the product of the factors x - c over a finite ring is monic, and Exercise B1 there uses it for the degree of a composition. - A homomorphism out of R[x] is fixed by the constants and x. To show that two ring homomorphisms out of R[x] agree, check that they agree on the constants and on x (@thm-polynomial-substitution (b)). Named in Section 6.4, it proves there that composing polynomials matches composing their functions, and Exercise B3 of Section 6.4 uses it to invert the shift p \mapsto p \circ (x + c).

title: 6.1 Polynomials as Coefficient Sequences
content:
Polynomials as Coefficient Sequences At school a polynomial is an expression such as 3x^2 - x + 2, and x is a number that has not been chosen yet. This chapter replaces that picture by a definition that works over every commutative ring of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2 (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field): over 
Q, over the fields 
F_p of Chapter 4, and over rings such as 
Z/6
Z, where a product of two non-zero elements can be zero. This section makes the one decision the whole chapter rests on: a polynomial is its list of coefficients. It then collects the finite sums, powers and multiples that the next sections compute with. Throughout, R is a commutative ring, with a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). What goes wrong with “an expression in x” Take the field 
F_2 = \{0, 1\} of @def-field-fp, in which 1 + 1 = 0. Read x^2 + x the school way, as a rule: replace x by an element c and compute cc + c. The tables of @exm-finite-fields give 0 \cdot 0 + 0 = 0 , \qquad 1 \cdot 1 + 1 = 1 + 1 = 0 . So the rule c \mapsto cc + c and the rule c \mapsto 0 give the same output at both elements of 
F_2. As functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 they are equal, by @fd2:prp-function-equality: same domain, same codomain, same values. If a polynomial were the function it defines, then x^2 + x would be the zero polynomial over 
F_2. So would x^3 + x and x^4 + x^2, which also give 0 at 0 and 1 + 1 = 0 at 1. None of them would have a highest power of x, and the rule “the degree of a product is the sum of the degrees”, which we want over every field, would fail for x \cdot (x + 1) = x^2 + x: degrees 1 and 1, product “zero”. Over 
Q the problem never shows (Section 7.4 proves that over an infinite field a non-zero polynomial never gives the zero function), which is why school algebra can afford the picture. Over a finite ring with 1 
e 0 it cannot. So we decide the other way. Two polynomials are the same when their coefficients are the same, and the letter x is not a number at all. A polynomial is its list of coefficients; the letter x only marks the positions. Polynomials over a commutative ring A list of coefficients that goes on forever is a sequence, that is, a function on 
N. We keep only the sequences that stop being non-zero. [Polynomial] Let R be a commutative ring. A polynomial over R (in the indeterminate x) is a function p \colon 
N 	o R, written p = (p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots), such that only finitely many p_k are non-zero: there exists N \in 
N with p_k = 0 for every k > N. Such an N is called admissible for p. The element p_k is the coefficient of x^k in p. For a \in R and n \in 
N, the monomial a \, x^n is the polynomial with a in position n and 0 in every other position. We set x \coloneqq 1 \, x^1, and for a \in R the constant a is the monomial a \, x^0. The zero polynomial is 0 \coloneqq (0, 0, 0, \dots). The set of all polynomials over R is written R[x]. In words: the first clause says that a polynomial is an infinite list of elements of R, indexed from 0; the second says that from some position on, every entry is 0. The quantifiers are in the order “there is one N that works for every later k”: a sequence with infinitely many non-zero entries, however sparse, is excluded. A monomial has at most one non-zero entry, so n is admissible for it, and it is a polynomial. The symbol x is the particular sequence (0, 1, 0, 0, \dots): an element of R[x], never an element of R, and never a variable that takes values. Equality. Two polynomials p, q \in R[x] are functions with the same domain 
N and the same codomain R. By @fd2:prp-function-equality, p = q \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad p_k = q_k \ 	ext{ for every } k \in 
N . To prove an identity between polynomials we therefore compute the k-th coefficient of both sides, for an arbitrary k. We call this move compare coefficients. It is the “reduce to the level below” of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.3, once more: a statement about polynomials becomes a statement about elements of R, one position at a time. The display. If N is admissible for p, we write p = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k = p_0 + p_1 x + p_2 x^2 + \dots + p_N x^N . For now this is notation only. No addition of polynomials has been defined yet, so the plus signs are not an operation: the display names the sequence by listing its entries, each with a marker x^k for its position. We drop terms whose coefficient is 0, write a x for a x^1, a for a x^0, x^k for 1 x^k, and - a x^k for (-a) x^k. So 3x^2 - x + 2 over 
Q names the sequence with p_0 = 2, p_1 = -1, p_2 = 3 and p_k = 0 for k \ge 3. Section 6.2 defines the sum of two polynomials and proves that the display is then an honest sum of monomials. There is one thing to check about the display. The admissible N is not unique: if N is admissible, so is every M \ge N, since k > M implies k > N. Passing from N to M only adds the terms 0 x^k for N < k \le M, which the convention drops. So every admissible N names the same sequence, and the display is well defined. Why “only finitely many”. Two later uses need it. In Section 6.4 we put an element c \in R in place of x and form \sum_k p_k c^k; in a ring only finite sums are defined, and finiteness is what makes the sum finite. In Section 6.3 every non-zero polynomial gets a degree, the highest position holding a non-zero coefficient; without finiteness there may be no highest position. The degenerate cases. The zero polynomial has every N admissible, including N = 0, and it is the monomial 0 \, x^n for every n. It is the one polynomial with no non-zero coefficient at all, and Section 6.3 will need a convention for its degree. At the other extreme, let R be the zero ring \{0\} of the examples after @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, where 1 = 0. There is exactly one function 
N 	o \{0\}, so R[x] has exactly one element, the zero polynomial, and x = 1 \, x^1 = 0 \, x^1 = 0. This is why some results below assume 1 
e 0 in R. [Reading off coefficient sequences] Write the coefficient sequence of each polynomial, and check it against @def-polynomial. In a ring 
Z/n
Z, a natural number m written as an element stands for m \cdot [1] = [m] (@thm-integers-mod-n-ring (d)), just as @def-field-fp does for 
F_p. 1. 3x^2 - x + 2 \in 
Q[x]. 2. x^2 + x \in 
F_2[x]. 3. [3]x + [4] \in (
Z/6
Z)[x]. 4. The constant 7, over 
Z, over 
Z/5
Z and over 
F_2. 5. 0 \in R[x], for any R. (a) (2, -1, 3, 0, 0, \dots). The entries lie in 
Q, and N = 2 is admissible, so it is a polynomial over 
Q. (b) (0, 1, 1, 0, 0, \dots), with entries in 
F_2 and N = 2 admissible. It is not the zero sequence, since its entry in position 1 is 1 
e 0. So x^2 + x 
e 0 in 
F_2[x], although the rule c \mapsto cc + c is the zero function on 
F_2, as computed above. (c) ([4], [3], [0], [0], \dots): the constant term comes first. The entries lie in 
Z/6
Z (@def-integers-mod-n-ring) and N = 1 is admissible. (d) Over 
Z: (7, 0, 0, \dots). Over 
Z/5
Z: ([7], [0], [0], \dots), and [7] = [2] because 7 - 2 = 5 is a multiple of 5; so this is the constant [2]. Over 
F_2: (1, 0, 0, \dots), because 7 = 1 in 
F_2 (7 - 1 = 6 = 3 \cdot 2). The same symbol 7 names three different polynomials, one in each ring, and in each ring N = 0 is admissible. (e) (0, 0, 0, \dots), with every N admissible: the degenerate case. Now a non-example, by a minimal change. Start from 1 + x + x^2 \in 
Q[x], the sequence (1, 1, 1, 0, 0, \dots), and change every later 0 to 1. The result (1, 1, 1, 1, \dots), informally “1 + x + x^2 + \cdots”, is still a function 
N 	o 
Q. The one clause that fails is only finitely many: for every N, the entry in position N + 1 is 1 
e 0, so no N is admissible. It is a formal power series, met again in the exercises of Section 6.2, but not a polynomial. An expression such as x^{-1} + 1 fails for a more basic reason: it would need an entry in position -1, and a polynomial is a function on 
N. 
R and 
C are commutative rings too (for 
R, Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5; for 
C, Chapter 3), so 
R[x] and 
C[x] are defined, and they are the main examples of the linear-algebra companion. No proof in this chapter needs them; our examples come from 
Z, 
Q, 
Z/n
Z and 
F_p, the rings this series has built. Where R matters. Nothing in @def-polynomial mentions inverses, an order, or size. It makes sense word for word over 
Z/6
Z, where [2][3] = [0] (@exm-integers-mod-six), and over the zero ring. The price is that school rules about polynomials cannot be assumed: each one that survives is proved, here or (division with remainder, counting roots) in Chapter 7, and each result says what it needs from R (nothing at all, no zero divisors, a unit leading coefficient, finiteness with 1 
e 0, or, for the derivative, the characteristic of a field). p_2 is a coefficient; p(2) will be a value. Section 6.4 writes p(c) for the result of putting c \in R in place of x. For p = x^2 + 1 \in 
Z[x], the coefficient p_2 is 1, while the value at 2 will be 2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5. Both are integers, so a reader who writes p(k) for “the k-th coefficient” gets 1 = 5. This book never writes p(k) for a coefficient: the coefficient of x^k is p_k, always with a subscript. Is 6x^2 equal to the zero polynomial in (
Z/6
Z)[x]? In 
Z[x]? In (
Z/6
Z)[x], yes: 6x^2 is the monomial [6] \, x^2, and [6] = [0], so every entry is [0] and the two sequences agree in every position. In 
Z[x], no: the entry in position 2 is 6 
e 0, while the zero polynomial has 0 there. Same display, two rings, two answers. Sums, powers and multiples The next section defines the product of two polynomials by a formula whose k-th coefficient is a finite sum \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i q_{k-i} of products in R. Later sections raise elements of R, and polynomials, to powers, and use multiples k \cdot a. This subsection collects what we use about all three. Most of it is already proved: finite sums and powers in a commutative ring are Chapter 1’s (@lem-ring-finite-sums, @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring), multiples are Chapter 4’s (@lem-integer-multiples), and the recursions follow the patterns that Sets and Functions, Section 3.3 set up for real numbers (@fd2:def-sum-product, @fd2:def-power). The patterns are reused; no fact about 
R is. One point deserves care before we start. The sums of polynomials in Section 6.2 must be formed before we know that R[x] is a commutative ring, because they are used to prove it. So part (a) below asks for an addition and a left-neutral element 0, and nothing more. [Finite Sums, Powers and Multiples] Let R be a commutative ring. 1. (Sums.) Let T be a set with a function + \colon T 	imes T 	o T and an element 0 \in T with 0 + u = u for every u \in T. For a sequence (u_i)_{i \in 
N} in T there is exactly one way to define \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i \in T, for k \in 
N, such that \sum_{i=0}^{0} u_i = u_0 , \qquad \sum_{i=0}^{k+1} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + u_{k+1} , starting from the empty sum 0. The sum \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i depends only on u_0, \dots, u_k; so a finite list u_0, \dots, u_k has a sum, computed from any extension of the list to a sequence. Likewise, a finite list s_1, \dots, s_r in R has a product \prod_{j=1}^{r} s_j, with \prod_{j=1}^{0} s_j = 1 and \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} s_j =  igl( \prod_{j=1}^{r} s_j  igr) s_{r+1}. 2. (Rules for sums in R.) For k \in 
N, c \in R and elements u_i, v_i \in R: (Σ1) \sum_{i=0}^{k} (u_i + v_i) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + \sum_{i=0}^{k} v_i; (Σ2) c \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} c \, u_i; (Σ3) for j \in 
N: if u_i = 0 for every i \le k with i 
e j, then \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = u_j when j \le k, and \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = 0 when j > k; (Σ4) -\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} (-u_i). 3. (Powers.) For s \in R and n \in 
N, s^0 \coloneqq 1 and s^{n+1} \coloneqq s^n s define s^n for every n, and for all s, t \in R and m, n \in 
N, s^{m+n} = s^m s^n , \qquad (s^m)^n = s^{mn} , \qquad (st)^n = s^n t^n . 4. (Multiples.) For all a, b \in R and m, n \in 
Z,  egin{aligned} (m + n) \cdot a &= m \cdot a + n \cdot a , & m \cdot (a + b) &= m \cdot a + m \cdot b , \ (m \cdot a) b &= m \cdot (ab) , & (m \cdot 1) a &= m \cdot a , \ (mn) \cdot a &= m \cdot (n \cdot a) . \end{aligned} In words: (a) says that a finite list in a set with an addition has a sum, built one term at a time, and that terms beyond the list do not matter; it needs no law of addition beyond 0 + u = u. (b) says that a finite sum of ring elements can be split into two sums, multiplied through by a constant, collapsed to its one non-zero term, or negated term by term. (c) is the three laws of exponents in a commutative ring. (d) is the arithmetic of the multiples m \cdot a of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.4 (“Multiples”), extended to m \in 
Z in Chapter 4: a dot with an integer on its left is always a multiple, and the product of two ring elements is written by juxtaposition. Part (b) is cited from Chapter 1 and part (d) from Chapter 4: (Σ1)–(Σ4) are @lem-ring-finite-sums (a), (b), (d), (e) (for (Σ3), apply @lem-ring-finite-sums (d) to the sequence that agrees with u_0, \dots, u_k and is 0 beyond k; by the finite-lists clause of part (a) above it has the same sum), and the five rules of part (d) above are @lem-integer-multiples (c), (d). In (c), the powers are the recursion of @fd2:def-power read in R: @fd2:thm-recursion with X = R, starting value 1 and step (n, y) \mapsto y s gives exactly one such s^n for every n, and the three laws are @prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a), (b), (c) of Chapter 1. Part (a) is the recursion of Sets and Functions, Section 3.3, read in T; it is built by @fd2:thm-recursion, and its uniqueness and the dependence on the list are short inductions. The sum comes from @fd2:thm-recursion, and each claim about it is one induction on one index, following the clauses of the recursion: the base case uses the starting value, and the step peels off the last term. No law of addition beyond 0 + u = u is used. (a) Apply @fd2:thm-recursion (read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) with X = T, starting value 0 and step (j, y) \mapsto y + u_j, a function 
N 	imes T 	o T because + maps T 	imes T into T. It gives exactly one sequence (S_j)_{j \in 
N} in T with S_0 = 0 and S_{j+1} = S_j + u_j. Set \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i \coloneqq S_{k+1}. Then \sum_{i=0}^{0} u_i = 0 + u_0 = u_0 by the hypothesis on 0, and \sum_{i=0}^{k+1} u_i = S_{k+1} + u_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + u_{k+1}. Any assignment obeying the two displayed equations agrees with this one at every k, by @fd1:ax-induction on k. For the dependence on u_0, \dots, u_k, let (v_i) be a second sequence with v_i = u_i for i \le k, and let (S'_j) be its sequence of partial sums. We prove by @fd1:ax-induction on j the statement “if j \le k + 1, then S_j = S'_j”. For j = 0 both are 0. If j + 1 \le k + 1, then j \le k + 1 and j \le k, so S_j = S'_j by the hypothesis and u_j = v_j; hence S_{j+1} = S_j + u_j = S'_j + v_j = S'_{j+1}. At j = k + 1 this gives \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} v_i. The argument used only that + is a function on T. The product of a list is @fd2:thm-recursion with X = R, starting value 1 and step (j, y) \mapsto y \, s_{j+1} (with s_j \coloneqq 1, say, for j > r), the pattern of the product in @fd2:def-sum-product; its dependence on s_1, \dots, s_r only is the same induction. This proves (a). We will use (a) twice over: for sums of ring elements, as in the product formula of Section 6.2, and for sums in R[x] of finitely many monomials, which Section 6.2 forms with its coefficientwise addition before any ring law of R[x] is known. In both cases 0 + u = u holds, in R by (F1) and (F3), and in R[x] position by position. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Write the coefficient sequences of x^3 - 2x \in 
Z[x] and of [2]x^2 + [4]x \in (
Z/4
Z)[x]. Is the second one a monomial? 2. Is “1 + x + x^2 + \cdots”, the sequence (1, 1, 1, \dots) of rationals, a polynomial over 
Q? Name the clause of @def-polynomial that decides it. 3. True or false: two polynomials p, q over 
F_2 whose rules c \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k and c \mapsto \sum_{k=0}^{N} q_k c^k, for an N admissible for both, agree at 0 and at 1 are equal. Justify your answer. 4. Which N are admissible for 3x^2 - x + 2 \in 
Q[x]? (a) x^3 - 2x is (0, -2, 0, 1, 0, 0, \dots): the constant term is 0, the coefficient of x is -2, and that of x^3 is 1. The second is ([0], [4], [2], [0], \dots), and [4] = [0] in 
Z/4
Z, since 4 - 0 = 4. So it is ([0], [0], [2], [0], \dots), the monomial [2] x^2. (b) No. The clause only finitely many fails: for every N \in 
N the entry in position N + 1 is 1 
e 0, so no N is admissible. (c) False. The polynomials x^2 + x and 0 over 
F_2 give the rules c \mapsto cc + c and c \mapsto 0, which agree at 0 and at 1 (the computation at the start of the section). But x^2 + x = (0, 1, 1, 0, \dots) differs from 0 in position 1, so the polynomials are not equal. (d) Every N \ge 2. The coefficient of x^2 is 3 
e 0, so N = 0 and N = 1 fail (position 2 > N holds a non-zero entry); and every N \ge 2 works, since all positions k \ge 3 hold 0. B. Practice [B1: Polynomials of bounded length as tuples] Let N \in 
N and P_N \coloneqq \{ p \in R[x] : p_k = 0 	ext{ for every } k > N \}. Prove that \Theta \colon P_N 	o R^{N+1}, \qquad p \mapsto (p_0, p_1, \dots, p_N) , is a bijection (@fd2:def-bijective), where R^{N+1} is the set of (N + 1)-tuples of elements of R, indexed here from 0 (@fd2:def-cartesian-product; for N = 0, where the book has no 1-tuples, we read R^1 as R, with (a_0) standing for a_0, and \Theta as p \mapsto p_0). Hence list the elements of P_2 for R = 
F_2. Injective. Let p, q \in P_N with \Theta(p) = \Theta(q). Then p_k = q_k for k \le N, and p_k = 0 = q_k for k > N by the definition of P_N. So p_k = q_k for every k, and p = q by @fd2:prp-function-equality. Surjective. Let (a_0, \dots, a_N) \in R^{N+1}. Define p \colon 
N 	o R by p_k \coloneqq a_k for k \le N and p_k \coloneqq 0 for k > N: extend by zeros. Then N is admissible for p, so p \in R[x] and p \in P_N, and \Theta(p) = (a_0, \dots, a_N). So \Theta is a bijection; its inverse is “extend by zeros”. For R = 
F_2 and N = 2, each a_i is 0 or 1, and the eight triples (a_0, a_1, a_2) give the eight polynomials 0, \quad 1, \quad x, \quad x + 1, \quad x^2, \quad x^2 + 1, \quad x^2 + x, \quad x^2 + x + 1 . Section 6.4 returns to this list and asks which functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 they define. [B2: Determine which] Each formula below defines a sequence 
N 	o 
Z/4
Z. Determine which of them are polynomials over 
Z/4
Z. Justify your answer, and for each polynomial give the least admissible N and the polynomial in the notation of the display. 1. p_k \coloneqq [2^k]. 2. p_k \coloneqq [k^2]. 3. p_k \coloneqq [k(k - 1)(k - 2)(k - 3)]. 4. p_k \coloneqq [2k]. By @thm-integers-mod-n-ring (b), [0], [1], [2], [3] are four different classes; in particular [1] 
e [0] and [2] 
e [0]. (a) A polynomial. The first entries are [1], [2], [4], [8], \dots, and for k \ge 2, 2^k = 4 \cdot 2^{k-2} (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)), so [2^k] = [0]. The least admissible N is 1: N = 1 works, and N = 0 does not, since p_1 = [2] 
e [0]. The polynomial is 1 + [2]x. (b) Not a polynomial. For odd k = 2j + 1, k^2 = 4(j^2 + j) + 1, so p_k = [1] 
e [0]. Given any N, the odd number k = 2N + 1 > N has p_k 
e [0], so no N is admissible. (c) A polynomial: the zero polynomial. Let k \in 
N. By @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a), k = 4q + r with 0 \le r \le 3, so k - r = 4q is one of the four factors k, k - 1, k - 2, k - 3. Hence the product is a multiple of 4, and p_k = [0] for every k (for k \le 3 the multiple is 0, since then q = 0). Every N is admissible; the least is 0, and the display is 0. (d) Not a polynomial. For odd k = 2j + 1, 2k = 4j + 2, so p_k = [2] 
e [0], and as in (b) no N is admissible. The sequences in (b) and (d) have infinitely many non-zero entries even though their values repeat; (c) shows that a formula in k can describe the zero polynomial. C. Going deeper [C1: Finitely many, in the sense of finite sets] For a sequence p \colon 
N 	o R, let S \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : p_k 
e 0 \}, the set of positions that hold a non-zero entry. Prove that some N \in 
N is admissible for p if and only if S is finite (@fd2:def-finite). So “only finitely many p_k are non-zero” in @def-polynomial means exactly what it says. (\Rightarrow) Let N be admissible. If k \in S, then p_k 
e 0, so k \le N; hence S \subseteq \{0, \dots, N\}. The set \{0, \dots, N\} has N + 1 elements (the third example after @fd2:def-finite), so its subset S is finite by @fd2:prp-subset-finite. (\Leftarrow) We prove by @fd1:ax-induction on n \in 
N: every subset A \subseteq 
N with n elements has an upper bound b \in 
N, that is, a \le b for every a \in A. For n = 0, A = \emptyset (the first example after @fd2:def-finite), and b = 0 works vacuously. Suppose the statement holds for n, and let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n + 1\} 	o A be a bijection. Put z \coloneqq \varphi(n + 1) and A' \coloneqq A \setminus \{z\}. The restriction of \varphi to \{1, \dots, n\} maps into A' (if \varphi(j) = z then j = n + 1, by injectivity), is injective, and is onto A' (an element of A' is \varphi(j) with j 
e n + 1, so j \le n). So A' has n elements and an upper bound b'. By trichotomy (@fd3:thm-omega-order (a)), the larger b of b' and z is defined, and it bounds every element of A = A' \cup \{z\}. Now let S be finite, with an upper bound N. If k > N, then k 
otin S, that is, p_k = 0. So N is admissible. The proof of (\Leftarrow) never needed a greatest element of S, only an upper bound. The greatest element exists when S is non-empty and finite (an upper bound in 
N \subseteq 
Z gives one by @fd3:prp-integer-least-element), and Section 6.3 calls it the degree. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 3: (\Rightarrow) shows S \subseteq \{0, \dots, N\} and concludes that S is finite, citing that \{0, \dots, N\} is finite and that a subset of a finite set is finite (@fd2:prp-subset-finite). - 2: (\Leftarrow) sets up an induction on the number of elements of a finite A \subseteq 
N, with the claim that A has an upper bound, and handles A = \emptyset. - 2: in the step, removes one element z and shows that the rest A' has n elements (by restricting the bijection, or by @fd2:cor-remove-point). - 1: takes the larger of b' and z, by trichotomy, as a bound for A = A' \cup \{z\}. - 2: concludes that an upper bound N of S is admissible: k > N implies k 
otin S, so p_k = 0. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a greatest element of S without justification; overlooking S = \emptyset in (\Leftarrow).

title: 6.2 The Polynomial Ring
content:
The Polynomial Ring Section 6.1 made a polynomial a coefficient sequence, and the display \sum_k p_k x^k only a way of writing it down. This section gives the sequences their sum and product, read off from what school algebra does with expressions, and proves that the result obeys every law of a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field). The obvious proof of associativity needs a theorem about reordering double sums that we have not proved. We avoid it with one device, check on monomials, extend by additivity, which returns in Sections 6.4 and 6.5. Adding and multiplying coefficient sequences At school, (3x^2 - x + 2)(x + 1) is computed by multiplying every term of the first factor by every term of the second, using a_i x^i \cdot b_j x^j = a_i b_j x^{i+j}, and then collecting the terms with the same power. The coefficient of x^k in the result collects the products a_i b_j over all pairs with i + j = k, that is, over i = 0, \dots, k with j = k - i. Addition collects like powers too, so it adds coefficients position by position. We turn these two recipes into definitions. (b) With a = 2, m = 1, b = 3, n = 2, c = 1, l = 1:  igl( (2x)(3x^2)  igr) x = (6 x^3) x = 6x^4, using 2 \cdot 3 = 6, 1 + 2 = 3, then 6 \cdot 1 = 6, 3 + 1 = 4; and (2x) igl( (3x^2) x  igr) = (2x)(3x^3) = 6x^4, using 3 \cdot 1 = 3, 2 + 1 = 3, then 2 \cdot 3 = 6, 1 + 3 = 4. Both are 6x^4. (c) For \Phi: (pq)(r + r') = (pq)r + (pq)r', which is (\ast\ast) with pq in place of p. For \Psi: p igl( q(r + r')  igr) = p(qr + qr') = p(qr) + p(qr'), which is (\ast\ast) twice. (d) On monomials, associativity is a single product: (ab)c = a(bc) in R and (m + n) + l = m + (n + l) in 
N. Both sides of (pq)r = p(qr) are additive in each argument and every polynomial is a finite sum of monomials, so the monomial case extends to all polynomials, one argument at a time. B. Practice [B1: A product over two rings] Compute (2x^3 - x + 4)(-2x^3 + x^2 + 3) in 
Z[x] and in 
F_2[x], from @def-polynomial-ring. In 
Z[x], (p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3) = (4, -1, 0, 2) and (q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3) = (3, 0, 1, -2), with 3 admissible for both; so (pq)_k = 0 for k > 6, and  egin{aligned} (pq)_0 &= 4 \cdot 3 = 12 , \ (pq)_1 &= 4 \cdot 0 + (-1) \cdot 3 = -3 , \ (pq)_2 &= 4 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 3 = 4 , \ (pq)_3 &= 4 \cdot (-2) + (-1) \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 3 = -3 , \ (pq)_4 &= (-1)(-2) + 0 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 0 = 2 , \ (pq)_5 &= 0 \cdot (-2) + 2 \cdot 1 = 2 , \ (pq)_6 &= 2 \cdot (-2) = -4 , \end{aligned} where in positions 4, 5, 6 the terms with an index above 3 are 0 and have been left out. Hence pq = -4x^6 + 2x^5 + 2x^4 - 3x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x + 12 . In 
F_2[x] the displays name other sequences: 2 = 0, 4 = 0, -1 = 1, -2 = 0 and 3 = 1 in 
F_2, so the first factor is x and the second is x^2 + 1. By @lem-monomial-product (a) with a = 1, m = 1, the product shifts (1, 0, 1, 0, \dots) one place up: x(x^2 + 1) = x^3 + x. This agrees with reducing the integer coefficients 12, -3, 4, -3, 2, 2, -4 modulo 2, which gives 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0. [B2: Changing the sign of x] Define \sigma \colon R[x] 	o R[x] by \sigma(p)_k \coloneqq (-1)^k p_k, where (-1)^k is the power in R (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)). Then \sigma(p) is a polynomial, since (-1)^k \cdot 0 = 0. We want to prove that \sigma(pq) = \sigma(p) \sigma(q) for all p, q \in R[x]. You may use the following, without proof. The map \sigma is additive: \sigma(p + q) = \sigma(p) + \sigma(q), position by position by (F9). Hence, with (\ast) and (\ast\ast), the maps \Phi(p, q) \coloneqq \sigma(pq) and \Psi(p, q) \coloneqq \sigma(p) \sigma(q) are additive in each argument. The last step is blank. Name the move, then complete it. The move is check on monomials, extend by additivity. Let a, b \in R and m, n \in 
N. The monomial a x^m has only position m possibly non-zero, so \sigma(a x^m) =  igl( (-1)^m a  igr) x^m. By @lem-monomial-product (b), \Phi(a x^m, b x^n) = \sigma igl( (ab) x^{m+n}  igr) =  igl( (-1)^{m+n} ab  igr) x^{m+n} , \Psi(a x^m, b x^n) =  igl( (-1)^m a  igr) x^m \cdot  igl( (-1)^n b  igr) x^n =  igl( (-1)^m a \, (-1)^n b  igr) x^{m+n} . The two coefficients agree: (-1)^m a \, (-1)^n b =  igl( (-1)^m (-1)^n  igr) (ab) = (-1)^{m+n} ab, by (F5) and (F6) in R and the first power law of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c). So \Phi and \Psi agree on monomials, and by @lem-check-on-monomials with two arguments and T = R[x], \sigma(pq) = \sigma(p) \sigma(q) for all p, q. Also \sigma(1) = 1, since (-1)^0 = 1. Section 6.4 writes \sigma(p) as p(-x). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the ring laws] Let R be a commutative ring. Prove, from @def-polynomial-ring, that the multiplication of R[x] is commutative and associative. You may use the laws of R, @lem-finite-sums-and-powers, @fd1:ax-induction and @fd2:prp-function-equality, but no result of this section after @def-polynomial-ring. Distributivity. For p, p', q, q' \in R[x], the k-th coefficient of (p + p')q is \sum_{i=0}^{k} (p_i + p'_i) q_{k-i}. Inside each term, (F6), (F9), (F6) give p_i q_{k-i} + p'_i q_{k-i}, and (Σ1) splits the sum into (pq)_k + (p'q)_k. So (p + p')q = pq + p'q, and in the same way, with (F9) directly, p(q + q') = pq + pq'. Hence (p, q) \mapsto pq and (p, q) \mapsto qp are additive in each argument, and so are (p, q, r) \mapsto (pq)r and (p, q, r) \mapsto p(qr), by applying the two laws twice. Monomials. For a, b \in R and m, n \in 
N, the k-th coefficient of (a x^m)(b x^n) is \sum_{i=0}^{k} (a x^m)_i (b x^n)_{k-i}. Every term with i 
e m is 0, and the term with i = m (present when m \le k) is a \, (b x^n)_{k-m}, which is ab if k = m + n and 0 otherwise. By (Σ3), (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n}. Reduction. (i) For p \in R[x], the sum s_N \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k in (R[x], +) (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a)) has p_j in position j \le N and 0 beyond, by @fd1:ax-induction on N: s_0 = p_0 x^0, and s_{N+1} = s_N + p_{N+1} x^{N+1} has coefficients p_j + 0, 0 + p_{N+1} and 0 + 0 for j \le N, j = N + 1 and j > N + 1, by (F1) and (F3). So p = s_N for admissible N (@fd2:prp-function-equality). (ii) Let \Phi, \Psi \colon R[x] 	o R[x] be additive and agree on monomials. By @fd1:ax-induction on N, \Phi(p) = \Psi(p) for every p for which N is admissible: for N = 0, p = p_0 x^0 by (i); if N + 1 is admissible for p, then p = s_N + p_{N+1} x^{N+1} with N admissible for s_N, by (i), and \Phi(p) = \Phi(s_N) + \Phi(p_{N+1} x^{N+1}) = \Psi(s_N) + \Psi(p_{N+1} x^{N+1}) = \Psi(p) by additivity, the induction hypothesis with the monomial case, and additivity. Every polynomial has an admissible N, so \Phi = \Psi. (iii) With two arguments, fix a monomial u and apply (ii) to v \mapsto \Phi(u, v) and v \mapsto \Psi(u, v); then fix any q and apply (ii) to the first argument. With three, treat the third, the second and the first argument in turn. Commutativity. (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n} = (ba) x^{n+m} = (b x^n)(a x^m), by (F6) in R and m + n = n + m in 
N; the reduction gives pq = qp. Associativity.  igl( (a x^m)(b x^n)  igr)(c x^l) =  igl( (ab)c  igr) x^{(m+n)+l} and (a x^m) igl( (b x^n)(c x^l)  igr) =  igl( a(bc)  igr) x^{m+(n+l)}, equal by (F5) in R and associativity of + in 
N; the reduction with three arguments gives (pq)r = p(qr). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: both distributive laws from the coefficient formula, naming the rule for a single-index sum ((Σ1)) and the law of R used inside each term. - 2: the product of two monomials, (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n}, with the vanishing of the other terms shown. - 3: the reduction to monomials, with additivity in each argument stated and used one argument at a time (both inductions proved in the answer; citing @lem-check-on-monomials earns none of these points). - 1: commutativity on monomials, naming (F6) in R. - 2: associativity on monomials, naming (F5) in R and the law of 
N used for the exponents. Fatal errors (0 for the step): treating polynomials as functions on R and citing the laws of R “pointwise”; checking only on x^m and x^n, with no account of the coefficients (the coefficients are where (F5) and (F6) of R are needed). A direct route works with coefficients throughout: commutativity by (F6) and the reversal i \mapsto k - i of a finite sum, associativity by rewriting both triple products as one sum over all (i, j, l) with i + j + l = k. Each needs a lemma that (Σ1)–(Σ4) do not contain, proved by induction. Commutativity with the reversal proved earns 3 points (the monomial product and commutativity on monomials); associativity with the reindexing proved earns the other 7. An unproved reversal or reindexing earns 0 for that step. [C2: Formal power series] Let R^{
N} be the set of all sequences 
N 	o R, with sum and product given by the formulas of @def-polynomial-ring. 1. Show that the formulas define functions R^{
N} 	imes R^{
N} 	o R^{
N}. 2. Show that R[x] \subseteq R^{
N} is closed under the sum and the product. 3. Let s \coloneqq (1, 1, 1, \dots). Show that (1 - x) s = 1. 4. Which step of the proof of @lem-check-on-monomials (with one argument) does not reach the elements of R^{
N}? (a) For p, q \in R^{
N} and k \in 
N, p_k + q_k \in R, and \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i q_{k-i} is a sum of k + 1 elements of R, defined by @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a). No finiteness of p or q is needed: each coefficient of the product only looks at positions 0, \dots, k. So both formulas give sequences 
N 	o R. (b) This is the closure paragraph after @def-polynomial-ring: if m and n are admissible for p and q, then \max(m, n) is admissible for p + q and m + n for pq. (c) 1 - x = (1, -1, 0, 0, \dots). In position 0,  igl( (1 - x)s  igr)_0 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1. In position k \ge 1, write the i-th term as v_i + w_i (by (F1) and (F3)), with v_0 = 1 \cdot 1, w_1 = (-1) \cdot 1 and every other v_i, w_i equal to 0, since for i \ge 2 the term is 0 \cdot 1 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) with (F6)). By (Σ1) and (Σ3), the sum is 1 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 1 = 1 + (-1) = 0, by (F7) and (F4). So (1 - x)s = (1, 0, 0, \dots) = 1. (d) The induction proves \Phi(p) = \Psi(p) only for sequences p that have an admissible N; the step from it to \Phi = \Psi uses that every polynomial has one. The sequence s has none, and it is not a finite sum of monomials either, since by (b) such a sum is a polynomial. So @lem-check-on-monomials says nothing about s, and the proof of @thm-polynomial-ring-laws does not apply to R^{
N}. The ring laws do hold in R^{
N}, the ring of formal power series, though we do not prove this here; nothing in this book depends on it. So (1 - x)s = 1 among all sequences, while Section 6.3 shows that over 
Z, 1 - x is not a unit of 
Z[x].

title: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content:
Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains Section 6.2 made R[x] a commutative ring for every commutative ring R (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws). This section attaches to each non-zero polynomial its degree, the position of its last non-zero coefficient, and asks the school question: is the degree of a product the sum of the degrees? Over 
Z it is. Over 
Z/6
Z it is not, and the reason is a single product of two elements of R. Sorting out which rings behave like 
Z leads to the integral domains, and to the two facts later chapters use most: a polynomial ring over an integral domain has no zero divisors, and its units are the units of R. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), and polynomials are coefficient sequences (@def-polynomial), with the sum and product of @def-polynomial-ring. Degree and leading coefficient Here is the computation that drives the section. Multiply p = 2x + 1 by q = 3x^2 + x by the product formula of @def-polynomial-ring, once in 
Z[x] and once in (
Z/6
Z)[x]. The coefficients of p are 1, 2, 0, 0, \dots and those of q are 0, 1, 3, 0, \dots, so  egin{aligned} (pq)_0 &= p_0 q_0 = 0, \ (pq)_1 &= p_0 q_1 + p_1 q_0 = 1, \ (pq)_2 &= p_0 q_2 + p_1 q_1 + p_2 q_0 = 3 + 2 = 5, \ (pq)_3 &= p_0 q_3 + p_1 q_2 + p_2 q_1 + p_3 q_0 = 2 \cdot 3 = 6, \end{aligned} and (pq)_k = 0 for k \ge 4. Over 
Z the product is 6x^3 + 5x^2 + x, with its last non-zero coefficient in position 3 = 1 + 2. Over 
Z/6
Z the same sums are read modulo 6: (pq)_3 = [6] = [0], and the product is [5]x^2 + x, whose last non-zero coefficient sits in position 2. The top coefficient of the product was 2 \cdot 3, the product of the top coefficients of the factors, and in 
Z/6
Z that product is [0] (@exm-integers-mod-six). To state any of this we need a name for “the position of the last non-zero coefficient”. A non-zero polynomial has one, because only finitely many of its coefficients are non-zero. The degree of a polynomial is the position of its last non-zero coefficient; the leading coefficient is the coefficient sitting there. [Degree, Leading Coefficient, Monic] Let R be a commutative ring and p \in R[x]. 1. If p 
e 0, the degree \deg p is the largest n \in 
N with p_n 
e 0. The leading coefficient of p is \operatorname{lc}(p) \coloneqq p_{\deg p}, and p is monic if \operatorname{lc}(p) = 1. 2. The zero polynomial has degree \deg 0 \coloneqq -\infty, and no leading coefficient. Here -\infty is a symbol not in 
N, with the conventions -\infty < n and -\infty + n = n + (-\infty) = -\infty for every n \in 
N, and -\infty + (-\infty) = -\infty. In words: (a) looks along the coefficient sequence and stops at the last place where it is non-zero; that place is the degree, and the entry there is the leading coefficient. A polynomial is monic when that entry is 1. Clause (b) gives the zero polynomial, which has no non-zero coefficient at all, a degree below every natural number. Well-definedness. Let p 
e 0, and let N be admissible for p: p_k = 0 for every k > N (@def-polynomial). The set S \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : p_n 
e 0 \} is non-empty, since p is not the zero sequence, and every element of S is at most N. Read in 
Z \supseteq 
N (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers), S is a non-empty set of integers bounded above, so it has a greatest element (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element). That element is \deg p. Two facts come with it, and every proof below uses them: p_{\deg p} 
e 0 , \qquad p_k = 0 \ 	ext{ for every } k > \deg p . The second says that \deg p is itself admissible for p, and the least admissible N: any smaller N would leave the non-zero coefficient p_{\deg p} beyond it. Examples. - In 
Q[x], \deg(3x^2 - x + 2) = 2 with leading coefficient 3; x^2 + 1 is monic of degree 2. The monomial a x^n with a 
e 0 has degree n and leading coefficient a. - A non-zero constant a = a x^0 has degree 0. The constant 0 has degree -\infty, not 0: degree 0 means “a constant, and not the zero one”. - Degree depends on the ring. The integer polynomial 6x^3 + 5x^2 + x has degree 3 in 
Z[x]; its coefficients read in 
Z/6
Z give [5]x^2 + x, of degree 2. Read in 
Z/5
Z they give x^3 + x ([6] = [1], [5] = [0]), monic of degree 3. - The degenerate ring. If 1 = 0 in R, then every a \in R is a = a \cdot 1 = a \cdot 0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so R = \{0\}, and the only polynomial over R is the zero sequence. Every polynomial over the zero ring has degree -\infty, and no polynomial over it is monic. This is why “monic” will never need the hypothesis 1 
e 0: a monic polynomial is non-zero, so its ring has 1 = \operatorname{lc}(p) 
e 0. Non-example by minimal change. The sequence (1, 1, 1, \dots) has no degree: the set S of its non-zero positions is all of 
N, which has no greatest element. It fails exactly the clause “only finitely many” of @def-polynomial, which is what made S bounded above. Any value given to \deg 0 is a convention, and the choice is made so that the rule “degrees add under products” survives the zero polynomial. For every q, 0 \cdot q = 0, so the rule asks for \deg 0 = \deg 0 + \deg q. If \deg 0 were an integer d, then in any ring with 1 
e 0 the case q = x, of degree 1, would give d = d + 1. No integer works; a symbol -\infty with -\infty + n = -\infty does. The order -\infty < n then lets “\deg p \le n” include the zero polynomial, which is what the sets R[x]_{\le n} at the end of this section need. The leading coefficient is the coefficient of the highest power, not the first one written. In 2 + x - 5x^3 \in 
Q[x], the leading coefficient is -5, and the polynomial is not monic although its x has coefficient 1. And the zero polynomial has no leading coefficient at all: “\operatorname{lc}(p)” silently assumes p 
e 0. The degree of a sum A sum cannot raise the degree, because adding coefficients position by position creates no non-zero coefficient beyond the last non-zero ones of the summands. [Degree of a Sum] Let R be a commutative ring and p, q \in R[x]. Then \deg(p + q) \le \max(\deg p, \deg q) , with equality when \deg p 
e \deg q. Beyond the larger of the two degrees both summands have only zero coefficients, so the sum does too. When one degree is strictly larger, the other summand contributes 0 at that top position, and the top coefficient survives. Let M \coloneqq \max(\deg p, \deg q). If M = -\infty, then p = q = 0, so p + q = 0 and both sides are -\infty. Otherwise M \in 
N, and for k > M we have k > \deg p and k > \deg q, so p_k = 0 and q_k = 0 (by the two facts after @def-degree when the polynomial is non-zero, and trivially when it is 0). Hence (p + q)_k = p_k + q_k = 0 + 0 = 0 for every k > M, by @def-polynomial-ring and (F3). So either p + q = 0, with degree -\infty < M, or p + q 
e 0 and its last non-zero coefficient is at a position \le M. In both cases \deg(p + q) \le M. Now let \deg p 
e \deg q; by symmetry \deg q < \deg p, so p 
e 0 and M = \deg p. Then q_M = 0, and (p + q)_M = p_M + q_M = p_M + 0 = p_M 
e 0 , so p + q 
e 0 and \deg(p + q) \ge M. With the first part, \deg(p + q) = M. The inequality is strict exactly when \deg p = \deg q = M \in 
N and the leading coefficients cancel, p_M + q_M = 0: for example (x^2 + x) + (-x^2 + 1) = x + 1, of degree 1 < 2, and x + (-x) = 0, of degree -\infty < 1. The degree of a product The opening computation suggests how a product behaves at the top. In (pq)_k = \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i q_{k-i}, a term can be non-zero only if i \le \deg p and k - i \le \deg q; for k = \deg p + \deg q that leaves exactly one term. We call this move look at the top coefficient. [Degree of a Product] Let R be a commutative ring, let p, q \in R[x] be non-zero, and let m \coloneqq \deg p, n \coloneqq \deg q. 1. (pq)_k = 0 for every k > m + n, and (pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). Hence \deg(pq) \le \deg p + \deg q for all p, q \in R[x], zero or not; and if p = 0 or q = 0, then pq = 0 and \deg(pq) = -\infty = \deg p + \deg q. 2. \deg(pq) = m + n if and only if \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q) 
e 0, and then \operatorname{lc}(pq) = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). This holds in particular - when R has no zero divisors (ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0), for example when R is a field (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)); together with the last clause of (a), \deg(pq) = \deg p + \deg q then holds for all p, q \in R[x], zero or not; - when \operatorname{lc}(p) is a unit of R (@def-ring-unit), in particular when p is monic. In words: (a) says that the product has nothing above position m + n, and that what sits at m + n is the product of the two leading coefficients, in every commutative ring; (b) says that the degree formula holds precisely when that one product is non-zero, and names two common situations where it is. The top of a product comes from the tops of the factors alone. Above m + n every term p_i q_{k-i} has a factor beyond the top of p or beyond the top of q; at m + n exactly one term escapes, p_m q_n. So the only question is whether p_m q_n can be 0, and that is a question about R, not about polynomials. Before reading on: which line needs R to have no zero divisors, and which works in every ring? (a) Let k \ge m + n and 0 \le i \le k, and consider the term p_i q_{k-i} of (pq)_k (@def-polynomial-ring). If i > m, then p_i = 0. If i \le m, then k - i \ge k - m \ge n, and k - i > n (so q_{k-i} = 0) unless k = m + n and i = m. So every term with i 
e m, or with k > m + n, has a factor 0, and is 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) with (F6). For k > m + n, all terms of (pq)_k are 0, so (pq)_k = 0 by (Σ3) of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b) (with j = 0). For k = m + n, every term with i 
e m is 0, and m \le m + n, so (Σ3) with j = m leaves (pq)_{m+n} = p_m q_n = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q) . For the inequality, let p, q \in R[x] be arbitrary. If p = 0, every coefficient of pq is a sum of terms 0 \cdot q_{k-i} = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), (F6)), so pq = 0, and both sides of the inequality are -\infty by the conventions of @def-degree, which is also the last clause of (a); likewise if q = 0. If p, q 
e 0 and pq = 0, the left side is -\infty < m + n. Otherwise pq 
e 0, and since (pq)_k = 0 for every k > m + n, its last non-zero coefficient is at a position \le m + n: \deg(pq) \le m + n. (b) By (a), m + n is admissible for pq, and (pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). If this element is non-zero, then pq 
e 0, its last non-zero coefficient is at m + n, and so \deg(pq) = m + n and \operatorname{lc}(pq) = (pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). If it is 0, then (pq)_k = 0 for every k \ge m + n, so \deg(pq) < m + n. For the two situations: p_m 
e 0 and q_n 
e 0 by @def-degree, so if R has no zero divisors, p_m q_n 
e 0. If u \coloneqq p_m is a unit and u q_n = 0, then q_n = (u^{-1} u) q_n = u^{-1}(u q_n) = u^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0, by (F6), (F7), (F5) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), against q_n 
e 0; so p_m q_n 
e 0. A monic p has p_m = 1, a unit since 1 \cdot 1 = 1. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Part (a), including the inequality, uses only (F1)–(F7), (F9), @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), (Σ3) of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b), and the two facts after @def-degree and its conventions, all valid in every commutative ring: it holds over 
Z/6
Z as over 
Q. Part (b) as an equivalence also holds in every ring. “No zero divisors” enters in one line, the first sentence of the last paragraph, and only to decide that p_m q_n 
e 0; the unit hypothesis is a second, different way to decide the same thing. The degree formula is not automatic. In (
Z/6
Z)[x], the opening computation gives ([2]x + [1])([3]x^2 + x) = [5]x^2 + x , a product of polynomials of degrees 1 and 2 that has degree 2, not 3. The coefficient (pq)_3 is \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q) = [2][3] = [6] = [0] (@exm-integers-mod-six). Part (a) of @thm-degree-of-product holds here; the hypothesis of (b) fails. Let p, q \in 
Q[x] with \deg p = 3 and \deg q = 2. What are \deg(pq), \deg(p + q) and \deg(p^2), where p^2 \coloneqq pp? Can you say what \deg(p - x^3) is? \deg(pq) = 5 and \deg(p^2) = 6, by @thm-degree-of-product (b): 
Q is a field (@fd3:thm-rationals-field), so it has no zero divisors. \deg(p + q) = 3, by the equality case of @thm-degree-of-sum, since 3 
e 2. The degree of p - x^3 is not determined: it is 3 if \operatorname{lc}(p) 
e 1, at most 2 if p is monic, and -\infty if p = x^3. The difference has coefficient \operatorname{lc}(p) - 1 at position 3, and that coefficient decides. title: 6.4 Evaluation, Substitution, and Polynomial Functions
content:
Evaluation, Substitution, and Polynomial Functions A polynomial, in this chapter, is a sequence of coefficients (@def-polynomial), not a function. But every polynomial defines a function: put an element c of the ring in place of x and add up. More generally we can put in place of x a class modulo n, or another polynomial, after first moving the coefficients into the ring where the substitution happens. This section proves one theorem, the substitution principle, that covers all of these at once, because each is a ring homomorphism out of R[x] determined by where it sends the constants and x. Then it compares a polynomial with its function, and shows that over every finite ring other than the zero ring the passage from polynomials to functions loses information. Throughout, R and S are commutative rings (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), and powers s^n and finite sums are those of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers. Evaluating a polynomial To evaluate a polynomial at c, replace each monomial a x^k by the element a c^k and add. By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, P_{j+1}(c) = P_j(c) \, (c - c_{j+1}), using (x - c_{j+1})(c) = c - c_{j+1} (the sum rule, with (-a)(c) = -a for a constant). Hence \varepsilon(P) = \varepsilon(0) with P 
e 0, and \varepsilon is not injective. The smallest instance is the one this chapter opened with. [Different Polynomials, Equal Functions] Over 
F_2, compare x^2 + x with 0, and x^2 with x, first as polynomials, then as functions 
F_2 	o

e 0 in position 1, so it is not the zero polynomial; it has degree 2. And x^2 
e x, since their coefficients differ in position 2 (and in position 1). As functions. At 0: 0^2 + 0 = 0 and 0^2 = 0. At 1: 1^2 + 1 = 1 + 1 = 0 in 
F_2 (@exm-finite-fields), and 1^2 = 1. So the function of x^2 + x is the zero function, and x^2 and x have the same function, the identity of 
F_2. This is @prp-polynomial-function-map (d) with R = 
F_2, c_1 = 0, c_2 = 1: P = (x - 0)(x - 1) = x(x + 1) = x^2 + x, since -1 = 1 in 
F_2. A polynomial is not its function. “p(c) = 0 for every c \in R” does not give p = 0: over every finite ring with 1 
e 0 the polynomial P of @prp-polynomial-function-map (d) is a counterexample, and over 
F_2 it is x^2 + x. Over 
Q the implication does hold: Chapter 7 proves it for every infinite field, by bounding the number of roots of a non-zero polynomial. Over 
Z it follows, though we do not prove it here: read p \in 
Z[x] as a polynomial with the same coefficients in 
Q[x], where it vanishes at infinitely many points. In this chapter, two polynomials are equal only when their coefficients are equal. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about @thm-polynomial-substitution and its proof, except the last. 1. Where in the proof is \varphi(1) = 1 used? 2. Where is the commutativity of S used? 3. Run the theorem with R = 
Z, S =
