F_3[x], compute the values of (x + 2)(x^2 + x + 1) at 0, 1, 2, and find all its roots in 
F_3. (a) Twice: for \Phi(1) = \varphi(1) s^0 = 1, and for \Phi(x) = \varphi(1) s^1 = s. (b) Essentially once: in the monomial computation, to rewrite \varphi(a)\varphi(b) s^m s^n as  igl(\varphi(a) s^m igr) igl(\varphi(b) s^n igr), which moves \varphi(b) past s^m by (F6) in S. The proof also uses (F6) in S for 0 \cdot s^k = 0, for the right distributive law in the additivity steps, and for 1 \cdot s = s; these uses only give the mirror forms of a \cdot 0 = 0, (F9) and (F7). An answer that lists them too, with this distinction, is correct. (c) The coefficients of p are 1, 3, 1, so \Phi(p) = [1] + [3][2] + [1][2]^2 = [1 + 6 + 4] = [11] = [1]. For the uniqueness half: 3x^2 is the product of the constant 3 and x^2 (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (c)), so \Psi(3x^2) = \Psi(3)\Psi(x)^2 = [3][2]^2 = [12] = [2]. No other value is possible, because \Psi respects products. (d) A ring homomorphism out of R[x] has no freedom: it must send a x^n to \varphi(a) s^n, so the formula is forced and uniqueness follows by additivity. The only work is to show that the forced formula respects products, and that is a check on monomials, where it becomes the power law and one reordering of factors in the commutative ring S. (e) Evaluation respects products (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so the value is the product of the values of the factors. At 0: 2 \cdot 1 = 2. At 1: (1 + 2)(1 + 1 + 1) = 0 \cdot 0 = 0. At 2: (2 + 2)(4 + 2 + 1) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 (in 
F_3, 4 = 7 = 1). So the only root is 1. Multiplied out by the product formula, the polynomial is x^3 + 3x^2 + 3x + 2 = x^3 + 2 in 
F_3[x], the second example after @def-polynomial-evaluation, whose values 2, 0, 1 agree. B. Practice [B1: The degree of a composition] Let R be an integral domain, p, q \in R[x], p 
e 0, and \deg q \ge 1. Prove that \deg(p \circ q) = \deg p \cdot \deg q. Show by an example that the hypothesis \deg q \ge 1 cannot be dropped. Let d \coloneqq \deg p and e \coloneqq \deg q \ge 1. Powers of q. By @fd1:ax-induction on k, q^k 
e 0, \deg q^k = ke and \operatorname{lc}(q^k) = \operatorname{lc}(q)^k. For k = 0, q^0 = 1 has degree 0 and leading coefficient 1 (as 1 
e 0). For the step, q^{k+1} = q^k q, and since R has no zero divisors, @thm-degree-of-product (b) gives degree ke + e = (k + 1)e and leading coefficient \operatorname{lc}(q)^k \operatorname{lc}(q). The top term. By @def-polynomial-composition with N = d, p \circ q = \sum_{k=0}^{d} p_k q^k. The term p_d q^d is the product of the non-zero constant p_d (degree 0) and q^d, so by @thm-degree-of-product (b) it has degree de. Every other term p_k q^k with k < d is 0 or has degree ke < de, since e \ge 1 (@thm-degree-of-product (a)). By @thm-degree-of-sum and induction along the sum recursion, r \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} p_k q^k has \deg r < de (for d = 0, r is the empty sum 0). Then p \circ q = r + p_d q^d, and the equality case of @thm-degree-of-sum gives \deg(p \circ q) = de. The hypothesis on q. Take R = 
Z, p = x - 1 and q = 1, of degree 0. Then p \circ q = 1 - 1 = 0, of degree -\infty, while \deg p \cdot \deg q = 1 \cdot 0 = 0. A constant q can make the top terms cancel. [B2: All polynomials of degree at most two over the field with two elements] List the elements of 
F_2[x]_{\le 2} with their degrees and their functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 (given by the values at 0 and 1). How many functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 are there, and how many of the eight polynomials give each one? By @def-polynomials-bounded-degree, the elements are a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 with a_i \in \{0, 1\}; there are eight (@exr-degree-b3 for 
F_2, n = 2). The value at 0 is a_0, and the value at 1 is a_0 + a_1 + a_2 in 
F_2.  egin{array}{l|c|c|c} p & \deg p & p(0) & p(1) \ \hline 0 & -\infty & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \ x & 1 & 0 & 1 \ x + 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \ x^2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \ x^2 + 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \ x^2 + x & 2 & 0 & 0 \ x^2 + x + 1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \end{array} A function 
F_2 	o 
F_2 is determined by its two values, so there are 2 \cdot 2 = 4 of them, and each occurs for exactly two polynomials in the table: (0, 0) for 0 and x^2 + x; (1, 1) for 1 and x^2 + x + 1; (0, 1) for x and x^2; (1, 0) for x + 1 and x^2 + 1. In each pair the two polynomials differ by x^2 + x, the polynomial of @exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2. [B3: Shifting the variable] Let R be a commutative ring and c \in R. Define T_c \colon R[x] 	o R[x] by T_c(p) \coloneqq p \circ (x + c). Prove that T_c is a bijective ring homomorphism with inverse T_{-c}. By @def-polynomial-composition, T_c is a ring homomorphism that fixes every constant and sends x to x + c; likewise T_{-c} fixes constants and sends x to x - c. The composite T_{-c} \circ T_c is a ring homomorphism (after @def-ring-homomorphism) that fixes constants, and T_{-c}(T_c(x)) = T_{-c}(x + c) = T_{-c}(x) + T_{-c}(c) = (x - c) + c = x . The identity map of R[x] is also a ring homomorphism that fixes constants and sends x to x. By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-substitution (b), with S = R[x], \varphi the constants and s = x, T_{-c} \circ T_c = \id_{R[x]}. Exchanging c and -c (and -(-c) = c), T_c \circ T_{-c} = \id_{R[x]}. So T_c has the inverse T_{-c}, and is a bijection (@fd2:def-bijective). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the substitution principle] State and prove @thm-polynomial-substitution. Statement. Let R and S be commutative rings, \varphi \colon R 	o S a ring homomorphism and s \in S, and let \Phi(p) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} \varphi(p_k) s^k for N admissible for p. Then \Phi \colon R[x] 	o S is a well-defined ring homomorphism with \Phi(a) = \varphi(a) for constants and \Phi(x) = s, and it is the only ring homomorphism R[x] 	o S with these two properties. Well defined. Enlarging N by one adds the term \varphi(0) s^{k} = 0 \cdot s^k = 0, since \varphi(0) + \varphi(0) = \varphi(0) gives \varphi(0) = 0; by induction any two admissible N give the same sum. In particular \Phi(a x^m) = \varphi(a) s^m, the other terms being 0. Additive. With N admissible for p and q, \Phi(p + q) = \sum_k \varphi(p_k + q_k) s^k = \sum_k  igl(\varphi(p_k) s^k + \varphi(q_k) s^k igr) = \Phi(p) + \Phi(q), by additivity of \varphi, (F9) and (F6) in S, and (Σ1). Multiplicative. The maps (p, q) \mapsto \Phi(pq) and (p, q) \mapsto \Phi(p)\Phi(q) are additive in p for fixed q, and in q for fixed p: the first because multiplication in R[x] distributes over addition and \Phi is additive, the second because \Phi is additive and multiplication in S distributes. On monomials, \Phi igl((ab) x^{m+n} igr) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) s^m s^n =  igl(\varphi(a) s^m igr) igl(\varphi(b) s^n igr) , by multiplicativity of \varphi, s^{m+n} = s^m s^n, and (F5), (F6) in S to move \varphi(b) past s^m. Since (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n}, the two maps agree on pairs of monomials, so they agree everywhere by @lem-check-on-monomials. The one, constants and x. \Phi(1) = \varphi(1) s^0 = 1, \Phi(a x^0) = \varphi(a), and \Phi(x) = \varphi(1) s = s. Uniqueness. If \Psi is a ring homomorphism with \Psi(a x^0) = \varphi(a) and \Psi(x) = s, then, as a x^n is the constant a times the n-th power of x, \Psi(a x^n) = \varphi(a) s^n = \Phi(a x^n). Both maps are additive and agree on monomials, so \Psi = \Phi by @lem-check-on-monomials with one argument. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: gives the formula for \Phi and proves it does not depend on N, from \varphi(0) = 0. - 1: proves \Phi additive. - 3: reduces multiplicativity to monomials (in one argument or in both), justifying the additivity it uses. - 2: computes the monomial case correctly, justifying the reordering of factors in S (commutativity). - 1: shows \Phi(1) = 1 and \Phi(x) = s (and \Phi(a) = \varphi(a)). - 2: proves uniqueness: the values on monomials are forced, then additivity. Fatal errors (0 for the step): proving multiplicativity only for p, q of degree at most 1; assuming that a homomorphism is determined by its value at x alone, without using \Psi(a) = \varphi(a) on constants. A proof of multiplicativity by expanding \Phi(p)\Phi(q) as a double sum and regrouping by i + j = k earns the 3 points of the reduction step only if the regrouping is proved. [C2: Composition is associative] Let R be a commutative ring and p, q, r \in R[x]. Prove that (p \circ q) \circ r = p \circ (q \circ r). The first half of a proof is given. Fix q and r. Both sides are additive in p: the left side is p \mapsto p \circ q followed by u \mapsto u \circ r, two ring homomorphisms (@def-polynomial-composition), and the right side is p \mapsto p \circ (q \circ r), a ring homomorphism. The second half is blank. Name the move, then complete it. One move is check on monomials, extend by additivity. Let p = a x^n. Since u \mapsto u \circ q is a ring homomorphism fixing the constant a and sending x to q, and a x^n is the product of a and x^n (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (c)), (a x^n) \circ q = (a \circ q)(x \circ q)^n = a q^n , by the power property of ring homomorphisms (after @def-ring-homomorphism). Applying the ring homomorphism u \mapsto u \circ r in the same way, (a q^n) \circ r = (a \circ r)(q \circ r)^n = a \, (q \circ r)^n . On the other side, the same computation with q \circ r in place of q gives (a x^n) \circ (q \circ r) = a \, (q \circ r)^n. So the two sides agree on every monomial. Both are additive in p, so by @lem-check-on-monomials (with one argument and T = R[x]) they agree for every p. Also correct: the move a homomorphism out of R[x] is fixed by the constants and x. Both sides are ring homomorphisms R[x] 	o R[x] (composites of ring homomorphisms, after @def-ring-homomorphism), both fix every constant ((a \circ q) \circ r = a \circ r = a and a \circ (q \circ r) = a), and both send x to q \circ r: (x \circ q) \circ r = q \circ r and x \circ (q \circ r) = q \circ r. So they are equal by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-substitution (b), with S = R[x], \varphi \colon a \mapsto a x^0 and s = q \circ r. [C3: The factor theorem over any commutative ring] Let R be a commutative ring and c \in R. 1. Prove that for every n \ge 1, x^n - c^n = (x - c) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{\,n-1-j} x^j . 2. Prove that for p \in R[x], p(c) = 0 if and only if p = (x - c) q for some q \in R[x]. 3. In 
Z/8
Z, find all roots of x^2 - 1. The usual argument that a quadratic polynomial cannot have more than two roots goes: “if c_1 is a root, then p = (x - c_1) q with \deg q = 1; a second root c_2 
e c_1 has (c_2 - c_1) q(c_2) = 0, so q(c_2) = 0”. Which step fails in 
Z/8
Z? [Hint 1] For (a), compare coefficients: multiplying a polynomial by x shifts its coefficients up by one place (@lem-monomial-product (a)). For (b) (\Rightarrow), reduce to (a). [Hint 2] For (b), let N be admissible for p and start from p - p(c) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k - \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k, with p(c) read as a constant. (a) Let u \coloneqq \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{\,n-1-j} x^j, so u_j = c^{\,n-1-j} for 0 \le j \le n - 1 and u_j = 0 for j \ge n. By @lem-monomial-product (a) and @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (d), (x - c)u = xu - cu has coefficient -c u_0 at 0 and u_{k-1} - c u_k at k \ge 1. So: - at k = 0: -c \cdot c^{n-1} = -c^n; - at 1 \le k \le n - 1: c^{\,n-k} - c \cdot c^{\,n-1-k} = 0, by the power law; - at k = n: u_{n-1} - c u_n = c^0 - 0 = 1; - at k > n: 0 - 0 = 0. These are the coefficients of x^n - c^n. This is Chapter 1’s difference-of-powers identity (@lem-difference-of-powers), read in the commutative ring R[x] with z = x and w = c; the proof above does not use it. (b) (\Leftarrow) By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, p(c) = (c - c)\, q(c) = 0 \cdot q(c) = 0. (\Rightarrow) Let N be admissible for p. By @prp-polynomial-sum-of-monomials and @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (b), (c), and since the constants respect sums,  egin{aligned} p - p(c) &= \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k - \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k \ &= \sum_{k=1}^{N} p_k  igl(x^k - c^k igr) , \end{aligned} where the term k = 0 is p_0 (1 - 1) = 0. By (a), each x^k - c^k with k \ge 1 is (x - c) u^{(k)} for a polynomial u^{(k)}, so by the distributive law p - p(c) = (x - c) q with q \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{N} p_k u^{(k)}. If p(c) = 0, then p = (x - c) q. (c) The squares in 
Z/8
Z of [0], \dots, [7] are [0], [1], [4], [1], [0], [1], [4], [1] (for instance [5]^2 = [25] = [1], [7]^2 = [49] = [1]). So x^2 - 1 has the four roots [1], [3], [5], [7]. The failing step is “(c_2 - c_1) q(c_2) = 0, so q(c_2) = 0”: it needs 
Z/8
Z to have no zero divisors. With c_1 = [1], q = x + 1 and c_2 = [3], (c_2 - c_1) q(c_2) = [2][4] = [8] = [0], with both factors non-zero. Chapter 7 proves the factor theorem over a field again, by division with remainder. [C4: A second proof of Fermat’s little theorem] Let p be a prime. Give another proof that a^{p-1} = 1 for every non-zero a \in 
F_p, along the following steps, and then compare x^p - x with its function. 1. Let a \in 
F_p be non-zero. Show that b \mapsto ab is a bijection from 
F_p \setminus \{0\} to itself. 2. Deduce that a^{p-1} = 1, by computing the product of all non-zero elements of 
F_p in two ways. 3. Show that x^p - x 
e 0 in 
F_p[x], but \varepsilon(x^p - x) = 0. Write F \coloneqq 
F_p, a field (@def-field-fp); then F \setminus \{0\} has the p - 1 elements 1, \dots, p - 1 (@thm-integers-mod-n-ring (b)). (a) For b \in F \setminus \{0\}, ab 
e 0, since F has no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)); so b \mapsto ab maps F \setminus \{0\} to F \setminus \{0\}. It is injective: ab = ab' gives a(b - b') = 0, so b = b'. Its image is a subset of the finite set F \setminus \{0\} in bijection with F \setminus \{0\}; if the image were a proper subset, this would contradict @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy. So the map is surjective, hence a bijection. (b) A rearranged product is the same product. For a list t_1, \dots, t_r in a commutative ring and a bijection \sigma of \{1, \dots, r\}, we show \prod_{j=1}^{r} t_{\sigma(j)} = \prod_{j=1}^{r} t_j, by @fd1:ax-induction on r. For r = 0 both sides are the empty product 1. For the step, first a deletion rule: for a list u_1, \dots, u_{r+1} and a position k, the product equals u_k times the product of the list with position k deleted. For k = r + 1 this is the product recursion; for k \le r, it follows from the rule for the first r entries (induction on the length) and (F5), (F6):  egin{aligned} \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} u_j = \Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^{r} u_j\Bigr) u_{r+1} &= \Bigl( igl(	extstyle\prod_{j \le r,\, j 
e k} u_j igr) u_k\Bigr) u_{r+1} \ &= \Bigl( igl(	extstyle\prod_{j \le r,\, j 
e k} u_j igr) u_{r+1}\Bigr) u_k , \end{aligned} and the bracket in the last line is the product of the list with position k deleted, by the product recursion, since that list ends with u_{r+1}. Now let u_j \coloneqq t_{\sigma(j)} and k \coloneqq \sigma^{-1}(r + 1). Deleting position k leaves the list t_{\sigma'(1)}, \dots, t_{\sigma'(r)}, where \sigma'(i) \coloneqq \sigma(i) for i < k and \sigma'(i) \coloneqq \sigma(i + 1) for i \ge k, a bijection of \{1, \dots, r\}: its values lie in \{1, \dots, r\}, since \sigma(m) = r + 1 only for m = k and the index used (i for i < k, i + 1 for i \ge k) is never k; it is injective because \sigma and this index map are; and every j \le r is \sigma(m) for some m 
e k, so j = \sigma'(m) if m < k and j = \sigma'(m - 1) if m > k. By the deletion rule and the hypothesis for r, \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} t_{\sigma(j)} =  igl(\prod_{i=1}^{r} t_i igr) t_{r+1} = \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} t_j. The two computations. List F \setminus \{0\} as b_1, \dots, b_{p-1}, and let Q \coloneqq \prod_{j=1}^{p-1} b_j. By (a), a b_j = b_{\sigma(j)} for a bijection \sigma of \{1, \dots, p - 1\}, so the list a b_1, \dots, a b_{p-1} is a rearrangement of b_1, \dots, b_{p-1}, and its product is Q. By (F5), (F6) and induction on the length, the same product is a^{p-1} Q. So a^{p-1} Q = Q = 1 \cdot Q. Since Q is a product of non-zero elements of a field, Q 
e 0 (@thm-field-basic-properties (f), by induction), and canceling Q (@thm-field-basic-properties (b)) gives a^{p-1} = 1. (c) The polynomial x^p - x has coefficient 1 at position p (since p \ge 2, the positions p and 1 differ), and 1 
e 0 in F; so it is not the zero polynomial. For every c \in F, c^p - c = 0: if c 
e 0, c^p = c^{p-1} c = c by (b); and 0^p = 0 since p \ge 1. So \varepsilon(x^p - x) is the zero function. This gives a second proof, by Fermat rather than by the factors x - c, that \varepsilon is not injective over 
F_p. The two witnesses are in fact the same polynomial: Chapter 7 shows that x^p - x = \prod_{c \in 
F_p} (x - c), the P of @prp-polynomial-function-map (d) with R = 
F_p (@exm-polynomial-function-finite-field (b)). This is the second proof of @thm-fermat-little (b); the first, in Chapter 4, went through the Frobenius map. Part (c) also follows directly from @thm-fermat-little (a).

title: 6.5 The Formal Derivative
content:
The Formal Derivative The polynomials of this chapter are coefficient sequences, and @thm-polynomial-substitution showed how to evaluate them and how to substitute into them. One more operation from school survives the passage to an arbitrary commutative ring: the derivative. This section defines it by its coefficients, proves the sum, product and power rules with the move of @lem-check-on-monomials, and asks when a derivative can be 0. Over a field the answer depends on the characteristic of Chapter 4, and over 
F_p it is not the answer of calculus. At school a double root shows itself in the graph. The parabola y = (x - 1)^2 touches the axis at 1 instead of crossing it, and its slope there is 0: the derivative 2(x - 1) vanishes at 1 as well. Over 
F_p there is no graph and no slope; the field has p elements and no limits. What survives is the formula: the derivative of a x^n is n a x^{n-1}. We keep the formula and drop the limit. Chapter 7 uses the result to detect repeated roots; this section builds the tool. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field). Polynomials are written f, g, h, with coefficients f_k, g_k, h_k, because the letter p is kept for a prime. A dot with an integer on its left is a multiple, n \cdot a = a + \dots + a with n terms (the “Multiples” paragraph of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.4, collected in @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (d)); the product of two ring elements is written by juxtaposition. The derivative by coefficients At school, (3x^4 + 5x^2)' = 12x^3 + 10x. Each term moves down one place, and its coefficient is multiplied by the exponent it had. In R[x] “multiplied by the exponent” has a meaning without any division or limit: the exponent n is a natural number, and n \cdot a is the n-th multiple of a. That recurring computation deserves a name. The formal derivative moves every coefficient down one place and takes it as many times as its old exponent. [Formal Derivative] Let R be a commutative ring and f \in R[x]. The formal derivative of f is the sequence f' \colon 
N 	o R given by (f')_k \coloneqq (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1} \qquad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N , where (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1} is the (k + 1)-th multiple of f_{k+1}. The higher derivatives are defined by f^{(0)} \coloneqq f , \qquad f^{(k+1)} \coloneqq  igl( f^{(k)}  igr)' \quad (k \in 
N) , and we write f'' for f^{(2)}. In words: the coefficient of x^k in f' is read off from the coefficient of x^{k+1} in f, added to itself k + 1 times. The definition uses only the addition of R, so it makes sense, word for word, over 
Z, 
Q, 
Z/6
Z and

title: Polynomials over a Field
content:
Polynomials over a Field Chapter 2 of this volume did arithmetic in 
Z: divide with a remainder (from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5), take the least positive element of a set closed under combinations, and the greatest common divisor, Bézout’s identity, Euclid’s lemma and unique factorization follow. Chapter 6 of this volume built the ring F[x] and its degree, but it did not divide one polynomial by another with a remainder. This chapter shows that over a field F the polynomials have the same arithmetic, with the degree in the part of the size and “monic” in the part of “positive”. It also proves what 
Z has no analogue for. A polynomial can be evaluated, so it has roots, and roots occupy the second half of the chapter. A root c is a factor x - c; a non-zero polynomial has no more distinct roots than its degree; a repeated root shows up in the formal derivative of Section 6.5; and values at enough points determine a polynomial, which is interpolation. Interpolation turns out to be the Chinese remainder theorem for the moduli x - c, and the ring F[x]/\langle m angle, built by the quotient construction of Section 2.3, is a field exactly when m is irreducible. The chapter ends with the question that algebra courses usually leave to analysis: does every non-constant complex polynomial have a root? It does, and Section 7.6 proves it with no convergent sequences, no compactness, no continuity theorem and no polar form. The one analytic input is the supremum property of 
R. It is used directly twice, to find a point where \abs{p} is smallest, and indirectly through the real square roots behind the modulus and behind the complex square roots. The factorization of real polynomials into linear factors and quadratics without real roots follows. Two rings, one arithmetic. The first half of the chapter runs Chapter 2 again, with these substitutions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ In

The integer twins are compared with, never cited as a reason for a polynomial statement. The general facts about ideals, quotient rings and units are cited, not proved again. Integers enter only as integers: as coefficients, in the rational root test of Section 7.3 and the integer polynomials of Section 7.1, and as degrees and exponents. What you need. Chapter 6 above all, and Chapter 4; Chapter 3 for Section 7.6 and a few examples; Chapter 2 for comparison and for the general theorems it proved once; Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, for division with remainder and for its 
R in Section 7.6; Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–5; and induction from Logic and Proof, Chapter 4. - From Chapter 6: the ring F[x] and its laws (@def-polynomial, @def-polynomial-ring, @thm-polynomial-ring-laws, @lem-finite-sums-and-powers, @lem-monomial-product); the degree and the leading coefficient, with the degree of a sum and of a product, the absence of zero divisors and the units (@def-degree, @thm-degree-of-sum, @thm-degree-of-product, @exm-integral-domains, @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors, @prp-polynomial-units); evaluation, substitution and ring homomorphisms (@def-polynomial-evaluation, @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, @thm-polynomial-substitution, @def-ring-homomorphism), with the polynomial over 
F_2 that vanishes everywhere (@exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2); and, for Sections 7.4 and 7.5, the formal derivative and its rules (@def-formal-derivative, @thm-formal-derivative-rules, @prp-formal-derivative-zero). - From Chapter 4: fields and the rule that a product of non-zero elements is non-zero (@def-field, @thm-field-basic-properties); the fields 
F_p (@def-field-fp); subfields (@def-subfield, @prp-subfield-test), for Section 7.2; the characteristic, integer multiples and Fermat’s little theorem (@def-characteristic, @exm-characteristics, @lem-integer-multiples, @thm-fermat-little), for Sections 7.4 and 7.5; and, in Section 7.6, the field 
Q(i) and complex conjugation (@exm-subfields-gaussian, @exm-complex-conjugation-automorphism). Section 7.5 meets the four-element field of @exr-finite-fields-from-modular-arithmetic-c1 again, and Exercise R2 of Section 7.6 returns to @exm-q-sqrt2-field. - From Chapter 3, for Section 7.6 (and the difference of powers also for Exercises B2 and B3 of Section 7.1): the complex numbers as a field containing 
R (@def-complex-numbers, @thm-complex-numbers-field, @prp-reals-embed-complex); the conjugate and the modulus and their rules (@def-conjugate-modulus, @thm-conjugate-properties, @prp-modulus-of-real, @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus); the triangle inequality and its variants (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @cor-complex-triangle-variants); powers (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring, @lem-difference-of-powers); complex square roots (@prp-complex-square-roots); and conjugate roots (@prp-real-coefficients-conjugate-roots). Sections 7.2 and 7.5 use 
Q \subseteq 
R \subseteq 
C in examples, and Exercise B3 of Section 7.5 compares 
R[x]/\langle x^2 + 1 angle with 
C. Chapter 3’s polar form and k-th roots are not used, and Chapter 4 is not used. - From Chapter 2, with division with remainder and parity from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5: ideals, quotient rings and units (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal, @def-ring-unit), cited for F[x]; the rules for divisibility, Euclid’s lemma and fractions in lowest terms (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @thm-euclid-lemma-integers, @prp-rationals-lowest-terms), for the rational root test; even and odd integers (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd); the integer gcd and its Euclidean step (@def-integer-gcd, @lem-gcd-remainder-step), in two exercises; and the integer twins compared with in Sections 7.1–7.5: those in the table above and @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @thm-integer-ideals-principal, @thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers, @exr-gcd-and-bezout-c2, @lem-least-divisor-prime, @thm-integers-mod-n-ring and @thm-units-mod-n. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3: 
N = \omega, its order and well-ordering, and even and odd exponents (@fd3:cor-omega-identification, @fd3:thm-omega-order, @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering, @fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity); commutative rings and the rules of an ordered ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules); greatest elements of bounded sets of integers (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element), for multiplicities; the irrationality of \sqrt2 (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two), and the gap at \sqrt2 in 
Q (@fd3:thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2), in Exercise C1 of Section 7.6; and maps on classes (@fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes), for the Chinese remainder theorem. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 4–6, for Section 7.6: absolute values and powers in an ordered field (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field, @fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field), from Chapter 4; 
R as a complete ordered field, its Archimedean property and the bound on powers of 2 (@fd3:def-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, @fd3:lem-power-two-bound), with @fd3:exm-representatives-need-choice compared with, from Chapter 7; and non-negative square roots in 
R (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), from Chapter 6, which also supply \sqrt2 for examples in Sections 7.2–7.5. - From Sets and Functions: bijections (@fd2:def-bijective), from Chapter 1; the well-ordering of 
N and the recursion theorem with its finite sums and products (@fd2:thm-well-ordering, @fd2:thm-recursion, @fd2:def-sum-product), from Chapter 2; equivalence classes and quotient sets, and suprema and infima (@fd2:thm-classes-partition, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:def-order-supremum), from Chapter 4; and finite and infinite sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count), from Section 4.1, for Section 7.4 and Exercise C3 of Section 7.3. - From Logic and Proof: induction and strong induction (@fd1:ax-induction, @fd1:thm-strong-induction), from Section 4.2, and, for the two find-the-error exercises, the catalogue of moves that are not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), from Section 8.6. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - Division with Remainder. Divisibility over a field, associates and the one monic associate of a non-zero polynomial; division with remainder, with existence by an element of least degree and uniqueness by comparing degrees, and long division over 
Q and 
F_3; and the remainder and factor theorems, which make a root c the same thing as a factor x - c. - Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm. The ideal generated by finitely many polynomials; every ideal of F[x] generated by exactly one monic polynomial; the gcd defined as the monic common divisor that every common divisor divides, with Bézout’s theorem and coprimality; the Euclidean algorithm as a recursively defined sequence, with back-substitution; and division and the gcd unchanged when the field is enlarged. - Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization. Irreducibility over a field, decided by roots in degrees 2 and 3 and not beyond, as x^4 + 4 shows; Euclid’s lemma and its consequences for irreducibles; an irreducible factor of least degree; unique factorization into monic irreducibles, with uniqueness stated by a bijection of indices; the factorizations of x^4 - 1 over five fields; and the rational root test. - Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative. At most n roots for a non-zero polynomial of degree n; a polynomial fixed by its values at n + 1 points, and over an infinite field by its function, but not over 
F_p; the expansion in powers of x - c; multiplicity, splitting off all roots, and splitting over a field; and repeated roots and repeated factors detected by the formal derivative and by \gcd(f, f'). - Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Lagrange polynomials and the unique interpolating polynomial of degree at most n; congruence modulo a polynomial and the ring F[x]/\langle m angle, named by the remainders and a field exactly when m is irreducible, with a field of four elements and a copy of 
C; the Chinese remainder theorem for any number of pairwise coprime moduli; interpolation as its case of linear moduli; and values and derivatives prescribed at once. - The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. Why the field axioms cannot suffice; a growth bound and a Lipschitz bound in place of continuity; the minimum of \abs{p}, found by nested squares and two uses of the supremum property; d’Alembert’s lemma, with its direction found by square roots instead of polar form; the theorem and the splitting of complex polynomials; and real polynomials, whose irreducible factors are linear or quadratic without real root, so that one of odd degree has a real root. Review exercises return to Chapters 4 and 6 and to Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4. Named moves - Least degree, then divide. In a set of polynomials closed under the right operations, take a non-zero element d of least degree and divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and has smaller degree, so it is 0. It is Chapter 2’s “least positive element, then divide”, with degree in place of size. Named in Section 7.2, it proves there that every ideal of F[x] has one monic generator (@thm-polynomial-ideals-principal), and Bézout’s theorem with it; its first, unnamed use is the existence half of division with remainder in Section 7.1. Exercise C1 of Section 7.2 asks for the whole proof, Exercise B2 of Section 7.3 leaves its last step to you, and Exercise C2 of Section 7.6 asks you to name it and carry it out. - Evaluate at a root. In f = qg + r, evaluate at a root of g: the term qg vanishes, and the value of r is read off. Named in Section 7.1, it proves the remainder theorem and finds remainders without dividing (@exm-polynomial-remainders-without-dividing, Exercise C2). In Section 7.5 it makes each Lagrange polynomial vanish at the other nodes, turns a congruence modulo x - c into a value at c (@prp-interpolation-as-chinese-remainder), and reads a value and a derivative off a congruence modulo (x - c)^2 (@exm-hermite-by-chinese-remainder). - Compare degrees. To show that two polynomials are equal, show that their difference has smaller degree than any non-zero polynomial of its kind can have: a non-zero multiple of g has degree at least \deg g, and a non-zero polynomial with n + 1 distinct roots has degree at least n + 1. Named in Section 7.1, it gives the uniqueness of the quotient and the remainder in Section 7.1, of the expansion in powers of x - c in Section 7.4, of the representative of degree less than \deg m in each class and of the solution of the Chinese remainder theorem in Section 7.5, and, with the root count, of the polynomial through given points in Sections 7.4 and 7.5. - Keep the quarter that keeps the infimum. To find a point where a quantity bounded below attains its infimum, halve a square, keep the first quarter in a fixed order whose infimum is the same, and take the point common to all the squares, which completeness supplies. It is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5’s bisection, now in the plane, and the fixed order makes each step a rule, so no choice is made. Named in Section 7.6, it proves there that \abs{p} attains its minimum (@thm-complex-polynomial-minimum); Exercise A1 there runs it for x^2 + 1, and Exercise C3 uses it to repair a flawed proof. - Multiply the Bézout identity, reused from Chapter 2. From af + bg = 1, multiply by h and read off what divides h. It proves Euclid’s lemma for polynomials (@thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma) and the rule for coprime divisors (@prp-polynomial-coprime-divisors-product) in Section 7.3. In Section 7.5 two such identities multiplied together show that coprimality survives products (@lem-polynomial-coprime-to-product), the identity read modulo m gives inverses in F[x]/\langle m angle, and one identity per modulus builds the solution of the Chinese remainder theorem. That chapter’s third move, computing on representatives, is not repeated: Section 7.5 cites its quotient-ring theorem.

title: 7.1 Division with Remainder
content:
Division with Remainder Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.1 divided -17 by 5 and kept the remainder 3: a quotient times the divisor, plus something smaller than the divisor. Chapter 6 built the ring F[x] of polynomials over a field and gave every non-zero polynomial a degree. For polynomials, “smaller” will mean “of smaller degree”. For instance, in 
Q[x], x^4 + 2x^3 - x + 3 = (x^2 + x)(x^2 + x - 1) + 3 , and the leftover 3 has degree 0, below the degree 2 of x^2 + x - 1. Three questions are open. Why can one always go on until the degree drops below that of the divisor? Why is the answer unique? And where does it matter that the coefficients lie in a field? This section answers all three, and then uses the answer to connect a root of a polynomial with a factor of degree 1. Throughout the chapter, F is a field (@def-field), and F[x] is the ring of polynomials over F (@def-polynomial-ring), a commutative ring by @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a). A field is an integral domain (@exm-integral-domains), so the results of Chapter 6 stated for integral domains apply to F[x]. We use the degree \deg p and the leading coefficient \operatorname{lc}(p) of @def-degree, with \deg 0 = -\infty, and the conventions -\infty < n and -\infty + n = -\infty for n \in 
N that come with it. A constant a \in F is identified with the polynomial a x^0 (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (b)), and (ap)_k = a p_k for a constant a (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (d)). Numerals in F are multiples of 1: 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, 3 \coloneqq 2 + 1, and so on, so that 2 = 0 in 
F_2 and 3 = 0 in 
F_3 (@def-field-fp). Divisibility over a field In 
Z, “a divides b” asked whether b is some integer times a. The same question makes sense in any commutative ring, and in F[x] it is the question this chapter is built on. The one new feature is that the answer can depend on the field. A polynomial g divides f when f is g times some polynomial over the same field. [Divisibility of Polynomials] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. 1. g divides f over F, written g \mid f, if there exists h \in F[x] with f = gh. Then g is a divisor (or factor) of f, and f is a multiple of g. We write g 
mid f when g does not divide f. 2. f and g are associates if f = cg for some non-zero constant c \in F. In words: (a) asks for a cofactor h, and the cofactor must have its coefficients in F; (b) says that two polynomials are associates when they differ by a non-zero constant factor. When two fields are in play, “g \mid f in F[x]” names the field. Four instances, chosen so that the same symbols give different answers: - x - 1 \mid x^2 - 1 in 
Q[x], since x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). - 2x - 2 \mid x^2 - 1 in 
Q[x], since x^2 - 1 = (2x - 2) igl(	frac12 x + 	frac12 igr). The polynomials x - 1 and 2x - 2 = 2(x - 1) are associates, and the cofactor 	frac12 x + 	frac12 needs the inverse of 2. - x + 1 \mid x^2 + 1 in 
F_2[x], since (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^2 + 1 there: 2 = 0 in 
F_2. - x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1 in 
Q[x]. Suppose x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)h with h \in 
Q[x]. Evaluating at -1 respects sums and products (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so (-1)^2 + 1 = (-1 + 1) \cdot h(-1), that is, 2 = 0 \cdot h(-1) = 0 in 
Q, which is false. Non-example by minimal change. The last two lines use the same symbols, x + 1 and x^2 + 1. Only the field changed, from 
F_2 to 
Q, and with it the value of 2: the evaluation argument gives 2 = 0, which is true in 
F_2 and false in 
Q. So “g \mid f” is a statement about g, f and F, which is why the definition says “over F”. Degenerate cases. Every g divides 0, since 0 = g \cdot 0. The zero polynomial divides only 0. And a non-zero constant c divides every f, since f = c(c^{-1}f); this is (F8), inverses of non-zero elements, at work in general (the cofactor of 2x - 2 above was one instance), and it means that non-zero constants are as invisible to divisibility as \pm 1 were in 
Z. In 
F_3[x], does x + 1 divide x^2 + 1? Evaluate at -1 = 2. No. If x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)h, evaluating at 2 (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives 2^2 + 1 = (2 + 1)h(2), that is, 5 = 0 \cdot h(2) = 0. In 
F_3, 5 = 2 
e 0. So x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1 in 
F_3[x]. The rules below are the ones the chapter uses. Parts (a)–(d) are identities in the commutative ring F[x], plus the inverse of a non-zero constant (F8) for the last clause of (a) and one degree count; parts (e) and (f) say exactly what “invisible” means. [Rules for Divisibility of Polynomials] Let F be a field and f, g, h \in F[x]. 1. g \mid 0. 0 \mid f if and only if f = 0. Every non-zero constant divides every polynomial. 2. If f \mid g and g \mid h, then f \mid h. 3. If h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid af + bg for all a, b \in F[x]. 4. If g \mid f and f 
e 0, then \deg g \le \deg f. 5. The units of F[x] (@def-ring-unit) are exactly the non-zero constants. 6. f \mid g and g \mid f if and only if f and g are associates (this includes f = g = 0). Every non-zero f has exactly one monic associate, namely \operatorname{lc}(f)^{-1} f. Two monic polynomials that divide each other are equal. Parts (a)–(c) are rearrangements of equations f = gh by the ring laws, except that the last clause of (a) also uses c^{-1}, from (F8). Part (d) is the degree of a product: a non-zero multiple of g has degree \deg g plus something in 
N. Part (e) is Chapter 6’s description of the units of R[x], read with R = F. For (f), mutual divisibility gives f = f \cdot uv, and canceling f makes u a unit, which (e) identifies as a non-zero constant. We use the ring laws of F[x] (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a)) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra without further mention. (a) 0 = g \cdot 0, so g \mid 0. If 0 \mid f, then f = 0 \cdot k = 0 for some k; conversely 0 \mid 0 by the first claim. If c \in F is a non-zero constant, then c^{-1} exists by (F8) of @def-field, and f = (c c^{-1}) f = c (c^{-1} f), so c \mid f. (b) Let g = fu and h = gv. Then h = (fu)v = f(uv), so f \mid h. (c) Let f = hu and g = hv. Then af + bg = a(hu) + b(hv) = h(au + bv), so h \mid af + bg. (d) Let f = gu with u \in F[x]. Since f 
e 0, neither g nor u is 0. The field F has no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)), so @thm-degree-of-product (b) gives \deg f = \deg g + \deg u. Here \deg u \in 
N, so \deg g \le \deg f. (e) By @prp-polynomial-units, applied to the integral domain F (@exm-integral-domains), the units of F[x] are the constants that are units of F. In a field every non-zero a is a unit, by (F8), and 0 is not, since 0 \cdot v = 0 
e 1 for every v (@thm-field-basic-properties (d) and (F7) of @def-field). So the units of F[x] are the non-zero constants. (f) (\Leftarrow) Let f = cg with c 
e 0 a constant. Then g \mid f, and g = c^{-1} f, so f \mid g. (\Rightarrow) Let f \mid g and g \mid f. If f = 0, then 0 \mid g, so g = 0 by (a), and f = 1 \cdot g. Otherwise write g = fu and f = gv. Then f = fuv, so f(1 - uv) = 0. Since f 
e 0, @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (a) gives 1 - uv = 0, that is, uv = 1. So v is a unit of F[x], hence a non-zero constant by (e), and f = vg: f and g are associates. The monic associate. Let f 
e 0 and a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(f) 
e 0. The polynomial a^{-1} f has the coefficients a^{-1} f_k (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (d)). These vanish exactly where the f_k do, since a^{-1} 
e 0 (as a \cdot 0 = 0 
e 1 = a a^{-1}, by @thm-field-basic-properties (d), (F7), (F8)) and F has no zero divisors, so \deg(a^{-1} f) = \deg f and \operatorname{lc}(a^{-1} f) = a^{-1} a = 1. If also cf is monic for a constant c 
e 0, the same computation gives \operatorname{lc}(cf) = ca = 1, so c = a^{-1} (uniqueness of inverses, @thm-field-basic-properties (c)). So a^{-1} f is the only monic associate of f. Monic and mutually dividing. Let f, g be monic with f \mid g and g \mid f. By what we proved, f = cg with a non-zero constant c, and comparing leading coefficients, 1 = \operatorname{lc}(f) = c \operatorname{lc}(g) = c. So f = g. This proves the proposition. Parts (e) and (f) are the polynomial form of a fact about 
Z: in @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (f) and (g), the units of 
Z were \pm 1, and two positive integers that divide each other are equal. In F[x] the units are the non-zero constants, and the role of “positive” is played by “monic”: among the associates of a non-zero polynomial, exactly one is monic. So whenever a polynomial is to be singled out from its associates, it is made monic. The hypothesis f 
e 0 in (d) cannot be dropped: x^5 \mid 0, and \deg x^5 = 5 > -\infty = \deg 0. In 
Q[x], list the associates of 3x + 6 that have integer coefficients and leading coefficient between -3 and 3. Which one is monic? The associates are c(3x + 6) with c \in 
Q, c 
e 0; the leading coefficient is 3c. Leading coefficients \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3 give \pm(x + 2), \pm(2x + 4), \pm(3x + 6), all with integer coefficients. The monic one is x + 2 = 	frac13 (3x + 6). Division with remainder Now the theorem. The tool is the one Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.1 used for integers, with degree in place of size: among all f - hg, take one of least degree, and show that its degree is below \deg g. [Division with Remainder in F[x]] Let F be a field, and let f, g \in F[x] with g 
e 0. 1. There are unique q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad \deg r < \deg g . 2. g \mid f if and only if r = 0. The polynomials q and r are the quotient and the remainder of f on division by g. Since \deg 0 = -\infty < \deg g, the remainder r = 0 is allowed. Look at all polynomials f - hg, h \in F[x]. If 0 is among them, f is a multiple of g and we are done. Otherwise their degrees are natural numbers, and well-ordering gives one, r, of least degree n. If n \ge \deg g, we can kill the leading term of r by subtracting a constant times a power of x times g: the constant is \operatorname{lc}(r) \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1}, and that inverse is where the field is needed. The result is again of the form f - hg and has smaller degree, against the choice of r. Uniqueness: two answers give (q - q')g = r' - r, and a non-zero multiple of g cannot have degree below \deg g. We call this move compare degrees. (a) Existence. Let m \coloneqq \deg g \in 
N and b \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(g) 
e 0, and let S \coloneqq \{ f - hg : h \in F[x] \} . If 0 \in S, say 0 = f - qg, then r \coloneqq 0 and this q satisfy f = qg + r and \deg r = -\infty < m. Suppose 0 
otin S. Then every element of S has a degree in 
N, and D \coloneqq \{ \deg s : s \in S \} \subseteq 
N is non-empty, since f = f - 0 \cdot g \in S. By the well-ordering of 
N (@fd2:thm-well-ordering; on 
N = \omega it is @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering), D has a least element n. Choose q \in F[x] with r \coloneqq f - qg of degree n, and let a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(r) 
e 0. Suppose n \ge m. Let t \coloneqq (ab^{-1}) x^{n-m}, a monomial with n - m \in 
N and non-zero coefficient ab^{-1}: b^{-1} 
e 0, since b \cdot 0 = 0 
e 1 = b b^{-1} (@thm-field-basic-properties (d), (F7), (F8)), so ab^{-1} 
e 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f). Then \deg t = n - m and \operatorname{lc}(t) = ab^{-1}, so by @thm-degree-of-product (b), tg has degree (n - m) + m = n and leading coefficient ab^{-1} b = a. Let r_1 \coloneqq r - tg = f - (q + t) g , an element of S. By @thm-degree-of-sum (with \deg(-p) = \deg p for every p, since (-p)_k = -p_k), \deg r_1 \le \max(\deg r, \deg tg) = n, and the coefficient of x^n in r_1 is a - a = 0. So \deg r_1 < n (or r_1 = 0). But r_1 
e 0, since 0 
otin S, and then \deg r_1 \in D is smaller than the least element n of D. This contradiction shows n < m. So f = qg + r with \deg r < \deg g. Uniqueness. Let f = qg + r = q'g + r' with \deg r < m and \deg r' < m. Then (q - q')g = r' - r , and \deg(r' - r) \le \max(\deg r', \deg r) < m by @thm-degree-of-sum (using \deg(-r) = \deg r as above). If q 
e q', then @thm-degree-of-product (b) gives \deg igl((q - q')g igr) = \deg(q - q') + m \ge m, a contradiction. So q = q', hence r' - r = 0 \cdot g = 0 and r = r'. (b) (\Leftarrow) If r = 0, then f = qg, so g \mid f. (\Rightarrow) If f = hg, then f = hg + 0 with \deg 0 < \deg g is a division with remainder; by the uniqueness in (a), r = 0. This proves the theorem. The field is used in two places. The first is the inverse b^{-1} of the leading coefficient of g, which builds the monomial t. The second is the degree of a product, in \deg(tg) = n and in the uniqueness: @thm-degree-of-product (b) needs the product of the leading coefficients to be non-zero, and a field has no zero divisors. The hypothesis g 
e 0 is needed as well: for g = 0 no r has \deg r < -\infty. The existence proof is also a procedure. Each pass replaces r by r - tg, which removes the leading term of r, and the degree drops by at least one. Starting from f, at most \deg f - \deg g + 1 passes are needed when \deg f \ge \deg g, and none when \deg f < \deg g: then q = 0 and r = f. This is the long division of school algebra, now with a proof that it stops and that its answer is the only one. Chapter 6 did not divide polynomials with remainder, so this is where the volume first does it. Its integer twin is @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, whose least-element proof the one above follows. [Long division in two fields] (i) In 
Q[x], divide f = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 4x - 1 by g = 2x^2 - x + 3. (ii) In 
F_3[x], divide f = x^4 + x + 2 by g = 2x^2 + 1. (i) Here \operatorname{lc}(g) = 2, with inverse 	frac12. Each pass subtracts t g, where t is the leading term of the current remainder divided by 2x^2:  egin{aligned} f - x^2 g &= -2x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 1, \ (-2x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 1) - (-x) g &= -3x^2 + 7x - 1, \ (-3x^2 + 7x - 1) -  igl(-	frac32 igr) g &= 	frac{11}{2} x + 	frac72 . \end{aligned} The last line has degree 1 < 2, so we stop. Adding up the t’s, 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 4x - 1 =  igl(x^2 - x - 	frac32 igr)(2x^2 - x + 3) + 	frac{11}{2} x + 	frac72 . Check:  igl(x^2 - x - 	frac32 igr)(2x^2 - x + 3) = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 - 	frac32 x - 	frac92, and adding 	frac{11}{2} x + 	frac72 gives f. (ii) In 
F_3, 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 1, so \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1} = 2^{-1} = 2. The first t is 1 \cdot 2 \cdot x^2 = 2x^2, and 2x^2 \cdot g = 4x^4 + 2x^2 = x^4 + 2x^2. The second t is 2, and 2g = 4x^2 + 2 = x^2 + 2:  egin{aligned} f - 2x^2 g &= -2x^2 + x + 2 = x^2 + x + 2, \ (x^2 + x + 2) - 2g &= x . \end{aligned} So x^4 + x + 2 = (2x^2 + 2)(2x^2 + 1) + x in 
F_3[x]. Check: (2x^2 + 2)(2x^2 + 1) = 4x^4 + 6x^2 + 2 = x^4 + 2 in 
F_3, and adding x gives f. Find two different pairs (q, r) with x^2 = q(x^2 + 1) + r in 
Q[x] and \deg r \le 2. Which condition in part (a) of the theorem does the second one fail? (q, r) = (1, -1): 1 \cdot (x^2 + 1) - 1 = x^2, with \deg(-1) = 0 < 2. And (q, r) = (0, x^2): 0 \cdot (x^2 + 1) + x^2 = x^2, with \deg r = 2. The second fails \deg r < \deg g = 2. Uniqueness holds only among remainders of degree strictly below that of the divisor; (1, -1) is the quotient and remainder. Division with remainder needs the leading coefficient of the divisor to be invertible. Take the polynomials in 
Q[x] all of whose coefficients lie in 
Z, and try to divide x^2 by 2x among them: x^2 = q \cdot 2x + r with \deg r < 1. Comparing the coefficients of x^2 gives 1 = 2q_1 (@lem-monomial-product (a)), and no integer q_1 satisfies it, since 1 is odd (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a)). In 
Q[x] there is no problem: x^2 = 	frac12 x \cdot 2x + 0. Exercise C1 shows that integer coefficients are kept when the divisor is monic. Roots and factors of degree one Division by a polynomial of degree 1 has a remainder of degree at most 0, that is, a constant. Which constant? Evaluate: the divisor x - c vanishes at c, so the quotient term disappears and the remainder is read off. We call this move evaluate at a root. [Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] and c \in F. 1. The remainder of f on division by x - c is the constant f(c). 2. c is a root of f if and only if x - c \mid f. 3. f has a factor of degree 1 in F[x] if and only if f has a root in F. Divide by x - c and evaluate at c: the term with the quotient vanishes, and what is left is the remainder. Part (b) is then the divisibility test of @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (b), and for (c) a factor ax + b of degree 1 is made monic, which turns it into some x - c. (a) The polynomial x - c is non-zero, of degree 1 and monic. By @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a), f = q \cdot (x - c) + r with \deg r < 1, so r is a constant (possibly 0). Evaluation at c respects sums and products, sends x to c and a constant to itself (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so f(c) = q(c) \cdot (c - c) + r = q(c) \cdot 0 + r = r . (b) By (a), f = q \cdot (x - c) + f(c) is the division of f by x - c. By @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (b), x - c \mid f if and only if this remainder is 0, that is, f(c) = 0. (c) (\Leftarrow) If f(c) = 0, then x - c \mid f by (b), and x - c has degree 1. (\Rightarrow) Let ax + b \mid f with a, b \in F, a 
e 0. Then ax + b = a igl(x - (-a^{-1}b) igr), so x - (-a^{-1}b) \mid ax + b, and by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b), x - (-a^{-1}b) \mid f. By (b), -a^{-1}b is a root of f. Part (b) is the factor theorem, and it turns a question about values (is f(c) = 0?) into a question about divisibility. Part (c) turns the search for factors of degree 1 into a search for roots. [Remainders without dividing] (a) In 
Q[x], find the remainder of f = x^5 - 3x^3 + 2x + 7 on division by x - 2. (b) In 
Q[x], find the remainder of x^5 on division by x^2 - x. (a) By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a), the remainder is f(2) = 32 - 24 + 4 + 7 = 19 . (b) The divisor x^2 - x has degree 2, so the remainder has degree at most 1: x^5 = q \cdot (x^2 - x) + ax + b with a, b \in 
Q (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a)). The divisor vanishes at 0 and at 1. Evaluating at both (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), 0 = q(0) \cdot 0 + b, \qquad 1 = q(1) \cdot 0 + a + b , so b = 0 and a = 1. The remainder is x. Check: x^5 - x = (x^2 - x)(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1). Without dividing, decide whether x + 1 divides x^7 + 1 in 
Q[x], and whether x - 1 does. x + 1 = x - (-1), and (-1)^7 + 1 = -1 + 1 = 0, so x + 1 \mid x^7 + 1 by @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b). For x - 1, the remainder is 1^7 + 1 = 2 
e 0 in 
Q, so x - 1 
mid x^7 + 1. (Over 
F_2, 2 = 0 and both divide.) [Looking ahead] Section 7.5 builds, for any finite list of distinct points of F, the polynomial of least degree that takes prescribed values there. Exercise C2 below is the case of two points: the remainder of f on division by (x - a)(x - b). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @thm-polynomial-division-remainder with every hypothesis. 2. Name the two places in its proof where “F is a field” is used. 3. Let f \in F[x], and let c \in F be a non-zero constant. What are the quotient and the remainder of f on division by c? 4. True or false, with a reason: for f, g \in 
Q[x], if f \mid g and g \mid f, then f = g. The same question in 
F_2[x]. (a) Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x] with g 
e 0. Then there are unique q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r and \deg r < \deg g; and g \mid f if and only if r = 0. (b) The inverse \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1}, which builds the monomial t = \operatorname{lc}(r)\operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1} x^{n-m}; and the absence of zero divisors in F, through @thm-degree-of-product (b), which gives \deg(tg) = n and, in the uniqueness, \deg igl((q - q')g igr) \ge \deg g. (c) q = c^{-1} f and r = 0: indeed f = (c^{-1} f) c + 0, and \deg 0 = -\infty < 0 = \deg c. By uniqueness this is the division. (d) In 
Q[x]: false. x \mid 2x and 2x \mid x (x = 	frac12 \cdot 2x), but x 
e 2x. By @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f), mutual divisibility only makes f and g associates. In 
F_2[x]: true. By (f), f = cg with c a non-zero constant, and the only non-zero element of 
F_2 is 1; so f = g. B. Practice [B1: Two long divisions] 1. In 
Q[x], divide x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5 by 3x^2 - 1. 2. In 
F_5[x], divide x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 by 2x^2 + 3, and decide whether 2x^2 + 3 divides x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 in 
F_5[x]. (a) \operatorname{lc}(3x^2 - 1)^{-1} = 	frac13. The passes subtract 	frac13 x^2, -x and 	frac19 times the divisor:  egin{aligned} (x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5) - 	frac13 x^2 (3x^2 - 1) &= -3x^3 + 	frac13 x^2 + 2x - 5, \ (-3x^3 + 	frac13 x^2 + 2x - 5) + x(3x^2 - 1) &= 	frac13 x^2 + x - 5, \ (	frac13 x^2 + x - 5) - 	frac19 (3x^2 - 1) &= x - 	frac{44}{9} . \end{aligned} So the quotient is 	frac13 x^2 - x + 	frac19 and the remainder is x - 	frac{44}{9}, of degree 1 < 2. Check: (3x^2 - 1) igl(	frac13 x^2 - x + 	frac19 igr) = x^4 - 3x^3 + x - 	frac19, and adding x - 	frac{44}{9} gives x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5. (b) In 
F_5, 2 \cdot 3 = 6 = 1, so 2^{-1} = 3. The passes subtract 3x^2, x and 3 times the divisor, with 3x^2(2x^2 + 3) = x^4 + 4x^2, x(2x^2 + 3) = 2x^3 + 3x and 3(2x^2 + 3) = x^2 + 4:  egin{aligned} (x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1) - (x^4 + 4x^2) &= 2x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 1, \ (2x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 1) - (2x^3 + 3x) &= x^2 + 1, \ (x^2 + 1) - (x^2 + 4) &= 2 , \end{aligned} using -4 = 1 and -3 = 2 in 
F_5. So the quotient is 3x^2 + x + 3 and the remainder is the constant 2. Since 2 
e 0 in 
F_5, @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (b) gives 2x^2 + 3 
mid x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 in 
F_5[x]. [B2: A factor of a difference of powers] Let F be a field, c \in F and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Deduce from @lem-difference-of-powers that x^n - c^n = (x - c) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^j x^{n-1-j} , and hence that x - c \mid x^n - c^n. Then give a second proof of the divisibility with @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor. F[x] is a commutative ring (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a)), so @lem-difference-of-powers applies in it. Take z = c and w = x: c^n - x^n = (c - x) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^j x^{n-1-j} . Negate both sides: -(c^n - x^n) = x^n - c^n and - igl((c - x) s igr) = (x - c) s for every s \in F[x] (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a), (c)). This is the displayed identity, and it shows x - c \mid x^n - c^n. Taking z = c, w = x rather than z = x, w = c gives the sum in the stated order, with no re-indexing. Second proof. By @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (c), x^n is the monomial 1 x^n, whose value at c is 1 \cdot c^n = c^n (@def-polynomial-evaluation, the monomial example after it). So the value of x^n - c^n at c is c^n - c^n = 0 (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations, for the sum and the constant -c^n), so c is a root and x - c \mid x^n - c^n by @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b). This proof gives the divisibility at once but not the quotient. [B3: One remainder over every field] Let F be any field. Show that the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 1 in F[x] is 1. Then explain why, over 
Q, evaluating at the roots 1 and -1 also finds it, and why that method alone does not settle the question over 
F_2. By @lem-difference-of-powers in F[x] with z = x^2, w = 1 and n = 50, since (x^2)^k = x^{2k} and 1^k = 1 (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)), (x^2 - 1) \sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j} = x^{100} - 1 . So x^{100} =  igl(\sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j} igr)(x^2 - 1) + 1, and \deg 1 = 0 < 2 = \deg(x^2 - 1). By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a), the remainder is 1, over every field. Over 
Q by evaluation. Write x^{100} = q(x^2 - 1) + ax + b. Evaluating at 1 and -1 gives 1 = a + b and 1 = -a + b; subtracting, 2a = 0, so a = 0 since 2 
e 0 in 
Q; then b = 1. Over 
F_2. There -1 = 1, so the two roots coincide and evaluation gives the single equation 1 = a + b. It does not determine a and b (both (0, 1) and (1, 0) satisfy it), so the uniqueness argument above is needed. C. Going deeper [C1: Monic divisors keep integer coefficients] Call p \in 
Q[x] an integer polynomial if every coefficient of p lies in 
Z. 1. Let f, g be integer polynomials with g monic. Prove that the quotient and the remainder of f on division by g in 
Q[x] are integer polynomials. 2. Prove the same if \operatorname{lc}(g) = -1. 3. Explain why the least-degree argument of @thm-polynomial-division-remainder still works when S is replaced by \{ f - hg : h 	ext{ an integer polynomial} \}, for g monic. [Hint 1] Rerun the existence proof of @thm-polynomial-division-remainder, but only with integer polynomials h. [Hint 2] Let S_
Z \coloneqq \{ f - hg : h 	ext{ an integer polynomial} \}. If 0 
otin S_
Z, take r = f - qg \in S_
Z of least degree n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering) and suppose n \ge \deg g. Sums, negatives and products of integer polynomials are integer polynomials: their coefficients are sums of products of coefficients (@def-polynomial-ring), and 
Z is closed under +, -, \cdot. (c) and (a). Let m \coloneqq \deg g and S_
Z \coloneqq \{ f - hg : h 	ext{ an integer polynomial} \} \subseteq 
Q[x] , whose elements are integer polynomials. Run the existence proof with S_
Z in place of S. If 0 \in S_
Z, then f = qg with q an integer polynomial and r = 0. Otherwise take r = f - qg \in S_
Z of least degree n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering), and suppose n \ge m. With a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(r) \in 
Z and b = 1, the monomial t = a x^{n-m} is an integer polynomial, so r - tg = f - (q + t)g \in S_
Z, and it has degree < n or is 0, exactly as in the proof. Both contradict the choice of r. So \deg r < m, and f = qg + r with q, r integer polynomials. This is a division with remainder in 
Q[x], so by uniqueness (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a)) these q, r are the quotient and remainder. The argument works because the step r \mapsto r - tg never leaves S_
Z: it needs b^{-1} \in 
Z, and b = 1 gives b^{-1} = 1. That answers (c). (d) If \operatorname{lc}(g) = -1, then b^{-1} = -1 \in 
Z, and the same proof runs with t = -a x^{n-m}. (Alternatively, divide f by the monic -g: f = q(-g) + r = (-q)g + r.) [C2: The remainder modulo a quadratic with known roots] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] and a, b \in F. 1. If a 
e b, prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)(x - b) is f(a) (a - b)^{-1} (x - b) + f(b) (b - a)^{-1} (x - a) . 2. If a = b, write f = (x - a)h + f(a) (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a)) and prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)^2 is h(a)(x - a) + f(a). 3. Hence find the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 3x + 2 in 
Q[x]. [Hint 1] The remainder has degree at most 1. Which values does it take at a and at b? [Hint 2] Write f = q(x - a)(x - b) + r with \deg r \le 1, and let s be the displayed polynomial. (a) The divisor (x - a)(x - b) is monic of degree 2 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), so @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a) gives f = q (x - a)(x - b) + r with \deg r \le 1. Evaluating at a and at b (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) kills the first term: r(a) = f(a) and r(b) = f(b). Let s be the displayed polynomial; it has degree at most 1, and s(a) = f(a) \cdot 1 + f(b) \cdot 0 = f(a), s(b) = f(b). So r - s has degree at most 1 and the two roots a 
e b. If r - s 
e 0, then x - a \mid r - s (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b)), say r - s = (x - a)k, and \deg k \le 0 by @thm-degree-of-product (b), so k is a constant; evaluating at b gives 0 = (b - a) k, so k = 0 because b - a 
e 0, and then r - s = 0 after all. Hence r = s. (b) Divide h by x - a: h = (x - a)h_2 + h(a) (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a)). Then f = (x - a)^2 h_2 + h(a)(x - a) + f(a) , and h(a)(x - a) + f(a) has degree at most 1 < 2. By uniqueness, it is the remainder. (c) x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2). By (a) with a = 1, b = 2, f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 2^{100}, the remainder is 1 \cdot (-1)^{-1} (x - 2) + 2^{100} \cdot 1^{-1} (x - 1) = (2^{100} - 1)x + (2 - 2^{100}) .

title: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content:
Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm Section 7.1 gave F[x] a division with remainder (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder). This section asks what two polynomials have in common. Here is a concrete version of the question. Which polynomials over 
Q can be written as a \cdot (x^2 - 1) + b \cdot (x^2 + x - 2) \qquad 	ext{with } a, b \in 
Q[x] \, ? Taking a = -1 and b = 1 gives x - 1, and hence, multiplying a and b by any h, every multiple h \cdot (x - 1). Nothing else can occur: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) and x^2 + x - 2 = (x - 1)(x + 2), so x - 1 divides every such combination (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)). So the answer is “all multiples of x - 1, and nothing else”. Why x - 1, and why should the answer be the set of multiples of a single polynomial? The integer version of this question, in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.2, was answered by a least element; here the answer is a polynomial of least degree. As in Section 7.1, F is a field and F[x] is a commutative ring (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a)). So the general notions of Chapter 2 apply to it without change: ideals (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, clauses (I1)–(I3)), quotient rings (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal) and units (@def-ring-unit). We recall the clauses: a subset I \subseteq F[x] is an ideal if (I1) 0 \in I, (I2) a + b \in I for all a, b \in I, and (I3) ra \in I for all a \in I and all r \in F[x]. The ideal generated by finitely many polynomials The combinations in the opening question form a set that deserves a name and a symbol. [Ideal Generated by Polynomials] Let F be a field, k \in 
Z_{>0} and f_1, \dots, f_k \in F[x]. The set \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle \coloneqq \{ a_1 f_1 + \dots + a_k f_k : a_1, \dots, a_k \in F[x] \} is the ideal generated by f_1, \dots, f_k. For one polynomial, \langle f angle = \{ af : a \in F[x] \} is the set of multiples of f. In words: \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle collects every way of multiplying each f_i by a polynomial and adding up. The coefficients a_i range over all of F[x], not over F. The name is earned by two facts. It is an ideal, and it contains every f_i. (I1): 0 = 0 \cdot f_1 + \dots + 0 \cdot f_k. (I2): \sum_i a_i f_i + \sum_i b_i f_i = \sum_i (a_i + b_i) f_i. (I3): r \sum_i a_i f_i = \sum_i (r a_i) f_i. These are the ring laws of F[x] applied to finite sums (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b)). Taking a_i = 1 and the other coefficients 0 shows f_i \in \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle. It lies inside every ideal that contains every f_i. If J is an ideal with f_1, \dots, f_k \in J, then each a_i f_i \in J by (I3), and their sum lies in J by (I2), applied k - 1 times. So \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle \subseteq J. So \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle is the smallest ideal containing f_1, \dots, f_k. This “smallest” clause is how we will compare two such ideals: to show \langle g_1, \dots, g_l angle \subseteq \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle, it is enough to show that each g_j lies in \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle. Examples: - \langle 0 angle = \{ a \cdot 0 \} = \{0\}, the degenerate case. It is the only ideal generated by one polynomial that contains no non-zero element, and the main theorem below treats it separately. - \langle c angle = F[x] for a non-zero constant c: every f equals (c^{-1} f) \cdot c. - For c \in F, let I_c \coloneqq \{ f \in F[x] : f(c) = 0 \}, the polynomials with root c. It is an ideal: 0(c) = 0, (f + g)(c) = f(c) + g(c) = 0, and (rf)(c) = r(c) f(c) = 0, by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. Moreover I_c = \langle x - c angle: by the factor theorem (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b)), f(c) = 0 if and only if x - c \mid f, that is, f \in \langle x - c angle. - In the opening question, \langle x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2 angle = \langle x - 1 angle. The set T \coloneqq \{ f \in F[x] : \deg f \ge 3 \} \cup \{0\} satisfies (I1) and (I3) (a non-zero multiple of a polynomial of degree at least 3 has degree at least 3, by @thm-degree-of-product (b)). But (I2) fails: x^3 and -x^3 + x lie in T, and their sum x has degree 1. So T is not an ideal. “Large degree” is not a property that sums keep, because leading terms can cancel. Is \{ f \in 
Q[x] : f(0) = 1 \} an ideal of 
Q[x]? Name the first clause that fails. No. (I1) fails already: the zero polynomial has 0(0) = 0 
e 1. (So do (I2), since (1 + 1)(0) = 2, and (I3), with r = 0.) Compare I_0 = \{ f : f(0) = 0 \} = \langle x angle, which is an ideal. Every ideal has one generator Every example above turned out to be the set of multiples of a single polynomial. That is no accident. [Ideals of F[x] Are Principal] Let F be a field and I an ideal of F[x]. 1. If I = \{0\}, then I = \langle 0 angle. 2. If I 
e \{0\}, there is exactly one monic d \in F[x] with I = \langle d angle. Moreover d is the only monic element of I of least degree among the non-zero elements of I. Take a non-zero element of I of least degree, and scale it to be monic; call it d. Its multiples lie in I by absorption. Conversely, divide any f \in I by d: the remainder f - qd lies in I and has smaller degree than d, so it cannot be a non-zero element of I. It is 0, and f is a multiple of d. Uniqueness comes from @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f): two monic generators divide each other. Before reading on: where is “least degree” used, and why is d made monic? (a) If I = \{0\}, then I = \{0\} = \langle 0 angle. (b) Existence. Let I 
e \{0\}. The set D \coloneqq \{ \deg e : e \in I, \ e 
e 0 \} is a non-empty subset of 
N, so it has a least element n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering; on 
N = \omega it is @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering). Choose a non-zero e \in I with \deg e = n, let a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(e) 
e 0, and let d \coloneqq a^{-1} e. Then d \in I by (I3), and d is monic of degree n (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f), @thm-degree-of-product (b)). (\supseteq) For h \in F[x], hd \in I by (I3). So \langle d angle \subseteq I. (\subseteq) Let f \in I. Since d 
e 0, @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a) gives q, r \in F[x] with f = qd + r and \deg r < \deg d = n. Then r = f + (-q)d \in I, by (I3) and (I2). If r
