Back-substitution: 2x + 2 = g - x(x^2 - 1) = g - x(f - g) = (-x) f + (x + 1) g , so x + 1 =  igl(-	frac12 x igr) f + 	frac12 (x + 1) g . Check: -	frac12 x f = -	frac12 (x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x) and 	frac12 (x + 1) g = 	frac12 (x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 2); the sum is 	frac12 (2x + 2) = x + 1. Common roots. f(-1) = -1 + 1 - 1 + 1 = 0 and g(-1) = -1 - 1 + 2 = 0, so -1 is a common root. Let c \in 
Q be any common root. By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b), x - c divides f and g, so it divides x + 1 by @thm-polynomial-bezout (b). Both are monic of degree 1, so they are associates by @thm-polynomial-bezout (e) (equal degree), hence equal (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f)). So x - c = x + 1, and c = -1. [B2: A gcd over the field with two elements] In 
F_2[x], let f = x^4 + x^3 + x + 1 and g = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1. Show that \gcd(f, g) = x^2 + 1 and that x^2 + 1 = 1 \cdot f + x \cdot g. In 
F_2, -1 = 1 and 1 + 1 = 0. First, x g = x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x, so f - x g = -x^2 + 1 = x^2 + 1 , that is, f = x \cdot g + (x^2 + 1), a division with remainder. Next, (x + 1)(x^2 + 1) = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 = g, so g = (x + 1)(x^2 + 1) + 0. The algorithm stops with u_2 = x^2 + 1, which is monic, so \gcd(f, g) = x^2 + 1. Finally x^2 + 1 = f - xg = 1 \cdot f + x \cdot g, since -x = x in 
F_2[x]. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: ideals of F[x] and Bézout] Let F be a field. 1. Prove that for every ideal I 
e \{0\} of F[x] there is exactly one monic d with I = \langle d angle. 2. Let f, g \in F[x], not both 0, and let d be the monic generator of \langle f, g angle. Prove that d \mid f, d \mid g, that every common divisor of f and g divides d, that d = \gcd(f, g), and that d = af + bg for some a, b \in F[x]. (a) A generator. The degrees of the non-zero elements of I form a non-empty subset of 
N, which has a least element n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering). Let e \in I be non-zero of degree n, and d \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(e)^{-1} e. Then d \in I by (I3), and d is monic of degree n. Every multiple hd lies in I by (I3), so \langle d angle \subseteq I. Conversely, let f \in I, and divide: f = qd + r with \deg r < n (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a)). Then r = f + (-q)d \in I by (I3) and (I2). If r 
e 0, it is a non-zero element of I of degree less than n, against the choice of n; so r = 0 and f \in \langle d angle. Hence I = \langle d angle. Uniqueness. If also I = \langle d' angle with d' monic, then d \in \langle d' angle and d' \in \langle d angle, so d and d' divide each other. Then d' = cd for a non-zero constant c (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f)), and comparing leading coefficients gives c = 1. (b) The ideal \langle f, g angle is not \{0\}, since it contains f and g; let d be its monic generator, from (a). Since f, g \in \langle d angle, d \mid f and d \mid g. Since d \in \langle f, g angle, d = af + bg for some a, b \in F[x]. If h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid af + bg = d (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)). So d is a monic common divisor that every common divisor divides: d = \gcd(f, g) by @def-polynomial-gcd. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: a non-zero element of least degree exists, with the well-ordering of 
N cited. - 1: it is made monic, and the monic element is shown to lie in I (absorption). - 3: an arbitrary element of I is divided by d, and the remainder is shown to lie in I. - 2: minimality of the degree forces the remainder to be 0. - 1: uniqueness of the monic generator (by any route: mutual divisibility, or minimality of the degree applied to the difference). - 2: d \mid f, d \mid g, d = af + bg, and “every common divisor divides d” are read off from \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle, and d = \gcd(f, g) is concluded from the definition. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming that the gcd is a combination of f and g (circular); “d divides f because d has least degree”, with no division step; citing @thm-euclidean-algorithm-polynomials (c) or the gcd clause of @lem-polynomial-gcd-remainder-step for (b) (both are proved from Bézout’s theorem). A second route for (b), the Euclidean algorithm with back-substitution by induction on the number of steps, may use the ideal equality of @lem-polynomial-gcd-remainder-step; it earns the 2 points of (b) when it shows that the monic associate of the last non-zero remainder divides f and g, is a combination of them, and is divisible by every common divisor. Existence in (a) has no second route here. [C2: Scaling the gcd] Let F be a field, f, g \in F[x], and h \in F[x] monic. Prove that \gcd(hf, hg) = h \gcd(f, g). [Hint 1] Compare the ideals \langle hf, hg angle and \langle f, g angle. [Hint 2] Show first that \langle hf, hg angle = \{ hu : u \in \langle f, g angle \}. If f = g = 0, then hf = hg = 0, and both sides are 0: \gcd(0, 0) = 0 = h \cdot 0. Otherwise let d \coloneqq \gcd(f, g), monic, with \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle (@thm-polynomial-bezout (c)). Since h is monic, h 
e 0, and one of hf, hg is non-zero (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (a)); so @thm-polynomial-bezout applies to (hf, hg) as well. The ideals. For a, b \in F[x], a(hf) + b(hg) = h(af + bg). As a, b range over F[x], af + bg ranges over \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle, so \langle hf, hg angle = \{ h \cdot cd : c \in F[x] \} = \{ c \cdot hd : c \in F[x] \} = \langle hd angle . The generator. hd is monic, since \operatorname{lc}(hd) = \operatorname{lc}(h)\operatorname{lc}(d) = 1 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)). By @thm-polynomial-bezout (c), \langle hf, hg angle = \langle \gcd(hf, hg) angle with \gcd(hf, hg) monic; by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-ideals-principal (b), \gcd(hf, hg) = hd = h \gcd(f, g). This is the polynomial twin of @exr-gcd-and-bezout-c2 (\gcd(ka, kb) = k \gcd(a, b) for k > 0), with “monic” in place of “positive”. Without “monic” the formula fails: \gcd(2x, 2) = 1 
e 2 = 2 \gcd(x, 1) in 
Q[x]. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: treats f = g = 0 by the convention, and checks that hf, hg are not both 0 otherwise (no zero divisors in F[x]). - 4: shows \langle hf, hg angle = \langle hd angle, citing \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle. - 2: shows hd is monic. - 2: concludes \gcd(hf, hg) = hd by the uniqueness of the monic generator. Fatal errors (0 for the step): asserting that every common divisor of hf and hg is h times a common divisor of f and g (false: 1 divides x \cdot x and x \cdot (x + 1), and 1 is not x times a polynomial); using factorizations into irreducibles, which this section does not have. A second route (hd = (hf)a + (hg)b is a monic common divisor and a combination, so every common divisor divides it) scores 2 for the zero case, 3 for “monic common divisor and combination”, 3 for “every common divisor divides hd”, 2 for the conclusion by @def-polynomial-gcd. [C3: The gcd of two binomials] Let F be a field. For m, n \in 
N, not both 0, prove that \gcd(x^m - 1, \, x^n - 1) = x^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1 in F[x] (here x^0 - 1 = 0, and \gcd(m, n) is the integer gcd). Compute \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1). Two remarks. For m \ge 1, x^m - 1 is monic of degree m. And for m \ge n \ge 1, by the power laws (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)), x^m - 1 = x^{m-n}(x^n - 1) + (x^{m-n} - 1) , since x^{m-n} x^n - x^{m-n} + x^{m-n} - 1 = x^m - 1. We prove, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) on s, the statement P(s): “for all m, n \in 
N, not both 0, with m + n \le s, the displayed formula holds”. P(0) holds vacuously: m + n \le 0 forces m = n = 0. Suppose P(s), and let m + n \le s + 1, not both 0. If m + n \le s, use P(s). Otherwise m + n = s + 1. Case n = 0. Then m \ge 1. The gcd of x^m - 1 and 0 is the monic generator of \langle x^m - 1, 0 angle = \langle x^m - 1 angle (@thm-polynomial-bezout (c)), which is x^m - 1. On the integer side, the common divisors of m and 0 are the divisors of m, and the greatest is m (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a), (e)), so \gcd(m, 0) = m. Both sides are x^m - 1. Case m = 0 is the same, since both gcds are symmetric. Case m, n \ge 1. Both gcds are symmetric, so we may suppose m \ge n. By the identity above and @lem-polynomial-gcd-remainder-step, \gcd(x^m - 1, x^n - 1) = \gcd(x^n - 1, x^{m-n} - 1) . The pair (n, m - n) is not (0, 0), since n \ge 1, and n + (m - n) = m < m + n = s + 1, so P(s) applies to it: the right side is x^{\gcd(n, m - n)} - 1. Finally m = 1 \cdot n + (m - n), so @lem-gcd-remainder-step gives \gcd(m, n) = \gcd(n, m - n). This proves P(s + 1). Since every pair (m, n) has m + n \le s for s = m + n, the formula holds for all m, n. For m = 12, n = 18: \gcd(12, 18) = 6, so \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1) = x^6 - 1. Each polynomial step is one step (m, n) \mapsto (n, m - n) of the subtractive Euclidean algorithm on the exponents.

title: 7.3 Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization
content:
Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization Over every field, x^4 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + 1). Over 
Q the last factor cannot be split further; over 
F_5 it can, and x^4 - 1 becomes a product of four factors of degree 1; over 
F_2 all of them coincide, and x^4 - 1 = (x + 1)^4. So the “primes” of F[x] depend on the field F. Once F is fixed, though, every polynomial of positive degree splits into such primes in essentially one way, as every positive integer does in Section 2.2, and for the same reason: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. Sections 7.1 and 7.2 supplied the tools: division with remainder (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder), the monic greatest common divisor and its Bézout identity (@thm-polynomial-bezout). This section spends them. Throughout, F is a field, and F[x] is a commutative ring with no zero divisors (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a), @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors); degrees of products add (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), and the units of F[x] are the non-zero constants (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (e)). Irreducible polynomials In 
Z, a prime is a number p \ge 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p. Two features of that definition need adjusting for polynomials. “Positive” has no meaning in F[x], and its job there was to ignore the units \pm 1; in F[x] the units are the non-zero constants, so we ignore those. And “p \ge 2” kept the units themselves from counting as primes; in F[x] the condition becomes “degree at least 1”. An irreducible polynomial is one that cannot be split into two factors of smaller degree. [Irreducible Polynomial] Let F be a field and p \in F[x]. The polynomial p is irreducible over F if \deg p \ge 1 and, whenever p = gh with g, h \in F[x], one of g, h is a constant. A polynomial of degree at least 1 that is not irreducible over F is reducible over F. In words: the first clause rules out 0 and the non-zero constants; the second says that every way of writing p as a product uses a constant factor. That constant is never 0, since p 
e 0. So p is reducible exactly when p = gh with \deg g \ge 1 and \deg h \ge 1; then \deg g + \deg h = \deg p (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), so both factors have degree strictly less than \deg p. Examples. - Every polynomial of degree 1 is irreducible. If p = gh with \deg p = 1, the degrees of g and h are natural numbers adding up to 1, so one of them is 0. - x^2 + x = x(x + 1) and x^3 = x \cdot x^2 are reducible over every field: each is a product of two factors of degree at least 1. - x^2 + 1 is reducible over 
F_2, where (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^2 + 1 because 2 = 0. Over 
Q it is irreducible, as the next proposition shows. The polynomial is the same; the field changed, and with it the answer. This is why the definition says “over F”. - If p is irreducible and a \in F is non-zero, then ap is irreducible. First, \deg(ap) = \deg p \ge 1 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), and a factorization ap = gh gives p = (a^{-1}g)h, so a^{-1}g or h is a constant, and then so is g or h. Associates of irreducibles are irreducible. The constants are kept out by the first clause, and each for a reason. Without it, the polynomial 0 would pass the second clause, since every factorization 0 = gh has g = 0 or h = 0 (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors), a constant. But every polynomial divides 0 (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (a)), so 0 behaves like the integer 0, not like a prime. A non-zero constant a is a unit: it divides everything, and every factorization a = gh has two constant factors, since the degrees add up to 0. If units counted as irreducible, every factorization could be padded with as many of them as we like, just as (1, 2, 2, 3, 5) would pad the factorization of 60 if 1 were prime. The clause \deg p \ge 1 plays the part of the integer condition p \ge 2. For polynomials of degree 2 and 3, irreducibility can be decided by looking for roots. [Irreducibility in Low Degree] Let F be a field and p \in F[x]. 1. If \deg p \ge 2 and p has a root in F, then p is reducible over F. 2. If \deg p \in \{2, 3\}, then p is irreducible over F if and only if p has no root in F. (a) Let c \in F be a root of p. By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b), p = (x - c)q for some q \in F[x]. Then \deg q = \deg p - 1 \ge 1 by @thm-degree-of-product (b), and \deg(x - c) = 1, so neither factor is a constant and p is reducible. (b) (\Rightarrow) is (a), read contrapositively. (\Leftarrow) Suppose p is reducible, so p = gh with \deg g, \deg h \ge 1 and \deg g + \deg h = \deg p \in \{2, 3\}. Two natural numbers, each at least 1, with sum 2 or 3: one of them is 1. So p has a factor of degree 1, and @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (c) gives a root of p in F. For x^2 + 1 over 
Q: for every c \in 
Q, c^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), with 0^2 = 0), so c^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0 by (b) and (e) of the same proposition. There is no rational root, and (b) makes x^2 + 1 irreducible over 
Q. The same lines work in every ordered field, so x^2 + 1 is irreducible over 
R as well. “No root” does not mean “irreducible” in degree 4 and above. For c \in 
Q, c^4 = (c^2)^2 \ge 0, so c^4 + 4 \ge 4 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)): the polynomial x^4 + 4 has no rational root. Yet x^4 + 4 = (x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2) , as expanding the right side shows: the terms in x^3, x^2 and x cancel. Proposition @prp-irreducible-low-degree (b) is about degrees 2 and 3 only, where every splitting must contain a factor of degree 1; in degree 4 a splitting may be 2 + 2, with no factor of degree 1 and so no root. Is 2x^2 + 4 irreducible over 
Q? Is x^2 + 2 irreducible over 
F_3? Over 
Q, yes: 2x^2 + 4 = 2(x^2 + 2), and x^2 + 2 has no rational root (c^2 + 2 \ge 2 > 0, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (h)), so it is irreducible by @prp-irreducible-low-degree (b), and so is its associate 2x^2 + 4. The factor 2 is a constant, so 2 \cdot (x^2 + 2) is not a splitting into non-constants. Over 
F_3, no: 1^2 + 2 = 3 = 0, so 1 is a root, and indeed x^2 + 2 = x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) in 
F_3. Euclid’s lemma for polynomials The definition of an irreducible p speaks about the factors of p. Unique factorization needs a statement about the polynomials that p divides. As in 
Z, the bridge is the Bézout identity, and the move is the one of Section 2.2: multiply the Bézout identity. Euclid’s Lemma for Polynomials Let F be a field and f, g, h \in F[x]. If f \mid gh and \gcd(f, g) = 1, then f \mid h. Since \gcd(f, g) = 1, @cor-polynomial-coprime-iff-combination gives a, b \in F[x] with af + bg = 1. Multiplying by h, h = h(af + bg) = (ah)f + b(gh) . Now f \mid f and f \mid gh, so f divides the combination (ah)f + b(gh) (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)). Hence f \mid h. The hypothesis \gcd(f, g) = 1 is needed. In 
Q[x], x^2 \mid x \cdot x, but x^2 
mid x, since a divisor of a non-zero polynomial has degree at most its degree (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d)); here \gcd(x^2, x) = x. For an irreducible p, the coprimality comes almost free, exactly as it did for a prime number. [An Irreducible Dividing a Product] Let F be a field and p \in F[x] irreducible over F. 1. For every f \in F[x]: p \mid f or \gcd(p, f) = 1. 2. For all g, h \in F[x]: if p \mid gh, then p \mid g or p \mid h. 3. If (q_1, \dots, q_l) is a list of polynomials in F[x], with l \in 
N, and p \mid q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l, then l \ge 1 and p \mid q_j for some j \in \{1, \dots, l\}. 4. If p and q are monic and irreducible over F and p \mid q, then p = q. Here q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l, also written \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, is the product of a finite list in the commutative ring F[x], given by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product as @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a) reads it: the empty product is 1, and \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j =  igl(\prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j igr) q_{l+1}. For (a), the gcd of p and f is a monic divisor of p, and an irreducible p has only two kinds of divisors: constants and associates of itself. Part (b) is Euclid’s lemma in the coprime case of (a). For (c), peel the last factor off the product and apply (b); induction on the length does the rest. For (d), the cofactor of p in q must be a constant, and comparing leading coefficients makes it 1. (a) Since p 
e 0, the gcd d \coloneqq \gcd(p, f) is monic (@def-polynomial-gcd, @thm-polynomial-bezout (c)). It divides p: write p = du with u \in F[x]. As p is irreducible, d or u is a constant. If d is a constant, it is a monic constant, so d = 1. If u is a constant, then u 
e 0 (as p 
e 0) and d = u^{-1}p; since d \mid f, f = dk = p(u^{-1}k) for some k \in F[x], so p \mid f. (b) Let p \mid gh. By (a), p \mid g or \gcd(p, g) = 1, and in the second case @thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma gives p \mid h. (c) By @fd1:ax-induction (on 
N = \omega, @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) we prove, for every l \in 
N, the statement P(l): “for every list (q_1, \dots, q_l) in F[x] with p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, we have l \ge 1 and p \mid q_j for some j \le l”. Base case P(0). The empty product is 1, and p 
mid 1: otherwise \deg p \le \deg 1 = 0 by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d), against \deg p \ge 1. So the hypothesis of P(0) never holds, and P(0) is true. Step. Assume P(l), and let p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j =  igl(\prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j igr) q_{l+1}. By (b), p divides the first factor or p \mid q_{l+1}. In the first case P(l) gives j \le l with p \mid q_j; in the second, take j = l + 1. Either way l + 1 \ge 1, and P(l + 1) holds. (d) Write q = pu with u \in F[x]. As q is irreducible, p or u is a constant, and p is not, since \deg p \ge 1. So u is a non-zero constant, and comparing leading coefficients (@thm-degree-of-product (b)) gives 1 = 1 \cdot u. Hence u = 1 and p = q. Part (b) fails for reducible polynomials: x^2 \mid x \cdot x with x^2 
mid x. Part (d) needs “monic”: x and 2x are irreducible over 
Q, and each divides the other. The same multiplication of a Bézout identity combines two coprime divisors. [Coprime Divisors of a Polynomial] Let F be a field and m, n, h \in F[x] with m \mid h, n \mid h and \gcd(m, n) = 1. Then mn \mid h. Write h = mk with k \in F[x]. Then n \mid mk, and \gcd(n, m) = \gcd(m, n) = 1, since the clauses of @def-polynomial-gcd do not depend on the order of the two polynomials. By @thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma, n \mid k; say k = nt. Then h = m(nt) = (mn)t, so mn \mid h. Without coprimality the conclusion fails: x \mid x twice over, yet x \cdot x = x^2 
mid x. In 
F_2[x], the polynomial x^2 + 1 divides (x + 1)(x + 1), but divides neither factor. Does this contradict @cor-irreducible-divides-product (b)? No. In 
F_2[x], (x + 1)(x + 1) = x^2 + 1, so x^2 + 1 is reducible over 
F_2, and the corollary says nothing about it. (It divides neither factor because each factor has degree 1 < 2, @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d).) Factors that cannot be split further The existence half of unique factorization needs a supply of irreducibles: every polynomial of positive degree must have an irreducible factor. In 
Z, the least divisor at least 2 was prime (@lem-least-divisor-prime). For polynomials, size becomes degree, and the “least divisor” becomes a monic divisor of least positive degree. [An Irreducible Factor Exists] Let F be a field and f \in F[x] with \deg f \ge 1. Then f has a monic irreducible divisor in F[x]. Among the monic divisors of positive degree, take one of least degree. A splitting of it into two non-constants would produce a monic divisor of smaller positive degree. Let c be the leading coefficient of f, and let D \coloneqq \{ \deg d : d \in F[x] 	ext{ monic}, \ \deg d \ge 1, \ d \mid f \} \subseteq 
N . The monic associate c^{-1}f has degree \deg f \ge 1 and divides f = c \cdot (c^{-1}f), so D is non-empty. By @fd2:thm-well-ordering (on 
N = \omega it is @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering), D has a least element n_0; let p be a monic divisor of f of degree n_0. Then \deg p = n_0 \ge 1. Suppose p = gh with \deg g \ge 1 and \deg h \ge 1. Then \deg g = n_0 - \deg h < n_0 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)). Let g_1 be the monic associate of g, so g = \operatorname{lc}(g)\, g_1 and \deg g_1 = \deg g. Then g_1 \mid g, g \mid p and p \mid f, so g_1 \mid f (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b)), and \deg g_1 \in D is smaller than n_0, against the choice of n_0. So every factorization p = gh has a constant factor, and p is irreducible. This is @lem-least-divisor-prime with degree in place of size; the twin is compared with, not used. Unique factorization Two facts about products of lists. The proof below handles lists of polynomials, and it uses two facts about their products, both proved by induction on the length from the recursion of the product. Let (q_1, \dots, q_l) be a list in F[x], with l \in 
N. 1. If every q_j is non-zero, then \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j 
e 0, and its degree is \sum_{j=1}^{l} \deg q_j. If every q_j is monic, so is the product. 2. If l \ge 1 and j \in \{1, \dots, l\}, let (q'_1, \dots, q'_{l-1}) be the list with the entry j removed: q'_t \coloneqq q_t for t < j and q'_t \coloneqq q_{t+1} for j \le t \le l - 1. Then \prod_{t=1}^{l} q_t =  igl(\prod_{t=1}^{l-1} q'_t igr) q_j. In particular every entry of a list divides its product. The names (L1), (L2) are used throughout this chapter. (L1). Induction on l. For l = 0 the product is 1, which is monic of degree 0, the empty sum. The failing line is (3). @prp-irreducible-low-degree (b) is stated for polynomials of degree 2 or 3, and x^4 + 1 has degree 4: the line applies a result outside its hypotheses, a “fact” that is not available, entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A counterexample to the step: x^4 + 4 has no rational root and is reducible (the warning after @prp-irreducible-low-degree). Repair. Suppose x^4 + 1 = gh with \deg g, \deg h \ge 1. The leading coefficients multiply to 1, so replacing g, h by their monic associates we may take both monic. The degrees add up to 4. If one of them is 1, that factor has a root in 
Q (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (c)), against lines (1)–(2). So both have degree 2: g = x^2 + ax + b, h = x^2 + cx + d with a, b, c, d \in 
Q. Comparing coefficients in (x^2 + ax + b)(x^2 + cx + d) = x^4 + (a + c)x^3 + (b + d + ac)x^2 + (ad + bc)x + bd with x^4 + 1 gives c = -a, b + d - a^2 = 0, a(d - b) = 0 and bd = 1. Since 
Q has no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)), a = 0 or d = b. - If a = 0: d = -b and -b^2 = 1, impossible since b^2 \ge 0 > -1 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). - If d = b: b^2 = 1, so b = \pm 1 (@cor-field-squares-equal), and a^2 = 2b = \pm 2. Now a^2 = 2 is impossible by @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two, and a^2 = -2 < 0 is impossible since squares are non-negative. So no splitting exists, and x^4 + 1 is irreducible over 
Q. [C3: Infinitely many irreducibles] 1. Let F be a field. Prove that no finite list contains every monic irreducible polynomial of F[x]: for every list (p_1, \dots, p_k) of monic irreducibles, k \in 
N, some monic irreducible is not an entry of it. 2. Let p be prime. Prove that there are exactly p^n monic polynomials of degree n in 
F_p[x], for each n \in 
N, and deduce that 
F_p[x] has monic irreducibles of arbitrarily large degree. [Hint 1] For (a), copy the integer argument: consider p_1 \cdots p_k + 1. For (b), a monic polynomial of degree n is determined by its n lower coefficients. [Hint 2] For (a): by (L1) the product has degree at least 1 when k \ge 1, so N \coloneqq p_1 \cdots p_k + 1 has a monic irreducible factor (@lem-polynomial-irreducible-factor). (a) If k = 0, the polynomial x is monic and irreducible and not an entry. Let k \ge 1 and P \coloneqq p_1 \cdots p_k. By (L1), P is monic of degree \sum_i \deg p_i \ge 1. Then N \coloneqq P + 1 has \deg N = \deg P \ge 1 (@thm-degree-of-sum, the degrees of P and 1 differ), so N has a monic irreducible divisor q (@lem-polynomial-irreducible-factor). If q = p_i for some i, then q \mid P by (L2), and q \mid N - P = 1 (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)), so \deg q \le 0 (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d)), against \deg q \ge 1. So q is a monic irreducible that is not an entry of the list. (b) A monic polynomial of degree n has n lower coefficients a_0, \dots, a_{n-1} \in 
F_p, and by @def-polynomial (equality coefficientwise) the map sending it to (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}) is a bijection onto the set T_n of such tuples; its inverse puts 1 in position n and zeros above. We show \card{T_n} = p^n by @fd1:ax-induction on n. T_0 has one element, the empty tuple, and p^0 = 1. The tuples of length n + 1 split by their last entry into p pairwise disjoint sets, one for each element of 
F_p, which has p elements (@def-field-fp); each is in bijection with T_n (drop the last entry). Applying @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count p - 1 times (an induction on the number of pieces), \card{T_{n+1}} = p \cdot p^n = p^{n+1}. So for each M \in 
N, the monic polynomials of degree at most M form a finite set: a union of the finitely many finite sets for n = 0, \dots, M, pairwise disjoint, again by @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count. Suppose every monic irreducible of 
F_p[x] had degree at most M. Then they would form a subset of a finite set, hence a finite set (@fd2:prp-subset-finite), and a bijection \{1, \dots, k\} 	o that set (@fd2:def-finite) would be a list containing every monic irreducible, against (a). So for every M there is a monic irreducible of degree greater than M. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) builds a polynomial N of degree \ge 1 that is 1 more than a multiple of p_1 \cdots p_k (e.g. p_1 \cdots p_k + 1, or x \, p_1 \cdots p_k + 1), and shows \deg N \ge 1 for every k, k = 0 included (or treats k = 0 separately). - 3: (a) takes a monic irreducible factor q of N and shows q is no p_i, since it would divide 1. - 3: (b) counts the monic polynomials of degree n through their coefficient tuples, with an induction or a cited counting result. - 2: (b) concludes by contradiction with (a): a bound on the degrees would make the irreducibles a finite set, hence a list. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that N itself is irreducible; taking “the product of all monic irreducibles” without a finite list. [C4: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple] Let f, g \in F[x] be monic, d \coloneqq \gcd(f, g), and write f = d f_1, g = d g_1. 1. Prove that \gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1. 2. Prove that L \coloneqq d f_1 g_1 is a monic common multiple of f and g that divides every common multiple of f and g, and that d \cdot L = fg. 3. In 
Q[x], let f = g = 2x (not monic). The gcd is x, and the monic common multiple dividing every common multiple is x. Show that \gcd(f, g) \cdot x 
e fg. (a) Since f 
e 0, d is monic, so d 
e 0. By @thm-polynomial-bezout (d), d = af + bg for some a, b \in F[x], so d \cdot 1 = d(af_1 + bg_1). Canceling d (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (b)), af_1 + bg_1 = 1, and \gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1 by @cor-polynomial-coprime-iff-combination. (b) Comparing leading coefficients in f = d f_1 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)) gives \operatorname{lc}(f_1) = 1; likewise g_1 is monic, so L is monic (L1). It is a common multiple: L = f g_1 = g f_1. Let h be a common multiple, h = fk = g m with k, m \in F[x]. Then d f_1 k = d g_1 m, and canceling d, f_1 k = g_1 m. So g_1 \mid f_1 k, and \gcd(g_1, f_1) = 1 by (a), hence g_1 \mid k by @thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma; say k = g_1 t. Then h = d f_1 g_1 t = L t, and L \mid h. Finally d \cdot L = (d f_1)(d g_1) = fg. (c) \gcd(2x, 2x) = x by @def-polynomial-gcd: x is monic and divides 2x, and every common divisor h of 2x and 2x divides 2^{-1}(2x) = x (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b)). Next, x is monic and a common multiple of f = g = 2x, since 2^{-1}(2x) = x. It divides every common multiple h: x \mid 2x and 2x \mid h, so x \mid h by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b). Any other monic L' with these two properties satisfies x \mid L' and L' \mid x, so L' = x by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f). But x \cdot x = x^2 
e 4x^2 = fg, since 1 
e 4 in 
Q. The identity of (b) needs f and g monic. For non-zero f, g, the monic associates \operatorname{lc}(f)^{-1} f and \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1} g have the same common divisors and the same common multiples as f and g, since each divides the other; so (b) applied to them gives d \cdot L = \operatorname{lc}(f)^{-1} \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1} fg.

title: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content:
Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative Over 
Q, the polynomial x^4 - 2x^3 + 2x - 1 vanishes at 1 and at -1, and nowhere else. Yet it has degree 4, and 1 behaves like three roots at once: x^4 - 2x^3 + 2x - 1 = (x - 1)^3(x + 1). This section counts roots properly. It proves that a non-zero polynomial of degree n has at most n roots, that a polynomial over an infinite field is determined by its values, and what it means for a root to be repeated; then it shows how to see a repeated root without factoring, through the formal derivative of Section 6.5. Here the integers have no twin. Section 7.3 followed Section 2.2 step by step, but an integer cannot be evaluated at a point. The main new tool is one fact from Section 7.1, the factor theorem (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor): c is a root of f if and only if x - c \mid f. Throughout, F is a field. Counting roots A root of f gives a factor of degree 1. Several distinct roots give several factors, and degrees add, so there cannot be too many of them. Counting Roots Let F be a field, f \in F[x], k \ge 1, and let c_1, \dots, c_k \in F be distinct roots of f. Then (x - c_1)(x - c_2) \cdots (x - c_k) \mid f . If f 
e 0, then k \le \deg f. In particular, a non-zero polynomial of degree n has at most n distinct roots in F. Peel the roots off one at a time. If f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_{k-1}) \, h, then the next root c_k must be a root of h: at c_k the product of the factors c_k - c_i is non-zero, because the roots are distinct and a field has no zero divisors. Then the factor theorem splits x - c_k off h. Counting degrees at the end gives k \le \deg f. For k \ge 1 let P_k \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{k} (x - c_i), the product of a list in F[x] (the recursion of Section 7.3, after @cor-irreducible-divides-product). We prove “P_k \mid f for all distinct roots c_1, \dots, c_k of f” by @fd1:ax-induction on k \ge 1 (on \omega, @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)). For k = 1, P_1 = x - c_1, and x - c_1 \mid f by @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b). Suppose the claim holds for k, and let c_1, \dots, c_{k+1} be distinct roots of f. By the claim for c_1, \dots, c_k, f = P_k h for some h \in F[x]. Evaluating at c_{k+1} (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations, applied factor by factor along the recursion), 0 = f(c_{k+1}) = (c_{k+1} - c_1)(c_{k+1} - c_2) \cdots (c_{k+1} - c_k) \, h(c_{k+1}) . Each c_{k+1} - c_i with i \le k is non-zero, since the roots are distinct, and a product of non-zero elements of a field is non-zero (@thm-field-basic-properties (g), by induction on the number of factors). So h(c_{k+1}) = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f). By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b), h = (x - c_{k+1}) h_1 for some h_1 \in F[x], and by the recursion f = P_k (x - c_{k+1}) h_1 = P_{k+1} h_1 . So P_{k+1} \mid f. Now let f 
e 0 and write f = P_k h_1. Then h_1 
e 0, P_k is monic of degree k by (L1) of Section 7.3, and \deg f = k + \deg h_1 \ge k by @thm-degree-of-product (b). Both hypotheses have a job: “distinct” in the factors c_{k+1} - c_i 
e 0, and “field” in the step “a product of non-zero elements is non-zero”. Without “distinct”: 1, 1 is a list of two roots of x - 1, but (x - 1)^2 
mid x - 1, by degrees (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d)). Without “field”: over the ring 
Z/8
Z, which has zero divisors, the polynomial x^2 - 1 of degree 2 has the four roots 1, 3, 5, 7, since 3^2 - 1 = 8, 5^2 - 1 = 24 and 7^2 - 1 = 48 are multiples of 8; there (3 - 1)(3 + 1) = 8 = 0 with both factors non-zero. Can a polynomial over 
Q of degree 3 vanish at 1, 2, 3 and 4? Can a polynomial of degree at most 3? Not one of degree 3: it is non-zero, so it has at most 3 distinct roots (@thm-polynomial-root-count). A polynomial of degree at most 3 can, but only the zero polynomial, whose degree is -\infty \le 3. Values determine the polynomial Section 6.4 insisted that a polynomial is not a function: over 
F_2, x^2 + x and 0 have the same values (@exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2). Its warning promised that over a field such as 
Q the values do determine the polynomial. Counting roots pays that promise. [Polynomials Determined by Values] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. 1. Let n \in 
N. If \deg f \le n, \deg g \le n, and f(c_i) = g(c_i) for n + 1 distinct elements c_0, \dots, c_n \in F, then f = g. 2. If F is infinite and f(c) = g(c) for every c \in F, then f = g. Two polynomials that agree at a point differ by a polynomial with a root there. If they agree at more points than their degree allows, the difference has too many roots, so it is 0. An infinite field has as many points as we need. (a) By @thm-degree-of-sum, \deg(f - g) \le \max(\deg f, \deg g) \le n (the degree of -g is that of g). By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, (f - g)(c_i) = f(c_i) - g(c_i) = 0, so c_0, \dots, c_n are n + 1 distinct roots of f - g. If f - g 
e 0, @thm-polynomial-root-count gives n + 1 \le \deg(f - g) \le n, which is false. So f - g = 0. (b) We first find enough distinct elements. An infinite set S contains, for every m \in 
N, a list of m distinct elements: an injective function \{1, \dots, m\} 	o S. By @fd1:ax-induction on m. For m = 0 the empty function works. Suppose s_1, \dots, s_m are distinct elements of S. The set A \coloneqq \{s_1, \dots, s_m\} has m elements, through the bijection i \mapsto s_i, so it is finite (@fd2:def-finite). Since S is infinite (@fd2:def-infinite), A 
e S, and as A \subseteq S, there is s \in S with s 
otin A. Then s_1, \dots, s_m, s are m + 1 distinct elements of S. The claim is proved by induction on a statement of the form “there exists a list”, and each step takes one element from a non-empty set, once; no sequence of choices is made, so no axiom of choice is used. Now let n \coloneqq \max(\deg f, \deg g, 0) \in 
N. The claim with S = F and m = n + 1 gives n + 1 distinct elements of F, at which f and g agree, and (a) gives f = g. Over 
Q, 
R and 
C, which are infinite, equality of polynomials and equality of polynomial functions are therefore the same thing. Two polynomials with integer coefficients that agree at every integer are equal too: read them in 
Q[x], and apply (a) at n + 1 distinct integers. Part (a) says more, and it says it over every field: n + 1 values fix a polynomial of degree at most n. A line is fixed by two points, a parabola by three. Over a finite field, (b) fails. For a prime p, every c \in 
F_p satisfies c^p = c (@thm-fermat-little (a)), so the polynomial x^p - x, which is not 0 (its coefficient of x^p is 1), vanishes at every element of 
F_p. For p = 2: 0^2 - 0 = 0 and 1^2 - 1 = 0, which is @exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2. For p = 3: the values at 0, 1, 2 are 0, 0 and 8 - 2 = 6 = 0. There is no conflict with (a): a polynomial of degree p needs p + 1 points, and 
F_p has only p. [Polynomial Functions over a Finite Field] (a) Show that x^3 + 2x and 0 have the same values on 
F_3, and factor x^3 + 2x in 
F_3[x]. (b) Let p be prime. Show that, in 
F_p[x], x^p - x = \prod_{c=0}^{p-1} (x - c) = x(x - 1)(x - 2) \cdots (x - (p - 1)) . (a) In 
F_3, 2 = -1, so x^3 + 2x = x^3 - x. Its values at 0, 1, 2 are 0, 1 - 1 = 0 and 8 - 2 = 6 = 0: the same as those of 0, although x^3 - x 
e 0. So 0, 1, 2 are three distinct roots, and by @thm-polynomial-root-count, x(x - 1)(x - 2) \mid x^3 - x. Both are monic of degree 3, so the cofactor has degree 0 and, comparing leading coefficients, is 1: x^3 + 2x = x(x - 1)(x - 2) \quad 	ext{in } 
F_3[x] . Expanding confirms it: x(x - 1)(x - 2) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x = x^3 + 2x, since 3 = 0. (b) The elements 0, 1, \dots, p - 1 of 
F_p are distinct (@def-field-fp), and each is a root of x^p - x by the warning. By @thm-polynomial-root-count, the product P of the x - c divides x^p - x; P is monic of degree p by (L1) of Section 7.3, and so is x^p - x, because p \ge 2 > 1. As in (a), x^p - x = P \cdot u with \deg u = 0, and comparing leading coefficients gives u = 1. Re-centering at a point To study a polynomial near a point c, it helps to write it in powers of x - c instead of powers of x. For x^2 and c = 1: x^2 = 1 + 2(x - 1) + (x - 1)^2. Such an expansion always exists and is unique, and it is found by dividing by x - c repeatedly. [Expansion in Powers of x - c] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] with \deg f = n \ge 0, and c \in F. 1. There are unique b_0, b_1, \dots, b_n \in F with f = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j (x - c)^j . 2. b_0 = f(c), and b_n is the leading coefficient of f. 3. For every h \in F, f(c + h) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j h^j. By @thm-degree-of-product (b) and induction on j, each (x - c)^j is monic of degree j; so a sum \sum_{j=0}^{J} d_j (x - c)^j with d_J 
e 0 has degree exactly J: the term d_J (x - c)^J has degree J, every other non-zero term has smaller degree, and @thm-degree-of-sum (with equality when the degrees differ, applied one term at a time) does the rest. The uniqueness half of (a) below uses this fact; part (b) uses its first clause, that (x - c)^n is monic of degree n. Divide f by x - c: the remainder is the constant f(c), and the quotient has degree one less. Expand the quotient the same way, by induction, and multiply back by x - c. For uniqueness, compare degrees: a non-trivial combination of the powers (x - c)^j has the degree of its highest term, so it is not 0. (a), existence. By @fd1:ax-induction on n, for every f of degree n. If n = 0, f is a non-zero constant b_0 = b_0 (x - c)^0. Let \deg f = n + 1. By @thm-polynomial-division-remainder and @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a), f = (x - c) q + f(c) with q \in F[x]. Since \deg f \ge 1 > \deg f(c), @thm-degree-of-sum gives \deg((x - c) q) = n + 1, so q 
e 0 and \deg q = n (@thm-degree-of-product (b)). By the induction hypothesis, q = \sum_{j=0}^{n} d_j (x - c)^j. Then f = f(c) + \sum_{j=0}^{n} d_j (x - c)^{j+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{n+1} b_j (x - c)^j , with b_0 \coloneqq f(c) and b_{j+1} \coloneqq d_j, by the distributive law for finite sums (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b), (Σ2)) and a shift of the summation index. (a), uniqueness. If \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j (x - c)^j = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b'_j (x - c)^j, then \sum_{j=0}^{n} (b_j - b'_j)(x - c)^j = 0 (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b), (Σ1), (Σ4)). If some b_j - b'_j were non-zero, the largest such j would be the degree of this sum, by the fact before the Idea; but the sum is 0. So b_j = b'_j for every j. (b) Evaluate at c (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations): (c - c)^0 = 1 and (c - c)^j = 0 for j \ge 1, so f(c) = b_0. The terms with j < n have degree less than n, and b_n (x - c)^n has coefficient b_n at x^n, since (x - c)^n is monic of degree n; so the coefficient of x^n in f, its leading coefficient, is b_n. (c) Evaluate at c + h: (x - c) takes the value h there, and @thm-evaluation-respects-operations carries sums, products and powers through. The coefficients b_j are computed by the existence proof: divide by x - c, keep the remainder as b_0, divide the quotient by x - c, keep the remainder as b_1, and so on until the quotient is a constant, which is b_n. The next example runs this. Expand x^3 in powers of x - 1 over 
Q. x^3 = (x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1) + 1, x^2 + x + 1 = (x - 1)(x + 2) + 3, x + 2 = (x - 1) \cdot 1 + 3. So b_0 = 1, b_1 = 3, b_2 = 3, b_3 = 1: x^3 = 1 + 3(x - 1) + 3(x - 1)^2 + (x - 1)^3 . Multiplicity The hook’s polynomial (x - 1)^3(x + 1) is divisible by (x - 1)^3 and not by (x - 1)^4. That exponent is what “three roots at once” means. The multiplicity of a root counts how many factors x - c can be split off. [Multiplicity of a Root] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] non-zero, and c \in F. The multiplicity of c in f, written \operatorname{mult}_c(f), is the largest m \in 
N with (x - c)^m \mid f. The root c is simple if \operatorname{mult}_c(f) = 1 and multiple if \operatorname{mult}_c(f) \ge 2. In words: keep dividing f by x - c while the division comes out exact; the number of exact divisions is the multiplicity. Well defined. The set M \coloneqq \{ m \in 
N : (x - c)^m \mid f \} contains 0, since (x - c)^0 = 1 divides f. For m \in M, m = \deg (x - c)^m \le \deg f (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d)), so M is bounded above, and it has a greatest element (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element, with 
N \subseteq 
Z). By the factor theorem (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b)), 1 \in M exactly when f(c) = 0, so \operatorname{mult}_c(f) = 0 \iff f(c) 
e 0 . For the direction from right to left: if f(c) 
e 0, no m \ge 1 lies in M either, since (x - c)^m = (x - c)^{m-1} (x - c) (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)), so (x - c)^m \mid f would give x - c \mid f (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b)), that is, 1 \in M. Hence M = \{0\}. A multiplicity 0 means “not a root”. The zero polynomial is excluded because every power of x - c divides it, and M would have no greatest element. Examples. In 
Q[x], \operatorname{mult}_1((x - 1)^2) = 2: (x - 1)^2 divides itself, and (x - 1)^3 does not, by degrees. \operatorname{mult}_0(x^2 + x) = 1: the value at 0 is 0, and x^2 does not divide x^2 + x, since division with remainder gives x^2 + x = x^2 \cdot 1 + x with remainder x 
e 0. And \operatorname{mult}_2(x^2 + x) = 0, since the value at 2 is 6 
e 0. The definition asks for a largest exponent, which is awkward to check directly. The next lemma replaces it by a single evaluation. [Multiplicity through the Cofactor] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] non-zero, c \in F and m \in 
N. 1. \operatorname{mult}_c(f) = m if and only if f = (x - c)^m g for some g \in F[x] with g(c) 
e 0. 2. Such a g is unique. 3. If f = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j (x - c)^j is the expansion of @thm-polynomial-taylor-shift, then \operatorname{mult}_c(f) is the least j with b_j 
e 0. If the cofactor g vanished at c, one more factor x - c would split off; if one more factor split off, cancellation would make g vanish at c. For (c), the expansion displays the cofactor directly. (a) (\Rightarrow) Let m = \operatorname{mult}_c(f), so f = (x - c)^m g for some g. If g(c) = 0, then g = (x - c) g_1 (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b)) and (x - c)^{m+1} \mid f, against the maximality of m. So g(c) 
e 0. (\Leftarrow) Let f = (x - c)^m g with g(c) 
e 0; then m \in M. Suppose some m' > m were in M. Then (x - c)^{m+1} divides (x - c)^{m'}, hence f: say f = (x - c)^{m+1} k = (x - c)^m  igl((x - c) k igr). Canceling (x - c)^m 
e 0 (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (b)) gives g = (x - c) k, so g(c) = 0, a contradiction. So m is the largest element of M. (b) If (x - c)^m g = (x - c)^m g', cancel (x - c)^m 
e 0. (c) The coefficient b_n is the leading coefficient of f, so it is non-zero, and the set of j with b_j 
e 0 has a least element J (@fd2:thm-well-ordering). The terms with j < J vanish, so, taking the factor (x - c)^J out of the remaining terms, f = (x - c)^J g , \qquad g \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{n-J} b_{J+i} (x - c)^i . Evaluating at c, as in @thm-polynomial-taylor-shift (b), g(c) = b_J 
e 0. By (a), \operatorname{mult}_c(f) = J. The factor g is the cofactor of c in f. Multiplicities of a product add, because cofactors multiply. [Multiplicity of a Product] Let F be a field, f, g \in F[x] non-zero and c \in F. Then \operatorname{mult}_c(fg) = \operatorname{mult}_c(f) + \operatorname{mult}_c(g). Let m \coloneqq \operatorname{mult}_c(f) and n \coloneqq \operatorname{mult}_c(g). By @lem-polynomial-multiplicity-cofactor (a), f = (x - c)^m u and g = (x - c)^n v with u(c) 
e 0 and v(c)

If \operatorname{mult}_c(f) = m \ge 1 and m \cdot 1

F_p (@exm-characteristics: \operatorname{char}

By @thm-formal-derivative-rules, f' = (2 \cdot 1) p p' g + p^2 g' = p  igl( (2 \cdot 1) p' g + p g'  igr) , so p divides both f and f', and hence divides \gcd(f, f') (@thm-polynomial-bezout (b); f

An admissible order is (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii): We use induction on k; for k = 1, x - c_1 \mid f by the factor theorem. Assume the claim for every list of k - 1 distinct roots, and let c_1, \dots, c_k be distinct roots of f. Write f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_{k-1}) h. Evaluate at c_k: 0 = (c_k - c_1) \cdots (c_k - c_{k-1}) h(c_k). Each c_k - c_i, i < k, is non-zero, since the roots are distinct. A product of non-zero elements of a field is non-zero, so h(c_k) = 0. e 0 says nothing about c_k - c_i. The distractor (vi′) skips the cancellation: f(c_k) = 0 only says that the product in (iv) is 0, and passing to h(c_k) = 0 needs both (v) and the absence of zero divisors. Over a ring with zero divisors the step fails: over

F_p[x]. Prove that f(c) = g(c) for every c \in

F_5 as x^7 + x. (\Leftarrow) If f - g = (x^p - x) h, then for c \in 
F_p, f(c) - g(c) = (c^p - c) h(c) = 0, since c^p = c (@thm-fermat-little (a)). (\Rightarrow) If f and g agree on 
F_p, then 0, 1, \dots, p - 1 are p distinct roots of f - g, so \prod_{c=0}^{p-1} (x - c) \mid f - g by @thm-polynomial-root-count, and that product is x^p - x (@exm-polynomial-function-finite-field (b)). F_5, and its degree is 3 < 5. C. [Hint 2] By induction on j,  igl((x - c)^i igr)^{(j)} =  igl( (i(i - 1) \cdots (i - j + 1)) \cdot 1  igr) (x - c)^{i-j} for j \le i, and 0 for j > i. The derivatives of the powers. If j + 1 = i + 1, the i-th derivative is the constant (i! \cdot 1), whose derivative is 0; and the derivative of 0 is 0 for larger j. The coefficients. Since the derivative is additive with (af)' = af' for constants a (@thm-formal-derivative-rules (a)), so is the j-th derivative (induction on j), and f^{(j)} = \sum_{i=j}^{n} b_i  igl( (i \cdots (i - j + 1)) \cdot 1  igr) (x - c)^{i-j} . At x = c, every term with i > j vanishes, and the term i = j is b_j (j! \cdot 1). So f^{(j)}(c) = (j! \cdot 1) b_j. In characteristic 0, j! \cdot 1 
e 0 (@def-characteristic, as j! \ge 1), and dividing gives the formula. Check. For f = x^3 - 2x + 5, f'' = 6x and f''(1) = 6, so b_2 = 6/2 = 3, as in Exercise B2 (a). [C2: Repeated factors through the gcd] 1. Using only \gcd(f, f'), decide whether f \coloneqq x^4 - 2x^3 + 2x - 1 \in 
Q[x] has a repeated irreducible factor. 2. Over 
F_2, let f \coloneqq x^4 + 1. Compute f' and \gcd(f, f'), and explain why part (b) of @cor-polynomial-squarefree-gcd does not apply. (a) f' = 4x^3 - 6x^2 + 2. The Euclidean algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-polynomials):  egin{aligned} f &= \Bigl( 	frac{1}{4} x - 	frac{1}{8} \Bigr) f' - 	frac{3}{4} (x^2 - 2x + 1) , \ f' &= \Bigl( -	frac{3}{4} (x^2 - 2x + 1) \Bigr) \Bigl( -	frac{8}{3} (2x + 1) \Bigr) + 0 . \end{aligned} The last non-zero remainder is -	frac{3}{4}(x^2 - 2x + 1), so \gcd(f, f') = x^2 - 2x + 1

Q has characteristic 0, @cor-polynomial-squarefree-gcd (b) says that f has a repeated irreducible factor. (Indeed f = (x - 1)^3 (x + 1), @exm-polynomial-multiplicity-run.) (b) f' = (4 \cdot 1) x^3 = 0 in 
F_2. Then \langle f, 0 angle = \langle f angle, whose monic generator is f itself, so \gcd(f, f') = f = x^4 + 1 
e 1 (@thm-polynomial-bezout (c)). Part (b) of the corollary assumes characteristic 0, and

e 0, 2 \cdot 1 = 0). Its proof uses that hypothesis at \deg p' = \deg p - 1, which fails in characteristic 2: (x^2 + 1)' = 0. Here the conclusion happens to hold anyway, since x^4 + 1 = (x + 1)^4 in

title: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content:
Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem Section 7.4 proved a uniqueness statement: two polynomials of degree at most n that agree at n + 1 distinct points are equal (@thm-polynomial-identity-from-values (a)). It said nothing about existence. Is there, for instance, a quadratic through the points (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 7)? This section builds one by a formula. It then reads the same question as three congruences. By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a), “the value at c is y” says that f leaves the remainder y on division by x - c. So we look for f with f \equiv 1 \pmod{x} , \qquad f \equiv 3 \pmod{x - 1} , \qquad f \equiv 7 \pmod{x - 2} . Three congruences to coprime moduli: that is the Chinese remainder theorem of Chapter 2 (@thm-chinese-remainder-two), with polynomials in place of integers. Polynomials through given points The points at which values are prescribed are called nodes. Suppose the nodes are c_0, \dots, c_n \in F and the values y_0, \dots, y_n \in F. Fitting all the values at once is hard. Fitting one value while ignoring the others would be easy if we had, for each node c_i, a polynomial that is 1 at c_i and 0 at every other node: then y_0 times the first, plus y_1 times the second, and so on, has every value right. Its value at c_i is the product of the numbers c_i - c_j, and dividing by that product makes the value 1. Each Lagrange polynomial is 1 at its own node and 0 at all the others. That is the existence of an interpolating polynomial and its uniqueness at once, without the formula for \ell_i; identifying it with \sum_i y_i \ell_i still needs @thm-polynomial-interpolation (a). (c) The route in (a) is shorter in what it needs: evaluation and the root count. The route in (b) passes through @lem-polynomial-coprime-to-product and Bézout identities for the moduli. The Lagrange route is shorter because linear moduli are special: “divisible by x - c” can be tested by evaluating at c, which turns every congruence into an equation in F. For moduli of higher degree, evaluation at a single point is no longer enough. For (x - c)^2, @exm-hermite-by-chinese-remainder (a) needs the derivative as well as the value. For x^2 + 1 over 
Q in @exm-polynomial-chinese-remainder-run, the modulus has no root in 
Q, so no evaluation in 
Q detects divisibility at all. The Chinese remainder route handles every modulus in the same way. [C2: Every function on a prime field is a polynomial] Let p be a prime. Prove that every function \varphi \colon 
F_p 	o 
F_p is the polynomial function c \mapsto f(c) of exactly one f \in 
F_p[x] with \deg f < p. The elements 0, 1, \dots, p - 1 of 
F_p are p distinct elements (@def-field-fp), and there are no others. Use them as nodes, c_i \coloneqq i for i = 0, \dots, p - 1, so n = p - 1. Existence. With y_i \coloneqq \varphi(i), @thm-polynomial-interpolation (b) gives f with \deg f \le p - 1 < p and f(i) = \varphi(i) for every i. Since the i are all the elements of 
F_p, the polynomial function of f is \varphi. Uniqueness. If g also has degree less than p and the function \varphi, then f and g have degree at most p - 1 and agree at the p distinct nodes, so f = g by @thm-polynomial-interpolation (c). So over 
F_p every function is a polynomial function, and the polynomials of degree less than p correspond one to one to the functions 
F_p 	o 
F_p. (As a count: both sets have p^p elements, p choices for each of p coefficients, or for each of p values.) Interpolation over 
F_p can use at most p nodes, since 
F_p has no more distinct elements. Polynomials of degree p or more are no longer determined by their functions: x^p and x have the same function by @thm-fermat-little (a), which is the warning of Section 7.4.

title: 7.6 The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
content:
The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra Over 
Q the polynomial x^2 - 2 has no root, and over 
R the polynomial x^2 + 1 has none. Chapter 3 announced that over 
C this stops: every non-constant complex polynomial has a root. This section proves it, and then reads off what it says about factoring complex and real polynomials. No argument from the field axioms alone can prove the theorem. The field 
Q(i) = \{ a + bi : a, b \in 
Q \} of @exm-subfields-gaussian satisfies every field axiom, and it contains an element i with i^2 = -1, just as 
C does. Yet x^2 - 2 has no root in it. If (a + bi)^2 = 2 with a, b \in 
Q, then comparing real and imaginary parts (@def-complex-numbers), a^2 - b^2 = 2 and 2ab = 0, so a = 0 or b = 0 (
Q has no zero divisors, @thm-field-basic-properties (f), and 2 
e 0). If b = 0, then a^2 = 2, which no rational satisfies (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two). If a = 0, then -b^2 = 2, impossible since -b^2 \le 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). So the proof must use a property of 
R that 
Q lacks. It is the supremum property of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). The plan has two halves. First, \abs{p} attains a smallest value on 
C (@thm-complex-polynomial-minimum). Second, at any point where p is not 0, some nearby point gives \abs{p} a smaller value (@lem-complex-polynomial-descent). So at a point where the smallest value is attained, p must be 0. The first half is where completeness is invoked directly (Steps 2 and 5); the second half uses it only indirectly, through square roots (see the remark after the minimum theorem). Throughout, p is a polynomial in 
C[x], and p(z) is its value at z \in 
C (@def-polynomial-evaluation). Inequalities are between real numbers; the modulus \abs{z} is a non-negative real (@def-conjugate-modulus). Two estimates All of them are from Chapter 3. For z, w \in 
C: \abs{z}^2 = (\operatorname{Re} z)^2 + (\operatorname{Im} z)^2 (@def-conjugate-modulus); \abs{\operatorname{Re} z} \le \abs{z}, \abs{\operatorname{Im} z} \le \abs{z} and \abs{z} \le \abs{\operatorname{Re} z} + \abs{\operatorname{Im} z} (@lem-real-part-at-most-modulus); \abs{zw} = \abs{z} \abs{w}, so \abs{z^j} = \abs{z}^j by induction on j, and \abs{z} = 0 only for z = 0 (@thm-conjugate-properties (d), (e)); \abs{z_1 + \dots + z_m} \le \abs{z_1} + \dots + \abs{z_m} and \abs{z} - \abs{w} \le \abs{z + w} (@cor-complex-triangle-variants (b), (c)). For a real number the modulus is the absolute value of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 (@prp-modulus-of-real), so the rules of @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field apply to it. Three facts about powers of non-negative reals are used as well, each by induction on the exponent with @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c): if 0 \le a \le b, then a^j \le b^j; if a \ge 1 and i \le j, then a^i \le a^j; if 0 < t \le 1 and i \le j, then t^j \le t^i. The first estimate says that \abs{p(z)} is large when \abs{z} is large, so the search for a smallest value can be confined to a bounded region. [Growth of a Complex Polynomial] Let p = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j x^j \in 
C[x] with n = \deg p \ge 1, so a_n 
e 0. Let A \coloneqq \abs{a_0} + \dots + \abs{a_{n-1}} , \qquad R \coloneqq \max\Bigl\{ 1,  rac{2A}{\abs{a_n}} \Bigr\} . Then for every z \in 
C with \abs{z} \ge R, \abs{p(z)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_n} \abs{z}^n \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_n} \abs{z} . In words: beyond the radius R, the top term outweighs all the others together, at least by half. Let \abs{z} \ge R. Then \abs{z} \ge 1, so \abs{z}^j \le \abs{z}^{n-1} for 0 \le j \le n - 1. Write p(z) = a_n z^n + w with w \coloneqq \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_j z^j (the sum recursion). By @cor-complex-triangle-variants (b) and @thm-conjugate-properties (d), \abs{w} \le \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \abs{a_j} \abs{z}^j \le A \abs{z}^{n-1} . By @cor-complex-triangle-variants (c), which is the reverse triangle inequality (a) with the second number negated, \abs{p(z)} \ge \abs{a_n} \abs{z}^n - \abs{w} \ge \abs{z}^{n-1}  igl( \abs{a_n} \abs{z} - A  igr). Since \abs{z} \ge 2A/\abs{a_n} and \abs{a_n} > 0, A \le 	frac12 \abs{a_n} \abs{z}, so \abs{a_n} \abs{z} - A \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_n} \abs{z}. Hence \abs{p(z)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_n} \abs{z}^n. Finally \abs{z}^n \ge \abs{z}, since \abs{z} \ge 1 and n \ge 1. The second estimate replaces continuity, which this volume does not have. It bounds how much p can change between two points of a bounded region, with an explicit constant. [A Lipschitz Bound for a Complex Polynomial] Let p = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j x^j \in 
C[x] and let M \in 
R with M \ge 0. Put L \coloneqq \sum_{j=1}^{n} j \abs{a_j} M^{j-1} \qquad (j \abs{a_j} 	ext{ the multiple } (j \cdot 1)\abs{a_j} 	ext{ in } 
R) . Then \abs{p(z) - p(w)} \le L \abs{z - w} for all z, w \in 
C with \abs{z} \le M and \abs{w} \le M. In words: on the disc of radius M, p moves at most L times as far as its argument. Let \abs{z}, \abs{w} \le M. Termwise (the sum rules (Σ1), (Σ2), (Σ4) of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers), p(z) - p(w) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_j (z^j - w^j), and the term j = 0 is 0. For j \ge 1, @lem-difference-of-powers gives z^j - w^j = (z - w) \sum_{i=0}^{j-1} z^i w^{j-1-i} . Each of the j terms of the sum has modulus \abs{z}^i \abs{w}^{j-1-i} \le M^i M^{j-1-i} = M^{j-1}. So \abs{z^j - w^j} \le j M^{j-1} \abs{z - w} by @cor-complex-triangle-variants (b), and summing over j with the same corollary, \abs{p(z) - p(w)} \le \sum_{j=1}^{n} \abs{a_j} \, j M^{j-1} \abs{z - w} = L \abs{z - w}. This is the only “continuity” the proof below needs, and it comes with a constant that can be computed. For p = x^2 + 1, compute A and R of @lem-complex-polynomial-growth, and the constant L of @lem-complex-polynomial-lipschitz for M = 4. Here a_0 = 1, a_1 = 0, a_2 = 1, n = 2. So A = \abs{1} + \abs{0} = 1 and R = \max\{1, 2 \cdot 1/1\} = 2. For M = 4, L = 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 4^0 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 4^1 = 8. (Check of the Lipschitz bound in one case: \abs{p(z) - p(w)} = \abs{z^2 - w^2} = \abs{z + w} \abs{z - w} \le 8 \abs{z - w} when \abs{z}, \abs{w} \le 4.) The smallest value of the modulus is attained We now look for a point where \abs{p} is smallest. The infimum of the values \abs{p(z)} exists by completeness; the work is to find a point at which it is attained. We trap such a point in smaller and smaller squares. For \sigma, 	au \in 
R and s \in 
R with s > 0, let S(\sigma, 	au, s) \coloneqq \{ z \in 
C : \sigma \le \operatorname{Re} z \le \sigma + s , \ 	au \le \operatorname{Im} z \le 	au + s \} , the closed square with lower-left corner \sigma + 	au i and side s. (In this section \sigma and 	au are real numbers. Chapter 5 uses the same letters for permutations, which do not appear here.) Each such square contains its corner, so it is non-empty. Its four quarters, in this fixed order, are  egin{aligned} &S(\sigma, 	au, s/2) , && S(\sigma + s/2, 	au, s/2) , \ &S(\sigma, 	au + s/2, s/2) , && S(\sigma + s/2, 	au + s/2, s/2) . \end{aligned} Each quarter lies in the square, and every point of the square lies in some quarter: \operatorname{Re} z \le \sigma + s/2 or \operatorname{Re} z \ge \sigma + s/2, and likewise for \operatorname{Im} z, since \le is a total order on 
R (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). [The Modulus of a Complex Polynomial Attains Its Minimum] For every p \in 
C[x] there is z^* \in 
C with \abs{p(z^*)} \le \abs{p(z)} for every z \in 
C. Confine the search to one big square S_0 by the growth lemma. The infimum m of \abs{p} over S_0 exists. Cut S_0 into four quarters: the infimum over S_0 is the least of the four infima, so some quarter has the same infimum m; keep the first such quarter, and repeat. We call this move keep the quarter that keeps the infimum. The squares shrink to a single point z^*, which completeness supplies as a supremum of corners. Near z^* every square still has points where \abs{p} is almost m, and the Lipschitz bound says \abs{p(z^*)} is almost the same; so \abs{p(z^*)} = m. This is the bisection of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5, now in the plane. Before reading on: why keep a quarter whose infimum equals the square’s, rather than a quarter containing a point where \abs{p} is smallest? If p is a constant a_0 (including 0), then p(z) = a_0 for every z, and z^* \coloneqq 0 works. Let n \coloneqq \deg p \ge 1, with leading coefficient a_n 
e 0, let R be as in @lem-complex-polynomial-growth, and let ho \coloneqq \max\Bigl\{ R,  rac{2\abs{p(0)}}{\abs{a_n}} \Bigr\} , so ho \ge 1. Step 1 (a square that suffices). Let S_0 \coloneqq S(-ho, -ho, 2ho). It contains 0. If z 
otin S_0, then \abs{\operatorname{Re} z} > ho or \abs{\operatorname{Im} z} > ho (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)), so \abs{z} > ho \ge R (@lem-real-part-at-most-modulus), and by @lem-complex-polynomial-growth, \abs{p(z)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_n} \abs{z} > 	frac12 \abs{a_n} ho \ge \abs{p(0)} . 	ag{1} Step 2 (the infimum; completeness, first use). For a square S, the set V(S) \coloneqq \{ \abs{p(z)} : z \in S \} \subseteq 
R is non-empty and bounded below by 0. So it has an infimum m(S) in 
R (@fd2:def-order-supremum); the fold after the proof derives this from the supremum property. Two consequences are used: m(S) \le \abs{p(z)} for every z \in S; and for every \varepsilon > 0 there is z \in S with \abs{p(z)} < m(S) + \varepsilon, since otherwise m(S) + \varepsilon would be a lower bound of V(S) larger than the greatest one. If S' \subseteq S, then m(S) is a lower bound of V(S') \subseteq V(S), so m(S) \le m(S'). Step 3 (a quarter with the same infimum). Let S be a square and Q_1, \dots, Q_4 its quarters. Each m(Q_i) \ge m(S) by Step 2. Let \mu be the least of the four numbers m(Q_i). Every z \in S lies in some Q_i, so \abs{p(z)} \ge m(Q_i) \ge \mu: \mu is a lower bound of V(S), hence \mu \le m(S). So \mu = m(S), and some quarter has m(Q_i) = m(S). Let q(S) be the first quarter, in the fixed order, with m(Q_i) = m(S). This is a rule: q is a function from squares to squares. Step 4 (the nested squares). Identify the square S(\sigma, 	au, s) with the triple (\sigma, 	au, s). By @fd2:thm-recursion (read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification), there is exactly one sequence of squares S_k = S(\sigma_k, 	au_k, s_k), k \in 
N, with S_0 as in Step 1 and S_{k+1} = q(S_k). By induction on k: - s_k = 2ho/2^k, the power 2^k taken in 
R (@fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field), since each quarter has half the side; - m(S_k) = m, where m \coloneqq m(S_0), by the choice of q; - \sigma_k \le \sigma_{k'} \le \sigma_k + s_k - s_{k'} and 	au_k \le 	au_{k'} \le 	au_k + s_k - s_{k'} for all k' \ge k, since the corner of a quarter is \sigma or \sigma + s/2 and its far edge \sigma + s/2 or \sigma + s. In particular S_{k'} \subseteq S_k \subseteq S_0. Step 5 (the common point; completeness, second use). The set \{ \sigma_k : k \in 
N \} is non-empty and bounded above by \sigma_0 + s_0 (Step 4 with k = 0). By @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field it has a supremum \sigma^* (@fd3:def-complete-ordered-field). Fix k. Then \sigma_k \le \sigma^*, and \sigma_k + s_k is an upper bound of the set: for k' \ge k, \sigma_{k'} \le \sigma_k + s_k by Step 4, and for k' < k, \sigma_{k'} \le \sigma_k by Step 4 with the roles of k and k' exchanged. So \sigma_k \le \sigma^* \le \sigma_k + s_k for every k. In the same way 	au^* \coloneqq \sup \{ 	au_k : k \in 
N \} satisfies 	au_k \le 	au^* \le 	au_k + s_k. Hence z^* \coloneqq \sigma^* + 	au^* i lies in every S_k. Step 6 (the value at the common point). For z, w \in S_k, \abs{\operatorname{Re}(z - w)} \le s_k and \abs{\operatorname{Im}(z - w)} \le s_k, so \abs{z - w} \le 2 s_k (@lem-real-part-at-most-modulus). Every point of S_0 has modulus at most ho + ho = 2ho, by the same lemma. Let L be the constant of @lem-complex-polynomial-lipschitz for M = 2ho. Let \varepsilon \in 
R with \varepsilon > 0. By @fd3:thm-constructed-reals-archimedean there is k \in 
N with k > 8ho L/\varepsilon; then 2^k \ge k + 1 > 8ho L/\varepsilon by @fd3:lem-power-two-bound, so 2 s_k L =  rac{4ho L}{2^k} <  rac{\varepsilon}{2} . 	ag{2} This k depends on \varepsilon (and on p, through ho and L). Since m(S_k) = m, Step 2 gives a point w \in S_k with \abs{p(w)} < m + \varepsilon/2 (ulename{\exists E}: the point w is used only inside this argument for this \varepsilon). Both z^* and w lie in S_k \subseteq S_0, so by the triangle inequality (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality), the Lipschitz bound and (2), \abs{p(z^*)} \le \abs{p(w)} + \abs{p(z^*) - p(w)} < m +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} + L \cdot 2 s_k < m + \varepsilon . As \varepsilon > 0 was arbitrary, \abs{p(z^*)} \le m: otherwise \varepsilon \coloneqq \abs{p(z^*)} - m > 0 would give \abs{p(z^*)} < \abs{p(z^*)}. Also \abs{p(z^*)} \ge m, since z^* \in S_0. So \abs{p(z^*)} = m. Step 7 (the minimum over all of the plane). Let z \in 
C. If z \in S_0, then \abs{p(z)} \ge m = \abs{p(z^*)}. If z 
otin S_0, then \abs{p(z)} > \abs{p(0)} \ge m by (1), since 0 \in S_0. This proves the theorem. Let V \subseteq 
R be non-empty and bounded below by 0, and let B be the set of lower bounds of V. Then 0 \in B, and every element of V is an upper bound of B, so B is non-empty and bounded above; by @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field it has a supremum m (@fd3:def-complete-ordered-field). Each v \in V is an upper bound of B, so m \le v: m is a lower bound of V. Each lower bound u of V is in B, so u \le m. Thus m is the greatest lower bound of V, its infimum in the sense of @fd2:def-order-supremum. The answer to the prompt. A quarter containing a point where \abs{p} is smallest is what the theorem is trying to prove exists, so it cannot be used to choose quarters. The infimum of a quarter always exists, by completeness, and Step 3 shows that some quarter keeps it. Choosing “the first such quarter in a fixed order” makes the step a rule, so the recursion theorem applies and no choice is made at any stage; compare @fd3:exm-representatives-need-choice, where a proof that picks infinitely many objects without a rule uses the axiom of choice. The supremum property is invoked directly in Steps 2 and 5 and nowhere else in this chapter. It also enters indirectly, through the non-negative real square roots of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots, which that result derives from the supremum: they give the modulus used in every inequality of this section, and the complex square roots of @prp-complex-square-roots used in the next lemma. In 
Q(i), with 
Q in place of 
R, both fail; Exercise C1 (c) asks where. In Step 3, why does it matter that there are only four quarters? The proof takes \mu, the least of the numbers m(Q_1), \dots, m(Q_4). A finite list of real numbers has a least element, so \mu exists and equals one of them; that is what produces a quarter with m(Q_i) = m(S). With infinitely many pieces, the infimum of their infima need not be attained by any one piece. A direction in which the modulus decreases The second half of the plan is algebra, together with complex square roots (@prp-complex-square-roots). Near a point z_0, write p(z_0 + h) = b_0 + b_k h^k + (	ext{higher powers of } h), with b_0 = p(z_0). If we can choose the direction of h so that b_k h^k points back toward 0 from b_0, and h so small that the higher terms do not undo the gain, then \abs{p} decreases. Dividing by b_0, the first need is a \zeta for which c\zeta^k has negative real part. [A Direction with Negative Real Part] Let c \in 
C with c 
e 0, and let k \in 
N with k \ge 1. Then there is \zeta \in 
C with \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta^k) < 0. Try it first (ten minutes): for c = i, find \zeta with \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta^3) < 0. Then find \zeta with \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta^2) < 0. For k = 3, the four “axis” directions \zeta \in \{1, -1, i, -i\} already turn c around: \zeta^3 runs through 1, -1, -i, i, and i \cdot i = -1. For k = 2 they do not: \zeta^2 \in \{1, -1\} for these four, and c\zeta^2 \in \{i, -i\} has real part 0. What works for k = 2 is a square root of a direction that works for k = 1: \eta = i gives \operatorname{Re}(i \cdot i) = -1, and if \zeta^2 = \eta, then c\zeta^2 = c\eta. So odd k is handled by the axes, and even k = 2j by a square root of a direction for j, which is strong induction. Square roots of complex numbers come from real square roots (@prp-complex-square-roots), so no polar form is needed. We prove, by strong induction on k (@fd1:thm-strong-induction, on 
N = \omega), the statement: if k \ge 1, then for every non-zero c \in 
C there is \zeta with \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta^k) < 0. For k = 0 there is nothing to prove. Let k \ge 1, assume the statement for every smaller exponent, and let c 
e 0. By @fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity (d), k = 2j + 1 or k = 2j for some j \in 
N. Case 1: k odd, k = 2j + 1. Since i^2 = -1, the power laws (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (a)–(c)) give i^k = (i^2)^j i = (-1)^j i \in \{ i, -i \}, (-1)^k = -1 and (-i)^k = (-1)^k i^k = -i^k. So as \zeta runs through 1, -1, i, -i, the products c\zeta^k run through c, -c and ic, -ic (in some order). If \operatorname{Re} c 
e 0, one of \operatorname{Re} c and \operatorname{Re}(-c) = -\operatorname{Re} c is negative. If \operatorname{Re} c = 0, then c = bi with b \coloneqq \operatorname{Im} c 
e 0, and ic = -b, -ic = b: one of them has negative real part. Case 2: k even, k = 2j with 1 \le j < k. By the induction hypothesis for j, there is \eta with \operatorname{Re}(c\eta^j) < 0. Then \eta 
e 0, since otherwise c\eta^j = 0. By @prp-complex-square-roots there is \zeta with \zeta^2 = \eta, and \zeta^k = (\zeta^2)^j = \eta^j (@prp-power-laws-commutative-ring (b)). So \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta^k) = \operatorname{Re}(c\eta^j) < 0. This proves the lemma. With polar form one would take \zeta to be a k-th root of -\conj{c}/\abs{c}. This volume’s k-th roots of complex numbers (@thm-complex-nth-roots) rest on the cosine and sine of @ax-cosine-sine, which it borrows from analysis. The proof above uses only the complex square roots of @prp-complex-square-roots, which Section 3.4 builds from the real square roots of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). For c = i and k = 1, which \zeta \in \{1, -1, i, -i\} gives \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta) < 0? \zeta = i: c\zeta = i \cdot i = -1, with real part -1 < 0. The others give i, -i and -i \cdot i = 1, with real parts 0, 0, 1. Now the descent itself. Re-centering at z_0 is @thm-polynomial-taylor-shift of Section 7.4. [d’Alembert’s Lemma] Let p \in 
C[x] be non-constant, and let z_0 \in 
C with p(z_0) 
e 0. Then there is z \in 
C with \abs{p(z)} < \abs{p(z_0)}. Expand around z_0: p(z_0 + h) = b_0  igl( 1 + (b_k/b_0) h^k + \dots  igr), where k is the first index j \ge 1 with b_j 
e 0. With h = t\zeta, t > 0 real and \zeta from the previous lemma, the bracket is 1 + t^k u + E with \operatorname{Re} u < 0. For small s > 0, \abs{1 + su} is about 1 - s\alpha with \alpha = -\operatorname{Re} u, and E is of order t^{k+1}, smaller than the gain t^k \alpha. The proof fixes t first and then checks the inequality. Before reading on: where is k, the first index with b_k 
e 0, used? Let n \coloneqq \deg p \ge 1. By @thm-polynomial-taylor-shift there are b_0, \dots, b_n \in 
C with p = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j (x - z_0)^j, b_0 = p(z_0) 
e 0 and b_n 
e 0 (the leading coefficient of p). So the set of j \in \{1, \dots, n\} with b_j 
e 0 contains n, and it has a least element k (@fd2:thm-well-ordering): k \ge 1, b_k 
e 0, and b_j = 0 for 1 \le j < k. Let c \coloneqq b_k/b_0 
e 0. By @lem-complex-direction-negative-real-part there is \zeta with \operatorname{Re}(c\zeta^k) < 0. Put u \coloneqq c\zeta^k , \qquad \alpha \coloneqq -\operatorname{Re} u > 0 , \qquad B \coloneqq \sum_{j=k+1}^{n} \Bigl|  rac{b_j}{b_0} \Bigr| \abs{\zeta}^j \ge 0 . Then \alpha \le \abs{u} (@lem-real-part-at-most-modulus), so \abs{u} > 0. Divide q by d: q = hd + r with \deg r < \deg d (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder). Then r = q - hd \in J, and a non-zero r would have smaller degree than the least; so r = 0 and d \mid q. R[x] non-constant, both have degree 1, and 0 = q(\alpha) = g(\alpha) h(\alpha) (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so g(\alpha) = 0 or h(\alpha) = 0 (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)): an element of J of degree 1, which was just excluded. So q is irreducible. [C3: Find the error] Here is an argument. Claim. For every non-constant p \in 
C[x], \abs{p} attains a minimum on 
C. Proof. (1) Let m \coloneqq \inf \{ \abs{p(z)} : z \in

C with \abs{p(z_k)} < m + 1/k. (3) Since \abs{p(z_k)} < m + 1 \le \abs{p(0)} + 1, @lem-complex-polynomial-growth puts the z_k in a bounded set. (4) So they converge to some z^* \in 
C. (5) Then \abs{p(z^*)} = \lim \abs{p(z_k)} = m. Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? Name the line that fails and the reason, give a counterexample to the illegal step, and say how the proof in the text avoids it. [Hint 1] For each line, ask which result of this volume or of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R justifies it. [Hint 2] Is every bounded sequence of real numbers convergent? The claim is true: it is @thm-complex-polynomial-minimum. The argument does not prove it. Line (4) fails. “The z_k lie in a bounded set, so they converge” uses a general “fact” that is neither proved here nor true: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue.
