(What is true, that a bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence, is not available in this volume; and the subsequence would still have to be chosen by a rule.) There is no counterexample to the conclusion. Two further slips. Line (2) picks infinitely many z_k with no rule given, which is a use of the axiom of choice (compare @fd3:exm-representatives-need-choice). Line (5) moves \abs{p} past a limit, which needs continuity; @lem-complex-polynomial-lipschitz would supply it, but the line cites nothing. The repair is the bisection of @thm-complex-polynomial-minimum: it chooses squares by a rule (“the first quarter with the same infimum”), finds the common point as a supremum of corners, and replaces the limit by the Lipschitz estimate of Step 6. No sequence is ever asked to converge. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the claim is true and the argument, as written, does not prove it. - 3: names line (4) and the reason: “bounded implies convergent” is unproved and false, (N9). - 2: a counterexample to the step, such as z_k = (-1)^k. - 1: names one further slip: the rule-less choice in line (2), or the unproved continuity in line (5). - 2: describes the repair: squares chosen by a rule, the common point from completeness, the Lipschitz bound in place of a limit. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a counterexample to the conclusion (there is none); “repairing” line (4) by citing Bolzano–Weierstrass as if it were proved in this volume. R. Review [R1] Let F be a field. Show that there are no non-zero f, g \in F[x] with f^2 = x g^2. This uses the degree of a product from Chapter 6 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), which holds over a field since a field has no zero divisors. Suppose f, g 
e 0 and f^2 = xg^2. Then \deg(f^2) = 2\deg f, and \deg(xg^2) = 1 + 2\deg g. So the natural number 2\deg f would equal 2\deg g + 1: even and odd at once, which @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a) rules out. Hence no such f, g exist. [R2] In 
Q[x]/\langle x^2 - 2 angle, show that every non-zero class [a + bx] (a, b \in 
Q) is a unit, by multiplying it by [a - bx]. Compute [1 + x]^{-1}. In 
Q[x], (a + bx)(a - bx) = a^2 - b^2x^2 = (a^2 - 2b^2) - b^2(x^2 - 2), so [a + bx][a - bx] = [a^2 - 2b^2]. If (a, b) 
e (0, 0), the rational number N \coloneqq a^2 - 2b^2 is non-zero: if b = 0, then N = a^2 
e 0; if b 
e 0, then N = 0 would give (a/b)^2 = 2, against @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two. So [a + bx] \cdot [N^{-1}(a - bx)] = [1], and [a + bx] is a unit. Every class is [a + bx] for exactly one pair (@thm-polynomial-quotient-ring (b)), and the zero class is the pair (0, 0), so every non-zero class is a unit: 
Q[x]/\langle x^2 - 2 angle is a field, as @thm-polynomial-quotient-field also says (x^2 - 2 is irreducible over 
Q). For 1 + x: N = 1 - 2 = -1, so [1 + x]^{-1} = [-(1 - x)] = [x - 1]. Check: (1 + x)(x - 1) = x^2 - 1 = 1 + (x^2 - 2). This is the computation of @exm-q-sqrt2-field in Chapter 4, “multiply by the conjugate”, with [x] in place of \sqrt2: the class [a + bx] behaves as a + b\sqrt2, and (1 + \sqrt2)^{-1} = \sqrt2 - 1. [R3] Let m, n \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that \gcd(2^m - 1, 2^n - 1) = 2^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1 in 
Z. The method is the integer Euclidean step of Chapter 2 (@lem-gcd-remainder-step), used on the exponents and on the numbers at once. We prove the claim for all m, n \ge 1 by strong induction on m + n (@fd1:thm-strong-induction). If m = n, both sides are 2^m - 1: the gcd of a positive integer with itself is that integer (it divides both, and every common divisor is at most it, @def-integer-gcd), and \gcd(m, m) = m. If m > n, then 2^m - 1 = 2^{m-n}(2^n - 1) + (2^{m-n} - 1) , and 2^n - 1 > 0, so @lem-gcd-remainder-step gives \gcd(2^m - 1, 2^n - 1) = \gcd(2^n - 1, 2^{m-n} - 1). Likewise m = 1 \cdot n + (m - n) gives \gcd(m, n) = \gcd(n, m - n). Since n + (m - n) = m < m + n and m - n \ge 1, the induction hypothesis gives \gcd(2^n - 1, 2^{m-n} - 1) = 2^{\gcd(n, m-n)} - 1 = 2^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1. If m < n, exchange the roles (the gcd is symmetric). For example, \gcd(2^{12} - 1, 2^{18} - 1) = \gcd(4095, 262143) = 63 = 2^6 - 1. This is the integer twin of Exercise C3 of Section 7.2 (@exr-polynomial-gcd-c3), where x^m - 1 and x^n - 1 play the parts of 2^m - 1 and 2^n - 1. [R4] Is x^4 + x + 1 irreducible over 
F_2? Yes. The tool is a degree count over a finite field: list the possible factorizations and check each. The values are 0 + 0 + 1 = 1 at 0 and 1 + 1 + 1 = 1 at 1, so f \coloneqq x^4 + x + 1 has no root in 
F_2, and hence no factor of degree 1 (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (c)). A factorization into non-constant factors would then be f = gh with \deg g = \deg h = 2. Over 
F_2 the only non-zero constant is 1, so g and h are monic. A root of g or h would be a root of f, so both are rootless quadratics, hence irreducible (@prp-irreducible-low-degree (b)). The monic quadratics over 
F_2 are x^2, x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)^2, x^2 + x = x(x + 1) and x^2 + x + 1; only the last is rootless. So g = h = x^2 + x + 1, and gh = x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^4 + x^2 + 1 
e f in 
F_2[x]. So f is irreducible. Look-alikes that fail. “No root, hence irreducible” (@prp-irreducible-low-degree) applies only in degrees 2 and 3; in degree 4 it is the error of Exercise C2 of Section 7.3, and x^4 + x^2 + 1 = (x^2 + x + 1)^2 is a rootless reducible quartic over 
F_2. The rational root test (@thm-rational-root-test) is about 
Q, not 
F_2. Eisenstein’s criterion is not in this volume.

title: Real Functions and Their Graphs
content: Real Functions and Their Graphs Analysis studies functions of a real variable, and it studies them with a short list of questions. Where does the function increase? What is the largest value it takes on a set? Does it have an inverse? What happens when it is combined with the integer part of a number, which jumps at every integer? This chapter fixes the objects and answers every such question that does not need a limit. A real function is a rule with a domain and a graph, and functions can be added, multiplied and composed. A strictly monotone function has an inverse, and the inverse is monotone too. When the values of a function on a non-empty set are bounded, they have a supremum, and there are rules for comparing suprema. The exponential, the logarithm and real powers are built from three facts about the exponential that Integration, Series, and Function Spaces proves. The last section collects strange functions on which later definitions of continuity and the integral will be tested. Part III of this volume begins here. Its three chapters, 8, 9 and 10, are the tools that Analysis on the Real Line assumes on its first page. They use the algebra of Part II (Chapters 4–7) only a little, mostly for polynomials. What you need. - Functions, composition and inverse functions, from Sets and Functions, Chapter 2 (@fd2:def-inverse-function). - The supremum of an ordered set, from Sets and Functions, Chapter 5 (@fd2:def-order-supremum). - The real numbers as a complete ordered field, with the absolute value, the Archimedean property and the integer part, from Number Systems: From \nN to \nR (@fd3:thm-cof-complete-archimedean). - Roots and rational powers, from Chapter 1 (@def-rational-power). - Polynomial functions, from Chapters 6 and 7, in Sections 8.1, 8.3 and 8.6 (@def-polynomial-evaluation). Time. About 30 hours if you read the main text and do every A exercise and one B and one C exercise per section; about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - Real Functions and Their Graphs. A real function is a rule with a domain and a graph (@def-real-function), and functions are added, multiplied, divided and composed. - Monotone Functions and Inverse Functions. A strictly monotone function has an inverse that is monotone in the same direction (@thm-monotone-inverse), which makes roots into functions. - Bounded Functions and Their Suprema. The supremum of a function on a set, found by bounding every value and then finding a value close to the bound, and rules for comparing suprema (@thm-sup-function-rules). - Floor, Distance to the Integers, and Step Functions. The floor, the ceiling and the fractional part (@def-floor-ceiling), the distance to the nearest integer, periodic functions and step functions. - The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers. From three borrowed facts about the exponential come the logarithm and the powers a^x for every real x, with the laws of powers (@prp-real-power-laws). - A Table of Strange Functions. The Dirichlet function, Thomae’s function and other strange examples (@def-thomae-function), each with a question that a later volume answers.

title: 8.1 Real Functions and Their Graphs
content:
Real Functions and Their Graphs Part II of this volume (Chapters 4–7) ended with polynomials as formal objects and with what their values can and cannot do. Part III (Chapters 8–10) turns to functions of a real variable, the objects that analysis adds, composes, inverts and bounds. This section fixes what a real function is, how two of them combine, how a graph moves when the formula changes, and how a function splits into an even and an odd part. Everything is proved from Sets and Functions, the complete ordered field 
R and the polynomials of Chapters 6 and 7; no limit appears. A formula is not yet a function Let f(x) = x^2/x. What is f(0)? The tempting answer cancels: x^2/x = x, so f(0) = 0. But the formula x^2/x asks us to divide by 0 at 0, and no field rule allows that. Another reader says f(0) is undefined. Both readers have a function in mind, and they have different ones. In Sets and Functions, a function is given by a graph, in which every input of its domain has exactly one value, together with a codomain (@fd2:def-function). A formula supplies the values but not the domain. Until the domain is named, the question has no answer. Here is a small case. Take the inputs D = \{1, 2, 3\} and send each input to its square. The values are 1, 4 and 9, and the function is recorded by the three pairs (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9). With the inputs \{-1, 1\} and the same rule, the pairs are (-1, 1) and (1, 1): a different function. A real function is a set of inputs together with one real value for each of them. The inputs are part of the function, and every input gets exactly one real number. [Real Function, Graph] Let D \subseteq 
R. A real function on D is a function f \colon D 	o 
R (@fd2:def-function). Its graph is \operatorname{graph} f \coloneqq \{ (x, f(x)) : x \in D \} \subseteq 
R^2 , where 
R^2 \coloneqq 
R 	imes 
R (@fd2:def-cartesian-product). The set D is always stated; there is no “natural domain” convention. The graph is exactly the relation G in the definition of a function (@fd2:def-function), since each element of G is the pair (x, f(x)). The codomain of a real function is always 
R. So the test for equal functions in Sets and Functions (@fd2:prp-function-equality) reads: two real functions are equal if and only if they have the same domain and the same value at every point of it. With D = 
R \setminus \{0\}, the function of the opening question is x \mapsto x^2/x on 
R \setminus \{0\}, and 0 is not an input. [First Real Functions] Each of the following is a real function; check that each input has exactly one value. 1. A constant x \mapsto c on 
R, and the identity x \mapsto x on 
R. 2. The absolute value x \mapsto \abs{x} on 
R (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field). 3. x \mapsto 1/x on 
R \setminus \{0\}. 4. x \mapsto \sqrt{x} on [0, \infty). 5. A restriction f|_A (@fd2:def-restriction-extension), for instance x \mapsto x^2 on [0, \infty). 6. An indicator \ind_A for A \subseteq 
R (@fd2:def-indicator), with codomain 
R in place of \{0, 1\}. 7. The function equal to x on (-\infty, 0) and to x^2 on [0, \infty). (a), (b) One formula, defined everywhere; \abs{x} is given by two cases that cover 
R and do not overlap. (c) 1/x exists exactly when x 
e 0. (d) For x \ge 0, \sqrt{x} is the unique b \ge 0 with b^2 = x. It exists because 
R is a complete ordered field. (e) A restriction keeps the old values on the smaller domain. (f) Enlarging the codomain changes no value. (g) The two pieces are disjoint and cover 
R, so they glue to one function, as in @fd2:exm-piecewise-as-gluing. @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field (
R is a complete ordered field); @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots (square roots exist). The figure shows, from left to right, the graphs of \abs{x}, 1/x, \sqrt{x} and \ind_{[0, \infty)}; an open dot marks a point that is not on the graph. Which subsets of the plane are graphs? Reading the definition of a function (@fd2:def-function) as a statement about vertical lines answers this. Take D = \{1, 2\}. The set \{ (1, 5), (2, 5) \} is a graph over D: above 1 and above 2 it has one point each. The set \{ (1, 5), (1, 6), (2, 5) \} is not, since it has two points above 1. Nor is \{ (1, 5), (2, 5), (3, 5) \}, since it has a point above 3, and 3 
otin D. [Vertical Line Test] Let D \subseteq 
R and G \subseteq 
R^2. Then G is the graph of a real function on D if and only if 1. for every a \in D there is exactly one y \in 
R with (a, y) \in G, and 2. every (a, y) \in G has a \in D. Let G = \operatorname{graph} f for f \colon D 	o 
R. Then (i) is the condition in the definition of a function. And (ii) holds because every element of G is a pair (x, f(x)) with x \in D. Conversely, (ii) gives G \subseteq D 	imes 
R. With (i), the pair f \coloneqq (G, 
R) is then a function D 	o 
R. Each (a, y) \in G has y = f(a) by the definition of the value, and each (x, f(x)) with x \in D lies in G by the same definition, so G = \operatorname{graph} f. @fd2:def-function (one value for each input; the value f(a)). In words: the vertical line through a meets G exactly once when a \in D, and not at all when a 
otin D. No natural domain. The function x \mapsto x^2/x on 
R \setminus \{0\} is the restriction of the identity of 
R to 
R \setminus \{0\}; it is not the identity, because the domains differ. And not every curve is a graph: the circle \{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : x^2 + y^2 = 1 \} contains (0, 1) and (0, -1). Every point must lie above D, by (ii), so 0 \in D. But then there are two points above 0, and (i) fails at 0, whatever D is. Is each set a graph, and over which D? (1) \{ (x, y) : y = x^2 \}; (2) \{ (x, y) : x = y^2 \}; (3) \{ (x, y) : y \ge 0, \ x = y^2 \}. (1) Yes, over 
R. (2) No: (1, 1) and (1, -1) both lie in it. Every point lies above D, by (ii), so 1 \in D, and there are two points above 1, so (i) fails. (3) Yes, over [0, \infty): every element has x = y^2 \ge 0, and for a \ge 0 the only y \ge 0 with y^2 = a is \sqrt{a}. It is the graph of \sqrt{\cdot}. Combining real functions Two real functions with different domains can still be added; the sum lives where both are defined. Composition needs more care, because g(f(x)) needs f(x) to be an input of g. Here is a small case. Let f(x) = 1/x on 
R \setminus \{0\} and g(x) = 1/(x - 1) on 
R \setminus \{1\}. Their sum 1/x + 1/(x - 1) makes sense where both do, on 
R \setminus \{0, 1\}; at x = 2 it is 	frac12 + 1 = 	frac32. The composite g(f(x)) = 1/(1/x - 1) needs x 
e 0 and 1/x 
e 1, so it is defined on 
R \setminus \{0, 1\} too. At x = 2 it is 1/(	frac12 - 1) = -2. [Operations on Real Functions] Let f \colon D_f 	o 
R and g \colon D_g 	o 
R be real functions and c \in 
R. On D_f \cap D_g define, for each x, (f + g)(x) \coloneqq f(x) + g(x), \quad (fg)(x) \coloneqq f(x) g(x), and \max(f, g)(x) \coloneqq \max(f(x), g(x)), likewise \min(f, g); here \max(a, b) is b if a \le b and a otherwise, and \min(a, b) is a if a \le b and b otherwise. On D_f define (cf)(x) \coloneqq c f(x), -f \coloneqq (-1) f and \abs{f}(x) \coloneqq \abs{f(x)}; and f - g \coloneqq f + (-g) on D_f \cap D_g. The quotient f/g, x \mapsto f(x)/g(x), has domain \{ x \in D_f \cap D_g : g(x) 
e 0 \}. The composite g \circ f, x \mapsto g(f(x)), has domain \{ x \in D_f : f(x) \in D_g \} . For instance, \abs{f} = \max(f, -f) on D_f. Fix x \in D_f. If f(x) \ge 0, then -f(x) \le f(x), so \max(f(x), -f(x)) = f(x) = \abs{f(x)}. If f(x) < 0, then f(x) < -f(x), so the maximum is -f(x) = \abs{f(x)}. This composite is the composite of Sets and Functions (@fd2:def-composition), applied to a restriction of f. Write E for its domain. Every value of f|_E lies in D_g, so f|_E may be regarded as a function E 	o D_g, and g after it is a composite in that sense, with values g(f(x)). Composition stays associative. The functions h \circ (g \circ f) and (h \circ g) \circ f have the same domain and the same values h(g(f(x))), so they are equal. This is associativity of composition (@fd2:prp-composition-associative) for the restricted maps. Let h \colon D_h 	o 
R as well. The domain of h \circ (g \circ f) is the set of x in the domain of g \circ f with g(f(x)) \in D_h, that is, \{ x \in D_f : f(x) \in D_g, \ g(f(x)) \in D_h \}. R \setminus \{0\}) = (0, \infty). The composite has domain \{ x \in 
R : x - 1 \in [0, \infty) \} = [1, \infty). Polynomial and rational functions Chapter 6 defined, for a polynomial p \in 
R[x], its polynomial function c \mapsto p(c) on 
R (@def-polynomial-evaluation). In this chapter the letter x usually names a real number, so we write this function as x \mapsto p(x); the polynomial x \in

R. A polynomial function on D is the restriction to D of the polynomial function x \mapsto p(x) of some p \in 
R[x]. For p, q \in 
R[x] with q 
e 0, the rational function p/q is x \mapsto p(x)/q(x) on \{ x \in 
R : q(x) 
e 0 \}. Chapters 6 and 7 proved what these functions need. Since

Choosing n + 1 distinct points of D, part (a) of that theorem gives p = q. So on an interval with more than one point, the degree and leading coefficient of a polynomial function are well defined. - Few roots. A non-zero q has at most \deg q roots (@thm-polynomial-root-count), so a rational function is defined at every real number except at most \deg q of them. On a finite set the second fact fails: on D = \{0, 1\}, the polynomials x^2 and x have the same function. Is \abs{x} on [0, \infty) a polynomial function? Are the rational function (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) and the polynomial function x + 1 on

R. Its vertex is (-1, 2). Even and odd functions Two symmetries of a graph are common enough to have names. A set D \subseteq 
R is symmetric if -x \in D for every x \in D; then -D = D. For example, take D = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}. On -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 the function x^2 takes the values 4, 1, 0, 1, 4: the value at -x equals the value at x. The function x^3 takes the values -8, -1, 0, 1, 8: the value at -x is minus the value at x. R. Then f is even if f(-x) = f(x) for every x \in D, and odd if f(-x) = -f(x) for every x \in D. Indeed, both f and x \mapsto f(-x) have domain -D = D, so they are equal exactly when their graphs are. The odd case uses the method of reading a graph as a set of pairs (@exm-method-graph-pairs), with M(u, v) = (-u, -v), which is its own inverse. For (x, y) \in

Conversely, let the graph be unchanged by M. Then for x \in D the point (-x, -f(x)) lies on it, so f(-x) = -f(x). Some examples: - x^2, \abs{x} and the constants on

R. The terms x^2 and 1 do not change when x is replaced by -x, and 2x changes sign. So f is the even function x^2 + 1 plus the odd function 2x. [Even and Odd Parts] Let D \subseteq 
R be symmetric and f \colon D 	o 
R. There is exactly one pair of functions e, o \colon D 	o

Replacing x by -x swaps f(x) and f(-x), so e(-x) = e(x) and o(-x) = -o(x); and e(x) + o(x) = f(x). Uniqueness. Let f = e + o = e' + o' with e, e' even and o, o' odd, and put h \coloneqq e - e' = o' - o. As a difference of even functions h is even, and as a difference of odd functions it is odd. So h(x) = h(-x) = -h(x), hence 2h(x) = 0. Since 2 
e 0, h(x) = 0 for every x \in D. Thus e = e' and o = o'. For a polynomial function on 
R, the even part keeps the even powers, since (-x)^k = x^k for even k and -x^k for odd k. For (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1, the formulas give the even part x^2 + 1 and the odd part 2x, as found above. R. Prove that \max(f, g) = 	frac12 (f + g + \abs{f - g}) and \min(f, g) = 	frac12 (f + g - \abs{f - g}). Both sides have domain D; fix x \in D. If f(x) < g(x), then \abs{f(x) - g(x)} = g(x) - f(x), and the right sides are g(x) and f(x), again the max and the min. The values agree at every x, so the functions are equal. [B2] Obtain the graph of x \mapsto 2\abs{x - 1} - 3 on

The zeros solve \abs{x - 1} = 	frac32, so x = -	frac12 or x = 	frac52. [B3] Find the even and odd parts of f(x) = 1/(1 - x) on D = 
R \setminus \{-1, 1\}. Why is -1 removed from D? For x \in D, the formulas of @prp-even-odd-decomposition give  egin{aligned} e(x) &= 	frac12 \Bigl(  rac{1}{1 - x} +  rac{1}{1 + x} \Bigr) = 	frac12 \cdot  rac{2}{1 - x^2} =  rac{1}{1 - x^2} , \ o(x) &= 	frac12 \Bigl(  rac{1}{1 - x} -  rac{1}{1 + x} \Bigr) = 	frac12 \cdot  rac{2x}{1 - x^2} =  rac{x}{1 - x^2} . \end{aligned} The formula 1/(1 - x) makes sense at -1. But even and odd functions need a symmetric domain: with 1 removed, -1 must go too. @def-even-odd-function (symmetric domain). [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and refute each false one with a counterexample. 1. The product of two odd functions on a symmetric D is even. 2. A function on a symmetric D that is both even and odd is the zero function. 3. The composite of two odd functions

title: 8.2 Monotone Functions and Inverse Functions
content:
Monotone Functions and Inverse Functions Section 8.1 made real functions into objects with a domain and a graph, and combined them. This section asks how a function treats the order of 
R: does a larger input give a larger output? We give the property its definition, a method for proving it, and rules for building monotone functions from others. Then we prove the main result: a strictly monotone function is a bijection onto its image, and its inverse is monotone in the same direction. That gives the n-th root as a function, for every real input when n is odd. Increasing and decreasing functions Ask a reader whether x \mapsto 1/x is decreasing, and the answer is usually yes. On 
R \setminus \{0\} it is not: -1 < 1, but 1/(-1) = -1 < 1 = 1/1, so a larger input gave a larger output. The function decreases on (-\infty, 0) and on (0, \infty), and the jump across 0 spoils the union. So “decreasing” is never a property of a formula alone. It is a property of a function on a set, and the definition must name the set. A small case first. On the set \{1, 2, 3\}, the function x \mapsto x^2 takes the values 1, 4, 9. Each larger input gives a larger output, so the function keeps the order there. On the set \{-2, 1\} it does not: -2 < 1, but (-2)^2 = 4 > 1 = 1^2. A function is increasing on a set when moving right inside the set never moves its value down. [Monotone Function] Let f \colon D 	o 
R be a real function (@def-real-function) and let A \subseteq D. The function f is - increasing on A if, for all x, y \in A, x < y implies f(x) \le f(y); - strictly increasing on A if, for all x, y \in A, x < y implies f(x) < f(y); - decreasing on A if, for all x, y \in A, x < y implies f(x) \ge f(y); - strictly decreasing on A if, for all x, y \in A, x < y implies f(x) > f(y). It is monotone on A if it is increasing on A or decreasing on A, and strictly monotone on A if it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on A. Without “on A”, the set is the whole domain D. In symbols, “increasing on A” is  orall x \in A \ \  orall y \in A \ \  igl( x < y 	o f(x) \le f(y)  igr) . In words: we pick two points of A, name the smaller one x, and ask that the values come in the same order (\le or <) or in the reverse order (\ge or >). Since x \le y means x < y or x = y, an increasing function also satisfies x \le y \Rightarrow f(x) \le f(y), and a decreasing one satisfies x \le y \Rightarrow f(x) \ge f(y). A strictly monotone function satisfies the same non-strict forms; the strict inequality fails at x = y. Negating quantifier by quantifier (@fd1:prp-quantifier-negation), “f is not increasing on A” is \exists x \in A \ \ \exists y \in A \ \  igl( x < y \wedge f(x) > f(y)  igr) , so a failure is shown by two witnesses, as -1 and 1 were for 1/x above. The identity x \mapsto x on 
R is strictly increasing, and so is x \mapsto x^3. Sets and Functions used the same word, and proved there that x \mapsto x^3 is strictly increasing (@fd2:exm-maps-from-calculus (a)). It also proved that every strictly increasing map between subsets of 
R is injective (@fd2:prp-strictly-monotone-injective). We use both facts without proving them again. Sets and Functions called a map f \colon A 	o B between subsets of 
R strictly increasing when x < x' implies f(x) < f(x'). Our f \colon D 	o 
R is strictly increasing on A exactly when its restriction f|_A \colon A 	o 
R (@fd2:def-restriction-extension) is strictly increasing in that sense: both say the same thing about the same pairs of points of A. The codomain plays no part. Sets with one point: on a set A with at most one point there is no pair x < y, so every function is strictly increasing and strictly decreasing on A, vacuously. Monotonicity says something only about pairs. Monotone on two sets does not give monotone on their union. The function 1/x is strictly decreasing on (-\infty, 0) and on (0, \infty), yet not decreasing on 
R \setminus \{0\}, by the witnesses -1 < 1 found at the start of this section. A proof that splits A into pieces must also compare a point of one piece with a point of the other. Is a constant function on 
R increasing? Is 1/x decreasing on 
R \setminus \{0\}? Is the indicator \ind_{[0, \infty)} (@fd2:def-indicator) increasing on 
R? For each “yes”, say whether “strictly” holds too. A constant is increasing, since f(x) = f(y) satisfies \le; it is decreasing too, and strictly neither: 0 < 1 and the values are equal. The function 1/x is not decreasing on 
R \setminus \{0\}: -1 < 1 and 1/(-1) < 1/1. The indicator is increasing: for x < y, if its value at x is 1, then 0 \le x < y and its value at y is 1 too. It is not strictly increasing: -2 < -1 with both values 0. The method: factor out the difference of the inputs To prove f strictly increasing on A, we fix x < y in A and must show f(y) - f(x) > 0. The hypothesis is about the difference y - x, which is positive. So the natural plan is to make y - x appear as a factor of f(y) - f(x), and then to sign what is left. [Method: factor out y − x] How it goes. “Let x, y \in A with x < y.” Write f(y) - f(x) = (y - x) \, Q(x, y) by algebra on the formula for f. Since y - x > 0, the sign of f(y) - f(x) is the sign of Q(x, y): show Q(x, y) > 0 for strictly increasing, Q(x, y) \ge 0 for increasing, and < 0 or \le 0 for the decreasing kinds (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), (d)). Differences of powers factor by @lem-difference-of-powers: y^n - x^n = (y - x) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} y^k x^{n-1-k} . Quotients are brought over a common denominator first. When to use it. f is given by a formula built from +, \cdot and /, and the claim is that f is monotone on a set. Common mistakes. One mistake is to conclude “strictly” from Q \ge 0: a positive number times a non-negative one may be 0. Another is to use a sign of Q that holds on part of A only. In that case, split A first, and also compare a point of one piece with a point of another. -------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want -------------------------------------- ----------------------------------- x, y \in A, x < y; the formula for f f(x) < f(y) y - x > 0 f(y) - f(x) > 0 f(y) - f(x) = (y - x) \, Q(x, y) Q(x, y) > 0: what is left to show -------------------------------------------------------------------------- For a quotient, the obvious argument fails. [A quotient of two increasing functions] Let g \colon (-2, \infty) 	o 
R, g(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 2}. Prove that g is strictly increasing. [Scratch work] The naive attempt. “The numerator x - 1 increases with x, so the quotient does.” The denominator increases too, and a quotient of two increasing positive things can do anything: x/x is constant. So the naive attempt proves nothing. Factor out y - x. For -2 < x < y, bring the difference over the common denominator (x + 2)(y + 2), which is positive. The numerator is  egin{aligned} &(y - 1)(x + 2) - (x - 1)(y + 2) \ &\quad = (xy + 2y - x - 2) - (xy + 2x - y - 2) = 3(y - x) . \end{aligned} So Q(x, y) = 3/ igl((x + 2)(y + 2) igr). ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want --------------------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------- -2 < x < y g(y) - g(x) > 0 g(y) - g(x) = 3(y - x)/ igl((x + 2)(y + 2) igr) Q(x, y) = 3/ igl((x + 2)(y + 2) igr) > 0 x + 2 > 0, y + 2 > 0 done: a quotient of positive elements is positive ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Let x, y \in (-2, \infty) with x < y. A counterexample to the step: 1 \cdot 0 = 0. This is the first mistake @exm-method-factor-difference warns against: strictness concluded from Q \ge 0. Repair. Line (i) gives more than (iii) uses: y > x \ge 1, so y^2 > 1 (@lem-reals-nth-root (a)), while x^2 \ge 1 and xy \ge x \ge 1. Hence y^2 + xy + x^2 > 3, the bracket is > 0, and (iv) holds. [C2, used later] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R be increasing, with f(f(x)) = x for every x \in 
R. Prove that f = \id_{
R}. Then show that “increasing” cannot be dropped. [Hint 1] Fix x, and split by the sign of f(x) - x. [Hint 2] Suppose f(x) > x, and apply f to both sides. Let x \in 
R. By trichotomy, f(x) > x, f(x) < x or f(x) = x. If x < f(x), then, f being increasing, f(x) \le f(f(x)) = x, against x < f(x). If f(x) < x, then f(f(x)) \le f(x), that is, x \le f(x), against f(x) < x. So f(x) = x for every x, and f = \id_{
R} by @fd2:prp-function-equality. Without “increasing” the claim fails: x \mapsto -x satisfies -(-x) = x for every x, and it is not the identity, since it sends 1 to -1. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: fixes an arbitrary x and compares x with f(x) (the three cases of trichotomy, or the two of totality). - 3: in one case (f(x) > x, or x \le f(x)), applies the monotonicity of f to the inequality between x and f(x) and uses f(f(x)) = x to reach a contradiction or, by antisymmetry, f(x) = x. - 2: handles the other case, or says that it is symmetric with the reason. - 1: concludes f = \id_{
R} from equality at every point. - 2: gives a function with f \circ f = \id_{
R}, f 
e \id_{
R}, and checks both properties. Slips that lose the step. Applying f to a strict inequality and keeping it strict, when f is only increasing. Assuming f is injective or continuous without proof.

title: 8.3 Bounded Functions and Their Suprema
content:
Bounded Functions and Their Suprema Number Systems proved that 
R is a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). By the definition of completeness (@fd3:def-complete-ordered-field), every non-empty set of real numbers that is bounded above has a supremum. A supremum is a least upper bound, as in Sets and Functions (@fd2:def-order-supremum). A real function f \colon D 	o 
R hands us such sets, one for each A \subseteq D: the set f(A) of its values on A. This section asks when f(A) is bounded, names its supremum and infimum, and fixes one method for computing them: bound every value, then find a witness. It then gives rules for comparing suprema without computing them, measures the spread of values, and shows that non-constant polynomials are unbounded on 
R. A least upper bound that is never reached Let f(x) = x/(1 + x) on [0, \infty). A few values: f(0) = 0 , \qquad f(1) =  rac12 , \qquad f(9) =  rac{9}{10} , \qquad f(99) =  rac{99}{100} . Every value is below 1, since x < 1 + x and 1 + x > 0. The values creep toward 1 and never reach it. “Its maximum is 1” is false: a maximum is a value, and 1 is not a value of f. “Its least upper bound is 1” is true, and proving it takes two halves. First, 1 bounds every value. Second, no number below 1 bounds every value. The first half is one line. The second half is the real work, and the epsilon test below turns it into a search for a single point. The infimum and the epsilon test Suprema come with a mirror image. Sets and Functions defined the infimum of a set as its greatest lower bound (@fd2:def-order-supremum), but completeness speaks only of suprema. Reflection in 0 turns one into the other. For A \subseteq 
R, write -A \coloneqq \{ -a : a \in A \}, the image of A under x \mapsto -x (@fd2:exm-sets-of-numbers-as-images). A small case first. Let A = \{ 1, 2, 3 \}, so -A = \{ -1, -2, -3 \}. The lower bound 1 of A becomes the upper bound -1 of -A. The supremum of -A is -1, and \inf A = 1 = -(-1). Number Systems set part (b) of the next proposition as an exercise (@fd3:exr-the-least-upper-bound-property-b1). We prove it here so that later sections can cite it. [Infimum by Reflection] Let A \subseteq 
R. 1. A real number l is a lower bound of A if and only if -l is an upper bound of -A. 2. If A is non-empty and bounded below, then A has an infimum, and \inf A = -\sup(-A). (a) For a \in A, l \le a holds if and only if -a \le -l, by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a) together with the case of equality. The elements of -A are exactly the numbers -a with a \in A, so l \le a for every a \in A if and only if b \le -l for every b \in -A. (b) Let l be a lower bound of A. By (a), -l is an upper bound of -A, and -A is non-empty because A is. Since 
R is complete (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), s \coloneqq \sup(-A) exists. By (a), applied to -s, the number -s is a lower bound of A, since -(-s) = s is an upper bound of -A. Let l' be any lower bound of A. Then -l' is an upper bound of -A by (a). A supremum is at most every upper bound, (S2), so s \le -l', that is, l' \le -s. So -s is the greatest lower bound of A. @fd2:def-order-supremum (S2: least upper bound). Every statement about suprema thus has a twin about infima, obtained by reflection. The second half of “least upper bound” says that nothing smaller is an upper bound. In 
R “smaller” can be measured by a positive gap \varepsilon, and “not an upper bound” means that some element sticks out above. That gives a test with an explicit witness. Here is the test on a small case. Take A = [0, 1) and the upper bound s = 1. For the gap \varepsilon = 1/10, the element 0.95 of A lies above 1 - 1/10 = 0.9. For \varepsilon = 1/100, the element 0.995 lies above 0.99. Every gap, however small, has such an element. [The Epsilon Test for a Supremum] Let A \subseteq 
R be non-empty and let s be an upper bound of A. Then s = \sup A if and only if, for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists a \in A with a > s - \varepsilon. In symbols:  orall \varepsilon > 0 \ \ \exists a \in A \ \ a > s - \varepsilon . Likewise, if i is a lower bound of A, then i = \inf A if and only if for every \varepsilon > 0 there exists a \in A with a < i + \varepsilon. (\Rightarrow) Let s = \sup A and \varepsilon > 0. Then s - \varepsilon < s. If s - \varepsilon were an upper bound of A, the least-upper-bound property (S2) would give s \le s - \varepsilon, which is false. So some a \in A fails a \le s - \varepsilon; by totality of the order (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), a > s - \varepsilon. (\Leftarrow) Assume the condition, and let u be an upper bound of A. Suppose u < s, and put \varepsilon \coloneqq s - u > 0. The condition gives a \in A with a > s - \varepsilon = u, against u being an upper bound. So s \le u by totality. Hence s is an upper bound, (S1), and is at most every upper bound, (S2): it is the supremum. For the infimum, apply the supremum statement to -A and the upper bound -i (@prp-real-infimum (a)). By the proof of @prp-real-infimum (b), i = \inf A if and only if -i = \sup(-A); and -a > -i - \varepsilon if and only if a < i + \varepsilon. @fd2:def-order-supremum (S1, S2). The element a is a witness for \varepsilon. It may depend on \varepsilon, and it usually does: a smaller \varepsilon asks for an element closer to the top. Is 0.99 the supremum of [0, 1)? Use the test. No, and the test does not even apply: it is stated for an upper bound s, and 0.99 is not one, since 0.995 \in [0, 1) and 0.995 > 0.99. The supremum is 1: it bounds [0, 1), and for \varepsilon > 0 the element \max(0, 1 - \varepsilon/2) of [0, 1) exceeds 1 - \varepsilon. Bounded functions and their suprema A real function (@def-real-function) on D has a set of values on each A \subseteq D, and the words of the previous subsection apply to that set. A small case first. Let f(x) = x^2 and A = [-1, 2]. For x \in A, \abs{x} \le 2, so f(x) \le 4; and f(x) \ge 0. One number, 4, lies above every value on A, and 0 lies below every value. A function is bounded on A when its values on A stay inside a fixed window. That is, some fixed interval contains every value on A. [Bounded Function] Let f \colon D 	o 
R and A \subseteq D. The function f is bounded above on A if the set f(A) = \{ f(x) : x \in A \} (@fd2:def-image) is bounded above: there exists M \in 
R with f(x) \le M for every x \in A. It is bounded below on A if f(A) is bounded below, and bounded on A if there exists M \in 
R with \abs{f(x)} \le M for every x \in A. When A = D, “on D” may be dropped. In words: one number M, chosen before x, works for all x \in A. By @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), \abs{f(x)} \le M says -M \le f(x) \le M, so a bounded function is bounded above and below. Conversely, if L \le f(x) \le U on A, then M \coloneqq \max(\abs{L}, \abs{U}) gives f(x) \le \abs{U} \le M and -f(x) \le -L \le \abs{L} \le M, so \abs{f(x)} \le M. The two meanings of “bounded” agree. Examples. The function x/(1 + x) from the start of the section is bounded on [0, \infty), with 0 \le f(x) < 1. A constant function c is bounded on every A, by \abs{c}. The function 1/x on (0, 1] is bounded below by 0 but not above: given M, the point x \coloneqq 1/(\abs{M} + 1) lies in (0, 1] and 1/x = \abs{M} + 1 > M. Change only the set to [1, 2] and the same formula is bounded, with 1/2 \le 1/x \le 1 (@fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (c)). Boundedness belongs to the pair (f, A), not to the formula. Before the next definition, one more small case. On A = \{ 0, 1, 2 \} the function x^2 takes the values 0, 1, 4. The least upper bound of these values is 4, and it is a value, at x = 2. The greatest lower bound is 0, at x = 0. [Supremum and Infimum of a Function] Let f \colon D 	o 
R and let A \subseteq D be non-empty. If f is bounded above on A, the supremum of f on A is \sup_A f \coloneqq \sup f(A) , also written \sup_{x \in A} f(x). If f is bounded below on A, its infimum on A is \inf_A f \coloneqq \inf f(A). The supremum is attained if \sup_A f \in f(A), that is, \sup_A f = f(x_0) for some x_0 \in A; it is then the maximum of f on A, written \max_A f. Likewise an attained infimum is the minimum \min_A f. Both exist under the stated hypotheses: f(A) is non-empty because A is, so completeness gives \sup f(A), and @prp-real-infimum (b) gives \inf f(A). The set A must be non-empty, since every real number bounds the empty set and no least one exists. An attained supremum f(x_0) is an upper bound of f(A) that lies in f(A), so it is the largest value. Conversely, a largest value f(x_0) is an upper bound, and every upper bound is at least f(x_0). So it is the supremum. The supremum need not be a value. A proof that starts “let x_0 be the point where f reaches \sup_A f” has assumed that the supremum is attained. For x/(1 + x) on [0, \infty) no such point exists. The supremum also depends on A: \sup_{[0, 1]} x^2 = 1 and \sup_{[0, 2]} x^2 = 4. The two halves we used for x/(1 + x) at the start of the section now become a general method. [Method: bound every value, then find a witness] How it goes. To prove \sup_A f = M for a non-empty A and a candidate M \in 
R: - (\le) Bound every value. Let x \in A be arbitrary and prove f(x) \le M. - (\ge) Find a witness. Let \varepsilon > 0 be arbitrary and produce x \in A, depending on \varepsilon, with f(x) > M - \varepsilon. The first half shows that f is bounded above on A and that M is an upper bound of f(A); then M = \sup_A f by @prp-real-sup-approximation. For an infimum, reverse the inequalities: f(x) \ge m for every x \in A, and for each \varepsilon > 0 some x with f(x) < m + \varepsilon. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want ------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ f on A 
e \emptyset; a candidate M (\le)  orall x \in A \ \ f(x) \le M; (\ge)  orall \varepsilon > 0 \ \exists x \in A \ \ f(x) > M - \varepsilon -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- When to use it. Whenever a supremum or infimum is to be computed. An inequality \sup_A f \le M needs only the first half, since the supremum is the least upper bound; an equality needs both. Common mistakes. Proving only (\le) shows that M is an upper bound, not that it is the least one. A witness for one \varepsilon, such as 1/10, is not enough: the second half needs a witness for every \varepsilon. A witness for f must not be paired with a different witness for g, as if f(x) + g(y) were a value of f + g. Exercise B4 shows where that mistake leads. Two worked examples The first example returns to x/(1 + x). Its witness has to move with \varepsilon. [A supremum that is not attained] Let f(x) = x/(1 + x) on A = [0, \infty). Prove that \sup_A f = 1 and that it is not attained. Find \inf_A f. [Scratch work] The bounding half: x/(1 + x) \le 1 means x \le 1 + x, after multiplying by 1 + x > 0, and that holds, even strictly. The witness half is the gap. Given \varepsilon > 0, we want x \ge 0 with  rac{x}{1 + x} > 1 - \varepsilon . For \varepsilon \ge 1 the right side is at most 0 and any x > 0 works. For 0 < \varepsilon < 1, work backwards: multiply by 1 + x, collect x: x > (1 - \varepsilon)(1 + x) \iff \varepsilon x > 1 - \varepsilon \iff x >  rac{1}{\varepsilon} - 1 . So x \coloneqq 1/\varepsilon is a clean choice, a little larger than needed. Does it also cover \varepsilon \ge 1? At x = 1/\varepsilon the value is 1/(1 + \varepsilon), and 1/(1 + \varepsilon) > 1 - \varepsilon means 1 > (1 - \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon) = 1 - \varepsilon^2, true for every \varepsilon > 0. One choice, no cases; the restriction \varepsilon < 1 was needed only while solving backwards. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want ------------------------------------------------------ -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- x \in [0, \infty) x/(1 + x) \le 1 \varepsilon > 0 some x \ge 0 with x/(1 + x) > 1 - \varepsilon x \coloneqq 1/\varepsilon, value 1/(1 + \varepsilon) 1/(1 + \varepsilon) > 1 - \varepsilon, i.e. 1 > 1 - \varepsilon^2: the gap is closed --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The proof runs forwards: bound, then choose x from \varepsilon, then check. Bound every value. Let x \ge 0. Then 1 + x > 0 and x < 1 + x; multiplying by 1/(1 + x) > 0 (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order (a), @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c)) gives f(x) < 1. Find a witness. Let \varepsilon > 0 and put x \coloneqq 1/\varepsilon, which lies in A. Then f(x) =  rac{1/\varepsilon}{1 + 1/\varepsilon} =  rac{1}{1 + \varepsilon} . Since (1 - \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon) = 1 - \varepsilon^2 < 1 and 1 + \varepsilon > 0, dividing by 1 + \varepsilon gives 1 - \varepsilon < 1/(1 + \varepsilon) = f(x). By the method of @exm-method-sup-two-halves, \sup_A f = 1. It is not attained, because f(x) < 1 for every x \in A. For the infimum, f(x) \ge 0 for x \ge 0, as a quotient of x \ge 0 by 1 + x > 0, and f(0) = 0. So \inf_A f = 0, attained: \min_A f = 0. For \varepsilon = 2, which x does the proof choose, and is its value above 1 - \varepsilon? x = 1/2, with f(1/2) = (1/2)/(3/2) = 1/3, and 1/3 > -1 = 1 - \varepsilon. The proof needs no separate case for large \varepsilon. In the second example the candidate is a value, and the witness half costs nothing. [A supremum that is attained] Find \sup and \inf of g(x) = x(1 - x) on [0, 1]. Completing the square, x(1 - x) =  rac14 -  igl( x -  rac12  igr)^2. Bound every value. Since  igl( x -  rac12  igr)^2 \ge 0, g(x) \le  rac14 for every x. Find a witness. g(1/2) = 1/4, and  rac14 >  rac14 - \varepsilon for every \varepsilon > 0. So x = 1/2 is a witness for every \varepsilon at once. Hence \sup_{[0, 1]} g = 1/4, attained at 1/2: it is \max_{[0, 1]} g. For the infimum, on [0, 1] both x \ge 0 and 1 - x \ge 0, so g(x) \ge 0, and g(0) = 0: \min_{[0, 1]} g = 0. An attained value is its own witness, which is why the witness in the second solution does not depend on \varepsilon. Find \sup and \inf of x^2 on (-1, 2), and of \ind_{
Q} \colon 
R 	o \{0, 1\} (@fd2:def-indicator) on [0, 1]. Which are attained? For x^2: the values on (-1, 2) form [0, 4), so \sup = 4, not attained (x^2 = 4 needs x = \pm 2), and \inf = 0, attained at 0. For \ind_{
Q}: \sup = 1, attained at any rational point such as 0, and \inf = 0, attained at any irrational point of [0, 1]. One is \sqrt2/2, with \sqrt2 from @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots: it lies in [0, 1] since 0 \le \sqrt 2 \le 2. First, \sqrt 2 is irrational. If \sqrt 2 = q \in 
Q, then q^2 = 2 in 
R. The copy of 
Q in 
R respects products and is injective (@fd3:thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field), so q^2 = 2 would hold in 
Q. That is impossible, since no rational number has square 2 (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two). Then \sqrt2/2 is irrational too: \sqrt2/2 = q \in 
Q would make \sqrt 2 = 2q rational. Rules for suprema of functions Suprema are compared more often than they are computed. Each comparison below, except (e), which is reflection, is one or both halves of the method. A small case first. On A = \{ 1, 2 \} let f take the values f(1) = 1, f(2) = 3, and let g take g(1) = 2, g(2) = 2. Then \sup f = 3 and \sup g = 2. The sum f + g takes the values 3 and 5, so \sup (f + g) = 5 = 3 + 2. The function 2f takes 2 and 6, so \sup (2f) = 6 = 2 \cdot 3. Rules for Suprema of Functions Let f, g \colon D 	o 
R, let A \subseteq D be non-empty, let f and g be bounded above on A, and let c \in 
R. All suprema are on A, and f + g, cf, \abs{f} are as in @def-function-algebra. 1. If f(x) \le g(x) for every x \in A, then \sup f \le \sup g. 2. \sup (f + g) \le \sup f + \sup g. 3. \sup (f + c) = \sup f + c. 4. If c \ge 0, then \sup (cf) = c \sup f. 5. If f is bounded below on A, then -f is bounded above on A and \sup (-f) = -\inf f. 6. If B \subseteq A is non-empty, then \sup_B f \le \sup_A f. 7. If f and g are bounded (above and below) on A, then  igl| \sup f - \sup g  igr| \le \sup \abs{f - g}. Parts (a), (b) and (f) are inequalities between suprema, so only the bounding half is needed: the right side bounds every value of the left side, and the left supremum is the least such bound. Parts (c) and (d) are equalities and take both halves; (d) treats c = 0 apart, since a witness for cf comes from \varepsilon/c. Part (e) is @prp-real-infimum applied to the set of values. Part (g) uses that f lies between g shifted down and g shifted up by the constant \sup \abs{f - g}. Write S_f \coloneqq \sup_A f and S_g \coloneqq \sup_A g. (a) For x \in A, f(x) \le g(x) \le S_g. So S_g is an upper bound of f(A). A supremum is at most every upper bound, (S2), so S_f \le S_g. (b) Bound every value. For x \in A, f(x) \le S_f and g(x) \le S_g. Adding the two inequalities, f(x) + g(x) \le S_f + S_g. So f + g is bounded above on A, and S_f + S_g is an upper bound of (f + g)(A). Least upper bound. The supremum is at most every upper bound, so \sup (f + g) \le S_f + S_g. (c) For x \in A, f(x) + c \le S_f + c. For \varepsilon > 0, @prp-real-sup-approximation gives x \in A with f(x) > S_f - \varepsilon, so f(x) + c > (S_f + c) - \varepsilon. By the method, \sup (f + c) = S_f + c. (d) If c = 0, then cf is the constant 0 on the non-empty set A, so \sup (cf) = 0 = 0 \cdot S_f. Let c > 0. Bound every value. For x \in A, f(x) \le S_f, so cf(x) \le c S_f (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), with equality allowed). Find a witness. Let \varepsilon > 0. Then \varepsilon/c > 0, and @prp-real-sup-approximation gives x \in A with f(x) > S_f - \varepsilon/c; multiplying by c > 0, cf(x) > c S_f - \varepsilon. By the method, \sup (cf) = c S_f. (e) Let l be a lower bound of f(A). Then -f(x) \le -l for x \in A, so -f is bounded above. The set of values of -f on A is -f(A), so \sup (-f) = \sup(-f(A)) = -\inf f(A) = -\inf f by @prp-real-infimum (b). (f) f(B) \subseteq f(A), so S_f is an upper bound of f(B), and f(B) is non-empty. Hence f is bounded above on B, and \sup_B f \le S_f, since a supremum is at most every upper bound. (g) If \abs{f(x)} \le M and \abs{g(x)} \le N on A, then \abs{f(x) - g(x)} \le M + N by the triangle inequality (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)), so d \coloneqq \sup \abs{f - g} exists. For x \in A, f(x) = g(x) +  igl( f(x) - g(x)  igr) \le g(x) + \abs{f(x) - g(x)} \le g(x) + d , since a number is at most its absolute value. By (a) and then (c), S_f \le \sup (g + d) = S_g + d. Swapping f and g, and using \abs{g - f} = \abs{f - g}, gives S_g \le S_f + d. So -d \le S_f - S_g \le d, which is \abs{S_f - S_g} \le d. @fd2:def-order-supremum (S2: least upper bound); @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b) (adding inequalities); @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) (\abs{g - f} = \abs{f - g}), (c) (t \le \abs{t}), (d) (\abs{t} \le d as two inequalities). Rule (b) bounds the supremum of a sum, and rule (g) says that two functions close at every point have close suprema. Rule (b) is an inequality, and it can be strict. On [0, 1] let f(x) = x and g(x) = 1 - x. Then \sup f = \sup g = 1, while f + g is the constant 1, so \sup (f + g) = 1 < 2. The two suprema are reached at different points, 1 and 0. Which half of the method does rule (f) use, and why is the other half not needed? Only (\le), bounding every value: every value of f on B is a value on A, so \sup_A f bounds f(B), and the least upper bound of f(B) is at most it. No witness is needed because the claim is an inequality, not an equality. How far apart can two values be? For a bounded function, the largest gap between two of its values measures how much the function varies on A. The obvious guess is “the top minus the bottom”, and the next result confirms it, with the top and bottom read as supremum and infimum. A small case first. On A = \{ 1, 2, 3 \} let f take the values 1, 4, 2. The gaps \abs{f(x) - f(y)} are 0, 1, 2, 3, and the largest is 3 = 4 - 1, the largest value minus the smallest. [The Spread of Values] Let A be non-empty and let f \colon D 	o 
R be bounded (above and below) on A \subseteq D. Then \sup  igl\{ \abs{f(x) - f(y)} : x, y \in A  igr\} = \sup_A f - \inf_A f . Try it first (ten minutes): which two points make \abs{f(x) - f(y)} almost \sup_A f - \inf_A f? The natural attempt takes x where f is largest and y where it is smallest. That attempt fails at once: neither point need exist, as x/(1 + x) on [0, \infty) showed. What does exist, for each \varepsilon > 0, is a point x with f(x) within \varepsilon/2 of the supremum and a point y with f(y) within \varepsilon/2 of the infimum (@prp-real-sup-approximation). Their gap falls short of \sup_A f - \inf_A f by less than \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon. The bounding half needs two inequalities, one for each sign of f(x) - f(y). Before reading on: why \varepsilon/2, and not \varepsilon? Let S \coloneqq \sup_A f and I \coloneqq \inf_A f, which exist by @def-sup-of-function, and let T \coloneqq \{ \abs{f(x) - f(y)} : x, y \in A \}, a non-empty set. Bound every value. Let x, y \in A. Then I \le f(x) \le S and I \le f(y) \le S, so f(x) - f(y) \le S - I and f(y) - f(x) \le S - I. Thus -(S - I) \le f(x) - f(y) \le S - I, and \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le S - I by @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d). So S - I is an upper bound of T. Find a witness. Let \varepsilon > 0. Then \varepsilon/2 > 0. By @prp-real-sup-approximation there are x \in A with f(x) > S - \varepsilon/2 and y \in A with f(y) < I + \varepsilon/2. A number is at most its absolute value, so \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \ge f(x) - f(y) > \Bigl( S -  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \Bigr) - \Bigl( I +  rac{\varepsilon}{2} \Bigr) = (S - I) - \varepsilon . By @prp-real-sup-approximation, \sup T = S - I. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (b) (\varepsilon/2 > 0); @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c) (t \le \abs{t}). With \varepsilon in place of each \varepsilon/2, the last display would end in (S - I) - 2\varepsilon, and the test asks for -\varepsilon; any two positive tolerances adding up to \varepsilon would do. The proof never used a point where f is largest. The result holds for x/(1 + x) on [0, \infty), where the spread is 1 - 0 = 1 and is not attained. Polynomials are unbounded On a set like [0, 1] many functions are bounded. On all of 
R, no polynomial function of degree at least 1 is. Chapter 7 proved how fast a complex polynomial grows (@lem-complex-polynomial-growth), and a real polynomial is a complex one whose coefficients happen to be real. Nothing new has to be estimated. A small case first. Let p(x) = x^2 - 3x. Then p(10) = 70 and p(100) = 9700. Once \abs{x} is large, the top term x^2 outweighs the rest, and the values grow without limit. [Polynomials of positive degree are unbounded] Let p = \sum_{j=0}^{d} a_j x^j \in 
R[x] with d = \deg p \ge 1, and put K \coloneqq \abs{a_0} + \dots + \abs{a_{d-1}} , \qquad R \coloneqq \max\Bigl\{ 1,  rac{2K}{\abs{a_d}} \Bigr\} . Show: 1. \abs{p(x)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_d} \abs{x} for every real x with \abs{x} \ge R; 2. every real root of p lies in (-R, R); 3. the polynomial function of p on 
R (@def-polynomial-rational-function) is not bounded. Regard p as an element of 
C[x], with coefficients a_j \in 
R \subseteq 
C (@prp-reals-embed-complex). The inclusion respects sums and products. So, for real x, the value of p at x computed in 
C is the real number p(x). The modulus of a real number is its absolute value (@prp-modulus-of-real). So the numbers K and R above are the A and R of @lem-complex-polynomial-growth, with n = d. (a) For real x with \abs{x} \ge R, the lemma gives \abs{p(x)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_d} \abs{x}^d \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_d} \abs{x}. (b) If \abs{x} \ge R, then \abs{x} \ge 1 and a_d 
e 0, so (a) gives \abs{p(x)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_d} > 0, and x is not a root. So every real root has \abs{x} < R, that is, -R < x < R (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). (c) Let M \in 
R and put x \coloneqq R + 2\abs{M}/\abs{a_d}. Then x \ge R > 0, so \abs{x} = x \ge R, and (a) gives \abs{p(x)} \ge 	frac12 \abs{a_d} \, x = 	frac12 \abs{a_d} R + \abs{M} > \abs{M} \ge M , since 	frac12 \abs{a_d} R > 0. So no M satisfies \abs{p(x)} \le M for every x \in 
R. The growth bound says where roots can be, not that one exists: x^2 + 1 has no real root. That a real polynomial of odd degree has a real root came from factoring, in Chapter 7 (@cor-real-odd-degree-root), and (b) now adds that such a root lies in (-R, R). For example x^3 - 4x + 1 has K = 5 and R = 10, so its roots lie in (-10, 10). Is x^3 - 100x bounded on [-20, 20]? On 
R? On [-20, 20], yes: \abs{x^3 - 100x} \le \abs{x}^3 + 100\abs{x} \le 8000 + 2000 = 10000, by the triangle inequality and \abs{x} \le 20. On 
R, no, by @exm-polynomial-unbounded (c). Boundedness depends on the set, as it did for 1/x on (0, 1] and on [1, 2]. Suprema over a product A function of two variables can be bounded in two stages: first over one variable with the other frozen, then over the other. The order of the stages does not matter. Here A and B are any sets, not necessarily of numbers, and \sup_{A 	imes B} f means \sup f(A 	imes B), the supremum of the set of values, as in @def-sup-of-function; likewise for the inner suprema. A small case first. Let A = B = \{ 1, 2 \}, and write the values of f as a table with rows a = 1, 2 and columns b = 1, 2: the first row is 1, 5 and the second is 3, 2. The row tops are 5 and 3, and the larger is 5. The column tops are 3 and 5, and the larger is again 5, the largest entry. [Iterated Suprema] Let A and B be non-empty sets and let f \colon A 	imes B 	o 
R be bounded above. Then \sup_{A 	imes B} f = \sup_{a \in A} \, \sup_{b \in B} f(a, b) = \sup_{b \in B} \, \sup_{a \in A} f(a, b) . In words: to find the top of a table of numbers, take the top of each row and then the top of those, or the same with columns. Let S \coloneqq \sup_{A 	imes B} f, which exists since A 	imes B is non-empty. For fixed a \in A, every f(a, b) is a value of f, so f(a, b) \le S for every b \in B. Hence b \mapsto f(a, b) is bounded above on the non-empty B. A supremum is at most every upper bound, (S2), so \varphi(a) \coloneqq \sup_{b \in B} f(a, b) \le S. So \varphi is bounded above on A by S, and \sup_A \varphi \le S for the same reason. Conversely, for (a, b) \in A 	imes B, f(a, b) \le \varphi(a) \le \sup_A \varphi. So \sup_A \varphi is an upper bound of the values of f, and S \le \sup_A \varphi. Hence S = \sup_A \varphi, the first equality. Exchanging the roles of A and B gives the second. If B = \{ b_0 \} is a singleton, the inner supremum is f(a, b_0), and the statement says only that \sup_{A 	imes \{b_0\}} f = \sup_{a \in A} f(a, b_0): the same set of values, written twice. The hypothesis that A and B are non-empty cannot be dropped, since an empty factor makes A 	imes B empty and leaves nothing to take the supremum of. [Looking ahead] Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 2, calls the number \sup_A f - \inf_A f of @prp-sup-oscillation the oscillation of f on A, and measures integrability with it. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Parts (a)–(c) are about the proof of @prp-sup-oscillation. Parts (d)–(f) are true or false: give a reason or a counterexample (here A is non-empty and f bounded on A). 1. Run the statement on f(x) = x^2 on A = [-1, 2): find \sup_A f, \inf_A f and the supremum of \abs{f(x) - f(y)}. Is that supremum attained? 2. Which line of the proof uses that f is bounded below on A? 3. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 4. \sup_A f \in f(A). 5. \inf_A f \le \sup_A f. 6. \sup_A \abs{f} = \max igl( \abs{\sup_A f}, \abs{\inf_A f}  igr). (a) The values of x^2 on [-1, 2) form [0, 4), so \sup_A f = 4 and \inf_A f = 0, and the supremum of \abs{f(x) - f(y)} is 4 - 0 = 4. It is not attained: both values lie in [0, 4), so \abs{f(x) - f(y)} < 4, and equality would need f(x) = 4, that is, x = \pm 2, neither of which lies in A. (b) The opening sentence, first: I = \inf_A f exists only because f is bounded below on A (@prp-real-infimum (b)). It is then used in the choice of y with f(y) < I + \varepsilon/2. The infimum version of @prp-real-sup-approximation then gives y. (The bounding half also uses I \le f(y).) (c) A largest and a smallest value need not exist, so take points whose values are within \varepsilon/2 of the supremum and of the infimum. Their gap is within \varepsilon of \sup_A f - \inf_A f, which also bounds every gap. (d) False: @exm-sup-not-attained. (e) True: pick any x \in A, possible since A 
e \emptyset; then \inf_A f \le f(x) \le \sup_A f. (f) True. Write S = \sup_A f, I = \inf_A f, m = \max(\abs{S}, \abs{I}). Bound every value: I \le f(x) \le S gives f(x) \le \abs{S} \le m and -f(x) \le -I \le \abs{I} \le m, so \abs{f(x)} \le m. Find a witness, for \varepsilon > 0. If S \ge 0 and m = \abs{S} = S, take x with f(x) > S - \varepsilon; then \abs{f(x)} \ge f(x) > m - \varepsilon. If I \le 0 and m = \abs{I} = -I, take x with f(x) < I + \varepsilon; then \abs{f(x)} \ge -f(x) > m - \varepsilon. No other case occurs: S < 0 forces I \le S < 0, so m = \abs{I} = -I; and I > 0 forces S \ge I > 0, so m = \abs{S} = S. B. Practice [B1] Let A be non-empty and f, g bounded below on A. Here is a proof that \inf_A (f + g) \ge \inf_A f + \inf_A g, with its last step left out. For each x \in A, f(x) \ge \inf_A f and g(x) \ge \inf_A g, so f(x) + g(x) \ge \inf_A f + \inf_A g. Say which method this is, then complete it. The method is the bounding half of @exm-method-sup-two-halves, mirrored for an infimum, followed by “the infimum is the greatest lower bound”. The displayed line shows that \inf_A f + \inf_A g is a lower bound of (f + g)(A); in particular f + g is bounded below on A, so \inf_A (f + g) exists (@def-sup-of-function). The infimum is greater than or equal to every lower bound (@fd2:def-order-supremum), so \inf_A (f + g) \ge \inf_A f + \inf_A g. [B2: Prove or disprove] Let A be non-empty and f, g bounded on A. Prove or disprove each statement; all suprema and infima are on A. 1. \sup (f + g) = \sup f + \sup g. 2. \sup \max(f, g) = \max(\sup f, \sup g). 3. If f(x) > 0 and g(x) > 0 for every x \in A, then \sup (fg) = \sup f \cdot \sup g. 4. \sup f = -\inf (-f). (a) False. On [0, 1], f(x) = x and g(x) = 1 - x give \sup (f + g) = 1 and \sup f + \sup g = 2, as in the warning after @thm-sup-function-rules. (b) True. Let m \coloneqq \max(\sup f, \sup g). Bound every value: \max(f(x), g(x)) is f(x) \le \sup f \le m or g(x) \le \sup g \le m. So \sup \max(f, g) \le m. Other half: f \le \max(f, g) and g \le \max(f, g) on A, so rule (a) of @thm-sup-function-rules gives \sup f \le \sup \max(f, g) and \sup g \le \sup \max(f, g), hence m \le \sup \max(f, g). (c) False. On (0, 1) let f(x) = x and g(x) = 1 - x, both positive. Then \sup f = \sup g = 1, but fg = x(1 - x) \le 1/4 by @exm-sup-attained-parabola, with \sup (fg) = 1/4 attained at 1/2 \in (0, 1). So 1/4 
e 1. (d) True. -f is bounded (above and below) on A, and rule (e) of @thm-sup-function-rules applied to -f gives \sup (-(-f)) = -\inf (-f), that is, \sup f = -\inf(-f). [B3] Find \sup and \inf of h(x) = x/(x^2 + 1) on 
R, and say whether each is attained. Hence \abs{h(x)} \le 	frac12 for every real x. Hint: compare h(x) with 	frac12 over a common denominator. For every real x, x^2 + 1 > 0, and  rac12 -  rac{x}{x^2 + 1} =  rac{x^2 - 2x + 1}{2(x^2 + 1)} =  rac{(x - 1)^2}{2(x^2 + 1)} \ge 0 , \qquad  rac{x}{x^2 + 1} +  rac12 =  rac{(x + 1)^2}{2(x^2 + 1)} \ge 0 . So -	frac12 \le h(x) \le 	frac12 for every x: every value is bounded. Witnesses: h(1) = 	frac12 and h(-1) = -	frac12 are values, each its own witness for every \varepsilon. Hence \sup_{
R} h = 	frac12 = \max_{
R} h and \inf_{
R} h = -	frac12 = \min_{
R} h, both attained. The two-sided bound is \abs{h(x)} \le 	frac12 by @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d). [B4: Find the error] Here is an argument for “\sup_A (f + g) = \sup_A f + \sup_A g for f, g bounded above on a non-empty A.” 1. The inequality \le is rule (b) of @thm-sup-function-rules. 2. For \ge, let \varepsilon > 0. Choose x \in A with f(x) > \sup f - \varepsilon/2 and y \in A with g(y) > \sup g - \varepsilon/2. 3. Then f(x) + g(y) > \sup f + \sup g - \varepsilon. 4. So \sup f + \sup g passes the epsilon test for the values of f + g, and equality holds. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, and why? The conclusion is false: @exr-bounds-and-suprema-b2 (a) gives f(x) = x, g(x) = 1 - x on [0, 1], with 1 
e 2. Lines (i)–(iii) are correct. Line (iv) fails: the epsilon test needs an element of the set of values (f + g)(A) = \{ f(z) + g(z) : z \in A \}, and f(x) + g(y) with x 
e y is not of that form. In the counterexample, x = 1 and y = 0 (each a witness for every \varepsilon) give f(1) + g(0) = 2, while every value of f + g is 1. This is the mistake of pairing a witness for f with a different witness for g, listed in @exm-method-sup-two-halves. C. Going deeper [C1: Chapter check: the supremum of a square] Let A be non-empty and let f \colon D 	o 
R be bounded on A \subseteq D, with f(x) \ge 0 for every x \in A. Prove that \sup_A f^2 =  igl( \sup_A f  igr)^2. [Hint 1] Use both halves of @exm-method-sup-two-halves, with s \coloneqq \sup_A f. [Hint 2] For the witness, aim at f(x) > s - \delta and expand (s - \delta)^2; then choose \delta from \varepsilon and s. Let s \coloneqq \sup_A f. Since A 
e \emptyset and f \ge 0 on A, s \ge f(x) \ge 0 for any x \in A. Bound every value. For x \in A, 0 \le f(x) \le s, so f(x)^2 \le s^2 by @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d), applied with both factors equal. So f^2 is bounded above on A by s^2. Find a witness. Let \varepsilon > 0. If s = 0, then f(x) = 0 on A, so f^2 is the constant 0 and any x \in A has f(x)^2 = 0 > s^2 - \varepsilon. Let s > 0 and put \delta \coloneqq \varepsilon/(2s) > 0, chosen from \varepsilon and s. By @prp-real-sup-approximation there is x \in A with f(x) > s - \delta. Case s - \delta \ge 0. Then 0 \le s - \delta < f(x), so (s - \delta)^2 < f(x)^2 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), and (s - \delta)^2 = s^2 - 2s\delta + \delta^2 = s^2 - \varepsilon + \delta^2 > s^2 - \varepsilon . So f(x)^2 > s^2 - \varepsilon. Case s - \delta < 0. Then s < \delta = \varepsilon/(2s), so s^2 < \varepsilon/2, and s^2 - \varepsilon < -\varepsilon/2 < 0 \le f(x)^2. In every case f(x)^2 > s^2 - \varepsilon. By the method, \sup_A f^2 = s^2. The hypothesis f \ge 0 is needed: f(x) = x on [-2, 1] has \sup f = 1, but \sup f^2 = 4. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: names s = \sup_A f and states both halves as the goal (every f(x)^2 \le s^2; for every \varepsilon > 0 some f(x)^2 > s^2 - \varepsilon). - 3: proves the bounding half, naming the nonnegativity of f(x) (and of s) as what allows squaring the inequality. - 3: chooses the witness tolerance from \varepsilon (and s) before taking the witness, and verifies f(x)^2 > s^2 - \varepsilon. - 2: handles the cases the choice leaves open (s = 0, and s - \delta < 0 or its equivalent in another route). A route that writes f(x)^2 - s^2 = (f(x) - s)(f(x) + s) and bounds \abs{f(x) + s} \le 2s earns the same points for the same steps. A route that bounds s by \sqrt{\sup_A f^2}, using the least-upper-bound property and squaring non-negative numbers (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)), earns the 3 + 2 points of the witness bullets for those steps. Slips that lose the step (0 points for it): squaring an inequality between numbers that may be negative; a witness that does not depend on \varepsilon; dividing by s without treating s = 0. [C2] Let a < b, L \ge 0, and let f \colon [a, b] 	o 
R satisfy \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le L \abs{x - y} for all x, y \in [a, b]. Here is the first half of a proof that f is bounded and \sup f - \inf f \le L(b - a), all suprema on [a, b]. For x \in [a, b], \abs{f(x)} \le \abs{f(a)} + \abs{f(x) - f(a)} \le \abs{f(a)} + L(x - a) \le \abs{f(a)} + L(b - a), so f is bounded. By @prp-sup-oscillation, \sup f - \inf f = \sup \{ \abs{f(x) - f(y)} : x, y \in [a, b] \}, so it suffices to bound this supremum. Say which method this is, then complete it. The method is the bounding half of @exm-method-sup-two-halves, followed by “the supremum is the least upper bound”. Bound every value. Let x, y \in [a, b]. Both lie between a and b, so -(b - a) \le x - y \le b - a, that is, \abs{x - y} \le b - a (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). Since L \ge 0, \abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le L \abs{x - y} \le L(b - a) . So L(b - a) is an upper bound of \{ \abs{f(x) - f(y)} : x, y \in [a, b] \}, and its supremum is at most L(b - a), since a supremum is at most every upper bound, (S2). Hence \sup f - \inf f \le L(b - a). (The first half used the triangle inequality, @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e), and 0 \le x - a \le b - a.) The bound can be an equality: f(x) = Lx has \sup f - \inf f = Lb - La.

title: 8.4 Floor, Distance to the Integers, and Step Functions
content:
Floor, Distance to the Integers, and Step Functions Number Systems: From 
N to 
R gave every element of an Archimedean field an integer part (@fd3:prp-integer-part-ordered-field). Here the integer part becomes a function on all of 
R, one that jumps at every integer. From it we build the distance to the nearest integer and the step functions. Section 8.6 builds its strange functions from these pieces. The floor and the ceiling Nobody needs a definition to round 3.7 down to 3. The integer 3 is the one with 3 \le 3.7 < 3 + 1. Rounding up gives 4, and the part left over, 3.7 - 3 = 0.7, lies between 0 and 1. For a number such as \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3, with no decimal expansion handed to us, we need to know that the answer exists and is unique. Both facts are already proved: - 
R is a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field); - a complete ordered field is Archimedean (@fd3:thm-cof-complete-archimedean); - in an Archimedean field every element lies in exactly one interval [m, m + 1) with m \in 
Z (@fd3:prp-integer-part-ordered-field). Throughout, integers are read inside 
R, as in Number Systems. The embedding \iota_{
R} respects sums, products and order and reflects order (@fd3:thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field). So a sum, product or comparison of integers means the same in 
Z and in 
R. The floor of x is the integer you reach by stepping down from x to the nearest integer at or below it. [Floor, Ceiling, Fractional Part] Let x \in 
R. The floor of x, written  loor{x}, is the unique m \in 
Z with m \le x < m + 1 . The ceiling of x is \ceil{x} \coloneqq - loor{-x}. The number x -  loor{x} is the fractional part of x; it lies in [0, 1). Existence and uniqueness are @fd3:prp-integer-part-ordered-field for F = 
R. So x \mapsto  loor{x} is a function 
R 	o 
R with values in 
Z, a real function in the sense of @def-real-function. The fractional part lies in [0, 1) because subtracting  loor{x} from m \le x < m + 1 gives 0 \le x -  loor{x} < 1. For a rational x the floor is the integer part of @fd3:prp-rational-integer-part. Sets and Functions used the floor map as a school fact (@fd2:exm-maps-from-calculus (b)). Now it rests on a proof. Examples.  loor{3.7} = 3, since 3 \le 3.7 < 4.  loor{5} = 5, since 5 \le 5 < 6: at an integer the floor is the integer itself.  loor{-0.2} = -1, since -1 \le -0.2 < 0. \ceil{3.7} = - loor{-3.7} = -(-4) = 4. The graph of the floor is a staircase: on each [m, m + 1) a horizontal segment at height m, with a filled dot at its left end and a hollow dot at its right end. The figure shows the graph of  loor{x} on [-2, 3), with the dashed line y = x: the staircase never rises above the line and never falls a full unit below it, which is rule (a) below. The floor is not “drop the decimals”. For x = -2.5, dropping the decimals gives -2, but -2 \le -2.5 is false; the integer with m \le -2.5 < m + 1 is m = -3. For negative non-integers the floor is one below the truncation. Compute  loor{-7/2}, \ceil{-7/2} and  loor{7/2} +  loor{-7/2}. -4 \le -7/2 < -3, so  loor{-7/2} = -4. Next, 3 \le 7/2 < 4 gives  loor{7/2} = 3, so \ceil{-7/2} = - loor{7/2} = -3. Finally  loor{7/2} +  loor{-7/2} = 3 - 4 = -1, not 0: the floor does not commute with negation. Each of these floors was found the same way: name a candidate integer and verify the two inequalities. That is the whole method for floors. [Method: pin the floor by its inequality] How it goes. To show  loor{A} = m for a real expression A, use one of two forms. - First form. Check that m is an integer and that m \le A < m + 1. Uniqueness in @def-floor-ceiling does the rest. - Second form. Check that m is an integer and that every j \in 
Z satisfies j \le A \iff j \le m. This form rests on rule (g) of @prp-floor-rules, which turns j \le A into a statement about  loor{A}. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want ---------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- an expression A; a candidate integer m m \le A < m + 1 (first form), or  orall j \in 
Z \colon j \le A \iff j \le m (second form) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- When to use it. Every identity with a floor on one side. The first form suits a candidate given by a formula; the second suits an A built from floors and divisions, where each step of the argument is an equivalence. Common mistakes. One mistake is to drop the decimals, as in the warning above. Another is to forget that m must be an integer. For example, x - 	frac12 \le x < (x - 	frac12) + 1 holds for every real x, yet x - 	frac12 is  loor{x} only when it is an integer. Here are the rules for the floor that later chapters use. Most of them are one application of the method; rule (g) is discreteness of 
Z. [Rules for the Floor] Let x, y \in 
R, n \in 
Z and k \in 
Z_{>0}. 1. x - 1 <  loor{x} \le x, and  loor{x} = x if and only if x \in 
Z. 2.  loor{x + n} =  loor{x} + n. 3. The floor is increasing: if x \le y, then  loor{x} \le  loor{y}. 4.  loor{x} +  loor{y} \le  loor{x + y} \le  loor{x} +  loor{y} + 1. 5.  loor{-x} = - loor{x} if x \in 
Z, and  loor{-x} = - loor{x} - 1 if x 
otin 
Z. 6. \ceil{x} is the unique m \in 
Z with m - 1 < x \le m. 7. For every j \in 
Z: j \le x \iff j \le  loor{x}. 8.  loor{ loor{x}/k} =  loor{x/k}. Parts (a), (b), (d), (e) and (f) use the first form of @exm-method-floor-inequality: write down the candidate and check two inequalities. Part (g) is discreteness of 
Z: no integer lies strictly between  loor{x} and  loor{x} + 1. Part (c) is (g) applied once, and (h) needs a separate argument. Write m \coloneqq  loor{x}, so m \in 
Z and m \le x < m + 1. (a) The inequality m \le x is half of the definition, and subtracting 1 from x < m + 1 gives x - 1 < m. If x \in 
Z, the integer x satisfies x \le x < x + 1, so  loor{x} = x by the first form. Conversely, if  loor{x} = x, then x is an integer, because  loor{x} is. (b) The number m + n is an integer, and adding n to m \le x < m + 1 gives m + n \le x + n < (m + n) + 1. By the first form,  loor{x + n} = m + n. (c) Let l \coloneqq  loor{y}, and write s \coloneqq x - m and t \coloneqq y - l, both in [0, 1). Then x + y = (m + l) + (s + t) with 0 \le s + t < 2. Case s + t < 1. Then m + l \le x + y < (m + l) + 1, so  loor{x + y} = m + l by the first form. Case s + t \ge 1. Then m + l + 1 \le x + y < (m + l + 1) + 1, so  loor{x + y} = m + l + 1.
