Slips that lose the step (0 points for it): shifting only forward, although x < 0 needs a backward shift; treating  loor{x + 1} as  loor{x}. [C2: Multiplying the distance] Let n \in 
Z_{>0}. 1. Prove that \dist(nx, 
Z) \le n \dist(x, 
Z) for every x \in 
R. 2. Prove that equality holds whenever \dist(x, 
Z) \le 1/(2n). 3. Find x with strict inequality for n = 2. Hint: if \abs{y - k} \le 	frac12 for an integer k, then \dist(y, 
Z) = \abs{y - k}. (a) By induction on n \ge 1 (@fd2:thm-induction, with base 1). For n = 1 both sides are \dist(x, 
Z). If \dist(nx, 
Z) \le n \dist(x, 
Z), then subadditivity (@prp-distance-to-integer (d)) gives \dist((n + 1)x, 
Z) \le \dist(nx, 
Z) + \dist(x, 
Z) \le (n + 1)\dist(x, 
Z) . (b) First the hint. Let \abs{y - k} \le 	frac12 with k \in 
Z, and let j \in 
Z with j 
e k. Then \abs{j - k} \ge 1 by discreteness (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)). The reverse triangle inequality (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (f)) gives \abs{y - j} \ge \abs{j - k} - \abs{y - k} \ge 1 - 	frac12 = 	frac12 \ge \abs{y - k} . So \abs{y - k} is the least of the numbers \abs{y - j}, j \in 
Z, and equals \dist(y, 
Z). Now let \dist(x, 
Z) \le 1/(2n). By @prp-distance-to-integer (a) there is k \in 
Z with \abs{x - k} = \dist(x, 
Z); put t \coloneqq x - k. Then nx = nk + nt with nk \in 
Z and \abs{nx - nk} = n\abs{t} \le 	frac12. By the hint, \dist(nx, 
Z) = n\abs{t} = n \dist(x, 
Z). @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) (\abs{nt} = n\abs{t}, as n > 0). (c) x = 	frac12: \dist(1, 
Z) = 0 < 1 = 2 \dist(	frac12, 
Z). Here \dist(x, 
Z) = 	frac12 > 	frac14 = 1/(2n), so (b) does not apply. Exercise A2 (c) gave the inequality only; (b) adds where it is an equality.

title: 8.5 The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers
content:
The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers Chapter 1 gave every non-negative real number its n-th roots (@lem-reals-nth-root). It gave every positive real number its rational powers (@def-rational-power), so a power with a rational exponent such as 2^{3/2} = (\sqrt 2)^3 already has a meaning. A power such as 2^{\sqrt 2} does not, and no root will give it one. This section borrows three facts about a single function, the exponential, and derives everything else from them: the logarithm, real powers and their laws, and how fast the exponential grows. Its main theorem shows that two of the three facts already determine the function completely. Powers that roots cannot reach A power a^{m/n} with a > 0 is a power of an n-th root, (\sqrt[n]{a})^m. The exponent \sqrt 2 is not of the form m/n, because \sqrt 2 is irrational, as Section 8.3 showed from @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two. So 2^{\sqrt 2} is not a root of anything we know. The naive answer, “the limit of 2^q as rational q approach \sqrt 2”, needs limits of functions, which this volume does not have. Our route goes through one function, the exponential, and one rule, a^x \coloneqq \exp(x \log a). Constructing the exponential needs power series, so we borrow it: three facts, and everything else is proved. What this volume borrows about the exponential The exponential should turn sums into products, and near 0 it should look like 1 + x. Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 7 constructs it as a power series and proves the facts below. Its 
R is a complete ordered field, so by @fd3:thm-cof-uniqueness it is our 
R, up to the one order-preserving field isomorphism, and the function carries over along it. What This Volume Borrows about the Exponential There is a function \exp \colon 
R 	o 
R with the following properties. They are assumed here and proved in Integration, Series, and Function Spaces, Chapter 7. 1. \exp(x + y) = \exp x \cdot \exp y for all x, y \in 
R. 2. \exp x \ge 1 + x for every x \in 
R. 3. For every y \in 
R with y > 0 there is x \in 
R with \exp x = y. In words: the addition rule (E1) turns addition of arguments into multiplication of values. The tangent-line bound (E2) puts the graph of \exp on or above the line y = 1 + x. The value property (E3) says that every positive real number is a value of \exp. Chapter 3 borrowed cosine and sine in the same way (@ax-cosine-sine). Nothing in Sections 8.1–8.4, and nothing earlier in this section, uses these three facts. From here on we use these three facts about \exp and no others, and each proof that uses one names it. The addition rule and the tangent-line bound carry most of the weight. The value property is what makes the logarithm defined on all of (0, \infty). Neither of the first two facts follows from the other. The constant function 1 satisfies the addition rule, since 1 = 1 \cdot 1, but not the tangent-line bound: at x = 1 it would need 1 \ge 2. The function x \mapsto 1 + x satisfies the tangent-line bound with equality, but not the addition rule: at x = y = 1 it gives 3, while (1 + 1)(1 + 1) = 4. The three facts say nothing about continuity or derivatives. That \exp is continuous, and equal to its own derivative, is true. But it is not among the three facts, and no proof in this volume may quote it. Nor is e^x a notation yet. Until real powers are defined and shown to agree with \exp, we write \exp x, never e^x. First consequences Negative integer exponents appear as soon as we divide. For a real u 
e 0 and n \in 
Z_{>0}, the power u^{-n} = (u^{-1})^n = (1/u)^n is the integer power of Chapter 1 (@def-integer-power). By @prp-integer-power-laws (d), u^{-n} = 1/u^n. We also write \exp(t)^n for (\exp t)^n. The first proposition collects what the addition rule and the tangent-line bound say at once. [First Consequences of the Addition Rule and the Tangent-Line Bound] 1. \exp 0 = 1. 2. \exp x > 0 and \exp(-x) = 1/\exp x for every x \in 
R. 3. \exp is strictly increasing on 
R. 4. \exp x \le 1/(1 - x) for every x \in 
R with x < 1. 5. \exp(nx) = (\exp x)^n for every x \in 
R and every n \in 
Z. Part (a) is the addition rule at x = y = 0, with the tangent-line bound to rule out \exp 0 = 0. Part (b) writes \exp x as a square, \exp(x/2)^2. Part (c) factors a difference, as in @exm-method-factor-difference, but with a product. The addition rule factors \exp y - \exp x as \exp x \cdot (\exp(y - x) - 1), and the tangent-line bound shows that the bracket is positive. Part (d) is the tangent-line bound at -x, turned upside down. (a) By the addition rule, \exp 0 = \exp(0 + 0) = (\exp 0)^2, so \exp 0 \cdot (\exp 0 - 1) = 0. By the tangent-line bound, \exp 0 \ge 1 + 0 = 1, so \exp 0 
e 0. A product that is zero with one factor non-zero has its other factor zero, so \exp 0 - 1 = 0. (b) By the addition rule and (a), \exp x \cdot \exp(-x) = \exp 0 = 1. Hence \exp x 
e 0, and \exp(-x) = 1/\exp x because inverses are unique. The same holds at x/2, so \exp(x/2) 
e 0. By the addition rule, \exp x = \exp(x/2 + x/2) = (\exp(x/2))^2, which is > 0 because it is the square of a non-zero number. (c) Let x < y. By the addition rule, \exp y = \exp x \cdot \exp(y - x), so \exp y - \exp x = \exp x \cdot  igl( \exp(y - x) - 1  igr) \ge \exp x \cdot (y - x) > 0 . The first inequality is the tangent-line bound at y - x, multiplied by \exp x > 0 from (b). The last step holds because a product of two positive numbers is positive, (O4): here \exp x > 0 and y - x > 0. (d) Let x < 1. By the tangent-line bound at -x, \exp(-x) \ge 1 - x > 0. Both numbers are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the inequality: 1/\exp(-x) \le 1/(1 - x). And 1/\exp(-x) = \exp x by (b) applied to -x. (e) For n \in 
N we induct on n. For n = 0, \exp(0 \cdot x) = \exp 0 = 1 = (\exp x)^0 by (a). If \exp(nx) = (\exp x)^n, then by the addition rule \exp((n + 1)x) = \exp(nx + x) = \exp(nx) \exp x = (\exp x)^n \exp x = (\exp x)^{n+1} . For n \in 
Z_{>0}, (b) and the case just proved give \exp(-nx) = 1/\exp(nx) = 1/(\exp x)^n = (\exp x)^{-n}. @fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules (d) (zero products), (a) (inverses are unique). @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) (non-zero squares are positive), (c) (multiplying by a positive number). @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (c) (reciprocals reverse order). @prp-integer-power-laws (d) (1/u^n = u^{-n}). @fd1:ax-induction. The value property (E3) appears nowhere in this proof. So every part of @prp-exp-first-consequences holds for any function that satisfies the addition rule and the tangent-line bound. The main theorem below depends on that. Which of the three borrowed facts does each of the following use: \exp 0 = 1; \exp is strictly increasing; the inverse of \exp is defined at every point of (0, \infty)? \exp 0 = 1 uses the addition rule (E1) and the tangent-line bound (E2), by the proof of (a). Strict increase uses the same two facts, through (b) and (c). The inverse being defined on all of (0, \infty) needs every positive number to be a value, which is the value property (E3). That the inverse is a function at all is (c), so the first two facts enter too. Squeeze, then close the gap by Archimedes The main theorem computes \exp x as a supremum. To show L = \sup S, @fd2:def-order-supremum asks that L be an upper bound and that no smaller number be one. The second half often comes from members of S approaching L at a known rate. A small case first. Let S be the set of the numbers 1 - 1/n for n \in 
Z_{>0}, and let L = 1. Every member of S is at most 1. The member with index n is L - 1/n, so the members come within 1/n of L. Given any L' < 1, a large n has 1/n < 1 - L', and then 1 - 1/n > L'. So no L' < 1 is an upper bound, and \sup S = 1. The method below does the same with any constant C in place of 1 in L - 1/n. [Method: squeeze, then close the gap by Archimedes] How it goes. To prove \sup S = L for a set S \subseteq 
R: 1. show that every s \in S satisfies s \le L; 2. find a constant C > 0, fixed before n is chosen, and an N_0 \in 
Z_{>0} such that for every integer n \ge N_0 some s_n \in S satisfies s_n \ge L - C/n; 3. given L' < L, put \varepsilon \coloneqq (L - L')/C > 0. By @fd3:prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is N with 1/n < \varepsilon for all n \ge N. For n \ge \max\{N, N_0\} we get s_n \ge L - C/n > L - C\varepsilon = L'. So no L' < L is an upper bound, and L is the least upper bound. When to use it. A supremum has been guessed, and the members of S come with an index n and an error estimate of the form C/n. Common mistakes. - The “constant” C is allowed to depend on n. With C = n, the estimate s_n \ge L - 1 says nothing about small gaps. - The constant is C = 0, which leaves \varepsilon undefined. If the estimate seems to come with C = 0, enlarge C: a lower bound L - C/n stays true when C grows. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------- every s \in S has s \le L; for n \ge N_0 some s_n \in S has s_n \ge L - C/n, with C > 0 fixed in advance no L' < L is an upper bound of S L' < L; \varepsilon \coloneqq (L - L')/C > 0; 1/n < \varepsilon for n \ge N some s \in S with s > L': take s_n, n \ge \max\{N, N_0\} --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The real numbers form a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). Every complete ordered field is Archimedean (@fd3:thm-cof-complete-archimedean), so the Archimedean property, which the last step of the method uses, holds in 
R. Two facts determine the exponential For a fixed x, the numbers (1 + x/n)^n are built from x by arithmetic alone. At x = 1 and n = 2, 3, 4 they are 9/4 = 2.25, 64/27 \approx 2.370 and 625/256 \approx 2.441. The theorem says that these numbers squeeze \exp x from below, and that their supremum is \exp x. [The Exponential Is Determined by Its Addition Rule and Tangent-Line Bound] Let x \in 
R, and let S_x \coloneqq \Bigl\{ \Bigl(1 +  rac{x}{n}\Bigr)^{n} : n \in 
Z_{>0},\ n > \abs{x} \Bigr\} . Then S_x is non-empty and bounded above, and \exp x = \sup S_x. Consequently, if E \colon 
R 	o 
R is any function satisfying the addition rule (E1) and the tangent-line bound (E2) with E in place of \exp, then E = \exp. [Scratch work] We want two bounds on (1 + x/n)^n: above by \exp x, and below by \exp x minus something of size C/n. Upper. The tangent-line bound at x/n gives \exp(x/n) \ge 1 + x/n. Raising both sides to the n-th power gives \exp(x/n)^n \ge (1 + x/n)^n, and \exp(x/n)^n = \exp x by @prp-exp-first-consequences (e). But raising an inequality to a power is allowed only between non-negative numbers (@lem-reals-nth-root (a)). At x = -3, n = 2, the base 1 + x/n = -1/2 is negative. So we ask for n > \abs{x}, which makes 1 + x/n > 0. Lower. Part (d) of the same proposition at x/n gives \exp(x/n) \le 1/(1 - x/n), valid when x/n < 1, so \exp x \le (1 - x/n)^{-n}. To compare this with (1 + x/n)^n, multiply and divide by (1 - x/n)^n: \Bigl(1 +  rac{x}{n}\Bigr)^{n} = \Bigl(1 -  rac{x^2}{n^2}\Bigr)^{n} \Bigl(1 -  rac{x}{n}\Bigr)^{-n} . The middle factor is close to 1: Bernoulli’s inequality gives (1 - x^2/n^2)^n \ge 1 - x^2/n. That is the C/n we need. ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- the addition rule and the tangent-line bound; @prp-exp-first-consequences; n > \abs{x} (1 + x/n)^n \le \exp x and (1 + x/n)^n \ge \exp x - C/n, C > 0 not depending on n 1 \pm x/n > 0; \exp x \le (1 - x/n)^{-n} (1 - x^2/n^2)^n \ge 1 - (	ext{const})/n: Bernoulli ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Then @exm-method-archimedes-squeeze finishes, with C \coloneqq (x^2 + 1)\exp x. The +1 keeps C > 0 at x = 0. Before reading on: why must n exceed \abs{x}? Find every place it is used. Fix x \in 
R. By the Archimedean property there is N_0 \in 
Z_{>0} with N_0 > \abs{x}, so S_x 
e \varnothing. Let n \in 
Z_{>0} with n > \abs{x}. Then \abs{x/n} < 1, so 1 + x/n > 0 and 1 - x/n > 0 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). Upper bound. By the tangent-line bound at x/n, 0 < 1 + x/n \le \exp(x/n). Raising to the n-th power keeps an inequality between non-negative numbers, so (1 + x/n)^n \le \exp(x/n)^n. And \exp(x/n)^n = \exp(n \cdot x/n) = \exp x by @prp-exp-first-consequences (e). So \exp x is an upper bound of S_x, and \sup S_x exists. Lower estimate. Since x/n < 1, @prp-exp-first-consequences (d) gives \exp(x/n) \le 1/(1 - x/n). Both sides are positive, so raising to the n-th power, with part (e) on the left, gives \exp x = \exp(x/n)^n \le \Bigl(1 -  rac{x}{n}\Bigr)^{-n} . Splitting the power of a product, (1 + x/n)^n = (1 - x^2/n^2)^n (1 - x/n)^{-n}. Here (1 - x^2/n^2)^n > 0, since 1 - x^2/n^2 = (1 + x/n)(1 - x/n) > 0. Multiply the display by this positive number, and then apply Bernoulli’s inequality (@fd2:thm-bernoulli) to -x^2/n^2 \ge -1, using \exp x > 0:  egin{aligned} \Bigl(1 +  rac{x}{n}\Bigr)^{n} &\ge \Bigl(1 -  rac{x^2}{n^2}\Bigr)^{n} \exp x \ge \Bigl(1 -  rac{x^2}{n}\Bigr) \exp x \ &\ge \exp x -  rac{(x^2 + 1) \exp x}{n} . \end{aligned} Conclusion. Put C \coloneqq (x^2 + 1)\exp x. It depends on x only, and C > 0 by @prp-exp-first-consequences (b). For every integer n \ge N_0 the member s_n \coloneqq (1 + x/n)^n of S_x satisfies s_n \ge \exp x - C/n. By @exm-method-archimedes-squeeze, \sup S_x = \exp x. Uniqueness. Let E satisfy the addition rule (E1) and the tangent-line bound (E2), with E in place of \exp. The proof of @prp-exp-first-consequences used only these two facts and field and order rules, so its conclusions hold for E. The argument above used only those conclusions, the tangent-line bound, and facts about 
R. So E(x) = \sup S_x = \exp x for every x \in 
R. Two functions with the same domain, codomain and values are equal, so E = \exp. @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (powers keep order). @fd2:prp-power-laws (c) (power of a product). @fd2:prp-function-equality (equal functions). The set S_x never mentions \exp, so the theorem is a formula: \exp x is pinned between computable numbers, as the next definition shows at x = 1. And the three borrowed facts describe a function that the first two already determine. The number e [Euler’s Number] e \coloneqq \exp 1. By the proof of @thm-exp-unique at x = 1, for every integer n \ge 2, \Bigl(1 +  rac1n\Bigr)^{n} \le e \le \Bigl(1 -  rac1n\Bigr)^{-n} . At n = 2 this reads 9/4 \le e \le 4, so e > 2. Exercise B1 below squeezes harder. Now we can say more about what fails without the tangent-line bound, beyond the constant function 1. The function F(x) \coloneqq \exp(2x) satisfies the addition rule, since F(x + y) = \exp(2x)\exp(2y). It also has the value property, since \exp t = y gives F(t/2) = y. It is not \exp: F(1) = \exp 2 = (\exp 1)^2 = e \cdot e by @prp-exp-first-consequences (e), and e \cdot e 
e e because e > 1. So, by @thm-exp-unique, it must fail the tangent-line bound. It does, at x = -1/2: F(-1/2) = \exp(-1) = 1/e < 1/2 = 1 + (-1/2), as e > 2. Without the tangent-line bound, the addition rule and the value property leave the speed of the function free. The logarithm By @prp-exp-first-consequences (b) and (c), \exp is a strictly increasing map from 
R into (0, \infty). By the value property, every point of (0, \infty) is a value. So \exp \colon 
R 	o (0, \infty) is a bijection. The logarithm undoes the exponential. The Logarithm The logarithm \log \colon (0, \infty) 	o 
R is the inverse of the bijection \exp \colon 
R 	o (0, \infty): for y > 0, \log y is the unique x \in 
R with \exp x = y. In words: the existence of x is the value property. Its uniqueness holds because a strictly increasing map is injective (@fd2:prp-strictly-monotone-injective). So \exp(\log y) = y for every y > 0 and \log(\exp x) = x for every x \in 
R. By @thm-monotone-inverse, \log is strictly increasing, and its graph is the graph of \exp with the coordinates swapped, that is, reflected in the line y = x. We write \log and never \ln. The picture shows \exp above the line y = 1 + x, touching it at (0, 1), and \log as its mirror image in y = x, through (1, 0). It illustrates; no proof below reads anything off it. What are \log(\exp 2) and \log(1/e)? \log(\exp 2) = 2, since \log undoes \exp. And \exp(-1) = 1/\exp 1 = 1/e by @prp-exp-first-consequences (b), so \log(1/e) = -1. Each rule for \log comes from a rule for \exp: apply \exp to both sides and use that \exp is injective. [Rules for the Logarithm] Let x, y \in 
R with x, y > 0. 1. \log 1 = 0 and \log e = 1. 2. \log(xy) = \log x + \log y and \log(1/x) = -\log x. 3. 1 - 1/x \le \log x \le x - 1, and each inequality is an equality only at x = 1. For (a) and (b), compute \exp of each side. For (c), the tangent-line bound at t = \log x gives x \ge 1 + \log x, and at t = \log(1/x) it gives the other half. Strictness needs \exp t > 1 + t for t 
e 0, which the three facts do not state. We get it by writing \exp t as a square, \exp(t/2)^2 \ge (1 + t/2)^2 = 1 + t + t^2/4, valid while 1 + t/2 \ge 0. (a) We have \exp 0 = 1 by @prp-exp-first-consequences (a), and \exp 1 = e by the definition of e. So \log 1 = 0 and \log e = 1, by the definition of \log. (b) By the addition rule, \exp(\log x + \log y) = \exp(\log x)\exp(\log y) = xy, so \log(xy) = \log x + \log y by the definition of \log. Then \log x + \log(1/x) = \log 1 = 0 by (a). (c) First, \exp t > 1 + t for every t 
e 0. Case t \ge -2. Then 1 + t/2 \ge 0, and \exp(t/2) \ge 1 + t/2 by the tangent-line bound. Squaring keeps an inequality between non-negative numbers, so by the addition rule \exp t = \exp(t/2)^2 \ge \Bigl(1 +  rac t2\Bigr)^{2} = 1 + t +  rac{t^2}{4} > 1 + t , the last step because t^2 > 0. Case t < -2. Then 1 + t < -1 < 0 < \exp t by @prp-exp-first-consequences (b). Now the tangent-line bound at t = \log x gives x = \exp(\log x) \ge 1 + \log x, that is, \log x \le x - 1. By the strict inequality just proved, it is strict when \log x 
e 0, that is, when x 
e 1. By (b), \log(1/x) = -\log x. The tangent-line bound at t = -\log x gives 1/x \ge 1 - \log x, that is, \log x \ge 1 - 1/x, again strict when x 
e 1. At x = 1 all three numbers are 0. @def-euler-number (e = \exp 1). @def-logarithm (\log inverts \exp). @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (squares keep order). @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e) (non-zero squares are positive). Part (c) gives numbers: 1/2 < \log 2 < 1, for example. Real powers A real power is the exponential of a multiple of a logarithm. For example, the rule below sets 2^{\sqrt 2} \coloneqq \exp(\sqrt 2 \log 2) and 8^{1/3} \coloneqq \exp(	frac13 \log 8). The second should be 2, the cube root of 8, and we will check that it is. Real Powers Let a, x \in 
R. - If a > 0, then a^x \coloneqq \exp(x \log a). - If a = 0 and x > 0, then 0^x \coloneqq 0. No other pair (a, x) is given a value by this definition; in particular there are no real powers of a negative base. In words: to raise a to the power x, take the logarithm, multiply by x, and exponentiate. By @def-logarithm, \log(a^x) = x \log a for a > 0. This is the definition with \log applied to both sides, not a theorem. The symbol a^x was already in use for x \in 
N (@fd2:def-power), and Chapter 1 gave \sqrt[n]{a} and a^{m/n}. The next proposition shows that the new definition agrees with both wherever they overlap, so no symbol now has two meanings. Base zero. For x = n \in 
Z_{>0} both definitions give 0^n = 0. For x = 0, the definition of real powers says nothing. The symbol 0^0 keeps the value 1 that @fd2:def-power gives it as a natural-number power. For x < 0, 0^x would have to be 1/0^{-x} = 1/0, so it is left undefined. Negative bases. \log a is defined only for a > 0, so the formula \exp(x \log a) cannot start. One could set (-8)^{1/3} \coloneqq -2, but the rule (a^x)^y = a^{xy} would then break. With x = 2 and y = 1/6 it would give (-8)^{1/3} = ((-8)^2)^{1/6} = 64^{1/6} = 2, not -2. The real cube root of a negative number is a separate object, \sqrt[3]{-8} = -2 of @exm-odd-roots, and it keeps its own symbol. Does @def-real-power give 0^0 a value? Is (1/2)^{-1} = 2? No: base 0 is covered only for x > 0. The symbol 0^0 keeps its natural-number value 1 from @fd2:def-power, which this definition does not touch. Yes: (1/2)^{-1} = \exp(-\log(1/2)) = \exp(\log 2) = 2, since -\log(1/2) = \log 2 by @prp-log-rules (b). [Real Powers Agree with Roots and Integer Powers] Let a \in 
R with a > 0. 1. For m \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}, the real power a^{m/n} is (\sqrt[n]{a})^m, the rational power of @def-rational-power, where (\sqrt[n]{a})^m is the integer power of Chapter 1. 2. In particular, for n = 1, the real power a^m is the integer power a^m (for m \ge 0, the power of @fd2:def-power). 3. e^x = \exp x for every x \in 
R. Show that a^{1/n} is a non-negative number whose n-th power is a; the uniqueness of roots makes it \sqrt[n]{a}. Then take the m-th power. (a) By the definition of real powers, c \coloneqq a^{1/n} = \exp((1/n) \log a), and c > 0 by @prp-exp-first-consequences (b). By part (e) of the same proposition, with the integer n, c^n = \exp\Bigl(n \cdot  rac 1n \log a\Bigr) = \exp(\log a) = a . So c \ge 0 and c^n = a. By the uniqueness in @lem-reals-nth-root (b), c = \sqrt[n]{a}. By part (e) again, now with (1/n) \log a in place of x and the integer m, a^{m/n} = \exp\Bigl(m \cdot  rac 1n \log a\Bigr) = c^m = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m , and part (e) states c^m with the integer powers of @def-integer-power when m < 0. (b) At n = 1, \sqrt[1]{a} is the unique b \ge 0 with b^1 = a, which is a itself. So (a) gives a^{m/1} = a^m. (c) By @prp-log-rules (a), e^x = \exp(x \log e) = \exp(x \cdot 1) = \exp x. @def-real-power (a^x = \exp(x \log a)). From now on e^x and \exp x are the same thing, and we use whichever reads better. Is 4^{1/2} = 2? Answer from @prp-real-power-consistent. Yes. By (a) with m = 1, n = 2, 4^{1/2} = (\sqrt 4)^1 = \sqrt 4, the unique non-negative real number whose square is 4. Since 2 \ge 0 and 2^2 = 4, that number is 2. The laws of exponents now come in one line each, because each is a law of \exp or of \log in disguise. For whole-number exponents they are school rules: 2^3 \cdot 2^2 = 8 \cdot 4 = 32 = 2^5, and (2^3)^2 = 64 = 2^6. The proposition says that they hold for every real exponent. [Laws of Real Powers] Let a, b, x, y \in 
R with a, b > 0. 1. a^{x + y} = a^x a^y and a^{-x} = 1/a^x. 2. (a^x)^y = a^{xy}. 3. (ab)^x = a^x b^x. 4. a^x > 0. 5. As a function of x on 
R: x \mapsto a^x is strictly increasing if a > 1, strictly decreasing if a < 1, and constant 1 if a = 1. 6. As a function of a on (0, \infty): a \mapsto a^x is strictly increasing if x > 0 and strictly decreasing if x < 0. Write each power as \exp of a product and use the addition rule, the log rules, and the monotonicity of \exp and \log. (a) a^{x+y} = \exp(x \log a + y \log a) = a^x a^y by the addition rule. Also a^{-x} = \exp(-x \log a) = 1/a^x by @prp-exp-first-consequences (b). (b) a^x > 0 by (d), and \log(a^x) = x \log a, so (a^x)^y = \exp(y x \log a) = a^{xy}. (c) (ab)^x = \exp(x \log a + x \log b) = a^x b^x, by @prp-log-rules (b) and the addition rule. (d) This is @prp-exp-first-consequences (b). (e) If a > 1, then \log a > \log 1 = 0, since \log is strictly increasing. So x \mapsto x \log a is strictly increasing, because multiplying by a positive number keeps order. Composing with the strictly increasing \exp gives a strictly increasing function (@prp-monotone-algebra (e)). If a < 1, then \log a < 0, and x \mapsto x \log a is strictly decreasing, because multiplying by a negative number reverses order. The composite is strictly decreasing by the same rule. If a = 1, a^x = \exp 0 = 1. (f) Let 0 < a < b. Then \log a < \log b. If x > 0, then x \log a < x \log b, and \exp keeps the order. If x < 0, the order is reversed and \exp keeps the reversed order. @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), (d) (multiplying by a sign). @def-logarithm (\log increasing). @prp-log-rules (a) (\log 1 = 0). Is 2^{\sqrt 2} > 2? Is (\sqrt 2)^{\sqrt 2} < 2? Yes to both. Since 1^2 = 1 < 2 = (\sqrt 2)^2, we have \sqrt 2 > 1, because squares of non-negative numbers keep order. The map x \mapsto 2^x is strictly increasing by @prp-real-power-laws (e), so 2^{\sqrt 2} > 2^1 = 2. For the second, \sqrt 2 = 2^{1/2} by @prp-real-power-consistent (a). So (\sqrt 2)^{\sqrt 2} = 2^{\sqrt 2/2}, by @prp-real-power-laws (b). Since (\sqrt 2)^2 = 2 < 4 = 2^2, \sqrt 2 < 2, so \sqrt 2/2 < 1 and 2^{\sqrt 2/2} < 2^1 = 2. @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) (comparing squares). The exponential outruns every power How fast does \exp x grow? The tangent-line bound gives only \exp x \ge 1 + x, which a linear function matches. Raising the tangent-line bound to a power, as in the proof of @thm-exp-unique, does much better. A small case first. Split 10 into two halves. By the addition rule, \exp 10 = (\exp 5)^2, and the tangent-line bound gives \exp 5 \ge 6, so \exp 10 \ge 36. The tangent-line bound at 10 alone gives only \exp 10 \ge 11. Splitting into more pieces does better still. [The Exponential Beats Every Power] 1. For every x > 0 and every k \in 
N, \exp x >  igl(x/(k + 1) igr)^{k+1}. Hence, for every M > 0, \exp x > M x^k for all x > M (k + 1)^{k+1}. 2. For every x > 0 and every m \in 
Z_{>0}, \log x < m x^{1/m}. Hence, for every \varepsilon > 0, \log x < \varepsilon x for all x > 4/\varepsilon^2. For (a), split x into k + 1 equal parts and apply the tangent-line bound to each: \exp x = \exp(x/(k + 1))^{k+1} \ge (1 + x/(k + 1))^{k+1}. Dropping the 1 loses a little, and gives a strict inequality. For (b), apply \log t \le t - 1 not at x but at x^{1/m}, which is much smaller. (a) Let x > 0, k \in 
N, t \coloneqq x/(k + 1) > 0. By the tangent-line bound, \exp t \ge 1 + t > t \ge 0. Raising to the power k + 1 keeps a strict inequality between non-negative numbers, so by @prp-exp-first-consequences (e), \exp x = (\exp t)^{k+1} > t^{k+1} =  rac{x^{k+1}}{(k + 1)^{k+1}} = x^k \cdot  rac{x}{(k + 1)^{k+1}} . If M > 0 and x > M(k + 1)^{k+1}, then x > 0, x^k > 0 and x/(k + 1)^{k+1} > M, so the right side exceeds M x^k. (b) Let x > 0 and m \in 
Z_{>0}. By the definition of real powers, \log(x^{1/m}) = (1/m) \log x. So, by @prp-log-rules (c) at x^{1/m} > 0, \log x = m \log(x^{1/m}) \le m (x^{1/m} - 1) < m x^{1/m} . Now let \varepsilon > 0 and x > 4/\varepsilon^2, and take m = 2. Here x^{1/2} = \sqrt x by @prp-real-power-consistent (a). Since \sqrt x \ge 0 and (\sqrt x)^2 = x > (2/\varepsilon)^2, we get \sqrt x > 2/\varepsilon, because squares of non-negative numbers keep order. So 2 < \varepsilon \sqrt x and 2\sqrt x < \varepsilon \sqrt x \sqrt x = \varepsilon x. Hence \log x < 2\sqrt x < \varepsilon x. @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (powers keep order). @fd2:prp-power-laws (c) (power of a product). @def-integer-power, @prp-integer-power-laws (d) ((1/u)^n = 1/u^n). @def-real-power (\log(a^x) = x \log a). @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) (comparing squares). The thresholds are explicit: \exp x > 1000\, x^2 once x > 1000 \cdot 27 = 27{,}000, and \log x < x/100 once x > 40{,}000. They are far from the best, and need not be good. They need to exist, depending on M, k or \varepsilon only, never on x. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-exp-unique. 1. Which of the addition rule (E1), the tangent-line bound (E2) and the value property (E3) does the proof use, including through @prp-exp-first-consequences? 2. Where does Bernoulli’s inequality enter, and at which real number is it applied? 3. Write out the two bounds on e that the proof gives at x = 1, n = 2. 4. Take x = -3 and n = 2. Which step of the upper-bound argument fails? Is its conclusion (1 + x/n)^n \le \exp x still true for this pair? (a) Only the addition rule (E1) and the tangent-line bound (E2). The proof of @prp-exp-first-consequences uses these two and field and order rules. The proof of the theorem adds the tangent-line bound at x/n. The value property (E3) is not used, which is why the uniqueness sentence asks only for the first two. (b) In the lower estimate, to bound (1 - x^2/n^2)^n below by 1 - x^2/n. It is applied at -x^2/n^2, which is \ge -1 because n > \abs{x}. (c) (1 + 1/2)^2 = 9/4 \le e \le (1 - 1/2)^{-2} = 4. (d) Here n = 2 < 3 = \abs{x}, and 1 + x/n = -1/2 < 0. The step “raise 1 + x/n \le \exp(x/n) to the n-th power” fails: @lem-reals-nth-root (a) needs a non-negative smaller side. The conclusion fails too: (-1/2)^2 = 1/4, while \exp(-3) = 1/\exp 3 < 1/4, because \exp 3 > 1 + 3 = 4. The inequality \exp 3 > 4 is strict by the first step of the proof of @prp-log-rules (c). [A2] True or false? Give a reason or a counterexample. 1. \exp(2x) = (\exp x)^2 for every x \in 
R. 2. \log(x + y) = \log x + \log y for all x, y > 0. 3. @def-real-power defines (-8)^{1/3}. 4. a^x b^y = (ab)^{x + y} for all a, b > 0 and x, y \in 
R. (a) True, by the addition rule (E1) with y = x, or by @prp-exp-first-consequences (e) with n = 2. (b) False. At x = y = 1 the left side is \log 2 and the right side is 0. But \log 2 > \log 1 = 0, since \log is strictly increasing. (c) False: the base -8 is negative, and @def-real-power gives no real powers of a negative base. The real number \sqrt[3]{-8} = -2 is the odd root of @exm-odd-roots, a different symbol. (d) False. With a = 1, b = 2, x = 1, y = 0: the left side is 1^1 \cdot 2^0 = 1, the right side 2^1 = 2 (values by @prp-real-power-consistent (b)). B. Practice [B1] Prove that 2.5 < e < 3. Hint: one value of n in the bounds after @def-euler-number does both. Take n = 6. The lower bound gives e \ge \Bigl( rac76\Bigr)^{6} =  rac{117649}{46656} >  rac52 , because 2 \cdot 117649 = 235298 > 233280 = 5 \cdot 46656. The upper bound gives e \le \Bigl(1 -  rac16\Bigr)^{-6} = \Bigl( rac65\Bigr)^{6} =  rac{46656}{15625} < 3 , because 46656 < 46875 = 3 \cdot 15625. Hence 2.5 < e < 3. Smaller n is not enough: at n = 2, 3, 4, 5 the upper bound (n/(n - 1))^n is 4, 27/8, 256/81, 3125/1024, all above 3. [B2: Prove or disprove] Prove each true statement and give a counterexample to each false one. 1. \exp x \ge 1 + x + x^2/2 for every x \ge 0. 2. \log x \le x/e for every x > 0. 3. If 0 < a \le b, then a^x \le b^x for every x \in 
R. 4. There is a polynomial function p on 
R (@def-polynomial-rational-function) with p(x) = \exp x for every x \in 
R. (a) True. Let x \ge 0 and n \in 
Z_{>0} with n > x and n \ge 2. By the binomial theorem in the commutative ring 
R (@thm-binomial-commutative-ring), (1 + x/n)^n is a sum of non-negative terms. Among them are 1, n \cdot x/n = x and  inom n2 x^2/n^2 = (1 - 1/n) x^2/2. Dropping the others, \exp x \ge \Bigl(1 +  rac xn\Bigr)^{n} \ge 1 + x +  rac{x^2}{2} -  rac{x^2}{2n} , where the first inequality is the upper-bound half of @thm-exp-unique. Suppose \delta \coloneqq 1 + x + x^2/2 - \exp x > 0. Then x 
e 0, since at x = 0 we have \delta = 0. The display gives x^2/(2n) \ge \delta for every integer n \ge 2 with n > x. By @fd3:prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is n \ge 2 with n > x and 1/n < 2\delta/x^2, a contradiction. So \delta \le 0. (b) True. By @prp-log-rules (b), (a) and (c), \log x = \log(e \cdot x/e) = 1 + \log(x/e) \le 1 + (x/e - 1) = x/e. (c) False. Take a = 1, b = 2, x = -1: 1^{-1} = 1 > 1/2 = 2^{-1}. The statement holds for x \ge 0 (@prp-real-power-laws (f), with equality at x = 0) and reverses for x < 0. (d) False. Suppose p(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} a_i x^i = \exp x for all x. Put S \coloneqq \sum_{i<d} \abs{a_i} and M \coloneqq S + \abs{a_d} + 1 \ge 1. For x \ge 1 we have x^i \le x^d for i \le d. So the triangle inequality gives \abs{p(x)} \le (S + \abs{a_d}) x^d < M x^d. By @prp-exp-beats-powers (a) with k = d, any x > M(d + 1)^{d+1}, which is \ge 1, has \exp x > M x^d > \abs{p(x)} \ge p(x), a contradiction. @fd2:prp-power-laws (e) (powers of x \ge 1). @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e) (triangle inequality). [B3: Put the proof in order] Here are lines of the lower estimate in the proof of @thm-exp-unique, shuffled, with two lines that do not belong. Write an order of the correct lines that makes a proof, and say why each distractor fails. 1. Fix x \in 
R and an integer n > \abs{x}. 2. Then 1 + x/n > 0 and 1 - x/n > 0. 3. By @prp-exp-first-consequences (d), \exp(x/n) \le 1/(1 - x/n), so \exp x \le (1 - x/n)^{-n}. 4. (1 + x/n)^n = (1 - x^2/n^2)^n (1 - x/n)^{-n}. 5. So (1 + x/n)^n \ge (1 - x^2/n^2)^n \exp x. 6. Bernoulli’s inequality at -x^2/n^2 \ge -1 gives (1 - x^2/n^2)^n \ge 1 - x^2/n. 7. Hence (1 + x/n)^n \ge \exp x - x^2 \exp x / n. 8. (D1) By the tangent-line bound, \exp x \ge 1 + x, so (1 + x/n)^n \ge 1 + x. 9. (D2) Bernoulli’s inequality at x^2/n^2 gives (1 - x^2/n^2)^n \ge 1 + x^2/n. Each line may come only after the lines it uses. Line (ii) uses (i). Line (iii) uses (ii), since it needs x/n < 1 and positive sides. Line (iv) uses (ii), since it divides by 1 - x/n 
e 0. Line (v) uses (iii) and (iv). Line (vi) uses only (i), since it needs x^2/n^2 \le 1. Line (vii) uses (v) and (vi). Every order respecting these constraints is accepted. One is (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii); another is (i), (vi), (ii), (iv), (iii), (v), (vii). (D1) bounds the wrong thing: the goal is a lower bound by \exp x - C/n, and 1 + x is not one. Its “so” is also unjustified: (1 + x/n)^n \ge 1 + x is Bernoulli’s inequality, not a consequence of \exp x \ge 1 + x. (D2) has the wrong sign: Bernoulli’s inequality at u = -x^2/n^2 gives 1 + nu = 1 - x^2/n. The claimed bound is false, since for x 
e 0 the left side is < 1 and the right side > 1. C. Going deeper [C1: Find the error] Here is a proof that \exp is strictly increasing: “Let x < y. By the addition rule, \exp y - \exp x = \exp(y - x), and by the tangent-line bound, \exp(y - x) \ge 1 + (y - x) > 0. So \exp y > \exp x.” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? Name the line that fails, and show that it fails with numbers. The conclusion is true: it is @prp-exp-first-consequences (c). The argument does not prove it. The first equality is false: the addition rule (E1) gives the quotient \exp y / \exp x = \exp(y - x), not the difference. At x = 0, y = 1: \exp 1 - \exp 0 = e - 1, while \exp(1 - 0) = e, and e - 1 
e e. The correct line is \exp y - \exp x = \exp x \cdot (\exp(y - x) - 1). After it, the tangent-line bound gives \exp(y - x) - 1 \ge y - x > 0, and multiplying by \exp x > 0 finishes. [C2: Chapter check: the logarithm is slower than every root] 1. Prove that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is X such that \log x < \varepsilon \sqrt x for every x > X. 2. Let m \in 
Z_{>0}. Prove that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is X such that \log x < \varepsilon x^{1/m} for every x > X. [Hint 1] For (a), compare \log x with a root of x smaller than \sqrt x, using @prp-exp-beats-powers (b). [Hint 2] For (b), put y \coloneqq x^{2/m}. What is \log x in terms of \log y? (a) Let \varepsilon > 0 and X \coloneqq (4/\varepsilon)^4 = 256/\varepsilon^4; it depends on \varepsilon only. Let x > X, and put s \coloneqq x^{1/4}. By @prp-exp-beats-powers (b) with m = 4, \log x < 4s. By @prp-real-power-consistent (a), s = \sqrt[4]{x}, so s \ge 0 and s^4 = x > (4/\varepsilon)^4. Hence s > 4/\varepsilon, because fourth powers of non-negative numbers keep order. So 4 < \varepsilon s and 4s < \varepsilon s \cdot s. Finally s \cdot s = x^{1/4 + 1/4} = x^{1/2} = \sqrt x, by the addition law for real powers and @prp-real-power-consistent (a). Hence \log x < 4s < \varepsilon \sqrt x. (b) Let \varepsilon > 0 and put \delta \coloneqq 2\varepsilon/m. Let Y \coloneqq 256/\delta^4 = 16m^4/\varepsilon^4, the threshold of (a) for \delta, and X \coloneqq Y^{m/2}; both depend on \varepsilon and m only. Let x > X and y \coloneqq x^{2/m} > 0. The map a \mapsto a^{2/m} is strictly increasing on (0, \infty) by @prp-real-power-laws (f). So y > X^{2/m} = Y^{(m/2)(2/m)} = Y^1 = Y, by part (b) of the same proposition and @prp-real-power-consistent (b). By (a) applied to y and \delta, \log y < \delta \sqrt y. Here \sqrt y = y^{1/2} = x^{(2/m)(1/2)} = x^{1/m}, by @prp-real-power-consistent (a) and the law (a^x)^y = a^{xy}. By the definition of real powers, \log y = (2/m) \log x, so \log x =  rac m2 \log y <  rac m2 \, \delta \, x^{1/m} = \varepsilon x^{1/m} . What a complete answer needs (10 points) - 3: a bound \log x \le c\, x^{1/k} with k > 2, with the result or log rule it comes from named. - 3: an explicit X depending on \varepsilon only, and a check that x > X gives \log x < \varepsilon \sqrt x. - 2: passes from x > X to the bound in (b), for example by the substitution y = x^{2/m} with the monotonicity of a \mapsto a^{2/m} cited, or directly by @prp-exp-beats-powers (b) with 2m and X = (2m/\varepsilon)^{2m}. - 2: the quantifiers in the order \varepsilon, then X, then every x > X. A route through @prp-exp-beats-powers (a) (put x = \exp t) earns the same points step for step. Slips that lose the step (0 for the step): X chosen depending on x; any use of derivatives, l’Hôpital’s rule or limits of functions. @lem-reals-nth-root (a) (powers keep order). @prp-real-power-laws (a), (b) (a^{x+y} = a^x a^y, (a^x)^y = a^{xy}). @def-real-power (\log(a^x) = x \log a).

title: 8.6 A Table of Strange Functions
content:
A Table of Strange Functions The later volumes will define continuity, limits of functions and the integral, and each definition will be tested on functions that resist being drawn. This section collects those functions in one place. For each we prove what can be proved with the tools of this chapter: the order, the floor, suprema and finite counting. What needs a limit we only ask, and the questions go into a table at the end. Irrationals between any two reals Most of the functions below treat rational and irrational points differently, so we need both kinds in every interval. The rationals are dense (@fd3:thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). The irrationals are dense too. Number Systems left this as an exercise (@fd3:exr-rationals-inside-the-reals-c2), and we prove it here. A real number is irrational if it is not in 
Q. [Irrationals Are Dense] For all a, b \in 
R with a < b there is an irrational x with a < x < b. Let a < b. The real numbers form a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). So there is \sqrt 2 \ge 0 with (\sqrt 2)^2 = 2, and 
R is Archimedean. Since a - \sqrt 2 < b - \sqrt 2, the density of the rationals gives q \in 
Q with a - \sqrt 2 < q < b - \sqrt 2 (@fd3:thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). Put x \coloneqq q + \sqrt 2; then a < x < b. Suppose x were rational. Then \sqrt 2 = x - q would be rational, as a difference of rationals. But \sqrt 2 is irrational, as Section 8.3 showed from @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two and the copy of 
Q inside 
R, a contradiction. Hence x is irrational. @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots (square roots exist); @fd3:thm-cof-complete-archimedean (
R is Archimedean); @fd3:thm-rationals-embed-ordered-field (
Q sits inside 
R). The argument for irrationality works for every rational q: q + \sqrt 2 is irrational. Why does the proof shift by \sqrt 2, and not by 1/2? For rational q, the number q + 1/2 is rational, so the shift would land on a rational. The proof needs a shift that turns every rational into an irrational, and an irrational shift does that. The Dirichlet function The simplest function that no pencil can draw is the indicator of the rationals. The Dirichlet Function The Dirichlet function is D \coloneqq \ind_{
Q} \colon 
R 	o 
R (@fd2:def-indicator): D(x) = 1 for x \in 
Q, and D(x) = 0 for x 
otin 
Q. [Properties of the Dirichlet Function] 1. A real p 
e 0 is a period of D (@def-periodic-function) if and only if p \in 
Q. 2. For all a < b, \sup_{(a, b)} D = 1 and \inf_{(a, b)} D = 0, both attained, and \sup \{ \abs{D(x) - D(y)} : x, y \in (a, b) \} = 1. 3. For all a < b, D is neither increasing nor decreasing on (a, b). (a) Let p \in 
Q, p 
e 0. Since 
Q is closed under sums and negatives, x \in 
Q if and only if x + p \in 
Q, so D(x + p) = D(x) for every x. Let p 
otin 
Q. Then D(0) = 1 and D(0 + p) = 0, so p is not a period. (b) Every value of D is 0 or 1. The interval (a, b) contains a rational, where D is 1 (@fd3:thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). It also contains an irrational, where D is 0 (@lem-irrationals-dense). An upper bound of D((a, b)) that is itself a value is its supremum, so \sup_{(a, b)} D = 1 is attained; likewise \inf_{(a, b)} D = 0. Since D is bounded on the non-empty set (a, b), @prp-sup-oscillation gives \sup \{ \abs{D(x) - D(y)} : x, y \in (a, b) \} = 1 - 0 = 1. (c) By @lem-irrationals-dense there is an irrational t \in (a, b). The rationals are dense, so there are rationals q_1 \in (a, t) and q_2 \in (t, b). Then q_1 < t and D(q_1) = 1 > 0 = D(t), so D is not increasing on (a, b). Also t < q_2 with D(t) = 0 < 1 = D(q_2), so it is not decreasing. @fd2:def-order-supremum (a bound that is a value); @fd3:thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field (the rationals are dense). The Dirichlet function on [0, 1]: the rational points sit on the upper dotted line, the irrational points on the lower one, and every stretch of either line contains points of both kinds. Multiplying by x. Let g(x) \coloneqq x D(x) on 
R: g(x) = x on 
Q and 0 off 
Q. Then \abs{g(x)} \le \abs{x} for every x, so near 0 the values of g are small. Away from 0 they are not. Let a 
e 0 and \delta > 0. If a \in 
Q, an irrational x with \abs{x - a} < \delta (@lem-irrationals-dense) gives \abs{g(x) - g(a)} = \abs{a}. If a 
otin 
Q, a rational x with \abs{x - a} < \min\{\delta, \abs{a}/2\} gives \abs{g(x) - g(a)} = \abs{x} \ge \abs{a} - \abs{x - a} > \abs{a}/2 , by the triangle inequality (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (e)). So every interval around a 
e 0, however short, holds points where g differs from g(a) by at least \abs{a}/2. Thomae’s function The Dirichlet function gives every rational the same value. Thomae’s function gives a rational a value that shrinks with its denominator. For example, it gives 1/2 the value 1/2, both 1/3 and 2/3 the value 1/3, and 3/4 the value 1/4. At an irrational point it is 0. Thomae’s Function For x \in 
Q, let x = p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0} and \gcd(p, q) = 1; the pair (p, q) is unique (@prp-rationals-lowest-terms (a)). Thomae’s function T \colon 
R 	o 
R is T(x) \coloneqq  egin{cases} 1/q & 	ext{if } x = p/q \in 
Q 	ext{ in lowest terms,} \ 0 & 	ext{if } x 
otin 
Q . \end{cases} Since 0 = 0/1 and \gcd(0, 1) = 1, T(0) = 1; likewise T(n) = 1 for every n \in 
Z. On 
Q, 0 < T \le 1, since q \ge 1. The denominator is read after cancelling: T(2/4) = T(1/2) = 1/2, not 1/4. Without lowest terms, “1/q at p/q” is not a function at all, since 1/2 = 2/4 would get the two values 1/2 and 1/4. Compute T(3/4), T(-6/8), T(0.6) and T(\sqrt 2/2). - T(3/4) = 1/4. - T(-6/8) = 1/4, since -6/8 = -3/4 and \gcd(-3, 4) = 1. - T(0.6) = 1/5, since 0.6 = 3/5. - T(\sqrt 2/2) = 0, since \sqrt 2/2 is irrational. Indeed, if \sqrt 2/2 = r \in 
Q, then \sqrt 2 = 2r \in 
Q. But \sqrt 2 is irrational, as shown in Section 8.3. Large values of T are rare. On [0, 1], the points with T(x) \ge 1/3 have denominator 1, 2 or 3. They are 0, 1, 1/2, 1/3 and 2/3: only five. For all a < b, the interval (a, b) contains points with T > 0 and points with T = 0. A large value needs a small denominator: T(x) \ge \varepsilon forces q \le 1/\varepsilon. There are finitely many such q, and for each q only finitely many multiples of 1/q lie in [a, b]. The same point appears under several q (1/2 = 2/4), so we take a union of finite sets rather than add up counts. (a) For x 
otin

otin 
Q, and both values are 0. Let x = p/q in lowest terms. Then x + 1 = (p + q)/q. A positive common divisor of p + q and q divides (p + q) - q = p. It divides q as well, so it is a common divisor of p and q and is at most their greatest common divisor \gcd(p, q) = 1; hence it equals 1. So \gcd(p + q, q) = 1 and T(x + 1) = 1/q = T(x). (b) Let \varepsilon > 0 and Q \coloneqq  loor{1/\varepsilon} (@def-floor-ceiling). For q \in 
Z_{>0} let S_q \coloneqq \{ p/q : p \in 
Z,\  loor{aq} \le p \le  loor{bq} \} . E \subseteq S_1 \cup \dots \cup S_Q. Let x \in E. Then T(x) \ge \varepsilon > 0, so x \in 
Q; write x = p/q in lowest terms. From 1/q \ge \varepsilon we get q \le 1/\varepsilon, so q \le Q by @prp-floor-rules (g). From a \le p/q \le b and q > 0 we get aq \le p \le bq. Hence  loor{aq} \le aq \le p, and p \le  loor{bq} by @prp-floor-rules (g). So x \in S_q with 1 \le q \le Q. (If Q = 0, no q qualifies and E = \emptyset.) Each S_q is finite. If  loor{aq} >  loor{bq}, then S_q = \emptyset. Otherwise let m \coloneqq  loor{aq} and k \coloneqq  loor{bq} - m + 1. The map \{1, \dots, k\} 	o S_q, j \mapsto (m + j - 1)/q, is onto by the definition of S_q, and injective because q 
e 0. So S_q has k elements (@fd2:def-finite). A finite union of finite sets is finite. Let A and B be finite sets. Then A \cup B is the union of the disjoint sets A and B \setminus A. The second is finite, as a subset of B. So A \cup B is finite by @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count. Induction on the number of sets gives S_1 \cup \dots \cup S_Q finite. Hence E, a subset of a finite set, is finite by @fd2:prp-subset-finite. (c) The interval (a, b) contains a rational, where T > 0 (@fd3:thm-rationals-dense-ordered-field). It also contains an irrational, where T = 0 (@lem-irrationals-dense). @prp-floor-rules (a) (the floor is at most the number); @fd2:prp-subset-finite (subsets of finite sets); @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count (a disjoint union of finite sets is finite); @fd1:ax-induction (induction). otin

otin

otin 
Q, so J(J(x)) = J(-x) = -(-x) = x. So J is its own two-sided inverse, and it is a bijection by @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Let a < b. The function H of @exm-strange-jump, H(x) = x for x < 0 and H(x) = x + 1 for x \ge 0, is strictly increasing on

[The Staircase Hugs the Diagonal] 1. s is increasing on [0, 1]. 2. s takes infinitely many values. 3. For 0 < x \le 1, 0 \le s(x) - x < 2x^2.
