orm{x} by (b), so \abs{t} = t_0. Since \abs{t} is t or -t, we get t = t_0 or t = -t_0. This proves the proposition. @prp-dot-product-laws-rn (e), (b): the zero vector, scalars come out. @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (a), (b): \abs{c} \ge 0, \abs{c}^2 = c^2. @fd3:prp-reciprocal-order: 1/p > 0 for p > 0. @fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field: \abs{t} is \pm t. Part (b) says that stretching a vector by c stretches its length by \abs{c}; the absolute value is needed, since 
orm{-x} = 
orm{x}. Part (d) says that on 
R^1 = 
R the norm is the old absolute value, so the double bars extend the single ones and nothing clashes. Dividing a nonzero vector by its norm gives a vector of length 1. For example, (3, 4) has norm 5, and by (b) the vector  rac15 (3, 4) = (3/5, 4/5) has norm  rac15 \cdot 5 = 1. [Unit Vector] A unit vector is a vector u \in 
R^n with 
orm{u} = 1. For x 
e 0 we write \dfrac{x}{
orm{x}} \coloneqq \dfrac{1}{
orm{x}} \, x, and call it the unit vector in the direction of x. The division is allowed because

e 0, by part (a) of @prp-norm-basic-rn. Part (b) shows that x / 
orm{x} is a unit vector. By part (f), the only other unit vector parallel to x is -x / 
orm{x}. Replacing x by x / 
orm{x} is called normalizing x. For example, (3, 4)/5 = (3/5, 4/5) is the unit vector in the direction of (3, 4), and the standard vectors e_k are unit vectors by (e). Compute 
orm{(1, 2, 2)}. Is (3/5, 0, 4/5) a unit vector? 
orm{(1, 2, 2)} = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = \sqrt 9 = 3, since 3 \ge 0 and 3^2 = 9. And \inner{(3/5, 0, 4/5)}{(3/5, 0, 4/5)} = 9/25 + 0 + 16/25 = 1, so the norm is \sqrt 1 = 1: yes. The length of a vector is not the sum of the sizes of its coordinates. 
orm{(1, 1)} = \sqrt 2, not \abs{1} + \abs{1} = 2; since (1, 1) = e_1 + e_2, this also shows 
orm{e_1 + e_2} = \sqrt 2 
e 2 = 
orm{e_1} + 
orm{e_2}. (Here \sqrt 2 
e 2 because 2^2 = 4 
e 2.) The norm respects scalar multiples, by @prp-norm-basic-rn (b), but not sums. Distance The distance between two points should be the length of the displacement from one to the other, y - x in the language of Section 9.2. We use x - y; it has the same length, by part (b) below. Distance For x, y \in 
R^n, the distance from x to y is d(x, y) \coloneqq 
orm{x - y}. For example, d igl((1, 2), (4, 6) igr) = 
orm{(-3, -4)} = 5. For n = 1, d(x, y) = \abs{x - y} by @prp-norm-basic-rn (d). That is the distance on the line of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field). [Basic Properties of the Distance] For all x, y, z \in 
R^n and c \in 
R: 1. d(x, y) \ge 0, and d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y; 2. d(x, y) = d(y, x); 3. d(x + z, y + z) = d(x, y); 4. d(cx, cy) = \abs{c} \, d(x, y). Each part rests on a vector identity that is checked coordinatewise (@exm-method-coordinatewise). (a) This is @prp-norm-basic-rn (a), since x - y = 0 if and only if x = y. (b) y - x = (-1)(x - y), so @prp-norm-basic-rn (b) with \abs{-1} = 1 gives 
orm{y - x} = 
orm{x - y}. (c) (x + z) - (y + z) = x - y. (d) cx - cy = c(x - y), then @prp-norm-basic-rn (b). Part (c) says that sliding both points by the same vector does not change their distance; (d) says that scaling the picture by c scales distances by \abs{c}. The property that matters most is missing from the list: the triangle inequality d(x, z) \le d(x, y) + d(y, z). It is the one property of distance that needs an idea, and Section 9.5 supplies it. The plane is the complex plane Chapter 3 defined 
C as the set 
R^2 (@def-complex-numbers) and measured its elements with the modulus. This chapter has now put a second structure on the same set. The two fit together exactly. [The Plane and the Complex Numbers] Let z = (a, b) and w = (c, d) be elements of 
R^2 = 
C, and let t \in 
R. 1. The sum z + w is the same in 
R^2 and in 
C, and so is the difference z - w. The scalar multiple tz equals the complex product (t, 0)\, z, that is, the product in 
C of the real number t with z (@prp-reals-embed-complex). 2. \inner{z}{w} = \operatorname{Re}(z \conj{w}). 3. 
orm{z} = \abs{z}, and so d(z, w) = \abs{z - w}. Every part compares two formulas in the coordinates a, b, c, d. Write both sides out by the definitions of Chapter 3 and of this chapter, and read off that they agree. (a) Both sums are (a + c, b + d) by the two definitions. By the multiplication rule of @def-complex-numbers, (t, 0)(a, b) = (ta - 0 \cdot b, \; tb + 0 \cdot a) = (ta, tb), which is tz. In particular (-1)w = (-c, -d), and (c, d) + (-c, -d) = (0, 0), so (-c, -d) is the negative of w in 
C as well; hence both differences are (a - c, b - d). (b) The conjugate of w is \conj{w} = (c, -d) (@def-conjugate-modulus). By the multiplication rule, z \conj{w} =  igl(ac - b(-d), \; a(-d) + bc igr) = (ac + bd, \; bc - ad) . Its real part is ac + bd = \inner{z}{w} (@def-dot-product-rn). (c) Both are \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, by the definitions of the norm and of the modulus. Then d(z, w) = 
orm{z - w} = \abs{z - w} by (a). @def-vector-operations-rn: the sum in 
R^2. @def-complex-numbers: sum and product in 
C. @def-norm-rn. @def-conjugate-modulus: the modulus. So every result of this chapter about 
R^n, read at n = 2, is a result about 
C. The order of the factors in (b) does not matter: \operatorname{Re}(z \conj{w}) = \operatorname{Re}(\conj{z} w), since the two products are conjugate (@thm-conjugate-properties (a), (b)). The coordinate bound (a) at the end of this section is, for n = 2, the first two inequalities of @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus. In the other direction, the multiplication of 
C has no counterpart in 
R^n for general n in this chapter; Section 9.5 explains why that matters. Comparing lengths through their squares Norms do not expand: 
orm{x + y} is the root of a sum, and nothing splits it. Squared norms do, because 
orm{v}^2 = \inner{v}{v} and the dot product is linear in each slot. The first example is the theorem of Pythagoras, with “right angle” read as “dot product zero” (@def-orthogonal-rn). For instance, \inner{(3, 0)}{(0, 4)} = 0, and indeed

Write each squared norm as a dot product,

orm{x} is small, or every coordinate x_k is small. The two are equivalent, with constants that depend only on n. For example, for x = (1, -2, 2) the largest size of a coordinate is 2, and

[Norm against Coordinates] Let x \in 
R^n and M \coloneqq \max\{ \abs{x_1}, \dots, \abs{x_n} \}. 1. \abs{x_k} \le 
orm{x} for every k; hence M \le 
orm{x}. 2.

Keeping one term and dropping the rest makes it smaller, which gives (a); replacing every term by the largest one makes it larger, which gives (b). In both parts we work with squares and come back by comparing squares. By @prp-norm-basic-rn (c), 
orm{x}^2 = \inner{x}{x} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j^2. Every term x_j^2 is \ge 0, since a square is never negative. (a) Fix k. A sum of non-negative terms is at least each of its terms (@prp-sum-order (b)), so x_k^2 \le \sum_{j=1}^{n} x_j^2 = 
orm{x}^2. Since x_k^2 = \abs{x_k}^2, this reads \abs{x_k}^2 \le 
orm{x}^2. Both \abs{x_k} and 
orm{x} are \ge 0, so comparing squares gives \abs{x_k} \le 
orm{x}. The maximum M is one of the numbers \abs{x_k}, so M \le 
orm{x}. (b) For every j, 0 \le \abs{x_j} \le M, so \abs{x_j} \abs{x_j} \le M M by @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d), that is, x_j^2 \le M^2. A sum of n terms, each at most M^2, is at most n M^2 (@prp-sum-order (c)), so 
orm{x}^2 \le n M^2. The number \sqrt n \, M is \ge 0, and its square is (\sqrt n)^2 M^2 = n M^2. So

R^n and every k, \abs{x_k} \le 
orm{x}. Proof. (1) The other terms of 
orm{x}^2 = \sum_j x_j^2 are non-negative, so 
orm{x}^2 \ge x_k^2. (2) Taking non-negative square roots, which preserves \le, we get 
orm{x} \ge \sqrt{x_k^2}. (3) Since \sqrt{a^2} = a for every real a, this gives 
orm{x} \ge x_k. (4) Applying this to -x, whose norm is 
orm{x}, gives

It cites the “fact” \sqrt{a^2} = a for every real a, which is false. Citing a false general fact is never allowed; it is (N9) in the list of Logic and Proof (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). orm{x} and \sqrt{x_k^2} are non-negative with squares 
orm{x}^2 \ge x_k^2. - Line (4) uses

orm{x} (@prp-norm-basic-rn (b)). - Line (5) holds because \abs{x_k} is x_k or -x_k. Even line (3) can be saved. title: 9.5 Cauchy–Schwarz and the Triangle Inequality

Cauchy–Schwarz and the Triangle Inequality Section 9.4 gave 
R^n a length and a distance and proved every basic property of the distance except one: that a detour through a third point is never shorter than the direct route. This section proves it. Everything rests on one inequality between the dot product and the lengths, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. The method that proves it is called normalizing: shrink or stretch both vectors to length 1, prove the inequality there, and scale back. Two earlier proofs, and why neither transfers The triangle inequality has been proved before in this series in two settings, for real numbers and for complex numbers. Each proof used a tool that 
R^n lacks. In 
R. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.1, trapped each number between \pm its absolute value, -\abs{x} \le x \le \abs{x}, and added the two traps. That is how it proved the triangle inequality for absolute values, @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (c)–(e). The trap compares x with the number \abs{x}. For a vector x \in 
R^n with n \ge 2, “x \le 
orm{x}” compares a vector with a number, and 
R^n has been given no order at all. In 
C = 
R^2. Section 3.3 expanded \abs{z + w}^2 and met the cross term 2\operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}), which it bounded by \abs{z\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\abs{w} (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality). By @prp-plane-is-complex-plane, \operatorname{Re}(z\conj{w}) = \inner{z}{w} and \abs{z} = 
orm{z}, so the key step was \inner{z}{w} \le 
orm{z} \, 
orm{w} , proved with the multiplication of 
C: the product z\conj{w} and the rule \abs{z\conj{w}} = \abs{z}\abs{w}. For n \ge 3 this book defines no such multiplication on 
R^n. The expansion itself does survive. Section 9.4 compared lengths by comparing their squares (@exm-method-expand-the-square). Expanding both squares by @eq-expand-norm-squared gives

R^2, x = (3, 4) and y = (4, 3). Their dot product is \inner{x}{y} = 12 + 12 = 24, and both have length 5, so 
orm{x}\,

Equality can hold with either sign, and the sign tells which way y points along x. [Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality] Let n \ge 1 and x, y \in 
R^n. (a) \abs{\inner{x}{y}} \le 
orm{x}\,
orm{y}. (b) \abs{\inner{x}{y}} =

orm{u - v}^2 \ge 0. What does it say about \inner{u}{v}? What else could you expand? [Scratch work] The attempt gives 0 \le

orm{-y} =

orm{x}\,

orm{x}\,

orm{x}\,

orm{x}\,

e 0, y is parallel to x if and only if y = cx for some c. Section 9.2 noted this right after defining parallel vectors (@def-parallel-rn). This proves the theorem. @prp-dot-product-laws-rn (a), (b), (e) (symmetry, scalars, zero vector); @prp-norm-basic-rn (a)–(c) (length zero, scaling, squares); @def-unit-vector-rn; @prp-vector-space-laws-rn (e), (f), (i) (scalar rules, signs); @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (c), (e) (adding, multiplying, squares); @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b), (d) (products, two-sided bounds); @fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field. For n = 1 the theorem says little: \abs{xy} = \abs{x}\,\abs{y} always, and any two reals are parallel. The content is in n \ge 2, where most pairs of vectors are not parallel and the inequality is strict for them. For x = (1, 2, 2) and y = (2, 0, 1), compute both sides of (a). Is the inequality strict, and does (b) predict the answer? \inner{x}{y} = 2 + 0 + 2 = 4, 
orm{x} = 3 and 
orm{y} = \sqrt 5. Since 4^2 = 16 < 45 = (3\sqrt5)^2 and both numbers are non-negative, 4 < 3\sqrt5: strict. Yes: y = cx would need c = 2 from the first coordinate and c = 0 from the second. And x = cy is impossible since y_2 = 0 
e 2 = x_2. So x, y are not parallel and (b) forbids equality. Squaring (a) gives the form used for sums of real numbers. For example, with (1, 2, 3) and (4, 5, 6) the sum of products is 4 + 10 + 18 = 32, and the sums of squares are 14 and 77. The squared form reads 32^2 = 1024 \le 14 \cdot 77 = 1078. [Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality for Sums] Let n \ge 1 and x_1, \dots, x_n, y_1, \dots, y_n \in 
R. Then \Bigl( \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k y_k \Bigr)^2 \le \Bigl( \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k^2 \Bigr) \Bigl( \sum_{k=1}^{n} y_k^2 \Bigr) , with equality if and only if (x_1, \dots, x_n) and (y_1, \dots, y_n) are parallel vectors of 
R^n. Let x \coloneqq (x_1, \dots, x_n) and y \coloneqq (y_1, \dots, y_n). The three sums are \inner{x}{y}, 
orm{x}^2 and 
orm{y}^2. By @thm-cauchy-schwarz-rn (a), 0 \le \abs{\inner{x}{y}} \le 
orm{x}\,
orm{y}. Squaring keeps an inequality between non-negative numbers, so \abs{\inner{x}{y}}^2 \le 
orm{x}^2 
orm{y}^2. And \abs{\inner{x}{y}}^2 = \inner{x}{y}^2. Two non-negative reals with equal squares are equal (comparing squares, Section 9.4). So equality holds exactly when \abs{\inner{x}{y}} = 
orm{x}\,
orm{y}, that is, by @thm-cauchy-schwarz-rn (b), when x and y are parallel. @def-dot-product-rn; @prp-norm-basic-rn (c) (length squared); @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d) (multiplying inequalities); @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b) (\abs{t}^2 = t^2). For n = 2 that identity reads (ac + bd)^2 + (ad - bc)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)(c^2 + d^2). Chapter 3 mentioned this case as a second route in the solution of its chapter check, Exercise C1 of Section 3.3 (@exr-triangle-inequality-c1). The method: normalize The proof of @thm-cauchy-schwarz-rn did its work for unit vectors and then scaled back. This way of proving is called normalizing. [Method: normalize] How it goes. Suppose a statement about x and y is homogeneous: replacing x by ax with a > 0 multiplies both sides by the same positive factor, and likewise for y. Then: 1. Settle x = 0 and y = 0 separately. 2. For x, y 
e 0, put u \coloneqq x/
orm{x} and v \coloneqq y/
orm{y}, and prove the statement for the unit vectors u, v. 3. Scale back, multiplying by the positive factor. When to use it. Inequalities between \inner{x}{y} and products of lengths; statements about directions rather than sizes. Common mistakes. Normalizing the zero vector is impossible: it has no direction, and x/
orm{x} would divide by 0. Scaling by a negative factor breaks the method, since x \mapsto -x changes the sign of \inner{x}{y} but not of 
orm{x}\,
orm{y}. A statement that is not homogeneous cannot be normalized. For example, 
orm{u + v} \le 2 holds for all unit u, v. By Cauchy–Schwarz, 
orm{u + v}^2 = 2 + 2\inner{u}{v} \le 2 + 2
orm{u}\,
orm{v} = 4, and comparing squares of non-negative numbers gives 
orm{u + v} \le 2. And yet 
orm{x + y} \le 2 fails for x = y = 2e_1, where 
orm{x + y} = 4. The proof of @thm-cauchy-schwarz-rn is the first worked example. It settles the zero case, proves the bound for unit vectors by expanding

title: Chapter Review
content:
Chapter Review Summary 
R^n is the set of lists of n reals (@def-real-n-space). Addition and scaling coordinate by coordinate obey the laws of a vector space (@prp-vector-space-laws-rn). The dot product is symmetric, linear in each place and positive on non-zero vectors (@prp-dot-product-laws-rn). The norm 
orm{x} = \sqrt{\inner{x}{x}} and the distance 
orm{x - y} obey Pythagoras, the parallelogram law and polarization (@prp-pythagoras-rn, @prp-parallelogram-law-rn, @prp-polarization-rn). Cauchy–Schwarz, \abs{\inner{x}{y}} \le 
orm{x}
orm{y}, holds with equality exactly for parallel vectors (@thm-cauchy-schwarz-rn), and it gives the triangle inequality (@thm-triangle-inequality-rn). The projection of x onto y is the closest point of the line 
R y (@thm-projection-closest-point). The quotient \inner{x}{y}/(
orm{x}
orm{y}) lies in [-1, 1] (@prp-angle-cosine-properties). What is open: the angle itself, which needs the function \cos. Lines, hyperplanes and convex sets come next, in Chapter 10, built from this chapter. Distance and convergence for abstract spaces are taken up by the analysis volumes. Proof methods in this chapter - Work coordinatewise (@exm-method-coordinatewise). To prove an equation between vectors, fix a coordinate k and compute the k-th coordinate of each side. Prove the equation in 
R, naming the law used, and conclude that the vectors agree in every place. Introduced in Section 9.2. - Expand the square (@exm-method-expand-the-square). Lengths are roots of sums, and their squares are dot products. Compare squares, write 
orm{v}^2 = \inner{v}{v}, expand by linearity and symmetry, and return to lengths by comparing squares. Introduced in Section 9.4, where it proves the Pythagorean theorem and the parallelogram law. - Normalize (@exm-method-normalize). If a statement is homogeneous in x and in y, settle x = 0 and y = 0 separately and prove it for the unit vectors x/
orm{x} and y/
orm{y}. Introduced in Section 9.5, where it proves Cauchy–Schwarz. - Subtract the projection (@exm-method-subtract-the-projection). Given x and y 
e 0, split x into its projection onto y and the remainder, which is orthogonal to y. Introduced in Section 9.6, where it proves the closest-point theorem. Terms - box: the product [a_1, b_1] 	imes \dots 	imes [a_n, b_n] of closed intervals (@def-box-rn). - cosine of the angle: \inner{x}{y}/(
orm{x}
orm{y}) for non-zero x, y (@def-angle-cosine-rn). - distance: 
orm{x - y} (@def-distance-rn). - dot product: \inner{x}{y} = \sum_k x_k y_k (@def-dot-product-rn). - norm, length: 
orm{x} = \sqrt{\inner{x}{x}} (@def-norm-rn). - orthogonal vectors: vectors with dot product 0 (@def-orthogonal-rn). - parallel vectors: vectors one of which is a real multiple of the other (@def-parallel-rn). - projection onto a line: \operatorname{proj}_y x =  rac{\inner{x}{y}}{
orm{y}^2}\, y (@def-projection-rn). - standard vectors: the vectors e_1, \dots, e_n with a single coordinate 1 (@def-standard-basis-rn). - unit vector: a vector of norm 1 (@def-unit-vector-rn). Results used from earlier volumes Logic and Proof, Chapter 8: - the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for the find-the-error exercises of Sections 9.3 and 9.4. Sets and Functions: - ordered pairs (@fd2:def-ordered-pair), Cartesian products (@fd2:def-cartesian-product) and bijections (@fd2:def-bijective), in Section 9.1; - recursion (@fd2:thm-recursion) and induction (@fd2:thm-induction); - finite sums and products (@fd2:def-sum-product) and maxima of finite sets (@fd2:prp-finite-max). Number Systems: From 
N to 
R: - the rules of an ordered ring (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules) and an ordered field (@fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves), on nearly every page; - the absolute value (@fd3:def-absolute-value-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field); - the rules of a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra) and of fractions in a field (@fd3:lem-field-fraction-rules); - 
R as a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field) and its square roots (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), which define the length. Results used from earlier chapters - Chapter 1, Section 1.1: the rules for finite sums (@lem-ring-finite-sums), comparing sums termwise (@prp-sum-order) and double sums over a rectangle (@prp-double-sum), for the dot product laws and Cauchy–Schwarz for sums. - Chapter 3, for Sections 9.1, 9.2 and 9.4: the complex numbers as pairs (@def-complex-numbers, @prp-reals-embed-complex), the modulus and the conjugate (@def-conjugate-modulus, @prp-modulus-of-real, @thm-conjugate-properties). - Chapter 3, for Section 9.5: the triangle inequality in 
C and its variants (@thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @cor-complex-triangle-variants, @lem-real-part-at-most-modulus). - Chapter 3, for Section 9.6 only: the unit circle and polar form (@prp-polar-form) and the borrowed cosine and sine (@ax-cosine-sine). - Chapter 4, for one remark in Section 9.2: fields (@def-field). - Chapters 6 and 7, for one exercise of Section 9.6: degree and evaluation of polynomials (@def-degree, @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, @thm-polynomial-root-count). - Chapters 5 and 8, for the review exercises of Section 9.6 only: groups and homomorphisms with their kernels (@def-group, @def-group-homomorphism, @prp-homomorphism-injective-iff-kernel-trivial), and monotone functions (@def-monotone-function, @exm-method-factor-difference). Borrowed facts The chapter borrows nothing new. It defines the cosine of the angle between two vectors as a quotient, so it needs no function \cos and no \pi. Section 9.6 mentions the facts about cosine and sine borrowed in Section 3.5 only once, to compare the quotient with the cosine of a number 	heta when n = 2. Threads - Same statement, three places. The triangle inequality is proved three times, each time by a different route. It is proved for 
R in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.1 (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), for 
C in Section 3.3, and for every 
R^n in Section 9.5. Cauchy–Schwarz is stated here only for 
R^n and for finite sums. The linear algebra volumes prove it for abstract inner product spaces. - Chapter 10 on distances. Hyperplanes \inner{a}{x} = c, nearest points on lines and hyperplanes, and betweenness stated by distances all come from the dot product and the projection of this chapter. - The angle. Section 9.6 defines only the cosine of the angle between two vectors. An angle 	heta with that cosine needs the function \cos. For n = 2 Chapter 3 supplies it through polar form, and for general n the analysis volumes do.

title: Lines, Hyperplanes, and Convex Sets
content:
Lines, Hyperplanes, and Convex Sets Chapter 9 gave 
R^n a distance. This chapter asks how much of the familiar geometry that distance already decides. A great deal: lines and segments, spheres and balls are all sets cut out by distances, and “x lies between p and q” is a statement about three distances and nothing else. One linear equation \inner{a}{x} = c cuts out a hyperplane, and the distance from a point to it has a formula. A set is convex when it contains the segment between any two of its points. The smallest convex set containing a given set is the set of its convex combinations. Analysis uses all of this from its first chapters on. The mean value theorem moves along a segment, and a ball is the set of points where an estimate holds. In a convex set, an argument made along one segment works between any two points. What you need. - Vectors, the dot product, the norm and the distance, from Chapter 9, Sections 9.2 to 9.4 (@def-norm-rn). - The triangle inequality and its equality case, from Section 9.5 (@thm-triangle-inequality-rn). - Projection onto a line and the closest-point theorem, from Section 9.6 (@thm-projection-closest-point). - The rules of an ordered field and square roots in 
R, from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). - Finite sums and induction, from Chapter 1 and Sets and Functions, for convex combinations of many points (@fd2:thm-induction). Time. About 15 hours if you read the main text and do every A exercise and one B and one C exercise per section; about 20 hours for everything. Roadmap - Lines and Segments. Lines p + 
R v, segments [p, q], and the theorem that x lies on [p, q] exactly when 
orm{p - x} + 
orm{x - q} = 
orm{p - q} (@thm-betweenness). - Hyperplanes and Nearest Points. Hyperplanes \inner{a}{x} = c, the nearest point on a line or a hyperplane with the distance to it (@prp-nearest-point-on-hyperplane), and how a line meets a sphere. - Convex Sets and Hulls. Convex sets, which include balls (@prp-balls-convex), convex combinations, and the convex hull of a set as the set of convex combinations of its points.

R(2v) by @prp-line-parametrizations with \lambda = 2, but 2v 
e v, since 2v - v = v 
e 0. (e) True. If both lines contain a 
e b, both equal the line a + 
R(b - a) by @prp-line-through-two-points. C. Going deeper [C1: Chapter check: one point in the middle] Prove that of three distinct collinear points of 
R^n, exactly one lies on the segment between the other two. Let the three points lie on the line p + 
R v, v 
e 0. Each has one parameter, and distinct points have distinct parameters, since equal parameters give equal points. Since \le is a total order (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), three distinct reals can be listed in increasing order. So we can name the points x_i = p + t_i v with t_1 < t_2 < t_3. Existence. By @exr-lines-and-segments-b1 with a = t_1, b = t_3 and t = t_2, x_2 \in [x_1, x_3]. Uniqueness. Suppose x_1 \in [x_2, x_3]. By @exr-lines-and-segments-b1 with a = t_2 < b = t_3, this gives t_2 \le t_1, against t_1 < t_2. Suppose x_3 \in [x_1, x_2]. The same exercise with a = t_1 < b = t_2 gives t_3 \le t_2, against t_2 < t_3. So x_2 is the only one of the three between the other two. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 2: puts the three points on one parametrization, with distinct parameters, and says why they are distinct. - 2: orders the parameters. - 2: shows that the point with the middle parameter is between the others (by B1 or directly). - 2: excludes x_1, either by B1’s (\Rightarrow) (citing it suffices) or by comparing distances with @thm-betweenness. - 2: excludes x_3 in the same way. A route through @thm-betweenness (comparing 
orm{x_1 - x_3} = (t_3 - t_1)
orm{v} with the sums of the other distances) earns the same points step for step. Slips that lose the step (0 points for it): using one parameter for a point on two different parametrizations; excluding only one of the outer points.

title: 10.2 Hyperplanes and Nearest Points
content:
Hyperplanes and Nearest Points Section 10.1 described a line by a parametrization, one free parameter. In the plane a line is also the solution set of one equation a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 = c. This section takes one linear equation \inner{a}{x} = c in any 
R^n and names its solution set, a hyperplane. Distances to a hyperplane, and to a line, then have exact formulas. The main tool is the expansion of Chapter 9: squaring and expanding turns a condition on distances into an equation that can be solved, a linear one in the equidistant case. Hyperplanes Chapter 9 met equations of this kind twice. The vectors orthogonal to a fixed a are the solutions of \inner{a}{x} = 0 (@def-orthogonal-rn). The points equidistant from two given points satisfy an equation \inner{x}{b - a} = 	ext{constant} (@exr-length-and-distance-b3). In 
R^2 such a set is a line. In 
R^3 it is not: Section 10.1 found three points of \{ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1 \} on no common line. The solution set of one equation deserves its own name. Here is a small case. Take a = (1, 1, 1) and c = 1 in 
R^3, so the equation is x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1. The points (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1) satisfy it. The point 0 gives 0 < 1, and the point (1, 1, 1) gives 3 > 1. So these two points lie on opposite sides of the solution set. A hyperplane is the set where one non-zero linear expression takes one value. [Hyperplane] Let a \in 
R^n with a 
e 0, and let c \in 
R. The set H_{a,c} \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : \inner{a}{x} = c \} is a hyperplane, and a is a normal vector of it. The sets \{ x : \inner{a}{x} \le c \} and \{ x : \inner{a}{x} \ge c \} are the two closed half-spaces of H_{a,c}; with < and > strictly, they are the two open half-spaces, or the two sides of H_{a,c}. In words: one vector a, which must be non-zero, and one number c give one equation, and the hyperplane is everything that satisfies it. A subset of 
R^n is a hyperplane if it equals H_{a,c} for some such pair. A hyperplane is never empty. The point p_0 \coloneqq  rac{c}{
orm{a}^2} \, a is defined, since 
orm{a}^2 > 0 by @prp-norm-basic-rn (a), (c). It lies on the hyperplane: \inner{a}{p_0} = (c/
orm{a}^2)
orm{a}^2 = c by linearity (@prp-dot-product-laws-rn (b)). By linearity again, \inner{a}{x} - c = \inner{a}{x - p_0}, so x \in H_{a,c} \iff x - p_0 \perp a . The hyperplane is the set of points reached from p_0 by a step orthogonal to a. Examples. - n = 1. For a 
e 0 in 
R, H_{a,c} = \{ c/a \}: a hyperplane of the line is one point. Its sides are the two open rays. - n = 2. H_{(1,1),1} is the line x_1 + x_2 = 1. We will see shortly that every hyperplane of 
R^2 is a line. - Coordinate hyperplanes. H_{e_k, 0} = \{ x : x_k = 0 \} by @prp-dot-product-laws-rn (d). In 
R^3, H_{e_3, 0} is the plane of the first two axes. What goes wrong when a = 0. Change a = (1, 1) to a = (0, 0). Then \inner{0}{x} = 0 for every x (@prp-dot-product-laws-rn (e)), so \{ x : \inner{0}{x} = c \} is 
R^n when c = 0 and empty when c 
e 0. Neither looks like the sets above, and the formula for p_0 would divide by 0. The clause a 
e 0 is what fails. Why “a” normal and not “the” normal. The equations x_1 + x_2 = 1 and 2x_1 + 2x_2 = 2 have the same solutions. So one hyperplane has many pairs (a, c), and the next result says exactly how many. [The Normals of a Hyperplane] Let a, a' \in 
R^n be non-zero and c, c' \in 
R. Then H_{a,c} = H_{a',c'} if and only if (a', c') = (\lambda a, \lambda c) for some real \lambda 
e 0. The direction (\Leftarrow) multiplies an equation by \lambda. For (\Rightarrow), the equation \inner{a'}{x} = c' must hold at every p_0 + w with w \perp a, so a' is orthogonal to everything orthogonal to a. Subtracting the projection (@exm-method-subtract-the-projection) produces a vector orthogonal to a from a' itself, and that vector must be 0. (\Leftarrow) If a' = \lambda a and c' = \lambda c with \lambda 
e 0, then \inner{a'}{x} = \lambda\inner{a}{x} by linearity, and \lambda\inner{a}{x} = \lambda c holds if and only if \inner{a}{x} = c, multiplying by \lambda or by 1/\lambda. (\Rightarrow) Suppose H_{a,c} = H_{a',c'}, and let p_0 = (c/
orm{a}^2) a. For every w \perp a, the point p_0 + w lies in H_{a,c}, hence in H_{a',c'}: \inner{a'}{p_0 + w} = c'. Taking w = 0 gives \inner{a'}{p_0} = c', and subtracting, \inner{a'}{w} = 0 for every w \perp a. Let \mu \coloneqq \inner{a'}{a}/
orm{a}^2 and w \coloneqq a' - \mu a = a' - \operatorname{proj}_a a'. By @thm-projection-closest-point (a), w \perp a, so \inner{a'}{w} = 0. Hence, by linearity, 
orm{w}^2 = \inner{a' - \mu a}{w} = \inner{a'}{w} - \mu \inner{a}{w} = 0 - 0 = 0 , and w = 0, since only the zero vector has norm 0. So a' = \mu a. Since a' 
e 0, \mu 
e 0. Finally c' = \inner{a'}{p_0} = \mu \inner{a}{p_0} = \mu c. This proves the claim with \lambda = \mu. @prp-dot-product-laws-rn (b): linearity; @prp-norm-basic-rn (a), (c): norm zero only at 0, 
orm{w}^2 = \inner{w}{w}. A hyperplane has many normal vectors, and a = 0 gives none. H_{(1,1),1} = H_{(2,2),2} = H_{(-1,-1),-1}. “The normal” of a hyperplane means “a normal”: it is fixed only up to a non-zero factor (@prp-hyperplane-normals). So a formula that uses a normal, such as the distance and nearest-point formulas below, is only meaningful if it gives the same answer for (\lambda a, \lambda c) as for (a, c). We check that it does. And a = 0 is excluded on purpose: \{ x : \inner{0}{x} = c \} is \emptyset or 
R^n, and neither is a hyperplane. Indeed, every H_{a,c} contains p_0 and misses p_0 + a, where the value is c + 
orm{a}^2 
e c. In the plane, hyperplanes and lines are the same sets, and each description converts into the other by swapping two coordinates and changing one sign. [Lines of the Plane Are Its Hyperplanes] Work in 
R^2. 1. For a 
e 0, H_{a,c} = p_0 + 
R(-a_2, a_1), where p_0 = (c/
orm{a}^2) a. 2. For v 
e 0 and any p, p + 
R v = H_{a,c} with a \coloneqq (-v_2, v_1) and c \coloneqq \inner{a}{p}. (a) Since a 
e 0, also (-a_2, a_1) 
e 0, so the right side is a line (@def-line-rn). (\supseteq) \inner{a}{(-a_2, a_1)} = -a_1 a_2 + a_2 a_1 = 0, so \inner{a}{p_0 + t(-a_2, a_1)} = c + 0 = c. (\subseteq) Let x \in H_{a,c} and w \coloneqq x - p_0. Then a_1 w_1 + a_2 w_2 = 0. Put t \coloneqq (a_1 w_2 - a_2 w_1)/
orm{a}^2. Using a_2 w_2 = -a_1 w_1 and a_1 w_1 = -a_2 w_2,  egin{aligned} -t a_2 &=  rac{a_2^2 w_1 - a_1 (a_2 w_2)}{
orm{a}^2} =  rac{(a_2^2 + a_1^2) w_1}{

orm{a}^2} = w_2 . \end{aligned} So x = p_0 + t(-a_2, a_1). (b) a = (-v_2, v_1) 
e 0 since v 
e 0, and \inner{a}{v} = -v_2 v_1 + v_1 v_2 = 0. So \inner{a}{p + tv} = \inner{a}{p} = c: the line lies in H_{a,c}. By (a), H_{a,c} = p_0 + 
R(-a_2, a_1) = p_0 + 
R(-v). As p \in H_{a,c}, p = p_0 - sv for some s, so p_0 = p + sv \in p + 
R v; and -v = (-1)v. By @prp-line-parametrizations, p_0 + 
R(-v) = p + 
R v. So in 
R^2 the two descriptions are interchangeable: a direction v gives the normal (-v_2, v_1), and a normal a gives the direction (-a_2, a_1). In 
R^3 this fails. The hyperplane H_{(1,1,1),1} contains (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1), and Section 10.1 showed, after the definition of collinear points, that no line contains all three. A hyperplane of 
R^3 is not a line. Write the line through (1, 3) and (4, -1) as an equation a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 = c. A direction is v = (4, -1) - (1, 3) = (3, -4). By @exm-lines-in-the-plane (b), a normal is (4, 3) and c = 4 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 3 = 13. So the line is 4x_1 + 3x_2 = 13. Check at the second point: 16 - 3 = 13. @prp-line-through-two-points: direction q - p. Equidistant points At the end of Section 10.1 we found a point at equal distances from p and q that is not their midpoint, and asked for all such points. Chapter 9 found their equation in @exr-length-and-distance-b3. Here that set is named as a hyperplane. Its two sides are the points nearer to p and the points nearer to q. A small case first. In 
R^2, take p = (0, 0) and q = (2, 0). A point x is equally far from both exactly when x_1^2 + x_2^2 = (x_1 - 2)^2 + x_2^2, that is, when 4x_1 = 4, or x_1 = 1. This is a line through the midpoint (1, 0). The points with x_1 < 1 are nearer to p. [The Perpendicular Bisector] Let p, q \in 
R^n with p 
e q, and let c \coloneqq  rac12  igl( 
orm{q}^2 - 
orm{p}^2  igr). Then \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - p} = 
orm{x - q} \} = H_{q - p, \, c} , a hyperplane that contains the midpoint  rac12 (p + q). Moreover, 
orm{x - p} < 
orm{x - q} if and only if \inner{q - p}{x} < c. This hyperplane is the perpendicular bisector of p and q. Expand the square (@exm-method-expand-the-square): compare squares instead of norms. The two squared norms both contain 
orm{x}^2, which cancels, and what is left of their difference is linear in x. For non-negative reals s, u, we have s < u if and only if s^2 < u^2. Since the order of 
R is total, also s = u if and only if s^2 = u^2. Norms are non-negative, so both claims may be checked on squares. By @eq-expand-norm-squared and linearity,  egin{aligned} 
orm{x - p}^2 - 
orm{x - q}^2 &=  igl( 
orm{x}^2 - 2\inner{x}{p} + 
orm{p}^2  igr) -  igl( 
orm{x}^2 - 2\inner{x}{q} + 
orm{q}^2  igr) \ &= 2\inner{q - p}{x} - 2c . \end{aligned} So 
orm{x - p}^2 = 
orm{x - q}^2 if and only if \inner{q - p}{x} = c, and 
orm{x - p}^2 < 
orm{x - q}^2 if and only if \inner{q - p}{x} < c. Since p 
e q, q - p 
e 0, so H_{q - p, c} is a hyperplane. For the midpoint, linearity and symmetry give \inner{q - p}{p + q} = 
orm{q}^2 - 
orm{p}^2, so \inner{q - p}{ rac12 (p + q)} = c. @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g), (i): squares keep order, order is total; @prp-norm-basic-rn (a): norms are non-negative; @prp-dot-product-laws-rn (a), (b): symmetry, linearity. The open half-space \inner{q - p}{x} < c is the side of the bisector that contains p: the points strictly nearer to p than to q. The midpoint is the only point of the segment [p, q] on the bisector. Indeed, for a point of [p, q] the two distances add up to 
orm{p - q}, by @thm-betweenness. If they are also equal, the point is the midpoint (@cor-point-pinned-on-segment). For n \ge 2, though, the bisector has many other points. Find the points of 
R^2 equidistant from (0, 0) and (2, 4). Here q - p = (2, 4) and c =  rac12 (20 - 0) = 10, so the set is 2x_1 + 4x_2 = 10, that is, x_1 + 2x_2 = 5 (the same hyperplane, by @prp-hyperplane-normals with \lambda =  rac12). The midpoint (1, 2) satisfies it: 1 + 4 = 5. Nearest points Chapter 9 found the point of a line through the origin nearest to a given point (@thm-projection-closest-point). A general line p + 
R v is the line 
R v slid by p, and distances do not change under sliding (@prp-distance-basic-rn (c)). So the answer carries over: slide x by -p, project, slide back. For example, take the horizontal line (0, 1) + 
R(1, 0) in 
R^2 and the point x = (3, 5). The point of the line nearest to x is (3, 1), straight below x, at distance 4. The step from it to x is (0, 4), orthogonal to the direction (1, 0). [The Nearest Point on a Line] Let L = p + 
R v with v 
e 0, let x \in 
R^n, and put t_0 \coloneqq  rac{\inner{x - p}{v}}{
orm{v}^2} , \qquad m \coloneqq p + t_0 v . Then x - m \perp v, and for every t \in 
R, 
orm{x - (p + tv)}^2 = 
orm{x - m}^2 + (t - t_0)^2 
orm{v}^2 . Hence m is the unique point of L nearest to x. Apply @thm-projection-closest-point to the vectors x - p and v 
e 0. Its number is t_0, and x - m = (x - p) - t_0 v. Part (a) gives x - m \perp v. Part (b), since x - (p + tv) = (x - p) - tv, gives the identity, and with it 
orm{x - (p + tv)} \ge 
orm{x - m}, with equality if and only if t = t_0. So a nearest point p + tv has t = t_0, and is m. Since m is described as the nearest point, it depends only on L and x, not on the parametrization used to compute it. The number 
orm{x - m} is the distance from x to L. For p = 0 this is @thm-projection-closest-point. Two cases of it were computed in @exm-distance-to-a-line-through-the-origin. For a hyperplane the roles turn around. On a line we search along the direction v and the error is orthogonal to v. On a hyperplane the error should be parallel to the normal a: from x, move along a until the equation \inner{a}{x} = c holds. For example, take x_1 + x_2 = 2 in 
R^2, so a = (1, 1), and the point x = (3, 3). Moving to x - s(1, 1) changes the value x_1 + x_2 = 6 by -2s. The value is 2 when s = 2, at the point (1, 1). Its distance from x is 
orm{(2, 2)} = 2\sqrt 2. [Distance to a Hyperplane] Let a 
e 0, c \in 
R and x \in 
R^n, and put x^* \coloneqq x -  rac{\inner{a}{x} - c}{
orm{a}^2} \, a . Then x^* \in H_{a,c}, and for every y \in H_{a,c}, 
orm{x - y}^2 = 
orm{x - x^*}^2 + 
orm{x^* - y}^2 . Hence x^* is the unique point of H_{a,c} nearest to x, and the distance from x to H_{a,c} is 
orm{x - x^*} =  rac{\abs{\inner{a}{x} - c}}{
orm{a}} . Write s \coloneqq (\inner{a}{x} - c)/
orm{a}^2, so x^* = x - sa. By linearity, \inner{a}{x^*} = \inner{a}{x} - s

orm{x - y}^2 \ge 
orm{x - x^*}^2. Equality holds if and only if 
orm{x^* - y} = 0, that is, y = x^*. Comparing squares of non-negative numbers, as in the proof of @prp-perpendicular-bisector, gives the same for the norms. Finally, since 
orm{sa} = \abs{s} \, 
orm{a},

orm{a}} , using \abs{u/w} = \abs{u}/w for w > 0. @prp-dot-product-laws-rn (b): linearity; @prp-norm-basic-rn (a), (b): norm zero only at 0,

orm{a}; @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (b): \abs{u/w} = \abs{u}/\abs{w}. The formula does not depend on which normal is used. Replacing (a, c) by (\lambda a, \lambda c) multiplies the numerator \abs{\inner{a}{x} - c} by \abs{\lambda} and the denominator 
orm{a} by \abs{\lambda}; in x^* the coefficient is multiplied by \lambda/\lambda^2 and the vector by \lambda. Nothing changes. The sign of \inner{a}{x} - c, which the absolute value discards, says on which side of the hyperplane x lies. Find the distance from (1, 2, 3) to the hyperplane x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0, and the nearest point. Here a = (1, 1, 1), c = 0, \inner{a}{x} - c = 6 and 
orm{a}^2 = 3. So x^* = (1, 2, 3) - 2(1, 1, 1) = (-1, 0, 1), which satisfies -1 + 0 + 1 = 0, and the distance is 6/\sqrt 3 = 2\sqrt 3 (as (2\sqrt 3)^2 = 12 = 36/3). Spheres meet lines; segments cross hyperplanes A sphere is the set of points at one fixed distance from a center. In the plane, the points at distance 1 from the origin form the unit circle x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 1. On the number line, the points at distance r from c are the two points c \pm r. [Sphere] For c \in 
R^n and a real r > 0, the sphere with center c and radius r is S(c, r) \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - c} = r \}. In 
R^2 a sphere is called a circle. So the unit circle is S(0, 1) in 
R^2. How many points can a line share with a sphere? Try the unit circle and the horizontal line x_2 = h. A common point has x_1^2 = 1 - h^2. So there are two common points if \abs{h} < 1, one if \abs{h} = 1, and none if \abs{h} > 1. Here \abs{h} is the distance from the center to the line. In general, too, the answer depends only on that distance. [A Line Meets a Sphere] Let L = p + 
R v with v 
e 0, let c \in 
R^n and r > 0, and let m = p + t_0 v be the point of L nearest to c and d \coloneqq 
orm{c - m} its distance (@prp-nearest-point-on-line). Then L \cap S(c, r) is 1. empty if d > r; 2. \{ m \} if d = r; 3. the two points p +  igl( t_0 \pm \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}/
orm{v}  igr) v if d < r. Parametrize (@exm-method-parametrize): the point p + tv lies on the sphere exactly when one equation in t holds. The identity of @prp-nearest-point-on-line makes that equation a square equal to a number, (t - t_0)^2 = k, and the sign of k decides everything. Apply @prp-nearest-point-on-line to the point c. Since 
orm{y - c} = 
orm{c - y} for every y, its identity reads 
orm{(p + tv) - c}^2 = d^2 + (t - t_0)^2 
orm{v}^2 \quad 	ext{for every } t \in 
R . Both 
orm{(p + tv) - c} and r are non-negative, so we may compare squares, as in the proof of @prp-perpendicular-bisector. Thus p + tv \in S(c, r) if and only if (t - t_0)^2 = k , \qquad k \coloneqq  rac{r^2 - d^2}{
orm{v}^2} . Since d, r \ge 0, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g) and totality give: k < 0 if d > r, k = 0 if d = r, k > 0 if d < r. (a) A square is never negative (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)), so for k < 0 no t works. (b) For k = 0, (t - t_0)^2 = 0 forces t = t_0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), and the only common point is m. (c) For k > 0, let ho \coloneqq \sqrt k, the non-negative real whose square is k (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). Then ho > 0, since ho \ge 0 and ho^2 = k 
e 0. The equation (t - t_0)^2 = ho^2 says (t - t_0 - ho)(t - t_0 + ho) = 0. So t = t_0 + ho or t = t_0 - ho (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), and both work. They differ, as ho > 0. Distinct parameters give distinct points (Section 10.1). Finally ho = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}/
orm{v}, since the right side is non-negative and its square is k. Here we use that the non-negative square root is unique. @prp-distance-basic-rn (b): distance is symmetric. @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots: a non-negative square root exists and is unique. @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field: 
R is complete. When d = r the line is tangent to the sphere at m. Exercise B3 shows that the tangent lines at a point m of the sphere are exactly the lines through m whose direction is orthogonal to m - c. The last result of the section is about segments. If p and q are on opposite sides of a hyperplane, the segment between them must cross it, and it crosses exactly once. For example, p = (0, 0) and q = (4, 0) lie on opposite sides of the line x_1 = 1. The point (1 - t)p + tq = (4t, 0) is on the line only for t = 1/4, at (1, 0). [A Segment Crosses a Hyperplane Once] Let a 
e 0, c \in 
R, and let p, q \in 
R^n with \inner{a}{p} < c < \inner{a}{q}. Then [p, q] meets H_{a,c} in exactly one point, namely (1 - t_1)p + t_1 q with t_1 \coloneqq  rac{c - \inner{a}{p}}{\inner{a}{q} - \inner{a}{p}} \in (0, 1) . Write \alpha \coloneqq \inner{a}{p} and  eta \coloneqq \inner{a}{q}, so \alpha < c <  eta. Every point of [p, q] is (1 - t)p + tq with t \in [0, 1] (@def-segment-rn). By linearity (@prp-dot-product-laws-rn (b)), \inner{a}{(1 - t)p + tq} = \alpha + t( eta - \alpha) . This equals c if and only if t( eta - \alpha) = c - \alpha, and since  eta - \alpha > 0, if and only if t = t_1. Moreover 0 < c - \alpha <  eta - \alpha, so 0 < t_1 < 1. Hence the point with parameter t_1 lies on [p, q] and on H_{a,c}, and every common point has parameter t_1, so it is that point. Along the segment, the value of \inner{a}{x} grows from \alpha to  eta at a constant rate in t, so it passes the level c once. When p and q are on the same side, the segment does not reach H_{a,c} at all. Exercise B4 (d) treats the side \inner{a}{x} < c; the other side follows by replacing (a, c) with (-a, -c). Section 10.3 calls a set convex if it contains the segment between any two of its points. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Consider the hyperplane 2x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = 6 in 
R^3. 1. Give a normal vector, and a second normal vector different from the first. 2. Find the distance from 0 to the hyperplane. 3. Find the point of the hyperplane nearest to 0. title: 10.3 Convex Sets and Hulls
content:
Convex Sets and Hulls Much of analysis moves from one point to another along a segment. Here are three examples. - The mean value theorem compares f(q) with f(p) by walking from p to q. - A set is connected, in the simplest case, because any two of its points can be joined inside it. - Cauchy’s theorem in complex analysis is first proved on regions where every segment between two points stays inside. Each of these arguments needs the segment [p, q] of @def-segment-rn to lie in the set where the work is done. This section names the sets for which that holds for every pair of points, shows that balls, lines, segments, hyperplanes and half-spaces are among them, and describes the smallest such set containing a given one. Before the definition, test the property on a few sets of the plane. Which of these subsets of 
R^2 contain the segment between any two of their points? - the disc \{x : 
orm{x} \le 1\}; - the ring \{x : 1 \le 
orm{x} \le 2\}; - the line 
R(1, 1); - the two-point set \{(0, 0), (1, 0)\}; - the empty set; - the union of the two coordinate axes. The disc: yes; this section proves it for every ball. The ring: no; (3/2, 0) and (-3/2, 0) lie in it, and the midpoint (0, 0) of the segment between them has norm 0 < 1. The line: yes, since (1 - t)(s, s) + t(u, u) = (v, v) with v \coloneqq (1 - t)s + tu. The two points: no; the midpoint (1/2, 0) is neither of them. The empty set: yes, since there are no two points to test. The axes: no; (1, 0) and (0, 1) lie on them, and the midpoint (1/2, 1/2) lies on neither axis. Convex sets and balls The property tested above deserves a name. A set is convex when it never makes you leave it to walk straight from one of its points to another. In other words, the segment between any two of its points lies inside it. [Convex Set] A subset C \subseteq 
R^n is convex if [p, q] \subseteq C for all p, q \in C. In words: whenever p and q are in C, so is (1 - t)p + tq for every t \in [0, 1] (@def-segment-rn). The quantifier over t covers the whole interval [0, 1], not just the midpoint t = 1/2. This matters: the set 
Q^2 of points of the plane with rational coordinates contains every midpoint of two of its points and still is not convex (see the warning on midpoints below). The empty set is convex, since the condition has no instance to check. So is every one-point set \{p\}, since [p, p] = \{p\}. The ring and the axes tested above are not convex: in each, one pair of points already has a midpoint outside. The sets of analysis on which estimates hold are balls. The words “open” and “closed” below are names for now. Analysis on the Real Line explains them and defines balls for any distance. For instance, in 
R^2 take the points at distance less than 1 from (1, 0). The point (1/2, 0) is one of them, at distance 1/2. The point (1, 1) is not, since its distance is exactly 1; it lies on the circle around the disc. [Open and Closed Balls] Let c \in 
R^n and r > 0. The open ball and the closed ball of center c and radius r are B(c, r) \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - c} < r \} , \qquad \overline{B}(c, r) \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - c} \le r \} . For n = 1, 
orm{x - c} = \abs{x - c} (@prp-norm-basic-rn (d)). So B(c, r) is the interval (c - r, c + r), and \overline{B}(c, r) is [c - r, c + r] (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d)). For n = 2 they are discs without and with their circle S(c, r) (@def-sphere-rn). [Balls Are Convex] For every c \in 
R^n and r > 0, the balls B(c, r) and \overline{B}(c, r) are convex. [Scratch work] Unwind the goal. The definition of convexity says what to fix: two points of the ball and a parameter t \in [0, 1]. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- We know We want --------------------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
orm{p - c} < r, 
orm{q - c} < r, t \in [0, 1] 
orm{(1 - t)p + tq - c} < r the same; and c = (1 - t)c + tc 
orm{(1 - t)(p - c) + t(q - c)} < r the triangle inequality and 
orm{sx} = \abs{s}
orm{x} each of the two pieces is at most its weight times r; the gap closes, since (1 - t)r + tr = r --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The second row is the whole trick. The center is split with the same weights as the point. Then the vector inside the norm becomes a weighted sum of two vectors whose lengths we know. Let p, q \in B(c, r) and t \in [0, 1]. By the laws of the vector operations, (1 - t)p + tq - c = (1 - t)(p - c) + t(q - c). Since 1 - t \ge 0 and t \ge 0, the triangle inequality (@thm-triangle-inequality-rn (a)) gives 
orm{(1 - t)p + tq - c} \le (1 - t)
orm{p - c} + t
orm{q - c} . If t = 0 or t = 1, the point (1 - t)p + tq is p or q, which lies in B(c, r). If 0 < t < 1, both weights are positive. Multiplying by a positive number keeps a strict inequality, so (1 - t)
orm{p - c} < (1 - t)r and t
orm{q - c} < tr. Adding these bounds the right side by (1 - t)r + tr = r. Hence (1 - t)p + tq \in B(c, r), and B(c, r) is convex. For \overline{B}(c, r) the same display holds. Since all four factors are non-negative, (1 - t)
orm{p - c} \le (1 - t)r and t
orm{q - c} \le tr. Adding gives 
orm{(1 - t)p + tq - c} \le r. This proves the proposition. @prp-vector-space-laws-rn, @prp-norm-basic-rn (b): rearrangements, 
orm{sx} = \abs{s}
orm{x}; @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b), (c): adding, multiplying by positives; @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d): multiplying non-negative inequalities. A ball is convex; its boundary is not. Is the sphere S(0, 1) \subseteq 
R^2 convex? No. The points (1, 0) and (-1, 0) lie on it, and the midpoint (0, 0) of the segment between them has norm 0 
e 1. Exercise B3 shows that no point strictly inside a segment between two different points of a sphere lies on the sphere. The proof of @prp-balls-convex is the pattern for proving convexity from the definition. [Method: the two-point test] How it goes. To prove that C is convex: 1. Take p, q \in C and t \in [0, 1]. 2. Write down the condition that p and q satisfy. 3. Split the vector, or the expression, belonging to (1 - t)p + tq as (1 - t)(\dots) + t(\dots). Use the same weights on every term, including the center or the constant. 4. Conclude by the triangle inequality, or by linearity, using 1 - t \ge 0 and t \ge 0. When to use it. Proving that a set is convex straight from the definition: balls, half-spaces, sets cut out by inequalities. Common mistakes. Checking only the midpoint, t = 1/2, is not enough: the set 
Q^2 below passes that check and is not convex. Allowing t outside [0, 1] is also wrong, since then a weight is negative and the inequalities reverse. Midpoints are not enough. The set 
Q^2 of points of 
R^2 with rational coordinates contains the midpoint  igl( (a + c)/2, (b + d)/2  igr) of any two of its points (a, b), (c, d). Yet it is not convex. The field 
R is a complete ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). So the real number \sqrt 2 exists (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots). Since 1 < 2 < 4, comparing squares of non-negative numbers gives 1 < \sqrt 2 < 2 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (g)). So t \coloneqq \sqrt 2 / 2 lies in [0, 1]. Then (\sqrt 2 / 2, 0) = (1 - t)(0, 0) + t(1, 0) is a point of [(0, 0), (1, 0)]. It is not in 
Q^2: if t \in 
Q, then \sqrt 2 = 2t \in 
Q, against @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two. Examples and operations The sets of Sections 10.1 and 10.2 are convex: lines and half-spaces pass the two-point test with linearity. [Lines, Segments, Hyperplanes and Half-Spaces Are Convex] Each of the following is a convex subset of 
R^n: - every line (@def-line-rn); - every segment (@def-segment-rn); - every hyperplane H_{a,c} and each of its four half-spaces (@def-hyperplane-rn). Use the two-point test of @exm-method-two-point-test, with linearity in place of the triangle inequality. The weights 1 - t and t pass through the parameter of a line and through the dot product with a. Let t \in [0, 1]. Lines. For two points p + sv and p + uv of p + 
R v, the laws of the vector operations give (1 - t)(p + sv) + t(p + uv) = p +  igl( (1 - t)s + tu  igr)v, a point of p + 
R v. Segments. If x, y \in [p, q], then [x, y] \subseteq [p, q] by @lem-subsegment; that is the definition of convexity for [p, q]. Hyperplanes and half-spaces. For x, y \in 
R^n, linearity of the dot product (@prp-dot-product-laws-rn (b)) gives c - \inner{a}{(1 - t)x + ty} = (1 - t) igl( c - \inner{a}{x}  igr) + t igl( c - \inner{a}{y}  igr) . If x, y \in H_{a,c}, the right side is 0, so (1 - t)x + ty \in H_{a,c}. If \inner{a}{x} \le c and \inner{a}{y} \le c, both brackets are \ge 0, and so are both weights. A product of two non-negative numbers is \ge 0, and so is a sum of two such products; so the right side is \ge 0. If both brackets are > 0, the right side is > 0. Indeed, one weight is positive, so its term is a product of two positive numbers and is positive, and the other term is \ge 0. This settles \{ \inner{a}{x} \le c \} and \{ \inner{a}{x} < c \}. The half-spaces with \ge and > are those with \le and < for the normal -a and the constant -c, since multiplying by -1 reverses an inequality. Also -a 
e 0. @prp-vector-space-laws-rn (vector rearrangements); @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d): products of non-negatives; @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (a), (b), (c): negation, sums, positive products. New convex sets come from old ones by intersecting, translating and scaling, but not by joining. For example, (1, 0) + B igl( (0, 0), 1  igr) = B igl( (1, 0), 1  igr) and 2B igl( (0, 0), 1  igr) = B igl( (0, 0), 2  igr). [Operations on Convex Sets] 1. If (C_i)_{i \in I} is a family of convex subsets of 
R^n, then  igcap_{i \in I} C_i is convex. 2. If C \subseteq 
R^n is convex, b \in 
R^n and \lambda \in 
R, then b + C \coloneqq \{ b + x : x \in C \} and \lambda C \coloneqq \{ \lambda x : x \in C \} are convex. 3. A union of two convex sets need not be convex: for p 
e q, the sets \{p\} and \{q\} are convex and \{p\} \cup \{q\} is not. Each part checks one segment at a time. A segment that lies in every C_i lies in their intersection, and translating or scaling moves a segment onto a segment. (a) The intersection is taken in 
R^n, as Sets and Functions defined the intersection of a family (@fd2:def-family-union-intersection (b)). For I = \emptyset it is 
R^n, which is convex. Let p, q \in  igcap_{i} C_i. For each i, p, q \in C_i and C_i is convex, so [p, q] \subseteq C_i. Hence [p, q] \subseteq  igcap_i C_i. (b) For x, y \in C and t \in [0, 1], the laws of @prp-vector-space-laws-rn give (1 - t)(b + x) + t(b + y) = b +  igl( (1 - t)x + ty  igr) , \qquad (1 - t)\lambda x + t\lambda y = \lambda igl( (1 - t)x + ty  igr) , and (1 - t)x + ty \in C. (c) [p, p] = \{p\}, so a one-point set is convex. The midpoint m = (p + q)/2 of [p, q] is neither p nor q: m = p would give q = p, and likewise for q. Show that the triangle T \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^2 : x_1 \ge 0, \ x_2 \ge 0, \ x_1 + x_2 \le 1 \} is convex. T is the intersection of the three closed half-spaces \{ \inner{(-1, 0)}{x} \le 0 \}, \{ \inner{(0, -1)}{x} \le 0 \} and \{ \inner{(1, 1)}{x} \le 1 \}, each convex by @prp-convex-examples. By @prp-convex-operations (a), T is convex. Convex combinations and the hull A point of a segment is a sum of two points with non-negative weights adding up to 1. Allowing more than two points gives the general form. For example, the weights 	frac12, 	frac14, 	frac14 are non-negative and add up to 1. On the points (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 4) they give 	frac12(0, 0) + 	frac14(4, 0) + 	frac14(0, 4) = (1, 1). [Convex Combination] Let k \ge 1 and p_1, \dots, p_k \in 
R^n. A convex combination of p_1, \dots, p_k is a point \lambda_1 p_1 + \dots + \lambda_k p_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i p_i \quad 	ext{with every } \lambda_i \ge 0 	ext{ and } \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i = 1 . The numbers \lambda_i are its weights. For k = 1 the only convex combination of p_1 is p_1 itself. For k = 2, the weights are 1 - t and t with t \in [0, 1], and the convex combinations of p_1, p_2 form [p_1, p_2]. The points need not be distinct. A convex set is defined by a condition on two points. It controls combinations of any number of points. [Convex Sets Contain Their Convex Combinations] Let C \subseteq 
R^n be convex. Then every convex combination of finitely many points of C lies in C. Peel off the last point. Convexity speaks about two points at a time, so split one point off. Of k + 1 weighted points, keep the last one. Rescale the first k weights so that they add up to 1 again. By induction, the first k points then give one point y of C, and the whole combination is a point of the segment [y, p_{k+1}]. The rescaling divides by 1 - \lambda_{k+1}, so the case \lambda_{k+1} = 1 is set aside. For k \ge 1, let P(k) be the statement: for all p_1, \dots, p_k \in C, every convex combination of p_1, \dots, p_k lies in C. We prove P(k) for every k \ge 1 by induction from the base 1 (@fd2:thm-induction). Base case. A convex combination of one point p_1 \in C has \lambda_1 = 1, so it is p_1 \in C. Inductive step. Let k \ge 1 and assume P(k). Let p_1, \dots, p_{k+1} \in C and let x = \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \lambda_i p_i be a convex combination of them. If \lambda_{k+1} = 1, then \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i = 0 with every \lambda_i \ge 0, so every \lambda_i with i \le k is 0 (@prp-sum-order (e)). Then 0\,p_i = 0 (@prp-vector-space-laws-rn (i)), and x = 1\,p_{k+1} = p_{k+1} \in C. Suppose now \lambda_{k+1} 
e 1. The weights \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k are non-negative, so \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i \ge 0 (@prp-sum-order (a)), and \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i = 1 - \lambda_{k+1} by the recursion for sums. Hence s \coloneqq 1 - \lambda_{k+1} satisfies s \ge 0 and s 
e 0, so s > 0, and \lambda_{k+1} = 1 - s \in [0, 1]. The numbers \lambda_i / s, for i \le k, are non-negative and add up to s/s = 1, since the constant 1/s comes out of the sum. So y \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{k}  rac{\lambda_i}{s} \, p_i is a convex combination of p_1, \dots, p_k, and y \in C by P(k). By the recursion for sums, and by taking the constant s out of the sum in each coordinate, x = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i p_i + \lambda_{k+1} p_{k+1} = s\,y + \lambda_{k+1} p_{k+1} = (1 - \lambda_{k+1})\,y + \lambda_{k+1}\,p_{k+1} , a point of [y, p_{k+1}]. Since y, p_{k+1} \in C and C is convex, x \in C. This proves P(k + 1), and the theorem follows. @lem-ring-finite-sums (b): constants come out; @lem-vector-sums-coordinatewise (a): vector sums by coordinates; @prp-sum-order (a), (e): sums of non-negatives; @prp-vector-space-laws-rn (i): 0\,p = 0. Among all convex sets containing a given set S, there is a smallest one. It is built the way Sets and Functions built the smallest closed set (@fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set): intersect all candidates. For the two points (0, 0) and (1, 0), every convex set containing both contains the segment between them. That segment is itself convex, so it is the smallest convex set containing the two points. [Convex Hull] Let S \subseteq 
R^n. The convex hull of S is \operatorname{conv} S \coloneqq  igcap \{ C \subseteq 
R^n : C 	ext{ is convex and } S \subseteq C \} . The family being intersected is non-empty, since 
R^n is convex and contains S. So \operatorname{conv} S is a subset of 
R^n, and it has three properties: - it is convex, by @prp-convex-operations (a); - it contains S, since every member of the family does; - it lies inside every convex set that contains S, since it is the intersection of all of them. In short, \operatorname{conv} S is the smallest convex set containing S. For example, \operatorname{conv}\{p, q\} = [p, q]. Indeed, the segment is convex (@prp-convex-examples) and contains p and q, and every convex set containing p and q contains [p, q]. The definition says what the hull is, but not how to find its points. The next theorem does. [The Convex Hull Is the Set of Convex Combinations] Let S \subseteq 
R^n, and let K be the set of all convex combinations of finitely many points of S. Then \operatorname{conv} S = K. Try it first (ten minutes): for three points p, q, r of the plane, describe \operatorname{conv}\{p, q, r\} without the word “intersection”. The first guess is the three sides, [p, q] \cup [q, r] \cup [r, p]. It contains p, q, r, but it is not convex. For p = (0, 0), q = (2, 0), r = (0, 2), the points (1, 0) \in [p, q] and (0, 1) \in [r, p] have midpoint (1/2, 1/2), which lies on none of the three sides. So the hull must also contain every segment [x, r] with x \in [p, q]. A point of such a segment is (1 - t) igl( (1 - s)p + sq  igr) + tr: a convex combination of p, q, r. That suggests the theorem, and suggests its two halves: ① every convex combination of points of S lies in \operatorname{conv} S, which is @thm-convex-contains-combinations applied to the convex set \operatorname{conv} S; ② the set K is itself convex and contains S, so the smallest such set lies inside it. For ②, two convex combinations are mixed by writing their two lists of points one after the other. (\supseteq) The set \operatorname{conv} S is convex and contains S, as shown just after @def-convex-hull-rn. By @thm-convex-contains-combinations, it contains every convex combination of finitely many of its points, in particular of points of S. So K \subseteq \operatorname{conv} S. (\subseteq) First, S \subseteq K: each p \in S is the convex combination 1\,p. Next, K is convex. Let x = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i p_i and y = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \mu_j q_j be in K, with p_i, q_j \in S, and let t \in [0, 1]. Join the two lists: let r_i \coloneqq p_i and 
u_i \coloneqq (1 - t)\lambda_i for 1 \le i \le k, and r_{k+j} \coloneqq q_j and 
u_{k+j} \coloneqq t\mu_j for 1 \le j \le m. Each 
u_i is a product of two non-negative numbers, so 
u_i \ge 0. Split the sum over the joined list into its two parts, and take the constants out of the two sums. This gives \sum_{i=1}^{k+m} 
u_i = (1 - t)\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i + t\sum_{j=1}^{m} \mu_j = (1 - t) + t = 1 . The same two rules, applied in each coordinate, give \sum_{i=1}^{k+m} 
u_i r_i = (1 - t)\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i p_i + t\sum_{j=1}^{m} \mu_j q_j = (1 - t)x + ty . So (1 - t)x + ty is a convex combination of the points r_1, \dots, r_{k+m} of S, and lies in K. Thus K is a convex set containing S. Since \operatorname{conv} S lies inside every such set, \operatorname{conv} S \subseteq K. This proves \operatorname{conv} S = K. @prp-sum-reindex (b): splitting a sum; @lem-ring-finite-sums (b): constants come out; @lem-vector-sums-coordinatewise (a): vector sums by coordinates; @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d): products of non-negatives. The theorem turns membership in a hull, a statement about all convex sets at once, into a search for weights. [A Triangle as a Hull] Let p_1, p_2, p_3 \in 
R^2. (a) Show that \operatorname{conv}\{p_1, p_2, p_3\} is the set T of points \lambda_1 p_1 + \lambda_2 p_2 + \lambda_3 p_3 with \lambda_i \ge 0 and \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 1: the filled triangle with corners p_1, p_2, p_3. (b) For p_1 = (0, 0), p_2 = (3, 0), p_3 = (0, 3), decide whether (1, 1) and (2, 2) lie in the hull. (a) T \subseteq \operatorname{conv}\{p_1, p_2, p_3\} by @thm-convex-hull-combinations-rn. For the other inclusion it is enough that T is convex, since it contains p_1 (weights 1, 0, 0), p_2 and p_3. For two points of T with weights \lambda_i and \mu_i, and t \in [0, 1], (1 - t)\sum_{i=1}^{3} \lambda_i p_i + t\sum_{i=1}^{3} \mu_i p_i = \sum_{i=1}^{3}  igl( (1 - t)\lambda_i + t\mu_i  igr) p_i , and the new weights are non-negative and add up to (1 - t) + t = 1. This is the proof of @thm-convex-hull-combinations-rn with the two lists kept equal instead of joined. (b) The weights \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambda_3 = 1/3 give 	frac13(0, 0) + 	frac13(3, 0) + 	frac13(0, 3) = (1, 1), so (1, 1) is in the hull. For (2, 2): any weights with \lambda_1(0, 0) + \lambda_2(3, 0) + \lambda_3(0, 3) = (2, 2) have 3\lambda_2 = 2 and 3\lambda_3 = 2, so \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 4/3 and \lambda_1 = 1 - 4/3 < 0. No admissible weights exist, and (2, 2) is not in the hull. In this example the hull is \{ x_1 \ge 0, \ x_2 \ge 0, \ x_1 + x_2 \le 3 \}: by (a) its points are (3\lambda_2, 3\lambda_3) with \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \ge 0 and \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 1 - \lambda_1 \le 1, and conversely a point x of the set has the weights \lambda_2 = x_1/3, \lambda_3 = x_2/3, \lambda_1 = 1 - (x_1 + x_2)/3 \ge 0. It is three times the triangle \{ x_1 \ge 0, \ x_2 \ge 0, \ x_1 + x_2 \le 1 \} shown convex earlier, and (2, 2) breaks the third inequality. Star-shaped sets Some arguments need segments only from one fixed point, not between every pair of points. For instance, the union of the two axes of 
R^2 is not convex. Yet every segment from (0, 0) to one of its points stays inside it. [Star-Shaped Set] A set S \subseteq 
R^n is star-shaped about a point c \in S if [c, x] \subseteq S for every x \in S. It is star-shaped if it is star-shaped about some point of S. A non-empty convex set is star-shaped about each of its points: that is the definition of convexity with p = c. The converse fails. [The Axes: Star-Shaped, Not Convex] Let A \coloneqq 
R(1, 0) \cup 
R(0, 1) \subseteq 
R^2, the union of the two axes. Show that A is star-shaped about 0, is not convex, and is not star-shaped about (1, 0). For x = (s, 0) \in A and t \in [0, 1], (1 - t)\,0 + t(s, 0) = (ts, 0) \in A; points of the other axis are handled the same way. So A is star-shaped about 0. The points (1, 0) and (0, 1) lie in A, and the midpoint (1/2, 1/2) of the segment between them has both coordinates non-zero, so it lies on neither axis. This shows at once that A is not convex and that [(1, 0), (0, 1)] 
ot\subseteq A, so A is not star-shaped about (1, 0). Convex and star-shaped sets return throughout the series. Analysis on the Real Line uses convex balls to join points by segments, for connectedness. Analysis in Several Variables uses segments inside convex sets for the mean value inequality. Complex Analysis proves Cauchy’s theorem first on convex and star-shaped regions. Analysis on Manifolds proves the Poincaré lemma on star-shaped sets. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Decide which of these subsets of 
R^2 are convex. Justify each answer that is “no” with two points. 1. \{ (x, y) : y \ge x^2 \}. 2. \{ (x, y) : y \le x^2 \}. 3. 
Z^2. 4. \{ x : 1 \le 
orm{x} \le 2 \}. (a) Convex; Exercise B1 proves it with the two-point test. (b) Not convex: (1, 1) and (-1, 1) lie in the set (1 \le 1), and their midpoint (0, 1) does not, since 1 > 0 = 0^2. (c) Not convex: (0, 0), (1, 0) \in 
Z^2, and the midpoint (1/2, 0) 
otin 
Z^2. (d) Not convex: (3/2, 0) and (-3/2, 0) lie in the ring, and the midpoint (0, 0) has norm 0 < 1. [A2] 1. Is (1, 2) in \operatorname{conv}\{(0, 0), (3, 0), (0, 3)\}? 2. Consider the proof of @thm-convex-hull-combinations-rn. Which of its two inclusions uses @thm-convex-contains-combinations, and what does it apply that theorem to? Why is the family of convex sets containing S, in @def-convex-hull-rn, non-empty? (a) Yes: 0\,(0, 0) + 	frac13(3, 0) + 	frac23(0, 3) = (1, 2), with non-negative weights adding up to 1. (b) The inclusion K \subseteq \operatorname{conv} S. It applies the theorem to the convex set \operatorname{conv} S, which contains S, so it contains every convex combination of points of S. The family contains 
R^n, which is convex and contains S. B. Practice [B1] Prove that P \coloneqq \{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : y \ge x^2 \} is convex. We use the two-point test (@exm-method-two-point-test). Let (a, b), (c, d) \in P, so b \ge a^2 and d \ge c^2, and let t \in [0, 1]. The point (1 - t)(a, b) + t(c, d) has coordinates (1 - t)a + tc and (1 - t)b + td. Since 1 - t \ge 0 and t \ge 0, multiplying keeps the two inequalities, and adding them gives (1 - t)b + td \ge (1 - t)a^2 + tc^2 . Expanding the square, (1 - t)a^2 + tc^2 -  igl( (1 - t)a + tc  igr)^2 = t(1 - t)(a - c)^2 , since (1 - t) - (1 - t)^2 = t(1 - t) = t - t^2. The right side is \ge 0: t(1 - t) \ge 0 and (a - c)^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e)). Hence (1 - t)b + td \ge  igl( (1 - t)a + tc  igr)^2, and the point lies in P. @fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves (d): multiplying non-negative inequalities; @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (b): adding inequalities. [B2] For C, D \subseteq 
R^n, let C + D \coloneqq \{ x + y : x \in C, \ y \in D \}. Prove that if C and D are convex, so is C + D. Let x + y and x' + y' be points of C + D, with x, x' \in C and y, y' \in D, and let t \in [0, 1]. By the laws of @prp-vector-space-laws-rn, (1 - t)(x + y) + t(x' + y') =  igl( (1 - t)x + tx'  igr) +  igl( (1 - t)y + ty'  igr) . The first bracket lies in C and the second in D, by convexity. So the point lies in C + D. [B3] Let c \in 
R^n, r > 0, and let p 
e q be points of the sphere S(c, r). Prove that 
orm{(1 - t)p + tq - c} < r for every t with 0 < t < 1. We use the equality case, as in @exm-method-equality-case. Let u \coloneqq (1 - t)(p - c) and w \coloneqq t(q - c), so (1 - t)p + tq - c = u + w (@prp-vector-space-laws-rn). By @prp-norm-basic-rn (b), 
orm{u} = (1 - t)r and 
orm{w} = tr. So the triangle inequality gives 
orm{u + w} \le (1 - t)r + tr = r. Suppose 
orm{u + w} = r = 
orm{u} + 
orm{w}. Here u 
e 0, since 
orm{u} = (1 - t)r > 0. By the equality case of @thm-triangle-inequality-rn (a), w = \lambda u for some \lambda \ge 0, that is, t(q - c) = \lambda(1 - t)(p - c). Dividing by t > 0, q - c = \mu(p - c) with \mu \coloneqq \lambda(1 - t)/t \ge 0. Taking norms, r = \mu r, so \mu = 1 and q = p, a contradiction. Hence 
orm{u + w} < r. The result depends on the equality case of the triangle inequality, which belongs to the Euclidean norm. Measure distances in 
R^2 instead by \max(\abs{x_1 - y_1}, \abs{x_2 - y_2}): the “unit ball” about 0 is the square \{ \max(\abs{x_1}, \abs{x_2}) \le 1 \}, and its edge contains the whole segment [(1, -1), (1, 1)], so the analogue of this exercise fails. So does the analogue of @thm-betweenness: the point (1, 1) is at distance 1 from (0, 0) and from (2, 0), and 1 + 1 = 2 is the distance between them, yet (1, 1) is not on the segment [(0, 0), (2, 0)]. Analysis on the Real Line returns to this distance. [B4: Prove or disprove] Prove each statement or give a counterexample. Throughout, C, S, T are subsets of 
R^n. 1. The union of two convex sets is convex. 2. The complement 
R^2 \setminus C of a convex set C \subseteq 
R^2 is convex. 3. \operatorname{conv}(S \cup T) = \operatorname{conv} S \cup \operatorname{conv} T. 4. For p, q \in 
R^n, the set \{ x : 
orm{x - p} \le 
orm{x - q} \} is convex. 5. If C is convex and \lambda, \mu \ge 0, then \lambda C + \mu C = (\lambda + \mu)C (notation of Exercise B2 and @prp-convex-operations (b)). (a) False. @prp-convex-operations (c): \{p\} \cup \{q\} with p 
e q. (b) False. C = \overline{B}(0, 1) is convex (@prp-balls-convex). The points (2, 0) and (-2, 0) lie outside it, and their midpoint (0, 0) lies in it. (c) False. Take S = \{p\}, T = \{q\} with p 
e q. Then \operatorname{conv} S = \{p\} and \operatorname{conv} T = \{q\}, since one-point sets are convex; but \operatorname{conv}(S \cup T) = [p, q] (the example after @def-convex-hull-rn) contains the midpoint, which is neither p nor q. (d) True. If p = q, the set is 
R^n. If p 
e q, let c \coloneqq (
orm{q}^2 - 
orm{p}^2)/2. By @prp-perpendicular-bisector, 
orm{x - p} < 
orm{x - q} if and only if \inner{q - p}{x} < c, and 
orm{x - p} = 
orm{x - q} if and only if \inner{q - p}{x} = c. Since \le means “< or =” (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)), the set is the closed half-space \{ \inner{q - p}{x} \le c \}. It is convex by @prp-convex-examples. (e) True. (\supseteq) For x \in C, (\lambda + \mu)x = \lambda x + \mu x \in \lambda C + \mu C (@prp-vector-space-laws-rn (h)). (\subseteq) Let \lambda x + \mu y \in \lambda C + \mu C, with x, y \in C. If \lambda + \mu > 0, let s \coloneqq \mu/(\lambda + \mu) \in [0, 1]; then \lambda x + \mu y = (\lambda + \mu) igl( (1 - s)x + sy  igr) , and (1 - s)x + sy \in C by convexity. If \lambda = \mu = 0, both sides are \{0\} when C 
e \emptyset and \emptyset when C = \emptyset. Convexity is needed: for C = \{0, e_1\} \subseteq 
R^n and \lambda = \mu = 1, the point e_1 = 0 + e_1 lies in C + C but not in 2C = \{0, 2e_1\}. C. Going deeper [C1: Chapter check: convex subsets of the line] Let C \subseteq 
R be non-empty and convex. Let \alpha \coloneqq \inf C if C is bounded below, and \alpha \coloneqq -\infty otherwise; let  eta \coloneqq \sup C if C is bounded above, and  eta \coloneqq +\infty otherwise. Prove that every real x with \alpha < x <  eta lies in C, and that every c \in C satisfies \alpha \le c \le  eta. (So C is an interval with ends \alpha and  eta, each end included or not.) [Hint 1] For x strictly between \alpha and  eta, look for two points of C, one on each side of x. [Hint 2] Since x > \inf C, what can you say about x as a bound of C? Then ask what that says about the elements of C. The supremum and the infimum. If C is bounded above, \sup C exists, since C is non-empty and 
R is complete (@fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field). If C is bounded below, \inf C exists, again since C is non-empty (@prp-real-infimum (b)). Two points around x. Let \alpha < x <  eta. If C is bounded below, x > \inf C, so x is not a lower bound of C; if C is not bounded below, no real number is a lower bound. Either way there is a \in C with a < x (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (i)). In the same way, x is not an upper bound of C, and there is b \in C with x < b. The segment is the interval. For n = 1, (1 - t)a + tb = a + t(b - a). Let t \coloneqq (x - a)/(b - a), which is defined since b - a > 0. It lies in (0, 1). First, 1/(b - a) > 0, since otherwise 1 = (b - a) \cdot 1/(b - a) \le 0, against 1 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), (e)). Now 0 < x - a < b - a, and multiplying by 1/(b - a) > 0 keeps both inequalities, by the same rule (c). With this t, we get (1 - t)a + tb = x. So x \in [a, b] \subseteq C, by convexity. Conclusion. Every x with \alpha < x <  eta lies in C. For c \in C, \alpha \le c because \inf C is a lower bound (or \alpha = -\infty), and c \le  eta likewise. So C is one of the intervals (\alpha,  eta), [\alpha,  eta), (\alpha,  eta], [\alpha,  eta], where an infinite end is never included. What a complete answer needs. (10 points) - 3: handles the ends: \sup C by completeness when bounded above, \inf C when bounded below (@prp-real-infimum), and the unbounded cases. - 3: finds a, b \in C with a < x < b, from “x is not a lower (upper) bound”. - 2: shows x \in [a, b] by an explicit t \in [0, 1], or by the remark of Section 10.1 that a segment of 
R is an interval. - 2: concludes both inclusions. Slips that lose the step (0 for the step): using \inf C or \sup C without boundedness; assuming that C contains its supremum or infimum. @fd3:def-complete-ordered-field (bounded sets have suprema). R. Review [R1] Let Q \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : \abs{x_k} \le 1 	ext{ for every } k \}. Show that Q is convex and that \overline{B}(0, 1) \subseteq Q \subseteq \overline{B}(0, \sqrt n). By @fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field (d), \abs{x_k} \le 1 if and only if -1 \le x_k \le 1, that is, x_k \le 1 and -x_k \le 1. Since x_k = \inner{e_k}{x} and -x_k = \inner{-e_k}{x} (@prp-dot-product-laws-rn (a), (b), (d)), Q is the intersection of the 2n closed half-spaces \{ \inner{e_k}{x} \le 1 \} and \{ \inner{-e_k}{x} \le 1 \}, whose normals \pm e_k are non-zero. Each is convex by @prp-convex-examples. So Q, their intersection, is convex by @prp-convex-operations (a). If 
orm{x} \le 1, then \abs{x_k} \le 
orm{x} \le 1 for every k (@prp-norm-coordinate-bounds (a)), so x \in Q. If x \in Q, then M \coloneqq \max_k \abs{x_k} \le 1, so 
orm{x} \le \sqrt n \, M \le \sqrt n (@prp-norm-coordinate-bounds (b)), and x \in \overline{B}(0, \sqrt n). These two inclusions, a ball inside a box inside a larger ball, are the ones Analysis on the Real Line uses to compare balls and boxes. [R2] Identify the polynomial a + bx + cx^2 \in 
R[x] with the point (a, b, c) \in 
R^3. Show that the set P of such polynomials f with f(t) \ge 0 for every t \in [0, 1] is a convex subset of 
R^3. Fix t \in [0, 1]. Evaluation respects sums and products, sends a constant to itself and x to t (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations). So for f = a + bx + cx^2, by the definition of the dot product, f(t) = a + bt + ct^2 = \inner{(1, t, t^2)}{(a, b, c)} . So P_t \coloneqq \{ f : f(t) \ge 0 \} is the closed half-space \{ \inner{(1, t, t^2)}{y} \ge 0 \} of 
R^3. Its normal (1, t, t^2) is non-zero, since its first coordinate is 1. So P_t is convex by @prp-convex-examples. Then P =  igcap_{t \in [0, 1]} P_t is convex by @prp-convex-operations (a). The two-point test also works directly. Let f = a + bx + cx^2 and g = a' + b'x + c'x^2 be in P and s \in [0, 1]. Then (1 - s)f(t) + sg(t) \ge 0 for every t \in [0, 1]. By the displayed formula, this is the value at t of the polynomial with coefficient triple (1 - s)(a, b, c) + s(a', b', c'). So that polynomial is in P. @def-dot-product-rn (the dot product). [R3] Let c \in 
C, r > 0 and u \in 
T. Show that D \coloneqq \{ z \in 
C : \abs{z - c} < r \} is convex as a subset of 
R^2, and that z \mapsto uz maps D onto \{ w \in 
C : \abs{w - uc} < r \}. Reading 
C as 
R^2, \abs{z - c} = 
orm{z - c} (@prp-plane-is-complex-plane (a), (c)). So D = B(c, r), which is convex by @prp-balls-convex. For z \in D, \abs{uz - uc} = \abs{u}\,\abs{z - c} = \abs{z - c} < r by @thm-conjugate-properties (d) and \abs{u} = 1; so uz lies in the second disc. Onto: let \abs{w - uc} < r and put z \coloneqq \conj{u} w. Since \conj{u} = u^{-1} (@prp-unit-circle (a)), uz = w. Also \conj{u}\,u\,c = c, and \abs{\conj{u}} = \abs{u} = 1 by @thm-conjugate-properties (d). Hence \abs{z - c} = \abs{\conj{u}(w - uc)} = \abs{\conj{u}}\,\abs{w - uc} = \abs{w - uc} < r , and z \in D. Multiplying the plane by a unit complex number turns it about 0, and Complex Analysis opens with this picture.
