Chapter Review Summary A line in 
R^n is p + 
R v with v 
e 0, and two distinct points lie on exactly one line (@prp-line-through-two-points). A point lies on the segment [p, q] exactly when its distances to the ends add up to 
orm{p - q}, and then those two distances fix it (@thm-betweenness, @cor-point-pinned-on-segment). A hyperplane H_{a,c} determines its normal vector up to a non-zero factor (@prp-hyperplane-normals). The points equidistant from p 
e q form a hyperplane (@prp-perpendicular-bisector). Every point has exactly one nearest point on a line and on a hyperplane, with explicit formulas (@prp-nearest-point-on-line, @prp-nearest-point-on-hyperplane). A line meets a sphere in zero, one or two points according to its distance from the center (@prp-line-meets-sphere). Balls, lines, segments, hyperplanes and half-spaces are convex, and so is any intersection of convex sets (@prp-balls-convex, @prp-convex-examples, @prp-convex-operations). The convex hull of a set is the set of convex combinations of its points (@thm-convex-hull-combinations-rn). What is open: the words “open ball” and “closed ball” are only names here. Analysis on the Real Line explains them, defines balls for any distance, and starts the analysis that uses this chapter’s geometry. Proof methods in this chapter - Parametrize and solve (@exm-method-parametrize). Give each line or segment its own parameter, write one equation per coordinate, solve, and check every equation, with the range [0, 1] for a segment. Introduced in Section 10.1, where it decides whether two lines in space meet. It returns more briefly in Section 10.2, where a line meets a sphere at the parameters solving one quadratic equation. - Use the equality case (@exm-method-equality-case). When a known inequality holds with equality, write its equality condition with a named multiplier and solve. Introduced in Section 10.1, where it proves that a point with 
orm{p - x} + 
orm{x - q} = 
orm{p - q} lies on [p, q]. Exercise B3 of Section 10.3 uses it again, to show that the points strictly between two points of a sphere lie inside it. - The two-point test (@exm-method-two-point-test). To prove a set convex, take two of its points and t \in [0, 1], split (1 - t)p + tq into (1 - t)(\dots) + t(\dots), and finish by the triangle inequality or by linearity. Introduced in Section 10.3, where it shows that balls are convex. Exercise B2 there runs it for sums of convex sets, and review exercise R2 offers it as a second route. - Peel off the last point. Convexity speaks about two points at a time, so a statement about k + 1 points is reduced to one about k points and a segment. It proves in Section 10.3 that a convex set contains every convex combination of its points (@thm-convex-contains-combinations). Terms - closed ball, open ball: \overline{B}(c, r) = \{x : 
orm{x - c} \le r\} and B(c, r) = \{x : 
orm{x - c} < r\}, for r > 0 (@def-ball-rn). - collinear points: points that all lie on one line (@def-collinear). - convex combination: a sum \lambda_1 p_1 + \dots + \lambda_k p_k with every \lambda_i \ge 0 and \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_k = 1 (@def-convex-combination-rn). - convex hull: the intersection of all convex sets containing a set S, written \operatorname{conv} S (@def-convex-hull-rn). - convex set: a set that contains the segment between any two of its points (@def-convex-set-rn). - half-space: one of the sets \{\inner{a}{x} \le c\}, \{\inner{a}{x} \ge c\} (closed) or \{\inner{a}{x} < c\}, \{\inner{a}{x} > c\} (open), for a 
e 0 (@def-hyperplane-rn). - hyperplane: a set H_{a,c} = \{x \in 
R^n : \inner{a}{x} = c\} with a 
e 0 (@def-hyperplane-rn). - line: a set p + 
R v = \{p + tv : t \in 
R\} with v 
e 0; t \mapsto p + tv is a parametrization of it (@def-line-rn). - normal vector: the vector a in H_{a,c}, fixed by the hyperplane only up to a non-zero factor (@def-hyperplane-rn). - segment: [p, q] = \{(1 - t)p + tq : t \in [0, 1]\}, with midpoint (p + q)/2 (@def-segment-rn). - sphere: S(c, r) = \{x : 
orm{x - c} = r\}, for r > 0 (@def-sphere-rn). - star-shaped set: a set S with a point c \in S such that [c, x] \subseteq S for every x \in S (@def-star-shaped). Results used from earlier volumes Number Systems: From 
N to 
R: - the rules of an ordered ring (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules), an ordered field (@fd3:prp-ordered-field-halves) and the absolute value (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field), on nearly every page; - square roots in 
R (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots, @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field), for spheres meeting lines and for the warning of Section 10.3; - completeness (@fd3:def-complete-ordered-field), in Exercise C1 of Section 10.3; - the irrationality of \sqrt 2 (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two). Sets and Functions: - intersections of families (@fd2:def-family-union-intersection) and the smallest set with a property (@fd2:prp-smallest-closed-set), for convex hulls; - induction (@fd2:thm-induction), for convex combinations of many points. Results used from earlier chapters - Chapter 9, Sections 9.2 to 9.4: vectors and their operations (@def-vector-operations-rn), the norm (@def-norm-rn, @prp-norm-basic-rn), the distance (@def-distance-rn), expanding a square (@exm-method-expand-the-square) and Pythagoras (@prp-pythagoras-rn). - Chapter 9, Section 9.5: the triangle inequality with its equality case (@thm-triangle-inequality-rn), which Section 10.1 rests on. - Chapter 9, Section 9.6: projection onto a line (@def-projection-rn) and the closest-point theorem (@thm-projection-closest-point), which give every nearest point of Section 10.2. - Chapter 1, Section 1.1: the rules for finite sums (@lem-ring-finite-sums, @prp-sum-reindex), in Section 10.3. - Chapter 8, Section 8.3: the infimum by reflection (@prp-real-infimum), in Exercise C1 of Section 10.3. - For the review exercises of Section 10.3 only: - the coordinate bounds for the norm (@prp-norm-coordinate-bounds) and the plane read as 
C (@prp-plane-is-complex-plane), from Section 9.4; - the modulus (@thm-conjugate-properties) and the unit circle (@prp-unit-circle), from Sections 3.2 and 3.5; - evaluation of polynomials (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), from Section 6.4. Borrowed facts The chapter borrows nothing new. It uses no cosine, sine or \pi, and no angle: everything in it is proved from the ordered field 
R and the results listed above. It uses no linear algebra either, and no limits. Threads - Betweenness by distances. Section 10.1 says “x lies on [p, q]” using distances alone (@thm-betweenness). The equality case behind it belongs to the Euclidean distance. For the distance that measures by the largest coordinate, the square \{\max(\abs{x_1}, \abs{x_2}) \le 1\} has a whole segment in its edge, so the analogue of Exercise B3 of Section 10.3 fails. Analysis on the Real Line takes the distance-only form to sets with any distance. Affine and Projective Geometry uses it to show that distance-preserving maps keep segments. - Convex and star-shaped sets. Balls are convex (Section 10.3), and convex sets are star-shaped about each of their points. Analysis on the Real Line joins points of a ball by segments when it studies connectedness. Complex Analysis proves Cauchy’s theorem first on discs and convex sets, where a primitive is built by integrating along segments. Analysis on Manifolds proves the Poincaré lemma on star-shaped sets.

title: Example (Method: telescoping)
content: How it goes. To find \(\sum a_k\) , write \(a_k = b_{k+1} - b_k\) , or \(b_k - b_{k+1}\) , for a sequence \(b\) you choose. Then the sum is the last \(b\) minus the first (the first minus the last for \(b_k - b_{k+1}\) ) ( @thm-telescoping ). To verify a guessed formula \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = F(n)\) , check \(F(0) = a_0\) and \(F(k) - F(k-1) = a_k\) for \(1 \le k \le n\) . Telescoping over \(1 \le k \le n\) then gives \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = a_0 + F(n) - F(0) = F(n)\) . When to use it. Quotients whose denominator is a product of shifted factors; differences of powers or roots; any sum whose partial sums you can guess. Common mistakes. A common mistake is to use a difference \(b_{k+2} - b_k\) , which skips a step. Such a sum leaves two terms at each end, not one.

title: Example (Odd numbers by reversal)
content: Show that \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} (2k + 1) = (n + 1)^2\) for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Example (A telescoping sum)
content: Find \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k(k+1)}\) for \(n \ge 1\) with @thm-telescoping .

title: Example (The sum of the squares)
content: Find \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^2\) for \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Compute \(\sum_{k=5}^{4} k\) and \(\prod_{k=1}^{3} (k + 1)\) . True or false, with a reason: \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_k = \bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{n} b_k\bigr)\) for all \(n \in \nN\) and all reals \(a_k, b_k\) . Rewrite \(\sum_{k=2}^{6} k^2\) with the index starting at \(0\) . Which \(b_k\) makes \(a_k = 2k + 1\) a telescoping difference \(b_{k+1} - b_k\) ?

title: Exercise (B2: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove or disprove, for all \(n \ge 1\) and all reals \(a_k\) , \(b_k\) : \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (a_k + 1) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k + n\) . \(\bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\bigr)^2 = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k^2\) . \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{n-k} b_k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k}\) . \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k(k+2)} = \frac12 \bigl(1 - \frac{1}{n+2}\bigr)\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Name the method)
content: Say which method this is, then complete it. Show that, for every \(n \in \nN\) , \[ \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{2k+1}{k^2(k+1)^2} = 1 - \frac{1}{(n+1)^2} . \]

title: Exercise (B4: Find the error)
content: Claim: for every \(n \ge 1\) and all \(b_1, \dots, b_{n+1}\) in a commutative ring, \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (b_{k+1} - b_k) = b_n - b_1\) . Proof. With \(j = k - 1\) the sum is \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (b_{j+2} - b_{j+1})\) , and @thm-telescoping (a) with \(n - 1\) in place of \(n\) gives the last term minus the first, \(b_n - b_1\) . Find the wrong step. Is the claim true?

title: Exercise (C1: The sum of the cubes)
content: Prove that \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^3 = \Bigl( \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \Bigr)^2\) for every \(n \in \nN\) , by the verification form of @exm-method-telescoping .

title: Lemma 1.1.8 (Difference of Powers)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, let \(z, w \in R\) , and let \(n \in \nN\) with \(n \ge 1\) . Then \[ z^n - w^n = (z - w) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} z^k w^{n-1-k} . \] In particular \(z^n - 1 = (z - 1)(1 + z + z^2 + \dots + z^{n-1})\) .

title: Lemma 1.1.2 (Natural Multiples in a Commutative Ring)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(a, b \in R\) and \(m, k \in \nN\) . \((m + k) \cdot a = m \cdot a + k \cdot a\) . \(m \cdot (a + b) = m \cdot a + m \cdot b\) . \((m \cdot a) b = m \cdot (ab)\) . \((mk) \cdot a = m \cdot (k \cdot a)\) . \(m \cdot a = (m \cdot 1) a\) .

title: Lemma 1.1.3 (Finite Sums in a Commutative Ring)
content:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(n \in 
N\) , \(c \in R\) , and let \((a_k)_{k \in 
N}\) and \((b_k)_{k \in 
N}\) be sequences in \(R\) . \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} (a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k + \sum_{k=0}^{n} b_k\) . \(c \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} c\, a_k\) . \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} m \cdot a_k = m \cdot \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k\) for every \(m \in 
N\) . Let \(j \in 
N\) , and suppose \(a_k = 0\) for every \(k 
e j\) . Then \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = a_j\) if \(j \le n\) , and \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = 0\) if \(j > n\) . \(-\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-a_k)\) . (Splitting off the first term.) \(\sum_{k=0}^{n+1} a_k = a_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{k+1}\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.6 (Double Sums over a Rectangle)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(m, n \in \nN\) and \(a_{ij} \in R\) for \(0 \le i \le m\) , \(0 \le j \le n\) . Then \[ \sum_{i=0}^{m} \sum_{j=0}^{n} a_{ij} = \sum_{j=0}^{n} \sum_{i=0}^{m} a_{ij} . \] In particular, for \(x_0, \dots, x_m, y_0, \dots, y_n \in R\) , \[ \Bigl( \sum_{i=0}^{m} x_i \Bigr) \Bigl( \sum_{j=0}^{n} y_j \Bigr) = \sum_{i=0}^{m} \sum_{j=0}^{n} x_i y_j . \]

title: Proposition 1.1.1 (Laws of Powers in a Commutative Ring)
content:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring ( @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field ), let \(z, w \in R\) , and let \(m, n \in 
N\) . \(z^{m+n} = z^m z^n\) . \((z^m)^n = z^{mn}\) . \((zw)^n = z^n w^n\) . If \(R\) is a field and \(z 
e 0\) , then \(z^n 
e 0\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.5 (Comparing Sums Termwise)
content: Let \(F\) be an ordered field, \(n \in \nN\) and \(a_k, b_k \in F\) for \(0 \le k \le n\) . All sums run over \(0 \le k \le n\) unless bounds are shown. If \(a_k \le b_k\) for every \(k\) , then \(\sum a_k \le \sum b_k\) ; if moreover \(a_j < b_j\) for some \(j\) , the inequality is strict. If \(a_k \ge 0\) for every \(k\) , then \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k \ge \sum_{k=0}^{m} a_k\) for every integer \(m\) with \(-1 \le m \le n\) , and \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k \ge a_j\) for every \(j \le n\) . If \(a_k \le M\) for every \(k\) , then \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k \le (n + 1) \cdot M\) . (Triangle inequality for sums.) \(\abs{\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k} \le \sum_{k=0}^{n} \abs{a_k}\) . If \(a_k \ge 0\) for every \(k\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = 0\) , then \(a_k = 0\) for every \(k\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.4 (Reindexing a Finite Sum)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(n \in \nN\) and \(a_0, \dots, a_n \in R\) . (Reversal.) \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{n-k}\) . (Splitting.) For every integer \(m\) with \(-1 \le m \le n\) , \[ \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=0}^{m} a_k + \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} a_k . \]

title: Theorem 1.1.7 (Telescoping Sums and Products)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(n \in \nN\) and \(b_0, \dots, b_{n+1} \in R\) . \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} (b_{k+1} - b_k) = b_{n+1} - b_0\) . If \(R\) is a field and every \(b_k \ne 0\) , then \(\prod_{k=0}^{n} \frac{b_{k+1}}{b_k} = \frac{b_{n+1}}{b_0}\) .

R\) , \(x \ge 0\) and \(k \le n\) , then \((1 + x)^n \ge  inom{n}{k} x^k\) . If \(x \in 
R\) , \(x \ge 0\) and \(n \ge 2\) , then \((1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx +  rac{n(n-1)}{2} x^2\) .

title: Example (An absorbed sum)
content: Compute \(\sum_{k=1}^{4} k \binom{4}{k}\) in two ways: term by term, and by absorption.

title: Example (A lower bound for powers of two)
content: Show that \(2^n \ge \frac{n(n-1)}{2}\) , and hence \(\frac{n}{2^n} \le \frac{2}{n - 1}\) , for every integer \(n \ge 2\) .

title: Example (Three expansions)
content: Expand \((a + b)^4\) in \(\nZ\) . (b) Expand \((x - 1)^5\) in \(\nR\) . (c) Compute \(11^4\) from row \(4\) of the table.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: In the proof of @thm-binomial-commutative-ring , why is \(u_0 \coloneqq 0\) put in, and where is it used? Where does the proof use commutativity of multiplication, (F6)? Run the induction step from \(n = 1\) to \(n = 2\) : list \(u_0, u_1, u_2\) and \(w_0, w_1, w_2\) , and add them. True or false: \(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}\) for all \(n, k \in \nN\) with \(k \le n\) . Give the reason.

title: Exercise (B1: Expansions)
content: Write \((2x - 1)^5\) , for \(x \in \nR\) , as a sum of six terms. What multiplies \(x^3\) ? (b) Compute \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} 3^k\) for \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Exercise (B2: An absorbed sum)
content: Show that \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k \binom{n}{k} = n \, 2^{n-1}\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) . Hint: absorption.

title: Exercise (B3: A numerical lower bound)
content: Show that \((1.01)^{10} \ge 1.1045\) without multiplying out the power.

title: Exercise (C1: Chapter check: absorption twice)
content: Prove that, in \(\nZ\) , \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} k(k - 1) \binom{n}{k} = n(n - 1) \, 2^{n-2}\) for every integer \(n \ge 2\) .

title: Proposition 1.2.1 (Absorption Identity)
content: For all \(n, k \in \nN\) , \[ (k + 1) \binom{n + 1}{k + 1} = (n + 1) \binom{n}{k} . \]

title: Proposition 1.2.2 (Binomial Coefficients and Factorials)
content: Let \(n, k \in \nN\) with \(k \le n\) . \(\binom{n}{k} \, k! \, (n - k)! = n!\) . \(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}\) . \(\binom{n}{k} \, k! = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} (n - j)\) . Hence, in \(\nR\) , \(\binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}\) .

title: Theorem 1.2.3 (The Binomial Theorem in a Commutative Ring)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(x, y \in R\) and \(n \in \nN\) . Then \[ (x + y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \cdot \bigl( x^k y^{n-k} \bigr) . \]

title: Example (The compound-interest sequence increases)
content: Show that \(\bigl(1 + \frac1n\bigr)^n < \bigl(1 + \frac{1}{n + 1}\bigr)^{n+1}\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) .

title: Example (A bound for n factorial)
content: Show that \(n! \le \bigl(\frac{n + 1}{2}\bigr)^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) , with equality only for \(n = 1\) .

title: Example (Method: bound a product by a power)
content: How it goes. To bound a product of non-negative factors from above, arrange the factors so that their sum is known, or at least bounded. Then apply @thm-am-gm : the product is at most the \(n\) -th power of their mean. For a strict inequality, check that the factors are not all equal. When to use it. Products such as \(n!\) , \(x(1 - x)\) or \(\bigl(1 + \frac1n\bigr)^n\) ; and any problem that asks for the largest product under a condition on the sum. Common mistakes. One mistake is to apply the theorem to factors that may be negative, where it is false. Another is to choose factors whose sum is not under control. That gives a bound that grows faster than the product.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These parts are about the proof of @thm-am-gm . In the induction step, what is \(x\) , and which fact gives \(x > -1\) ? Which step uses that every \(a_k > 0\) , and not just \(a_k \ge 0\) ? Run the step from \(n = 1\) to \(n = 2\) with \(a_1 = 1\) and \(a_2 = 4\) : compute \(A_1\) , \(A_2\) and \(x\) , and the three members of the chain \(a_1 a_2 \le A_1 a_2 \le A_2^2\) . True or false: \(abc \le \bigl(\frac{a + b + c}{3}\bigr)^3\) for all real \(a, b, c\) .

title: Exercise (B1: Apply the means)
content: Let \(a, b, c > 0\) . Prove that \((a + b)(b + c)(c + a) \ge 8abc\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove or disprove each statement. \(\dfrac{x}{y} + \dfrac{y}{x} \ge 2\) for all real \(x, y > 0\) . \(\prod_{k=1}^{n} (1 - a_k) \le 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\) for every \(n \in \nN\) and all \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in [0, 1]\) . \((1 + x)^3 \ge 1 + 3x + 3x^2\) for every real \(x \ge -1\) . \(abcd \le \bigl(\frac{a + b + c + d}{4}\bigr)^4\) for all real \(a, b, c, d \ge 0\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A product near one)
content: Show that \(\prod_{k=1}^{10} \Bigl(1 - \dfrac{k}{100}\Bigr) \ge 0.45\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Find the error)
content: Here is an argument for part (a) of @thm-am-gm when all \(a_k > 0\) . Write \(A_m\) for the mean of \(a_1, \dots, a_m\) . We induct on \(n\) . For \(n = 1\) , \(a_1 = A_1\) . Suppose \(a_1 \cdots a_n \le A_n^n\) for all positive \(a_1, \dots, a_n\) , and let \(a_1, \dots, a_{n+1} > 0\) . Multiplying the hypothesis by \(a_{n+1} > 0\) gives \(a_1 \cdots a_{n+1} \le A_n^n\, a_{n+1}\) . Adding a number to a list never lowers its mean, so \(A_n \le A_{n+1}\) ; and the new number is at most the new mean, so \(a_{n+1} \le A_{n+1}\) . Hence \(A_n^n\, a_{n+1} \le A_{n+1}^n A_{n+1} = A_{n+1}^{n+1}\) , and \(a_1 \cdots a_{n+1} \le A_{n+1}^{n+1}\) . Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails and give a counterexample to that line.

title: Lemma 1.3.1 (Strict Bernoulli Inequality)
content: Let \(x \in \nR\) with \(x \ge -1\) and \(x \ne 0\) . Then \((1 + x)^n > 1 + nx\) for every integer \(n \ge 2\) .

title: Proposition 1.3.2 (Products of Factors Below One)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) and \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in \nR\) with \(0 \le a_k \le 1\) for every \(k\) . Then \[ \prod_{k=1}^{n} (1 - a_k) \ge 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k . \]

title: Theorem 1.3.3 (Arithmetic and Geometric Means)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) be an integer, let \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in \nR\) with \(a_k \ge 0\) for every \(k\) , and let \(A \coloneqq \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\) . \(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \le A^n\) . Equality holds in (a) if and only if \(a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_n\) .

title: Example (A limit that is not zero)
content: Show that \(a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{2n^2 + 3n}{n^2 - 5} \to 2\) .

title: Example (A first estimate in \nR)
content: Show that \(a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{n + 3}{2n^2 - 1} \to 0\) in \(\nR\) .

title: Example (Factorials beat powers of two)
content: Show that \(\dfrac{1}{n!} \le \dfrac{1}{2^{n-1}} < \dfrac{2}{n}\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) , and hence that \(\dfrac{1}{n!} \to 0\) .

title: Example (Method: keep the dominant term)
content: How it goes. In a quotient of sums, keep the term that grows fastest and absorb the others into it. From some \(n_0\) on, a lower-order term is at most a fixed fraction of the dominant term. For example, \(5 \le \frac12 n^2\) once \(n \ge 4\) , so \(n^2 - 5 \ge \frac12 n^2\) there. Then the quotient is bounded by a quotient of single powers. This is the bounding step of the method of @fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition , with \(n_0\) the largest of the ranges used. When to use it. Rational expressions in \(n\) , possibly with \(\sqrt{n}\) . Common mistakes. Subtracting in the denominator without stating a range. For instance, \(n^2 - 5 \ge \frac12 n^2\) is false for \(n \le 3\) .

title: Example (Method: bound a power from below)
content: How it goes. To make a quotient small when its denominator contains \(r^n\) with \(r > 1\) : Write \(r = 1 + h\) with \(h > 0\) . Keep one term of the expansion: \((1 + h)^n \ge nh\) by Bernoulli’s inequality, or \((1 + h)^n \ge \binom{n}{k} h^k\) by @cor-binomial-real (b). Take \(k\) one more than the power of \(n\) on top. Bound \(\binom{n}{k}\) below by \(c\,n^k\) for \(n \ge n_0\) . Invert, and finish with the method of @fd3:exm-method-limit-from-definition . When to use it. Quotients \(n^p / r^n\) . Powers \(\abs{r}^n\) with \(\abs{r} < 1\) , through \(1/\abs{r} = 1 + h\) . The \(n\) -th roots of Section 1.5. Common mistakes. One mistake is to choose \(k\) too small: then the bound does not tend to \(0\) . Another is to use the binomial bound with \(h < 0\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Write the negation of “ \(a_n \to 0\) ” with all its quantifiers. In @exm-first-estimate , on what does \(N\) depend? Could it depend on \(n\) ? Name the method used: \(\dfrac{n}{n^3 + 7} \le \dfrac{1}{n^2}\) for \(n \ge 1\) . True or false: if \(\abs{a_n} \le \dfrac{5}{n}\) for every \(n \ge 10\) , then \(a_n \to 0\) .

title: Exercise (B1: Say which method, then complete it)
content: Show that \(a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{n + 5}{2^n} \to 0\) . Start: write \(2 = 1 + 1\) . By @cor-binomial-real (b) with \(k = 2\) , \(2^n \ge \dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2} \ge \dfrac{n^2}{4}\) for \(n \ge 2\) . Say which method this is, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
content: The claim is \(a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{2n + 1}{n + 1} \to 2\) . Put the lines below in an order that proves it, and say which line does not belong. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . For \(n \ge N\) , \(\abs{a_n - 2} = \dfrac{1}{n + 1} < \dfrac{1}{n} \le \dfrac{1}{N} < \varepsilon\) . Choose \(N \in \nN\) with \(N > 1/\varepsilon\) and \(N \ge 1\) . Choose \(N \coloneqq n + 1\) . Hence \(a_n \to 2\) . \(\abs{a_n - 2} = \Bigl\lvert \dfrac{2n + 1 - 2n - 2}{n + 1} \Bigr\rvert = \dfrac{1}{n + 1}\) for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Prove or disprove)
content: Prove each true statement and refute each false one. In parts (a), (b), (c) and (e), \(a_n\) denotes the \(n\) -th term of the sequence in question. \(\dfrac{n^2 + 1}{n^3} \to 0\) . \(\dfrac{n}{n + 1} \to 0\) . \(\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n} \to 0\) . For every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , every integer \(n \ge 1/\varepsilon\) has \(\dfrac{1}{n^2} < \varepsilon\) . \(\dfrac{2^n}{n!} \to 0\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Chapter check: a rational limit)
content: Prove from the definition that \(a_n \coloneqq \dfrac{3n^2 - n}{n^2 + 4} \to 3\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Squares over powers)
content: Let \(r > 1\) and \(h \coloneqq r - 1\) . Show that \(\dfrac{n^2}{r^n} \to 0\) . Start: by @cor-binomial-real (b) with \(k = 3\) , \(r^n \ge \dfrac{n(n - 1)(n - 2)}{6} h^3\) for \(n \ge 3\) . Say which method this is, then complete it.

title: Proposition 1.4.2 (Powers Beat n)
content: Let \(r > 1\) and \(h \coloneqq r - 1\) . Then \(\dfrac{n}{r^n} \le \dfrac{4}{nh^2}\) for every integer \(n \ge 2\) , and \(\dfrac{n}{r^n} \to 0\) .

title: Proposition 1.4.1 (Geometric Sequences Tend to Zero)
content: Let \(r \in \nR\) with \(\abs{r} < 1\) . If \(r \ne 0\) and \(h \coloneqq \dfrac{1}{\abs{r}} - 1\) , then \(h > 0\) and \(\abs{r}^n < \dfrac{1}{nh}\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) . \(r^n \to 0\) .

title: Corollary 1.5.6 (Geometric Mean Below Arithmetic Mean)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) be an integer and let \(a_1, \dots, a_n \in \nR\) with \(a_k \ge 0\) for every \(k\) . Then \[ \sqrt[n]{a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n} \le \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k , \] with equality if and only if \(a_1 = a_2 = \dots = a_n\) .

title: Proposition 1.5.7 (Two Root Estimates)

title: Corollary 2.1.2 (Coprime Means 1 Is a Combination)
page: 2.1 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(a, b \in \nZ\) . Then \(a\) and \(b\) are coprime if and only if \(ax + by = 1\) for some \(x, y \in \nZ\) .

title: Definition 2.1.3 (Coprime Integers)
page: 2.1 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Integers \(a, b \in \nZ\) are coprime if \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: These questions are about the uniqueness half of the proof of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic . Why must the empty list count as a prime factorization? Run the induction step on \((p_1, p_2, p_3, p_4) = (2, 2, 3, 5)\) and a second prime factorization \((q_1, \dots, q_l)\) of \(60\) . Which equalities does the proof derive, and to which two lists is \(P(3)\) applied? Which line of the proof uses Euclid’s lemma, and through which result? Where is “non-decreasing” used? Give the idea of the uniqueness proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: The following lines contain a proof of @thm-euclid-lemma-integers , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Suppose \(a \mid bc\) and \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) . There are \(x, y \in \nZ\) with \(ax + by = 1\) . (ii′) Since \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) and \(a \mid bc\) , we have \(a \mid b\) or \(a \mid c\) . Multiplying by \(c\) : \(c = acx + bcy\) . (iii′) Dividing \(1 = ax + by\) by \(a\) : \(1/a = x + (b/a)y\) . \(a \mid acx\) , since \(acx = a(cx)\) . Write \(bc = ak\) ; then \(bcy = a(ky)\) , so \(a \mid bcy\) . Hence \(a \mid acx + bcy\) . So \(a \mid c\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Two factorizations and a gcd)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Find the prime factorizations of \(1001\) and of \(2^{10} - 1\) , proving that each entry is prime. Then show that \(\gcd(1001, 1023) = 11\) in two ways. First, use the factorizations to write \(1001 = 11 \cdot 91\) and \(1023 = 11 \cdot 93\) : show \(\gcd(91, 93) = 1\) , and deduce \(\gcd(1001, 1023) = 11\) from a Bézout identity for \(91\) and \(93\) ( @cor-coprime-iff-combination ). Second, use the Euclidean algorithm. Hint: the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime shortens each primality check. Do not use the school rule “the gcd is the product of the shared primes”: this chapter does not prove it.

title: Exercise (C1: Chapter check: unique factorization)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Prove that two prime factorizations of the same positive integer are equal: the uniqueness half of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic . You may cite @thm-euclid-lemma-integers and @cor-prime-divides-product .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. Let \(m, n, c \in \nZ\) . If \(m \mid c\) , \(n \mid c\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) , then \(mn \mid c\) . Argument. (1) Write \(c = mk\) and \(c = nl\) with \(k, l \in \nZ\) . (2) Then \(c^2 = c \cdot c = (mk)(nl) = mn \cdot kl\) . (3) So \(mn \mid c^2\) . (4) Hence \(mn \mid c\) . Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, and give a counterexample to the step.

title: Exercise (C3: There is no last prime)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Prove that no finite list contains every prime: for every list of primes \((p_1, \dots, p_k)\) , with \(k \in \nN\) , there is a prime that is not an entry of the list.

title: Lemma 2.2.4 (The Least Divisor Is Prime)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Let \(n \in \nZ\) with \(n \ge 2\) . The set \(D \coloneqq \{ d \in \nZ : d \ge 2 \text{ and } d \mid n \}\) has a least element, and that element is prime. In particular, \(n\) has a prime factor.

title: Proposition 2.2.3 (Coprime Divisors of a Number)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Let \(m, n, c \in \nZ\) with \(m \mid c\) , \(n \mid c\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) . Then \(mn \mid c\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Euclid’s Lemma)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Let \(a, b, c \in \nZ\) . If \(a \mid bc\) and \(\gcd(a, b) = 1\) , then \(a \mid c\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.5 (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic)
page: 2.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content: Every \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) has exactly one prime factorization.

title: Definition 2.4.1 (Unit of a Commutative Ring)

content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring ( @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field ). An element \(u \in R\) is a unit of \(R\) if there exists \(v \in R\) with \(uv = 1\) . The set of units of \(R\) is written \(R^{\times}\) . For a unit \(u\) , the element \(v\) is unique ; it is written \(u^{-1}\) and called the inverse of \(u\) .

title: Lemma 3.3.1 (Real and Imaginary Parts against the Modulus)
content: For every \(u \in \nC\) , \[ \abs{\operatorname{Re} u} \le \abs{u} , \qquad \abs{\operatorname{Im} u} \le \abs{u} , \qquad \abs{u} \le \abs{\operatorname{Re} u} + \abs{\operatorname{Im} u} . \] In particular \(\operatorname{Re} u \le \abs{u}\) .

title: Theorem 3.3.2 (Triangle Inequality for Complex Numbers)
content: For all \(z, w \in \nC\) , \[ \abs{z + w} \le \abs{z} + \abs{w} . \]

title: Corollary 4.1.2 (Equal Squares)
page: 4.1 The Field Axioms and the First Examples
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(x, y \in F\) . Then \(x^2 = y^2\) if and only if \(x = y\) or \(x = -y\) . In particular, \(x^2 = 1\) if and only if \(x = 1\) or \(x = -1\) .

title: Definition 4.1.1 (Field)
page: 4.1 The Field Axioms and the First Examples
content: A field is a set \(F\) together with two functions, addition \(+ \colon F \times F \to F\) , \((a, b) \mapsto a + b\) , and multiplication \(\cdot \colon F \times F \to F\) , \((a, b) \mapsto a \cdot b = ab\) , satisfying the following clauses. \(a + b = b + a\) for all \(a, b \in F\) . \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\) for all \(a, b, c \in F\) . There is an element \(0 \in F\) such that \(a + 0 = a\) for every \(a \in F\) . For every \(a \in F\) there is an element \(-a \in F\) such that \(a + (-a) = 0\) . \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a, b, c \in F\) . \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in F\) . There is an element \(1 \in F\) with \(1 \ne 0\) such that \(a \cdot 1 = a\) for every \(a \in F\) . For every non-zero \(a \in F\) there is an element \(a^{-1} \in F\) such that \(a a^{-1} = 1\) . \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a, b, c \in F\) . We write \(a - b \coloneqq a + (-b)\) , and \(a / b \coloneqq a b^{-1}\) for \(b \ne 0\) .

(2) Dividing both sides by \(x\) gives \(x = 1\) . (3) So \(x = 0\) or \(x = 1\) . Is the claim true? Does the proof prove it? If not, name the line that fails, the error, and give a counterexample to the step.

title: Proposition 4.1.3 (Linear Equations in a Field)
page: 4.1 The Field Axioms and the First Examples
content: Let \(F\) be a field and let \(a, b, c, d, e, f \in F\) . If \(a \ne 0\) , the equation \(ax = b\) has exactly one solution \(x \in F\) , namely \(x = a^{-1} b\) . If \(ad - bc \ne 0\) , the system \[ \begin{aligned} ax + by &= e, \\ cx + dy &= f \end{aligned} \] has exactly one solution \((x, y) \in F \times F\) , namely \[ x = \frac{ed - bf}{ad - bc}, \qquad y = \frac{af - ce}{ad - bc}. \]

title: Lemma 4.2.1 (Bézout’s Lemma for Integers)
content: Let \(a, n \in \nZ\) with \(n \ge 1\) , and suppose that the only positive integer dividing both \(a\) and \(n\) is \(1\) . Then there are \(x, y \in \nZ\) with \[ ax + ny = 1 . \]

title: Theorem 4.2.2 (\nZ/n\nZ Is a Field Exactly for Prime n)
content: Let \(n \ge 2\) be an integer. Then \(\nZ/n\nZ\) is a field ( @def-field ) if and only if \(n\) is prime.

title: Definition 4.3.2 (Prime Subfield)
content: The prime subfield of a field \(L\) is the smallest subfield of \(L\) , that is, \(K_{\emptyset}\) of @prp-subfield-intersection (b): the intersection of the set of all subfields of \(L\) .

title: Definition 4.3.1 (Subfield)
content: Let \(L\) be a field. A subfield of \(L\) is a subset \(K \subseteq L\) such that \(0 \in K\) and \(1 \in K\) ; \(K\) is closed under sums and products : \(a + b \in K\) and \(ab \in K\) for all \(a, b \in K\) ; \(K\) is closed under negatives : \(-a \in K\) for every \(a \in K\) ; \(K\) is closed under inverses : \(a^{-1} \in K\) for every non-zero \(a \in K\) . Here \(0\) , \(1\) , \(+\) , \(\cdot\) , \(-a\) and \(a^{-1}\) are those of \(L\) .

title: Proposition 4.3.2 (Intersections of Subfields)
content: Let \(L\) be a field. If \(\sK\) is a non-empty set of subfields of \(L\) , then \(\bigcap \sK\) is a subfield of \(L\) . For every subset \(S \subseteq L\) there is a smallest subfield of \(L\) containing \(S\) : a subfield \(K_S\) with \(S \subseteq K_S\) , contained in every subfield of \(L\) that contains \(S\) . It is \(K_S = \bigcap \sK_S\) , where \(\sK_S\) is the set of subfields of \(L\) that contain \(S\) .

title: Proposition 4.3.1 (The Subfield Test)
content: Let \(L\) be a field and \(K \subseteq L\) . If \(K\) is a subfield of \(L\) , then \(K\) , with the restrictions of \(+\) and \(\cdot\) to \(K \times K\) , is a field ( @def-field ). Its zero is \(0_L\) , its one is \(1_L\) , and the negative and the inverse of an element of \(K\) are those of \(L\) . Conversely, suppose that \(a + b \in K\) and \(ab \in K\) for all \(a, b \in K\) , and that \(K\) with the restricted operations is a field. Then \(K\) is a subfield of \(L\) : its zero \(0_K\) is \(0_L\) , its one \(1_K\) is \(1_L\) , and its negatives and inverses are those of \(L\) . \(K\) is a subfield of \(L\) if and only if \(1 \in K\) , \(a - b \in K\) for all \(a, b \in K\) , and \(ab^{-1} \in K\) for all \(a, b \in K\) with \(b \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 4.4.1 (Field Homomorphism)
content: Let \(F\) and \(L\) be fields. A homomorphism (of fields) \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) is a function such that, for all \(a, b \in F\) , \[ \varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b) , \qquad \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) , \qquad \varphi(1) = 1 . \] A bijective ( @fd2:def-bijective ) homomorphism is an isomorphism ; \(F\) and \(L\) are isomorphic , written \(F \cong L\) , if there is an isomorphism \(F \to L\) . An isomorphism \(F \to F\) is an automorphism of \(F\) .

content:
Let \(\varphi \colon F 	o L\) be a homomorphism of fields, and let \(a, b \in F\) . \(\varphi(0) = 0\) , \(\varphi(-a) = -\varphi(a)\) and \(\varphi(a - b) = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b)\) . If \(a 
e 0\) , then \(\varphi(a) 
e 0\) and \(\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}\) . \(\varphi\) is injective . title: Corollary 4.5.7 (A Finite Field Has Prime Characteristic)
page: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content: Let \(F\) be a finite field. \(\operatorname{char} F\) is a prime \(p\) . \(F\) contains a subfield isomorphic to \(\nF_p\) , namely its prime subfield. \(p \cdot a = 0\) for every \(a \in F\) .

page: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content:
Let \(\varphi \colon F 	o L\) be a homomorphism. Then \(\varphi \circ \iota_F = \iota_L\) , and \(\varphi\) maps the prime subfield of \(F\) onto the prime subfield of \(L\) . The identity is the only homomorphism \(
Q 	o 
Q\) , and the only homomorphism \(
F_p 	o 
F_p\) for each prime \(p\) . In particular the only automorphism of \(
Q\) , and of \(
F_p\) , is the identity. Every automorphism of a field \(F\) fixes each element of the prime subfield of \(F\) .

title: Definition 4.5.1 (Characteristic)
page: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content: Let \(F\) be a field. If there exists a positive integer \(n\) with \(n \cdot 1 = 0\) , the characteristic of \(F\) , written \(\operatorname{char} F\) , is the least such \(n\) . If there is none, \(\operatorname{char} F \coloneqq 0\) .

title: Lemma 4.5.1 (Integer Multiples)
page: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(a, b \in R\) , and \(m, k \in \nN\) . \((m \cdot 1) + (k \cdot 1) = (m + k) \cdot 1\) . \((m \cdot 1)(k \cdot 1) = (mk) \cdot 1\) . \((m \cdot 1)\, a = m \cdot a\) . The identities (a)–(c) hold for all \(m, k \in \nZ\) , and so do \[ \begin{aligned} (m + k) \cdot a &= m \cdot a + k \cdot a , & (-m) \cdot a &= -(m \cdot a) , \\ m \cdot (a + b) &= m \cdot a + m \cdot b , & (m \cdot a)\, b &= m \cdot (ab) , \\ (mk) \cdot a &= m \cdot (k \cdot a) . & & \end{aligned} \]

title: Proposition 4.5.4 (Subfields and Homomorphisms Preserve the Characteristic)
page: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content: If \(K\) is a subfield of \(L\) , then \(\operatorname{char} K = \operatorname{char} L\) . If \(\varphi \colon F \to L\) is a homomorphism, then \(\operatorname{char} F = \operatorname{char} L\) . There is no homomorphism between two fields of different characteristic.

title: Theorem 4.5.3 (The Characteristic Is Zero or a Prime)
page: 4.5 Integer Multiples, the Characteristic, and the Prime Subfield
content: Let \(F\) be a field. Then \(\operatorname{char} F\) is \(0\) or a prime.

title: Theorem 4.6.2 (The Frobenius Homomorphism)
page: 4.6 The Binomial Theorem, the Frobenius Map, and Fermat's Little Theorem
content: Let \(F\) be a field of characteristic \(p > 0\) . For all \(x, y \in F\) , \[ (x + y)^p = x^p + y^p , \qquad (xy)^p = x^p y^p , \] and \(1^p = 1\) . So the Frobenius map \(\mathrm{Fr} \colon F \to F\) , \(\mathrm{Fr}(x) \coloneqq x^p\) , is a homomorphism, and it is injective. \((x - y)^p = x^p - y^p\) for all \(x, y \in F\) . If \(F\) is finite, then \(\mathrm{Fr}\) is an automorphism of \(F\) .

title: Definition 5.1.1 (Group)
content: A group is a set \(G\) together with a binary operation on \(G\) , that is, a function \(G \times G \to G\) , \((a, b) \mapsto ab\) ( @fd2:def-function , with \(G \times G\) the Cartesian product of @fd2:def-cartesian-product ), such that: (Associativity) \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a, b, c \in G\) ; (Identity) there is an element \(e \in G\) with \(ea = ae = a\) for every \(a \in G\) ; (Inverses) for every \(a \in G\) there is \(b \in G\) with \(ab = ba = e\) , where \(e\) is the element of (G2). The group is abelian if moreover \(ab = ba\) for all \(a, b \in G\) .

title: Definition 5.1.3 (Integer Powers)
content:
Let \(G\) be a group and \(g \in G\) . For \(n \in 
N\) , the power \(g^n\) is the product of the constant list \((g, \dots, g)\) of length \(n\) ; so \[ g^0 = e , \qquad g^{n+1} = g^n g \quad 	ext{for } n \in 
N . \] For \(n \in 
Z\) with \(n < 0\) , write \(n = -m\) with \(m \in 
N\) ( @fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers (c)), and set \(g^n \coloneqq (g^{-1})^m\) . In additive notation the power is the multiple \(n \cdot g\) : \(0 \cdot g = 0\) , \((n + 1) \cdot g = n \cdot g + g\) , and \((-m) \cdot g = m \cdot (-g)\) .

title: Definition 5.1.2 (Product of a List)
content: Let \(G\) be a group and \(r \in \nN\) . A list of length \(r\) in \(G\) is a function \(\{1, \dots, r\} \to G\) , written \((g_1, \dots, g_r)\) ; for \(r = 0\) it is the empty list . Its product \(g_1 g_2 \cdots g_r \in G\) is given by recursion: the product of the empty list is \(e\) , and \[ g_1 \cdots g_{j+1} \coloneqq (g_1 \cdots g_j)\, g_{j+1} \quad \text{for } 0 \le j < r , \] where \(g_1 \cdots g_j\) is the product of the shortened list \((g_1, \dots, g_j)\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. In every group, \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\) . Argument. (1) By (G1)–(G3), \((b^{-1}a^{-1})(ab) = b^{-1}(a^{-1}a)b = b^{-1}eb = b^{-1}b = e\) . (2) Since \(xy = yx\) for all \(x, y\) in a group, also \((ab)(b^{-1}a^{-1}) = (b^{-1}a^{-1})(ab) = e\) . title: Proposition 5.1.2 (Laws for Products of Lists)
content: Let \(G\) be a group, and let \((g_1, \dots, g_r)\) and \((h_1, \dots, h_s)\) be lists in \(G\) . (Concatenation) \((g_1 \cdots g_r)(h_1 \cdots h_s) = g_1 \cdots g_r h_1 \cdots h_s\) , the product of the list \((g_1, \dots, g_r, h_1, \dots, h_s)\) of length \(r + s\) . (Brackets) If \(r \ge 1\) , every bracketing of \(g_1, \dots, g_r\) , in this order, has the value \(g_1 \cdots g_r\) . (Inverses) \((g_1 \cdots g_r)^{-1} = g_r^{-1} \cdots g_1^{-1}\) .

title: Proposition 5.1.4 (The Units Form a Group)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. Then \(R^{\times}\) , the set of units of \(R\) , is an abelian group under the multiplication of \(R\) , with identity \(1\) , and the inverse of \(u\) in this group is \(u^{-1}\) .

title: Theorem 5.1.1 (Basic Properties of Groups)
content: Let \(G\) be a group and \(a, b, c \in G\) . The identity element of \(G\) is unique. The inverse of \(a\) is unique. We denote it by \(a^{-1}\) . \((a^{-1})^{-1} = a\) and \((ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}\) . (Cancellation) If \(ab = ac\) , then \(b = c\) . If \(ba = ca\) , then \(b = c\) . The equations \(ax = b\) and \(ya = b\) have exactly one solution \(x \in G\) and exactly one solution \(y \in G\) : \(x = a^{-1}b\) and \(y = ba^{-1}\) .

title: Definition 5.2.1 (Subgroup)
page: 5.2 Subgroups and the Subgroups of the Integers
content: Let \(G\) be a group. A subset \(H \subseteq G\) is a subgroup of \(G\) if \(e \in H\) , and \(ab \in H\) and \(a^{-1} \in H\) for all \(a, b \in H\) .

title: Definition 5.2.2 (Subgroup Generated by an Element)
page: 5.2 Subgroups and the Subgroups of the Integers
content: Let \(G\) be a group and \(g \in G\) . The subgroup generated by \(g\) is \[ \langle g \rangle \coloneqq \{ g^n : n \in \nZ \} , \] with the powers of @def-group-integer-power . In additive notation, \(\langle a \rangle = \{ n \cdot a : n \in \nZ \}\) .

title: Definition 5.3.1 (Group Homomorphism)
content: Let \(G\) and \(H\) be groups. A function \(\varphi \colon G \to H\) is a homomorphism if \(\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in G\) . A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism . The groups \(G\) and \(H\) are isomorphic , written \(G \cong H\) , if there exists an isomorphism \(G \to H\) . The kernel of \(\varphi\) is \[ \ker \varphi \coloneqq \{ g \in G : \varphi(g) = e_H \} , \] where \(e_H\) is the identity of \(H\) .

title: Proposition 5.3.2 (Composites and Inverses of Homomorphisms)
content: Let \(G\) , \(H\) and \(K\) be groups. If \(\varphi \colon G \to H\) and \(\psi \colon H \to K\) are homomorphisms, then so is \(\psi \circ \varphi \colon G \to K\) . If \(\varphi \colon G \to H\) is an isomorphism, then its inverse function \(\varphi^{-1} \colon H \to G\) is an isomorphism. \(\id_G\) is an isomorphism. Consequently \(G \cong G\) ; if \(G \cong H\) , then \(H \cong G\) ; and if \(G \cong H\) and \(H \cong K\) , then \(G \cong K\) .

title: Proposition 5.3.3 (Injective Exactly When the Kernel Is Trivial)
content: A homomorphism \(\varphi \colon G \to H\) is injective if and only if \(\ker \varphi = \{e_G\}\) .

title: Theorem 5.3.1 (Basic Properties of Homomorphisms)
content: Let \(\varphi \colon G \to H\) be a homomorphism of groups, and let \(a \in G\) . \(\varphi(e_G) = e_H\) . \(\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}\) . \(\ker \varphi\) is a subgroup of \(G\) . \(\varphi(a^n) = \varphi(a)^n\) for every \(n \in \nZ\) . The image \(\varphi(G)\) is a subgroup of \(H\) .

title: Definition 5.4.2 (Cycle, Transposition)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) and \(k \ge 2\) , and let \(i_1, \dots, i_k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) be distinct . The \(k\) -cycle \((i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_k) \in S_n\) is the permutation \(\gamma\) with \[ \gamma(i_j) \coloneqq i_{j+1} \ \text{ for } 1 \le j < k , \qquad \gamma(i_k) \coloneqq i_1 , \] and \(\gamma(x) \coloneqq x\) for every \(x \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) not among \(i_1, \dots, i_k\) . A \(2\) -cycle \((i\ j)\) is a transposition . Two cycles are disjoint if their supports are disjoint.

title: Definition 5.4.1 (Permutations and the Symmetric Group)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A permutation of \(X\) is a bijection \(X \to X\) . The permutations of \(X\) , with the operation \(\sigma\tau \coloneqq \sigma \circ \tau\) , form the group \(S_X\) of @exm-groups (c). For \(n \in \nN\) , the symmetric group is \[ S_n \coloneqq S_{\{1, \dots, n\}} , \] where \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) is empty for \(n = 0\) . The support of \(\sigma \in S_X\) is the set of points it moves, \[ \supp \sigma \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \sigma(x) \ne x \} . \]

title: Lemma 5.4.1 (Permutations Fixing the Last Point)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , and let \(S' \coloneqq \{ \sigma \in S_{n+1} : \sigma(n + 1) = n + 1 \}\) , a subgroup of \(S_{n+1}\) . For \(\sigma \in S'\) , the restriction \(\sigma'\) of \(\sigma\) to \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) , with codomain \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) , is a permutation of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) . The map \(S' \to S_n\) , \(\sigma \mapsto \sigma'\) , is an isomorphism. Its inverse sends \(\rho \in S_n\) to its extension \(\bar\rho \in S'\) , defined by \(\bar\rho(i) \coloneqq \rho(i)\) for \(i \le n\) and \(\bar\rho(n + 1) \coloneqq n + 1\) .

title: Proposition 5.4.3 (Disjoint Permutations Commute)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) and \(\sigma, \tau \in S_n\) with \(\supp \sigma \cap \supp \tau = \emptyset\) . Then \(\sigma\tau = \tau\sigma\) . Moreover, every permutation \(\sigma\) maps \(\supp \sigma\) onto itself: \(\sigma(\supp \sigma) = \supp \sigma\) .

title: Proposition 5.4.2 (The Symmetric Group Has n! Elements)
content: For every \(n \in \nN\) , \(S_n\) is finite and has \(n!\) elements: \(\card{S_n} = n!\) .

title: Theorem 5.4.4 (Disjoint Cycle Decomposition)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) . Every \(\sigma \in S_n\) is a product \(\sigma = \gamma_1 \gamma_2 \cdots \gamma_s\) , \(s \in \nN\) , of pairwise disjoint cycles, each with support contained in \(\supp \sigma\) . For \(\sigma = \id\) the product is empty ( \(s = 0\) ).

title: Corollary 5.5.3 (Adjacent Transpositions Generate S_n)
content: Let \(n \ge 2\) . Every \(\sigma \in S_n\) is a product of adjacent transpositions \((i\ \ i{+}1)\) , \(1 \le i < n\) .

title: Definition 6.1.1 (Polynomial)
content:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. A polynomial over \(R\) (in the indeterminate \(x\) ) is a function \(p \colon 
N 	o R\) , written \(p = (p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots)\) , such that only finitely many \(p_k\) are non-zero: there exists \(N \in 
N\) with \(p_k = 0\) for every \(k > N\) . Such an \(N\) is called admissible for \(p\) . The element \(p_k\) is the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \(p\) . For \(a \in R\) and \(n \in 
N\) , the monomial \(a \, x^n\) is the polynomial with \(a\) in position \(n\) and \(0\) in every other position. We set \(x \coloneqq 1 \, x^1\) , and for \(a \in R\) the constant \(a\) is the monomial \(a \, x^0\) . The zero polynomial is \(0 \coloneqq (0, 0, 0, \dots)\) . The set of all polynomials over \(R\) is written \(R[x]\) .

title: Lemma 6.1.1 (Finite Sums, Powers and Multiples)
content:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. (Sums.) Let \(T\) be a set with a function \(+ \colon T 	imes T 	o T\) and an element \(0 \in T\) with \(0 + u = u\) for every \(u \in T\) . For a sequence \((u_i)_{i \in 
N}\) in \(T\) there is exactly one way to define \(\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i \in T\) , for \(k \in 
N\) , such that \[ \sum_{i=0}^{0} u_i = u_0 , \qquad \sum_{i=0}^{k+1} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + u_{k+1} , \] starting from the empty sum \(0\) . The sum \(\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i\) depends only on \(u_0, \dots, u_k\) ; so a finite list \(u_0, \dots, u_k\) has a sum, computed from any extension of the list to a sequence. Likewise, a finite list \(s_1, \dots, s_r\) in \(R\) has a product \(\prod_{j=1}^{r} s_j\) , with \(\prod_{j=1}^{0} s_j = 1\) and \(\prod_{j=1}^{r+1} s_j =  igl( \prod_{j=1}^{r} s_j  igr) s_{r+1}\) . (Rules for sums in \(R\) .) For \(k \in 
N\) , \(c \in R\) and elements \(u_i, v_i \in R\) : (Σ1) \(\sum_{i=0}^{k} (u_i + v_i) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + \sum_{i=0}^{k} v_i\) ; (Σ2) \(c \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} c \, u_i\) ; (Σ3) for \(j \in 
N\) : if \(u_i = 0\) for every \(i \le k\) with \(i 
e j\) , then \(\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = u_j\) when \(j \le k\) , and \(\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = 0\) when \(j > k\) ; (Σ4) \(-\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} (-u_i)\) . (Powers.) For \(s \in R\) and \(n \in 
N\) , \(s^0 \coloneqq 1\) and \(s^{n+1} \coloneqq s^n s\) define \(s^n\) for every \(n\) , and for all \(s, t \in R\) and \(m, n \in 
N\) , \[ s^{m+n} = s^m s^n , \qquad (s^m)^n = s^{mn} , \qquad (st)^n = s^n t^n . \] (Multiples.) For all \(a, b \in R\) and \(m, n \in 
Z\) , \[  egin{aligned} (m + n) \cdot a &= m \cdot a + n \cdot a , & m \cdot (a + b) &= m \cdot a + m \cdot b , \ (m \cdot a) b &= m \cdot (ab) , & (m \cdot 1) a &= m \cdot a , \ (mn) \cdot a &= m \cdot (n \cdot a) . \end{aligned} \]

title: Definition 6.2.1 (The Polynomial Ring)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. For \(p, q \in R[x]\) and \(k \in \nN\) define \[ (p + q)_k \coloneqq p_k + q_k , \qquad (-p)_k \coloneqq -p_k , \qquad (pq)_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i \, q_{k-i} . \] The set \(R[x]\) with this addition and this multiplication is the polynomial ring over \(R\) .

Lemma 6.2.3 (Check on Monomials)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, and let \(T\) be a set with a function \(+ \colon T \times T \to T\) . Let \(\Phi, \Psi\) be maps of one, two or three polynomial arguments to \(T\) , that is, both maps \(R[x] \to T\) , both \(R[x]^2 \to T\) or both \(R[x]^3 \to T\) , that are additive in each argument : for each argument position and all fixed values of the other arguments, \[ \Phi(\dots, u + u', \dots) = \Phi(\dots, u, \dots) + \Phi(\dots, u', \dots) \] with \(u, u'\) in that position, and the same for \(\Psi\) . If \(\Phi\) and \(\Psi\) take the same value whenever every argument is a monomial, then \(\Phi = \Psi\) .

title: Lemma 6.2.2 (Multiplying by a Monomial)
content: Let \(a, b \in R\) , \(m, n \in \nN\) and \(q \in R[x]\) . \(\bigl( (a x^m) q \bigr)_k = a \, q_{k-m}\) for \(k \ge m\) , and \(\bigl( (a x^m) q \bigr)_k = 0\) for \(k < m\) . \((a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) \, x^{m+n}\) .

title: Proposition 6.2.1 (A Polynomial Is the Sum of Its Monomials)
content: Let \(p \in R[x]\) and \(N \in \nN\) . The sum \(\sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k\) of the monomials \(p_k x^k\) , formed in \((R[x], +)\) , has coefficient \(p_j\) in position \(j\) for every \(j \le N\) , and \(0\) in every position \(j > N\) . In particular, if \(N\) is admissible for \(p\) , then \[ p = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k . \]

title: Theorem 6.2.4 (The Polynomial Ring Is a Commutative Ring)
content:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. \(R[x]\) , with the operations of @def-polynomial-ring , is a commutative ring ( @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field ), with zero the zero polynomial, negative \(-p\) as defined there, and one \(1 \coloneqq 1 \, x^0\) . Spelled out, for all \(p, q, r \in R[x]\) : (1) \(p + q = q + p\) and \((p + q) + r = p + (q + r)\) ; (2) \(p + 0 = p\) and \(p + (-p) = 0\) ; (3) \(pq = qp\) and \((pq)r = p(qr)\) ; (4) \(1 \cdot p = p\) ; (5) \(p(q + r) = pq + pr\) . The map \(R 	o R[x]\) , \(a \mapsto a \, x^0\) , is injective and satisfies \((a + b) x^0 = a x^0 + b x^0\) , \((ab) x^0 = (a x^0)(b x^0)\) and \(1 x^0 = 1\) . If \(1 
e 0\) in \(R\) , then \(1 
e 0\) in \(R[x]\) . For \(n \in 
N\) , the \(n\) -th power of \(x\) in the ring \(R[x]\) ( @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)) is the monomial \(1 \, x^n\) , and the product of the constant \(a\) with it is the monomial \(a \, x^n\) . Hence \(p = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k\) , for admissible \(N\) , is a sum of products of constants and powers of \(x\) . For a constant \(a\) and \(p \in R[x]\) , \((ap)_k = a \, p_k\) for every \(k\) .

title: Corollary 6.3.3 (Polynomial Rings over Integral Domains)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. If \(R\) is an integral domain, \(p, q \in R[x]\) and \(pq = 0\) , then \(p = 0\) or \(q = 0\) . So \(R[x]\) is an integral domain. (Cancellation) If \(R\) is an integral domain, \(p, q, r \in R[x]\) , \(pq = pr\) and \(p \ne 0\) , then \(q = r\) . Conversely, if \(R[x]\) is an integral domain, then so is \(R\) .

title: Definition 6.3.2 (Integral Domain)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: An integral domain is a commutative ring \(R\) with \(1 \ne 0\) and no zero divisors : for all \(a, b \in R\) , if \(ab = 0\) , then \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\) .

title: Definition 6.3.3 (Polynomials of Degree at Most n)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(n \in \nN\) . The set of polynomials of degree at most \(n\) is \[ R[x]_{\le n} \coloneqq \{ p \in R[x] : \deg p \le n \} . \]

title: Definition 6.3.4 (Polynomials of Degree Exactly n)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(n \in \nN\) . The set of polynomials of degree exactly \(n\) is \(R[x]_{= n} \coloneqq \{ p \in R[x] : \deg p = n \}\) .

title: Proposition 6.3.4 (Units of a Polynomial Ring)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: Let \(R\) be an integral domain. Then the units of \(R[x]\) are exactly the constants \(a\) with \(a \in R^{\times}\) ( @def-ring-unit ): identifying \(a\) with \(a x^0\) , \((R[x])^{\times} = R^{\times}\) .

title: Theorem 6.3.2 (Degree of a Product)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, let \(p, q \in R[x]\) be non-zero, and let \(m \coloneqq \deg p\) , \(n \coloneqq \deg q\) . \((pq)_k = 0\) for every \(k > m + n\) , and \((pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q)\) . Hence \(\deg(pq) \le \deg p + \deg q\) for all \(p, q \in R[x]\) , zero or not; and if \(p = 0\) or \(q = 0\) , then \(pq = 0\) and \(\deg(pq) = -\infty = \deg p + \deg q\) . \(\deg(pq) = m + n\) if and only if \(\operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q) \ne 0\) , and then \(\operatorname{lc}(pq) = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q)\) . This holds in particular when \(R\) has no zero divisors ( \(ab = 0\) implies \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\) ), for example when \(R\) is a field ( @thm-field-basic-properties (f)); together with the last clause of (a), \(\deg(pq) = \deg p + \deg q\) then holds for all \(p, q \in R[x]\) , zero or not; when \(\operatorname{lc}(p)\) is a unit of \(R\) ( @def-ring-unit ), in particular when \(p\) is monic.

title: Theorem 6.3.1 (Degree of a Sum)
page: 6.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(p, q \in R[x]\) . Then \[ \deg(p + q) \le \max(\deg p, \deg q) , \] with equality when \(\deg p \ne \deg q\) .

title: Corollary 6.4.3 (Changing the Coefficient Ring)
content: Let \(\varphi \colon R \to S\) be a ring homomorphism. For \(p \in R[x]\) , let \(\varphi_*(p)\) be the sequence with \(\bigl(\varphi_*(p)\bigr)_k \coloneqq \varphi(p_k)\) . Then \(\varphi_*(p) \in S[x]\) , and \(\varphi_* \colon R[x] \to S[x]\) is a ring homomorphism with \(\varphi_*(a x^n) = \varphi(a) x^n\) . Moreover \(\deg \varphi_*(p) \le \deg p\) for every \(p\) , and for \(p \ne 0\) , equality holds if and only if \(\varphi(\operatorname{lc}(p)) \ne 0\) .

title: Definition 6.4.3 (Composition of Polynomials)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(p, q \in R[x]\) . The composition \(p \circ q \in R[x]\) is \(\Phi(p)\) for the homomorphism \(\Phi\) of @thm-polynomial-substitution with \(S = R[x]\) , \(\varphi \colon a \mapsto a x^0\) and \(s = q\) : \[ p \circ q = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k \, q^k \qquad (N \text{ admissible for } p). \]

title: Definition 6.4.1 (Evaluation, Root, Polynomial Function)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(p \in R[x]\) and \(c \in R\) . The value of \(p\) at \(c\) is \[ p(c) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k \in R , \] for any \(N \in \nN\) with \(p_k = 0\) for every \(k > N\) . The element \(c\) is a root of \(p\) if \(p(c) = 0\) . The polynomial function of \(p\) is the function \(R \to R\) , \(c \mapsto p(c)\) .

title: Definition 6.4.2 (Ring Homomorphism)
content: Let \(R\) and \(S\) be commutative rings. A ring homomorphism \(\varphi \colon R \to S\) is a function such that, for all \(a, b \in R\) , \[ \varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b) , \qquad \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a) \varphi(b) , \] and \(\varphi(1) = 1\) .

title: Proposition 6.4.4 (Polynomials and Their Functions)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. The set \(R^R\) of functions \(R \to R\) ( @fd2:def-function ), with the pointwise operations \((f + g)(c) \coloneqq f(c) + g(c)\) and \((fg)(c) \coloneqq f(c) g(c)\) , is a commutative ring, whose zero and one are the constant functions with values \(0\) and \(1\) . The map \(\varepsilon \colon R[x] \to R^R\) , \(\varepsilon(p) \coloneqq (c \mapsto p(c))\) , is a ring homomorphism. For all \(p, q \in R[x]\) and \(c \in R\) , \((p \circ q)(c) = p(q(c))\) : composition of polynomials matches composition of their functions. If \(R\) is finite with \(1 \ne 0\) , then \(\varepsilon\) is not injective. Explicitly, if \(c_1, \dots, c_r\) lists the elements of \(R\) without repetition, then \[ P \coloneqq \prod_{j=1}^{r} (x - c_j) \] is monic of degree \(r\) , so \(P \ne 0\) , yet \(P(c) = 0\) for every \(c \in R\) .

title: Theorem 6.4.1 (Evaluation Respects the Operations)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(p, q \in R[x]\) and \(c \in R\) . Then \[ (p + q)(c) = p(c) + q(c) , \qquad (pq)(c) = p(c) \, q(c) , \] and \(a(c) = a\) for every constant \(a\) , and \(x(c) = c\) .

title: Theorem 6.4.2 (Substitution Principle)
content: Let \(R\) and \(S\) be commutative rings, \(\varphi \colon R \to S\) a ring homomorphism, and \(s \in S\) . Define \(\Phi \colon R[x] \to S\) by \[ \Phi(p) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} \varphi(p_k) \, s^k , \] for any \(N\) admissible for \(p\) . \(\Phi\) is well defined, and it is a ring homomorphism with \(\Phi(a) = \varphi(a)\) for every constant \(a \in R\) and \(\Phi(x) = s\) . \(\Phi\) is the only ring homomorphism \(R[x] \to S\) with these two properties.

content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and \(E \colon R[x] \to R[x]\) , \(E(f) \coloneqq f + f'\) . Show that \(E\) is an injective homomorphism of the group \((R[x], +)\) to itself. If \(1 \ne 0\) in \(R\) , show that \(E(fg) = E(f) E(g)\) fails for some \(f, g\) .

content: Find all \(f \in \nQ[x]\) with \(f \circ x^2 = f^2\) .

title: Proposition 6.5.2 (When the Formal Derivative Is Zero)
content: Let \(F\) be a field ( @def-field ) and \(f \in F[x]\) . If \(\operatorname{char} F = 0\) , then \(f' = 0\) if and only if \(f\) is constant. Moreover, \(\deg f' = \deg f - 1\) whenever \(\deg f \ge 1\) . If \(\operatorname{char} F = p > 0\) , then \(p\) is prime, and the following are equivalent: (i) \(f' = 0\) ; (ii) \(f_k = 0\) for every \(k \in \nN\) not divisible by \(p\) ; (iii) \(f = g \circ x^p\) for some \(g \in F[x]\) ( @def-polynomial-composition ).

title: Theorem 6.5.1 (Rules for the Formal Derivative)
content: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring, \(f, g \in R[x]\) , \(a, c \in R\) and \(m \in \nZ_{>0}\) . (Linearity) \((f + g)' = f' + g'\) , and \((af)' = a f'\) for the constant \(a\) ; moreover \(a' = 0\) . (Product rule) \((fg)' = f'g + fg'\) . (Power rule) \((g^m)' = (m \cdot 1) \, g^{m-1} g'\) . In particular \(\bigl( (x - c)^m \bigr)' = (m \cdot 1)(x - c)^{m-1}\) .

title: Definition 7.1.1 (Divisibility of Polynomials)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g \in F[x]\) . \(g\) divides \(f\) over \(F\) , written \(g \mid f\) , if there exists \(h \in F[x]\) with \(f = gh\) . Then \(g\) is a divisor (or factor ) of \(f\) , and \(f\) is a multiple of \(g\) . We write \(g \nmid f\) when \(g\) does not divide \(f\) . \(f\) and \(g\) are associates if \(f = cg\) for some non-zero constant \(c \in F\) .

title: Example (Remainders without dividing)
content: In \(\nQ[x]\) , find the remainder of \(f = x^5 - 3x^3 + 2x + 7\) on division by \(x - 2\) . In \(\nQ[x]\) , find the remainder of \(x^5\) on division by \(x^2 - x\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: State @thm-polynomial-division-remainder with every hypothesis. Name the two places in its proof where “ \(F\) is a field” is used. Let \(f \in F[x]\) , and let \(c \in F\) be a non-zero constant. What are the quotient and the remainder of \(f\) on division by \(c\) ? True or false, with a reason: for \(f, g \in \nQ[x]\) , if \(f \mid g\) and \(g \mid f\) , then \(f = g\) . The same question in \(\nF_2[x]\) .

content:
In \(

title: Exercise (B2: A factor of a difference of powers)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(c \in F\) and \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) . Deduce from @lem-difference-of-powers that \[ x^n - c^n = (x - c) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^j x^{n-1-j} , \] and hence that \(x - c \mid x^n - c^n\) . Then give a second proof of the divisibility with @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor .

title: Exercise (B3: One remainder over every field)
content: Let \(F\) be any field. Show that the remainder of \(x^{100}\) on division by \(x^2 - 1\) in \(F[x]\) is \(1\) . Then explain why, over \(\nQ\) , evaluating at the roots \(1\) and \(-1\) also finds it, and why that method alone does not settle the question over \(\nF_2\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The remainder modulo a quadratic with known roots)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) and \(a, b \in F\) . If \(a \ne b\) , prove that the remainder of \(f\) on division by \((x - a)(x - b)\) is \[ f(a) (a - b)^{-1} (x - b) + f(b) (b - a)^{-1} (x - a) . \] If \(a = b\) , write \(f = (x - a)h + f(a)\) ( @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a)) and prove that the remainder of \(f\) on division by \((x - a)^2\) is \(h(a)(x - a) + f(a)\) . Hence find the remainder of \(x^{100}\) on division by \(x^2 - 3x + 2\) in \(\nQ[x]\) .

title: Proposition 7.1.1 (Rules for Divisibility of Polynomials)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g, h \in F[x]\) . \(g \mid 0\) . \(0 \mid f\) if and only if \(f = 0\) . Every non-zero constant divides every polynomial. If \(f \mid g\) and \(g \mid h\) , then \(f \mid h\) . If \(h \mid f\) and \(h \mid g\) , then \(h \mid af + bg\) for all \(a, b \in F[x]\) . If \(g \mid f\) and \(f \ne 0\) , then \(\deg g \le \deg f\) . The units of \(F[x]\) ( @def-ring-unit ) are exactly the non-zero constants. \(f \mid g\) and \(g \mid f\) if and only if \(f\) and \(g\) are associates (this includes \(f = g = 0\) ). Every non-zero \(f\) has exactly one monic associate, namely \(\operatorname{lc}(f)^{-1} f\) . Two monic polynomials that divide each other are equal.

title: Theorem 7.1.2 (Division with Remainder in F[x])
content: Let \(F\) be a field, and let \(f, g \in F[x]\) with \(g \ne 0\) . There are unique \(q, r \in F[x]\) with \[ f = qg + r \quad \text{and} \quad \deg r < \deg g . \] \(g \mid f\) if and only if \(r = 0\) . The polynomials \(q\) and \(r\) are the quotient and the remainder of \(f\) on division by \(g\) .

title: Theorem 7.1.3 (Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem)
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) and \(c \in F\) . The remainder of \(f\) on division by \(x - c\) is the constant \(f(c)\) . \(c\) is a root of \(f\) if and only if \(x - c \mid f\) . \(f\) has a factor of degree \(1\) in \(F[x]\) if and only if \(f\) has a root in \(F\) .

title: Corollary 7.2.3 (Coprime Means 1 Is a Combination)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g \in F[x]\) . Then \(f\) and \(g\) are coprime if and only if \(af + bg = 1\) for some \(a, b \in F[x]\) .

title: Definition 7.2.3 (Coprime Polynomials)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field. Polynomials \(f, g \in F[x]\) are coprime over \(F\) if \(\gcd(f, g) = 1\) .

title: Definition 7.2.1 (Ideal Generated by Polynomials)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(k \in \nZ_{>0}\) and \(f_1, \dots, f_k \in F[x]\) . The set \[ \langle f_1, \dots, f_k \rangle \coloneqq \{ a_1 f_1 + \dots + a_k f_k : a_1, \dots, a_k \in F[x] \} \] is the ideal generated by \(f_1, \dots, f_k\) . For one polynomial, \(\langle f \rangle = \{ af : a \in F[x] \}\) is the set of multiples of \(f\) .

title: Definition 7.2.2 (Greatest Common Divisor of Polynomials)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g \in F[x]\) , not both \(0\) . A greatest common divisor of \(f\) and \(g\) is a monic \(d \in F[x]\) such that \(d \mid f\) , \(d \mid g\) , and \(h \mid d\) for every common divisor \(h\) of \(f\) and \(g\) . We set \(\gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0\) .

title: Example (A run of the Euclidean algorithm)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: In \(\nQ[x]\) , compute \(\gcd(f, g)\) for \(f = x^4 - x^3 - 3x^2 + x + 2\) and \(g = x^3 - 2x - 1\) , and write it as \(af + bg\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: These questions are about the proof of @thm-polynomial-ideals-principal . Where is “least degree” used? Why is \(d\) made monic, and what would fail without it? Run the proof on \(I \coloneqq \{ f \in \nQ[x] : f(1) = 0 \text{ and } f(-1) = 0 \}\) : show that \(I\) is an ideal, and find \(d\) . The polynomials in two indeterminates \(x, y\) over \(\nQ\) with zero constant term (such as \(x\) , \(y\) , \(x^2 y - 3y\) ) are closed under sums and under multiplication by any polynomial in \(x, y\) . Name the step of the proof that has no analogue there. (A prose answer; no proof that the theorem fails is asked for.) State the idea of the proof in two sentences.

title: Exercise (B1: A gcd and its common root)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: In \(\nQ[x]\) , let \(f = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1\) and \(g = x^3 + x + 2\) . Compute \(\gcd(f, g)\) with the Euclidean algorithm, and write it as \(af + bg\) . Hence show that \(-1\) is the only common root of \(f\) and \(g\) in \(\nQ\) .

title: Exercise (B2: A gcd over the field with two elements)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: In \(\nF_2[x]\) , let \(f = x^4 + x^3 + x + 1\) and \(g = x^3 + x^2 + x + 1\) . Show that \(\gcd(f, g) = x^2 + 1\) and that \(x^2 + 1 = 1 \cdot f + x \cdot g\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: ideals of F[x] and Bézout)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field. Prove that for every ideal \(I \ne \{0\}\) of \(F[x]\) there is exactly one monic \(d\) with \(I = \langle d \rangle\) . Let \(f, g \in F[x]\) , not both \(0\) , and let \(d\) be the monic generator of \(\langle f, g \rangle\) . Prove that \(d \mid f\) , \(d \mid g\) , that every common divisor of \(f\) and \(g\) divides \(d\) , that \(d = \gcd(f, g)\) , and that \(d = af + bg\) for some \(a, b \in F[x]\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Scaling the gcd)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f, g \in F[x]\) , and \(h \in F[x]\) monic. Prove that \(\gcd(hf, hg) = h \gcd(f, g)\) .

title: Exercise (C3: The gcd of two binomials)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field. For \(m, n \in \nN\) , not both \(0\) , prove that \[ \gcd(x^m - 1, \, x^n - 1) = x^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1 \] in \(F[x]\) (here \(x^0 - 1 = 0\) , and \(\gcd(m, n)\) is the integer gcd). Compute \(\gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1)\) .

title: Lemma 7.2.4 (One Step of the Euclidean Algorithm)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g, q, r \in F[x]\) with \(f = qg + r\) . Then \(\langle f, g \rangle = \langle g, r \rangle\) , and hence \(\gcd(f, g) = \gcd(g, r)\) .

title: Proposition 7.2.6 (Division and gcd Do Not Depend on the Field)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(L\) be a field, \(K \subseteq L\) a subfield, and \(f, g \in K[x]\) . If \(g \ne 0\) , the quotient and the remainder of \(f\) on division by \(g\) are the same in \(K[x]\) and in \(L[x]\) . If \(g \ne 0\) , then \(g \mid f\) in \(L[x]\) if and only if \(g \mid f\) in \(K[x]\) . \(\gcd(f, g)\) is the same computed in \(K[x]\) or in \(L[x]\) . In particular, \(f\) and \(g\) are coprime over \(K\) if and only if they are coprime over \(L\) .

title: Theorem 7.2.5 (The Euclidean Algorithm for Polynomials)

title: Theorem 7.2.2 (Bézout’s Theorem for Polynomials)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field, let \(f, g \in F[x]\) be not both \(0\) , and let \(d\) be the monic polynomial with \(\langle f, g \rangle = \langle d \rangle\) ( @thm-polynomial-ideals-principal ). \(d \mid f\) and \(d \mid g\) . Every common divisor of \(f\) and \(g\) divides \(d\) . \(d = \gcd(f, g)\) . So \(\gcd(f, g)\) exists, and \(\langle f, g \rangle = \langle \gcd(f, g) \rangle\) . \(\gcd(f, g) = af + bg\) for some \(a, b \in F[x]\) . \(\gcd(f, g)\) has the largest degree among the common divisors of \(f\) and \(g\) , and a common divisor of that degree is an associate of \(\gcd(f, g)\) .

title: Theorem 7.2.1 (Ideals of F[x] Are Principal)
page: 7.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(I\) an ideal of \(F[x]\) . If \(I = \{0\}\) , then \(I = \langle 0 \rangle\) . If \(I \ne \{0\}\) , there is exactly one monic \(d \in F[x]\) with \(I = \langle d \rangle\) . Moreover \(d\) is the only monic element of \(I\) of least degree among the non-zero elements of \(I\) .

title: Corollary 7.3.3 (An Irreducible Dividing a Product)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(p \in F[x]\) irreducible over \(F\) . For every \(f \in F[x]\) : \(p \mid f\) or \(\gcd(p, f) = 1\) . For all \(g, h \in F[x]\) : if \(p \mid gh\) , then \(p \mid g\) or \(p \mid h\) . If \((q_1, \dots, q_l)\) is a list of polynomials in \(F[x]\) , with \(l \in \nN\) , and \(p \mid q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l\) , then \(l \ge 1\) and \(p \mid q_j\) for some \(j \in \{1, \dots, l\}\) . If \(p\) and \(q\) are monic and irreducible over \(F\) and \(p \mid q\) , then \(p = q\) .

title: Definition 7.3.1 (Irreducible Polynomial)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(p \in F[x]\) . The polynomial \(p\) is irreducible over \(F\) if \(\deg p \ge 1\) and, whenever \(p = gh\) with \(g, h \in F[x]\) , one of \(g\) , \(h\) is a constant. A polynomial of degree at least \(1\) that is not irreducible over \(F\) is reducible over \(F\) .

content: Show that \(3x^3 + x^2 - 2\) is irreducible over \(\nQ\) .

content: List all irreducible polynomials of degree at most \(3\) over \(\nF_2\) , and prove that the list is complete.

content: Prove the uniqueness half of @thm-polynomial-unique-factorization : if \(c \, p_1 \cdots p_k = c' q_1 \cdots q_l\) with \(c, c' \in F\) non-zero and all \(p_i\) , \(q_j\) monic irreducible over the field \(F\) , then \(c = c'\) , \(l = k\) , and the two lists agree up to a bijection of indices. title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content:
Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. \(x^4 + 1\) is irreducible over \(
Q\) . Argument. (1) By @thm-rational-root-test , a rational root of \(x^4 + 1\) is \(u/v\) with \(u \mid 1\) and \(v \mid 1\) , so the only candidates are \(1\) and \(-1\) . (2) Both give the value \(1 + 1 = 2 
e 0\) , so \(x^4 + 1\) has no rational root. (3) By @prp-irreducible-low-degree , a polynomial without roots is irreducible. (4) Hence \(x^4 + 1\) is irreducible over \(
Q\) . Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, give a counterexample to the step, and repair the proof.

content:
Let \(F\) be a field. Prove that no finite list contains every monic irreducible polynomial of \(F[x]\) : for every list \((p_1, \dots, p_k)\) of monic irreducibles, \(k \in 
N\) , some monic irreducible is not an entry of it. Let \(p\) be prime. Prove that there are exactly \(p^n\) monic polynomials of degree \(n\) in \(
F_p[x]\) , for each \(n \in 
N\) , and deduce that \(
F_p[x]\) has monic irreducibles of arbitrarily large degree.

title: Exercise (C4: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple)
content: Let \(f, g \in F[x]\) be monic, \(d \coloneqq \gcd(f, g)\) , and write \(f = d f_1\) , \(g = d g_1\) . Prove that \(\gcd(f_1, g_1) = 1\) . Prove that \(L \coloneqq d f_1 g_1\) is a monic common multiple of \(f\) and \(g\) that divides every common multiple of \(f\) and \(g\) , and that \(d \cdot L = fg\) . In \(\nQ[x]\) , let \(f = g = 2x\) (not monic). The gcd is \(x\) , and the monic common multiple dividing every common multiple is \(x\) . Show that \(\gcd(f, g) \cdot x \ne fg\) .

title: Lemma 7.3.5 (An Irreducible Factor Exists)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f \in F[x]\) with \(\deg f \ge 1\) . Then \(f\) has a monic irreducible divisor in \(F[x]\) .

title: Proposition 7.3.1 (Irreducibility in Low Degree)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(p \in F[x]\) . If \(\deg p \ge 2\) and \(p\) has a root in \(F\) , then \(p\) is reducible over \(F\) . If \(\deg p \in \{2, 3\}\) , then \(p\) is irreducible over \(F\) if and only if \(p\) has no root in \(F\) .

title: Proposition 7.3.4 (Coprime Divisors of a Polynomial)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(m, n, h \in F[x]\) with \(m \mid h\) , \(n \mid h\) and \(\gcd(m, n) = 1\) . Then \(mn \mid h\) .

title: Theorem 7.3.2 (Euclid’s Lemma for Polynomials)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g, h \in F[x]\) . If \(f \mid gh\) and \(\gcd(f, g) = 1\) , then \(f \mid h\) .

title: Theorem 7.3.6 (Unique Factorization of Polynomials)
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f \in F[x]\) with \(\deg f \ge 1\) and leading coefficient \(c\) . Existence. There are \(k \ge 1\) and monic polynomials \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) , irreducible over \(F\) , with \(f = c \, p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) . Uniqueness. If also \(f = c' q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l\) with \(c' \in F\) , \(l \in \nN\) and monic polynomials \(q_1, \dots, q_l\) irreducible over \(F\) , then \(c' = c\) , \(l = k\) , and there is a bijection \(\sigma \colon \{1, \dots, k\} \to \{1, \dots, l\}\) ( @fd2:def-bijective ) with \(q_{\sigma(i)} = p_i\) for every \(i\) .

title: Theorem 7.3.7 (Rational Root Test)
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) , let \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in 
Z\) with \(a_n 
e 0\) , and let \(f \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{n} a_i x^i \in 
Q[x]\) . If \(u \in 
Z\) , \(v \in 
Z_{>0}\) , \(\gcd(u, v) = 1\) and \(f(u/v) = 0\) , then \(u \mid a_0\) and \(v \mid a_n\) in \(
Z\) .

title: Corollary 7.4.8 (Repeated Factors and the Greatest Common Divisor)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f \in F[x]\) with \(\deg f \ge 1\) . If \(p \in F[x]\) is irreducible and \(p^2 \mid f\) , then \(p \mid \gcd(f, f')\) . So if \(\gcd(f, f') = 1\) , no irreducible divides \(f\) twice, and \(f\) has no multiple root in \(F\) . If \(F\) has characteristic \(0\) ( @def-characteristic ) and \(\gcd(f, f') \ne 1\) , then \(p^2 \mid f\) for some irreducible \(p\) .

title: Definition 7.4.1 (Multiplicity of a Root)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) non-zero , and \(c \in F\) . The multiplicity of \(c\) in \(f\) , written \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f)\) , is the largest \(m \in \nN\) with \((x - c)^m \mid f\) . The root \(c\) is simple if \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f) = 1\) and multiple if \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f) \ge 2\) .

title: Definition 7.4.2 (Splitting over a Field)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f \in F[x]\) non-zero of degree \(n\) . The polynomial \(f\) splits over \(F\) if \[ f = a (x - a_1)(x - a_2) \cdots (x - a_n) \] for some \(a, a_1, \dots, a_n \in F\) , repetitions among the \(a_i\) allowed. For \(n = 0\) this says that \(f = a\) is a non-zero constant.

title: Example (Polynomial Functions over a Finite Field)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content:
Show that \(x^3 + 2x\) and \(0\) have the same values on \(

F_3[x]\) . Let \(p\) be prime. Show that, in \(

page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content:

title: Exercise (B1: Put the proof in order)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: The following lines contain a proof of the divisibility part of @thm-polynomial-root-count , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven correct lines in an order that makes a proof, say which other orders are also admissible, and say why each of the other two lines fails. We use induction on \(k\) ; for \(k = 1\) , \(x - c_1 \mid f\) by the factor theorem. Assume the claim for every list of \(k - 1\) distinct roots, and let \(c_1, \dots, c_k\) be distinct roots of \(f\) . Write \(f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_{k-1}) \, h\) . Evaluate at \(c_k\) : \(0 = (c_k - c_1) \cdots (c_k - c_{k-1}) \, h(c_k)\) . Each \(c_k - c_i\) , \(i < k\) , is non-zero, since the roots are distinct. (v′) Each \(c_k - c_i\) , \(i < k\) , is non-zero, since \(c_k \ne 0\) . A product of non-zero elements of a field is non-zero, so \(h(c_k) = 0\) . (vi′) \(h(c_k) = 0\) , because \(f(c_k) = 0\) . By the factor theorem, \(h = (x - c_k) h_1\) , so \(f = (x - c_1) \cdots (x - c_k) \, h_1\) .

page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative

Prove that \[ b_j = \frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j! \cdot 1} \qquad (0 \le j \le n) , \] where \(f^{(j)}\) is the \(j\) -th formal derivative ( @def-formal-derivative ).
