title: Lemma 7.4.4 (Multiplicity through the Cofactor)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content:
Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) non-zero, \(c \in F\) and \(m \in 
N\) . \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f) = m\) if and only if \(f = (x - c)^m g\) for some \(g \in F[x]\) with \(g(c) 
e 0\) . Such a \(g\) is unique. If \(f = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j (x - c)^j\) is the expansion of @thm-polynomial-taylor-shift , then \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f)\) is the least \(j\) with \(b_j 
e 0\) .

title: Proposition 7.4.5 (Multiplicity of a Product)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f, g \in F[x]\) non-zero and \(c \in F\) . Then \(\operatorname{mult}_c(fg) = \operatorname{mult}_c(f) + \operatorname{mult}_c(g)\) .

title: Theorem 7.4.2 (Polynomials Determined by Values)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f, g \in F[x]\) . Let \(n \in \nN\) . If \(\deg f \le n\) , \(\deg g \le n\) , and \(f(c_i) = g(c_i)\) for \(n + 1\) distinct elements \(c_0, \dots, c_n \in F\) , then \(f = g\) . If \(F\) is infinite and \(f(c) = g(c)\) for every \(c \in F\) , then \(f = g\) .

title: Theorem 7.4.7 (Repeated Roots and the Derivative)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) non-zero and \(c \in F\) . \(c\) is a multiple root of \(f\) if and only if \(f(c) = 0\) and \(f'(c) = 0\) . If \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f) = m \ge 1\) and \(m \cdot 1 \ne 0\) in \(F\) , then \(f' \ne 0\) and \(\operatorname{mult}_c(f') = m - 1\) .

title: Theorem 7.4.1 (Counting Roots)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) , \(k \ge 1\) , and let \(c_1, \dots, c_k \in F\) be distinct roots of \(f\) . Then \[ (x - c_1)(x - c_2) \cdots (x - c_k) \mid f . \] If \(f \ne 0\) , then \(k \le \deg f\) . In particular, a non-zero polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) distinct roots in \(F\) .

title: Theorem 7.4.6 (Splitting Off All Roots)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field and \(f \in F[x]\) non-zero. Let \(c_1, \dots, c_k \in F\) , \(k \in \nN\) , be the distinct roots of \(f\) in \(F\) (every root of \(f\) in \(F\) is one of them), and \(m_i \coloneqq \operatorname{mult}_{c_i}(f)\) . Then \[ f = (x - c_1)^{m_1} (x - c_2)^{m_2} \cdots (x - c_k)^{m_k} \, g \] for some \(g \in F[x]\) with no root in \(F\) , and \(m_1 + m_2 + \dots + m_k \le \deg f\) .

title: Theorem 7.4.3 (Expansion in Powers of x - c)
page: 7.4 Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative
content: Let \(F\) be a field, \(f \in F[x]\) with \(\deg f = n \ge 0\) , and \(c \in F\) . There are unique \(b_0, b_1, \dots, b_n \in F\) with \[ f = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j (x - c)^j . \] \(b_0 = f(c)\) , and \(b_n\) is the leading coefficient of \(f\) . For every \(h \in F\) , \(f(c + h) = \sum_{j=0}^{n} b_j h^j\) .

title: Definition 7.5.1 (Lagrange Polynomials)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content:
Let \(n \in 
N\) and let \(c_0, \dots, c_n \in F\) be distinct . For \(i \in \{0, \dots, n\}\) , the \(i\) -th Lagrange polynomial of these nodes is \[ \ell_i \coloneqq \prod_{\substack{j = 0 \ j 
e i}}^{n} (c_i - c_j)^{-1} (x - c_j) \in F[x] , \] the product, in increasing order of \(j\) , of the \(n\) polynomials \((c_i - c_j)^{-1}(x - c_j)\) with \(j 
e i\) .

title: Definition 7.5.2 (Congruence Modulo a Polynomial)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(m \in F[x]\) . Polynomials \(f, g \in F[x]\) are congruent modulo \(m\) , written \(f \equiv g \pmod{m}\) , if \(m \mid f - g\) ( @def-polynomial-divides ), that is, if \(f - g \in \langle m \rangle\) ( @def-polynomial-combinations ).

title: Lemma 7.5.4 (Coprime to Each Factor, Coprime to the Product)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(s \ge 1\) and \(p, q_1, \dots, q_s \in F[x]\) . If \(\gcd(p, q_j) = 1\) for every \(j\) , then \(\gcd(p, q_1 \cdots q_s) = 1\) . Let \(k \ge 1\) and let \(m_1, \dots, m_k \in F[x]\) be pairwise coprime : \(\gcd(m_i, m_j) = 1\) whenever \(i \ne j\) . If \(m_i \mid h\) for every \(i\) , then \(m_1 \cdots m_k \mid h\) .

title: Proposition 7.5.6 (Interpolation Is the Chinese Remainder Theorem for Linear Moduli)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(c_0, \dots, c_n \in F\) be distinct, let \(y_0, \dots, y_n \in F\) , and let \(m \coloneqq (x - c_0) \cdots (x - c_n)\) . The moduli \(x - c_0, \dots, x - c_n\) are pairwise coprime, and \(\deg m = n + 1\) . For \(f \in F[x]\) and each \(i\) : \(f \equiv y_i \pmod{x - c_i}\) if and only if \(f(c_i) = y_i\) . The polynomial of degree less than \(n + 1\) given by @thm-polynomial-chinese-remainder (c) for the right-hand sides \(y_0, \dots, y_n\) is \(\sum_{i} y_i \ell_i\) , the interpolating polynomial of @thm-polynomial-interpolation . In particular, the remainder of the polynomial \(e_i\) of @thm-polynomial-chinese-remainder (a) on division by \(m\) is the Lagrange polynomial \(\ell_i\) .

title: Theorem 7.5.5 (Chinese Remainder Theorem for Polynomials)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(k \ge 1\) , let \(m_1, \dots, m_k \in F[x]\) be non-zero and pairwise coprime, and let \(m \coloneqq m_1 \cdots m_k\) . For each \(i\) , let \(M_i\) be the product of the \(m_j\) with \(j \ne i\) (in increasing order of \(j\) ). For each \(i\) there are \(a_i, b_i \in F[x]\) with \(a_i M_i + b_i m_i = 1\) . Put \(e_i \coloneqq a_i M_i\) . Then \(e_i \equiv 1 \pmod{m_i}\) and \(e_i \equiv 0 \pmod{m_j}\) for \(j \ne i\) , and for all \(r_1, \dots, r_k \in F[x]\) the polynomial \(f \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{k} r_i e_i\) satisfies \[ f \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i} \qquad \text{for every } i \in \{1, \dots, k\} . \] A polynomial \(g\) satisfies the same \(k\) congruences if and only if \(g \equiv f \pmod{m}\) . Exactly one polynomial of degree less than \(\deg m\) satisfies the \(k\) congruences. The rule \(\Phi([f]_m) \coloneqq ([f]_{m_1}, \dots, [f]_{m_k})\) is a well-defined bijection \[ \Phi \colon F[x]/\langle m \rangle \to F[x]/\langle m_1 \rangle \times \dots \times F[x]/\langle m_k \rangle , \] and, with \(+\) and \(\cdot\) on the right taken componentwise, \(\Phi\) preserves \(+\) and \(\cdot\) and sends \([1]_m\) to \(([1]_{m_1}, \dots, [1]_{m_k})\) .

title: Theorem 7.5.1 (Lagrange Interpolation)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(c_0, \dots, c_n \in F\) be distinct, and let \(y_0, \dots, y_n \in F\) . Let \(\ell_0, \dots, \ell_n\) be the Lagrange polynomials of the nodes ( @def-lagrange-polynomials-for-nodes ). For all \(i, k \in \{0, \dots, n\}\) , \(\ell_i(c_k) = 1\) if \(k = i\) and \(\ell_i(c_k) = 0\) if \(k \ne i\) . Each \(\ell_i\) has degree exactly \(n\) . The polynomial \(p \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{n} y_i \ell_i\) satisfies \(\deg p \le n\) and \(p(c_k) = y_k\) for every \(k\) . It is the only polynomial of degree at most \(n\) with \(p(c_k) = y_k\) for every \(k\) . Every \(q \in F[x]\) with \(\deg q \le n\) satisfies \(q = \sum_{i=0}^{n} q(c_i) \ell_i\) .

title: Theorem 7.5.3 (The Quotient Is a Field Exactly When m Is Irreducible)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(m \in F[x]\) with \(\deg m \ge 1\) . Then \(F[x]/\langle m \rangle\) is a field ( @def-field ) if and only if \(m\) is irreducible over \(F\) ( @def-irreducible-over-field ).

title: Theorem 7.5.2 (The Ring of Polynomials Modulo m)
page: 7.5 Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
content: Let \(m \in F[x]\) with \(d \coloneqq \deg m \ge 1\) , and write \([f] = f + \langle m \rangle\) . \(F[x]/\langle m \rangle\) , with \([f] + [g] \coloneqq [f + g]\) and \([f][g] \coloneqq [fg]\) , is a commutative ring with zero \([0]\) and one \([1]\) , and \([1] \ne [0]\) . Each class contains exactly one polynomial of degree less than \(d\) : the remainder of any of its members on division by \(m\) . In particular \(f \equiv g \pmod{m}\) if and only if \(f\) and \(g\) leave the same remainder, and sending each class to its member of degree less than \(d\) is a bijection from \(F[x]/\langle m \rangle\) onto \(\{ r \in F[x] : \deg r < d \}\) . The map \(F \to F[x]/\langle m \rangle\) , \(c \mapsto [c]\) ( \(c\) a constant), is injective and preserves \(+\) and \(\cdot\) . \([f]\) is a unit of \(F[x]/\langle m \rangle\) ( @def-ring-unit ) if and only if \(\gcd(f, m) = 1\) . In that case \([f]^{-1} = [a]\) for any \(a, b \in F[x]\) with \(af + bm = 1\) .

title: Corollary 7.6.7 (Complex Polynomials Split)
content:
Every non-zero \(p \in 
C[x]\) splits over \(
C\) ( @def-splits-over-field ): \(p = a(x - z_1) \cdots (x - z_n)\) with \(n = \deg p\) , \(a\) the leading coefficient of \(p\) , and \(z_1, \dots, z_n \in 
C\) . The multiplicities of the roots of \(p\) add up to \(n\) . The irreducible polynomials of \(
C[x]\) are exactly those of degree \(1\) .

title: Corollary 7.6.9 (The Irreducible Real Polynomials)
content: A polynomial \(p \in \nR[x]\) is irreducible over \(\nR\) if and only if \(\deg p = 1\) , or \(\deg p = 2\) and \(p\) has no real root.

title: Corollary 7.6.11 (Real Polynomials of Odd Degree Have a Real Root)
content: Every \(f \in \nR[x]\) of odd degree has a root in \(\nR\) .

title: Exercise (C3: Find the error)
content:
Here is an argument. Claim. For every non-constant \(p \in 
C[x]\) , \(\abs{p}\) attains a minimum on \(
C\) . Proof. (1) Let \(m \coloneqq \inf \{ \abs{p(z)} : z \in 
C \}\) , which exists since the set is non-empty and bounded below by \(0\) . (2) For each \(k \ge 1\) , pick \(z_k \in 
C\) with \(\abs{p(z_k)} < m + 1/k\) . (3) Since \(\abs{p(z_k)} < m + 1 \le \abs{p(0)} + 1\) , @lem-complex-polynomial-growth puts the \(z_k\) in a bounded set. (4) So they converge to some \(z^* \in 
C\) . (5) Then \(\abs{p(z^*)} = \lim \abs{p(z_k)} = m\) . Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? Name the line that fails and the reason, give a counterexample to the illegal step, and say how the proof in the text avoids it.

title: Definition 8.1.4 (Even and Odd Functions)
content: Let \(D \subseteq \nR\) be symmetric and \(f \colon D \to \nR\) . Then \(f\) is even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\) for every \(x \in D\) , and odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for every \(x \in D\) .

title: Definition 8.1.2 (Operations on Real Functions)
content:
Let \(f \colon D_f 	o

On \(D_f \cap D_g\) define, for each \(x\) , \[ (f + g)(x) \coloneqq f(x) + g(x), \quad (fg)(x) \coloneqq f(x) g(x), \] and \(\max(f, g)(x) \coloneqq \max(f(x), g(x))\) , likewise \(\min(f, g)\) ; here \(\max(a, b)\) is \(b\) if \(a \le b\) and \(a\) otherwise, and \(\min(a, b)\) is \(a\) if \(a \le b\) and \(b\) otherwise. On \(D_f\) define \((cf)(x) \coloneqq c f(x)\) , \(-f \coloneqq (-1) f\) and \(\abs{f}(x) \coloneqq \abs{f(x)}\) ; and \(f - g \coloneqq f + (-g)\) on \(D_f \cap D_g\) . The quotient \(f/g\) , \(x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)\) , has domain \(\{ x \in D_f \cap D_g : g(x)

title: Example (Method: reading a graph as a set of pairs)
content:
How it goes. To prove that \(\operatorname{graph} g\) is \(\operatorname{graph} f\) moved by a bijection \(M \colon 
R^2 	o 
R^2\) , fix \((x, y) \in 
R^2\) and prove \[ (x, y) \in \operatorname{graph} g \iff M^{-1}(x, y) \in \operatorname{graph} f , \] by unwinding “ \((x, y) \in \operatorname{graph} g\) ” into “ \(x \in D_g\) and \(y = g(x)\) ”. Since \(M\) is a bijection, the right side says exactly that \((x, y) \in M(\operatorname{graph} f)\) . When to use it. Shifts, reflections and stretches of graphs; symmetry of a graph; the graph of an inverse function in the next section. Common mistakes. The usual mistake is to move the graph the wrong way. The formula for \(g\) contains \(M^{-1}\) , while the picture moves by \(M\) .

title: Proposition 8.1.3 (Even and Odd Parts)
content:
Let \(D \subseteq

title: Proposition 8.1.2 (Moving a Graph)
content: Let \(f \colon D \to \nR\) , \(a, b \in \nR\) and \(c > 0\) . The function \(x \mapsto f(x - a) + b\) on \(D + a\) has graph \(\operatorname{graph} f + (a, b)\) . The function \(cf\) on \(D\) has graph \(\{ (u, cv) : (u, v) \in \operatorname{graph} f \}\) , and \(x \mapsto f(x/c)\) on \(cD\) has graph \(\{ (cu, v) : (u, v) \in \operatorname{graph} f \}\) .

content:

title: Definition 8.2.1 (Monotone Function)
content: Let \(f \colon D \to \nR\) be a real function ( @def-real-function ) and let \(A \subseteq D\) . The function \(f\) is increasing on \(A\) if, for all \(x, y \in A\) , \(x < y\) implies \(f(x) \le f(y)\) ; strictly increasing on \(A\) if, for all \(x, y \in A\) , \(x < y\) implies \(f(x) < f(y)\) ; decreasing on \(A\) if, for all \(x, y \in A\) , \(x < y\) implies \(f(x) \ge f(y)\) ; strictly decreasing on \(A\) if, for all \(x, y \in A\) , \(x < y\) implies \(f(x) > f(y)\) . It is monotone on \(A\) if it is increasing on \(A\) or decreasing on \(A\) , and strictly monotone on \(A\) if it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on \(A\) . Without “on \(A\) ”, the set is the whole domain \(D\) . In symbols, “increasing on \(A\) ” is \[ \forall x \in A \ \ \forall y \in A \ \ \bigl( x < y \to f(x) \le f(y) \bigr) . \]

content:

R \setminus \{0\}\) and the set \(\{-1, 1, 2\}\) .

title: Example (Method: factor out y − x)
content: How it goes. “Let \(x, y \in A\) with \(x < y\) .” Write \[ f(y) - f(x) = (y - x) \, Q(x, y) \] by algebra on the formula for \(f\) . Since \(y - x > 0\) , the sign of \(f(y) - f(x)\) is the sign of \(Q(x, y)\) : show \(Q(x, y) > 0\) for strictly increasing, \(Q(x, y) \ge 0\) for increasing, and \(< 0\) or \(\le 0\) for the decreasing kinds ( @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), (d)). Differences of powers factor by @lem-difference-of-powers : \[ y^n - x^n = (y - x) \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} y^k x^{n-1-k} . \] Quotients are brought over a common denominator first. When to use it. \(f\) is given by a formula built from \(+\) , \(\cdot\) and \(/\) , and the claim is that \(f\) is monotone on a set. Common mistakes. One mistake is to conclude “strictly” from \(Q \ge 0\) : a positive number times a non-negative one may be \(0\) . Another is to use a sign of \(Q\) that holds on part of \(A\) only. In that case, split \(A\) first, and also compare a point of one piece with a point of another. title: Proposition 8.2.1 (Rules for Monotone Functions)
content:
Let \(f, g \colon D 	o 
R\) and \(A \subseteq D\) . If \(f\) and \(g\) are increasing on \(A\) , so is \(f + g\) ; it is strictly increasing if \(f\) or \(g\) is. If \(f\) is increasing on \(A\) and \(c \ge 0\) , then \(cf\) is increasing on \(A\) , strictly if \(f\) is and \(c > 0\) ; and \(-f\) is decreasing on \(A\) , strictly if \(f\) is strictly increasing. If \(f\) and \(g\) are increasing on \(A\) and \(f(x) \ge 0\) , \(g(x) \ge 0\) for every \(x \in A\) , then \(fg\) is increasing on \(A\) . If \(f\) is increasing on \(A\) and \(f(x) > 0\) for every \(x \in A\) , then \(1/f\) is decreasing on \(A\) , strictly if \(f\) is strictly increasing. Let \(f \colon D 	o 
R\) , \(g \colon E 	o 
R\) , \(A \subseteq D\) and \(B \subseteq E\) with \(f(A) \subseteq B\) . If \(f\) is monotone on \(A\) and \(g\) on \(B\) , then \(g \circ f\) is monotone on \(A\) . It is increasing if both are increasing or both decreasing, and decreasing if one is increasing and the other decreasing. It is strictly so if both are strictly monotone.

title: Proposition 8.2.2 (Strictly Monotone Functions Reflect the Order)
content: Let \(f \colon D \to \nR\) , \(A \subseteq D\) , and \(x, y \in A\) . If \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(A\) , then \(x < y \iff f(x) < f(y)\) , and \(x \le y \iff f(x) \le f(y)\) . If \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \(A\) , then \(x < y \iff f(x) > f(y)\) , and \(x \le y \iff f(x) \ge f(y)\) .

title: Theorem 8.2.3 (Inverse of a Strictly Monotone Function)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) and let \(f \colon A \to \nR\) be strictly increasing. Then: \(f\) , with codomain \(f(A)\) , is a bijection \(A \to f(A)\) ; write \(f^{-1} \colon f(A) \to A\) for its inverse; \(f^{-1}\) is strictly increasing; \(\operatorname{graph} f^{-1} = \{ (y, x) : (x, y) \in \operatorname{graph} f \}\) . The same holds with “strictly decreasing” in place of “strictly increasing”, in the hypothesis and in (b).

title: Definition 8.3.1 (Bounded Function)
content:
Let \(f \colon D 	o 
R\) and \(A \subseteq D\) . The function \(f\) is bounded above on \(A\) if the set \(f(A) = \{ f(x) : x \in A \}\) ( @fd2:def-image ) is bounded above: there exists \(M \in 
R\) with \(f(x) \le M\) for every \(x \in A\) . It is bounded below on \(A\) if \(f(A)\) is bounded below, and bounded on \(A\) if there exists \(M \in 
R\) with \(\abs{f(x)} \le M\) for every \(x \in A\) . When \(A = D\) , “on \(D\) ” may be dropped.

title: Definition 8.3.2 (Supremum and Infimum of a Function)
content: Let \(f \colon D \to \nR\) and let \(A \subseteq D\) be non-empty . If \(f\) is bounded above on \(A\) , the supremum of \(f\) on \(A\) is \[ \sup_A f \coloneqq \sup f(A) , \] also written \(\sup_{x \in A} f(x)\) . If \(f\) is bounded below on \(A\) , its infimum on \(A\) is \(\inf_A f \coloneqq \inf f(A)\) . The supremum is attained if \(\sup_A f \in f(A)\) , that is, \(\sup_A f = f(x_0)\) for some \(x_0 \in A\) ; it is then the maximum of \(f\) on \(A\) , written \(\max_A f\) . Likewise an attained infimum is the minimum \(\min_A f\) .

title: Example (Method: bound every value, then find a witness)
content: How it goes. To prove \(\sup_A f = M\) for a non-empty \(A\) and a candidate \(M \in \nR\) : \((\le)\) Bound every value. Let \(x \in A\) be arbitrary and prove \(f(x) \le M\) . \((\ge)\) Find a witness. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be arbitrary and produce \(x \in A\) , depending on \(\varepsilon\) , with \(f(x) > M - \varepsilon\) . The first half shows that \(f\) is bounded above on \(A\) and that \(M\) is an upper bound of \(f(A)\) ; then \(M = \sup_A f\) by @prp-real-sup-approximation . For an infimum, reverse the inequalities: \(f(x) \ge m\) for every \(x \in A\) , and for each \(\varepsilon > 0\) some \(x\) with \(f(x) < m + \varepsilon\) . We know We want \(f\) on \(A \ne \emptyset\) ; a candidate \(M\) \((\le)\) \(\forall x \in A \ \ f(x) \le M\) ; \((\ge)\) \(\forall \varepsilon > 0 \ \exists x \in A \ \ f(x) > M - \varepsilon\) When to use it. Whenever a supremum or infimum is to be computed. An inequality \(\sup_A f \le M\) needs only the first half, since the supremum is the least upper bound; an equality needs both. Common mistakes. Proving only \((\le)\) shows that \(M\) is an upper bound, not that it is the least one. A witness for one \(\varepsilon\) , such as \(1/10\) , is not enough: the second half needs a witness for every \(\varepsilon\) . A witness for \(f\) must not be paired with a different witness for \(g\) , as if \(f(x) + g(y)\) were a value of \(f + g\) . Exercise B4 shows where that mistake leads.

title: Example (Polynomials of positive degree are unbounded)
content: Let \(p = \sum_{j=0}^{d} a_j x^j \in \nR[x]\) with \(d = \deg p \ge 1\) , and put \[ K \coloneqq \abs{a_0} + \dots + \abs{a_{d-1}} , \qquad R \coloneqq \max\Bigl\{ 1, \frac{2K}{\abs{a_d}} \Bigr\} . \] Show: \(\abs{p(x)} \ge \tfrac12 \abs{a_d} \abs{x}\) for every real \(x\) with \(\abs{x} \ge R\) ; every real root of \(p\) lies in \((-R, R)\) ; the polynomial function of \(p\) on \(\nR\) ( @def-polynomial-rational-function ) is not bounded.

title: Example (A supremum that is attained)
content: Find \(\sup\) and \(\inf\) of \(g(x) = x(1 - x)\) on \([0, 1]\) .

title: Example (A supremum that is not attained)
content: Let \(f(x) = x/(1 + x)\) on \(A = [0, \infty)\) . Prove that \(\sup_A f = 1\) and that it is not attained. Find \(\inf_A f\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Parts (a)–(c) are about the proof of @prp-sup-oscillation . Parts (d)–(f) are true or false: give a reason or a counterexample (here \(A\) is non-empty and \(f\) bounded on \(A\) ). Run the statement on \(f(x) = x^2\) on \(A = [-1, 2)\) : find \(\sup_A f\) , \(\inf_A f\) and the supremum of \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)}\) . Is that supremum attained? Which line of the proof uses that \(f\) is bounded below on \(A\) ? State the idea of the proof in two sentences. \(\sup_A f \in f(A)\) . \(\inf_A f \le \sup_A f\) . \(\sup_A \abs{f} = \max\bigl( \abs{\sup_A f}, \abs{\inf_A f} \bigr)\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Let \(A\) be non-empty and \(f, g\) bounded below on \(A\) . Here is a proof that \(\inf_A (f + g) \ge \inf_A f + \inf_A g\) , with its last step left out. For each \(x \in A\) , \(f(x) \ge \inf_A f\) and \(g(x) \ge \inf_A g\) , so \(f(x) + g(x) \ge \inf_A f + \inf_A g\) . Say which method this is, then complete it.

title: Exercise (B2: Prove or disprove)
content: Let \(A\) be non-empty and \(f, g\) bounded on \(A\) . Prove or disprove each statement; all suprema and infima are on \(A\) . \(\sup (f + g) = \sup f + \sup g\) . \(\sup \max(f, g) = \max(\sup f, \sup g)\) . If \(f(x) > 0\) and \(g(x) > 0\) for every \(x \in A\) , then \(\sup (fg) = \sup f \cdot \sup g\) . \(\sup f = -\inf (-f)\) .

title: Exercise (B3)
content: Find \(\sup\) and \(\inf\) of \(h(x) = x/(x^2 + 1)\) on \(\nR\) , and say whether each is attained. Hence \(\abs{h(x)} \le \tfrac12\) for every real \(x\) . Hint: compare \(h(x)\) with \(\tfrac12\) over a common denominator.

title: Exercise (B4: Find the error)
content: Here is an argument for “ \(\sup_A (f + g) = \sup_A f + \sup_A g\) for \(f, g\) bounded above on a non-empty \(A\) .” The inequality \(\le\) is rule (b) of @thm-sup-function-rules . For \(\ge\) , let \(\varepsilon > 0\) . Choose \(x \in A\) with \(f(x) > \sup f - \varepsilon/2\) and \(y \in A\) with \(g(y) > \sup g - \varepsilon/2\) . Then \(f(x) + g(y) > \sup f + \sup g - \varepsilon\) . So \(\sup f + \sup g\) passes the epsilon test for the values of \(f + g\) , and equality holds. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, and why?

title: Exercise (C1: Chapter check: the supremum of a square)
content: Let \(A\) be non-empty and let \(f \colon D \to \nR\) be bounded on \(A \subseteq D\) , with \(f(x) \ge 0\) for every \(x \in A\) . Prove that \(\sup_A f^2 = \bigl( \sup_A f \bigr)^2\) .

title: Exercise (C2)
content: Let \(a < b\) , \(L \ge 0\) , and let \(f \colon [a, b] \to \nR\) satisfy \(\abs{f(x) - f(y)} \le L \abs{x - y}\) for all \(x, y \in [a, b]\) . Here is the first half of a proof that \(f\) is bounded and \(\sup f - \inf f \le L(b - a)\) , all suprema on \([a, b]\) . For \(x \in [a, b]\) , \(\abs{f(x)} \le \abs{f(a)} + \abs{f(x) - f(a)} \le \abs{f(a)} + L(x - a) \le \abs{f(a)} + L(b - a)\) , so \(f\) is bounded. By @prp-sup-oscillation , \(\sup f - \inf f = \sup \{ \abs{f(x) - f(y)} : x, y \in [a, b] \}\) , so it suffices to bound this supremum. Say which method this is, then complete it.

title: Proposition 8.3.5 (Iterated Suprema)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be non-empty sets and let \(f \colon A \times B \to \nR\) be bounded above. Then \[ \sup_{A \times B} f = \sup_{a \in A} \, \sup_{b \in B} f(a, b) = \sup_{b \in B} \, \sup_{a \in A} f(a, b) . \]

title: Proposition 8.3.1 (Infimum by Reflection)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) . A real number \(l\) is a lower bound of \(A\) if and only if \(-l\) is an upper bound of \(-A\) . If \(A\) is non-empty and bounded below, then \(A\) has an infimum, and \(\inf A = -\sup(-A)\) .

title: Proposition 8.3.2 (The Epsilon Test for a Supremum)
content: Let \(A \subseteq \nR\) be non-empty and let \(s\) be an upper bound of \(A\) . Then \(s = \sup A\) if and only if, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , there exists \(a \in A\) with \(a > s - \varepsilon\) . In symbols: \[ \forall \varepsilon > 0 \ \ \exists a \in A \ \ a > s - \varepsilon . \] Likewise, if \(i\) is a lower bound of \(A\) , then \(i = \inf A\) if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(a \in A\) with \(a < i + \varepsilon\) .

title: Proposition 8.3.4 (The Spread of Values)
content: Let \(A\) be non-empty and let \(f \colon D \to \nR\) be bounded (above and below) on \(A \subseteq D\) . Then \[ \sup \bigl\{ \abs{f(x) - f(y)} : x, y \in A \bigr\} = \sup_A f - \inf_A f . \]

title: Theorem 8.3.3 (Rules for Suprema of Functions)
content: Let \(f, g \colon D \to \nR\) , let \(A \subseteq D\) be non-empty , let \(f\) and \(g\) be bounded above on \(A\) , and let \(c \in \nR\) . All suprema are on \(A\) , and \(f + g\) , \(cf\) , \(\abs{f}\) are as in @def-function-algebra . If \(f(x) \le g(x)\) for every \(x \in A\) , then \(\sup f \le \sup g\) . \(\sup (f + g) \le \sup f + \sup g\) . \(\sup (f + c) = \sup f + c\) . If \(c \ge 0\) , then \(\sup (cf) = c \sup f\) . If \(f\) is bounded below on \(A\) , then \(-f\) is bounded above on \(A\) and \(\sup (-f) = -\inf f\) . If \(B \subseteq A\) is non-empty, then \(\sup_B f \le \sup_A f\) . If \(f\) and \(g\) are bounded (above and below) on \(A\) , then \(\bigl| \sup f - \sup g \bigr| \le \sup \abs{f - g}\) .

title: Definition 8.4.1 (Floor, Ceiling, Fractional Part)
page: 8.4 Floor, Distance to the Integers, and Step Functions
content: Let \(x \in \nR\) . The floor of \(x\) , written \(\floor{x}\) , is the unique \(m \in \nZ\) with \[ m \le x < m + 1 . \] The ceiling of \(x\) is \(\ceil{x} \coloneqq -\floor{-x}\) . The number \(x - \floor{x}\) is the fractional part of \(x\) ; it lies in \([0, 1)\) .

title: Definition 8.4.4 (Step Function)

Let \(a, b \in

The points \(x_0, \dots, x_n\) form a partition of \([a, b]\) adapted to \(\varphi\) , and the intervals \((x_{i-1}, x_i)\) are its open pieces .

title: Example (Method: pin the floor by its inequality)
page: 8.4 Floor, Distance to the Integers, and Step Functions
content: How it goes. To show \(\floor{A} = m\) for a real expression \(A\) , use one of two forms. First form. Check that \(m\) is an integer and that \(m \le A < m + 1\) . Uniqueness in @def-floor-ceiling does the rest. Second form. Check that \(m\) is an integer and that every \(j \in \nZ\) satisfies \(j \le A \iff j \le m\) . This form rests on rule (g) of @prp-floor-rules , which turns \(j \le A\) into a statement about \(\floor{A}\) . We know We want an expression \(A\) ; a candidate integer \(m\) \(m \le A < m + 1\) (first form), or \(\forall j \in \nZ \colon j \le A \iff j \le m\) (second form) When to use it. Every identity with a floor on one side. The first form suits a candidate given by a formula; the second suits an \(A\) built from floors and divisions, where each step of the argument is an equivalence. Common mistakes. One mistake is to drop the decimals, as in the warning above. Another is to forget that \(m\) must be an integer. For example, \(x - \tfrac12 \le x < (x - \tfrac12) + 1\) holds for every real \(x\) , yet \(x - \tfrac12\) is \(\floor{x}\) only when it is an integer.

title: Definition 8.5.3 (Real Powers)
page: 8.5 The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers
content: Let \(a, x \in \nR\) . If \(a > 0\) , then \(a^x \coloneqq \exp(x \log a)\) . If \(a = 0\) and \(x > 0\) , then \(0^x \coloneqq 0\) . No other pair \((a, x)\) is given a value by this definition; in particular there are no real powers of a negative base.

title: Example (Method: squeeze, then close the gap by Archimedes)
page: 8.5 The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers
content: How it goes. To prove \(\sup S = L\) for a set \(S \subseteq \nR\) : show that every \(s \in S\) satisfies \(s \le L\) ; find a constant \(C > 0\) , fixed before \(n\) is chosen , and an \(N_0 \in \nZ_{>0}\) such that for every integer \(n \ge N_0\) some \(s_n \in S\) satisfies \(s_n \ge L - C/n\) ; given \(L' < L\) , put \(\varepsilon \coloneqq (L - L')/C > 0\) . By @fd3:prp-archimedean-reciprocal there is \(N\) with \(1/n < \varepsilon\) for all \(n \ge N\) . For \(n \ge \max\{N, N_0\}\) we get \(s_n \ge L - C/n > L - C\varepsilon = L'\) . So no \(L' < L\) is an upper bound, and \(L\) is the least upper bound. When to use it. A supremum has been guessed, and the members of \(S\) come with an index \(n\) and an error estimate of the form \(C/n\) . Common mistakes. The “constant” \(C\) is allowed to depend on \(n\) . With \(C = n\) , the estimate \(s_n \ge L - 1\) says nothing about small gaps. The constant is \(C = 0\) , which leaves \(\varepsilon\) undefined. If the estimate seems to come with \(C = 0\) , enlarge \(C\) : a lower bound \(L - C/n\) stays true when \(C\) grows. We know We want every \(s \in S\) has \(s \le L\) ; for \(n \ge N_0\) some \(s_n \in S\) has \(s_n \ge L - C/n\) , with \(C > 0\) fixed in advance no \(L' < L\) is an upper bound of \(S\) \(L' < L\) ; \(\varepsilon \coloneqq (L - L')/C > 0\) ; \(1/n < \varepsilon\) for \(n \ge N\) some \(s \in S\) with \(s > L'\) : take \(s_n\) , \(n \ge \max\{N, N_0\}\)

title: Exercise (B3: Put the proof in order)
page: 8.5 The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers
content: Here are lines of the lower estimate in the proof of @thm-exp-unique , shuffled, with two lines that do not belong. Write an order of the correct lines that makes a proof, and say why each distractor fails. Fix \(x \in \nR\) and an integer \(n > \abs{x}\) . Then \(1 + x/n > 0\) and \(1 - x/n > 0\) . By @prp-exp-first-consequences (d), \(\exp(x/n) \le 1/(1 - x/n)\) , so \(\exp x \le (1 - x/n)^{-n}\) . \((1 + x/n)^n = (1 - x^2/n^2)^n (1 - x/n)^{-n}\) . So \((1 + x/n)^n \ge (1 - x^2/n^2)^n \exp x\) . Bernoulli’s inequality at \(-x^2/n^2 \ge -1\) gives \((1 - x^2/n^2)^n \ge 1 - x^2/n\) . Hence \((1 + x/n)^n \ge \exp x - x^2 \exp x / n\) . (D1) By the tangent-line bound, \(\exp x \ge 1 + x\) , so \((1 + x/n)^n \ge 1 + x\) . (D2) Bernoulli’s inequality at \(x^2/n^2\) gives \((1 - x^2/n^2)^n \ge 1 + x^2/n\) .

By the addition rule, \(\exp y - \exp x = \exp(y - x)\) , and by the tangent-line bound, \(\exp(y - x) \ge 1 + (y - x) > 0\) . So \(\exp y > \exp x\) .” Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? Name the line that fails, and show that it fails with numbers.

title: Proposition 8.5.7 (The Exponential Beats Every Power)
page: 8.5 The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers
content: For every \(x > 0\) and every \(k \in \nN\) , \(\exp x > \bigl(x/(k + 1)\bigr)^{k+1}\) . Hence, for every \(M > 0\) , \(\exp x > M x^k\) for all \(x > M (k + 1)^{k+1}\) . For every \(x > 0\) and every \(m \in \nZ_{>0}\) , \(\log x < m x^{1/m}\) . Hence, for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , \(\log x < \varepsilon x\) for all \(x > 4/\varepsilon^2\) .

title: Proposition 8.5.6 (Laws of Real Powers)
page: 8.5 The Exponential, the Logarithm, and Real Powers
content: Let \(a, b, x, y \in \nR\) with \(a, b > 0\) . \(a^{x + y} = a^x a^y\) and \(a^{-x} = 1/a^x\) . \((a^x)^y = a^{xy}\) . \((ab)^x = a^x b^x\) . \(a^x > 0\) . As a function of \(x\) on \(\nR\) : \(x \mapsto a^x\) is strictly increasing if \(a > 1\) , strictly decreasing if \(a < 1\) , and constant \(1\) if \(a = 1\) . As a function of \(a\) on \((0, \infty)\) : \(a \mapsto a^x\) is strictly increasing if \(x > 0\) and strictly decreasing if \(x < 0\) .

title: Lemma 8.6.1 (Irrationals Are Dense)
content: For all \(a, b \in \nR\) with \(a < b\) there is an irrational \(x\) with \(a < x < b\) .

title: Proposition 8.6.2 (Properties of the Dirichlet Function)
content: A real \(p \ne 0\) is a period of \(D\) ( @def-periodic-function ) if and only if \(p \in \nQ\) . For all \(a < b\) , \(\sup_{(a, b)} D = 1\) and \(\inf_{(a, b)} D = 0\) , both attained, and \(\sup \{ \abs{D(x) - D(y)} : x, y \in (a, b) \} = 1\) . For all \(a < b\) , \(D\) is neither increasing nor decreasing on \((a, b)\) .

content: \(s\) is increasing on \([0, 1]\) . \(s\) takes infinitely many values. For \(0 < x \le 1\) , \(0 \le s(x) - x < 2x^2\) . (At \(x = 0\) the left side is \(0\) and so is the right, so the strict inequality fails there.)

title: Proposition 8.6.3 (Thomae’s Function Has Few Large Values)
content: \(1\) is a period of \(T\) . For all real \(a \le b\) and every \(\varepsilon > 0\) , the set \(E \coloneqq \{ x \in [a, b] : T(x) \ge \varepsilon \}\) is finite. For all \(a < b\) , the interval \((a, b)\) contains points with \(T > 0\) and points with \(T = 0\) .

title: Proposition 8.6.5 (The Zigzag Takes Every Value Near 0)

title: Definition 9.2.3 (Parallel Vectors)
content:
Vectors \(x, y \in 
R^n\) are parallel if \(y = cx\) for some \(c \in 
R\) or \(x = cy\) for some \(c \in 
R\) .

title: Definition 9.2.2 (Standard Vectors)
content: For \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) , the \(k\) -th standard vector \(e_k \in \nR^n\) has \(k\) -th coordinate \(1\) and every other coordinate \(0\) : \[ (e_k)_j \coloneqq \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } j = k , \\ 0 & \text{if } j \ne k . \end{cases} \]

title: Definition 9.2.1 (Vector Operations in \nR^n)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . For all \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\) and \(y = (y_1, \dots, y_n)\) in \(\nR^n\) and every \(c \in \nR\) , define \[ \begin{aligned} x + y &\coloneqq (x_1 + y_1, \; \dots, \; x_n + y_n) , \\ c x &\coloneqq (c x_1, \; \dots, \; c x_n) . \end{aligned} \] The zero vector is \(0 \coloneqq (0, \dots, 0)\) , the negative of \(x\) is \(-x \coloneqq (-1)x\) , and the difference is \(x - y \coloneqq x + (-y)\) . The number \(c\) is called a scalar , and \(cx\) a scalar multiple of \(x\) .

title: Example (Method: work coordinatewise)
content:
How it goes. To prove an equation between vectors of \(
R^n\) : Fix an arbitrary \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) . Compute the \(k\) -th coordinate of each side from the definitions. Prove the resulting equation in \(
R\) , naming the field law used. Since \(k\) was arbitrary, conclude that the vectors agree in every place, so they are equal. When to use it. Equations built from \(+\) , scalar multiples, coordinates and finite sums of vectors. Every law of @prp-vector-space-laws-rn below except (j) is one application. Common mistakes. Treating a condition that is not “for every \(k\) ” as if it were. The statement \(x 
e 0\) means that some coordinate \(x_k\) is non-zero. It does not mean that every coordinate is non-zero. Similarly, “ \(x\) and \(y\) are parallel”, defined below, asks for one scalar shared by all coordinates, so it is not a separate condition in each coordinate. In these cases, first unwind the condition into a statement about one chosen coordinate; then the method helps. Examples. Law (g) of the proposition below, planned in the table above, and law (j), where the condition \(x 
e 0\) has to be unwound.

title: Lemma 9.2.2 (Sums of Vectors, Coordinatewise)
content:
Let \(m \in 
N\) , let \(v_1, \dots, v_m, w_1, \dots, w_m \in 
R^n\) , and let \(c_1, \dots, c_m, d_1, \dots, d_m \in

title: Proposition 9.2.3 (Expansion in the Standard Vectors)
content: Every \(x \in \nR^n\) satisfies \[ x = \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k e_k , \] and the coefficients are unique: if \(c_1, \dots, c_n \in \nR\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} c_k e_k = x\) , then \(c_k = x_k\) for every \(k\) .

title: Definition 9.3.1 (Dot Product)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . The dot product of \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\) and \(y = (y_1, \dots, y_n)\) in \(\nR^n\) is the real number \[ \inner{x}{y} \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k y_k = x_1 y_1 + \dots + x_n y_n . \]

title: Definition 9.3.2 (Orthogonal Vectors)
content: Let \(n \ge 1\) . Vectors \(x, y \in \nR^n\) are orthogonal , written \(x \perp y\) , if \(\inner{x}{y} = 0\) .

title: Proposition 9.3.1 (Laws of the Dot Product)
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) , let \(x, y, z \in 
R^n\) and \(c \in 
R\) , and let \(e_1, \dots, e_n\) be the standard vectors ( @def-standard-basis-rn ). (Symmetry.) \(\inner{x}{y} = \inner{y}{x}\) . (Linearity in each slot.) \(\inner{x + y}{z} = \inner{x}{z} + \inner{y}{z}\) and \(\inner{cx}{z} = c\inner{x}{z}\) ; and likewise in the second slot, \(\inner{z}{x + y} = \inner{z}{x} + \inner{z}{y}\) and \(\inner{z}{cx} = c\inner{z}{x}\) . (Positivity.) \(\inner{x}{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} x_k^2 \ge 0\) , and \(\inner{x}{x} = 0\) if and only if \(x = 0\) . (Standard vectors.) \(\inner{x}{e_k} = x_k\) for every \(k\) , and \(\inner{e_j}{e_k} = 1\) if \(j = k\) , \(\inner{e_j}{e_k} = 0\) if \(j 
e k\) . (Zero.) \(\inner{x}{0} = \inner{0}{x} = 0\) .

title: Proposition 9.3.2 (The Orthogonality Test)
content:
Let \(n \ge 1\) and \(x, y \in 
R^n\) . If \(\inner{x}{z} = 0\) for every \(z \in 
R^n\) , then \(x = 0\) . The following are equivalent: (i) \(x = y\) ; (ii) \(\inner{x}{z} = \inner{y}{z}\) for every \(z \in 
R^n\) ; (iii) \(\inner{x}{e_k} = \inner{y}{e_k}\) for every \(k \in \{1, \dots, n\}\) .

title: Definition 9.4.3 (Distance)
content: For \(x, y \in \nR^n\) , the distance from \(x\) to \(y\) is \(d(x, y) \coloneqq \norm{x - y}\) .

title: Definition 9.4.1 (Norm)
content: Let \(x \in \nR^n\) . The norm (or length ) of \(x\) is the real number \[ \norm{x} \coloneqq \sqrt{\inner{x}{x}} = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \dots + x_n^2} , \] the non-negative square root of @fd3:prp-cof-square-roots .

title: Definition 9.4.2 (Unit Vector)
Example (Method: expand the square)
content:
How it goes. To prove an identity or an inequality between norms: If lengths are compared, compare their squares instead. This is allowed because both sides are \(\ge 0\) . Write each squared norm as a dot product, \(
orm{v}^2 = \inner{v}{v}\) . Expand by linearity and symmetry, as in @eq-expand-norm-squared . Compare the expansions. Then return from squares to lengths by comparing squares. When to use it. Identities and inequalities among the norms of sums, differences and multiples of vectors; conditions such as \(d(x, a) = d(x, b)\) . Common mistakes. A common mistake is to drop the cross term \(2\inner{x}{y}\) , which turns every expansion into Pythagoras. Another is to square a side that may be negative, such as \(
orm{x} - 
orm{y}\) ; comparing squares does not apply there.

title: Exercise (A1)

For \(x = (2, -1, 2, 0)\) , compute \(M\) , \(\norm{x}\) and \(\sqrt n \, M\) , and check both bounds of @prp-norm-coordinate-bounds . State the idea of the proof of @prp-norm-coordinate-bounds (b) in two sentences.

content:
How it goes. Suppose a statement about \(x\) and \(y\) is homogeneous : replacing \(x\) by \(ax\) with \(a > 0\) multiplies both sides by the same positive factor, and likewise for \(y\) . Then: Settle \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\) separately. For \(x, y

Inequalities between \(\inner{x}{y}\) and products of lengths; statements about directions rather than sizes. Common mistakes. Normalizing the zero vector is impossible: it has no direction, and \(x/
orm{x}\) would divide by \(0\) . Scaling by a negative factor breaks the method, since \(x \mapsto -x\) changes the sign of \(\inner{x}{y}\) but not of \(

orm{p - x} = s\) and \(
orm{x - q} = r\) . If \(p 
e q\) , it is \[ x = p +  rac{s}{
orm{p - q}} (q - p) ; \] if \(p = q\) , it is \(p\) .

title: Definition 10.1.2 (Collinear Points)
content: Points of \(\nR^n\) are collinear if one line contains them all.

title: Definition 10.1.1 (Lines in \nR^n)
content:
Let \(p, v \in 
R^n\) with \(v 
e 0\) . We write \[ p + 
R v \coloneqq \{ p + tv : t \in 
R \} . \] A subset \(L \subseteq 
R^n\) is a line if \(L = p + 
R v\) for some \(p \in 
R^n\) and some \(v 
e 0\) . The map \(t \mapsto p + tv\) from \(
R\) to \(L\) is a parametrization of \(L\) , with base point \(p\) and direction \(v\) ; the number \(t\) is the parameter of the point \(p + tv\) .

title: Definition 10.1.3 (Segment)
content: Let \(p, q \in \nR^n\) . The segment from \(p\) to \(q\) is \[ [p, q] \coloneqq \{ (1 - t)p + tq : t \in [0, 1] \} . \] Its midpoint is \(\frac12 (p + q)\) , the point with \(t = \frac12\) .

title: Example (Method: use the equality case)
content: How it goes. A known inequality \(A \le B\) is given, or proved, to hold with \(A = B\) . Recall its exact equality condition. Typically it reads “one vector is a non-negative multiple of the other, or is zero”. Write that condition with a named multiplier. Then solve for what you want, keeping every case of the condition. When to use it. A sum of distances equals a distance. Cauchy–Schwarz holds with equality. A question asks for all extreme cases of an inequality. Common mistakes. Dropping the sign condition loses the point: \(c \ge 0\) is exactly what separates \([p, q]\) from the rest of the line through \(p\) and \(q\) . Forgetting the case \(u = 0\) leaves a gap, because when \(u = 0\) and \(w \ne 0\) no multiplier exists.

title: Example (Method: parametrize and solve)
content: How it goes. Give each line or segment its own parameter, with a different letter for each. Write “the point lies on both” as one equation per coordinate. Solve some of the equations, then check every equation with the values found. For a segment, also check that the parameter lies in \([0, 1]\) . When to use it. Deciding whether a point lies on a line, a segment or a ray. Finding where two lines meet, or showing that they do not. Later, finding where a line meets a sphere or a hyperplane. Common mistakes. Using one letter for both parameters looks only for a point reached “at the same time” on both lines, and so misses most meeting points. Solving two equations and forgetting to test the rest can produce a meeting point that does not exist.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Parametrize the line through \((1, -1, 2)\) and \((3, 0, 0)\) . Is \((5, 1, -2)\) on it? Find the midpoint of the segment between these two points. Show that \((1, 2)\) , \((3, 5)\) and \((7, 11)\) are collinear, and find one of them that lies on the segment between the other two. In the proof of @thm-betweenness , direction \((\Leftarrow)\) , where is \(c \ge 0\) used? Take \(p = 0\) , \(q = (1, 0)\) and \(x = (2, 0)\) , a point of the line through \(p\) and \(q\) . Which hypothesis of the theorem fails, and what does the equality case of the triangle inequality say about \(u = x - p\) and \(w = q - x\) ?

content: Let \(p, v \in \nR^n\) with \(v \ne 0\) , and let \(a < b\) be real numbers. Prove that \(p + tv \in [p + av, p + bv]\) if and only if \(a \le t \le b\) .

title: Lemma 10.1.3 (A Segment Contains Its Subsegments)
content: Let \(p, q \in \nR^n\) . If \(x, y \in [p, q]\) , then \([x, y] \subseteq [p, q]\) .

content:

content:
Let \(p, q \in

content:
Let \(p, q, x \in

orm{x - q} =

title: Definition 10.2.1 (Hyperplane)
content:
Let \(a \in 
R^n\) with \(a 
e 0\) , and let \(c \in 
R\) . The set \[ H_{a,c} \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : \inner{a}{x} = c \} \] is a hyperplane , and \(a\) is a normal vector of it. The sets \(\{ x : \inner{a}{x} \le c \}\) and \(\{ x : \inner{a}{x} \ge c \}\) are the two closed half-spaces of \(H_{a,c}\) ; with \(<\) and \(>\) strictly , they are the two open half-spaces , or the two sides of \(H_{a,c}\) .

title: Definition 10.2.2 (Sphere)
content:
For \(c \in 
R^n\) and a real \(r > 0\) , the sphere with center \(c\) and radius \(r\) is \(S(c, r) \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - c} = r \}\) . In \(
R^2\) a sphere is called a circle .

content: Consider the hyperplane \(2x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = 6\) in \(\nR^3\) . Give a normal vector, and a second normal vector different from the first. Find the distance from \(0\) to the hyperplane. Find the point of the hyperplane nearest to \(0\) .

content: Prove that three non-collinear points \(p, q, s\) of \(\nR^2\) lie on exactly one circle. Find it for \((0, 0)\) , \((4, 0)\) , \((0, 2)\) .

content:

content:
Let \(a

R^n\) , and put \[ x^* \coloneqq x -  rac{\inner{a}{x} - c}{

orm{x - y}^2 = 
orm{x - x^*}^2 +

orm{x - x^*} =  rac{\abs{\inner{a}{x} - c}}{

Let \(p, q \in

title: Proposition 10.2.6 (A Segment Crosses a Hyperplane Once)
content:
Let \(a 
e 0\) , \(c \in 
R\) , and let \(p, q \in

title: Definition 10.3.2 (Open and Closed Balls)
content:
Let \(c \in 
R^n\) and \(r > 0\) . The open ball and the closed ball of center \(c\) and radius \(r\) are \[ B(c, r) \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - c} < r \} , \qquad \overline{B}(c, r) \coloneqq \{ x \in 
R^n : 
orm{x - c} \le r \} . \]

title: Definition 10.3.3 (Convex Combination)
content: Let \(k \ge 1\) and \(p_1, \dots, p_k \in \nR^n\) . A convex combination of \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) is a point \[ \lambda_1 p_1 + \dots + \lambda_k p_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i p_i \quad \text{with every } \lambda_i \ge 0 \text{ and } \sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i = 1 . \] The numbers \(\lambda_i\) are its weights .

title: Definition 10.3.4 (Convex Hull)
content: Let \(S \subseteq \nR^n\) . The convex hull of \(S\) is \[ \operatorname{conv} S \coloneqq \bigcap \{ C \subseteq \nR^n : C \text{ is convex and } S \subseteq C \} . \]

title: Definition 10.3.1 (Convex Set)
content: A subset \(C \subseteq \nR^n\) is convex if \([p, q] \subseteq C\) for all \(p, q \in C\) .

title: Definition 10.3.5 (Star-Shaped Set)
content: A set \(S \subseteq \nR^n\) is star-shaped about a point \(c \in S\) if \([c, x] \subseteq S\) for every \(x \in S\) . It is star-shaped if it is star-shaped about some point of \(S\) .

title: Example (Method: the two-point test)
content: How it goes. To prove that \(C\) is convex: Take \(p, q \in C\) and \(t \in [0, 1]\) . Write down the condition that \(p\) and \(q\) satisfy. Split the vector, or the expression, belonging to \((1 - t)p + tq\) as \((1 - t)(\dots) + t(\dots)\) . Use the same weights on every term, including the center or the constant. Conclude by the triangle inequality, or by linearity, using \(1 - t \ge 0\) and \(t \ge 0\) . When to use it. Proving that a set is convex straight from the definition: balls, half-spaces, sets cut out by inequalities. Common mistakes. Checking only the midpoint, \(t = 1/2\) , is not enough: the set \(\nQ^2\) below passes that check and is not convex. Allowing \(t\) outside \([0, 1]\) is also wrong, since then a weight is negative and the inequalities reverse.

title: Example (The Axes: Star-Shaped, Not Convex)
content:
Let \(A \coloneqq 
R(1, 0) \cup 
R(0, 1) \subseteq 
R^2\) , the union of the two axes. Show that \(A\) is star-shaped about \(0\) , is not convex, and is not star-shaped about \((1, 0)\) .

title: Example (A Triangle as a Hull)
content: Let \(p_1, p_2, p_3 \in \nR^2\) . (a) Show that \(\operatorname{conv}\{p_1, p_2, p_3\}\) is the set \(T\) of points \(\lambda_1 p_1 + \lambda_2 p_2 + \lambda_3 p_3\) with \(\lambda_i \ge 0\) and \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = 1\) : the filled triangle with corners \(p_1, p_2, p_3\) . (b) For \(p_1 = (0, 0)\) , \(p_2 = (3, 0)\) , \(p_3 = (0, 3)\) , decide whether \((1, 1)\) and \((2, 2)\) lie in the hull.

content:

title: Exercise (C1: Chapter check: convex subsets of the line)
content: Let \(C \subseteq \nR\) be non-empty and convex. Let \(\alpha \coloneqq \inf C\) if \(C\) is bounded below, and \(\alpha \coloneqq -\infty\) otherwise; let \(\beta \coloneqq \sup C\) if \(C\) is bounded above, and \(\beta \coloneqq +\infty\) otherwise. Prove that every real \(x\) with \(\alpha < x < \beta\) lies in \(C\) , and that every \(c \in C\) satisfies \(\alpha \le c \le \beta\) . (So \(C\) is an interval with ends \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) , each end included or not.)

title: Exercise (R1)
content: Let \(Q \coloneqq \{ x \in \nR^n : \abs{x_k} \le 1 \text{ for every } k \}\) . Show that \(Q\) is convex and that \(\overline{B}(0, 1) \subseteq Q \subseteq \overline{B}(0, \sqrt n)\) .

content:
Identify the polynomial \(a + bx + cx^2 \in 
R[x]\) with the point \((a, b, c) \in

content:
Let \(c \in

title: Proposition 10.3.1 (Balls Are Convex)
content: For every \(c \in \nR^n\) and \(r > 0\) , the balls \(B(c, r)\) and \(\overline{B}(c, r)\) are convex.

title: Proposition 10.3.2 (Lines, Segments, Hyperplanes and Half-Spaces Are Convex)
content: Each of the following is a convex subset of \(\nR^n\) : every line ( @def-line-rn ); every segment ( @def-segment-rn ); every hyperplane \(H_{a,c}\) and each of its four half-spaces ( @def-hyperplane-rn ).

title: Proposition 10.3.3 (Operations on Convex Sets)
content:
If \((C_i)_{i \in I}\) is a family of convex subsets of \(
R^n\) , then \( igcap_{i \in I} C_i\) is convex. If \(C \subseteq 
R^n\) is convex, \(b \in 
R^n\) and \(\lambda \in 
R\) , then \(b + C \coloneqq \{ b + x : x \in C \}\) and \(\lambda C \coloneqq \{ \lambda x : x \in C \}\) are convex. A union of two convex sets need not be convex: for \(p 
e q\) , the sets \(\{p\}\) and \(\{q\}\) are convex and \(\{p\} \cup \{q\}\) is not.

title: Theorem 10.3.4 (Convex Sets Contain Their Convex Combinations)
content: Let \(C \subseteq \nR^n\) be convex. Then every convex combination of finitely many points of \(C\) lies in \(C\) .

title: Theorem 10.3.5 (The Convex Hull Is the Set of Convex Combinations)
content: Let \(S \subseteq \nR^n\) , and let \(K\) be the set of all convex combinations of finitely many points of \(S\) . Then \(\operatorname{conv} S = K\) .
